en: The *Bodhicaryāvatāra* composed by Śāntideva,
accompanied by the commentary titled *Pañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.

*Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!* Chapter One: The Praise of the Awakening Mind (*Bodhicittānuśaṃsa*) Having prostrated with devotion to the Sugatas, together with their Sons and their Dharma-bodies, and to all those worthy of praise;
I shall explain, in brief and according to the scriptures, the entry into the vows of the sons of the Sugata.

"......and all those worthy of praise," refers to [the author's] spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) and others. "The entry into the vow of the sons of the Sugata" is the statement of the subject matter (abhidheya).
"I shall explain" is the statement of the purpose (prayojana).
However, there is no explicit word for the demonstration of the relationship;
rather, that must be understood through the very force of the context.
The phrase "according to the tradition" is a term intended to avoid independence [of judgment].
The statement "from the compound" is a remark intended to avoid the fault of tautology;
such is the collective meaning.
As for the meaning of the individual parts, it is now stated.
In the term *sugata*, the word *gata* demonstrates the distinction of the Blessed Ones from all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*),
because the latter remain within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), whereas the Blessed Ones have emerged from cyclic existence.
The word *su* (well), however, is distinguished by its occurrence in three senses, such as "praiseworthy" (*praśasta*) and so forth.

By this, the meaning is as follows: the *sugatas* are those who have gone (*gata*) by means of the middle way (*madhyamapratipadā*) in such a manner that it is "praiseworthy" (*praśasta*), namely, through the abandonment of the obscurations of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and so forth.
By this, the perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃpatti*) is expressed.
Alternatively,

they are "Well-Gone" (sugata) because they have gone to— that is, attained— the praiseworthy reality of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena; by this, the perfection of realization is demonstrated.
Alternatively, the distinction of the Blessed Ones from the teachers of the non-Buddhist schools is demonstrated;
for due to their adherence to the existence of a self and so forth, they lack the excellent destination,
and because such things as a self are sublated by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, their going is not praiseworthy because it is not an antidote to *saṃsāra*.
Alternatively, they have "gone" by way of non-return;

they are "Well-Gone" (*sugata*) because, through the purification of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), the ignorance that is the seed of the ego-sense has been abandoned in every respect, resulting in no further rebirth through passion and so forth.
By this, the distinction of the Blessed Ones even from the Bodhisattvas who are Stream-enterers and Once-returners is shown;
for although their progress is praiseworthy, because they have not abandoned all the realms [of existence], the possibility of returning again remains.

Alternatively, they are called "Well-gone" (Sugata) because they have completely abandoned everything—including the latencies (*vāsanā*) characterized by defects of body, speech, and intellect, or the lack of proficiency in teaching the path they themselves have realized—in every respect.
By this much, the state of being "one who goes to the full" (saṃpūrṇagāmin) has been established for the Blessed Ones.
By this also, it is made known that the Blessed Ones possess qualities not shared with the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas who are Non-returners (anāgāmin).
This is because in those [latter], there is the possibility of deficiencies in body, speech, and intellect, as well as a lack of proficiency in explaining the path they themselves have realized.
And thus, Buddhahood—which possesses the essence of all qualities without exception and is uncommon to other practitioners—is designated by the term "Sugata.
Having prostrated with supreme devotion and reverence to those Sugatas who are of such a nature, [he says]: (Bcp 2)
The connection [of the verse] is: "Having paid homage, I shall explain the entry into the vow of the sons of the Sugata. Of what nature are they? They are "together with their sons" (*sasutān*).
And here, the "sons" of the Munis are understood to be none other than the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) such as the Joyous (*pramuditā*) and so forth.
Because they alone are the subject under discussion here,
by this qualification, the homage to the Noble Saṅgha is included along with them.
He states another qualification: "possessing the Dharma-body" (*sadharmakāyān*).
The essential Dharma-body (*svābhāviko dharmakāya*) of the Blessed Ones is liberated from all obscurations; and that very body is the Dharma whose nature is realization (*adhigama*).
Alternatively, the word *kāya* has the sense of a "collection," as in "the body of people" (*janakāya*) or "the body of troops" (*balakāya*).
By this [usage], the teaching (*pravacana*) is also included;
[therefore, it means] together with that.
By this as well, the homage to the Dharma is included;
thus, it is said that "this is the homage to the Triple Gem."
Is it not the case that the sequence is: from the Buddha comes the Dharma, and from the Dharma the Noble Saṅgha?
Why then is there this transposed presentation, wherein the Noble Saṅgha follows immediately after the Buddha, and the Dharma follows after that? True.
In this case, it should be understood that the mention [of the objects] is presented out of order for the sake of conforming to the structure of the verse;
however, in terms of actual application, the sequence is precisely as follows: "having prostrated to the Sugatas, together with their Dharma-bodies and their Sons."
There is no fault here whatsoever.
Alternatively,
since Bodhisattvas have also realized the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the Dharma-body exists for them as well, in accordance with their respective attainment.
For them as well, homage must be proffered together with the *dharmakāya*;
for they too, by virtue of having realized the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), are fixed in the state of a Sugata and are virtually Sugatas.
Thus, they are mentioned prior to the Dharma.
Thus, nothing is improper.
Are these the only ones?
No; he says: "and all those worthy of praise."
"Having prostrated with reverence even to all other venerable ones, such as preceptors (ācārya) and teachers (upādhyāya),"—

having thus expressed the salutation to the Sugatas and others by means of the first half-verse, he states the subject matter and so forth by means of the second half-verse, beginning with "O son of the Sugata," and so on.
"Born from oneself" means *ātmaja*.
The "sons of the Sugatas" (*jinaputra*) are the sons of the Sugatas;
the meaning is *bodhisattvas*.
Regarding their entry into the vow (*saṃvara*):
it is called a "vow" (*saṃvara*) because it is a restraint (*saṃvaraṇa*), or that by which one is restrained;
it consists of the formal undertaking of the bodhisattva training preceded by the grasping of the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
And we shall explain that in its proper place. Its introduction:
it is called an "introduction" (*avatāra*) because one enters into it, or because by means of it one enters; thus, it is the path (*mārga*).
I shall explain and establish that by which, upon attaining the state of a bodhisattva, the condition of a Sugata is achieved; this is the meaning of "by means of this treatise."
Since it is being presented in this manner, "the entry into the vows" is its subject matter (*abhidheya*),
and "this [work]" is the designation (*abhidhāna*) for that entry into the vows;
thus, by implication, the relationship characterized as that between the designation and the designated has also been stated.
The statement of that [purpose] is the purpose of the designation (*abhidhāna*).
However, in the ultimate sense, the purpose of that is precisely the analytical understanding (*vyutpatti*) of the nature of the subject matter (*abhidheya*).

Furthermore, since the subject matter leads to the removal of all obscurations through the gradual production of the wisdom consisting of hearing and so forth, its purpose is indeed Buddhahood; such is the finality of the purpose.
And this is included within the very title *Entrance into the Vows of the Sons of the Sugata*,
because it is mentioned immediately thereafter,
and because [the author] will indicate it by means of a statement regarding its benefits.
"Having taken this image of impurity, one fashions it into an invaluable image of the Jewel of the Victor.
Thus, the connection, the subject matter, and the purpose have been set forth as the necessary factors for engaging with the work.
Otherwise, due to the suspicion that [the subject matter] is inexpressible and so forth, the engagement of discerning people (*prekṣāvat*) with this [work] would not occur.

To the objection, "How will they accept a statement made by you independently (*svātantryeṇa*? he says: "In accordance with tradition" (*yathāgamaṃ*). This means: without transgressing the scriptures (*āgama*).
Just as it has been set forth by the Blessed Ones in the scriptures, so too must I set it forth without overstepping its meaning; by this,
independence from the scriptures is avoided.
The meaning is that this does not contradict the sūtra;
furthermore, by means of this straightforwardness, he has demonstrated his own depth of comprehension regarding the meaning of the teaching.
This, too, is indeed a factor for engaging [in practice].
Now, one might object: "If it is to be explained according to the scriptures, then those who desire that [explanation] will simply engage with the scriptures themselves;
so what is the use of this? To this he replies: "In brief."
In brief:
even if it has indeed been taught in the scriptures (*āgama*),
nevertheless, because it is presented there with great detail across various sūtras, [it is summarized here].
The distinction is that I, however, shall speak by condensing [the material] into a summary.
By this, the objection that "this is a redundancy" is refuted; furthermore, this also serves as a rebuttal to the charge that it lacks the constituent parts for engaging [the audience].

Therefore, because it serves as a factor for engagement (*pravṛtty-aṅga*), the statement regarding the subject matter and so forth is not irrelevant. [Objection: In that case, the act of paying homage (*praṇāma*) is purposeless. [Response:
Even that, being uttered for the sake of attaining the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) and other benefits, how could it be purposeless?

This is the intended meaning: for one whose mental continuum is pervaded by the accumulation of merit arising from prostrating to the Sugata and others, the activity of previously committed sins becomes extremely attenuated; and for one whose obstacles have been pacified, the completion of the task undertaken comes to pass.
Furthermore, by this [homage], his own adherence to the path followed by all virtuous people is made manifest.
By hearing the salutation to the chosen deity and others, the listeners will conceive a sense of faith (*āstikatva*), which will engender respect for his own work.

And here, by hearing the majesty of the Blessed One’s qualities as evoked by the word "Sugata," those who desire it and whose minds are inclined toward its attainment will strive to fully understand the entry into the vows of the Sons of the Sugata.
In this [work], these things proceed;
this is the fruit of prostrating to one's chosen deity and so forth.
By this, it is also shown that whatever one desires or intends to accomplish—
Let him do that very thing and nothing else; for if he were to do something else, it would constitute an irrelevant statement and lead to an over-extension of the argument.
Thus, having already set his intention upon explaining the entry into the vows, why does he perform an irrelevant salutation to his chosen deity and so forth?
As for the claim that "it would entail the two faults previously mentioned," that too is refuted,
because its utility has been described; thus, there is no mention of something irrelevant.
Only that which is relevant to the subject at hand should be stated, and nothing else;
thus, there is no excessive prolixity, and everything is well-established.

One might object: "Even if it is stated concisely, how could this work be adopted by anyone as a specific means for engaging in practice, given that it contains nothing beyond the traditional scriptures (āgama) and lacks any specific subject matter or distinction?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"Indeed, there is nothing new here to be said, nor do I possess any skill in composition."
Therefore, I have no concern for the welfare of others; this was composed by me merely to cultivate my own mind.
There is nothing whatsoever new, different, or exceeding what is found in the scriptures that remains to be said by me;
for the word "hi" (indeed) is used here in the sense of "because.
One might then object: even if there is no statement of a subject matter exceeding those [scriptures], there may still be a particular arrangement of the meanings of words.
Therefore, there would also be activity specifically [for that purpose].
To this, he says: "And not...
Nor is composition (*saṃgrathana*) a particular arrangement of words and meanings.
In this regard, I possess skill and proficiency;
or, the word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis.
If this is so, one might ask: how does this serve the welfare of others?
He says: "Precisely for this reason.
He accepts exactly what has been established by the opponent, because he lacks the power to state anything new.
Nor do I possess skill in composition,
nor even the thought of benefiting others;
I have not even the conceptualization that "this will be useful for the sake of others."
If it is asked, "In that case, since there is a deficiency in my ability, for what purpose is this effort toward composition? he says:
"For my own sake. This treatise was composed and offered by me in order to increasingly perfuse my own mind with the flavor of practicing the entry into the vows of the sons of the Sugatas.
Or it is the discourse on entering the vows;
this is the instruction regarding the past time, having placed within the mind the perfected inner reality.

Now, it may be objected that the composition of a treatise is never seen to be for one's own sake, nor does the mere act of composing it by oneself produce any excellence within the self, since such a specific refinement already exists within the self beforehand. To this, he replies:
First, by this means, the surge of my own faith to cultivate virtue increases;
furthermore, if another person of a nature similar to mine should see it, then for that reason as well, this [practice] is meaningful. (Bca 1.3)
By means of this text, or by cultivating and accomplishing wholesome and virtuous mental attention,
the force of serene confidence increases.
The activity [of the mind] proceeds as a continuous flow, with the continuum of the serene mind increasing further and further.
By this, he demonstrates that its performance of one's own welfare is established by direct experience.
Showing that its performance of the welfare of others also occurs to some extent, he says: "Then, having met with me," and so forth.
The word "atha" (now/then) introduces an alternative perspective.
First of all, its capacity to fulfill its own purpose is established by experience;
furthermore, if some other person of a nature similar to my own were to see—that is, perceive—it.
This treatise or its meaning is meaningful and purposeful even for this reason, because it is also useful for the benefit of others;
for the utility of benefiting others is possible in some way or another.
By this verse, he demonstrates his own freedom from conceit.
Now, providing an introduction in order to cause one to grasp the discourse on entering the vows, he says:
"This attainment of the favorable conditions for a moment is extremely difficult to find; it has been obtained as the means for accomplishing the goals of human endeavor.
If one does not contemplate what is beneficial here, how will such an opportunity ever come together again? (Bca 1.4)

The perfection and completeness of this moment, which is free from the eight inopportune states, is extremely difficult to obtain; it is acquired with great hardship and is attained only by some rare chance. It is comparable to a turtle, living in a vast ocean, placing its neck through the hole of a yoke floating upon the waves.
It has been attained and acquired,
and it is the means for accomplishing the human goal;
the human goal is characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
Its *sādhanī* is that which brings it to completion;
that is to say, it is capable therein because it is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to it.
And even if this [perfection] is of such a nature...
When one does not contemplate what is beneficial,
and does not adopt the means for achieving heaven and liberation— the cause of happiness for oneself and others—
then once again, this birth as a human being, which is free from the opportunity for faith, is merely a coming together, an entering into, or a meeting; that is to say, a convergence.
Why? How?
It will not happen in any way whatsoever because it is extremely difficult to attain;
for during a state of the inopportune moments (*akṣaṇa*), it is impossible to perform the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*).
This is the intended meaning.
As it is said in the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, in the liberation of the noble Jayoṣmāyatana:
"The turning away from the eight inopportune states is difficult to obtain."
The attainment of human existence is difficult to find;
the purity of the perfection of the opportune moment is difficult to find;
the arising of a Buddha is difficult to find.
The possession of unimpaired faculties is difficult to obtain;
hearing the Buddha's Dharma is difficult to obtain;
meeting with a true person is difficult to obtain.
True spiritual friends are difficult to find;
the imparting of instruction according to the true method is difficult to find;
and a right livelihood in the human world is difficult to find.
It was with this very intention that it was said:
"Human birth is difficult to obtain in the world; the arising of a Buddha is exceedingly difficult to obtain."
Even more difficult to obtain than that is the practice of going forth out of faith.
With compassion for all sentient beings, one should make the mind firm in awakening;
for the sake of pacifying all suffering, there is a succession of things most difficult to obtain.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, these are the inopportune states (akṣaṇas):
hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, barbarians, long-lived gods,
those with wrong views, the two [extremes of] Buddha-less eras, and muteness— these are the eight inopportune states here.
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, exertion must be undertaken right now.
Now, in order to inspire a longing for the adoption of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), he introduces the benefits by saying:

"Just as lightning momentarily reveals light in the thick darkness of a night clouded with clouds, so too, through the power of the Buddhas, a mind directed toward meritorious deeds may occasionally arise in the world for a moment. (Bca 1.5)

Just as at night, during the season of the arrival of clouds, when darkness is thick with rain-clouds, a flash of lightning illuminates and reveals some small portion of material objects for only a moment or an instant—this very same analogy applies here as well; thus he says, "By the power of the Buddhas," and so forth.

For it is the Blessed Buddhas alone who, in order to bring about welfare and happiness, remain constantly observing the mental continuums of all sentient beings according to their being worthy or unworthy [of the teaching].
When, where, by what means, for whom, and seeing what is suitable, they then empower that [being] there with that means;
however, in a state of unsuitability, they remain indifferent.
Thus, through the empowerment of the Tathāgata, [the appearance of a Buddha] is somehow difficult to encounter.

May the intellect of the world’s people be directed for even a single moment toward virtuous deeds— wholesome actions that are the causes of benefit and happiness; for in this regard, their minds are unstable, having been habituated throughout beginningless saṃsāra solely to the side of unwholesomeness.
(Bcp 6) If this is indeed so, what follows from it? He says:
Therefore, virtue is always weak, while the power of evil is great and most terrible.
By what other virtue could that [mind] be surpassed, were it not for the mind of complete enlightenment? (Bca 1.6)
Since this is so, therefore, auspicious merit is weak and indeed devoid of efficacy; it is extremely slender because it is like a flash of lightning.
It is "constant," meaning at all times.
To whom, then, does superior power belong? He says: "But power... The capacity of the unwholesome (*aśubha*), moreover, is great, because it is like the dense darkness of thick clouds.
It is extremely terrible and most fearsome because it bestows the sufferings of hell and other realms, and because it is very difficult to overcome;
let it indeed possess great power.
Nevertheless, that [obstacle] will be overcome by another powerful merit, and thus there is no harm whatsoever;
to this he says: "That," and so forth.
Such great power as that is "conquered," meaning it is overcome; by what else? By nothing at all—this is the meaning.
Why, then, is it said thus: "In perfect enlightenment," and so forth?

Regarding perfect enlightenment—that is, Buddhahood—the mental attention (*manasikāra*) with resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) is the mental state directed toward the goal of attaining it, motivated by the aspiration to deliver all sentient beings.
If that were not the case,
its great power would indeed be overcome by something even greater, just as the darkness of night is overcome by the sun;
yet no other antidote more powerful than the spirit of enlightenment can possibly exist.
Therefore, the intention is that for the sake of counteracting that [obstacle], only the mind of complete enlightenment (saṃbodhicitta) is to be adopted, and nothing else.
For this reason as well, the thought of awakening (saṃbodhicitta) should be adopted; thus he says:
"Having reflected for many eons, the Lords of Sages have seen that this alone is beneficial;
for by means of happiness itself, happiness increases and carries across immeasurable multitudes of beings. (Bca 1.7)
One intermediate kalpa is a kalpa;
twenty intermediate kalpas are a kalpa;
eighty intermediate kalpas are a kalpa.
And that is designated as a *mahākalpa*;
here, therefore, it is precisely a *mahākalpa* that is intended—
many, not few, [aeons] included within the first incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*).
By those who contemplate with diligence and thoroughly investigate,
it was seen and realized by the Lords of Sages— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— while they were in the state of Bodhisattvas.
It is beneficial because it is capable of accomplishing all goals, as it serves as their seed;
this very thing is the mind of complete enlightenment (saṃbodhicitta).
But how is this alone beneficial? To this he says: "Since," and so forth.
Because [this] happiness, having increased and reached its culmination, is characterized by Buddhahood;
[it benefits] those who are immeasurable and beyond measure.
It carries across and delivers the multitudes of people— the masses of sentient beings— from the great ocean of the suffering of saṃsāra;
therefore, this alone is beneficial.
Alternatively: because happiness, characterized by the prosperity of gods and humans,
has increased— that is, attained growth—
precisely from the mind of awakening (*saṃbodhicitta*).
It causes to overflow; that is, it satisfies exceedingly.
That which becomes more abundant due to its ease is called "overflowing" (*utplāvana*).
For example, in the expression "we have been overflowed by curd," the meaning is that the curd has become more abundant due to its ease [of digestion].
Alternatively, it should be construed as follows: because happiness has increased from that very mind of complete enlightenment (*saṃbodhicitta*).
He explains how it has increased: "by means of ease alone," meaning not with difficulty,
nor through great hardship such as the plucking out of one's hair and so forth.

For it is precisely through the vow of the mind of awakening that a bodhisattva, increasing from the very accumulation of immeasurable merit and wisdom and attaining the happiness of the prosperity of gods and humans, brings even greater satisfaction to sentient beings by means of those [prosperities]. As he will say:
Thus, proceeding from happiness to happiness, what conscious person would despair,
having obtained the chariot of the awakening mind that removes all weariness and fatigue?
Thus [Bodhicaryāvatāra 7.30].
But surely, even in the *Jātakas* of the Blessed Ones, such as the *Maitrībala-jātaka* (*Jātakamālā* 8), great hardships are heard of;
how then can it be said that happiness increases only through happiness?
This is not a fault; for those whose nature is compassion, suffering that brings about the welfare and happiness of others is indeed something to be produced for both themselves and others.
It will be demonstrated that for the wise who suffer at the suffering of others, such happiness is indeed suffering.

Showing that for this reason as well—because it is the cause of one's own and others' welfare—the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) must never be abandoned, he says: "Even by those who wish to cross over hundreds of worldly sufferings, by those who wish to remove the misfortunes of sentient beings, and by those who wish to enjoy hundreds of manifold pleasures, the thought of awakening must indeed never be relinquished. (Bca 1.8)

Those belonging to the lineage of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, desiring to cast off and wishing to abandon hundreds of sufferings of saṃsāra— the hundreds of sufferings of the states of existence such as the hells, which are experienced as pain in their infinite multitude— and those belonging to the lineage of the Bodhisattvas,
who desire not only to remove but to utterly eliminate for all people the sufferings of birth and so forth, even though they do not belong to themselves; [for them, this treatise is composed].
Not only by those who wish to remove the sufferings of themselves and others,
but also by those who desire to experience many hundreds of various pleasures— the happiness obtainable through rebirth as gods or humans— even by those who long for the pleasures of saṃsāra.
The meaning is that the *bodhicitta* must always, at all times, never be released nor abandoned; it must be adopted.
Alternatively, these are qualifiers specifically for those who desire perfect enlightenment.
For this special quality as well, one should adopt the thought of awakening (bodhicitta); thus it is said:
"The wretched one, bound in the prison of existence, is called a son of the Sugatas in an instant;
indeed, as soon as the thought of awakening has arisen, he becomes worthy of veneration by the world of humans and gods. (Bca 1.9)
Samsara itself is a prison; the analysis of the compound is: "one for whom the bondage—namely, attachment and so forth—is the binding.
Being such a wretched and miserable person, [he remains there].
At the very moment the thought of awakening has arisen, specifically at the time of first taking up the vow of bodhicitta,
one is called a "son of the Sugatas" and is designated as a "son of the Buddha."
"In an instant" means at that very moment.
To show that it is not merely thus, he says:
"Together with men and gods," and so forth. (Bcp 8)
He became one to be venerated, saluted, and praised even by those worlds such as the asuras and others who exist together with humans and gods— that is, with men and deities.
By the use of the word "sma," which indicates the past tense, it is shown that he was already such at the very moment the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) arose.
For this reason as well—seeing these qualities and benefits—one should exert effort in taking up the thought of awakening (bodhicitta). Thus it is said:

"Having taken this image of impurity, one makes of it an image of the jewel-like Victor, priceless. Take hold with great firmness of that which is called the thought of awakening, which is like a highly penetrating elixir. (Bca 1.10)
This [body] is like excrement; its nature is that of the corpse of a human being and so forth, consisting of those elements and having that as its intrinsic character.
The meaning is: "having been nourished by that" [i.e., food]. "Having taken it" means having grasped it.
The Victor alone is the jewel,
because he possesses qualities such as being difficult to encounter;
one who produces or brings to completion an image of him produces the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
The meaning is that it brings about the form of the Tathāgata.
Of what nature is it? It is priceless (*anarghā*); that is, its value (*argha*) or price does not exist.
Because its qualities surpass all those of the three realms and because the limit of its qualities cannot be fully known,
it is described as such;
for this very reason, it is called a "collection of flavors" (rasajāta), meaning a variety of flavors.
Because it causes piercing that is exceedingly high, it is "to be pierced excessively" (*atīva vedhanīyam*).
The suffix *-anīya* is used either in the sense of the agent (*kartari*) or the instrument (*karaṇe*).
That [piercing] is of such a kind.
The perception of this produced essence is *bodhicitta*;
it is designated by no other name than *bodhicitta*.

"Grasp it very firmly so that once grasped, it does not waver"—this is the sense of the imperative "grasp" (*gṛhṇata*), which is used here according to the reading of the authoritative scripture (*āgama*).
Therefore, those who wish to make themselves a jewel among Jinas should firmly grasp the great elixir of the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
And it is said in the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa* (Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra 502):
"O son of good family, for example, there exists a type of alchemical elixir called 'Golden Radiance' (*hāṭakaprabhāsa*)."
A single *pala* of it turns a thousand *palas* of iron into gold;
yet that single *pala* of the elixir cannot be exhausted or turned back into iron by those thousand *palas* of iron.

In the very same way, a single atom of the elixir of the resolve for omniscience (*sarvajñatā-cittotpāda*), when embraced by the wisdom of the dedication of roots of merit, exhausts all the iron of the obscurations of karma and afflictions, and transforms all phenomena into the gold of omniscience.
It acts [in this way];
yet the flavor-element of the arousal of the mind of omniscience cannot be exhausted or altered by the iron and other metals of all karmic and afflictive obscurations.

Showing that even those who desire power within the realms of existence should have no doubt or misconception regarding this, he says: "O you whose nature is to wander through the cities of the various states of existence, take hold with firm resolve of the jewel of the spirit of enlightenment (bodhicitta)—that which has been thoroughly examined by those of immeasurable wisdom as being of great value, the sole caravan leader for the world. (Bca 1.11)
The "ports" (pattana) here are indeed the destinations (gati), which are cities for the buying and selling of the commodities of karmic actions;
likewise, the ports of rebirth are the places for the buying and selling of the commodities of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Those whose very nature or habit (śīla) is to dwell far away—meaning to be constantly departing—from those [ports] are so described.
This is their address:
"O you who are habituated to wandering away from the city of the destination, take hold most firmly of the jewel of the thought of awakening!"
The thought of awakening itself is a jewel, just like a precious gem;
for just as the great jewel, the wish-fulfilling gem, is the cause for pacifying all poverty and miserable rebirths, so too is this jewel of the thought of awakening.
This is the intended meaning: You are indeed merchants seeking the attainment of happiness and prosperity;
therefore, accept this very great jewel with great respect.
Why? Because it is "of great value"—this is the reason given.
Because this is priceless—since it excels all things by being the causal basis for both mundane and supramundane prosperity—therefore, the meaning is that this alone is what should be accepted.
If one asks, "How is this known? he says: "It has been thoroughly examined."
"Thoroughly investigated" means correctly determined.
By whom? He says: "by those of immeasurable intellect.
That is, by those of great wisdom—the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—whose intellect (*dhī*) or cognition (*buddhi*) is immeasurable, meaning impossible to measure.
By this much, it is said that the examination is "well-examined" because there is not even the slightest error in the investigation.
Furthermore, by what kind of beings?
By those who are the sole caravan-leaders of the world.
The suffix *aṇ* is applied in the sense of "leading a caravan.
The Buddhas, Blessed Ones, and Bodhisattvas—who are subject to the power of compassion—are the sole caravan leaders (*sārthavāha*) of all worlds; by them [it is led].

Just as merchants have leaders who are caravan leaders—wise and seeking their welfare—who guide them in the attainment of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful, so too [are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas].
Thus, there is no possibility of contradiction in that case,
and the intention here is the same;
therefore, this very jewel of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), priceless and most firm, should be grasped.
And this has been stated in that very same place:
"For example, noble son, as long as the moon and sun illuminate with their orb-like radiance,
within that interval, whatever enjoyments there may be— whether wealth, grain, jewels, gold, silver, flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, or other articles of use— "

All of those are not equal to the value of the great wish-fulfilling jewel, the King of Subjugation (*vaśirāja-mahāmaṇiratna*); in the same way, even so far as the omniscient wisdom (*sarvajñajñāna*) illuminates the sphere of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) throughout the three times,

whatever roots of merit there may be belonging to all gods, humans, and all sentient beings— including all those that are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*)— all of them [are not equal] to the great wish-fulfilling jewel, the King of Subjugation, which is the production of the thought of awakening (*bodhicittotpāda*).
"They do not tolerate a price," [as stated in the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra, 500].
Demonstrating another extraordinary and preeminent greatness of this [bodhicitta], like that of the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), he says:
"Indeed, all other virtue perishes once it has yielded its fruit, just as a plantain tree perishes after bearing its fruit.
But the tree of the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta) constantly bears fruit, never perishes, and indeed continues to produce [more]. (Bca 1.12)
Just as a plantain tree does not bear fruit again after yielding its fruit once,
so too all other wholesome deeds apart from the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), no matter how slight, become incapable of yielding further fruit once their maturation has ripened;
for they are exhausted by that alone.
Furthermore, because maturation (*vipāka*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it lacks a subsequent connection to further fruit.
He states "constantly" (*satatam*) and so forth to show that this is the specific distinction of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*):
at all times it bears fruit by bestowing happiness and prosperity upon rebirths as gods and humans; unlike other forms of merit, it does not go to exhaustion.

Because it possesses a stable nature and because it is filled at every moment by streams of clouds of various kinds of merit, the tree of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) indeed continues to grow,
since it produces the fruit of uninterrupted success and happiness.
And because it generates ever-increasing and ever-superior special qualities,
the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is like a tree;
this is a compound [formed] according to the rule "compounded with *vyāghra* and so forth."
Since this is so,

therefore those who are discerning and desire to attain all perfections of happiness— which are uninterrupted and possess excellence— should grasp precisely this. And this has been stated in the *Āryākṣayamatinirdeśa*:
(VIII.4) "Venerable Śāradvatīputra, it is just as, for example, a drop of water that has fallen into the great ocean does not undergo exhaustion or depletion in the interim until the end of the eon;
even so, there is no exhaustion or depletion in the interim of a root of virtue dedicated toward awakening until one sits at the seat of awakening. Thus it is said.
Bodhicitta is not only the cause for the accumulation of all that is virtuous, but also the cause for the exhaustion of the unwholesome side; this he states in a verse and a half:
"Even after committing most terrible sins, by relying upon it, one crosses over in an instant."
Just as one does not resort to great dangers by taking refuge with a hero, why then do ignorant beings not refrain from such [fearful] things?

Even if one has previously committed sins and unwholesome deeds— which are great, extremely terrifying, and most dreadful because they bestow unbearable suffering in the hells and other realms— one crosses over and completely transcends them by relying upon that bodhicitta; that is, by means of its characteristics of generating, protecting, increasing, and cultivating it.
The meaning is that he transcends by overcoming its power;
for in a single moment— indeed, in one and the same instant— he fully accumulates a vast mass of merit merely by its production.
How does one cross over?

Just as by relying on a hero one crosses over great dangers, or as someone who, even after committing a great offense, crosses over and becomes free from fear regarding the consequences of that offense—
so it is in this case as well.
Why, then, is such a bodhicitta not relied upon, not cultivated?
The meaning is: by ignorant beings, those devoid of wisdom, that is, by deluded people.
The underlying sense is that it ought indeed to be relied upon.
This too is stated in that very same place:

"O son of good family, just as a man who relies upon a hero does not fear any enemies, even so a bodhisattva who relies upon the hero that is the production of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) does not fear any enemies that are evil deeds."
He provides another illustration regarding the destruction of evil through the thought of awakening (bodhicitta):

"Just as the fire at the end of an eon consumes great evils in an instant. At the end of an eon, during the time of universal dissolution, the fire—the conflagration arising from the rising of the seven suns—consumes the entire realm of desire (kāmadhātu) along with the first dhyāna.
Just as it burns everything without remainder so that not even ashes are left behind,
so too are the sins.
Of what nature are they?

The great [sins], resembling Mount Sumeru, which result in the ripening of suffering in the Mahāraurava and other hells— whatever the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) incinerates, it eradicates by destroying that ripening.
"In an instant, not after a long time"—
this is how the connection should be understood with the phrase "it is not resorted to by ignorant beings."
This too has been stated in that very same place: "It is like the fire at the end of an eon, by virtue of incinerating all misdeeds;
it is like the subterranean realm (pātāla), by virtue of exhausting all unwholesome dharmas."
But surely the Blessed One is a proponent of the non-perishing of performed actions; so how can this be stated?
It is rightly said.

Because it is included within the great flood of merit—which is generated by the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and pervades the realm of space at every moment—it remains undiscernible according to the analogy of a single *palā* of salt [in the ocean].
Furthermore, because it has been overwhelmed by a powerful counteragent, that [merit] is indeed burnt and incapable of yielding its fruit; thus, there is no fault.
Or rather, it was said with the intention of referring to those who lack the means: "Karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced.
But this [practice] is the great means for uprooting all evil.

For instance, when a bodhisattva reflects with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), thinking, "I shall rescue all sentient beings, who pervade the realm of space, from all suffering and establish them in the perfection of all happiness," and simultaneously exhausts previously committed sins through the practice of remorse (*vidūṣaṇā*) and other means,
then by the power of that very thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), what possibility is there for sin to exist within his mental continuum?
Thus, everything is rendered free from confusion, so that there would be no room for objection.
By this much, what was stated— "By what other virtue could that be overcome?"— has also been made perfectly clear.
Others, however, say: "All this is said with reference to karma of indefinite ripening, for it is impossible for anyone to prevent karma that has definite ripening."
Thus, he says that the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) should be adopted:
"The wise Lord Maitreya proclaimed its immeasurable benefits to Sudhana. (Bca 1.14)
The Lord Maitreya, the Blessed One Ajita— what kind of being? A wise Bodhisattva— spoke, that is, he declared, the immeasurable and infinite natural qualities and benefits of that bodhicitta.
To Sudhana, that is, to the Bodhisattva named Sudhana;
and likewise it is described in the noble Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra:
"O son of good family, the thought of awakening is indeed the seed of all the qualities of a Buddha."
He is like a field, because he causes all the pure dharmas of the entire world to grow;
he is like the earth, because he is the refuge for all the world;
and so on, up to being like a father, because he protects all bodhisattvas.
/ He is like Vaiśravaṇa because he cuts off all poverty;
he is like the king of wish-fulfilling jewels because he accomplishes all aims.
It is like a vessel of fortune because it fulfills all intentions;
it is like a spear because it conquers the enemy of the afflictions.
Such is the detailed exposition.
"How is it that ignorant beings do not resort to this?"—this too should be applied here.

Now, showing the divisions of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), he says: "In brief, that mind of awakening should be understood as being of two kinds: the mind of the aspiration for awakening (bodhipraṇidhicitta) and the mind of the setting out toward awakening (bodhiprasthānacitta). (Bca 1.15)
That bodhicitta, which possesses the benefits just demonstrated, should be understood as being of two kinds and two types.
Although many varieties exist—such as those pertaining to the lineage-ground (*gotrabhūmi*) and so forth—he asks how it is of two kinds and answers: "In brief.
Even though other types are possible, it is said to be of these two kinds by way of summary.
How is it twofold? One is the mind of aspiration for enlightenment (bodhipraṇidhicitta), and the second is the mind of application toward enlightenment (bodhiprasthānacitta).
The aspiration for enlightenment; that very mind, or the mind directed toward it—
that mind which has arisen from the aspiration but is devoid of engagement in generosity and the other perfections.
That is the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*).
For example, it is the volition (*cetanā*) in the form of an initial prayer: "May I become a Buddha for the sake of protecting the entire world.
The mind of application (*prasthānacitta*) is either the mind that sets out or the very act of setting out itself.
Because the mind has that as its intrinsic nature;

for it is from the moment one begins to engage in the accumulations preceded by the undertaking of the vow and preceded by a prior mental attention that it is the "mind of setting out" (*prasthānacitta*).
Thus, by the sequence stated, there is a twofold division.
He indicates with the word "only" (*eva*) that the difference is precisely this much. The two *ca*-particles are for the purpose of mutual conjunction (*parasparasamuccaye*).
This demonstrates that both [types of bodhicitta] possess the nature of bodhicitta;
thereby, it dispels the doubt that the former [conventional] bodhicitta is not [true] bodhicitta,
because the *Śūraṃgamasamādhi-sūtra* declares that even the first-arisen bodhicitta is the cause of Buddhahood.

Likewise, it is said in the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha* (Bcp 12): "Noble son, rare are those beings in the world of beings who direct their minds toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; rarer still than they are those beings who have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
Now, making clear that very distinction just mentioned by means of an illustration, he says:

"Just as the difference between one who desires to go and one who is going is perceived, so too should the difference between these two be understood by the wise according to their respective order. (Bca 1.16)
Just as a certain person, desiring to reach a desired location and having the intention to go, does not actually set out; whereas another, having set out for its attainment, indeed goes.
Just as their difference— that is, their distinction— is perceived and understood,
so too should the difference, the diversity between these two— the mind of the aspiration for enlightenment and the mind of the practice— be known and comprehended by the wise and discerning.
How so? By way of numerical correspondence (*yāthāsaṃkhyena*).
The suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (*svārthe*).
The meaning of the number is that the former is an illustration of the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*), while the latter is that of the mind of application (*prasthānacetas*).

The Blessed One has described this very mind of aspiration (*praṇidhicitta*), even when devoid of practice (*pratipatti*), as having great fruit within *saṃsāra*. Thus he says: "The fruit of the mind of aspiration for enlightenment is great even in *saṃsāra*, even if it is indeed devoid of practice."
Nevertheless, let alone his Buddhahood,
even within saṃsāra, the fruit consisting of birth among gods and humans— characterized by happiness and prosperity— is great, being more vast than any other wholesome [action].
Because it is characterized by such attributes as "it bears fruit constantly," and so forth.
Thus it is said in the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa* (the *Gaṇḍavyūha Sūtra*, chapter 508):
"For example, noble son, even when broken, a diamond jewel surpasses all other gold ornaments, being preeminent in every way."
It does not lose its name as a diamond-jewel,
and it dispels all poverty;

in the same way, noble son, even when separated from correct practice, the diamond-jewel of the production of the mind set on omniscience surpasses the golden ornaments of all the qualities of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It does not abandon what is called the thought of awakening (bodhicitta),
and it turns back the poverty of cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
Therefore, even one who is entirely incapable of training in the perfections in every way and by every means must nevertheless generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*);
for, through the embrace of such skillful means, it yields a great fruit.
As it is said in the *Āryāpararājāvavādaka-sūtra*:
"Because you, Great King, have many duties and much to be done, you are unable to train in the perfection of generosity in every way, at all times, and in its entirety."
...up to training in the perfection of wisdom.
Therefore, O Great King, you should likewise maintain this very desire for perfect awakening, as well as faith, aspiration, and the vow,
whether walking, standing, sitting, lying down, waking, eating, or drinking.
Constantly recollect, attend to, and cultivate [this].

Having gathered together and weighed the roots of merit of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, noble Śrāvakas, and ordinary beings— both your own and those of others— past, future, and present, rejoice in them.
With the foremost rejoicing, having rejoiced,
dedicate the acts of worship to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Noble Śrāvakas;
and having dedicated them, make them common to all sentient beings.

Therefore, for the sake of all sentient beings until the attainment of omniscience and for the fulfillment of all Buddha-qualities, dedicate [your merit] three times every day toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
In this way, O Great King, by practicing accordingly, you shall exercise your sovereignty and yet not neglect the duties of kingship.
And you will bring the accumulations for awakening to full completion.

Having said this and more, he continued: "Furthermore, O Great King, by the ripening of the roots of merit from the thought of perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhicitta*), you have indeed been reborn many times among the gods,
and you have been reborn many times among human beings."
And you shall exercise sovereignty over all rebirths among gods and humans;
such is the detailed account.
Thus, one should not despise the bodhicitta even when it is deficient in practice, because that too brings forth happiness throughout the infinite cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, it is established that the bodhicitta which has practice as its essence yields an exceedingly vast fruit; thus he says:
But it is not the uninterrupted nature of merit that is like that of one whose mind is set upon departure.
"But not," however, means "not again.

The sense is that it is not like the state of the mind of setting out (prasthānacitta), which possesses uninterrupted merit— that is, the quality of flowing with a continuous stream of the auspicious— but such is not the case for this [mind].
Establishing this very quality of uninterrupted merit through two verses, he says:
"From the moment one takes up that mind for the sake of liberating the boundless realm of sentient beings with an irreversible resolve," (Bca 1.18)
From that time forward, even while one is asleep or heedless, uninterrupted streams of merit flow forth like the sky, in manifold ways. (Bca 1.19)
"From which time," meaning starting from which point;

"of the boundless," meaning that which has no limit or measure, [referring to] the realm of sentient beings that pervades the realm of space; "for the sake of liberation," meaning for their complete release, which is the cause for the pacification of all suffering.
He takes up that mind;
having taken up the mind of perfect enlightenment, he abides in it. How? With an irreversible intention and a mind that has not strayed from its engagement.
From that time forward, beginning with that as the starting point,
it applies to both cases: even to one who is asleep with a mind overcome by torpor, and to one who is heedless or whose mind is distracted.
And this is an illustration;
it should be understood that [this occurs] even when walking, standing, sitting, eating, or even in states such as fainting, and so forth.
"Many times" means...
At every moment, many times over,
uninterrupted streams of merit— continuous successions and impetuses of virtue—
proceed forth, equal to the sky, with a measure as vast as the realm of space at every instant.
Therefore, a bodhisattva must be one whose essence is practice.
And it is said in the *Āryasamādhirāja*:
"Therefore, I shall become one whose essence is practice."
In this way, O youth, one should train.
Why is that?
Because for one whose essence is practice, O youth, unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is not difficult to attain. [Samādhi 10]
Demonstrating that the Blessed One himself has stated that his merit is uninterrupted, he says:
"The Tathāgata himself spoke this, along with its logical justification, in the *Subāhupṛcchā* for the sake of beings who have inferior inclinations. (Bca 1.20)
The Tathāgata, the Buddha, the Blessed One himself, has personally declared and explained this very quality of immeasurable merit.
Where? In the *Subāhupṛcchā*, that is, in the sutra named *Subāhupṛcchā*. How? With supporting evidence and with logical reasoning.

For what purpose? For the sake of beings who have inferior inclinations (*hīnādhimukti*). Those whose inclination—meaning faith or desire—is directed toward the inferior vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; they are the "beings" referred to here.
"For them, this is for that purpose";
that is to say, with that objective in view.

For instance, those of indefinite lineage (*aniyatagotra*) who, fearing the accumulation of a greater mass of merit over a much longer period of time, turn their minds away from the Mahāyāna and [seek] the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas—which can be accomplished by a smaller mass of merit in a shorter period of time—[are the ones for whom this was intended].
To refute that [view], the Blessed One stated the following reasoning.
Explaining that very rebirth in two verses, he says:
"Thinking, 'I shall destroy the headaches of sentient beings,' he who possessed the altruistic intention was seized by immeasurable merit. (Bca 1.21)
How much more so for one who desires to remove the incomparable spear of each [being], and who wishes to establish each being in immeasurable virtue? (Bca 1.22)
Thinking, "I shall dispel the headache of a few people by means of a mantra or medicine," one who possesses such a virtuous intention should be seen as being embraced by immeasurable merit;
how much more so, then, for one who desires to remove the immeasurable suffering of cyclic existence for every single being in the immeasurable world?

Moreover, for one who desires to remove that suffering and to endow all sentient beings with every virtue, how could there not be immeasurable merit? This should be construed by changing the case-ending [of the subject].
Furthermore, how could streams of merit not flow for him without interruption, equal to the sky?
Therefore, just as Buddhahood is to be accomplished through a vast accumulation of provisions,

and just as even within that vastness of accumulation it occurs at every moment— due to such specific causes, there is a great gain in this very Mahāyāna. Thus, it is demonstrated that our minds should not turn back out of cowardice from this state of fearlessness.
As it will be said:
"Exhausting former sins and receiving oceans of merit,
by the power of the thought of awakening alone, one proceeds more swiftly even than the Śrāvakas."

Thus [Bodhicaryāvatāra 7.29]. And he who thus exerts himself for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings is praiseworthy even compared to the gods and others, because his qualities are uncommon; demonstrating this, he says:
Whose mother or father could have such a hope for their welfare?
Or will it belong to the gods, the sages, or the Brahmās? (Bca 1.23)
Of which being?
Of the mother, the progenitor;
or of the father, the begetter.
Of the deities, such as Soma, Varuṇa, and others;
or of the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha, Gotama, and others;
or of the Brahmins, the knowers of the Vedas.

For such is this hope for the welfare [of others] and this intention to bring about their benefit— just as it has been demonstrated immediately following [the previous discussion]— that it will belong to a bodhisattva;
let alone whether it has occurred or is occurring, even in the future it will never belong to anyone other than a bodhisattva.
To the question "Why is this so?", he says:
"Even for those very same beings, such a desire has never arisen before even in a dream for their own sake; how, then, could it possibly exist for the sake of others? (Bca 1.24)

Even for those [beings], such as their mothers and others, even for their own sake—that is, even for the sake of themselves—this aspiration to remove all suffering and to establish immeasurable virtues has never arisen before; it was unprecedented, not having occurred even in a dream.
Let alone arising intentionally during the waking state.
He says that [compassion] might sometimes arise for the sake of others: "How can there be a birth [of compassion] for the sake of another?
For one's own self is dearer to the world than another; if [compassion] does not exist even for that [self], [how much less for another]?"

How could there even be the possibility of acting for the sake of others? Or rather, one should construe it thus: "How could there even be the occurrence of acting for the sake of others even in a dream?"
Having thus established the unique quality of the bodhisattva, he concludes by saying:
"How can this unprecedented and extraordinary jewel among beings be born, whose intention for the sake of others does not arise even for its own self? (Bca 1.25)
Thus, because he performs such exceedingly marvelous deeds and his arising is difficult to encounter, he is indeed a special jewel among sentient beings— one unprecedented and never before perceived.
How is it that he is born with such qualities as have been described here?
"How so? [is asked] regarding the marvelous.
Why, then, is it said thus? He says: "Because it is for the sake of others."
Because that great being’s intention is directed toward the welfare of others, it does not arise even for his own sake among other sentient beings in the manner described above.
And here, other qualities of one who has generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) should also be stated,
such as those revealed by the Blessed One, the noble Maitreya, concerning Sudhana in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*;
and these have also been shown in great detail by the author of the treatise in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
It should be understood in that very same way.

Furthermore, by way of the benefits of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), he speaks of the immeasurable merit of the bodhisattva: "How indeed can the merit of that jewel of a mind be measured—that seed of joy for the world and the medicine for the suffering of the world? (Bca 1.26)

Since it is the cause of all joy for all sentient beings and the fundamental source of all prosperity for gods and others, how indeed could the merit of that jewel of the mind— bodhicitta— be measured? In what manner, indeed, could it be numbered?
Because it is so vast as to be impossible to measure.
This has been stated in the *Āryavīradattaparipṛcchā*: "If the merit arising from the thought of awakening were to possess form..."
Having completely filled the realm of space, it would further extend beyond that.
Thus it is said.

Even though the instruction is given in general terms, it should nevertheless be understood as referring to the "mind of setting out" (prasthānacitta), because that alone is the subject under discussion.
Furthermore, he states another qualification of that very [bodhicitta]: "and of the medicine for the suffering of the world.
This is because, by way of eliminating all physical and mental sufferings of all living beings, it has the nature of a great elixir that removes every disease.
By this, the fact that bodhicitta is the cause of both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is established.
Therefore, it is rightly said that this possesses an incalculable amount of merit.
Anticipating the doubt as to how this is logical, he explains:
"The worship of the Buddha is distinguished by the mere wish for their welfare;
how much more so when one exerts oneself for the sake of all the happiness of all sentient beings. (Bca 1.27)

(Bcp 16) The meaning is: from the *bodhicitta* that consists solely of aspiration and prayer—the intense resolve (*adhyāśaya*) thinking, "May I become a Buddha for the sake of protecting the entire world"—but which is devoid of actual practice;
whatever merit arises from this, it surpasses even the worship of a Buddha, according to the scriptures. Thus, it truly becomes the cause for generating a mass of merit.
In this way, the greatness of the first *bodhicitta* has been explained.
This too has been stated in that very same place: "Suppose a person were to give to the Lords of the World Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filled with the finest jewels."
But whoever, with palms joined, should direct their mind toward awakening—
this worship is superior, for its end is not to be found.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, how could there not be extraordinary merit from making the effort, "I shall remove all suffering from all suffering beings and endow them with every happiness"?

"Now, beings are themselves discerning regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful; so what is the use of effort?"—anticipating this objection, he replies with three verses:
"They rush headlong toward suffering alone, with the intention of escaping from suffering."
Out of delusion and a mere desire for pleasure, they destroy their own happiness like an enemy.

Whoever would bring satisfaction with all forms of happiness to those who are repeatedly afflicted by the miseries of the world, and whoever would cut through all their sufferings— [that person should be honored]. (Bca 1.29)
He even destroys delusion; how could there be anyone equal to such a virtuous person?
Where is such a friend, or where is such merit?
Intending to escape from suffering, yet desiring to counteract the pain of hunger and so forth through unwholesome actions such as taking life,
they run toward suffering itself— the very nature of which is the experience of falling into the precipices of hell and other realms— and proceed directly facing it.
The meaning is that they enter only into suffering,
like moths entering the flame of a lamp.
For this very reason, by the mere desire for pleasure— that is, by the longing for happiness— they destroy their own happiness like an enemy.

If it is asked how they become their own enemies for the sake of destroying their own happiness, it is because of delusion; due to the power of perversion, there is a lack of thorough knowledge regarding the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful.

Therefore, that virtuous person who is compassionate without cause should provide satisfaction and nourishment through all forms of happiness—both physical and mental—to those who are perverted, attached to pleasure, longing for happiness, entirely deprived of it, afflicted, and suffering; that is, to those who have been tormented in many ways by hundreds of various sufferings.
Or alternatively: [the text continues as follows:]... [The provided text ends here].
It should be understood that [the Bodhisattva] should repeatedly and in many ways bring about satisfaction through all forms of happiness.
It does not merely produce satisfaction in terms of pleasure;
rather, it cuts through and pacifies all afflictions and all painful sensations.
It not only brings about the pacification of suffering and the satisfaction of happiness,
but it also destroys delusion and eliminates ignorance.
"This is not the path; this is the path. From here there is danger; go from here, do not sit down"—thus he reveals the paths of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
And he who is thus devoted to turning others away from calamity, and intent on providing for their welfare and happiness (Bcp 17).
Among all beings,
where is there a virtuous person equal to him?
Where is there a virtuous person equal to that great-souled one?
It does not exist at all from anywhere, because its nature is that of supreme affection without cause;
or rather, from where could such a friend come— one whose mind is inclined toward bestowing benefit and happiness, a locus of supreme trust, and a friend equal to him?
Whence comes a friend? It is not possible at all.
Whence comes such merit?
Whatever merit arises for a bodhisattva dwelling in this manner,
that too is not equal to any other merit.
Even one who returns a favor for a service received is praised;
how much more, then, should a Bodhisattva be praised, who acts as a benefactor even when not solicited?
When someone has previously assisted one during times of fear, crisis, or calamity, and then returns that assistance once the help has been rendered,

he too is praised by the world and extolled as "this person is virtuous. How much more so, then, the Bodhisattva who is a naturally benevolent being— one who brings about the welfare of others without being prompted and without being requested?
What more can be said, what else remains to be told?
The meaning is that it is impossible to offer praise for him.

Even with reference to worldly conventions, he speaks in order to manifest the greatness of the Bodhisattva’s merit: "A doer of virtue who gives alms to a few people is honored by the world for giving a mere meal for a single moment, even if it lasts only half a day and is accompanied by contempt. (Bca 1.32)

By undertaking the gift of merely food and drink for a limited number of beings, one is honored and venerated by people as "this person is one of meritorious deeds," by those in the world who delight in virtuous actions;
yet even that gift lasts but a moment, not the entire day.
Or even half of that,
or indeed for a single moment;
this is by virtue of giving merely a portion of food.
"Meat" (maṃsa) refers to contemptible food,
that is, inferior nourishment; it is merely that, nothing more.
It is devoid of such indirect expressions.
From the giving of that—that is, from its relinquishment—how so? With contempt.
This is an adverbial modifier. It means:
with contempt, preceded by a salutation;
that is to say, having struck [him] with a slap on the cheek or a blow from a stick as he was entering the sacrificial hall by force.
Furthermore, from what state?
From passing half the day, that is, from being sustained for two watches;
having eaten at midday, one again seeks food in the evening.

Furthermore, demonstrating that the giving of a bodhisattva is the opposite of this, he says: How much more so for one who bestows gifts for an infinite duration of time, to an infinite number of sentient beings—giving inexhaustibly until the end of space and all its inhabitants, and thereby completely fulfilling every wish? (Bca 1.33)
There is no limit or measure;
he does not give by counting sentient beings, thinking, "I shall give to this many— hundreds, thousands, lakhs, or crores— and after that, no more."
However, it is not for a limited number of sentient beings,
nor for a fixed period of time, but rather for an infinite duration of time.
"I shall give for a hundred thousand lakhs of koṭis of kalpas, but beyond that, no," thus he does not give with a time limit.
"Like the sky" [means...]
"Sky-beings" (gaganajana) refers to people who are like the sky;
the meaning is that just as space is limitless, so too are these beings. Alternatively:
The sky and those people are "sky-people" (*gaganajana*);
their complete exhaustion is their total purification.
This has as its limit the extent of the element of space and as long as sentient beings have not attained final nirvana.
As he will say:
"As long as space endures, and as long as the world endures, may my own endurance continue. [Bodhicaryāvatāra 10.55]
Therefore, it is inexhaustible, because its exhaustion or limit does not exist.
This is the intended meaning: that gift which lasts until the end of the destruction of the world and the sky is, in reality, truly inexhaustible.
Because there is no exhaustion of them;
nor is it a specific, limited object, but rather the complete fulfillment of all desires.

If a bodhisattva, with a joyful mind, bestows everything that is desired by another—provided it is all blameless and brings delight to their intention—preceded by supreme affection, respect, honor, and kind words, how could it not be fitting for this to be an act of worship? Indeed, it is most certainly fitting; thus it should be understood.
As it is said in the *Nārāyaṇaparipṛcchā*:
"That object should not be grasped in which one does not give rise to the thought of renunciation, nor in which the intention to relinquish would fail to proceed."
To the extent that this very body of mine has been surrendered and relinquished for the sake of all sentient beings,
let alone external objects;
whatever purpose shall serve whichever sentient being, by whatever means, and in whatever way.
To each of them I shall give that very thing;
whatever is available, I shall give my hand to those who ask for a hand, up to and including giving away my head to those who ask for a head.
What need is there to mention external objects?

That is to say, wealth, grain, gold, silver, jewels, ornaments, horses, chariots, elephant-vehicles, villages, cities, market towns, districts, kingdoms, nations, royal capitals, ports, female and male slaves, laborers, servants, sons, daughters, and retinues— thus it is said in detail.

Thus, demonstrating that those who desire their own welfare must protect their own minds with great effort toward a Bodhisattva—who stands as a repository for a collection of jewel-like virtues and whose sole supreme vow is the accomplishment of the benefit and happiness of others—the Lord has said: "Whoever conceives a defiled thought in his own heart toward a son of the Conqueror, the master of the sacrificial feast (sattrapati), shall dwell in the hells for as many eons as there are moments of that defilement’s arising. (Bca 1.34)

In this manner, according to the sequence stated, regarding the Bodhisattva— the son of the Victor, the son of the Sugata, the lord of the gift of happiness at all times, and the master of the sacrificial session (*sattra*)—
that evil-natured person who, within his own heart, that is, in the continuum of his own mind, harbors or generates turbid, sinful thoughts; [he is as described].
"He dwells in the hells," so said the Lord, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Although the rule *upānvadhyāḍ vasah* would have required the accusative case, there is here an intention to express the locative sense of the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*).
For how long? For as many eons as the number of the arising of his defilements.
The meaning is that for as many moments as a defiled mind arises in one's continuum, for that many eons— one numbering according to those moments of defiled mind— one remains in the hells.
As it is said in the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra*:

Mañjuśrī, for as many moments as a bodhisattva gives rise to thoughts of resentment or thoughts of contempt toward another bodhisattva, for that many eons must he don the armor [of resolve]: "I must dwell in the great hells."

Is it not said that for one who sheds the blood of a Tathāgata with a malicious mind, there is no dwelling in the Avīci hell for as many eons as the number of moments in which the thought was produced?
Since there is nothing more exalted than a Tathāgata in the three worlds, how is this most difficult point to be reconciled? True.
Indeed, in this system, the reality of things is not established according to their literal sense,
because the entire teaching is established by way of being either of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) or of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
For no one in the world, including the gods, is able to give rise to a malicious thought toward the Tathāgata.

Because through practice over the course of no small number of aeons, the mind of loving-kindness becomes habitualized toward all sentient beings, weapons do not strike his body; this is stated as a description of the benefits of the mind of loving-kindness.
Furthermore, in this case, the transmigration of karma is not actually demonstrated.

Because the Buddhas have abandoned the obscuration of karma, that [offense] was displayed through an intentional accommodation (*abhisaṃdhi*) toward those to be trained, and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). However,
in the case of harming a bodhisattva, Buddhahood itself would be destroyed along with its very root.
In this way, the welfare of the world including its gods would be impaired;
this has been stated in accordance with the scriptures.
Here, only the Blessed One knows the ultimate truth.

And this was said in the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā-sūtra*: "Mañjuśrī, if some son of good family or daughter of good family were to destroy or burn as many stūpas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā,

and another son of good family or daughter of good family, having conceived a mind of malice, harshness, and anger toward a bodhisattva mahāsattva who is devoted to the Mahāyāna, were to revile and abuse him..."
This person enters into a sin even more incalculable than that.
Why is that?
For it is from the Bodhisattvas that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are born.
Stūpas originate from the Buddha, as do all articles of comfort and all the assemblies of devas.
By showing disrespect to a bodhisattva, one shows disrespect to all Buddhas;
by honoring a bodhisattva, one honors all Buddhas. And so forth.
Furthermore, as for one who generates a serene mind toward that [stūpa], how much fruit of merit arises for them? To this he says:
"Now, for one whose mind attains serenity, the fruit produced for him shall be even greater than that."
For an evil deed committed against the Sons of the Conqueror requires great effort [to undo], whereas a virtuous one is accomplished without effort.
Furthermore, for that meritorious person whose mind attains clarity toward a bodhisattva,

a fruit greater than that would be produced; for that one with a clear mind, a fruit greater than that would be produced and arise— namely, from the specific distinction of ripening, a fruit of meritorious action much more abundant than the fruit of the previous evil would be produced and arise.
Alternatively,
it is precisely the karma that brings about a ripened fruit equal to or exceeding that [previous karma] which is called the "fruit";
that is to say, karma that produces a more abundant fruit arises.
And it is said in the *Niyatāniyatāvatāramudrāsūtra*:

"Mañjuśrī, suppose that in all the world-systems in the ten directions, all sentient beings were to have their eyes plucked out, based on mere conceptual construction. Then, suppose some son of good family or daughter of good family, with a mind of loving-kindness toward all those sentient beings, were to restore those eyes for them, based on mere conceptual construction."

Or, Mañjuśrī, if another son of good family or daughter of good family, with a devout mind, should behold a bodhisattva who is resolved upon the Mahāyāna, this person generates incalculably more merit than that. Thus it is said.
Therefore, those who know themselves should cultivate only a virtuous mind in this great field of merit.
Moreover, for this reason as well, it is proper to cultivate only a virtuous mind.
This is because even with great force and through extreme hardship, an evil deed— indeed, only an evil deed, being contemptible or a misdeed— is committed against Bodhisattvas,
since their entire conduct of body, speech, and mind produces clarity and faith.
And due to the power of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), no one gives rise to a mind of malice toward Bodhisattvas.
This has been stated in the *Āryamañjuśrī-vimokṣa*:
"For example, noble son, for the great Naga kings who have bound upon their heads the crest-jewel of the king of wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi-ratna-rāja*), there is no fear of harm from others."

In the same way, for those Bodhisattvas who have bound upon their crowns the king of wish-fulfilling jewels—the great compassion of the thought of awakening—there is no fear of miserable rebirths, the lower realms, or the machinations of others. Thus it is said.
Therefore, for what purpose is this effort undertaken toward them, which results in the acquisition of misfortune and bitter fruit?

For this very reason, however, virtue arises without effort, because through the means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth, one performs actions for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, thereby performing perfectly pure deeds.
And because there is no lapse whatsoever in any respect,
joy, serene confidence, and gladness arise toward them quite effortlessly;
therefore, the wholesome again arises without effort.
Now, manifesting mental clarity through his own excellence toward those who have generated the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), the author of the treatise pays homage to them, saying:

"I pay homage to their bodies, in which that precious jewel of the sublime mind has arisen; I go for refuge to those mines of happiness, in whom even an injury results in a succession of bliss. (Bca 1.36)
I prostrate and pay homage to the bodies and personhoods of those elephant-like men,
in whose mental continuums that excellent jewel of the mind— possessing the aforementioned benefits— has arisen and been produced.

The mind alone is the jewel, resembling a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); it is excellent and supreme because it removes all the suffering of poverty. And that is the analysis of the compound: "that [which is] both that [mind] and the excellent jewel of the mind."
The word "that" (tat) may be taken separately;
this refers to the honoring of one who is a vessel of superior qualities.
He states another qualification of that [vessel]: "even where there is harm."

The intended meaning is this: even when harm or defeat is inflicted upon those Bodhisattvas whose hearts are supremely virtuous, it results in a continuous succession of happiness for the perpetrator and ultimately brings about his welfare. This is because it is impossible to inflict harm upon them;
or, even if such harm were somehow possible, those with malicious intentions who act with that very harm as their motive will, through some subsequent cause, develop faith toward them once again.
In that regard, even an act of harm results in a succession of happiness within nirvāṇa;
as it was said concerning the Five [Monks] in the *Maitrībalajātakamālā* (Jātakamālā 8).
Or, because of the Bodhisattva’s vow, even harm is said to result in a succession of happiness.
As he will say:
"Those who slander me, and others who do me harm, as well as those who mock me—
may they all partake in enlightenment."
Thus [Bodhicaryāvatāra 3.16].

Alternatively, there are those for whom even an injury—even an act of harm—due to the resolute intention of great compassion, produces only happiness despite being a cause of suffering, as if it were performed by one's own beloved son;
as we shall explain in the chapter on Patience (Kṣānti).

Thus, because they are in every way the cause of happiness, he demonstrates that Bodhisattvas are to be resorted to by those seeking happiness, just as a mine of jewels is resorted to by those seeking jewels:
"I go for refuge to them, the sources of happiness.
They are sources of happiness because they are the sole origin of all happiness.
I go for refuge to them, who, according to the sequence already described, are causes of happiness even when they cause harm; the sense is: "May they be my protection."
