Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Benefits of the Awakening Mind," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
The Second Chapter, titled "Confession of Evil.

Now, having thus attained this rare convergence of favorable conditions and having understood the benefits of the spirit of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), for the purpose of taking up that spirit of enlightenment—

Bringing the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas before his eyes, he performs prostration, worship, going for refuge, confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, entreaty to the Buddhas, supplication, and the dedication toward enlightenment, saying:

"In order to grasp that jewel of the mind, I shall properly perform worship of the Tathāgatas, of the stainless jewel of the True Dharma, and of the sons of the Buddha, who are oceans of virtue. (Bca 2.1)
In order to grasp— that is, to take up— the jewel of the mind whose benefits have just been explained;
that is to say, in order to produce it,
I perform worship to the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
"This is I"—thus the grasper of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) points out the self.
This is the exposition of the Jewel of the Buddha;
and [it is also] of the Jewel of the True Dharma, characterized by scripture (āgama) and realization (adhigama).
"Of the stainless" means that which is pure in its three excellences, purified of the three spheres, and naturally luminous;
for it is never the locus of any impurities,
since the afflictions are merely adventitious.
And because it is skillful at removing all impurities,
this is an exposition of the jewel of the Dharma and of its offspring, the sons of the Buddha.

This, however, is the exposition of the Jewel of the Saṅgha, [referring] to those who are oceans of virtues, oceans of the jewels of qualities, such as the noble Avalokiteśvara, Mañjughoṣa, and others.
This concludes the procedure for worshiping the Three Jewels.
The phrase "I perform worship" is to be connected with every [instance].
"Properly" (*samyak*) is an adjective qualifying the worship itself; it means that it should be done correctly, without error.
Or rather, it is a qualification of the grasping by means of an intense clarity of mind;
that is, for the sake of correct grasping, one should grasp with a mind exceptionally serene, and not out of compliance with others or the like,
so that what has been grasped does not fall away again.
Speaking specifically of worship, he says:
"Whatever flowers and fruits there are, whatever kinds of medicinal herbs exist, whatever jewels there are in the world, and whatever waters are clear and delightful; [Bca 2.2]"
As for their measure, it is as many as there are flowers and fruits without exception; all of these, extending to the very limits of the expanse of space, are without ownership.
"Taking [these] with my intellect, I offer them to the bulls among sages together with their sons"—this should be applied everywhere in the preceding [verses].
"Kinds of medicine" refers to various types of medicinal herbs.
"Clear and beautiful" is also an epithet for the jewels.
Likewise, there are mountains made of jewels, as well as forest regions delightful for their solitude,
creepers radiant with the ornaments of flowers, and trees whose branches are bent low by excellent fruit.

And in the worlds of the gods and others, there are perfumes and incenses, wish-fulfilling trees, and trees made of jewels; there are lakes adorned with lotuses, and the sounds of swans are utterly enchanting. (Bca 2.4)
The "bearers of the earth" are the mountains;
"consisting of jewels" means having the nature of jewels;
"delightful through seclusion" means delightful because of their solitude, captivating to the mind.
That is to say, they are conducive to discernment (*viveka*).

"Resplendent with ornaments of beautiful flowers" means that the very flowers—which are excellent because they are endowed with fine color, fragrance, and taste—serve as their ornaments and decorations; they are thus exceedingly brilliant and radiant. "With branches bent by good fruit" means those whose branches are bent down, drooping, as if touching the ground, by those fruits which are both excellent and beautiful. These are the *kalpa* trees.
There were wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpavṛkṣas*).
"Adorned with lotuses" means those for whom the very lotuses (*padmas*) serve as ornaments; they were thus.
"Exceedingly charming with the cries of swans" means those that were delightful, being exceedingly captivating through the sounds—the calls—of swans; they were thus.
And all these various kinds of crops grown without cultivation, or other objects worthy of worship and adornment,
extending as far as the limits of the expanse of space— all these, too, are without ownership.
"Unplowed" means produced or manifested without the act of plowing with a plowshare.

"Species of grain" refers to varieties of rice or other such crops. "Other ornaments for those worthy of worship" refers to the decorations that bring beauty to those who are venerable and to be propitiated.

Others, moreover, extend as far as the limits of the realm of space; "the extension of the realm of space" means its scope, its room, or its breadth, and these [worlds] have that as their limit or boundary.
All of these are said to be unappropriated and without "mine-ness," meaning they have not been claimed by anyone.
Taking this with my intellect, I offer it to the bulls among sages together with their sons;
may they, who are worthy of the finest offerings and possess great compassion, accept it from me out of pity for me.
Having taken up— that is, having grasped— with the intellect by means of the mental consciousness,
I offer and present [this] to the bulls among sages, the preeminent sages,
together with their sons and accompanied by the assembly of bodhisattvas.
May they accept and take possession of all these articles of my offering;
the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are the most excellent recipients of offerings and supreme vessels for gifts,
who possess great compassion and whose sole intention is to provide for the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings.
Having compassion for me, a being distressed by misery, and feeling pity for me— that is to say, for the sake of favoring me.

This might be the case: why is it that only mental worship is prescribed in this way, when one might instead directly offer those various charming objects? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "I am meritless and exceedingly poor; I have nothing else for the sake of worship. Therefore, O Protectors, whose minds are intent on the welfare of others, please accept these things for my sake through your own power. (Bca 2.7)
I have not performed meritorious deeds; for that very reason, I am greatly impoverished.
Through merit, one comes to possess the perfection of all necessary requisites.
Because of that absence, I have no other requisites whatsoever for the purpose of worship.

Therefore, for my sake—and out of a desire for my merit—may the Blessed Ones accept these spoken articles of worship offered by me; for they possess minds intent on the welfare of others, they long for the benefit and happiness of others, and they are endowed with great compassion. Thus, O Protectors, please accept this.
"By one's own power" means by one's own capability.
Furthermore, this personal existence of mine is under my own control;
thinking, "I shall offer it," he says:
"And I give myself entirely and in every way to the Victors and to their sons."
O supreme beings, please accept me as your own; out of devotion, I enter into the state of servitude toward you.
And I offer myself to the Victors in every way,
entirely and in all respects;
having relinquished my self-possessiveness, I offer it even to their sons.
Accept me, O bulls among men;
I accept servitude and the state of a slave unto you,
not out of greed for a livelihood or the like.
Rather, it means with devotion, with supreme reverence, and with a mind overflowing with faith.
Now, one might ask: "What benefit is there in this? To which he replies:
"By being accepted by you, I shall become fearless and work for the welfare of sentient beings within existence;
I shall transcend my former evil and shall not commit further sin again. (Bca 2.9)

"By means of your great support provided by you, I am free from fear and accomplish for the welfare of the world within cyclic existence. Even with such great support, one who is shrouded by unwholesome karma lacks the capacity even to achieve their own welfare; thus he says, 'And previously,' and so forth.
Previously, due to lack of full understanding, I committed unwholesome karma, which I now transcend."
I eliminate [these defilements] through the practice of thorough examination and so forth.
When it is said "he transcends," it is said "I transcend" because there is no concern for mere verbal conventions in these linguistic usages,
and because the primary emphasis lies on the meaning and the underlying elements (dhātu).
Furthermore, I shall not commit evil again;
I establish the restraint of non-doing for the future.
Having thus offered all these gifts of worship, beginning with the surrender of one's own self, he speaks again in order to perform a particularly distinguished form of worship:
"In those fragrant bathing halls, delightful with pillars radiant with jewels, with canopies shimmering with pearls, and with floors of clear, brilliant crystal. (Bca 2.10)
(Bcp 25) "Radiant" means shining with jewels such as sapphire and the like; "charming" means beautiful because of those pillars. It should be construed as: "I perform my bath in those bathing-houses.
Furthermore, of what nature are they?
In those [palaces] which were like canopies— canopies that were radiant and shining, inlaid with pearl-work consisting of pearls—
and which were transparent, perfectly pure, and brilliant, full of luster.

These are made of crystal (sphāṭika), being the floors (kuṭṭima) which are specific types of ground decorations; in those [floors], which are fragrant, being perfumed and scented with the incense of black agallochum, sandalwood, and so forth.
There are houses for them for bathing.
With jars filled with pleasing fragrant water and flowers, and with many great treasures of jewels,
I perform this bath for the Tathāgatas and their sons, accompanied by song and instrumental music.
And water, and flowers of delightful fragrance; with those [flowers],
the jars and pots were filled—
those [vessels] made of great jewels, consisting of vast quantities of lapis lazuli and so forth.
And those jewels were of many hundreds of thousands of millions of varieties of their own natures.
Accompanied by song and instrumental music, together with enchanting singing, dancing, drums, and other musical instruments.
I shall wipe their bodies with incomparable garments that have been thoroughly perfumed and cleansed of impurities;
thereafter, I shall give them excellent robes, beautifully dyed and well-incensed.
By means of incenses such as agallochum (agaru) and others that have been well-perfumed;
by those whose impurities have been washed away—
that is to say, by those who are stainless.
With incomparable and peerless garments of fine linen,
[he honored] those Tathāgatas and their sons.
The body is the physical frame; "I wipe" means I cleanse it. "Then," that is, immediately after that wiping.
Deeply red, meaning beautifully colored or perfectly dyed,
and perfumed with exquisite incense—
I offer these to those Victors.
Excellent robes, unsurpassed coverings.
With divine garments that are soft, smooth, and variously beautiful, and with those various excellent ornaments,
I shall adorn Samantabhadra, Ajita, Mañjughoṣa, Lokeśvara, and the others as well.
Divine, meaning originating in heaven and worthy of the gods; soft, meaning having a delicate touch, and smooth,
meaning subtle.
By means of those garments which possess a manifold splendor produced by various colors;
and by the finest ornaments, the most excellent of decorations;
"by this and that" refers to crowns, bracelets, armlets, necklaces, anklets, and so forth.
I also adorn and embellish the Bodhisattvas, such as Samantabhadra, Ajita, Mañjughoṣa, Lokeśvara, and others.

I anoint those bodies of all the lords of sages, which blaze with the luster of gold that is well-heated, polished, and well-washed, with the finest perfumes whose scents spread throughout the entire triple-thousandfold world system.
A thousand sets of four continents, as well as a thousand each of moons, suns, Mount Merus, the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadēva*), and the worlds of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*),
is considered a "small chiliocosm" (*sāhasracūḍika*).
That same [system] multiplied by a thousand is the "dichiliocosm" (*dvisāhasra*).
A thousand of those is a trisāhasra;
this means one hundred billion four-continent world systems (*cāturdvīpika*).
In this way, the world-systems in all directions are infinite and boundless.
Those whose nature it is to spread throughout all the three-thousandfold world systems are "those who are thus. Those who possess such fragrances and scents are "those who are thus."

With those supreme perfumes, such as yakṣakardama and haricandana, I anoint and smear the bodies of those lords of sages. Of what nature are they? They are well-heated, having had their internal impurities purified by processes such as puṭapāka.
"Thoroughly polished" means cleansed with emery and other gems;
"well-washed" means its external impurities have been removed by rinsing with alkaline, acidic, and saline substances; and it is gold that has become such as this.
Its radiance means its luster; [the trees] are blazing like that, meaning they possess such luster.
And this has been described according to worldly convention;
however, there is no worldly analogy whatsoever for the splendor of the Tathāgata’s body.
Now he introduces the worship with garlands:

"Worship the most worshipful Lords of Sages with all fragrant and pleasing flowers, such as the *māndārava*, *indīvara*, and *mallikā*, and with garlands that are beautiful in their arrangement. (Bca 2.15)
The *māndārava* is a specific flower among the gods;
the *indīvaram* is the blue lotus (*utpala*);
and the *mallikā* is the jasmine (*vārṣikī*).
With all these and other such beautiful fragrances and captivating flowers, I worship the most venerable lords of sages;
and with garlands and wreaths, rendered lovely by their exquisite weaving and arrangement.
He speaks of the offering of incense:
"I thoroughly perfume them with clouds of incense, delightful with abundant and diffusing fragrances.
"Abundant" (sphīta) means thick or copious.
And with such clouds of incense— trembling, pervading the ends of the quarters, emitting abundant fragrance,
and possessing such scents—
as clouds of incense whose forms hang down from the surface of the sky.
The compound is formed according to the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.56);
it means "clouds of incense," by which [they are characterized].
The meaning is "rising like clouds";
"them" refers to those lords of sages (munīndras), whom I shall honor with incense.
Regarding the offering of food, he says:
"I present as an offering to them various kinds of foods to be enjoyed, foods to be chewed, and drinks. (Bca 2.16)
*Bhojya* is that which is eaten by filling the mouth;
*khādya* is that which is eaten in morsels; *chedya* is that which is cut, such as *dhṛtapūra* (fried cakes).
Whatever is to be drunk, such as beverages and the like,
prepared in these various and manifold ways—
I offer them, having presented them, to those Lords of Sages.
He speaks of the lamp offering:
"I present rows of jewel lamps set within golden lotuses;
upon the mosaic floors smeared with perfumes, I scatter pleasing heaps of flowers. (Bca 2.17)
Those lamps made of jewels;
those whose rows and garlands are arranged [therein] are such. Where? Upon golden lotuses.
The compound is justified because it conveys meaning despite being dependent [on external factors].
"Smeared with fragrance" means anointed with the scents of sandalwood, saffron, and so forth.

I offer to those whose nature is loving-kindness clouds of celestial palaces, which shine with the splendor of long, dangling strings of pearls and gems, which adorn the face of every direction, and which are delightful with songs of praise.
Those celestial cloud-masses, which are collections of palaces, possess beauty through long hanging strings of pearl necklaces; they provide illumination and bring splendor to all directions.
I shall hold aloft the most beautiful jeweled parasols of the great sages— exquisitely formed with golden handles and adorned with closely set pearls.
The parasols, made of jewels and inlaid with pearls, were raised high upon beautiful golden staffs. "Samucchritāni" means they were held aloft on their poles.

Now, concluding the offering of worship, he says: "From this point forward, let there arise delightful clouds of worship, and clouds of the music of cymbals and song that bring joy to all sentient beings. (Bca 2.20)
From this moment forth, may these clouds of offerings presented by me,
or those brought forth by gods and others, remain for an eon or the remainder of an eon, and may they abide in a state of supreme excellence.
And as for the clouds of musical performance, "tūryas" refers to musical instruments such as drums and the like.
*Saṃgītayaḥ* means songs sung together;
that is to say, collective songs.
Alternatively:
Ensembles of music—consisting of instrumental and vocal performances performed in concert—are what is meant by "assemblies.
Their clouds are multitudes of such groups;
and they bring joy to all sentient beings, producing delight for all living creatures.
Furthermore, they are not impossible to hear;
the connection [of the sentence] is "let them be established."
Summarizing in general, he speaks of the worship toward the true Dharma and so forth:
"May showers of flowers, jewels, and other offerings fall continuously upon all the jewels of the true Dharma, upon the shrines, and upon the images. (Bca 2.21)
Among all the jewels of the true Dharma consisting of the twelvefold scriptural teachings,
it is like a jewel because it illuminates the reality of things and because it is the cause of supreme nirvana.
Upon the stupas, the shrines of the Blessed One, and the images— that is, the representations of the forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
there were showers of flowers and showers of jewels.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), showers of sandalwood powder, garments, and so forth are meant.
"Uninterruptedly" (nirantaram) means without cessation throughout the duration of saṃsāra.

(Bcp 28) Extending this to the unsurpassed worship, he says: "Just as Mañjughoṣa and the others worship the Victors, so do I worship the Tathāgatas, the Protectors, together with their Sons. (Bca 2.22)

Just as the Bodhisattvas who are lords of the ten stages— headed by Mañjughoṣa, Samantabhadra, and Ajitalokanātha— worship the Tathāgatas with such a resolute intention (adhyāśaya) and through such a conviction (adhimokṣa), so too do I worship the Tathāgatas together with their sons, the hosts of Bodhisattvas.
Regarding praise and worship, he says:
"I praise those oceans of virtues with hymns that are like oceans of vocal qualities and limbs;
and may clouds of melodic praise arise from them, never otherwise. (Bca 2.23)
The seven notes are Gāndhāra and the others;
their limbs or subdivisions are Kāmōda and the rest.
Because of their extreme abundance, like the ocean, they are called "oceans" (sāgara).
By those hymns;
"hymns" (stuti) themselves are "chants" (saṃgīti), or rather, "chants" are the collections (samudāya) of hymns.
May clouds arise for them and attend upon these Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
"not otherwise" means that they shall be exactly as I have envisioned, without error.
Regarding the prostration and worship to the Jewels of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, he says:
"With prostrations as numerous as the atoms in all fields, I bow down to all the Buddhas of the three times, together with the supreme assembly of their Dharma. (Bca 2.24)
With as many prostrations as there are atoms in all the Buddha-fields throughout the ten directions.

"Those belonging to all three times" refers to the Tathāgatas of the past, present, and future. Of what nature are they? "Together with the Dharma and the supreme assembly": the assembly that is supreme among assemblies is the assembly of Bodhisattvas; [they are together] with both the Dharma and that supreme assembly.

Regarding prostration at the stūpas of the Tathāgatas, he says: "I pay homage to all caityas, as well as those which are the abodes of Bodhisattvas; I offer salutations to my preceptors and likewise to the ascetics who are worthy of veneration. (Bca 2.25)
The meaning is: "I prostrate to the stūpas, both those containing a body and those without a body, in the upward, horizontal, and downward directions, as well as in the intermediate directions.
Furthermore, the phrase "also to the bases of the Bodhisattvas" refers to the places of his births and so forth, such as those described in the Jātakas and Avadānas.
"Those worthy of salutation" refers to the elders who are deserving of homage;
by this, the procedure for worship and salutation has been stated.
And this procedure for worship was taught in the *Trisamayarāja*, as it has been said: "There are jewel-mountains born of the land;
there are jewel-mountains born of the water."
It is said that gems produced on land and in water, situated in the ten directions, which are without the sense of "mine" and unappropriated, are to be given as gifts.
And in this same manner, all medicinal herbs, all elixirs, all waters,
all faultless circles,
and all golden circles [are to be understood].
Or, in world-systems that have unfolded, there are layers of earth-essence endowed with the touch of supreme flavor and immortal creepers;
there are rice grains that grow without being sown or ploughed;
and there are delightful objects of enjoyment in all the Uttarakuru continents and in purified world-systems.
As it is said in the *Āryaratnamegha*: "Whatever sublime offerings and services he hears of in the sūtras,
those he [performs] with an intense, resolute intention."
He dedicates [the merit] to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
in that way, he reflects upon various kinds of worship and service.
Now, preceded by going for refuge to the Three Jewels, he speaks of the confession of misdeeds:
I go for refuge to the Buddha until I reach the seat of enlightenment;
I go for refuge to the Dharma and likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas. (Bca 2.26)
For the purpose of protection and for the purpose of refuge, "going" means the fulfillment of that [refugee's] command; for whoever goes for refuge to someone, [that person is their protector].
The meaning is that he does not transgress that command.
Regarding the phrase "from the seat of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍata*):
this word *maṇḍa* signifies the essence (*sāra*).
It is just as with the phrase "the cream of ghee.
And that being so, it means: "until [I have] made awakening my primary goal," up to "as long as I do not attain perfect complete enlightenment."
With palms joined in reverence, I make this request to the Perfectly Awakened Ones who dwell in all directions, and also to the Bodhisattvas of great compassion.
By the phrase "I inform," it is shown that one should speak this with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), having visualized oneself standing before the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"With palms joined" refers to a bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*); the meaning is that one has formed a hollowed cup with both hands.
In this beginningless saṃsāra, or even in this very life,
whatever evil I have committed or caused to be committed while like a beast;
And whatever I have rejoiced in for the sake of my own destruction out of delusion, I confess that transgression, tormented by remorse.
"Beginningless" refers to the succession of previous births;
"in this very birth" means even in this present life, not only in former ones.
"By means of an animal" indicates the abundance of delusion within oneself.
"Threefold action" refers to that performed by body, speech, and mind; therein, it was also caused to be done by all three.
"Consented to by speech and mind" means that because the fruit of that sinful karma ripens within myself for the sake of my own destruction,
"its transgression" refers to that downfall.
I teach, I reveal, I make clear,
and I do not conceal;
[this is said] regarding remorse, because one hears that unwholesome karma results in the ripening of suffering in the hells and other realms.
Now, he states the confession of transgressions according to their relative importance:
"Whatever harm to the Three Jewels, or toward my mother and father, or toward other gurus, has been committed by me through the impetuosity of body, speech, or mind," (Bca 2.30).
"In the Three Jewels" refers to the field of unsurpassed qualities;
"mother," and so forth, refers to the field of benefactors,
because harm done toward them results in the ripening of extensive and intense suffering.
O Leaders, whatever terrible sin has been committed by me, a wicked person defiled by manifold faults, all of that I confess.
"Corrupted by manifold defects" means defiled by afflictions such as passion and so forth;
the meaning is that it is not independent.
And how may I escape from this, O Leaders? I am constantly filled with anxiety:
"May death not come upon me before my accumulation of evil has been exhausted. (Bca 2.32)
(Bcp 30) Regarding the agitation over evil karma, he says: "And how shall I escape from this? Save me quickly!
"How" means by what manner or method.
"From this impurity;
quickly, that is, swiftly.
To the question, "What is this haste of yours? he says:
May death not come too soon for me while my sins remain undestroyed.
"As long as I do not bring about the destruction of my evil deeds, death will not come to me;
otherwise, there would be the fear of falling into an evil rebirth."
But surely, for one who has not exhausted their accumulated sins, what opportunity is there for death? To this he says:
This death, which destroys all trust, does not examine what has been done or left undone; it cannot be relied upon by the healthy or the sick alike, like a sudden, great thunderbolt. (Bca 2.34)
Death does not examine whether "this has been done" or "this has not yet been done.
Trust is confidence;
by means of that [trust], it is a slayer.
Nor is it to be trusted that one is free from disease, young, or possesses a strong body;
why? Because it is like a sudden great thunderbolt, resembling the unexpected fall of a vajra.
If there is fear of evil in this way, for what purpose then was it committed? To this he says:
"For the sake of the pleasant and the unpleasant, evil has been committed in many ways."
It has not been understood that one must depart, leaving everything behind.
That which is dear consists of oneself and one's own possessions, while that which is not dear consists of those who cause harm to them.

By one desiring benefit and happiness for the dear and the opposite for the not dear, evil has been committed in many ways, through various types such as the taking of life, taking what is not given, and so forth.
Now, one might object: "Since all of this must be abandoned and departed from before long, why is this useless and sinful accumulation being pursued? To this he says, "All," and so forth.
One must go, having cast off and left behind everything, whether pleasant or unpleasant.
But this was not reflected upon by me, being deluded.
Those who are unpleasant will not exist; those who are dear to me will not exist;
I myself will not exist, and everything will not exist.
"What remains now? To this he says:
"Whatever object is experienced becomes a mere memory;
like everything experienced in a dream, once gone, it is no longer seen. (Bca 2.37)
"Whatever object"—whether it be a cause of pleasure or a cause of suffering—is "experienced," that is, perceived.
How is this so? He says: "like what is experienced in a dream."
Just as that which is perceived in the state of dream, once destroyed, is not seen again,
there remains only the memory thereof.
Likewise, demonstrating that everything else associated with loved ones and so forth is unstable even within this very life, he says:
"Even while remaining right here, many loved ones and those not loved have already passed away;
yet the terrible evil committed for their sake remains standing before you. (Bca 2.38)
(Bcp 31) While I remain standing, or even while I am merely sitting and watching, they have gone, swallowed up by impermanence.
If this is so, then the evil committed for their sake will also go along with them; thus he says: "For that purpose," and so forth.
The evil committed for the sake of, or on account of, those [objects] such as beloved ones—that remains standing right before me;
the meaning is that it will go along with me.
One might ask: "Even though you see this, why have you fainted? To this he says:
"I did not reflect that I am merely a guest;
thus, through delusion, attachment, and aversion, I have committed manifold sins. (Bca 2.39)
"I do not belong to anyone,
nor does anyone belong to me"— thus have I neither examined nor investigated.
For that reason,
attachment is clinging to the self and what belongs to the self;
aversion is hostility.
He acts in opposition to that.
Since you possess such exceedingly long life, what cause for fear of death could there be?
To the question, "Why then do you fear thus? he replies:
"The expenditure of life increases day and night without respite."
There is no arrival of life, yet I shall not die; what indeed am I? (Bca 2.40)
Day and night, the expenditure of life increases and the formative forces of life (āyuḥ-saṃskāra) are consumed;
"without rest" means there is not even a single moment when this expenditure ceases.
"Āgama" means arrival or entry; yet not even a trace of such an increase or accumulation is found there. Therefore, why should I not die?
For even if life persists for a long time, it ends in death."
It might be argued: "Those for whose sake you have committed evil will not share in the experience of the suffering that is its fruit when you are in hell and other such realms;
so why do you resort to such despondency? To this, he says:
"Let alone the next world..."
Even here, while lying on my bed and standing in the midst of my kinsmen,
I alone must endure the agonies of the severing of my vital organs and other such pains.
In this very life, even while amidst one's own kinsmen and attendants during the affliction of suffering at the end of death and so forth—
such as the sensation of the cutting of the vital organs, the pain of thirst, and the burning of the limbs— all of that must be endured by me alone;
not even the slightest portion of it can belong to another.
How much more so, then, in the case of hell and other such realms? He says:
"For one seized by the messengers of Yama, where is the kinsman? Where is the friend? At that time, merit alone is protection; yet that was not cultivated by me. (Bca 2.42)

For one seized by the messengers of Death, held fast, bound with a noose around the neck, beaten with mallets, his feet pierced by thorns and jagged fragments of stone in the dense thickets of the forest wilderness, and led helpless to the ground where his karma is experienced—whence comes a kinsman? Whence a friend? No companions whatsoever can provide protection there.
At that time, merit alone would be the protection;
yet I did not cultivate it, and I did not acquire that merit which serves as a refuge.

(Bcp 32) Again, he speaks of the agitation regarding evil: "O Protectors, because of my attachment to this impermanent life, and not knowing this danger, I, being heedless, have accumulated much evil. (Bca 2.43)
While life is transient,
through attachment and grasping,
one fails to know and fails to see this impending fear of suffering in the hells and other realms.
"By one who is heedless" means by one intoxicated with the pride of youth, beauty, wealth, sovereignty, and so forth.
Why then do you remain so full of worldly attachment? To this he says:

"Even if one were being led away today for the purpose of having one's limbs severed, one becomes parched with thirst; with a wretched gaze, one looks upon the world as something entirely different. (Bca 2.44)
This suffering of having one's hands, feet, and so forth cut off is very slight compared to the suffering of hell;
nevertheless, even there, such a state occurs:
one withers away entirely and undergoes total desiccation.
"Thirsty" means afflicted by thirst.
"With a wretched look" means with a miserable look.
"Quite another" means contrary.

He describes the intensity of the suffering in hell: "How much more so when one is presided over by the terrifying forms of Yama’s messengers, seized by the fever of great terror, and overwhelmed by the discharge of excrement? (Bca 2.45)
With timid glances, seeking protection in the four directions;
"of terrifying aspect" means having a fearsome form;
"presided over" means taken under one's own power.
He was seized and gripped by a fever of great terror;
"purīṣa" means excrement,
and its "utsarga" is the discharge or emission thereof.
Enveloped and smeared by that, he was distressed; "by the wretched" means by those who were miserable;
he searched for protection in the four directions.
To the question "How so?", he says:
"Who will be my virtuous protector from this great fear? (Bca 2.46)
He is the virtuous one, affectionate without cause;
he is the refuge and the protector.
Seeing all directions devoid of protection, I shall again fall into utter confusion;
what then shall I do in that place of great terror?
Even so, when one perceives no refuge anywhere at all, then, due to the absence of refuge, one falls once more into delusion;
what shall I do at that time?
Being incapable of all activities,
he remains in that place, on the ground of the Pratāpana and other hells.

Therefore, it is appropriate to practice the remedy right now; thus he says: "Even today, I go for refuge to the Jinas, the Lords of the World, who possess great power, who are intent upon protecting the world, and who remove all fear. (Bca 2.48)
The lords of the worlds, who have become the source of all consolation and peace;

the leaders, who possess great strength—that is, whose power is everywhere unimpeded; and those who are intent upon protecting the world—that is, who are dedicated to the rescue and protection of all sentient beings.

Even so, if there were no cessation of fear without relying on a protector, then what would be the point of going for refuge? To this he says: "who remove all terror," meaning those who take away all calamities.
Regarding the going for refuge to the Dharma and the Saṅgha, he says:
"I go for refuge with my whole being to the Dharma realized by them, which destroys the fear of cyclic existence, and likewise to the assembly of Bodhisattvas. (Bca 2.49)
By those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
"attained" means realized directly;
"dharma" means Nirvana.

It destroys the fear of saṃsāra because it is the antidote to all afflictions. "With devotion" means with supreme faith, not with deceit, hypocrisy, or doubt. "The host of bodhisattvas" refers to the Saṅgha.
"Thus it is," with such an attitude.
Now, offering himself to the Bodhisattvas according to their preeminence, he says:
"Overwhelmed by fear, I give myself to Samantabhadra;
and again, I give myself to Mañjughoṣa by my own self. (Bca 2.50)
To the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra,
I give myself; I offer myself up,
being overwhelmed by fear and agitated by the terrors of hell and the other realms.
Furthermore, "to Mañjughoṣa" means to Mañjunātha; "by oneself" means not by the instigation of another, but with a mind that is spontaneously serene.
And to that Lord Avalokita, whose conduct is agitated by compassion, I cry out with a piteous voice in my fear; may he protect me, a sinner.
To Āryāvalokiteśvara—whose conduct and character are agitated by compassion, thus he is "one whose conduct is agitated by compassion"—this is his very qualification. I cry out; I raise a cry.
"Artaravam" is an adverbial modifier meaning "with a voice distressed by suffering, wretched, and timid"; "bhītaḥ" means "terrified," [specifically] terrified of the fruit of evil karma.
May that Blessed One Avalokita protect me, a sinner; may he deliver me, who have committed evil deeds.
Seeking protection, I call out with sincerity to the noble Ākāśagarbha and Kṣitigarbha, and to all those who possess great compassion.
And the noble Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha,
and the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha; this is to be connected with the subsequent phrase "I cry out."
And all those of great compassion, even those not mentioned by name— those supremely merciful ones who suffer with the suffering of others.
I pay homage to that Vajrin, at the mere sight of whom the wicked messengers of Yama and others flee in terror in the four directions.
By the mere sight of whom the messengers of Yama and others—
the word "others" including yakṣas, rākṣasas, and other malevolent beings— becoming terrified, flee and depart to a great distance.
I bow to him; I pay homage to him.
"Vajrin" refers to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi, so called because he possesses a vajra (*vajram asyāsti*).
Thus, by means of this taking of refuge and so forth, the power of reliance (*āśrayabala*) is demonstrated for the purpose of exhausting evil deeds.
As it is said in the *Caturdharmaka-sūtra* (Bcp 34):

"In that regard, the power of the basis (*āśrayabala*) consists of going for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, and not abandoning the bodhicitta. By means of this powerful support, one cannot be overcome by evil."
Furthermore, in order to dispel any suspicion of changeability, he says:
"Having transgressed your command, I now seek refuge in you out of fear; being terrified, quickly destroy my fear! (Bca 2.54)
Having transgressed your command;
now, at this very moment;
because of seeing [this] danger.
Because it is observed that undesirable consequences arise from its transgression,
I, being afraid— terrified of those undesirable consequences— go to you for refuge;
therefore, you should not entertain any further doubts to the contrary.
Therefore, fear is not for those who have perished; dispel the fear arising from previously committed sins—
swiftly, that is, quickly.
The word "mine" (mama) is to be supplied [as an ellipsis].
One might object: "Even so, who will believe this?
Anticipating this doubt, he speaks again to establish firmness in this matter:
"Even one terrified by a fleeting illness should not disregard the physician's word."
How much more so when one is seized by the four hundred and four types of diseases?
"Transitory" (itvara) means that which goes away, perishes, or does not remain for long; or it means "light.
And that [is] this very disease.
Therefore, out of fear, one should not transgress the physician’s word; one should not overstep the physician’s instruction,
lest this disease of mine should increase.
"How much more so," that is to say, "how much less" [could one overcome it]?
"Seized by hundreds of diseases" means one would have to leap over four hundred and four— that is, four hundred with four added— diseases.
There are one hundred untimely deaths and one timely death, making one hundred and one types of death in total.
Each of these is further divided into those caused by wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), phlegm (*śleṣman*), and their combination (*saṃnipāta*), resulting in four hundred and four varieties.
Thus, from the difference in causes arises the difference in effects, and from the difference in effects follows the determination of the difference in causes.
One might ask: "Even so, what is the cause for fear here, since [the disease] does not exist? To this he says:
"For by even one of these, all the people dwelling in Jambudvīpa perish—those for whom no medicine can be found in any direction. (Bca 2.56)
For when even a single disease becomes aggravated, all living beings and humans dwelling in Jambudvīpa perish and die;
furthermore,
there are diseases for which no medicine, remedy, or treatment can be found anywhere.
In this regard, the Padmaka Jātaka of the King of Kāśi should be cited.
It is thus heard: while practicing the conduct of awakening, this very Blessed One was in a past age a king of Kāśi named Padma.
At that time, all the people of Jambudvīpa were overwhelmed by a great disease and were dying.
They reflected thus: "This very lord of ours, the King, who is supremely compassionate, will provide a remedy; let us report our own suffering to him.
Having thus resolved and gathered together, they said, "O Great King,"
"Even though our lord, who desires our supreme welfare, is still present, we have reached this state"—thus they manifested their suffering before the king.
And that king, his heart overcome by compassion and unable to endure their distress, commanded the physicians: "Quickly remove these people's affliction of disease!"

Having promised "So be it," they too examined the medical treatises; finding no medicine other than the flesh of a fish that had just been caught and was still bleeding, they replied to the king exactly as before.
Such is the detailed account.
This very Jātaka demonstrates the characteristic of existence (bhava).
"In this matter, to think 'I shall transgress the word of the omniscient physician who removes all thorns'—fie upon me, utterly deluded! (Bca 2.57)
Having extracted many physical and mental thorns,
he loathes himself, thinking,
"Shame on me, who have been utterly deluded!"
Even knowing this, if I were to practice in opposition to the command of the Tathāgata, then there would be no end to my delusion;
the meaning is that I would be contemptible.
Why is this so? He says: "I remain extremely vigilant even regarding other precipices;
how much more so regarding a precipice a thousand yojanas deep that lasts for a long time! (Bca 2.58)
In even very small precipices such as those of mountains, where there might be the mere breaking of bones or the suffering of death itself— how much more so in one measuring a thousand *yojanas*?
The suffix *aṇ* is used here because its measure (*parimāṇa*) is a thousand *yojanas*.
The meaning is: in a precipice such as the Avīci hell, which measures many thousands of yojanas;
"for a long time" means where the exhaustion of one's lifespan occurs through intermediate kalpas and so forth.
"Why do you abandon your comfort out of cowardice so prematurely, without even seeing death arrive? To this he says:
"Death does not come this very day; therefore, my comfort is not unjustified. Yet that hour will inevitably come when I shall no longer exist. (Bca 2.59)
"This is certainly determined as inevitable."
Nevertheless, he says that fear is inappropriate:
"Who has granted me freedom from fear? Or how shall I escape?
I shall certainly cease to exist; why then is my mind so well-composed? (Bca 2.60)
The intention is: "By which noble person has fearlessness been granted to me, saying 'Do not fear,' so that I may dwell without fear?
Or rather, even if there were a means of escape, nevertheless, fear would still be improper.
That too does not exist;
[one wonders], "How shall I escape from this suffering?
or "I shall certainly no longer exist."
"It has been said by the Blessed One that the end of all life is death."
He says that for this reason as well, my dwelling in ease is not appropriate:
"What essence remains to me from those things previously experienced and now lost, through which, by being attached, I have transgressed the words of my gurus? (Bca 2.61)
"By one who is attached" means by one who is clinging.
"Of the gurus" refers to the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitras).
Therefore, he says that it is appropriate for me to keep this in mind day and night:
"Having abandoned this world of living beings, as well as my kinsmen and acquaintances, I shall go somewhere all alone; what use have I for all these things, pleasant or unpleasant? (Bca 2.62)
The world of living beings (*jīvaloka*) is the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*), characterized by the commonality (*sabhāgatā*) of humans and so forth;
"alone" means without a companion.
"Somewhere" (*kvāpi*) refers to an unspecified location.
But this alone was my appropriate reflection day and night at that time:
"Since suffering is certain to arise from the unwholesome, how might I escape from it? (Bca 2.63)
"From the impure" means from unwholesome karma;
"from that" means from the impure.
Now, having reached the certainty that the fruits of actions are bound to one's own deeds, he begins once more to confess his transgressions with great earnestness, saying:
"Whatever evil I have accumulated as a foolish and deluded child—both that which is inherently blameworthy and that which is blameworthy by convention. (Bca 2.64)
Standing before the Protectors with palms joined, fearing suffering and prostrating again and again, I confess all of that.
May the leaders accept this transgression as a transgression:
[committed] by one who is childish, meaning ignorant;
by one who is deluded, meaning blinded by confusion.
"Whatever" refers to that which is committed by body, speech, or mind.

"Natural offenses" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are those whose nature consists of the ten unwholesome actions, such as taking life and so forth. "Proscribed offenses" (*prajñapti-sāvadya*) are those such as eating at improper times and so forth, which were proscribed by the Blessed One specifically for those who have taken vows.
"I shall teach" gives rise to a vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*);
"with palms joined" is a bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*);
and "having prostrated again and again" demonstrates an exceptional intensity of mental agitation (*cittasaṃvega*).
That by which one goes excessively into the hells and other realms is *atyaya*, namely, unwholesome karma.
May they accept it as such—that is, as a fault; may they recognize, perceive, understand, and discern it as it has been made manifest by me.
With an unobstructed mind;
the sense here is that "I have no concealment."
Furthermore, in order to dispel the apprehension of future lapses, he speaks while undertaking the restraint of non-repetition:
"O Protectors, this was not good; it must not be done by me again. (Bca 2.66)
That which is not beloved by the noble ones, nor praised by the wise, is called an unwholesome, censurable, and ignoble action.
From this day forward, knowing and seeing [this], I shall not perform it again intentionally or with deliberate thought;
the meaning is that I shall undertake the restraint of non-doing for the future.
And this will be made clear in the context of the exposition of the three aggregates [in Bodhicaryāvatāra 5.98–99].
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "Confession of Evil," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 37) Chapter Three, titled "The Embracing of the Thought of Enlightenment.
Now, immediately following the confession of misdeeds, he speaks of the rejoicing in merit:
I rejoice with great joy in all the merit performed by all sentient beings, which brings rest from the suffering of the lower realms; may those who are suffering dwell in happiness.

For those who, having experienced suffering in the realms of hell and so forth, become exhausted, attain the ripening of their good deeds and, having obtained happiness, rest for a short time; with a serene mind, I rejoice in them—that is, I gladden them with a clear heart. Furthermore, rejoicing is threefold: by means of the mind, the body, and speech.
There, with a serene mind, he gladdens it mentally;

experiencing with his body the bristling of hair, the shedding of tears, the trembling of limbs, and so forth, and with speech, his heart being thus delighted, he utters words of a corresponding nature.

The meaning is: "Well done! A good deed has been performed!"—that is, may that purpose for which they performed those actions, namely, "may those who are suffering find happiness," also be fulfilled for them.

Having rejoiced in worldly deeds, he, rejoicing in the supramundane, said: "I rejoice in the liberation of embodied beings from the suffering of saṃsāra; and I rejoice in the state of a bodhisattva and the state of a Buddha for the Protectors. (Bca 3.2)

"Liberation from suffering" refers to the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas or the enlightenment of the Pratyekabuddhas; or rather, it is said that way because the mind has been generated for that purpose. In that case, even the three types of enlightenment are included within that grasp.
"Of embodied beings" refers to living creatures.

"The state of being a bodhisattva and the state of being a Buddha" means that the state of being a bodhisattva is the causal stage of the Blessed Ones, while the state of being a Buddha is the resultant stage.
"Tāyinām" refers to those who teach the path they have themselves realized.
As it has been said: "Tāya is the proclamation of the path seen by oneself. [The term refers to those] in whom that [quality] exists.
Alternatively, *tāya* has the meaning of "continuity" for those who abide in non-abiding nirvana as long as saṃsāra endures.
Rejoicing in the merit of the Bodhisattvas, he says:
"I rejoice in the oceans of the generation of the thought of enlightenment, which bring happiness to all sentient beings and establish the welfare of all beings, belonging to the Teachers. (Bca 3.3)
The productions of the thought of awakening (*cittotpāda*), which arise at every moment, are like oceans because they are limitless and unfathomable; [the text says] "those [oceans].
Of what nature are they? They bring happiness to all sentient beings, meaning that their very essence is inclined solely toward that flavor (*rasa*) of bringing happiness to all sentient beings.
[The phrase] "bestowing benefit upon all sentient beings" means those who provide welfare.

Regarding the term "śāsinām": *śāsa* means teaching (*śāsana*), which is the practice of the means to Buddhahood; they are called *śāsins* (teachers) metaphorically because they possess that [practice] as their purpose. for Bodhisattvas, having gathered sentient beings through the means of attraction such as generosity and so forth, lead them onto the true path.

Now, speaking of the request, he says: "With palms joined in reverence, I entreat all the Perfectly Awakened Ones in every direction."

Demonstrating the act of entreating, he says:
"With palms joined in reverence, I entreat the Victors who desire to enter nirvāṇa."
May they remain for infinite eons; let this world not be blind.
To him who, having accomplished what was to be done, intends to enter final nirvana,
I pray that he remain for boundless eons;
let it not be as before— that there be blindness, meaning a lack of discernment regarding the knowledge of the path.

Immediately following the request for prayers, he now speaks of the dedication of merit:
"Having thus performed all this, whatever virtue I have acquired, by that may I become the pacifier of all the sufferings of all sentient beings. (Bca 3.6)

I shall dispel it and turn back [the danger] by raining down food and drink— that is, by providing a continuous supply of food and drink.

the aeon concludes through weapons, disease, and famine. Thus it is said.

seven months, and seven days. As it is said:
The eon concludes through weapons, disease, and famine,
lasting for seven days, seven months, and seven years respectively.
Thus it is said.
Therein, due to the absence of food and drink, their only sustenance is the eating of each other's flesh and bones.

In that place, may I become food and drink.
May I become an inexhaustible treasure for sentient beings who are poor,
and may I appear before them in the form of various useful articles.
"For the poor" means for those lacking wealth.
"Inexhaustible" means that which does not diminish even when its wealth is being drawn out.
"In the forms of various implements" refers to whatever sentient beings desire, such as beds, seats, clothing, food, ornaments, ointments, and so forth.
"In whatever various forms of excellent requisites, may I myself attend upon them,
being present before those poor beings.
And this dedication has been explained in detail in the noble Vajradhvaja Sūtra.
In this regard, it is said:
while dedicating those roots of merit, he dedicates them in this way: "By this root of merit, may I become a shelter for all sentient beings by turning back the entire mass of suffering;

May I become a refuge for all sentient beings by protecting them from all fears; may I become a destination for all sentient beings by following along through all stages; may I become the ultimate resort for all sentient beings by bringing about the attainment of absolute security.

"May I become a light for all sentient beings by means of demonstrating knowledge free from darkness; may I become a torch for all sentient beings by means of dispelling the blinding darkness of ignorance," and so forth, in detail.
Having said this, he spoke further: "In that regard, one dedicates through resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), not by mere words;
and one dedicates with an uplifted mind, one dedicates with a joyful mind."
With a serene mind, he dedicates;
with a joyful mind and a tender mind, he dedicates;
with a mind of loving-kindness, a mind of affection, a mind of favor, a mind of benefit, and a mind of happiness, he dedicates.
Thus is the detailed explanation.

"Self-existences" (*ātmabhāvān*) refers to all bodies throughout the deaths and rebirths in all realms of existence.

"Whatever wholesome productions of the thought arise, I shall dedicate them toward unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment. This is skillfulness regarding the future.

Having fulfilled the resolute conviction in the relinquishment of everything, through the force of the mind of renunciation and by means of that physical application, he has abandoned all grasping.
Being liberated from the suffering of existence, which is rooted in all grasping, he is called "liberated."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
(Bcp 40) But is it not proper to preserve at least something for one's own sake? To dispel such stinginess, he says:

The nirvāṇa of all things, including the contaminated personal existence and so forth, is liberation;
my mind seeks that, and my consciousness seeks that.

if at the time of nirvāṇa I must necessarily depart having relinquished my entire personal existence and so forth, then it would be better to give it away to sentient beings.

Everything has been surrendered by me to them in every respect; why should I concern myself with whether it is fair or unfair?
Let them perform blameless actions. This is precisely what he says:
May no one ever suffer misfortune by taking me as their refuge.
May nothing undesirable ever happen to any living being by depending on me, whether in this world or in the next.
For those whose minds become either angry or pleased by taking me as their object,

For those whose intellect or mind is angry or not serene,

The masculine gender of that word [sarvārthasiddhi] is due to its coreferentiality with its cause;

Those who slander me, as well as others who do me harm, and even those who mock me—
may they all partake in enlightenment.
"They will slander" means they will defame by falsely imputing faults;
"others also who will cause harm, whether physical or mental";
"mockers" means those who ridicule.
Or those who act as mockers;
likewise, others who are indifferent or even hostile—
may they all become attainers of Buddhahood.
I am the protector of the protectorless, the caravan leader for those traveling on the road,
and for those desiring to reach the further shore, I am the boat, the bridge, and the causeway.
"Of the helpless" means those seeking sacrificial offerings (*sāṃnāyya*).
"And the caravan leader for those traveling" means the chief of the caravan for those who have set out on the road.
"For those desiring to reach the further shore" means those wishing to go to the opposite bank of rivers and so forth.
May I be a lamp for those who seek a lamp; may I be a bed for those who seek a bed;

"For those seeking lamps" means for those situated in darkness.
"For those seeking beds" means for those desiring a place to lie down.
"For those seeking servants" refers to those who desire attendants, laborers, and so forth, for the sake of service.
May I become for embodied beings a wish-fulfilling gem, a jar of fortune, a perfected spell, a great medicinal herb, a wish-granting tree, and a cow of plenty. (Bca 3.19)

The *cintāmaṇi* is a particular kind of jewel that grants whatever fruit one has thought of. The *bhadraghaṭa* is such that if one places one's hand into it while intending whatever object one desires,
all of that is accomplished.
"Siddhavidyā" means one whose mantra is perfected; whatever rite is performed by her, all that succeeds.
"Mahauṣadhi" means that which, being singular, is the cause for pacifying all calamities and afflictions.
The *kalpavṛkṣa* is a specific kind of tree that fulfills imagined desires;
the *kāmadhenu* is that which yields whatever one wishes to milk.
The elements, such as earth and the rest, serve as the various kinds of enjoyments for immeasurable beings dwelling throughout the entirety of space. (Bca 3.20)
Thus, for the realm of sentient beings who abide in space, may I be their source of sustenance in manifold ways until all have attained nirvāṇa.
"Earth and so forth" refers to earth, which is the supporter of all things; by the word "and so forth," water, fire, and air are included—these being the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
These [elements] function, for instance, as the support for beds, seats, crops, fruits, roots, and so on.
Likewise, they serve as causes for crossing over [to the other shore], bathing, and so forth;
this should be applied similarly in other cases as well.
They become the objects of enjoyment for countless sentient beings who pervade the infinite realm of space.

In the very same way, may I also become an object of enjoyment for all sentient beings in manifold ways, until all have attained parinirvāṇa and until all are completely liberated from the sufferings of saṃsāra.
Therefore, one who seeks awakening must practice the relinquishment of these things, beginning with one's own person.
This generosity has been demonstrated in great detail in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
For example, it is stated in that very same work, the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*:
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva produces the perception of "belonging to others" regarding all phenomena and does not grasp at any entity whatsoever.
Why is that?
"For clinging is indeed fear.
Having said this, it was further stated in that very same place:
"Moreover, Śāriputra, Bodhisattvas are indeed courageous in mind."

To the extent that he becomes one who renounces his own hand, renounces his feet, renounces his nose, renounces his head, renounces his limbs and minor members, up to the point of renouncing all his possessions.

Thus it is said; moreover, O son of good family, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should generate this thought: "This body of mine has been surrendered and relinquished for the sake of all sentient beings, let alone external things.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Likewise, it is taught in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"I must exhaust this body in performing services for all sentient beings.

Just as these four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—[serve] through various pleasures, various means, various objects, various implements, and various enjoyments..."
Just as [these things] become the objects of enjoyment for sentient beings,

even so shall I make this body, a collection of the four great elements, a means of subsistence for all sentient beings in detail— through various pleasures, various methods, various objects, various requisites, and various enjoyments; such is the detailed explanation.
All of this that has preceded, beginning with that jewel of the mind, should be understood as the preliminary practice for undertaking the vow of bodhicitta.

Thus, having performed the worship and so forth, and having relinquished the gift of one's own person and so on, one who has realized the benefits of having undertaken bodhicitta— recognizing the excellence of this moment as supremely difficult to find— firmly establishes faith as the root and, feeling compassion for sentient beings who are without protection or refuge, [proceeds].

Indifferent to one's own happiness and pained by the suffering of others, with the intention and resolve to eradicate it, perceiving that Buddhahood alone is the means for that end, one binds on the armor for it— since neither fear nor suffering is dear to oneself or to others.
What distinction is there for oneself such that one protects this [self] and not another?
Thus:
by one who desires to bring an end to suffering for oneself and for the realm of sentient beings, and who wishes to reach the ultimate limit of happiness.
Having made firm the root of faith, one should make the mind steadfast in enlightenment.
Thus, [Śikṣāsamuccaya-kārikā 2],
he begins to generate the mind of perfect enlightenment:
"Just as the mind of enlightenment was previously taken up by the Sugatas of old..."
They remain established in the training of a bodhisattva according to the proper sequence.
With whatever intention [it is generated], namely for the sake of abandoning all the sufferings of all sentient beings;
or rather, the Blessed Ones know it exactly as it was taken up.
Regarding "bodhicitta": *bodhi* is buddhahood, which is the realization of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena through the abandonment of all obscurations.
And we shall explain this, along with its accumulation, in the section on wisdom (*prajñāpariccheda*).

In that context, "mind" refers to the mental attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) for the sake of attaining it; the meaning is: "May I become a Buddha in order to accomplish the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings."

Having thus established the generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicittotpāda*) with the first half [of the verse], he speaks—beginning with "Those bodhisattvas," etc.—to establish the undertaking of the vows of training (*śikṣāsaṃvara*).
The meaning is: "In that regard," namely, that which must always be performed by a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening, which is the training of a bodhisattva.
"Successive order" means following in sequence...
(Bcp 43) Just as he did, so shall I generate the spirit of enlightenment for the welfare of the world;
and just as he did, I shall train myself in those precepts in due order. (Bca 3.23)
Having thus taken up the thought of awakening with serene faith, the wise one should further gladden the mind in this way for the sake of increasing what has already been nourished. (Bca 3.24)
Today my birth has become fruitful; I have well attained this human state.
Today I am born into the family of the Buddhas; I am now truly a son of the Buddha.

Just as a blind man might find a jewel among heaps of refuse,

it is an inexhaustible treasure that pacifies the world's poverty.

it is the tree of rest for the world weary from wandering on the path of existence.
The moon of the mind has arisen as a common bridge for all travelers to cross over the miserable realms, and as a pacifier of the afflictions of the world.

it has arisen as the fresh butter produced from churning the milk of the sublime Dharma.
For this caravan of people traveling on the path of existence, who are hungry for the enjoyment of happiness,

Today I have invited the world to the state of a Sugata and to happiness in the interim;
indeed, before all the Protectors, may the gods, asuras, and others rejoice!
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Embracing of the Awakening Mind," in the *Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 44) Chapter Four: Heedfulness Regarding the Awakening Mind.
Having thus firmly grasped the awakening mind, the son of the Conquerors—
One should always strive, without indolence, to avoid transgressing the training.
Even regarding that which was undertaken impulsively or that which was not properly deliberated upon, it is appropriate to make a vow, thinking, "I shall or shall not do this. (Bca 4.2)
That which has been investigated by the Buddhas and their sons of great wisdom—why should I hesitate to do the same therein according to my ability? (Bca 4.3)
And if, having made such a vow, I were not to accomplish it through action,
what would be my destiny after deceiving all these beings?
It is said that even for a person who, after having thought of something in their mind, does not give it away—even if the object is of little value—that person becomes a preta. Bca_4.5.
What will become of my destiny if, having loudly proclaimed with sincere devotion the unsurpassed happiness, I have deceived the entire world?
Only the Omniscient One knows this inconceivable course of action,
whereby even by relinquishing the thought of enlightenment, he nonetheless liberates those people.
For a bodhisattva, every transgression is thus particularly grave,
because by committing it, he causes the ruin of the welfare of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, for anyone else who creates even a moment's obstacle to his merit—
that destroyer of the welfare of sentient beings— there is no end to his miserable rebirths.
For by destroying the welfare of even a single sentient being, one is destroyed;
how much more so for all embodied beings dwelling as far as the limits of space!
Thus, wavering in saṃsāra due to the power of transgressions and the power of the thought of awakening, one is delayed in attaining the [bodhisattva] stages.
Therefore, I must respectfully accomplish what I have vowed;
if I do not exert effort today, I shall go from the depths to the very depths.
Immeasurable Buddhas, seeking the welfare of all sentient beings, have passed away;
yet, through my own fault, I have not come within the range of their healing power.
If even now I were to remain just as I am, I would repeatedly encounter the miseries of miserable rebirths, disease, death, cutting, and breaking.
When shall I obtain the arising of a Tathāgata, faith, and human birth itself, as well as the fitness for practicing virtue—all of which are so exceedingly difficult to find? (Bca 4.15)
This day is healthy, provided with food, and free from calamity;
yet this moment of life is deceptive, like a jar filled with poison. (Bca 4.16)
Indeed, by such conduct as mine, human birth will not be obtained again;
and when human birth is not obtained, how can there be virtue, since only evil prevails?
When, though worthy of virtue, I do not practice virtue,
being utterly deluded by the sufferings of the miserable realms, what shall I do then?
For one who performs no wholesome deed and instead accumulates evil,
even the very word "happy rebirth" is lost for hundreds of millions of eons.

For a sin committed in a single moment, one dwells in Avīci for an eon;

And he is not liberated merely by experiencing that [suffering];
therefore, while experiencing it, he produces yet another evil.
There is no greater deception than this, nor any greater delusion, that having obtained such a moment as this, I have not practiced virtue. (Bca 4.23)
If, however, I reflect in this way and again sink down, deluded,
I shall grieve for a long time once more, impelled by the messengers of Yama.
The unbearable fire of hell will burn my body for a long time;
the fire of remorse will burn my untrained mind for a long time.
Having somehow reached this ground of benefit so difficult to find,
even though I know it, shall I be led back once again to those very same hells?
In this matter, I have no volition, as if deluded by spells;
I do not know by whom I am bewildered, nor who dwells within me. (Bca 4.27)
The enemies of craving, hatred, and the like lack hands, feet, and other limbs;
they are neither brave nor wise. How is it that I have been enslaved by them? (Bca 4.28)
"Remaining well-established within my very own mind, they strike at me alone;
even then, I do not become angry—fie on this endurance of what is improper! (Bca 4.29)
Even if all the gods and humans were to become my enemies,

For even the very long lives of all other enemies do not equal such a duration as that of my enemies,

When cultivated in accordance with their nature, all things conduce to one's welfare;

Thus, while these constant and long-standing enemies— the sole cause for the production of a flood of calamities—

Having pledged to liberate the world, as far as the limits of space in the ten directions, from its afflictions,

unless it be toward such afflictions as are inherently bound up with the destruction of afflictions.
Let my entrails gush out at will, and let my head indeed fall;
I shall by no means bow down before the enemies that are the afflictions.
Even for an enemy who has been banished, there may still be the acquisition of a dwelling place in another land;
however, such is not the case for the enemy of the afflictions, for once he has regained his strength, he returns. (Bca 4.45)
(Bcp 47) This is not [the case] with the enemy that is the affliction (*kleśa*).
Its conduct is not seen to be like that of other enemies.
To the question, "How then can this be obtained by will? he says:

Where could that [affliction] go, residing as it does within my own mind, once it has been cast out? For where could it stay and strive for my destruction? O dull-witted one, this is not merely a matter of effort for me; those wretched afflictions are to be overcome by wisdom and right view.
Where could this enemy, the affliction, go after being expelled from my mind and take up residence, such that, having established itself there, it might strive for my destruction?
I do not perceive any such place at all.
The sense is that once it has been uprooted, its resurgence is impossible;
however, I alone am lacking in resolve because my mental faculties are not sharp.
Furthermore, O ascetic, these afflictions, being rootless, are to be abandoned solely by the vision of the reality of ultimate truth.
Establishing this very point, he says:
"The afflictions do not reside in objects, nor in the collection of sense faculties, nor in between; nor do they exist elsewhere. Where, then, do these reside that they churn up the entire world?"

Even when viewing objects such as the pleasant and so forth, afflictions do not arise for some whose sense faculties are restrained; furthermore, even when analyzed down to the level of atoms, they are not perceived therein.
Thus, [the afflictions] do not reside in the objects, nor in the collection of sense faculties such as the eye, as previously explained.

Furthermore, they do not abide in the interval between the object and the sense faculty, because those [faculties] that are perceptible are simply not perceived even when the sense faculties are present during states such as reflection on the Dharma.
Nor are they determined to abide anywhere else apart from these;
therefore, being rootless and empty of reality, they are merely adventitious, because they are produced solely from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*).
Even though they are such as this, they churn the entire world;
and so, what is appropriate here? He says:
This is merely an illusion; therefore, release the terror from your heart and apply yourself to effort.
For the sake of wisdom, why do you needlessly torment yourself in the hells?

For just as a magical illusion (māyā), although empty of the form of an elephant, appears through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs as that very form by way of this-conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā*), even though it is devoid of reality by means of the mantra;

so too these afflictions (*kleśa*), having error as their cause and arising from improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), appear merely through the principle of dependence (*idaṃpratītyatāmātra*) while being entirely without reality.
Therefore, O heart, abandon your fear of the afflictions.
Who indeed are these wretched beings when examined from the perspective of ultimate reality?
Therefore, devote yourself to effort; exert enthusiasm for the sake of wisdom, in order to attain the discernment of reality.
"Why do you, having fallen under the power of the afflictions, needlessly and without purpose torment and oppress yourself in the hells, such as Saṃghāta and the rest?
Now, summarizing the entire previous subject matter, he says:
"Having thus resolved, I shall exert effort for the sake of practicing the training as it has been taught."
For one who deviates from the physician’s instruction, how can there be freedom from disease for that which is to be cured by medicine?
(Bcp 48) Having thus ascertained and firmly established the meaning set forth in all the preceding chapters, I shall now apply myself to the nature of illusion;
for what purpose? For the sake of practicing the training as it has been described.

It is for the purpose of training in those precepts of a bodhisattva which have been set forth as duties in various sūtras, or which have been briefly indicated here in this very treatise in their respective places.
And the training precepts for bodhisattvas have been taught by the Blessed One in the sūtras.
As it is said in the *Ārya-ratnamegha*:
"And how, noble son, does a bodhisattva become one who is restrained by the vow of bodhisattva training?"
In this regard, a bodhisattva reflects thus: "I cannot realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment by means of the mere Prātimokṣa restraint alone.
Rather, I must train myself in those bodhisattva modes of conduct and bodhisattva training precepts which have been prescribed by the Tathāgata in various sūtras."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
Therefore, for one of dull intellect such as myself,
the vow of the bodhisattva is difficult to understand because it has been explained in detail. What, then, is appropriate?
Therefore, one should know the vital points so that one may remain free from transgression.
And what are those vital points? Namely—

The relinquishing of one's person, enjoyments, and all merit accumulated throughout the three times for the sake of all sentient beings, as well as its protection, purification, and increase; this is [the perfection of giving].

Thus it has been said: "This is the compendium of the Bodhisattva, wherein even during the intervals between practices, transgressions are established. As it is stated in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣasūtra*:

If a path has been embraced by a bodhisattva for the sake of all sentient beings, leading to the exhaustion of suffering, and while that bodhisattva remains having embraced that path, even after the passing of ten million eons, not even a single thought of pleasure should arise— even, at the very least, a thought of sitting down [in rest].
In that regard, a bodhisattva should generate this thought: "Having taken upon myself the urgent needs of all sentient beings, it is much for me even that I sit down."
For this very reason, he says: "By the instruction of a physician.

Just as for a patient who does not follow the instructions of a physician—whether it be a task to be accomplished by medicine or a disease to be cured by medicine—how can there be freedom from illness or health?

Likewise, for one who does not practice the training prescribed by the Great Physician, the Omniscient One, how can there be freedom from illness—the liberation from the great terror of the sufferings of birth and so forth, produced by karma and mental afflictions?

Thus, the general characteristic of an offense for one who has undertaken the vows is stated; by means of this characteristic of an offense, one should personally discern and avoid whatever object is endowed with it, and one should not be confused regarding those things that resemble offenses or those that resemble non-offenses.

A bodhisattva, for the sake of pacifying all present and future suffering and mental distress of all sentient beings, and for the sake of producing all present and future happiness and mental well-being, acts through his efforts of body, speech, and mind without guile.
He makes no effort,
does not seek out the collection of conditions for that [attainment], and does not strive to counteract its obstacles.

One does not produce even a small amount of suffering or mental distress that serves as a remedy for great suffering and mental distress; nor does one inflict even a slight loss for the sake of accomplishing a great purpose; nor does one remain indifferent for even a moment.
One becomes guilty of an offense;
in brief, there is no offense regarding tasks that lie beyond one's own capacity, because since they are fruitless in such cases, there is no prescription of training for them.
Or rather, another [type of transgression] is indeed understood as being inherently reprehensible (*prakṛtisāvadya*).
However, that case where an offense might occur through the power of yoga even when it is beyond the scope of one's own capacity need not be considered.
Liberation from that [fault] occurs because it is included within the general confession of misdeeds.
This, in brief, is the essence of the bodhisattva training;
however, in detail, it would require an exposition lasting until the end of immeasurable eons.
Alternatively, in brief, there are two types of transgressions for a bodhisattva:
undertaking an action without considering whether it is appropriate or inappropriate according to one's capacity,
and neither withdrawing from it nor remaining indifferent toward it.
He becomes guilty of an offense;
having deliberated, he transgresses what is appropriate even when exhorted by a caṇḍāla slave,
he becomes guilty of an offense.

Furthermore, whoever desires to master this for the sake of practice should apply themselves to the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* at least for the purpose of training in the gateway of conduct, because the very commencement of such training yields great fruit.
As it is described in the *Praśāntaviniścayaprātihāryasūtra*:
"Thus, the training of a bodhisattva has been briefly explained according to the instruction."
Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Heedfulness regarding the Awakening Mind, in the *Pañjikā* (Detailed Commentary) on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 50) Chapter Five: Guarding Vigilant Awareness.
Having thus established the relinquishing and the protection of the person and so forth, he now begins to explain in detail the protection, purification, and increase [of the bodhicitta].

For a bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), even though he has relinquished his own person (*ātmabhāva*), he must still perform its protection, purification, and increase. This is because: "The body and so forth are given for the enjoyment of sentient beings; if it is not protected, how can there be enjoyment? What is given that is not enjoyed?"
Therefore, for the sake of the enjoyment of sentient beings, one should protect one's own person and so forth,
by not abandoning spiritual friends and by constantly looking toward the sūtras.
And that [protection], such as the preservation of one's own person and so forth, would come about only through the guarding of the training;
