otherwise, because of falling into the miserable states such as the hells, it would not exist.
Therefore, this is said: "By one who desires to protect the training, the mind must be guarded with effort;
the training cannot be protected by one who does not guard the flickering mind. (Bca 5.1)
Training (*śikṣā*) consists in undertaking and adopting [the precepts] by one who has taken the vow; it is the performance of what is prescribed and the non-performance of what is forbidden.
Since it will be stated that "a bodhisattva who desires to guard and protect that training must diligently guard his own mind," [this follows from that].
Now, regarding the section on guarding the training, he asks why the mind is guarded and says: "Not the training.
Otherwise, the training itself cannot be guarded by one who does not guard the fickle and uncontrolled mind;
for when the mind is wavering, stability in the training is impossible.
For this reason as well, he says that the mind alone must be guarded:
"Even untamed, intoxicated elephants do not cause such agony here as the elephant of the mind causes once it is unleashed in the Avīci hell and other realms. (Bca 5.2)
Untamed, excellent elephants do not cause such suffering in this world;
rather, it is the mind itself—like an elephant—that, when established in its own arbitrary will, inflicts the suffering experienced in the next world in the Avīci hell and other realms.
This is because [the mind] can somehow be brought under control by the goad of the Tathāgata’s command.
Regarding the benefit of bringing it under control, he says:
"If the elephant of the mind is bound on all sides with the rope of mindfulness, all fear has vanished and every excellence has arrived. (Bca 5.3)
If it should somehow be bound,
"mindfulness" (smṛti)— whose definition will be stated below—
is itself the rope, because it is the means of binding.
Because the activity of the faction of the non-existent has been obstructed in every way and on all sides,
at that time fear has set and completely vanished without remainder;
everything characterized by worldly prosperity and the supreme good is entirely auspicious.
"Arrived" means having reached [its destination],
just as one says, "If it has rained, the rice has ripened."
(Bcp 51) But surely there are many other sources of affliction, such as wild beasts and predators;
how then will there be no fear of them through the mastery of the mind? To this he says:
Tigers, lions, elephants, bears, snakes, and all enemies—
And all the guardians of hell, as well as the ḍākinīs and rākṣasas.
All these become bound by the binding of the single mind;
and by the taming of the single mind, all become tamed.
This is easy to understand.
Why is this so? He says: "Because all fears and immeasurable sufferings arise from the mind alone—this has been taught by the Speaker of Reality. (Bca 5.6)
For all of these become givers of what is undesirable through the power of the projection of karma; and karma is indeed the mind itself, according to the statement: "Volition is karma."
Mind alone is the originator of both vocal and bodily actions,
because they do not arise in its absence,
and because of the scriptural statement: "Action is that which has been willed."
Therefore, everything here is produced solely by karma, and that is not other than the mind. Thus it is said:
"The variety of the world is born of karma; it consists of volition and what is produced by it."
Volition is mental action; from it arise vocal and bodily actions. (Abhidharmakośa 4.1)
Furthermore, for one whose mind is free from malice, there are no such things as "harms-doers. For it is said: "In this world, there is no fear of enemies for one whose mind has ceased from evil;
there is no loss of happiness for him whose mind stands under control."
Therefore, this was said:
"The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."
The Blessed One is a speaker of reality because his nature is to discourse on the true state of things.
Therefore, he has declared and revealed this reality: "Everything is produced from the mind.
Consequently, in all cases, the mind alone is primary.
Establishing that "this is exactly so and not otherwise," he says:
"By whom were the weapons in hell diligently fashioned?
By whom was the floor of glowing iron made, and from where did those women arise? (Bca 5.7)
By whom were the spears, swords, clubs, and so forth of the hell-wardens made, or the [weapons] produced from the Sword-Leaf Forest?
There is no creator there, such as Īśvara or anyone else.
Because its agency has been refuted elsewhere and will also be refuted here;
furthermore, by whom was this ground made of heated iron fashioned?
And from what causal complex were those women born,
who are seen by adulterers both below and above the *śālmalī* tree? And what is that *śālmalī* tree?
Therefore, no other cause need be postulated here apart from the mind. As it has been said:
"The mind alone fashions the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel in its extreme variety;
for the entire world is said to be born of karma, and karma does not exist apart from the mind."
Thus [it is said].
Therefore, since the mind alone is the cause here and nothing else, the Sage declared: "All that arises from a sinful mind;
therefore, there is nothing more terrifying in the three worlds than the mind. (Bca 5.8)

The Blessed One has declared that the mind itself, conditioned by evil karma, is the cause for them and nothing else. Since this is so, there is no cause for fear in the three worlds other than an evil mind.
Therefore, the mind alone must be brought under control.
As it is said in the *Ārya-ratnamegha*:
"All phenomena are preceded by the mind."
When the mind is fully understood, all phenomena become fully understood.
Moreover:
The world is led by the mind; the mind does not see the mind.
By the mind is karma accumulated, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.
The mind wanders like a firebrand;
the mind fluctuates like a wave;
the mind burns like a forest fire.
"The mind grows like a great ocean," and so it is said.
Investigating in this way, he dwells with mindfulness well-established in the mind,
and does not fall under the power of the mind;
rather, it is the mind that comes under his power.
"When the mind has come under one's control, all phenomena come under control."
It might be argued: "In what way is the mind primary in the perfections such as generosity (*dānapāramitā*)?
For that [generosity] is characterized by the removal of poverty for all sentient beings. To this, he says:
"If the perfection of generosity were [fulfilled] only after making the world free from poverty..."
How is it that even now the world remains poor, despite those former saviors?
For poverty indeed consists of either a mental wretchedness due to the craving for the enjoyment of tainted pleasures or a deficiency of requisites.
If it is said that the perfection of the virtue of generosity is achieved by removing this from the world, then how is that so?
In no way whatsoever was it appropriate for the former Protectors, the Blessed Ones who had previously attained perfect enlightenment. Why? Because the world is still impoverished even today;
as long as the poverty of the world has not been stilled, [it remains so].
(Bcp 53) If this is not accepted, how does that [generosity] come about? He says:
"When there is the mental state of relinquishing all one's possessions together with the fruit, toward all people..."
The perfection of generosity has been proclaimed; therefore, it is indeed the mind itself.

When one gives away all things— both external and internal— as well as the fruit of that giving— to all sentient beings, and through the cultivation of this practice it reaches its peak such that the mind arises free from the stain of stinginess and without attachment,
then it is said that the perfection of generosity (dānapāramitā) is accomplished.
Therefore, that is mind alone; it is not something other than the perfection of generosity.
But since the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*) is even more essentially the mind itself, he says:
"Where could fish and other creatures be taken so that I might not kill them?
When the mind of abstinence is attained, however, it is considered the perfection of ethical discipline. (Bca 5.11)
For morality (*śīla*) is precisely the mental state of abstaining from all faults such as taking life;
it does not, however, have the nature of the external objects that serve as its basis being ceased.

If, on the other hand, morality were to exist simply because of the absence of killing and so forth due to the non-existence of the objects of killing and so forth, [then morality would be non-existent].
In that case, where should those fish and others be taken so that they would no longer be seen?
Otherwise, their virtue (*śīla*) would not exist when the process of killing them begins;
yet this is not the case.

Therefore, even while those [defilements] exist, when the mind of renunciation has been attained and there is mental attention toward cessation, that is considered and agreed upon by those who know its nature to be the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*).
Consequently, it is the mind itself.
The perfection of patience, too, is not distinct from the mind; thus he says:
"How many wicked people can I kill, when they are like space?
But when the mind of anger is killed, all enemies are killed. (Bca 5.12)
Patience (*kṣānti*) is the state of the mind being unperturbed even when harm from others and the like occurs.

Otherwise, if one were to seek the repayment of enmity by destroying all enemies, there would be no one left to cause harm once that enmity had been pacified through the absence of any remaining hostility;
thus, patience is the act of enduring.
In that case, this would be impossible to carry out;
for enemies, being as limitless as space, are infinite,
and their killing is impossible.
Therefore, the very mind that has turned away from anger and the like is, for them, like their execution by means of a skillful method;
because they disregard the harm done by such [enemies] and because the possibility of enmity in future lives is eliminated, those enemies are as good as dead.
Regarding this impossibility, he states that it is indeed possible through the application of skillful means by showing an illustrative example:
"Where could there be enough leather to cover the entire earth? Yet, with just the leather of a single sandal, the whole world is covered. (Bca 5.13)
The earth ought to be covered for the sake of protection against injury from thorns and the like;
yet this is not possible, because there is not enough leather for that purpose.
Even though concealment exists, it is impossible [to conceal everything];
however, it is possible by means of a skillful method (upāya).
By means of leather alone, as in the case of shoes, the entire ground becomes covered.
Applying to the present context the meaning stated in the analogy, he says:
"Just as [external objects], so too external things cannot be warded off by me.
I shall ward off my own mind; what is the use of other things being warded off? (Bca 5.14)
(Bcp 54) Phenomena such as enemies and the like cannot be warded off by me; likewise, harmful actions are impossible to prevent, just as it is impossible to cover the entire earth with leather.
Therefore, I shall ward off only my own mind, for that alone is possible.
Because restraining anything else would be purposeless, since that [restraint] is accomplished simply by restraining one's own mind;
therefore, it is the mind itself.

The perfection of vigor (vīryapāramitā), however, has the nature of enthusiasm for the wholesome; thus it is said that it is most clearly the mind itself: "Even with speech and body, because their activity is sluggish, there is no such fruit as the state of Brahmā and so forth, which belongs even to a single moment of sharp mind. (Bca 5.15)

Even for a mind accompanied by speech and body that is sluggish in its activity toward the side of the wholesome, such a result does not arise as that which results from a mind that, though solitary, is keenly active toward objects such as meditative absorption (dhyāna) and so forth— namely, the state of becoming Brahmā and the like.
Therefore, it is the mind alone [that is the primary agent].

But since meditation is characterized by one-pointedness of mind and cannot be described as anything other than the mind itself, the Omniscient One said: "All recitations and all ascetic practices, even if performed for a long time, are in vain if the mind is distracted or dull. (Bca 5.16)
Recitations (*japa*) are verbal activities characterized by the repetition of mantras and the like;
and austerities (*tapas*) are physical, characterized by the subduing of the senses.
Even if these are practiced for an exceedingly long time, they [are fruitless] if the mind is attached elsewhere or if the mind is impaired by drowsiness and so forth.
The meaning is "devoid of equal proficiency.
It is "in vain" (vṛthā), that is, fruitless,
because its result is exceedingly meager.
Or, because he is of no use for the desired purpose,
even a son is as good as sonless, just like one who does not perform the duties of a son.
Thus said the Blessed One, the Omniscient One;
therefore, the perfection of meditation is also nothing but the mind.
But wisdom is beyond dispute; it is the mind itself. Thus he says:
"To destroy suffering and to attain happiness, those by whom this secret mind—the very essence of all dharmas—has not been cultivated, wander in vain through the sky. (Bca 5.17)

In order to abandon the suffering of birth and so forth within the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies, and to attain the bliss of nirvāṇa through that abandonment, those beings wander in saṃsāra in vain and without purpose, like a kāśī flower in the sky— fruitless. That which is performed yet adheres nowhere at all is thus described as the vow of practicing the five fires, plucking out the hair, and so forth.
Who, then, wander in this way?

Those who, though terrified by the fear of saṃsāra and seekers of happiness, have not cultivated the mind—the entirety of the Dharma and the source of all mundane and supramundane activities—which is secret because its nature is beyond the sphere of experience of the foolish; nor have they repeatedly stabilized it through the realization of the true nature of mind.
Therefore, this is nothing other than the mind itself;
as it is described in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*:
"The basis of all bodhisattva conduct is one's own mind."
The empowerment of one's own mind is the ripening and disciplining of all sentient beings.
[And so on. Noble son, it occurred to me: "One's own mind alone must be sustained by all roots of virtue."
One's own mind alone should be moistened by the clouds of Dharma;
one's own mind alone should be purified of obstructive states;
one's own mind alone should be strengthened through vigor—and so forth.
(Bcp 55) Having thus established that the nature of the mind is present everywhere, he concludes by saying:
"Therefore, I must keep my own mind well-guarded and under my control.
Apart from the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many other vows for me? (Bca 5.18)

One who has thus generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and strives to guard the trainings should reflect as follows: "With my mind one-pointed, I must make my own mind well-established through mindfulness and well-guarded through vigilant awareness (*saṃprajanya*) in the manner to be described hereafter;
for within this alone all [virtues] are included."
Therefore, the protection of the mind alone is the primary vow.
Abandoning that, what need have I for many other vows? None at all;
for without it, they are fruitless.

And this training of a bodhisattva is precisely this: the cultivation of the mind, because it is the root of all activities for the benefit of sentient beings. As it is proclaimed in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:

The bodhisattva Mativikrama said: "This phenomenon which is called 'phenomenon' does not abide in a location, nor does it abide in a specific place; rather, this phenomenon is dependent solely upon one's own mind.
Therefore, I must make my own mind well-pleased, well-sustained, thoroughly mastered, well-exerted, and well-restrained."
For what reason? Wherever there is mind, there are virtues and faults.
Therefore, the bodhisattva, having restrained the mind from faults, directs it toward virtues.
Thus it is said: "Dharma is dependent on the mind;
awakening is dependent on Dharma."
Having thus ascertained that everything depends upon the mind, he provides an illustration regarding the firmness of the mind:
"Just as one situated among the fickle protects a wound with care, so too should one situated among the wicked always protect the wound of the mind. (Bca 5.19)

Furthermore, out of fear of harm among people who are not composed in meditation, one whose mind is fixed upon that [meditation] should protect it with vigilance; just as someone protects a wound, so too should one who desires to guard the training, dwelling among foolish people who are enemies without cause, protect the mind at all times like a wound, being intent upon that task.
This example is given according to common worldly understanding;
however, he states that there is not even the slightest resemblance [between this and the case at hand]:
"Fearing even a tiny fraction of the pain from a wound, I protect the wound with great care."
Are you not afraid of a wound in the mind from being struck by the mountain Saṃghāta?
Even a slight pain is a mere fragment of suffering caused by a wound;
therefore, fearing it, I protect the wound.
In accordance with the context, the reading "rakṣati" (protects) is appropriate.
"With devotion" means with focused intent.

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: being terrified of the origin of the Saṃghāta hell—the suffering experienced for many thousands of years—and of being struck by mountains from all sides, would one not protect the wound of the mind?
Alternatively, it should be construed with the thought: "Why indeed do I not protect [them]?
Or else:
Thus, it is introduced that one who has generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) should reflect with the mind:
"Then I shall protect [them]."
"What benefit, then, would there be in this? To this he says:
"For by dwelling in this manner of abiding, even among the wicked and even in the midst of women, the steadfast ascetic is not brought to ruin. (Bca 5.21)

Because one who wanders with such mental attention even in the midst of women is like one on the roof of a palace— unassailable and exceedingly free from sensual passions— it is said that he is a "steadfast ascetic.
His mind is thoroughly settled in this mental attention.
He does not violate his mental attention toward guarding the training, nor does he stumble.
Showing firm resolve regarding the point that "this must indeed be done once again," he says:
"Let my gains perish at will; let honor, body, and life perish; let all other merit perish as well, but never, under any circumstances, let my mind [forsake its resolve]. (Bca 5.22)
Let my robes, alms-food, and so forth perish; let them go to destruction according to my desire and as I wish.
As for "honor," it refers to worship consisting of respectful treatment, such as offering seats and prostrating at the feet.
"May this body and life—all of it—perish;
may whatever else there is that serves as a cause for pleasure and mental ease also perish;
but may my virtuous mind never perish at any time whatsoever."
Furthermore, in order to inspire respect for this subject, the author of the treatise says:
"To those who desire to guard the mind, I join my palms in reverence; protect mindfulness and situational awareness with every effort. (Bca 5.23)
With palms joined, I pray:
for what purpose? For mindfulness and clear comprehension—not mindfulness alone.
Nor is it merely clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*); thus, two *ca*s are used in mutual dependence.
In that regard, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is explained in the *Āryaratnacūḍasūtra*: "That mindfulness by which the manifestation of all afflictions (*kleśa*) does not occur."
By means of which mindfulness one does not allow an entry for any of the deeds of Māra; by means of which mindfulness one does not fall onto a wrong path or a bad road;
and by means of which mindfulness, acting as a gatekeeper, one allows no opportunity for any unwholesome mental states or mental factors.
This is called right mindfulness.

In brief, this mindfulness (smṛti) is defined as follows: mindfulness is the recollection of what is prescribed and what is prohibited, as appropriate; and as it has been said, "mindfulness is the non-forgetting of the object of focus."
Regarding clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), it is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*: "When walking, one clearly knows, 'I am walking';
when standing, one clearly knows, 'I am standing.'"
When sitting, he knows, "I am sitting";
when lying down, he knows, "I am lying down.
In whatever way his body is positioned, he knows it exactly as it is.
...and so forth.
Whether going forward or returning, he acts with clear comprehension;
whether looking ahead or looking aside, whether bending or stretching his limbs, whether carrying his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl, or whether eating, drinking, chewing, or tasting.

He acts with clear comprehension when dispelling drowsiness and fatigue; whether coming or going, standing or sitting, sleeping or waking, speaking or remaining silent, and when practicing meditative seclusion.
This very point will be stated:
"This alone is, in brief, the definition of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*):
that which is the repeated examination of the body and the mind."
Thus [it is said]. But what is the fault in the absence of these two, such that they are described as things to be guarded with effort? To this he says:
Just as a man distressed by disease is incapable of all activities, so too a mind impaired by these two is incapable of all activities. (Bca 5.24)

Just as a person whose capacity is impaired by disease becomes incapable of all actions such as walking or eating, so too a mind devoid of mindfulness and clear comprehension is incapable of all activities characterized by meditation, study, and the like.

Having stated the fault when both are absent as a whole, he speaks in order to explain the fault when each is individually absent: "For one whose mind lacks clear comprehension, that which has been heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon does not remain in memory, like water in a cracked jar. (Bca 5.25)
That in which clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) does not exist is "lack of clear comprehension" (*asaṃprajanya*). For one who possesses that mind,
the object perfected by the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation does not abide in memory.
And all that is auspicious has its root in that [faith].
How so? Just as water poured into a leaking jar flows out from below and does not remain.
He states another fault regarding its absence: "Even those who are learned, faithful, and devoted to effort, become defiled by transgressions through the fault of lack of introspection. (Bca 5.26)

Even many who are learned, as well as those who possess faith and are devoted to effort, showing respect in their training, become defiled by transgressions through the fault of lack of clear awareness (*asaṃprajanya*), because they fail to examine the movements of body and mind.
Furthermore, he states another defect in its absence: "By the thief of lack of clear awareness, which follows the theft of mindfulness..."
Even after accumulating merits, those who are robbed [of them] go to an evil rebirth.

Lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*) is indeed the absence of clear comprehension; it is a thief whose very nature is the afflictions (*kleśa*), because it carries away the wealth of the wholesome. Following that which pursues the loss of mindfulness, and by following the disappearance and absence of mindfulness—which serves as its guardian—they become robbed, their wealth of the wholesome being plundered. Thus, even though they have accumulated merits, having made a collection of the wealth of the wholesome, [they are ruined].
They become destined for the miserable realms.
To clarify the very point just stated—asking "Why, moreover, is it so?"—he says:
"This host of thieves that are the afflictions seeks an opportunity; having found an opening, they plunder and destroy the life of the good rebirth. (Bca 5.28)
Thieves are robbers; their assembly seeks an opportunity, like a *piśāca* watching for a way of entry.
The meaning is that they are intent on searching for a vulnerability.
Having found an opportunity—that is, having secured a point of entry—they plunder.
Consequently, one destroys the attainment of life for the sake of a beautiful rebirth, due to the absence of the provisions for merit.
Now, concerning mindfulness, he says:
"Therefore, mindfulness should never be removed from the door of the mind; even when it has departed, it should be re-established by recollecting the agonies of the miserable realms. (Bca 5.29)
Since such a fault would arise in the absence of mindfulness,

therefore, seeing this defect here, one must not remove mindfulness— which is characterized by non-forgetfulness of the object— from the gateway of the mind, that is, from the path leading into the house of the mind;
the meaning is that it should always be firmly established.
Now, if at some time one should depart from that through negligence, then even though one has departed, one must be brought back again and reinstated right there.
How so? By recollecting and keeping in mind the suffering of the miserable states, such as the hells and other evil rebirths.

In this regard, there are these twelve recollections for the purpose of avoiding fruitless activity, such as the recollection of the gravity of the ripening [of karma] resulting from not transgressing the commands of the Tathāgata; these have been demonstrated in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, and should therefore be understood with discernment from that very source.
That mindfulness also arises from intense devotion;
and devotion, having understood the greatness of tranquility (*śamatha*), is born through ardent application (*ātāpa*).
We shall explain this in its proper place.
Furthermore, for some, mindfulness arises even in other ways.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"For those who act with reverence out of fear of their preceptor’s instruction..."
For the fortunate, mindfulness arises easily through dwelling with a guru.

For those living in the presence of their teacher (ācārya) or preceptor (upādhyāya), or in the presence of any other venerable celibate student (brahmacārin), there is respect for their instructions; even out of fear—that is, through dread of them—there should be devotion in all duties and an orientation toward them with one's whole being.
This is the dharma that is the opposite of contempt.

For those who act accordingly, who are diligent, and who are virtuous—those who favor the instructions [of the Buddha] regarding the rules for what is beneficial and what is harmful—their mindfulness arises without any difficulty.

Showing that by dwelling in this manner one becomes one who frequently dwells in mindfulness and mental attention, he says in two verses: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have unimpeded vision everywhere; everything is right before them, and I stand before them. (Bca 5.31)
Having reflected thus, one should remain in that state, endowed with shame, reverence, and fear;
in this way, the recollection of the Buddha will arise for him again and again.
At all times, for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— who possess the unimpeded eye of knowledge regarding the entire range of all things— all categories of phenomena indeed stand before them;
I too stand before them,
just like every other phenomenon.
Keeping this in mind, one should remain thus with a self-restrained mind,
endowed with shame, respect, and fear; for "shame" (trapā) in the case of an improper action is modesty (lajjā).
Respect for the training, fear regarding its transgression,
or a sense of shame and so forth toward the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This being the case, he says "buddha... and so forth, [implying] that there would also be another distinction:
for one who dwells in this manner, the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) would occur at every moment, even against his will.

Explaining that mindfulness alone is the cause for the arising and stabilization of clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*), he says: "Clear comprehension arrives and does not depart once it has arrived, when mindfulness stands guard at the gateway of the mind. (Bca 5.33)

When mindfulness stands like a gatekeeper at the door of the house of the mind, preventing the entry of the multitude of thieves that are the afflictions, then clear comprehension arises effortlessly;
and once arisen, it becomes stable.

Thus, having first explained the virtues and faults of these two through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he speaks of the avoidance of fruitless movement for the sake of abandoning what is harmful:
"First of all, this mind must always be established in such a manner;
I should always remain like a piece of wood, as if I were without sense faculties. (Bca 5.34)
First, one reflects within oneself: "This is the mind. At all times, it should be established in this manner according to the sequence described.

Thereafter, for the sake of abandoning fruitless movement, one should remain as if devoid of the collection of sense organs, by withdrawing all conceptual constructions that grasp at fruitless objects such as forms.
Like what? Like a piece of wood.
Because it is devoid of the activity of the eyes and other sense faculties.
This very point is clarified: "Eye-glances that are fruitless should never be made;
rather, the gaze should always be directed downwards, as if constantly gazing inward. (Bca 5.35)
The gaze should be made such that the pair of eyelashes are slightly closed, fixed upon the tip of the nose, and looking only as far as the distance of a yoke.
For the sake of abandoning affliction through continuous practice by one who has just begun, it is said:
"However, for the sake of resting the gaze, one may occasionally look toward the directions;
having seen a mere appearance, one should look about to welcome [the object]. (Bca 5.36)
In order to abandon weariness of view and mind, he should occasionally look toward the directions.
Then, if someone should ever approach his vicinity,
he should look upon them with a greeting to satisfy them, having recognized them merely by their reflection.
Otherwise, by failing to pay him respect there, one would produce unwholesome karma.
Since one sees [dangers] even on the path, he says— so as to avoid injury while traveling—
that one should repeatedly look in the four directions to perceive fear at the start of the path and so forth;
having rested, one should look toward the quarters, and indeed turn back to look behind.
The phrase "in the four directions" is used in sequence for the purpose of perceiving thieves and other sources of fear;
otherwise, protection of one's person would not be achieved.
Furthermore, this surveying of all directions must be performed while standing, in order to avoid the impairment caused by agitation.
Looking back means turning around and facing backward.
And he speaks of the protection against lack of concentration:
"One should advance or retreat after examining what is ahead and behind;
likewise, in all circumstances, one should act having understood what must be done. (Bca 5.38)
One should advance forward and retreat backward,
having carefully observed dangers such as precipices;
thus, according to the direction of the stated sequence, one should understand the purpose of benefiting oneself and others and make the essence of practice one's primary concern.

Now, in order to teach the practice of vigilant awareness (*saṃprajanya*), he says: "Having first directed the action with the thought, 'The body must be positioned in this way,' one should then repeatedly observe, 'How is the body situated? during the intervals. (Bca 5.39)
In one of the four postures—remaining thus with the body either standing or sitting—one should maintain that posture.
Immediately thereafter, having begun an activity such as recitation, one must again examine the interval: "How is the body positioned? while remaining in that very same posture.
Or, if his deportment has been broken,
it must be restored as before.
(Bcp 60) Having explained the examination of the body, he speaks of the examination of the mind:
"In this way, the wild elephant of the mind must be scrutinized with every effort, so that once it is bound to the great pillar of reflection on the Dharma, it is not released. (Bca 5.40)
The very contemplation of the Dharma, characterized by the welfare of oneself and others, is the great pillar, because it is the cause for bringing [the mind] under control through binding.
Even when bound [to the object], it must be examined again and again; thus he says:
"One should examine the mind in this way: 'Where does it dwell? so that one never abandons the yoke of meditative concentration for even a single moment. (Bca 5.41)
Furthermore, where does this mind of mine dwell— is it on the previous object or has it gone elsewhere?
Having understood that it has gone, one should withdraw it from there and apply it to that very same [object].
When [the mind] flows spontaneously, it should be left in equanimity.
Thus, one should maintain [the practice] in such a way that one does not abandon even a single moment of the burden of *śamatha*.
By this much, it is said that ethical discipline (*śīla*) indeed conduces to meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"One quickly attains a stainless concentration; these are the benefits of pure ethical discipline."
Thus it is said.
From this it is understood that whatever applications are causes for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), [they all lead to it].
"They are followers of ethical discipline" means that,
therefore, one who seeks concentration must possess the ethical discipline of mindfulness and clear comprehension;
likewise, even one who seeks ethical discipline must apply effort toward concentration.

He states the occasion for relinquishing meditative concentration: "If one is unable [to maintain it] due to involvement in fear, festivals, and so forth, one may act as one pleases; for it has been taught that equanimity toward ethical discipline is appropriate at the time of giving. (Bca 5.42)
Fear such as that of fire or burning;
likewise, festivals performed for the sake of worshiping the Three Jewels and so forth,
or even the welfare of sentient beings and the like, which are exceedingly great.
If, despite the possibility of that [practice], one is unable to remain [in it], then acting according to one's desire is permitted;
the meaning is that one does not become guilty of an offense.
From where, then, is this lack of restriction obtained? To this he says: "Giving," and so forth.

Although ethical discipline (*śīla*) is superior to giving (*dāna*), nevertheless, for one who is training in the lower instruction and has not yet attained proficiency through practice while established in the subsequent higher instruction, there is no transgression even if they should somehow turn away from it for that duration of time.
This is the time for giving, not for ethical discipline;
therefore it was said, "if one is incapable. This illustration is based on this much alone.
As it has been said: "In that regard, for one who is unable to accomplish a single training, there is no transgression due to the non-practice of the other trainings.
The *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra* also spoke thus: "At the time of giving, there is equanimity toward the undertaking of ethical discipline."
Thus it is said;
and for this reason, one must not be lax.
Since there might be an obstruction to meditative concentration even while engaged in the cultivation of wholesome factors, he says that such [distraction] should not be adopted:
"Having understood what one has begun to do, one should not think of anything other than that."
That alone should first be accomplished with an inner self directed toward it.

(Bcp 61) However, having determined for oneself— as far as one's strength permits— through reasoning, scripture, or the words of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), whatever action such as meditation or study one has begun,
that very thing must first be brought to completion with a mind inclined toward it; one must not abandon it while still unfinished and begin something else.
Furthermore, what would happen if it were not so? He says:
"For in this way all that is well-done will be accomplished; otherwise, neither would come to pass.
Moreover, the affliction of non-discernment (asaṃprajanya) will likewise increase. (Bca 5.44)
Because for one who practices in this manner, everything will be performed in a well-integrated way;
whereas in the opposite case, both would be poorly integrated— the former having been previously accepted and the latter subsequently taken up—
and there would be a lack of clear comprehension due to unstable engagement.
Upon entry, there shall be prosperity.
He says that one should likewise avoid fruitlessness in this way:
"While various kinds of idle chatter are occurring in many ways, one should destroy the curiosity that has arisen regarding all such diversions. (Bca 5.45)

When there occurs the expression of various kinds of incoherent speech, when one engages in that which is devoid of external conditions, and regarding all marvelous things, one should personally restrain the fluctuations of speech and mind during the performance of those actions for the sake of seeing or hearing them.
Furthermore, he says that one should practice what is prescribed in the *Prātimokṣa* in order to avoid fruitless actions:
"Having remembered the training of the Tathāgata, one should abandon at that very moment any fruitless activity—such as kneading clay, cutting grass, or drawing lines—out of fear. (Bca 5.46)

One should avoid, at once— without allowing any delay of time— drawing lines, scratching, or writing with fingernails, sticks, or other tools upon floors, planks, and the like, even if such actions occur spontaneously and without purpose; for one should remember that the Blessed One has commanded abstention from these, out of fear of the ripening fruit of transgressing that command.
In order to teach the practice of constant vigilance (*saṃprajanya*) regarding the manifestation of afflictions, he says through seven verses beginning with "When one wishes to move," and so forth:
"When one desires to move, or even when one desires to speak, one should first examine one's own mind and, with steadfastness, act in a manner that is appropriate. (Bca 5.47)
Having first examined one's own mind,
it was stated that [the practice] to be performed during the state of non-affliction has been explained.
He demonstrates this very point:
"When one perceives one's own mind to be either attracted or repelled, then one should neither act nor speak, but remain like a piece of wood. (Bca 5.48)
When one perceives one's own mind as being attached or hostile,
then not even the slightest movement of the hands or feet should be made, nor should any speech be uttered.
Otherwise, even the bodily and vocal intimations produced by that [mind] would be defiled.
Therefore, having withdrawn the conceptualizations of the activity of the external senses, one should remain like a piece of wood at that time,
keeping in mind that all phenomena are devoid of activity because they are free from all functional exertion.
Another says:
When the mind becomes agitated or mocking, filled with pride and intoxication, excessively sarcastic, crooked, and deceitful— (Bca 5.49).
"Agitated" means agitated even by negligence such as listening to the true Dharma and so forth;
it means being full of distraction.
It consists of the commencement of verbal harassment accompanied by derision,
or that which is joined with such [derision];
pride (*māna*) is the inflation of the mind.
Pride (*mada*) is the mind’s attachment to its own qualities (*svadharma*).
That which is accompanied by these two is "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) with them.
Utprāsa is physical harassment; with that, it is intense.
It is crooked, devious, or deceitful.
If the mind were to become deceptive, delusive, or illusory,
then it should remain like a piece of wood; such is the connection [of the sentence].
Whenever there appears the semblance of self-exaltation or the disparagement of others—
accompanied by reproach and agitation— one should then remain like a piece of wood.
Self-exaltation is the manifestation of the excellence of one's own qualities;
it is a semblance (*tadābhāsa*) and a reflection (*tatpratibhāsa*) thereof, because it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpana*) of that.
It is likewise appropriate [to define] disparagement of others as either attacking another, or exposing their faults.
*Adhikṣepa* is the verbal disparagement of another.
*Saṃrambha* is a state of mental affliction caused by constant strife and dispute. The analysis of the compound (*vigraha*) is: that which exists together with both of these.
Thus, when one perceives one's own mind, it should remain like a log; this general statement is connected here.
If my mind seeks gain, honor, or fame, or seeks a retinue, or seeks service for myself, then I shall remain like a piece of wood.
Fame is renown;
retinue consists of female and male servants, laborers, and so forth;
attendance includes washing the feet, massaging, and similar services.
My mind has such a longing for these objects;
therefore, I remain like a piece of wood.
My mind desires to speak either harshly regarding the welfare of others, or for the sake of its own self-interest, or out of a desire for an audience; therefore, I shall remain like a piece of wood.
Cruel toward the interests of others and averse to the welfare of others;
seeking one's own interest and intent upon one's own interest; "assembly" refers to a gathering of people such as disciples, pupils, and so forth.
Desiring that, one seeks its retinue.
Because [others] are intolerant, lazy, fearful, arrogant, talkative,
and likewise obstinately attached to their own side, I therefore remain like a piece of wood.
Intolerant means having a disposition of non-endurance;
lazy means unfit for action, which is to say, indolent.
"Bhīta" means one who is afraid of the body or life, or afraid of the causes of fear;
"pragalbha" means audacious;
"mukhara" means one who speaks harshly.
Disregarding what is logical or illogical, it is either expressive [of a position] or,
regarding one's own side— such as disciples, students, kinsmen, or blood relatives— it is characterized by attachment and an excessive degree of partiality.
Now he states the instruction on the remedy:
"Having thus observed that the mind is afflicted or engaged in fruitless undertakings, the hero should always firmly restrain it by means of the antidote. (Bca 5.54)

Having recognized his own mind as defiled, associated with afflictions, or engaged in fruitless activity according to the sequence previously shown, he should suppress and overcome it by restraining all mental fluctuations, rendering its power weak, so that it no longer possesses the nature of manifesting again. Thus, the heroic Bodhisattva, having girded himself for victory in the battle against the afflictions and other obstacles, remains steadfast.

The meaning is: by means of whatever [remedy] has been taught as the antidote for a particular [affliction], such as the meditation on the foul (*aśubha*) for passion (*rāga*) and so forth, through the application of its opposite; "always" means at all times.
Whenever it is perceived as being afflicted,
it was stated in the *Ugraparipṛcchā* with reference to the householder bodhisattva:
"He must abstain from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, intoxicants, and the basis for negligence."
[He should be] sober, not insane, not fickle, not wavering, not confused, not talkative, not arrogant, and possessed of established mindfulness and clear comprehension. Thus.
And concerning the Bodhisattva who has gone forth in this very [state], it is said: "It is the non-distraction of mindfulness and clear comprehension."
Likewise, it is shown in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*:

"Furthermore, noble son, the speech of a bodhisattva is not passionate, nor hateful, nor deluded, nor afflicted; it is not subject to momentary prediction, nor is it speech that exalts one's own side, nor speech that suppresses the side of others, nor speech that is attached to praising oneself."
Or speech that obstructs the excellence of others, or speech for the sake of rescuing one's own thesis, or speech consisting of the predictions of those with overweening pride.
Thus, by abandoning fruitless activity, the protection of one's person from harm is established.
Therefore, I must remain well-established in ethical discipline, unshakable and not lax.
And this is accomplished by one whose mind is concentrated;
therefore, having understood this greatness of calm abiding (*śamatha*), it should be cultivated with earnest application.
By means of this, intense reverence for the trainings arises.
By that means, mindfulness is established;
with mindfulness established, one avoids what is fruitless,
and for such a person, misfortunes do not arise.
Therefore, one who wishes to protect their own person (ātmabhāva) should seek the root of mindfulness and always remain possessed of established mindfulness. Regarding this very point, it is said:
"In that regard, what is the protection of one's person? It is the avoidance of what is harmful. By what means is that obtained? By avoiding all fruitless activity."
This [liberation] is accomplished through constant mindfulness; mindfulness arises from intense devotion;
and devotion is born of fervor after one has understood the greatness of tranquility.
Thus [it is said].
The greatness of *śamatha*, however, will be explained right here at the appropriate occasion.
The summarized meaning here is that one must resolve to avoid what is harmful; showing this through three verses, he says:
"Extremely firm, very serene, steadfast, with respectful reverence, possessing a sense of shame and fear, peaceful, and intent upon pleasing others. (Bca 5.55)
This world is not weary of childish desires that are mutually contradictory;
rather, it is filled with compassion for them, thinking, "For this [suffering] arises from their afflictions. (Bca 5.56)
I constantly hold my mind under the control of myself and other beings regarding blameless things, remaining free from pride like a magical creation.
"Well-ascertained" means free from doubt and error. "Well-purified" means always abounding in joy and mental well-being.
"Steadfast" means unshakable.
Respect has already been explained.
Reverence is the mind's humility toward those worthy of worship;
it exists together with those two.
"Modest" is as before.
"Terrified" means being afraid upon seeing a lapse.
"Tranquil" means having the sense faculties restrained.
Like one who exerts effort in pleasing sentient beings.
That which produces delight for one person is the opposite for another;
[the teaching] is untiring and free from regret because of the mutually contradictory desires of ordinary people.
How so? Because it is endowed with compassion.
This is a statement of the cause.
Why? Because, thinking that this mutual conflict of conduct among these fools arises from the production of afflictions and not from independence, [the Blessed One spoke thus].
At all times, one should be under the control of oneself and sentient beings, and dependent upon both self and others.
In what respect? Not everywhere;
rather, in regard to blameless matters—those things that are free from fault for both parties.
Like what? Like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*), as if created by transformation. One should hold a mind free from pride (*vigatamāna*).
A bodhisattva should fix this thought in his mind: "I am this [very person]."
For this reason as well, one must provide protection for the mind by avoiding what is harmful through the mental application of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

Thus it is said: "Remembering again and again, over and over, that this excellent opportunity has been obtained after a long time, I shall hold such a mind steady, unshakable like Mount Sumeru. (Bca 5.58)
Having recalled with mindfulness this excellent moment obtained after a very long time, I shall repeatedly stabilize within my mind such a nature as has been described—
unshakable and impossible to shake by the winds of discursive thoughts such as sensual desire, like the king of mountains.
Thus, through these two—ethical discipline and meditative concentration—which mutually foster one another, there is the complete perfection of mental action.
Therefore, it is established that the training of a bodhisattva is precisely the cultivation of the mind.
Consequently, as it has been said:
"Apart from the vow of guarding the mind, what is the use of many vows for me?"—
thus it is concluded.
Furthermore, in order to ascertain that very solitude, he speaks of the contemplation of the body:
"Dragged here and there by vultures greedy for flesh, why does this body not offer any resistance? (Bca 5.59)
The body has no activity whatsoever anywhere, because it lacks capacity even with respect to itself;
otherwise, the body of a dead person would be devoid of mind.

One asks why he does not provide a remedy here and there to protect himself while being torn apart by vultures and other scavengers; the answer is that this is because he is devoid of all capacity for such action.
For this very reason, the cultivation of the mind alone is what must be accomplished; for when the mind has been cultivated, the cultivation of the body is achieved effortlessly.
What is meant is that it [the effect] is dependent upon that [the cause].
Thus, casting aside attachment toward this body which is useless in every respect, he says: "Why do you protect this body by making it your own?
If this [body] is indeed distinct from you, then what loss do you suffer in its regard? (Bca 5.60)

(Bcp 65) O mind, having accepted as a self that which is utterly devoid of self—the heap of flesh and bones known as the body—for what reason do you protect it? If you ask why this is so: because this body is indeed distinct from you.
Therefore, when this [body] decays, what of yours decays?
If you say, "I have long since accepted it as my own," he replies:
"O fool, you do not accept that a wooden puppet is pure."
Why do you protect this putrid machine constructed of impurities?
O fool, this is merely the manifestation of your delusion:
that [this] is pure and holy,
while this other is impure.
This very point is stated as "impure" (amedhya); it is putrid and subject to decay.
It might be asked: "Is a fault being asserted that does not even exist in another? To this he says:
"First, by means of your own intellect alone, separate this leather bag from the skeletal frame;
strip the flesh away from the cage of bones with the weapon of wisdom. (Bca 5.62)
Having even separated the bones, look at the marrow within;
investigate for yourself whether there is any essence here at all.
This leather bag—
separate it by means of your own superior intelligence;
remove it from your body by cutting the flesh with the weapon of wisdom from the mechanical frame constructed of bones.
Immediately after that, having even broken the bones into separate pieces, look at— and observe— the marrow.

If it will demonstrate in detail that the internal body is composed of the four great elements, born from the impurities of the parents' *kalala*, consisting of suffering, and ungrateful— then what essence is there here that is praised by the wise, or which is logical?
Thus, reflect upon this by yourself alone.
Having searched thus with effort, you have not seen any essence here;
now tell me, why do you still protect this body even today?
If you say that what has been stated according to this method is well said,
then tell me now: why do you still protect this body, which is devoid of all virtues?
Thus it is even for one who possesses such knowledge.
Nevertheless, if it is asked whether there is anything here worth adopting, he says:
"You must not eat the impure; you must not drink the blood; the intestines must not be sucked. What will you do with this body? (Bca 5.65)
The concise meaning is this: that which exists is not useful.
Therefore, what will you do with this useless body?
The meaning is that attachment to it is not appropriate.
Seeing that this alone is appropriate because there is no other purpose, he says:
"It is proper to preserve [the body] for the sake of food for vultures, jackals, and the like;
however, this little body of humans is merely an instrument for [performing] karma. (Bca 5.66)
(Bcp 66) For it is maintained that action is assisted by something as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhāva*).
Nevertheless, he says that one should not form an attachment to this:
"Even while you are thus protecting it, merciless Death will snatch away the body and give it to the vultures; what will you do then? (Bca 5.67)
"Having snatched away" means by force;
the intention is that when merciless Death seizes your body and gives it to the vultures, even then there will be no remedy whatsoever.
This might be so;
yet, even though this is the case, one might think that he should still be protected merely by providing clothing for his devotion. To this, he says:
"Clothing and the like are not given to a servant with the thought, 'He will not stay.'"
The body will depart after having eaten; why then do you incur such expense?
Even if it were indeed the case that one must perform the work of a servant, even then a wise person would act only after understanding that such a state is unstable by nature;
so too in this present case, with what intention, O mind, do you incur this expenditure— the depletion of your resources— toward that very subject?
Should this [mind] then be employed entirely without any scope? No, he says:
"Therefore, having given it its wages, now perform your own purpose with the mind; for not everything acquired by a wage-earner is given back to him. (Bca 5.69)
Wages are the price for labor;
having given only that much to this transient body,
because it is merely an instrument for work.
O mind, you must follow your own purpose!
If it is asked, "Why is that which has been acquired by this very [mind] not given to it?"—
the answer is no, because there is no principle that whatever is acquired by a laborer must all be given back to that laborer.
Therefore, having provided such mere support—
by conceiving of the body as a boat for the purpose of going and coming—
make the body move according to your will for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.

Forming the notion of a boat regarding the body, make the body subject to your will for the sake of engaging in or withdrawing from activity, for the purpose of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings or for [your own] perfection.
The word "O mind" is connected here as it was previously introduced.

Thus, having investigated its nature and utility through the contemplation of the body, and concluding the purpose of the body, he says: "One who has thus brought oneself under control should always have a smiling face;
one should abandon the contraction of the brow into a frown, and be the first to speak as a friend to the world. (Bca 5.71)
In accordance with the principle stated, one should bring under one's own control the self characterized by mind and body;
one should always maintain a serene countenance and abandon the contraction of the eyebrows and forehead, which causes the loss of serenity.
Even before being exhorted by others, he should be one whose nature it is to gladden them with greetings and the like;
and he should be a friend without cause to all sentient beings.
Thus, he says that this training must also be practiced for the sake of avoiding what is useless:
"One should not suddenly throw down chairs and the like with a loud thud; nor should one bang a door. One should always take delight in silence. (Bca 5.72)
(Bcp 67) One should not suddenly or hastily strike the door with one's hand, staff, or other objects without purpose;
in short, one should delight in being free from noise.
"What benefit would there be in this? he says:
"Like a heron, a cat, or a thief, moving silently and unobserved, one attains the desired goal; thus should the ascetic always conduct himself. (Bca 5.73)
All these, dwelling silently and without agitation, attain the intended goal;
likewise, one who observes the vow should also dwell by avoiding that which thorns concentration.
"One should train in this way as well," he says:
"One should always receive with one's head the words of those skilled in exhorting others and who act beneficially without being asked; one should always be a disciple to all. (Bca 5.74)

One should receive upon one's head the beneficial words of those who are capable of dispelling remorse and providing instruction and admonition, who are experts in the Vinaya and other disciplines, and who seek one's welfare even without being asked;
the sense is that one must not corrupt one's own mind toward them, nor should one treat them with contempt.
One should practice toward all sentient beings with a mind of reverence for a teacher; thus, one should learn everything from everyone.
Regarding the washing away of the stain of envy, he says:
One should utter words of approval for all well-spoken things;
seeing one who performs meritorious deeds, one should gladden them with praises. (Bca 5.75)
When speaking words that increase the virtues of others, one should utter the words "Excellent! Excellent! or "This is auspicious" with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) in order to please them.
Even upon seeing one who performs wholesome deeds,
one should encourage them with words of praise such as, "Well done! and "You are blessed, a performer of virtuous actions."
Dispelling the suspicion that this is mere flattery, he says:
"One should speak of virtues in one's absence and repeat them when others do so out of satisfaction;
and when one's own qualities are being praised, one should cultivate the recognition of those virtues [in others]. (Bca 5.76)
One should speak of the virtues of others, even when they are real, in their absence and not in their presence;
otherwise, someone might consider it mere flattery.
However, when another person speaks of the virtues of someone else in that person's presence, one may speak of them in their presence as well, by way of repeating what was said.
Otherwise, thinking "he has no taste for this," another person might become corrupted in mind.

However, when one's own virtues are being proclaimed— whether in one's presence or behind one's back— by someone who is partial to virtue and full of faith, one should prevent the mind from becoming puffed up and instead keep in mind the virtuous affection of that very person who speaks of those qualities.
Warding off resentment toward the virtues of others, he says:

"For all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction, which is difficult to obtain even with wealth; therefore, I shall enjoy the happiness of satisfaction through the virtues produced by the efforts of others. (Bca 5.77)
(Bcp 68) For all beings— whether inferior, middling, or superior—
all undertakings are for the sake of satisfaction through the removal of suffering;
the meaning is that satisfaction alone should be produced through the exertion of every endeavor.
Moreover, that contentment is difficult to obtain even through the expenditure of wealth;
it may or may not come to pass.

But here, since it is present and accomplished without effort, why should it be abandoned? Thinking thus, I shall enjoy—that is, experience—the happiness of contentment brought forth by qualities produced without other exertion.
For one should eliminate mental harshness upon hearing the virtues of others by cultivating the thought: "She is not possessed of intolerance because of the qualities of her beloved son."
Right here he states the accumulation [of merit]:
"In this case there is no loss for me at all, and in the next world there is great happiness;
whereas through hatreds there is the suffering of displeasure and great suffering in the next world. (Bca 5.78)

For me, who am thus engaged in this matter, not even a slight trace of diminution is possible in this world; rather, there is indeed an increase. He shows this by saying: "In the next world there is great happiness from rejoicing in the virtues of others.
Furthermore, it is observed that if one does not act in this way, there is a decrease.
In both worlds there is suffering because of an inability to endure the virtues of others.
Therefore, having abandoned all defilements, one should train in this appropriate practice of action; thus it is said:

One should speak with words that place the feet [of the composition] confidently, whose meaning is clear, which is delightful, pleasant to the ear, rooted in compassion, and uttered in a soft and gentle tone. (Bca 5.79)
It is distinguished because it is free from all faults;
its words are established in proper sequence;
and its meaning is beyond doubt.
It brings delight to the mind,
provides nourishment upon hearing,
is an outflow of the essence of compassion, and is not a cause for passion and the like.
With a gentle voice and non-harsh speech,
he utters a soft tone— neither less nor more than the sound required for the listener to achieve understanding.
One should always look upon sentient beings with a straight gaze, as if drinking them in with one's eyes;
by relying solely upon these, my Buddhahood shall come to be.

With eyes that were straight and not crooked, bowed down by the weight of the essence of supreme affection, he gazed upon sentient beings as if drinking them in with thirst for cool water— beings who bring him the highest joy;
yet he looked with neither passion, nor malice, nor delusion,
for these beings are indeed his greatest benefactors.
Why is that? Because by encountering these beings, Buddhahood—which is so difficult to attain—will become mine; it will arise.
And dwelling in this manner, one remains truly capable of benefiting sentient beings even in the present. As it is said:
"In all circumstances, being steady, one speaks with gentle, smiling, and affectionate words."
One should win over those who are worthy, and one will also become acceptable.
Thus it is said:
[Śikṣāsamuccaya, Verse 10].
And this indeed is the duty of a bodhisattva, namely, that which is called "winning over sentient beings."
As it was elucidated by the noble Bodhisattva Priyadarśana in the *Dharmasaṃgītisūtra*:
"O Blessed One, a bodhisattva should practice in such a way that sentient beings become serene at the mere sight of him.
For what reason? Because..."
"Blessed One, there is no other task for a bodhisattva than winning over sentient beings.
Blessed One, this ripening of sentient beings is itself the bodhisattva’s Dharma-recitation."
(Bcp 69) If it is asked, "What is the fault if one does not act in this way? [The answer is:
But the world, having disregarded that sprout of the Victor as unworthy of acceptance—like fire covered by ashes—will be cooked in the hells and other realms of suffering.
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, for a bodhisattva, the very act of pleasing sentient beings is the field of service, the uncommon cause for the production of merit."
In connection with that, showing something else as well, he says:

"Great merit arises from [giving] to those who are constantly attached [to worldly things], from that which arises through the cultivation of the antidotes, to a field of qualities and benefactors, and to those who are suffering. (Bca 5.81)
That which is performed through formal undertaking;
that which arises from attachment; that which is produced by intense faith;
and that which arises from the antidote, being born from the cultivation of emptiness and other factors that serve as antidotes to the afflictions.
The field of qualities consists of Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth;
the field of benefactors consists of mothers, fathers, and so forth; and the field of those suffering consists of the sick and others.
In these cases, even that which is performed by one of small intelligence arises as a cause for immeasurable merit.

He says that this too must be practiced by the bodhisattva: "One should always be skillful, endowed with diligence, and a doer oneself; one should not grant anyone an opportunity in any of one's tasks. (Bca 5.82)
He is skillful and possesses sharp activity in all matters;
endowed with exertion, he is possessed of vigor through the removal of indolence.
For this very reason, he performs everything that is to be done by himself.
One should not depend upon anything else in any action whatsoever;
this very point is shown by the passage beginning with "there is no opportunity" (nāvakāśa).
Regarding the practice of the perfections (*pāramitā*), he speaks of acting in successive order in order to avoid what is harmful:
"The perfections, beginning with generosity, are increasingly superior. One should not abandon a superior [perfection] for the sake of another, except in the case of the bridge of conduct. (Bca 5.83)
Higher and higher:
morality is superior to giving, patience is superior to morality, and so forth.
Therefore, for the sake of the supreme perfection, one should not abandon what is superior;
the meaning is that one should not practice anything that is contrary to it.
Is this to be done in every respect?
He says "no," [explaining] "elsewhere":
that very conduct of the Bodhisattvas, characterized by the vows of training (*śikṣā-saṃvara*), has been established as a dam for the protection of the waters of virtue;
therefore, "elsewhere" means apart from that, having abandoned it.
The meaning is that it does not break apart.
Therefore, he says that one who desires to gather the accumulations, being dependent upon compassion, must perform everything that has been taught:
"Having understood this, one should always be intent upon the welfare of others;
for a compassionate person who perceives the true benefit, even what is prohibited is permitted. (Bca 5.84)
Having thus understood this as supreme, one should always exert vigor for the sake of providing welfare and happiness to sentient beings.
If it is asked, "How is one not guilty of an offense when engaging in an activity that is prohibited? the answer is: no;
for in certain cases, even what is forbidden may be done for the sake of a particular benefit to sentient beings by means of the eye of wisdom.
It has been permitted by the Blessed One as something to be done for one who sees [the truth],
and the teaching of the Blessed One possesses an exit;
yet even that is not for everyone.

Rather, for one who is compassionate, whose activity proceeds from the excellence of compassion, who is dependent upon that [compassion], whose sole flavor is the welfare of others, and who is turned away from self-interest— namely,

for one who acts with skillful means as the function of benefiting others arises through wisdom and compassion— there is no transgression. In this regard, the distinction between transgression and non-transgression should be understood from the *Upāliparipṛcchā*.
Likewise, in the *Upāyakauśalya-sūtra*, in the section concerning the young brahmin Jyotiṣka.
This is the protection of one's person by means of medicine, clothing, and so forth;
in order to demonstrate this, he says:
Having shared [his food] with those who have fallen into misfortune, those who are protectorless, and those established in vows,
he should eat a moderate amount and discard three robes outside [the monastery].
For the physical body must be maintained through medicines, clothing, and so forth, because it is useful for the sake of others.
As was stated previously, there are two kinds of medicine: constant medicine and medicine for the occasion of illness.
Among these, constant medicine consists of rice and other such foods.
For that purpose, while wandering for alms in the proper range, one should enter the village with mindfulness applied to the prescribed training.
Then, from the alms-food obtained and divided into four portions, one should share with those who have fallen into misfortune, the destitute, and those established in vows;
one portion should be for those who have fallen into misfortune.
Having given the second portion to those who are destitute,
the third to his fellow practitioners of the holy life, he should consume the fourth portion himself.
While consuming it, he consumes it without passion and without attachment.
He is without greed and without attachment,
[using food] merely for the maintenance and sustenance of this body.
A moderate amount;
and he consumes it in such a way that he is neither too emaciated nor has a body that is too heavy.
For what reason?
Because one who is excessively emaciated becomes averse to the side of wholesome qualities, and one whose body is too heavy becomes overcome by drowsiness.
"Having consumed that alms-food, he should remain oriented toward the side of virtue.
Thus it is stated in the *Āryaratnamegha*.
It is also said in the *Āryaratnarāśi*:
And while consuming it, one should produce this mental attention: "There are eighty thousand families of worms in this body;
may they dwell in happiness through this very strength.
Now, I shall provide them with sustenance."
"And having attained awakening, I shall further gather [beings] through the Dharma," and so forth in detail.
Furthermore, it is said in this very same place: "Kāśyapa, I authorize two kinds of faith.
Which two?"
Of one who is disciplined and of one who is liberated. Thus.
In this manner, all enjoyments should be consecrated for the sake of sentient beings; otherwise, from enjoying them out of self-love, a defiled transgression arises.
Thus it is said.
[Śikṣāsamuccaya, Verse 13] (Bcp 71) As it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*:
"Having obtained food that is delicious, flavorful, and excellent, they eat it while lacking application in yoga."
For them, that food becomes a cause of death, just as unwashed lotus stalks are for young elephants.
This should be examined in detail in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
Medicine for the sick, however, is of three kinds: that which lasts for a watch of the night, that which lasts for seven days, and that which lasts for life.
This has been set forth in the Bhikṣu-vinaya and should be understood from that very source.
He speaks of protecting oneself with robes and other necessities: "One should cast away the three robes externally.
This means that if someone should come and ask a bodhisattva for his bowl and robes, [he should give them].
Therefore, one should not practice excessive renunciation;
rather, regarding that which was authorized by the Blessed One— the three robes as the ascetic’s equipment— and whatever may be in excess of that:
It must be given to one who asks, and not otherwise.

And it is said in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*: "If, moreover, someone should come and ask for an alms-bowl or a robe, and if he should have something in excess of the three robes permitted by the Buddha,"
One should give what has been relinquished.
However, if he should have fewer than three robes— those depending upon which he dwells in the holy life— that must not be relinquished.
For what reason?
Because the Tathāgata has declared that the three robes are not to be relinquished.
Śāriputra, if a bodhisattva, having renounced the three robes, were to become intent on begging for them, [he would be at fault].
By that, one would not have practiced fewness of desires. Thus it is said.
Prohibiting excessive renunciation and further demonstrating self-protection, he says:
One should not afflict the body, which serves the true Dharma, for the sake of other things;
for in this very way, one may swiftly fulfill the hopes of sentient beings. (Bca 5.86)
The Dharma of the virtuous, the true persons, the Bodhisattvas,
consists in the provision of supreme benefit and happiness for both worldly and transcendent beings;
one should not afflict the body that serves this Dharma for the sake of a trivial purpose.
Otherwise, there would be a loss of a great mass of benefit.
For this very reason, this is a statement of the cause regarding what preceded.
But why is it so?
For by being nurtured through this very gentle method of upbringing, he will very quickly become capable of accomplishing the welfare and happiness of sentient beings.
Since this is so, therefore:
One should not give up one's life as long as the disposition of compassion is impure;
however, when the disposition is equal [to that of others], it may be given up, and in this way one does not fall away.
It is prohibited that one should not perform acts such as the giving of one's own body or head.

When? When the mind of compassion is impure—that is, when it is active in a manner common to all people, whether friends, enemies, or others who are in distress. For if vigor is over-exerted, there would be an obstruction to the welfare of oneself and others.
Furthermore, when the mental disposition (*āśaya*) has become equal, whether toward oneself or others, it is not prohibited [to act as one pleases].

As it is said: "Likewise, giving and not giving—which cause obstacles to the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), learning, and so forth, for oneself or others—should not be practiced by one who possesses either superior capacity for the welfare of sentient beings or equal capacity. (Bcp 72)
It is thus established that for a bodhisattva, both giving and not giving—which respectively create excessive or insufficient obstacles to wholesome qualities—should not be practiced.

And with this very point in mind, it is stated in the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa*: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, how should a bodhisattva who has gone forth from the household life and is devoted to the factors of enlightenment give gifts?"
Which gift should be given?
Of what nature should the gift be given? [The rest as before.]

One should be a giver of the Dharma. Śāriputra, if a householder bodhisattva were to give as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, filled with the seven precious jewels, and if, Śāriputra,
a bodhisattva who has entered the life of renunciation were to proclaim even a single four-line stanza, [the latter would generate far more merit].
This alone produces much more merit than that.
Śāriputra, the Tathāgata has not authorized the giving of material gifts by one who has gone forth. [The rest as before.]

Furthermore, Śāriputra, whatever gain may come into one’s bowl or be contained within one’s bowl— whether it be righteous or obtained through the Dharma— one should share it in common with one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.
In that very same place it says: "Furthermore, Śāriputra, whatever bodhisattva has not yet gone forth from the household life must cultivate the Dharma;
he must be devoted to it."

For otherwise, for the sake of gathering the benefit of a single sentient being, there would be a loss of great benefit by creating an obstacle to the cultivation of the bodhisattva’s resolve for that great mass of beings and for that specific being; thus, dwelling by means of this skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*), one does not fall away from the path to enlightenment.
This is the intended meaning: he has already given his own person (*ātmabhāva*) to all sentient beings long ago.
It must simply be protected from use at an improper time;
therefore, there is no occasion for stinginess, nor is there any loss of what was promised. As it has been said:

Just as the seed of the beautiful medicinal tree, which provides enjoyment through its roots and so forth, must be protected even after it has been given by not using it at the wrong time, so too must the seed of the perfectly enlightened one, that medicinal tree, be protected.
Thus it is said.
One should protect oneself even by guarding the inclinations of sentient beings; thus it is said:
"One should not speak the Dharma to one who lacks respect, who is healthy, or whose head is wrapped;
nor to one with an umbrella, a staff, or a weapon, nor to one whose head is covered. (Bca 5.88)

For the Dharma of the Blessed One is honored by gods and humans; therefore, the gods and others find fault with one who fails to show respect when the Dharma is being proclaimed. Since this has been prohibited by the Blessed One, one would incur an offense by transgressing his command.

Nor [should one eat] with the head bound by a garment or similar object; the word "together" (saha) connects to all three cases; likewise, [one should not eat] when the head is covered by an upper robe or other such cloth.
The phrase "each being healthy" is to be connected [to each case].
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of one who is ill;
this is also an illustrative indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).
One should not [teach] while standing to one who is lying down or sitting;
nor while sitting to one who is lying down; nor while not seated to one who is sitting.
Not by one who does not travel the path with a traveler on the path,
nor by one who follows behind a leader,
nor even by one adorned with ornaments.
These and others should also be understood in this way.
He says that this too, as a cause for a root downfall, must not be committed in order to avoid misfortune:
"The profound and sublime [teaching] should not be given to those of little merit, nor to women in the absence of a man.
"Profound" means difficult for those of dull intellect to fathom because of its depth.
And it is "sublime" because it reaches the ultimate limit.
The connection with the context is that one should not speak such a Dharma to those who are few, whose intellects are unrefined, or who have inferior inclinations.
One should not speak the Dharma to a woman alone in a secluded place.
By speaking thus, one becomes guilty of an offense;
there is no fault if it should be a man.
One should practice equal reverence toward all phenomena, whether low or superior.
One should cultivate an equal degree of mental clarity and so forth toward the teachings spoken in the Śrāvakayāna as toward those spoken in the Mahāyāna;
otherwise, there would be a rejection of the true Dharma.
One should not employ a recipient of the vast Dharma in a base teaching,
nor should one, having abandoned proper conduct, entice others with sūtras and mantras.
Having recognized through signs that a sentient being is a vessel for the profound and vast Dharma, one should not introduce them to the teachings of the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth.

Furthermore, one should not lead those who desire the Dharma to believe that purification will come merely by reciting sūtras and the like, while setting aside proper conduct, the training in the vows, and what is to be practiced.
