Regarding this, it is said: another disadvantage is seen in the *Ratnakūṭa*: "To place trust in sentient beings who have not yet been ripened is a transgression of a bodhisattva."
To reveal the sublime Buddha-dharma to those who have not become fit vessels is a transgression of a bodhisattva;
to reveal the Hīnayāna to beings who possess sublime resolve is a transgression of a bodhisattva.
In the *Ārya-sarvadharma-vaipulya-saṃgraha*, even a subtle misfortune is described: "For the karmic obstruction of rejecting the true Dharma, Mañjuśrī, is indeed subtle.
For whoever, Mañjuśrī, forms the notion that some part of the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata is beautiful and the notion that another part is not beautiful,"
He rejects the true Dharma;
by that rejection of the true Dharma, he slanders the Tathāgata and reviles the Saṃgha.
He who speaks thus: "This is logical, this is illogical," and so forth in detail.

And in the *Āryākāśagarbhasūtra*, in the section concerning the root downfalls, it is said: "Furthermore, a beginner bodhisattva might say to certain people: 'O friend, what is the use of the Prātimokṣa discipline? By well-guarding your ethical conduct, you should quickly generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
read the Mahāyāna!'"
Whatever unwholesome karma has been accumulated by you through body, speech, and mind on account of the afflictions, by that there will be purification for you without ripening,
just as was stated previously.
This is the third root downfall of a beginner bodhisattva.

Therefore, he says that even this which is prohibited by the Prātimokṣa should not be practiced: "The discarding of tooth-sticks and spittle uncovered is not desired; it is also censurable in water, on land, or in places used for enjoyment, as is the case with urine and so forth. (Bca 5.91)
One should not discharge phlegm or saliva in an uncovered place; nor should one perform such despicable acts as voiding urine or excrement upon water or upon ground intended for enjoyment or use.
In these cases as well, by disrespecting the deities and others, one generates demerit.
One should not eat with the mouth full, nor with noise, nor with the mouth wide open;
one should not sit with legs dangling, nor rub both arms simultaneously.
Having filled the mouth by taking a large morsel,
one makes a sound with the *sukasuni* and other such noises;
"with the face spread out" means the mouth is opened wide.
One should not sit with the feet dangling, meaning with the feet not touching the ground or a seat such as a couch.
One should not rub both arms simultaneously at the same time;
there is no fault in rubbing them sequentially.
When the condition exists.

(Bcp 74) One should not engage in traveling, lying down, or sitting with another man’s wife, even if she is alone and has no second companion. The mention of "another" is used because this rule applies equally here to both householders and those who have gone forth.
One should not perform [actions such as] traveling by carriage and so forth.
Summarizing and showing the point briefly, he says:
"Having seen and having asked about everything that causes lack of confidence among the world, one should avoid it. (Bca 5.93)
Having seen all that which does not produce confidence among people, whether in a treatise or in worldly practice,
one should inquire from those who possess specialized knowledge.
One should avoid it.

By this, the following is shown: even when something is seen, if it is of such a nature that it causes harm, one should avoid it, for an offense occurs. As it was said in the *Ratnamegha*: "Therefore, the concise vow was taught by the Victor."
One should diligently abandon whatever causes a lack of faith among sentient beings.
Thus it is said.
[Śikṣāsamuccaya-kārikā 12] As it is said: "And what are those bodhisattva practices?
In this regard, a bodhisattva does not dwell in a lowly state, nor at an improper time."
He does not speak at an improper time;
he is not one who lacks knowledge of the proper time; he is not one who lacks knowledge of the proper place.
Since he would cause beings to experience a lack of faith in his presence due to that cause,
he maintains a correct deportment for the sake of protecting all beings and for the purpose of fulfilling his own equipment for enlightenment;
he speaks softly, speaks slowly, avoids excessive social contact, is inclined toward solitude, and has a very serene countenance.

A bodhisattva must never show contempt toward anyone; thus it is said: "One should not point with a finger at anything, but rather respectfully with the right hand; one should even indicate the path using the entire hand. (Bca 5.94)
One should not point out anything with a single finger, such as the index finger and so forth, but rather with the entire hand, the whole hand;
and with the right hand, not the left.
One should also explain the path;
let alone matters concerning [proper] respect.
To prevent causing displeasure among people, he says:
"One should not call out to anyone by raising one's arms even in a minor emergency; rather, a snap of the fingers or the like should be used, otherwise one would be lacking in restraint. (Bca 5.95)
One should not beckon anyone by raising one's arm when the difference in the importance of the purpose is slight; however, there is no fault in doing so when the purpose is great.
However, one should make a sound such as the snap of fingers;
for if that is not done, one would be unrestrained when walking with an unconcentrated mind.
By this much, the avoidance of restlessness is also demonstrated.

Showing how he should prepare his bed, [the author] says: "One should lie down in the desired direction like the bed of the Lord’s nirvāṇa; being fully conscious and intending to rise quickly, one must first necessarily [prepare it] according to rule. (Bca 5.96)
One should arrange one's bed like the Great Nirvāṇa-bed of the Blessed One,
placing the head toward the desired direction and lying on the right side.
Placing one foot upon the other,
making the right arm a pillow, and extending the left arm to rest it upon the thigh;
With his body well-covered by robes, mindful, and clearly comprehending.
Maintaining the perception of rising and the perception of light while lying down.
He is not overcome by mindlessness or torpor;
he does not relish the pleasure of sleep, nor the pleasure of reclining on his side, except for as much as is necessary for the maintenance and sustenance of these great elements.
One should rise quickly with lightness;
one should not rise slowly, overcome by sloth, yawning or stretching the limbs.
One should rise even before all of these [actions] occur.
Summarizing this further, he says:
"The conduct of Bodhisattvas is said to be immeasurable;
one should, for now, certainly practice that conduct which purifies the mind. (Bca 5.97)
Conduct (*ācāra*) is that which is to be trained in;
it is immeasurable and incalculable, as demonstrated in the *Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa* and other texts.
One should first practice conduct in the form of a summary of that [immeasurable training], which is precisely the purification of the mind.
Niyatam means necessarily or inevitably.
Regarding the purification of common downfalls, it is said:
"One should recite the Three-Section Sūtra three times during the day and night;
by that, through reliance on the Bodhicitta and the Victors, all remaining downfalls are pacified. (Bca 5.98)
Three times during the night;
three times during the day;
"three aggregates" (*triskandha*) refers to the collection of the three aggregates: the confession of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, and the dedication toward awakening.
One should perform the *triskandha* rite.
The remaining [downfalls] are other than those of the root category;
or alternatively, they are those committed through forgetfulness or without clear comprehension, as opposed to those committed intentionally and then counteracted.
Their pacification and remedy come through that threefold turning of the wheel and by taking refuge in the mind of awakening and the Blessed Victorious Ones.
By this, the practice of revulsion and so forth are demonstrated.
In that regard, the purification of evil is taught in the *Caturdharmaka-sūtra*:
"Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with four qualities overcomes evil that has been committed and accumulated. Which four?"
Namely: by means of the practice of revulsion, the practice of the antidote,
and the power of restoration.
And by the power of the basis (*āśrayabala*).

In that regard, the practice of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇāsamudācāra*) consists of the confession of evil after having committed unwholesome karma, taking the form of remorse and accompanied by self-reproach;
its performance is the practice thereof.
In that regard, the practice of the counteragent consists of the wholesome as the counteragent to the unwholesome;
it is the practice of that [counteragent],
which is the absolute application to wholesome action even after having committed unwholesome action.
In that context, the power of restoration is the attainment of the restraint of non-action through the formal undertaking of the vow (*saṃvara*).
In that context, the power of the basis consists of going for refuge to the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha,
as well as not relinquishing the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
By relying on that strength, he cannot be overcome by evil.
Maitreya, a bodhisattva mahāsattva endowed with these four qualities overcomes evil that has been committed and accumulated.
In particular, the confession of the bodhisattva transgressions—both grave and light—is taught in the *Āryopāliparipṛcchā*;
they should be consulted in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
A bodhisattva should confess all transgressions alone, day and night, in the presence of the thirty-five Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.

In this regard, the confession is as follows: beginning with "I, [name], go for refuge to the Buddha," and so on, up to "I go for refuge to the Saṅgha; homage to the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One."
Beginning with "Homage to Vajrapramardin" and continuing until—
"With palms joined, I go for refuge to all"—

having thus spoken in detail, he says: "In this way, Śāriputra, by taking these thirty-five Buddhas as the foremost, a bodhisattva achieves the purification of evil through mental engagements that follow after all the Tathāgatas."
It should be performed.
When he has thus purified his evil, those very Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, show their faces to him; [and so on].
That which constitutes a ground for remorse regarding an offense cannot be purified by the assemblies of all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

rather, a bodhisattva emerges from the remorse of an offense by maintaining and reciting the names of those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and by setting in motion the Dharma-discourse of the Three Aggregates day and night.
And he attains meditative concentration.
This should be understood in its entirety from the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*.
The practice of confession has been explained.
The power of the remedial practices and the power of restoration should also be seen in detail from the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* itself.
However, in the *Āryamaitreyavimokṣa*, the purification of evil through the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is taught.
And that has already been stated previously.
Regarding the purification of evil through reliance on the Victorious One, the *Sūkarikā-avadāna* (The Story of the Sūkarikā) should be cited:
"Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth."
Having abandoned human bodies, they obtain divine bodies.
In this way, the recitation concerning the Dharma and the Saṅgha expresses the power of the support.

Showing again that there is no fixed rule, he says: "In whatever states one may find oneself, whether by one's own will or under the power of another, one should diligently train in those very precepts appropriate for those states. (Bca 5.99)
Whether acting by himself or depending on others, he is engaged in performing deeds for the benefit of sentient beings.
Why, then, is this expressed with such lack of restriction? He says:
"For there is nothing whatsoever that is not to be learned by the sons of the Conquerors;
nor is there any merit that does not accrue to one who dwells in this manner. (Bca 5.100)

Because there is nothing whatsoever that must not be studied by the sons of the Buddha, who, having realized the reality of all things in all their aspects, strive for the sake of establishing the welfare and happiness of all beings;
otherwise, it would be impossible to accomplish the benefit of all sentient beings in every possible way.
For one who practices in this way, even the accumulation of merit would likewise be limitless.
One should also grasp this seal of the training precepts; thus it is said:

"Whether indirectly or directly, one should act for the benefit of sentient beings and not otherwise. And for the sake of sentient beings alone, one should dedicate everything toward enlightenment. (Bca 5.101)

Whether ultimately by one's own actions such as providing food and so forth, by the instigation of others, or by the dispatching of various messengers; or directly by oneself through the giving of material gifts and the like— whatever does not become a cause for the welfare and happiness of sentient beings [is not a gift].
One should neither perform nor cause others to perform that;
nor should one do only this alone.

Rather, for the sake of the liberation from cyclic existence of all sentient beings who have fallen into the suffering of saṃsāra, one should dedicate every root of virtue toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
By these two verses, the increase of merit is thus demonstrated.
Regarding what was stated [in Śikṣāsamuccaya, verse 6], "by not abandoning the spiritual friend," it says:
One should never abandon a spiritual friend, even for the sake of one's life—[a friend] who upholds the bodhisattva vow and is skilled in the meaning of the Mahāyāna. (Bca 5.102)
Regarding virtuous action, characterized by the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is an incomparable kinsman;
one should not abandon such a person even if terrified by the danger of losing one's body or life.
Furthermore, the benefits of having a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra-anuśaṃsā*) are to be understood from the *Sadāprarudita-parivarta* of the *Āryāṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (Chapter 30).

It is also said in the *Caturdharmaka-sūtra*: "O monks, a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) must not be abandoned by a bodhisattva mahāsattva for as long as life lasts, even for the sake of one's own life.
He states the characteristics of that spiritual friend who is not to be abandoned: "One who is established in the vow of the bodhisattva training and is learned in the meaning of the Mahāyāna."
Such as this is extremely difficult to obtain.
In order to fully understand the service of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), it is said:
"One should learn how to attend upon a teacher from the *Śrīsaṃbhava-vimokṣa*.
From the *Śrīsaṃbhava-vimokṣa*, that is, from the chapter of the noble *Gaṇḍavyūha*, one should learn—that is, come to know—the manner of attending upon a spiritual friend.

As stated by the noble Śrīsaṃbhava in the *Āryagaṇḍavyūha*: "Noble son, bodhisattvas who are sustained by spiritual friends do not fall into the miserable realms. And so on, until: "Spiritual friends are those who exhort one [to virtue]; they are those who prevent one from doing what should not be done; they are those who restrain one from states of negligence."
They are the ones who lead one out from the city of saṃsāra.
Therefore, noble son, you should approach spiritual friends with such mental attention, never ceasing,
with a mind like the earth because it does not grow weary while bearing all burdens.
With a mind equal to a vajra, by virtue of having an unbreakable intention; with a mind equal to the cosmic rim, by virtue of being unpierced by any suffering;
with a mind equal to a servant of the world, by virtue of not feeling disgust in undertaking any task.
With a mind like a dust-remover, by way of abandoning pride and arrogance;
with a mind like a vehicle, by way of carrying heavy burdens;
with a mind like a horse, by way of not becoming angry.
With a mind like a ship, by not being weary of coming and going;
with one resembling a good son, by looking toward the face of the spiritual friend;
and furthermore, noble son, you should conceive the perception of yourself as a patient and the perception of spiritual friends as physicians.
One should perceive the instructions as medicine and the practice as the eradication of disease;
and you, noble son, should conceive of yourself as a coward.
The perception of spiritual friends as heroes, the perception of their instructions as weapons, and the perception of one's practice as the destruction of enemies.
Regarding what was stated [in verse 6]: "And because of the constant inspection of the sūtras," he says the following to demonstrate that:
"This and other [teachings] spoken by the Buddha are to be known from reading the sūtras" (Bca 5.103).
This has been set forth here in this treatise;
if anything else was not mentioned here,
it was because it had already been taught by the Blessed Buddha as a duty to be performed by Bodhisattvas.
This should be understood through familiarity with the meaning of various sūtras.
He demonstrates this very point: "The trainings are seen in the sūtras; therefore, one should recite the sūtras.
The trainings of the bodhisattvas consist of the characteristics of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted."
Since this is so in the sūtras, such as the Mahāyāna sūtra-ends like the Ratnamegha and others, for that reason,
he states this specific explanation:
And one should examine the root downfalls in the Ākāśagarbha Sūtra.
In the *Āryākāśagarbhasūtra*, five root downfalls are specified for a consecrated Kṣatriya;
likewise, there is one root downfall in general;
and similarly, eight root downfalls are specified for a beginner Bodhisattva.

And so it is said there: "O son of good family, there are five root downfalls for an anointed Kṣatriya king; by these root downfalls, the anointed Kṣatriya king consumes all previously planted roots of merit, falls from his status, is defeated, and, deprived of all the happiness of gods and humans, becomes one who goes to the states of woe."

What are the five? Noble son, it is when a consecrated kṣatriya steals property belonging to a stūpa, or belonging to the Saṅgha, or dedicated to the Saṅgha of the four quarters; either he steals it himself or causes it to be stolen.

This is the first root transgression. Likewise, the second arises from rejecting the Dharma spoken in the three vehicles, or from taking away the saffron robes of one who has gone forth, whether that person be virtuous or immoral.
Because of making him a householder, because of striking his body,
and because of casting him into prison.
The third [type of transgression] arises from depriving one of life;
the fourth arises from committing any one of the five acts of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya);
and [the fifth] from wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi).
The fifth [offense] occurs from undertaking the ten unwholesome paths of action, or from inciting others to undertake them.
Likewise, there is one [offense] common to all, consisting of causing a schism in the community and so forth.
It is stated in that very same [text]:
"For sons of noble family and daughters of noble family who are beginners and have set out in the Mahāyāna, there are eight root downfalls."
By which root downfalls have beginners who have set out in the Mahāyāna stumbled—all those previously mentioned, and so forth, as before.
What are the eight?
They are those beings who, due to the cause of their own past misconduct, have been born in this afflicted world of the five degenerations.
They possess only meager roots of virtue;
indeed, when this most profound sūtra associated with emptiness is extensively recited and explained before them,
those foolish ordinary persons, having exerted no effort, become terrified upon hearing it.
As long as they turn back their minds from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and direct their minds toward the vehicle of the śrāvakas,
this is the first root downfall of a beginner bodhisattva.
"By which root downfall," and so forth, as before.

Therefore, a bodhisattva, having first understood the intentions (*āśaya*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of other beings and other individuals, should provide the teaching of the Dharma to beings according to their inclinations in a gradual sequence.

The second [root downfall] occurs when one causes another to turn away from the means-end of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) and generates in them a mind set upon the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

The third [point] is because it reveals the method of purification for this [Mahāyāna] through the mere generation of the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) and the recitation [of its teachings] within the Mahāyāna, while setting aside the restraint of the *prātimokṣa* training;
and because it reveals the concealment and disparagement of the Śrāvaka and other vehicles along with their fruits, whereas it reveals the complete purity within the Mahāyāna.
The fourth [type of transgression] arises from acting according to the words of others;
that is, for the sake of gaining fame, profit, and so forth, by reciting the Mahāyāna and the like,
as well as through speaking disparagement, censure, and so on toward others because of those same conditions.
The fifth [offense] arises from self-exaltation and from claiming to have attained superhuman states;
it occurs by merely reciting [the scriptures] while proclaiming an understanding of the profound Dharma.
The sixth [offense] arises from likewise inciting others [to do so].

When a king’s priests, ministers, or outcastes have punished monks with a monetary fine— having seized property belonging to the Saṅgha, to a stūpa, or to the Saṅgha of the four directions— and hand it over to those very individuals,
both the king and the officials incur a root offense.
This is the seventh [cause]:
because the training was established prior to disputes concerning dharma and adharma,
and because of the honoring of those whose conduct had fallen away from its root.
If those who practice asceticism use or enjoy articles of enjoyment other than those [permitted], except for the purpose of dedicating them [to others], both incur a root downfall;
this is the eighth.
For the sake of easy comprehension of these root downfalls, the summary verses shown by the author of the treatise are stated:
"By stealing the property of the Three Jewels, the first pārājika downfall is considered incurred;
by the rejection of the True Dharma, the second was taught by the Sage."
(Bcp 79) Or, even for a monk who is immoral, [the offense occurs] by stealing his saffron robe, by beating him, by casting him into prison, or by causing him to leave the religious life improperly.

The Conqueror has declared that a root downfall occurs through committing one of the five acts of immediate retribution, by grasping at wrong views, or even by the destruction of villages and the like.
Because of the teaching on emptiness to beings who have not yet developed wisdom,
and because of turning away from perfect enlightenment those who had set out for Buddhahood.
Because of abandoning the Prātimokṣa and enjoining [others] to the Mahāyāna,
or because of the apprehension that the Śrāvaka vehicle does not lead to the abandonment of passion and so forth.
Either by seizing the possessions of others, or again by proclaiming one's own virtues,
or by disparaging others for the sake of gain, honor, and fame.
Furthermore, by falsely claiming, "I possess profound patience," one might cause the śramaṇas to be punished or cause them to be deprived of the Three Refuges.
Or one may accept what is being given for the sake of abandoning [the practice of] *śamatha*,
as well as for the enjoyment of those in seclusion and for the offering of it to those engaged in recitation.
For these root offenses are the causes for the great hells;
they must be confessed in a dream while standing before the noble Ākāśagarbha.
By abandoning the thought of enlightenment, by not giving to a supplicant,
through intense stinginess and greed, or through striking a sentient being out of anger;
Even when being conciliated with effort, one does not exercise patience toward sentient beings—
either due to the afflictions, by following the whims of others, or by describing a counterfeit of the true Dharma.
Thus it is said.
In that very same sūtra, their extraction is stated.
Since the duties of Bodhisattvas are also taught in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, that too must be examined; thus he says:
"The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* should certainly be consulted again and again, because correct conduct is demonstrated therein in detail. (Bca 5.105)
The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* was also composed by these very same [authors] themselves;
it must certainly and invariably be consulted again and again, not just once.
The sense is that this is what should be practiced.
Why? Because for the virtuous—namely, the bodhisattvas—conduct (*ācāra*) means behavior, that is to say, the way of acting (*itikartavyatā*).
In that *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, it has been demonstrated and clearly elucidated through an extensive treatise; therefore.
If he is unable to practice that [extensively], then he should,

in brief, behold either the *Sūtrasamuccaya* or the compendium of selected portions from various sūtras composed by these very [masters]; he should see or examine it, whether in terms of the text or its meaning.
In this case as well, the purpose is the same as before. Or else: "And [this commentary] composed by the noble Nāgārjuna is the second [work], undertaken with great effort" (Bca 5.106).
One should diligently and respectfully examine the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and the *Sūtrasamuccaya*, both composed by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna;
the sense is that what is not seen here may be found there.
He states that even regarding the training in the mirror [of the Bodhisattva's discipline], it is of use to all in its entirety by way of a rule:
"Whatever one is restrained from, and whatever one is enjoined to do—one should practice that after having seen the training, for the sake of protecting the minds of the world. (Bca 5.107)
That from which one is turned away— namely, that which is to be abandoned and not to be done— is prohibited by the statement,
"This is not to be done," whether in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* or the *Sūtrasamuccaya*.
Whatever action is enjoined as something to be performed— that is, prescribed—
is well-known or established. For the sake of protecting the minds or intentions of people, [one should act accordingly].
Just as one would not cause it to be disturbed,
having seen the training in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* and other such works,
one should practice it step by step.
In whatever matter, in whatever way, and with whatever justification something is appropriate, one should conduct oneself accordingly;
otherwise, there would be the defilement of an offense due to conduct that is confused about the meaning.

By this much, the purification of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) has been explained. As it is said: "What is the purification of the personal existence? It is the cleansing of misdeeds and afflictions.
According to the words of the Perfectly Awakened One, in the absence of effort, one goes to the miserable states."
Thus it is said.
Regarding what was stated— that one should always act with mindfulness (*smṛti*) and clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*)— the essential nature of mindfulness is understood from its very name.
However, it is not known what kind of thing clear comprehension (*saṃprajanya*) is; therefore, in order to understand its essential nature, he says:
"This alone is, in brief, the definition of clear comprehension."
That which is the repeated examination of the state of one's body and mind.
It is the constant examination and investigation of the state of the body and the state of the mind during all modes of conduct, exactly as previously explained.
To establish that all this skill in the trainings taught must be accomplished through action and not by mere words alone, he says:
"I shall practice with my body itself; what would be the use of verbal recitation? What will happen to a sick person by merely reading a medical treatise? (Bca 5.109)
Since bodily activity is preceded by the mind,
that too has been established by this very [statement]:
"I shall accomplish everything through practice."
However, since mere verbal proclamation is fruitless, a bodhisattva must strive [to act accordingly].
How so? What result will be achieved for one afflicted by disease who merely studies the medical treatises but does not perform the treatment?
For the illness will not cease through that alone.
The sense is that "nothing [is attained by mere knowledge alone].
Therefore, all of this must be accomplished through the performance of ritual action.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "Guarding Vigilant Awareness," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-pañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 91) 6. The Sixth Chapter, titled "The Perfection of Patience" (*kṣāntipāramitā*).

Having thus established the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in many ways, and having established the protection and purification of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) and so forth, in order to establish the purification of the wholesome (*śubha*), it was said:
One should practice patience, seek out sacred learning, and thereafter take refuge in the forest;
one should apply oneself to meditative concentration and cultivate the contemplation of the foul and so forth.
And he begins to state this very point with the words "all this" and so forth:
"All this good conduct, giving, and worship of the Sugata..."
That which has been accomplished over a thousand eons is destroyed by a single act of resentment.
"All this" refers to wholesome action consisting of good conduct produced from the undertaking of the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*). Giving (*dāna*) is threefold.
In general, even the worship of the Sugatas is threefold;

whatever has been performed or acquired over many thousands of eons—all that is struck down and consumed by resentment and hatred toward sentient beings, just as a spark of fire consumes a heap of grass.
And it is said in the *Āryamañjuśrīvikrīḍitasūtra*: "O Mañjuśrī, 'hostility, hostility'—it destroys the merit accumulated over a hundred eons;
therefore it is called hostility."
The Noble Sarvāstivādins recite: "Behold, monks, this monk prostrating with his entire body at the stūpa of hair and nails and inspiring his mind with serene faith.
"Yes, Venerable Sir.
"Monks, by this monk, as much ground as has been traversed—"
Downward, for eighty-four thousand yojanas, as many grains of sand as there are within the interval between the golden and diamond circles—
that many thousands of universal monarchies must be enjoyed by this monk.

Then the Venerable Upāli, having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, regarding what was said by the Blessed One— that this monk possesses such great roots of merit—
where, Blessed One, do these roots of merit reach attenuation, exhaustion, and total depletion?"
"Upāli, I do not perceive any loss or harm as great as when a fellow practitioner of the holy life conceives a malicious thought toward another fellow practitioner of the holy life.
In that case, Upāli, these great roots of merit undergo diminution, exhaustion, and total destruction.
Therefore, Upāli, you should train yourself thus: 'We shall not harbor a corrupt mind even toward a burnt pillar.'"
How much more so, then, when the body is possessed of consciousness?
Therefore it is said:
"There is no evil equal to hatred, and no austerity equal to patience;
therefore, one should cultivate patience with effort through various methods. (Bca 6.2)
There is no evil or unwholesome state equal to hatred that serves as a cause for the overcoming of merit;
nor is there any austerity equal to or equivalent to patience and forbearance,
for well-performed merit is accomplished through immense exertion.
Since this is so, one should therefore cultivate and practice patience and forbearance with every effort,
by means of various and manifold methods that will be described hereafter.
(Bcp 82) Demonstrating the faults of hatred in this very life through three verses, he says:
"The mind finds no peace; it does not experience joy or happiness;
it finds neither sleep nor steadfastness while the dart of hatred remains in the heart. (Bca 6.3)
Even those whom he honors with wealth and respect, and those who have taken refuge in him,
desire to kill their master because they are ill-favored by his hatred.
Even friends are repelled by him; he gives nothing and is not served.
In short, there is nothing by which an angry person remains at ease.
He does not grasp at or rely upon tranquility or pacification;
being always unpacified because he is ablaze with the fire of hatred, he does not enjoy or attain the bliss of rapture or the bliss of mental well-being, for he is overwhelmed by that very [hatred].
One finds neither sleep, nor steadfastness, nor mental happiness, while the thorn of hatred— which causes torment to body and mind— dwells within the heart;
and even those dependents whom one honors, respects, and gratifies with gains and offerings [are likewise affected].
In this way, they wish to harm a hateful master. Why? Because "disagreeable due to hatred" and "unpleasant" are the causal phrases for this.
Even friends who are otherwise divided feel agitation and tremble before such a hateful person.
Even when intent on giving, he is not served nor approached by his circle of dependents;
what need is there for more? Let this be understood here in brief: there is no means whatsoever for the pacification of one who is prone to anger by which such a person might obtain happiness.
Hatred is the harsh state of the mind;
its manifest activity is anger, by the power of which one takes up sticks and other such weapons.
Thus, although there is a distinction between these two, they are taught as non-different because both must be abandoned.

Thus, even in this present life, one should strive to abandon hatred by understanding its faults; regarding this, he says: "He who, perceiving anger as an enemy because it produces such sufferings as these, destroys it through persistent effort, shall be happy both in this world and the next. (Bca 6.6)
Since it produces sufferings in the manner thus described, therefore, he who is of virtuous nature [should act] out of persistence— that is,
from intense resolve.
The meaning is that he has initiated vigor;
he is happy both in this world and in the next world.
Now, establishing a method to destroy hatred by striking at its cause, he says:
"Born from the doing of what is undesirable and from the obstruction of what is desired, hatred—having found its food in mental distress—proudly destroys me. (Bca 6.7)
Therefore, I shall obstruct the food of that enemy:
desire and aversion, which are born from the grasping at "self" and "mine.
In this context, that which is a means to the happiness of self and mine is desired.
The opposite of that is "undesirable";
thus, this is merely a product of conceptual construction.
In ultimate reality, however, nothing whatsoever exists that is either desirable or undesirable.

Therefore, due to the force of the latencies of false attachment, because of performing what is undesirable and obstructing what is desirable, mental distress— suffering of the mind— is produced; from that, hatred arises toward that which performs such [actions] or toward that which opposes it.

Thus, having determined that it is indeed mental distress (*daurmanasya*)— acting as powerful nourishment— that, once it has gained strength, destroys me through hatred, I shall first destroy its cause of growth;
when that is destroyed, there will be nothing but happiness.
Because of its destruction,
and because that which has been destroyed root and branch cannot arise again.
"Now, why do you have such an excessive attachment [to this body]? To this he says:
"Because for this enemy, there is no other task [to be accomplished] than my killing. (Bca 6.8)
For there is nothing else that my enemy, Hatred, must do day or night other than to bring about my death.

Having thus analyzed the faults of hatred, one should generate its antidote, patience (*kṣānti*), by every possible means. In this regard, three kinds of patience are taught in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*, namely:
the patience of enduring suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanākṣānti*).
There are the patience of reflecting on the Dharma and the patience of enduring the injuries of others.
Regarding these, he first speaks with reference to the patience of enduring suffering:
Even through the arrival of the most undesirable, my joy must not be disturbed;
for even in dejection there is no gain, whereas the wholesome is lost.
The opposite of the patience that endures suffering is the fear of attaining or encountering what is undesirable,
as well as attachment to pleasure when one encounters the loss of what is desired; from these two arises mental distress (*daurmanasya*).
From that, there arises either hatred or a state of mental dejection;
for this very reason, it is said in the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*: "Non-attachment to pleasure, and non-aversion toward suffering."
Thus it is said.
It is also stated in the *Ratnamegha-sūtra*: "Whatever internal sorrows, lamentations, sufferings, dejections, and despairs there may be, he endures and tolerates them."
Therefore, even if my head were to be cut off, I must not be disturbed nor should I allow my joy to be shaken;
for joy is the antidote to dejection.
Because there is no room for dejection when the mind is joyful even at the onset of suffering, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) must be protected with effort in order to eliminate dejection.
Why? Because even if dejection is produced when a desired object is thwarted, that which was desired and longed for will not be accomplished.
But this would be the distinction: wholesome [states], moreover, are destroyed.

And sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is described in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*: "In that regard, what is sympathetic joy? It is the gladness, clarity, and rapture arising from recollecting the qualities of a Buddha; it is the non-depression and non-subjugation of the mind, and the absence of thirsting desire, because it draws away all delights in sensual pleasures and establishes one in the delight in all [spiritual] dharmas."
Joy of the mind, buoyancy of the body,
and exhilaration of the intellect.
The mind is like a blue lotus,
delighting in the joy of the Tathāgata’s body;
such is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, he asks why dejection arises in one who does not investigate:
"If there is indeed a remedy, what is the use of dejection in that case?
But if there is no remedy, what is the use of dejection in that case? (Bca 6.10)
And if there exists another means— a remedy— to avert the destruction of what is desired and to prevent the onset of what is undesired,
then what is the use of mental distress in that case?
Let that very remedy be practiced.
If, on the other hand, it does not exist, then what is the use of mental distress in that regard? It serves no purpose whatsoever.
Since there is no means [to achieve it], this matter is entirely lost.
Having reflected thus, it is better simply to turn back dejection.
He begins to establish that suffering becomes non-obstructive through habituation:
"Suffering, humiliation, harshness, and infamy are undesirable;
for one's own dear ones and even for an enemy, it is the opposite. (Bca 6.11)
Suffering is twofold: physical and mental. Among these, physical suffering arises from being struck by sticks and the like; mental suffering has its cause in humiliation and the like.
In this context, "humiliation" (*nyakkāra*) means contempt (*dhikkāra*);
"harshness" (*pārūṣya*) is speech that strikes at one's vital points;
and "infamy" (*ayaśas*) is ill-repute, which is the manifestation of one's deficiencies.
All this is undesirable; yet, is it not indeed for the welfare of others? To address that point, he says: "of those who are dear."
Those who have been accepted as "mine" are objects of love for both themselves and for oneself;
however, for an enemy who causes suffering and the like, it is the opposite of this.
For him, suffering and so forth are indeed desired.
In that regard, he speaks first to dispel the inability to endure suffering:
"Happiness is obtained only with difficulty, while suffering remains effortlessly;
and liberation is attained through suffering alone. Therefore, O mind, be firm! (Bca 6.12)
Having cultivated the side of wholesome qualities with great effort, one occasionally and at some point attains the contaminated happiness within saṃsāra, which is extremely difficult to find;
suffering, however, is always easily obtained,
because it is established without effort.
Thus, the practice of that is not difficult, because it is familiar at all times.
Furthermore:
Even the means for escaping saṃsāra is nothing but suffering;
nevertheless, it is indeed appropriate to take hold of it as a form of provisions for the journey.
Since this is so, therefore, O mind:
Be firm for the experiencing of suffering;
do not resort to cowardice.
Furthermore, one should reflect in the mind that "this suffering is fit to be endured because it accomplishes a great purpose"; thus he says:
"The Durgā-putrakas and Karṇāṭas [endure] the pain of burning, cutting, and so forth."
They endure [suffering] in vain for the sake of liberation; why then am I so cowardly?

The Durgā-putrakas, the sons of Caṇḍī, having fasted for three nights or one day during the period of Mahānavamī and other such occasions, undergo painful sensations—inflicting burning, cutting, and piercing upon their own bodies—yet experience them entirely without fruit.

Likewise, the Southerners originating from regions such as Karṇāṭa, out of pride in merely writing their own names above others, compete with one another; experiencing suffering through various causes, they even cast away their lives.
But why should I become faint-hearted because of sufferings when I have exerted myself to achieve Buddhahood, which is most difficult for both myself and others to attain?
One might argue: "A very slight suffering can somehow be endured;
but how indeed should one endure the suffering of having one's hands, feet, and head cut off, or the sufferings of hell and so forth, for the sake of liberation? To this, he says:
There is no object whatsoever that is difficult for habituation to accomplish;
therefore, by practicing with mild pain, even great pain can be endured.

There is no object whatsoever—whether it be proficiency in the study of the scriptures, artistic skills, or the experience of mild, moderate, or intense suffering—that does not become the domain of practice.
The sense is that everything can indeed be mastered through practice.
Therefore, by practicing even the slightest pain, one becomes able to endure even the great torments of hell and the like.
As it has been said: "In that regard, the practice of what is more painful and most painful is accomplished by being preceded by the practice of slight pain.
And just as, through the power of habituation, sentient beings have the perception of pleasure in what is actually suffering," (Bcp 85)
Likewise, through the practice of establishing the perception of pleasure even amidst the arising of all sufferings, only the perception of pleasure arises.
In this way, as a natural outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), one attains the samādhi called "Pervaded by the Pleasure of All Dharmas.
For it is said in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*:
“Blessed One, there is a samādhi called ‘Pervaded by the Happiness of All Phenomena.
By the attainment of this samādhi, a bodhisattva experiences only pleasant feeling toward all objective referents, and not painful feeling,
nor neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.”
Even when undergoing the torments of hellish suffering, only the perception of pleasure arises for him; likewise even when undergoing human tortures,
even while his hands, feet, ears, and noses are being cut off.
The very perception of pleasure becomes present;
even when being struck with canes, or even with half-caned whips, or being lashed with whips, the perception of pleasure arises;
even for one cast into prisons, [the perception of pleasure arises].
Or while oil is being pressed,
or sugarcane is being crushed,
or reeds are being flattened.
Whether being burned by a lamp of oil, or being cut into pieces as small as a kārṣāpaṇa coin, or being cooked in a frying pan,
or being trampled by elephants, the perception of pleasure alone arises.
Thus is the detailed exposition.
This might indeed be so if there were practice in mild suffering from the very beginning;
however, that very thing does not exist. To this, he says:
"The sensations of gadflies, mosquitoes, hunger, thirst, and so forth..."
And do you not see that great suffering from itching and other ailments is entirely purposeless?
Do you not see the harm and suffering caused by gadflies and the like?
The point is that such [suffering] exists as something easily accomplished, serving as the cause for habituating oneself to mild pain.
Furthermore, in order to strengthen one's own mind in another way, he says:
"One should not cultivate delicacy toward cold, heat, rain, wind, travel, disease, imprisonment, and beating; otherwise, suffering increases. (Bca 6.16)
For one whose mind is exceedingly delicate, suffering becomes an extreme affliction;
however, for one whose mind is firm even in the face of suffering, the opposite is true.
[Objection: "But even when the mind is being strengthened, suffering remains indeed unbearable. To this, he says:
"Some, upon seeing their own blood, exert themselves all the more;
yet others, upon seeing the blood of another, fall into a swoon" (Bca 6.17).
Since that [suffering] has arrived through the mind's either firmness or its cowardice,
one should therefore become difficult for suffering to conquer and should overcome the affliction.
Indeed, for one whose mind is firm, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
For instance, certain heroic men, even upon seeing their own blood on the field of battle, exhibit an even greater degree of valor;
whereas others, whose mental continuums are characterized by cowardice, [faint] even at the sight of another's blood.
They experience the suffering that ends with death.

Considering that both of these result from the mind’s mutual habituation and its opposite, one should not be overcome by suffering; for, being unshakable even by sufferings, one would not be subject to them.
Then one overcomes suffering; one is no longer overcome by it.
Thinking, "In this way too, I shall overcome suffering," he says:
"Even in the face of pain, the wise person should not disturb the clarity of the mind;
for that is a battle with the afflictions, and in combat, suffering is easily encountered. (Bca 6.19)
A wise person should not allow the aforementioned clarity of mind to decline.
Why? Because this battle has been commenced against the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
And in a battle, it is difficult to ensure that there shall be no suffering.
But suffering is indeed easily obtained.

[Objection: "Even so, this appears to be exceedingly difficult. To this he says: "Those who, enduring even mortal blows with their chests, conquer their enemies—they are the victorious heroes; all others are merely slayers of the dead. (Bca 6.20)
Those who overcome the enemy face-to-face,
who receive his blows upon their own chests, and who conquer their foes in battle—
those heroic men, having achieved victory here through the conquest of the enemy, are highly praised.

Furthermore, those others who overcome an enemy by means of deceptive strikes and the like are merely killers of the dead; because they accomplish nothing, they are indeed objects of contempt for the truly brave.
For this reason as well, one should endure suffering by seeing its virtues; thus he says:

"And another virtue of suffering is that through it comes the loss of intoxication via spiritual urgency (saṃvega), compassion for those in cyclic existence, fear of evil, and longing for the Victor. (Bca 6.21)
This is another virtuous cause, a quality conducive to the path of awakening for this suffering:
that when suffering enters the mind, a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) arises;
and from that, the fall and destruction of the intoxication caused by youth, wealth, and so forth, occurs.
There is a mind of compassion toward those wandering in saṃsāra who are oppressed by the sufferings of saṃsāra;
a mind of fear regarding evil and a resolve not to commit it, thinking, "This is the fruit of evil";
and longing, devotion, faith, and clarity of mind toward the Buddha, the Blessed One.
For it was the Blessed One alone who taught the path leading to the destruction of suffering.
Reflecting on the endurance of suffering arising from external conditions, he says:
"I feel no anger even toward bile and other humors, though they cause great pain; why then should I be angry with sentient beings? For they too are provoked by external conditions. (Bca 6.22)

The body is composed of the three humors, beginning with bile (pitta). When these humors reach an unbalanced state due to the improper nature of diet and lifestyle, they give rise to diseases and become the causes of all suffering.
Nevertheless, I feel no anger toward them.
Because they lack consciousness,
they do not intentionally inflict suffering;
rather, they have become provoked by the power of the totality of their own causes.
If this is so, why be angry with sentient beings?
If you ask, "Why should it not be so?
[the answer is that] they too, due to the transgression of their past karma, become givers of suffering when provoked by the totality of their own causes.
Thus, as in the case of bile and other humors, anger toward them is not appropriate for me.

(Bcp 87) Demonstrating that dependence on causes is the same in both cases, he says: "Just as this pain arises even though it is not desired, so too anger arises by force even though it is not desired. (Bca 6.23)
Just as pain, though unintended, necessarily arises from bile and other humors whose capacities are produced by their own conditions,
so too does anger arise from dejection and other states whose powers are acquired through the transformation of their own causes; thus, both are equally dependent upon causes and conditions.
Now, it might be argued: "It has been stated here that those who possess consciousness act in such an undesirable manner after having reflected; however, others do not do so. To this he says:
"A person does not become angry by reflecting, 'I shall be angry,' but rather becomes angry of his own accord."
Thinking "I shall arise," anger does not actually arise.
Without the collection of conditions that serve as its cause, a person does not become angry at will, having first reflected with deliberate intent;
nor does anger arise independently, having intended for itself, "I shall arise."
Therefore, he says that this alone is established here by valid cognition:
"Whatever offenses there may be, and whatever various sins, all those arise through the power of conditions; nothing exists independently. (Bca 6.25)
All this has as its inherent nature that which is established solely through specific conditionality;
nothing whatsoever exists that functions independently.
The collection of conditions has no volition that "I shall produce," nor does that which has been produced have the volition "I have been produced. (Bca 6.26)
Even the totality of conditions (*pratyayasāmagrī*), while producing its own effect, does not produce it through volition;
for it produces such an effect by virtue of the nature of things (*dharmatā*) resulting from the transformation of its own causes, but not through volition.
Furthermore, once the effect has been produced, there is no thought or mental attention (*manasikāra*) on the part of that effect, thinking, "I have been produced by this totality of conditions."
Therefore, because all phenomena are devoid of activity,
when this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises.
Thus, this world is merely a matter of specific conditionality;
herein, nothing whatsoever exists independently,
because all phenomena are dependent upon causes and conditions.
It might be argued: "There certainly exists that which is independent, such as the *pradhāna* and the Self (*ātman*) for the Sāṃkhyas, and space (*ākāśa*) and so forth for the Naiyāyikas.
Why, then, is it said that nothing whatsoever exists here that is independent?"

Anticipating this objection, he says: "That which is indeed desired as the primary [cause] among these, and which is imagined to be the Self—that very thing arises without being consciously willed, out of fear of existence. (Bca 6.27)
That which is accepted by you as *prakṛti*, *pradhāna*, or the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—
the word "it is said" (*kila*) indicates a lack of conviction, signifying that this is not consistent with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, whatever entity is imagined or determined to be the *ātman* is likewise entirely inconsistent with valid means of knowledge.
He said: Because that very thing does not arise with the intention, "I shall come into being" or "I shall originate," since it lacks any other cause for itself.
Why?
Because that which is unarisen does not exist; who then could desire to become it at that time?
That [cause], such as Pradhāna and so forth, was previously non-existent;
and for that which is non-existent, like the son of a barren woman, what desire could there be to come into being or to arise?
Or, if nothing non-existent arises, [then...]
It is merely a transformation from the unmanifest state into the manifest state.
If this is so, how can a transformation—or the manifest state itself—arise if it is non-existent?
Since both the transformation and the manifest state possess that [unmanifest] as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it would follow that they too must arise [as something previously non-existent].
If there were difference, there would be an absence of relation;
and if one were to postulate a relation, there would be an infinite regress.
The Pradhāna will be refuted at length later [9.127–138].
It might be argued: "This fault does not apply to the self;
for we do not accept its production.
Since it is eternally of a permanent nature, it is indeed unproduced."
Let it be so;
nevertheless, in every respect, it is just like the horn of a donkey,
because of the absence of arising.
Therefore, one does not desist even here [from the argument]:
"For that which is unarisen does not exist; who then would desire to become it?
Thus.
Or even if he exists, he possesses no sovereignty even over himself;
for he experiences even an object only when it is presented by primordial nature (prakṛti).
And at that time, prior to the enjoyment of the object, his status as its enjoyer did not exist.
And that which arises later is of the very same nature [as the former],
for otherwise its status as an enjoyer would be untenable.
Since its arising implies the arising of that [self] as well, how can it be that the arising of the self is not admitted?
Thus, furthermore,
since that which has not arisen does not exist, who then would wish to become it? This conclusion follows.
He states another refutation here as well:
"And because it is occupied with its objects, it does not even strive to cease. (Bca 6.28)

Even if it is maintained that this [consciousness] proceeds for the sake of experiencing objects presented by the *pradhāna*, then the subsequent activity of that which was previously inactive is not logical.
Or, if it somehow does proceed, [how could this be?]
Even then, there would be no cessation for one who is still engaged with sense objects. This very point is stated: "He does not even strive to restrain [them].
He does not even have the resolve to turn away from the enjoyment of sense objects.
For at that time, it would possess that very nature,
and since that nature is eternal, it could not cease; or else, if it were to cease, it would follow that it is impermanent.
The designation of a self by the Naiyāyikas and others is due to its permanence.
He also states its specific distinction: "For the self is eternal, insentient, and clearly inactive like space;
here, insentiency is the distinction [from the Sāṃkhya view]."
Elsewhere there is equality:
in that regard, it is eternal, having one and the same nature in earlier and later times;
and it is insentient, having the nature of non-consciousness.
The meaning is that it is insentient;
it perceives through association with another consciousness;
and it is all-pervading like space.
For this very reason, it is clearly and manifestly inactive. As it has been said:
"Others, moreover, here desire the self to be the substratum of desire and the rest, inherently insentient by nature, eternal, and likewise all-pervading."
It is the agent of pure and impure actions and the experiencer of their fruit; it is conscious due to its association with consciousness, not by its own intrinsic nature.
And thus, it is indeed incapable of anything, because it is of no use in any effect whatsoever.
Now, if it is argued that its activity is admitted even though it is inactive when other auxiliary conditions are present— as it has been said:
"The connection with knowledge, effort, and so forth is said to be its agency.
To this, he replies:
"Even when there is contact with other conditions, what action can there be for that which is changeless? (Bca 6.29)
Even when in contact with other conditions such as knowledge, effort, and so forth, what action can there be for the self—which, being eternal and changeless, has not deviated from its prior nature?
No action whatsoever is possible.
As before, what has been done by that [agent] during the time of the action?
In the relationship "this is his action," what is the basis for that connection?
Just as it was previously at the time of non-action, so too at the time of action, that which is devoid of the nature of an agent— what has been done by it regarding action,
such that its action could be established upon contact with other conditions? Furthermore:
Since there is no connection with either [of the two], what other cause could there be for the relation that "this action belongs to that self"?
There is none at all.
Since the self will be refuted in detail [9.58–60] and God as well [9.119–126],
no one whatsoever can be independent. Having thus established the lack of independence everywhere, he concludes by saying:
Thus everything is under the control of another, and that [controller] too is without autonomy;
since all things are thus motionless like magical illusions, where is there any cause for anger?
In this manner, according to the principle stated, the entire collection of external and internal things is dependent on another and subject to others.
If it is argued that there must then be something under whose control these things are not dependent on another, [the answer is] no;
for even that which exercises such control is itself powerless, being dependent upon its own causes.
In this way, since that cause also arises from its own cause, no independence whatsoever is possible within the beginningless succession of saṃsāra.
Therefore, all phenomena are devoid of agency;
in ultimate reality, who harms whom, such that it would be appropriate for someone to feel hatred toward another who has committed an offense?
This very point is stated: because all conceptualization of activity has vanished like a magical creation, and since all phenomena are thus inactive and effortless, where could anger be directed?
The meaning is that for those possessed of discernment, anger toward anything whatsoever is not appropriate.

It might be argued as follows: "In this way, while one [alternative] is established, the second is undermined. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even prevention is not tenable in this manner; for if it is asked, 'Who prevents what?'—then by the very logic already established, even prevention—that is, cessation—is not tenable in the case of entities that are inactive, just like a magical creation (*nirmāṇa*)."
Thus, when not even the slightest thing is seen to be independent, and everything arises in dependence upon a collection of conditions, then even a prohibition is not tenable.
Or rather—let it not be so;
nevertheless, why is it not logical?
Who prevents it?

If it is asked, "The agent is independent; what is there to be negated? [Does he] prevent that which has proceeded independently?"—the intention here is this: for even when the principle is the same, activity does not occur in every case because it is a general property.
Therefore, it is correct to say that prevention is not logical.
If you think thus, he states the following reply:
"Dependence is logical, because the cessation of suffering is held [to result from it]. (Bca 6.32)
The refutation is appropriate; why?
Because of dependent nature:
since there exists the state of being dependently originated—namely, that "depending on this, this arises"—even among entities that are devoid of activity.
Therefore, the refutation is appropriate, and consequently there is no contradiction.
This is what is meant: although all phenomena are devoid of activity, [the refutation remains valid].
Nevertheless, dependence is demonstrated by the power of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), according to such statements as: "In this way, everything is under the control of another" (6.31).
Therefore, by the force of conditions such as ignorance, the successive stream of effects in the form of mental formations (saṃskāra) and so forth proceeds;
when each preceding factor ceases, the subsequent one ceases.
And this will be explained in detail later [at 9.75].
Therefore, the cessation and turning away from the suffering of saṃsāra is intended;
hence, the prevention of the engagement in evils such as hatred and so forth is logically consistent.
Depending upon that, a fruit consisting of the nature of higher worldly prosperity and the ultimate good arises.
Now, applying this very point to the subject at hand, he says:
"Therefore, whether seeing an enemy or a friend acting unjustly, one should remain happy by reflecting: 'Such are the conditions that have arisen for him. (Bca 6.33)
Since everything is dependently arisen, therefore one should take only happiness as the object of focus, even in relation to a non-friend, a friend, or a wrongdoer.
Why? Because such causes for performing harm belong to this non-friend or the other.
Having thus resolved, one should be happy and should not give way to dejection.
Furthermore, demonstrating that there is no cessation of suffering even when the mind is disturbed by the onset of pain, he says:
"If, however, success were achieved by one's own will for all embodied beings, no one would experience suffering, for no one desires suffering. (Bca 6.34)
For indeed, that which is not desired does not cease, nor does that which is desired appear, merely by the wish of the self in the absence of a cause;
if it were so, no sentient being would ever experience suffering.
Why is this? No one desires suffering for themselves;
for all sentient beings indeed desire their own happiness.

Having explained the patience of enduring suffering, he now speaks to demonstrate the patience of forbearing harm from others: "Out of negligence, they injure themselves with thorns and the like; out of anger, by depriving themselves of food and so forth; and out of a desire to obtain power and such things. (Bca 6.35)
Some kill themselves by hanging or by falling from heights, by consuming poison or unwholesome food,
and by the performance of non-virtuous deeds.
When, being under the power of the afflictions, they destroy even their own dear selves,
how then could there be any avoidance of harm toward the bodies of others?
(Bcp 91) Acting without due consideration is negligence (*pramāda*).

Those engaged in worldly activities (*karmapravṛtta*) themselves afflict their own bodies with thorns, stumps, debris, stones, pebbles, and the like on difficult paths, or by lying down upon beds strewn with thorns;
likewise, they afflict them through the avoidance of food and drink, and so forth.
Why? Out of anger, or with the desire to obtain that which is forbidden, such as another's wife or wealth.
Hanging is suspension by means of a rope; falling is tumbling down from a mountain or similar precipice;
[death] occurs through such means as entering water or fire.
By consuming poison, unwholesome food, and the like, and by excessive eating and drinking, certain deluded persons destroy— that is, kill— their own selves, their very bodies.
Through the killing of others and so forth,
and by the performance of non-meritorious actions;
through the intention to kill others and by unwholesome conduct in battles and similar situations.

When, according to the sequence thus described, these sentient beings— due to being subject to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and being dependent upon the afflictions— strike even their own dear and beloved selves and cause them pain,
then how could there be for them a cessation of harmful intent toward the bodies of others, the bodies of others? And in this way, they are indeed objects of compassion.
He says that there is no basis for hatred:
"When these people, maddened by afflictions, are engaged in self-destruction, not only is there no compassion, but how could anger even arise? (Bca 6.38).

When these doers of harm are seized as if by *piśācas* and proceed toward self-destruction—either directly or by way of harming others—according to the principle already stated, it is not merely that compassion is absent;
even indifference on the part of the virtuous would be improper there.
How could hatred arise toward those who are objects of compassion? This is a great perversion.

Thus, he says that one should likewise restrain one's own mind: "If it is the very nature of fools to cause harm to others, it is not fitting for me to feel anger toward them, just as it is not fitting to be angry at fire for its inherent quality of burning. (Bca 6.39)
For in this regard, there are two possible alternatives:
either the nature of foolish ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) is precisely such that it consists in causing harm to others,
in which case their nature does not admit of questioning— namely, "Why do they commit injury to others?"— or else [their nature is different].
Having reflected thus, it is not proper for me to feel hatred toward them; just as it is not proper toward fire, whose very nature is burning, because it performs the act of burning.
Otherwise, in the absence of that [act], there would follow the undesirable consequence of its losing its essential nature.
With reference to the second alternative, he says:
"Now, if this fault is adventitious and sentient beings are by nature gentle, nevertheless, their anger is improper, like pungent smoke in the sky. (Bca 6.40)
Now, this fault is adventitious and distinct from them; it does not constitute their intrinsic nature.
Sentient beings, moreover, because their mental continua are luminous by nature, are gentle and of an upright disposition. For faults are of a corrupt nature.
Sentient beings do not possess that nature;
nevertheless, anger toward those beings who are gentle by nature is improper.
Toward what, for instance, would it be appropriate?
Just as pungent smoke [appears] in the sky,
pungency is indeed not the intrinsic nature of the pure sky, but rather that of the smoke.
Therefore, it is appropriate that the fault belongs to the smoke itself due to its own defect, and not to the sky which is naturally pure.
Consequently, anger is fittingly directed toward faults alone, and not toward sentient beings.
Moreover, anger should indeed be directed toward that which is the primary cause of suffering, and not toward what is secondary; thus he says:
"If, having set aside the actual instrument such as the staff, one becomes angry with the instigator..."
Even if he is impelled by hatred, let there be hatred toward that hatred; this is better for me.
For when a blow from a stick falls upon the body, suffering arises for one whose mind is untrained;
therefore, the stick itself is the primary cause of the suffering, and it is thus appropriate to direct anger toward it.
But what fault is there in the stick being impelled by another?
Therefore, it is the instigator alone who becomes the object of hatred.
If that is the case, then since he too was impelled by hatred to wield the staff, my hatred is properly directed toward that hatred itself, not toward the instigator.

Moreover, reflecting that "neither pleasure nor pain is experienced by anyone without it being taken [from another]," one should not allow the mind to become corrupted even when others cause harm; thus it is said:
"In the past, I too inflicted such very same suffering upon sentient beings."
Therefore, this is indeed appropriate for me [to do] toward those who cause harm to sentient beings.

"In a previous birth, I too inflicted such suffering upon sentient beings; therefore, for me who have committed harm against others, this is entirely appropriate according to the principle of clearing a debt.
The meaning is that it arises from the ripening of the fruit of those actions."
Reflecting that "this arises from this cause and not from another," one should endure harm inflicted by others; thus, showing this, he says:
"That weapon and my body—both are causes of suffering.
Since I have taken up the body for the sake of that weapon, at what should I be angry? (Bca 6.43)
For it is established by valid cognition that the complete assembly of unimpaired causes is the cause of every effect, and such an assembly exists here;
namely, the weapon— such as a sword— and my own body belonging to that harmful person.
These two, being in the form of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), are the cause of suffering.
Thus, even though the efficient cause exists, why would the effect not arise?
Otherwise, that [complex] would not be its cause at all.
Furthermore, is there something else [than that], namely, the conjunction of its production (utpādayoga)—
that is to say, would there be another cause [besides] from its causal totality (sāmagrī)?
Therefore... if you are angry with the one who brings about the cause [of your suffering], then it is equally appropriate to be angry with yourself;
for you yourself carry and bring forth the causes of suffering.
The sense is that if there is no anger toward oneself, it is likewise not appropriate toward another.
Clarifying the very same point stated by way of another method, he says:
"This lump in the form of an image has been grasped by me, blinded by craving, though it is incapable of being struck. Why, then, should I be angry at the pain therein? (Bca 6.44)
This physical form is like a ripe boil that I have taken hold of;
because it is the cause of all suffering, it endures every kind of crushing;
and because it cannot be broken even by beating, striking, and the like.

Regarding that craving and longing for the avoidance of suffering and the attainment of happiness, when that pain exists, where can one be angry— especially by one who is blinded and whose eye of wisdom is covered?
Indeed, it is not at all appropriate for one who possesses discernment to be angry with anything when the pain of a boil arises from contact with a wall or similar object.
Moreover, one who has no need for an effect ought to avoid its very cause.
However, demonstrating his own reflection— that he possesses a perverted mind— he says:
"I do not desire suffering, yet as a fool I desire the cause of suffering; since suffering has come about through my own transgression, why am I angry with another? (Bca 6.45)

I do not desire suffering born from blows with sticks and the like; however, I do desire its cause—the body—which acts as an adversary. "Foolish" refers to the nature of a fool, which is perversion (*viparyāsa*).

Therefore, for this reason, whatever suffering exists within one's own body has arisen solely from one's own transgression. Why, then, does one become angry with another who is merely a cooperative condition for it?
It is said that anger toward another is not appropriate for me, just as it would be improper for one who has fashioned a weapon oneself for their own destruction to direct anger elsewhere.
Just as the forest of sword-leaves and the birds of hell are produced solely by my own karma, so too is this; at whom, then, should one be angry?
The Sword-Leaf Forest (Asipatravana) arises from hell;
it is so called because its leaves are indeed swords.
The mention of "swords" is used because they are the predominant feature.
Furthermore, other weapons and mechanical contrivances are also causes of suffering for those in hell;
likewise, the birds dwelling in that forest—such as vultures, owls, and crows—are produced solely by my own karma as causes of suffering.
There is no other cause of suffering here.
Likewise, this enemy weapon and so forth, which is the cause of suffering, is produced solely by my own karma; so why be angry at anyone?
To demonstrate that even in this way it is merely a misconception, he says:
Impelled by my own karma, they have become my wrongdoers;
since they will go to the hells, are they not indeed already slain by me?

"Since these wrongdoers, impelled and driven by my own past actions, have become injurious toward me—even though I previously inflicted injuries upon them—and are thus destined for hell, have they not been slain by me alone?
[The Bodhisattva] addresses his own mind: 'I have not been harmed by these.'"
This is the intended meaning: "If I had not performed such an action, then even these people would not have become my wrongdoers"; thus, it is by my own action alone that they become wrongdoers.
Showing this through two verses by stating, "Out of delusion, I perceive those who have been helpful as those who have harmed me," he says:
"Relying upon these very people, my great evil is destroyed through my forbearance;
yet, relying upon me, they go to hells of long-lasting suffering. (Bca 6.48)
"I alone am the wrongdoer toward these people, yet they are my benefactors;
why, having reversed this truth, do you, with a wicked mind, become angry? (Bca 6.49)

By relying upon these wrongdoers and taking them as the occasion, my evil—produced by the harm done to others in previous lives—is exhausted; it comes to an end through the ripening of experiencing that suffering. For one who is patient, who takes forbearance as their objective, much has been accomplished in many ways.
Relying upon me and impelled by my own karma, even after committing such harm, these beings again go to the hells, which involve intense sensations and the experience of unbearable suffering.
Therefore, according to the sequence explained, it is clearly understood that I alone am the one who harms them, and so forth.
(Bcp 94) Now, if you are the one who causes harm, then it is fitting that you alone go to hell, and not these others; to this he says:
If my own intention were virtuous, I would not go to the hells;
what concern of theirs is it here if I have protected myself? (Bca 6.50)
This culmination in the cessation of retaliation is the greatness of my intention (*āśaya*), which is the cause for the cessation of rebirth in the hell realms.
By the power of the greatness of that very intention, I do not go to the hells;
the sense is that it is not due to their evil intentions that I fall into the hells.
He says this very thing with the words beginning "of these" (*eṣām*).
The collective meaning here is as follows: if, even though I am an offender, I do not go to the hells due to some skillful means (*upāyakauśala*), then for these [beings]...
What has happened to those who have done harm, and what is lost to them?
The meaning is: what injury [is there]?
First, by my protecting only one person, the others would not be protected, nor would I myself be protected;
yet by this much, there would be no increase or decrease whatsoever in their virtues or faults.

Now, one might object: "Even if this were so, it is still not proper for you to protect them out of gratitude for their assistance. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even if I were to retaliate, even then these [beings] would not have been protected."
My conduct also declines; therefore, the ascetics have perished.
Even if I were to retaliate against those who inflict blows with sticks and the like,
they would still not be protected;
no remedy whatsoever would have been provided for them regarding their descent into the hells and other such states.
On the contrary, even when struck by me, I must not strike back;
likewise, I must never abandon a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings,
nor should I give rise to a mind of resentment even toward a burnt pillar.
If I were to do so, there would surely be a decline in my own bodhisattva conduct.
Therefore, since there is currently no means of remedy and these wretched, miserable beings cannot be protected, they are lost and have already fallen into the miserable realms;
thus, for now, they are left in neglect.
Afterwards, having attained the means for that, I shall act in such a way that not even a particle of suffering remains for them.
Having thus established the patience of enduring harm from others, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the patience of reflecting on the Dharma:
"The mind cannot be struck by anyone anywhere because it is formless;
however, due to attachment to the body, the consciousness is afflicted by suffering. (Bca 6.52)
Twofold suffering arises as an affliction for one who lacks discernment: that which is physical and that which is mental.
Among these, no one is able to inflict a staff or the like upon the mind, because the mind is formless.
Thus, suffering arising from that does not exist in the ultimate sense;
however, mental distress and the like produced by conceptual construction do exist.
This very point is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "in the body," and so forth.
Due to the force of the habitual tendencies of the conceptualization "this body is mine," the mind is afflicted by physical suffering.
In that regard, he states that the causes of suffering are indeed specific:
"This group—insult, harsh speech, and ill-repute—does not afflict the body; therefore, why does your mind become agitated? (Bca 6.53).
The group beginning with insults is not a cause of suffering for the body;
for it does not inflict any injury upon the body.
Therefore, for what reason does your mind become agitated?
Furthermore, one might think: "Even if insults and the like do not cause physical harm to the body, nevertheless, upon hearing them, people will develop a lack of faith toward me;
therefore, I cannot accept this. Anticipating such a concern, he says:
