If others have a lack of faith toward me, how will that devour me, whether in this life or in another, such that it would be undesirable to me? (Bca 6.54)
Let it be so; nevertheless, this must still be investigated:
regarding me, because of hearing reports of insults and the like, there is this lack of favor from people.

Having reflected, "Will he devour me in this world or in the next world, such that this lack of public confidence in me would be unpleasant? one should not harbor any obsessive attachment to this matter.

Is there not, then, a reason for attachment here, namely the obstruction of gain? To this he says: "If he is undesirable to me because he causes an obstacle to my gain, then my gain will perish right here, but my sin will certainly remain. (Bca 6.55)
For instance, upon hearing of insults and the like, people lose their confidence;
from that, they turn away from offering gifts and gains.
If you think, "Therefore, this collection of insults and so forth is undesirable to me," [the response follows].
That is incorrect;
it will perish, for it is subject to the nature of decay, and it will pass away.
My gain shall occur right here within these very specific days.
But it will not follow one into the next world.
On the contrary, the very sin that arises from being angry with those who treat one with contempt and the like will remain supreme; it will follow one into the next world.
This is certain because, as long as its fruit has not been exhausted, that [sin] does not perish.
This too should be reflected upon here:
"Better for me to die this very day than a long life of falsehood;
for even if I were to remain for a long time, that same suffering of death would eventually be mine."

This alone is better and more excellent: that my death occur this very day due to the absence of gain, rather than a long and protracted life of false livelihood through the acquisition of gain by means of harming others.
Why? Because even if one lives for a much longer time, life ends in death; thus, the suffering of that inevitable death shall be mine nonetheless.
"That which will happen after a hundred years has passed is exactly the same as what happens to me now as I am dying"; thus, there is no difference between those who live long and those who do not.
Showing that there is likewise no distinction even from this [point of view], he says in two verses:
"Whether one who has enjoyed happiness for a hundred years in a dream wakes up,
or another who, having been happy for a mere moment, wakes up," (Bca 6.57)
Surely, happiness ceases for both once they have awakened;
that very same analogy applies at the time of death to one who has lived long and one who has lived but a short while.

(Bcp 96) Just as someone who has awakened after experiencing a hundred years of happiness in a dream might consider himself happy for that duration, whereas another person, having awakened after only a single moment,
considers himself happy for that same length of time.
In both of these cases, when one has awakened from the experience of pleasure obtained in a dream, that pleasure which was obtained and then vanished does not return;
it does not persist in the waking state,
because it remains as nothing more than a mere memory.
That very comparison applies to two men who have experienced pleasure in a dream—the long-lived and the short-lived—at the time of death, at the moment of dying.
[The word *saukhya*] is formed with the suffix *-aṇ* in its own sense (*svārthe*), as in "pleasure ceases.
Thus, enough of this false life!
Showing that there is no difference whatsoever between gain and loss even for this reason, he says:
"Even after obtaining many gains and enjoying pleasures for a long time, I shall depart empty-handed and naked, like one who has been robbed. (Bca 6.59)
Even after obtaining very abundant gains and attaining them,
and even after enjoying pleasures for a long time,
one encounters death once more with empty hands and hollow hands.
Therefore, not even the slightest bit of provisions was taken from those gains; nor did anything remain as a remnant of my happiness.
Not even a mere waist-string was left behind, so that I shall go from this world to the next world naked, like one who has been plundered by thieves.

It might be argued as follows: there is indeed a distinction; because robes and other requisites are not lacking and because the life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) are sustained, one’s life would last for a much longer time.

Consequently, one could effect the exhaustion of previously committed evil through the practice of remorse and so forth, and the increase of the side of virtue through the preservation of the vows of training (*śikṣā-saṃvara*), the cultivation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), and so on—as it has been said:
As long as one who practices the Dharma lives, for that long they produce a continuous stream of virtue.
Thus it is said.
Anticipating the objection that "therefore, hatred toward one who creates an obstacle to gain is indeed appropriate," he says:

"If, while living by means of gain, I bring about the destruction of evil and merit... and so forth; that is, you think: "While being sustained and remaining alive by means of gain according to the manner described, I shall effect the destruction of evil and the production of merit."
Is this not stated by one who perceives a fault even greater than this? He says:
"Indeed, for one who becomes angry for the sake of gain, there is both the destruction of merit and sin. (Bca 6.60)
For one who, for the sake of gain and on account of gain, harbors hatred toward those who create obstacles to it, the very destruction of his merit arises.
As it was said: "All this is well-conducted behavior," and so forth.
However, there is this distinction: the mass of evil arising from impatience increases.

Now, it might be argued: "Life may somehow be sustained for a long time through gain; that alone is sufficient for our purpose. To this he says: "If that very purpose for which I live should perish," [what is the use?]
Of what use is even that life which performs nothing but unwholesome deeds?

(Bcp 97) Indeed, the life of a bodhisattva is not desired for its own sake alone, as is the case with other sentient beings; rather, it is for the purpose of increasing the accumulations and for the purpose of destroying evil.
Therefore, if that [life] were to result solely in the exhaustion of well-performed deeds, [it would be undesirable].
In that case, what is the use of such a life, whose very nature is the performance of exclusively unwholesome deeds?
The sense is that it is indeed contemptible.
It might be argued: "My mind does not give rise to resentment toward one who speaks ill of me because they obstruct my gain;
rather, it is because their actions, such as concealing my virtues, are a cause of suffering. To this, he says:
If you say that hatred toward one who speaks ill of others destroys living beings,
why does such anger not arise in you toward one who brings disgrace upon another?
If you think that this hatred of yours toward one who brings disrepute destroys you by exposing faults and concealing virtues through the utterance of blame;
and if, for that reason, [you feel such aversion]:
Alternatively,
he destroys beings and the worlds,
and causes them to be punished for speaking ill of me.
The meaning is that one whose own mind is not serene causes the minds of others as well to become unsereene.
If it is argued that there should be hatred toward one who speaks ill [of others], it is said in response:
even one who proclaims the infamy of other sentient beings [would be subject to such hatred].
Why does anger not arise toward him as well?
He too, being a slanderer, destroys sentient beings;
therefore, anger toward him is indeed appropriate.
Anticipating an objection to this, he says:
"Because their lack of serenity depends on others, you are patient toward those who are unserene.
This means that the lack of serenity belonging to them is dependent upon—reliant upon—other beings.
It arises having taken other sentient beings as its object;
its state is "thatness," and from that [state],

patience— namely, forbearance— arises in you toward those who are unpacified, that is, those with unpacified minds who speak ill of you, because it does not depend on others for its lack of pacification.
He asks about one's own mind itself. Regarding this, it is said:
"When one is dependent on the arising of afflictions, there is no patience toward those who speak ill. (Bca 6.63)
If you possess patience toward one whose lack of favor depends on another, then why do you not have patience toward one who speaks ill of yourself?
Of what nature is that person?

In the case of being dependent on the arising of afflictions—that is, being reliant on the production of afflictions—the state of impurity being dependent on another is the cause for forbearance; the meaning is that this is equal in both instances.
It is said that one should not give rise to a mind of resentment even out of devotion toward those who damage images and so forth:
"Even toward those who destroy images, stūpas, and the true Dharma, or who revile them, it is not fitting for me to feel hatred; for there is no suffering for the Buddha and the others. (Bca 6.64)
Those who destroy are those who cause disturbance; those who revile are those who, with the perception of fault, speak of deformity. Toward them, hatred is not appropriate for me.

Why is this? Because for the Buddhas and others—the Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas—there is no mental distress (*daurmanasya*), characterized by affliction of the mind, due to the absence of attachment resulting from the cessation of the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*) produced by false adherence. This is the intended meaning.
Therefore, one should not give rise to a mind of hatred toward those who destroy images;
rather, for the virtuous, only compassion is appropriate toward those who perform contrary dharmas.
Otherwise, because there would be no distinction [between them], only sin would arise.
If, however, it can be prevented in accordance with the Dharma, then there is no fault.

Furthermore, even when a mind of hatred arises toward those who harm one's teachers, mother, father, and so forth—out of a desire for the Dharma—that too must certainly be restrained. Thus it is said:
"Toward those who cause harm to one's teachers, blood relatives, and other loved ones..."
Having observed the arising of conditions as before, one should restrain anger.
Gurus are those who instruct in the path of Dharma and turn one away from unwholesome states; they include maternal relatives,
uterine brothers,
and others such as kinsmen, those of the same lineage, and blood relations.
The connection is that one should restrain anger toward those who harm them, as well as toward those who harm beloved ones or objects of affection.
How? By observing, as before, the arising of conditions.
As it was said: "Whatever offenses there may be," and so forth;
therefore, all these [beings] merely experience the fruit produced by their own prior karma.
There is no cause for remedy here whatsoever.
By this it is stated that the view held in other systems— that there is no fault even for one who commits evil for the sake of gods, teachers, the twice-born, or parents— is not accepted here.
Furthermore, reflecting on this reality of things, one should not harbor malice toward sentient beings; thus it is said:
"The suffering of embodied beings is invariably caused by both conscious and unconscious agents.
Since that suffering is seen to reside in the conscious being, therefore, endure this suffering. (Bca 6.66)
The cause characterized as a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), which is determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the producer of every effect,
is a certain [collection] that, by virtue of the nature of things, possesses a capable essence in some cases and in some places. Among these,
there is that which is produced by a conscious agent through the striking of hands, feet, and so forth.
By means of insentient things such as sticks, weapons, diseases, and so forth;
even in those cases, there is indeed the activity of a sentient being,
though the distinction lies in whether it is performed directly or indirectly.
In embodied beings—that is, those possessing a body—pain arises invariably, either spontaneously by chance or produced by impacts from clods of earth, walls, and the like.
There is no cause for pain other than these.
And although it is produced by such a collection of two kinds of causes, it is observed and established by valid cognition in the conscious body, which possesses cognition.
Therefore, that alone is the place of its origination and nothing else;
for it is insentient, as it lacks connection with sensation.
Therefore, whatever arises from a particular source exists only there and not elsewhere,
just as a lotus grows in the mud and not on dry land. By this principle, forgive and endure this twofold suffering just described.
To explain that since this fault is common to both parties, anger toward anyone is inappropriate, he says:
"Out of delusion some commit offenses; others, being equally deluded, become angry. Whom among these can we call blameless, or whom can we call the offender? (Bca 6.67)
Due to the perversion of grasping and adhering to the notions of "self" and "mine," some commit offenses by means of punishment and the like;
others, uttering insults and so forth, make themselves guilty of fault;
yet others become angry because of those offenses.

Being utterly deluded by ignorance alone, and failing to perceive the connection between their own past actions and their present results due to the veil of *avidyā*, they begin to strike and revile others.
Thus we say: among these people, who have been brought under the sway of possession by the *rākṣasa* of the afflictions (*kleśa*), who is without fault?
Whom shall we call the offender?
Since the fault is common to both parties.
(Bcp 99) Furthermore, thinking that this too pertains only to oneself, one should turn back the mind of resentment; thus it is said:
"Why was such a deed done previously by which you are now thus oppressed by others?
All are dependent upon their own karma; who am I here to act otherwise? (Bca 6.68)
For what reason, for what purpose, was this causal karma performed that results in such a fruit?
The expression "by which" (yena) is a common worldly idiom used in the sense of "that which" (yad).
That is to say: since it is thus.
Or rather, by whatever power of karma as a cause,
you are harmed and oppressed by others through insults, imprisonment, beatings, and so forth—
if indeed this is so, then...
Nevertheless, he says that a remedy is appropriate, beginning with "all," and so forth:

"All causes of suffering proceed from the conditions of karma; who am I here to act otherwise in order to turn back their fruit? No one at all, because it is impossible for anyone to turn back karma that is already oriented toward yielding its fruit."
Furthermore, he says that this is the appropriate course of action here:
"Having understood this, I shall likewise apply effort toward meritorious deeds, so that all may come to possess minds of loving-kindness toward one another. (Bca 6.69)
"These beings, being dependent on karma and afflictions, perform improper actions toward one another and cannot be turned back.
Having understood and realized this, I shall once again exert effort in meritorious and wholesome deeds; in that manner, I shall initiate vigor (*vīrya*).

Having attained such power as this, they shall proceed upon the true path; being thus, all shall become possessed of a mind of loving-kindness (*maitracitta*), intent upon providing benefit and happiness to one another.

Having turned away from thoughts of malice toward each other, one should eliminate hatred toward those who inflict harm upon beloved objects by means of a worldly illustration. To demonstrate this, he says in two verses:
"Just as when a house is burning, the fire, having gone to another house..."
If one becomes attached to grass or similar things, that [attachment] should be drawn out and removed.
When the mind is thus scorched by the fire of hatred due to attachment,
it must be abandoned at that very moment, for fear of the total combustion of one's merit.
Just as when a house is being consumed by fire, one moves from that house to another house;
out of fear that the fire might attach itself or cling to the grass, wood, and so forth therein, and thus burn other objects contained within it, those [objects] are pulled out and removed.
Having distinguished [the mind] and determined it,
he says— applying the observed sequence to the present case as well—
that by attachment to a certain object, the mind (*citta*) and the intellect (*manas*) become attached, and thus one is burned and tormented.

By the fire of hatred, with its burning heat, that object which is the locus of attachment must be abandoned at that very moment; it should not be relinquished through lingering over time, and one's clinging to it must be avoided.
For what reason?
The self is the body of merit;
that is to say, the aggregate of merit.
Let there be no burning up or total exhaustion of it according to the sequence previously described.
Otherwise, like an object situated within a house, the fire of hatred would consume him as well.
Moreover, this is indeed a gain that has been obtained, in that karma which would have resulted in hell ripens through human sufferings; demonstrating this, he says:
"If one who was to be executed is released after having his hand cut off, what is unwholesome in that?"
If one is freed from the hells by means of human sufferings, what could be inauspicious about that?
For if one who deserves death is released after having only his hand cut off, then there is no injury whatsoever to him.
On the contrary, one considers oneself to have gained a profit, thinking, "This pain of having a hand cut off is very slight compared to the pain of death.
Likewise, even for one who, having experienced human suffering such as beating, imprisonment, and humiliation, becomes liberated from the sufferings of hell,
not even the slightest diminution of that [suffering] occurs.
This suffering is nothing compared to the suffering of hell;
it is actually happiness.
Therefore, if one were discerning, [one would realize this].
In that case, mental gladness alone is appropriate for him here.

Now, it might be argued: "I am not able to practice patience even toward a very slight suffering. To this, he says: "If even this much suffering cannot be endured today, then why is anger—which is the cause of the torments of hell—not restrained? (Bca 6.73)
Even the slightest suffering caused by blows from sticks, slaps, clods of earth, and the like, cannot now be endured or tolerated.
Therefore, we ask you this: if it is indeed thus, for what reason is this anger and resentment—which leads to the sufferings of hell—not restrained?
For since this very thing bestows suffering in the hells to an even greater degree, it would be appropriate to turn away from anger only those who are afraid of suffering.
Furthermore, even if it cannot be endured,
nevertheless, because karma arises with that as its cause, suffering will befall you even against your will;
nor will any fruit whatsoever be produced.
Thinking that by enduring this there will be a great gain of purpose, he says in two verses to provide instruction:
"For the sake of anger alone, I have been made to undergo [suffering] in the hells thousands of times;
yet neither my own welfare nor the welfare of others has been accomplished by me. (Bca 6.74)
And this suffering is not of such a kind as to fail to accomplish a great purpose;
therefore, for one who removes the suffering of the world, it is only appropriate here to feel joy toward suffering.
It is precisely the cause of anger;
likewise, it is utterly fruitless in the hells, such as Saṃjīva and the others.

Thousands of times, on many occasions, I was made to suffer, tormented by causes such as being cut, pierced, and split open. Even while experiencing such suffering, I did not— indeed, not at all— accomplish or bring to completion my own welfare, which consists in the attainment of results both seen and unseen.
The welfare of another, or anyone else, is characterized by the provision of happiness;
thus, this humiliation consisting of thousands of hellish sufferings is indeed purposeless.
Therefore, he says that even now it is not right for me to be intolerant of it: "This suffering is not at all like that which arises from hell."
And yet, one will achieve Buddhahood, which is of great significance and consists in the provision of welfare and happiness for all sentient beings.
Therefore, the sense is that toward suffering—which removes the world's pain and pacifies the suffering of all beings included within the three realms—only joy is appropriate here, not aversion.

To wash away the stain of envy upon hearing of the virtues of others, he says: "If others have attained joy and happiness by praising one who is exalted by virtue, why does your mind not likewise rejoice when you praise him? (Bca 6.76)
If some have attained the happiness of joy by praising one who is superior in virtue,
then why, O mind, do you not experience the bliss of rapture through the celebration of those very virtues?
Why do you suddenly turn yourself into fuel for the blazing flames of the fire of envy?
(Bcp 101) But surely, since all pleasure is prohibited because its nature is attachment,
I shall not even adopt this [pleasure] due to my aversion to all pleasure?
For it will be said:
Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, finds delight,
there a suffering a thousand times greater arises and takes hold of it.
Thus it is said:
"And this joy and happiness of yours is blameless and gives rise to bliss."
And winning over others is the supreme quality, which has not been forbidden by those possessed of virtue.
For it is not all joy and happiness that has been rejected;
rather, it is that which is blameworthy and a cause of unwholesomeness.
And this joy and happiness of yours, which rests upon the virtues of others, is blameless.
Nor is it a cause of unwholesomeness;
therefore, it brings about the arising of happiness, because happiness arises from it.
For this very reason, it has not been prohibited by those endowed with virtue who understand the rules of the Blessed One’s teaching.
This is another of his virtues: that he wins over others through delight in their qualities. Thinking, "In this way, he is free from envy regarding virtues," other beings as well become won over.
Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to include joy and bliss here.
It might be argued: "I have no intolerance whatsoever toward the virtues of others; rather, it is because this is his happiness that I am unable to endure it. To this, he says:
"If this thought—that 'this is his happiness'—is not dear to you..."
By ceasing to give wages and other forms of support, one's merit in both the seen and unseen worlds would be destroyed.

If, with this intention—that happiness belongs only to the one who offers the praise—you do not find dear this happiness arising from the praise of another's virtues, then you have fallen into a most dire strait.
How so? Because of your refusal to provide wages and other such benefits.

Furthermore, because you are averse to and disinclined toward such acts as giving wages— that is, providing the price for labor— to your own servants and others for the sake of your own personal happiness, as well as returning a favor to one who has rendered you a service, and so forth;
Even that [act] ought not to be performed by one who hates the happiness of others,
because through that very act, his own happiness will be accomplished;
thus, the visible fruit is found in this world.
The unseen [result] pertaining to the next world is destroyed;
both are ruined by one who cannot endure the excellence and happiness of others.
Furthermore, demonstrating that this [position] of yours is indeed a false rejoinder, he says:
"When your own virtues are being proclaimed, you even desire the happiness of others;
yet when the virtues of another are being proclaimed, you do not even desire your own happiness. (Bca 6.79)
If someone extols your virtues,
you then desire happiness for that other person even if it is undesirable to them; yet, if they describe the virtues of another, [you feel otherwise].
Then, however, with your mind pierced by the thorn of envy,
you do not even desire your own happiness;
let alone the happiness of others— this is the meaning of the word "even" (*api*).
Therefore, it is merely envy toward the excellence of another's happiness that you feel,
not an inability to endure the happiness of those who praise you.
As it was said:
"If this [pleasure] of yours is not dear to you in the sense that 'this is my pleasure' alone."
[Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.78] (Bcp 102) Regarding this, he states a specific refutation:
"Having generated the thought of awakening out of a desire for the happiness of all sentient beings..."
Why are you angry today with sentient beings who have obtained happiness for themselves?
This is indeed particularly contemptible for one who has generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta): namely, the inability to endure the happiness and prosperity of others.

For it is with the mental orientation that "all sentient beings wandering within the three realms must be satisfied with every kind of happiness and prosperity and led to the attainment of Buddhahood by me" that the mind of awakening is generated.
Having produced that [merit], why does one become angry with sentient beings?
"Now" means at this very moment;
with what kind of beings? With those who are objects of confidence.
"Having inspired confidence in one's own mind regarding the happiness attained by oneself"—
the meaning is that such a mind which is averse to the happiness of others must certainly not be cultivated by a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, regarding one who, although having generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), perceives the gain, honor, and prosperity of another and, with a heart corrupted by envy, is consumed by that very grief—
for the purpose of censuring such a person, it is said:
"You indeed desire for sentient beings Buddhahood, which is worthy of worship by the three worlds."
Seeing that their honor is but momentary, why do you burn with envy for them?
Alternatively, it might be argued: "It is not that I simply cannot tolerate their happiness;
rather, it is the gain and honor offered to them by those whose minds are delighted by hearing of the other virtues they have manifested. To this, he says: *trailokya*, etc.
The three worlds (*trailokya*) are either characterized by the desire, form, and formless realms, or, according to worldly convention, consist of heaven and so forth.
Or it is the collection thereof;
because he is worthy of worship (*pūjā*), he is "to be worshipped" (*pūjya*), meaning he is to be honored.
By this, his state of surpassing all others is established.
"You indeed desire such Buddhahood for sentient beings.
By the word "indeed" (*kila*), he expresses a lack of approval upon perceiving a contradiction.
The term "honor" (*satkāra*) is an elliptical expression (an *upalakṣaṇa*).
Also gain;
the rest is easy to understand.
With a view toward gain, he says:
"He who nourishes those whom you ought to nourish gives to you alone; having obtained one who sustains your family, you do not rejoice, but instead become angry. (Bca 6.82)
Whoever nourishes those who are to be nurtured by you— such as your dear sons and others—
is giving them to you alone;
by that act, an increase has been brought about for you alone.
Therefore, having obtained—that is, having found—such a person who sustains your family by living upon your family's means, do you not rejoice?
He asks with an ironic intonation (kāku): "Do you not instead become enraged?"
The meaning is that you do not exult;
likewise, in the present case as well, for one who has grasped all sentient beings as belonging to oneself, it is only fitting that he should find happiness through their happiness.

It might be argued: "You have asserted that they shall attain only Buddhahood, and not some other happiness. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Why do you not desire for those beings that very enlightenment which you desire for them?"
But is this not also incorrect? Because:
"The world has been invited by me today to the state of a Sugata and to happiness in the interim."
[Bodhicaryāvatāra 3.33] (Bcp 103) Thus it has been asserted. Let it be so.
Nevertheless, one who has generated the mind of enlightenment and desires awakening— that is, Buddhahood— for those sentient beings—
would he not desire other categories of mundane and supramundane goals?
Or, if it is not accepted that he does so, [then...]
Then he says that even the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is lost: "Whence can the thought of awakening belong to one who is angry at the prosperity of others? (Bca 6.83).
Whence can there be the thought of enlightenment for one who has made a false vow regarding that very thought?
For whom? For one who becomes angry at the prosperity of another.
Regarding other forms of prosperity born from gain and honor— this "stinging at the vital point" (marmacodanā) is the cause for a bodhisattva’s cessation from unwholesome actions.
Moreover, even though another person lacks the attainment of gain and honor, it is not possible for you to possess them simply because of that.
Thus, demonstrating why one who hates such a person makes an effort to commit suicide without any valid reason, he says:
"If that [wealth] was not obtained by him, it remains in the house of the donor."
In every respect, that [body] does not belong to you; so what is the use of whether it is given away or not?
Even if that being, who was the object of your intolerance, did not receive the gift being offered by him, it nevertheless remained in the house of the donor;
what, then, has resulted for you from that?
In every respect, whether it has been acquired by him or remains in his house, that object does not belong to you.
Thus, what is the use to you of its being given or not given? It serves no purpose for you whatsoever.
Therefore, equanimity alone is appropriate for the wise person in that regard.

Furthermore, demonstrating that this too should be reflected upon, he says: "Or rather, what can merit do? Or what can one's own virtues do for those who are well-disposed? Tell me, why are you not angry when someone, receiving [something], does not accept it? (Bca 6.85)
How can he, who is honored with gains and respect by donors and masters of generosity who are exceedingly devoted,
ward off those merits performed in previous births that are now ready to ripen, and by the power of which these gains and honors come to him?
Or rather, let him restrain the gracious donors and masters of charity,
or else let him restrain his own virtues, depending upon which their faith has arisen.
"Do not even give rise to affection for them.
Or alternatively:
"Even if you receive [benefits] from them, do not accept them as your own."

Tell me, in what manner might you not find dissatisfaction here? For there is no cause for satisfaction: on the one hand, it is impossible to prevent merit and the like; and on the other, even if one does not grasp at what is obtained, it has already been stated that such [merit] does not belong to you in any way through the refutation beginning with "that is not yours.
Nevertheless, it might be argued: "The attainment of gain and honor belongs only to another, not to me."
Thinking, "If I do not possess this,
then let another also not possess it"—
this is the basis for my dissatisfaction; anticipating this objection, he says:
Not only do you not grieve for yourself for having committed evil deeds,
but you also desire to compete with others who have performed meritorious acts.
This is easily understood: "Whatever suffering there is, all of it arises from evil;
even the frustration of one's desires is suffering, as is that which one seeks but does not obtain."
Because of the statement: "That too is suffering."
As it will be said:
"And the frustration of desires arises for those who commit evil deeds."
[On Bodhi 7.41] (Bcp 104) "Whatever happiness there is, all that is born from merit.
Thus, one who desires happiness should exert effort in virtuous action.
As he will say: "But the desire for happiness by one who performs meritorious deeds... and so forth (*Bodhicaryāvatāra* 7.42–43).
Thus, how is rivalry with those who have performed meritorious deeds appropriate?
The meaning is that for those who desire happiness, rivalry is appropriate only in the performance of well-done deeds themselves.
Moreover, you should also be asked this:
"If something unpleasant were to happen to your enemy for your satisfaction, what would be the result?
That is to say, if something unpleasant—an undesirable thing—were to arise or occur for your enemy, who is the object of your hatred, merely by your wishing it so; [what would be the gain?].
What, moreover, would happen to you by this much?
Let that [undesirable consequence] befall him for now;
as for another, let it befall them or not.
Anticipating the opponent's thought that "I have need of only a very small amount," he says: "And it will not be causeless merely by your wishing for it. (Bca 6.87)
Your "expectation" (āśaṃsana) means desire,
that is to say, longing;
and it is not for that reason alone that [the cause] is without a cause.
No cause for this exists; thus, the object will be "causeless."
Granted that it may be unpleasant; having accepted this as "so be it," it is said:
"But even if, by your wish, that suffering of the enemy is accomplished, what pleasure do you have?
Even if, indeed, by your wish that which is unpleasant for the enemy is accomplished and brought about, [what benefit is there for you?].
Nevertheless, when suffering has arisen for him, what pleasure do you have? None at all;
the point is that this intended [pleasure] is purposeless. [Objection: But surely this very thing is the purpose, namely, my satisfaction in his suffering. To this, he says:
Even if this were for one's own benefit, what misfortune could possibly be greater than this?
Even so, if there were some purpose or benefit in taking pleasure in the suffering of others,
then what indeed could be a greater misfortune than this?
The word "nu" is used for emphasis.
This very thing is a great misfortune; such is the meaning.
But how is this a misfortune? He says:
"For this is a terrible hook cast by the fisherman of the afflictions (kleśa), by which the guardians of hell, having purchased you, will roast you in cauldrons. (Bca 6.89)
Because this very thing—such as it is—is a terrible hook, a source of great terror, consisting of a mind intent on the harm of others;
of what nature is it? It is "cast by the fisherman of the afflictions" (*kleśabāḍiśika*). Those who act with the hook are the "hook-men" (*bāḍiśikāḥ*); it is cast, that is, taken up, by them.
For,
like a fish from a fisherman's hook,
the wardens of hell— the servants of Yama— will buy you from the fisherman that is the affliction and will roast you; they will roast you.
In some versions, the reading is "kvacin nītvā" (having led somewhere). "Kumbhiṣu" refers to specific hells.
The sense is: therefore, do not form a longing for this place.
(Bcp 105) Furthermore, even the suffering that arises when one is deprived of praise and so forth occurs only for one who lacks discernment; teaching this, he says:
"Praise, fame, and honor lead neither to merit nor to long life."
Not for the sake of strength, nor for health, nor for my own physical pleasure.

And such indeed would be the self-interest of the wise person who understands his own interest. There are exactly five kinds of objects intended by the learned as being for the sake of man (puruṣārtha).
Namely: merit (puṇya),...
increase of lifespan, increase of strength, and attainment of health;
And as for bodily pleasure,
praises and the like are of no use whatsoever in these matters;
for such is the extent of your own self-interest, O wise one who understands what is truly beneficial to yourself.
"But for another, it might be otherwise," thus he reflects upon himself;
even though they may know their own purpose.
Nevertheless, because one who knows only his own self-interest lacks the proper means, he is shown separately;
by the word "of the wise," that [self-interest] is also mentioned as being inconsistent with such wisdom.
Now, one might object: "But there is also mental happiness;
therefore, this restriction is inappropriate. To this he says:
"One who desires mental happiness would have to indulge in liquor, gambling, and the like. (Bca 6.91)
Mental happiness is *saumanasya*.
One who desires that [happiness] would have to resort to liquor, gambling, courtesans, and adultery;
whereas, on the other hand, there is *saumanasya* arising from hearing the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Therefore, since that is included within the category of merit, there is no fault.
Consequently, even for you, the causes of mental pleasure—such as praise and the like—which bring joy to foolish people, are simply not to be adopted.

He says that even for this reason, praise and the like are merely the delusions of foolish people: "Some deluded persons, for the sake of fame, squander their wealth and even bring about their own destruction; though they themselves remain very far removed from such qualities, they are praised for the virtues of Śakra and others."
With eyes and faces wide open in joy, bards and others, seeking fame, bestow upon them wealth such as elephants and horses as if they were blades of grass.

Furthermore, out of the obsession that "by these very virtues, my fame— born from the conquest of enemies like Śakra— shall spread extensively throughout the world," they cause them to die by making them mount into unbearable battles, even though those men already esteem themselves for those very qualities.
And demonstrating that there is no purpose whatsoever here from the perspective of ultimate truth, other than [the result of] false conceptualization, he says:
"Are syllables edible? And whose happiness is it when one has died? (Bca 6.92).
Are the syllables (*varṇa*) that express praise and so forth edible, such that they should be chewed?
When one has died for the sake of fame, whose is that pleasure arising from hearing that fame?
Therefore, demonstrating that this [pursuit of fame] is like the play of children, he says:
Just as a child cries out with a cry of distress when a house of sand is broken—

just as some child, playing with great delight in a house made of dust, is seized by great sorrow when it is destroyed by someone, and like one tormented by extreme affliction, wails in a piteous voice, "My house is broken!"— so too is it here.
He says that this very same analogy applies here as well: "In the same way, when praise and fame are lost, my own mind appears [to me] in that manner. (Bca 6.93)
In the same way, when praise and fame decline or are obstructed, suffering enters my own mind and appears as such to me while I am reflecting;
even here, one must conclude that there is no deception by anything that exists as a real entity.

(Bcp 106) Furthermore, examining it in another way, [the author] says, reflecting with four verses that this is merely the characteristic of a fool: "First of all, because sound is insentient, it is impossible for it to praise me.
Sound consists of phonemes; as an external object, it is *acitta*—that is, unconscious.
The state of being that [is expressed by] "tasmāt" (therefore).
That word praises me and utters my praise.
"Asambhavaḥ" (impossibility): this is not possible.
To the question of how gladness arises, he says:
"Indeed, 'another is pleased with me'—this is the cause of gladness. (Bca 6.94)
"The other person is of the nature of consciousness"—
the word "kila" (allegedly) indicates a lack of conviction, signifying that even this [assertion] is meaningless.
The thought, "He is pleased with me," meaning he is well-disposed toward me, is the cause of his affection.
In that case as well, the connection is: "Because it is likewise unrelated, it is merely the behavior of a child" (Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.97).
This is the connection.
Imagining a lack of connection, he says:
"What indeed is the use to me of affection for another, whether directed toward someone else or toward myself?
That pleasure of affection belongs to him alone; from it, I do not receive even the slightest share."
Since [the pleasure] belongs to another, whether it be in someone else or in me, what comes to me by that affection residing in another's continuum? Nothing at all.
Why? Because that very person who is pleased—the one who performs the praise—possesses that happiness of pleasure, not anyone else.
Therefore, not even the slightest part, nor even a fraction, of that joy and happiness belonging to another's continuum belongs to me.
It might be argued: "The happiness of Bodhisattvas consists precisely in the happiness of others; so why is there no share for them [in that happiness]? To this he says:
"If their happiness is my happiness, then let that happiness be mine everywhere."
Why is it that I do not experience happiness when others are happy through the grace of someone else?
If happiness arises from the happiness of another, then when that other person is made happy by faith in someone else, may I too possess that happiness.
Why is it that joy in another does not arise through being delighted in oneself?
But my happiness does not arise from the favor shown toward others who are happy.
Therefore, he says this to show that it is merely words and not the ultimate truth:
"Therefore, the thought 'I am praised' gives rise to joy within oneself."
Even there, because it is likewise irrelevant, it is merely the behavior of a child.
Because there is no other cause for it, joy arises within oneself through the conceptualization "I have been praised," and not from being happy because of the happiness of another;
even in that case, it does not arise merely when another is made happy by one's favor.
Even with respect to the self, because there is no connection due to the lack of proximity according to the sequence just described, this is merely the play of the ignorant.

Moreover, demonstrating that praise and the like only bring about my own decline, he says: "Praise and the like destroy my security and spiritual urgency; they produce envy toward those with virtues and anger toward prosperity. (Bca 6.98)

These [qualities], beginning with praise, are my *kṣema*, that is, my welfare; furthermore, *kṣema* is the preservation of the side of virtue (*kuśalapakṣa*). Likewise, *saṃvega* is the sense of revulsion toward the suffering of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
They destroy and kill; it is not merely that much,
but furthermore, there is envy toward those possessed of virtues.
Out of pride in their own superior qualities, by concealing the qualities of others,
or through an inability to endure those qualities, they harbor anger and resentment toward those very same people regarding prosperity— which consists of gain, honor, and so forth— thinking,
"I alone am superior in quality."
Thinking, "All this prosperity is suitable for me alone, and not for others."
Since these faults can arise in the context of praise and so forth,
therefore, those who have appeared before me to destroy my praise and the like have, in fact, set out for the sake of protecting me from falling into the lower realms. (Bca 6.99)
For that reason,
those beings who have arisen against me, intent on destroying my praise and so forth and creating obstacles for me—
[their] falling into the miserable states is the falling into hell and the like.
Therefore, since they have indeed applied themselves and exerted themselves for the sake of guarding, protecting, and safeguarding me,
these are my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), not those who do me harm.

To demonstrate that it is entirely improper for one who seeks liberation to harbor a mind of resentment toward those who obstruct gain and the like, he says: "For me, who seeks liberation, attachment to gain and honor is improper; how could I feel hatred toward those who release me from bondage? (Bca 6.100)
For one who desires liberation, gain and honor are like a bond because they are a basis for attachment; it is improper and unsuitable for one seeking release to have such a bond.

Those who act as spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) liberate and separate me from bondage—characterized by the suffering of saṃsāra or by the nature of gain and so forth—even though they are regarded as enemies.
How can there be hatred toward them, who are my supreme benefactors and objects of affection? The intention is that such hatred is not appropriate.
How is it not reasonable? He says:
"For one who desires to enter [the city of liberation], those [enemies] have become like door-bolts;
how can I feel hatred toward them, as if it were through the empowerment of the Buddha? (Bca 6.101)
For one who desires liberation from the sufferings of saṃsāra by abandoning attachment to gain and honor, those distinguished noble beings have become like door-bolts or side-entrances.
Why? Because it is as if through the empowerment and majestic influence of the Buddhas;
how then could I harbor hatred toward them?
Restraining hatred even toward one who causes the destruction of virtue, he says:
"It is not fitting to feel anger thinking, 'An obstacle to my merit has been created by this person.
Is there no austerity equal to patience? Indeed, that very opportunity has now presented itself. (Bca 6.102)
(Bcp 108) Thinking, "This person has caused an obstruction to my virtue," one should not harbor hatred toward this destroyer of merit.
Why? Because there is no austerity (*tapas*) or well-performed deed equal to patience (*kṣānti*), since it is the cause of all wholesome actions.
As it is said: "And there is no austerity equal to patience" (Bodhicaryāvatāra 6.2).
Because of this statement:
"Is it not the case that this very thing has arrived and presented itself effortlessly? For, under the guise of being an obstacle to merit, there is actually the presence of a cause for merit."
Regarding that aversion, he says that one would be destroying one's own merit: "But if, through my own fault, I do not practice patience here,
then I myself have created an obstacle when the cause for merit has presented itself" (Bca 6.103).

Now, if, due to my own fault characterized by intolerance, I do not practice patience or forbearance toward this obstacle-maker, then the obstruction to this merit has been created by myself and not by anyone else.
Why? Because when that which is intended to be an obstacle to merit—namely, the cause of merit—has arisen and become present.
Or it is conceived that "here" means "in this cause of merit."
If it is a destroyer of merit,
how can it be a cause of merit?
To the objection that it is merely an obstacle, he says:
For that which does not exist without another, and which exists when that other is present—that alone is its cause; how can it be called an obstacle?
Whatever entity is considered an effect, which does not exist without that which is considered its cause— that is, which does not occur in its absence—
is precisely that which comes to be through the existence of the other.
Nothing else is the cause that produces that which is considered an effect,
because [the effect] conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [cause].
Likewise, in the present case as well, since it is indeed the producer, how can it be called an obstacle to that which is produced, or designated as the cause of its destruction?
Even in such a case, for one who conducts themselves accordingly, there is no contradiction.
Making the aforementioned point clear by means of an illustration, he says:
"For a petitioner who arrives at the proper time does not cause an obstacle to giving;
nor is it said that an obstacle to renunciation is created when a seeker of ordination has arrived. (Bca 6.105)
For it is not said that a petitioner or seeker who arrives at the very moment a certain donor intends to give has created an obstacle to that gift;
rather, such a person is itself the cause of the gift.
Likewise, for someone desiring to go forth, the encounter with one who can ordain them—which consists in the taking up of the vows of renunciation and so forth—is likewise a cause.
And that is not called an obstacle for it;
rather, it is indeed the cause of it,
because without it, that [result] would be impossible.
The same should be understood in the present case as well.
Furthermore, demonstrating that since the cause for patience is extremely rare, it is only appropriate to feel joy upon encountering it, he says:
"Suppliants are easy to find in the world, but those who do harm are rare."

Suppliants are exceedingly abundant everywhere in the world, because everyone is averse to refusing what is being given; however, those who do harm are rare, occurring only once in hundreds of thousands.
If one were to wonder whether someone might exist [who could harm me] or not, and from what cause this would be so, he says: "Because no one offends me, who am myself without offense. (Bca 6.106)
Because no one at all offends me— who am without fault and have ceased from harming others— without cause;
[here] the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

Thus, because they are so exceedingly rare and because they provide such supreme assistance, even a wrongdoer is to be welcomed; as it is said: "Therefore, an enemy is to be desired by me, for he is like a treasure discovered in one's home acquired without effort, since he is an aid to the practice of awakening. (Bca 6.107)

Since harmful persons are encountered with some difficulty, an enemy who has appeared in one's own home and been acquired without any effort at all should be desired by me, like a treasure discovered in the house;
for he acts as a cooperative cause in the practice of awakening and in the accumulation of the requisites for Buddhahood.

Demonstrating that it is appropriate for me, out of gratitude, to offer a reciprocal service to one who provides assistance toward such a supreme human goal, he says: "Since this fruit of patience was acquired by both myself and him, it should first be given to him; for this patience was preceded by his [action]. (Bca 6.108)
Since he was providing assistance there, he was indeed a cause and not an obstacle; therefore, both of us have earned [merit]: I by practicing patience, and he by doing me a service.

Regarding this: one should make the vow, "I must first give the fruit of patience—characterized by the attainment of the Dharma—to this companion in the Dharma, for whose sake I am providing assistance. This is just as the Bodhisattva Maitrībala made his vow concerning the group of five.
Regarding this, he states the reason: because it is "preceded by that";
that is to say, it is so called because this very thing is its prior cause.
For there is no other cause for patience apart from one who has caused harm.
This is indeed appropriate if he acts with that very intention; however, suspecting that this person might have a mere intent to cause harm, [the author] says:
"If his intention is not fixed on the accomplishment of patience, then he is neither a venerable one nor an enemy."
If even the True Dharma, though devoid of mind, is the cause of accomplishment, how can it be worshipped?
"The intention of this bodhisattva is: 'May his forbearance be perfected'; he has no desire for the harm of one intent on doing him wrong.
For that reason, even if an enemy is a cause of virtue, he is not to be honored."

If that is the case, then how can the True Dharma, characterized by the scriptures, which is the cause for the accomplishment of the wholesome, be worthy of worship even though it lacks intentionality?
The implication is that it too would not be worthy of worship because it is devoid of such an intention.
Now, since the True Dharma has no intentionality, it possesses not even the intent to cause harm;
yet its opposite is observed in this [person]. Thus he says: "If one who harbors the intent to cause harm toward him is not honored, then he is an enemy."
Otherwise, how could I possess patience toward one who strives for my benefit like a physician? (Bca 6.110)
Thinking, "This enemy has the intention to do me harm," if the enemy is not honored with gifts and respect, nor treated with hospitality—
if one acts otherwise, how can there be patience for me who does not restrain a mind of hatred toward the wrongdoer?
The meaning is that it is not at all appropriate for one who cannot endure such an injury, or for one who is returning an injury;
how, then, can there be patience in other circumstances?
Like a physician striving for the welfare of others,
and like a skilled doctor who provides benefit and happiness, there is always only love and reverence toward him;
not even a trace of the cause of aversion is found therein.
Patience (*kṣānti*) is so called because it turns back the mind of hatred;
therefore, patience belongs to one who turns back the mind of resentment precisely toward those who cause harm.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
Therefore, it is precisely by depending upon that evil disposition that patience arises;
for this reason, that very person is the cause of my patience and should be honored by me like the True Dharma.
Since patience is not appropriate toward one who, like a physician, is intent on one's welfare,
for this reason, forbearance arises only by relying upon and taking as its object that person’s very evil intention,
and not toward anyone who possesses a virtuous intention.
Therefore, it is that very person whose disposition gives rise to patience who is the cause of patience,

and not one who, like a physician, possesses a non-malicious disposition. Thus, even though he lacks the disposition for the accomplishment of patience, he is to be honored by me as if he were the True Dharma itself.
This is what is meant: what purpose do I have for this investigation of intention? If it is useful for the accomplishment of the desired goal, then by that alone it would be acceptable to me.
But the fruit of that defective intention belongs only to him who possesses that defective intention;
for me, however, this is solely a cause for the arising of merit.
Thus, how could he not be worthy of worship?
Therefore, what is the use of defining his essential nature when the cause for the accumulation [of merit] is already established?
Demonstrating through scripture that this very [nature] is the cause for the accumulation, he says:
Therefore, the Sage has declared that the field of sentient beings is the field of the Victors,
for by propitiating these [beings], many have reached the further shore of prosperity.
Because they are the cause for the production and development of the accumulations, sentient beings are a field;
likewise, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are a field.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, because they are the causal factors for the state of Buddhahood, they have been described by the Blessed One in many ways.

Why? Because, by propitiating these sentient beings as well as the Victors through the practice of acting in accordance with their wishes, many have attained Buddhahood and reached the pinnacle of all mundane and supramundane prosperity.
This might be thought: "Even if sentient beings are indeed causes of all prosperity,"

Nevertheless, it is argued that equality with the Tathāgatas is not appropriate. To this, he says: "When the acquisition of the Buddha-qualities is the same from both sentient beings and the Victors, what is the logic for having reverence toward the Victors but not toward sentient beings? (Bca 6.113)
Since the arrival and acquisition of both sets of Buddha-qualities— such as the powers (*bala*) and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*)— are equal and undifferentiated,
the sense is that their causality with respect to both is likewise undifferentiated.
Therefore, even though the causal status is common [to both], just as there is reverence toward the Victors (*jina*), [so it should be toward the Bodhisattvas].
In the same way, [it is not so] with regard to sentient beings.
Thus, what kind of sequence or order could there be for those who possess discernment?
The meaning is that it is simply not logical.

Now, one might object: "Since sentient beings possess intentions that are free from the stains of passion and so forth, even if they are the cause [of Buddhahood], how is it logical for them to be equal to the Blessed One? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The greatness of the intention is not inherent by itself, but rather through its effect; and since that greatness is equal [to the Buddha's], sentient beings are therefore equal to him. (Bca 6.114)

(Bcp 111) Although the Blessed Ones possess supreme majesty here, produced by immeasurable merit and gnosis, nevertheless, because the causal state [of their activity] is equal in its utility for what is required, their majesty is said to be equal.
For that reason, those beings are said to be "equal" to the Victors; thus, no distinction is made here.
Furthermore, in order to demonstrate that specific distinction which resides within each individual, he says:
"That one who is worthy of worship because of an intention of loving-kindness— that is indeed the greatness of a sentient being."
Whatever merit arises from faith in the Buddha, that is indeed the majesty of the Buddha himself.
Furthermore, that one who dwells with a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward sentient beings is honored by people—
that is the greatness inherent within his own mind of loving-kindness, and not that of anyone else.
Likewise, the merit that arises for one who gladdens their own mind by taking the greatness of the Tathāgata as an object—
This is the unique majesty of the Blessed One alone,
because no other possesses such qualities.
Having thus stated this uncommon quality, he says, pointing toward the subject at hand:
"Therefore, sentient beings are equal to the Victors by virtue of possessing a portion of the qualities of a Buddha;
however, no one is equal to the Buddhas in their infinite qualities, which are like oceans. (Bca 6.116)
This is the seed here; the meaning is that it pertains to the appropriation of equality.
However, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthatas*), there are no sentient beings whatsoever who are equal to the Blessed Buddhas.
If such beings were to exist, [then this would be so].
Then they too would indeed be Buddhas; by what means?
By being oceans of qualities.
They are oceans of virtues, mines of the jewels of virtue, because they are unfathomable and boundless;
he further provides another qualification for them: "by means of infinite parts."
"By those whose ocean of qualities has an infinite and boundless portion— that is, even a single part— such [qualities] as these."
Clarifying the very point already stated, he says:
"If even a minute quality is seen in someone who is a singular mass of the essence of virtues, even the three worlds would not be sufficient for the sake of honoring that person. (Bca 6.117)
Regarding those Blessed Ones who are the singular mass of the primary qualities among all qualities,
even their quality— be it as small as an atom (paramāṇu), that is to say,
even a mere particle of quality.
If it is seen or recognized in some particular being, then even the three worlds are not sufficient for the purpose of honoring that person who is the locus of such qualities;
that is to say, the jewels and other treasures produced within the three worlds are not worthy of comparison.

If this is so, how then is it said that "pleasing sentient beings" is taught? To this he says: "But a portion of the arising of the Buddha-dharmas exists within sentient beings; by acting in accordance with this portion, the worship of sentient beings is accomplished. (Bca 6.118)
This has been explained previously.

For this reason as well, pleasing sentient beings is appropriate; thus he says: Moreover, for those who are sincere friends and immeasurable benefactors, what other recompense could there be than the act of pleasing sentient beings? (Bca 6.119)
(Bcp 112) For the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas— who are friends without guile and sincere well-wishers,

and who have rendered boundless assistance— there is no repayment for the harm done to them other than their purification, which is to say, the expiation and cleansing of that injury. What else could there be besides the propitiation of sentient beings?
The meaning is that this alone is the supreme ransom.

Realizing that only a servant who acts in accordance with the master’s mind achieves his desired ends, [the author], demonstrating that the propitiation of sentient beings alone is what should be undertaken, says:
"For whose sake they break their bodies and enter the Avīci hell, when one does for them what is required for them, it will be as if done for them.
Therefore, even toward those who do great harm, one should practice only what is beneficial. (Bca 6.120)
Having repeatedly cut off their hands, feet, heads, eyes, and even their own flesh, they gave them away for the sake of establishing the welfare and happiness of others;
likewise, out of compassion for the suffering of others, they would enter even the Avīci hell for their sake in order to deliver them.
By virtue of the context, these refer to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

In that regard, [the merit] would be truly accomplished only with respect to those sentient beings; otherwise, even if it were accomplished, it would not be accomplished. Here, the word "accomplished" (*kṛta*) is used in the sense of performing well, because of its connection to the subject at hand.
Since this is so, one should not corrupt the mind even toward those who cause the greatest harm;
rather, one should perform every kind of wholesome action—whether by body, speech, or mind—exclusively for their benefit and happiness.
Establishing what has already been stated, he says:

"Since my masters themselves are so indifferent even toward their own bodies for the sake of [others], how can I not show respect to those various masters, rather than behaving as their servant? (Bca 6.121)
My masters alone, the Buddhas and others, [acted] by themselves, that is, by their own selves.
The word "tāvat" (so much) is used for the purpose of reference;
"yadartham" means for the sake of which, that is, on account of whom.
Even toward themselves— even toward their own bodies and lives— they, being indifferent and unattached according to the sequence described, renounce them like blades of grass;
how then can I, who am once again their servant, show pride toward those beings who are as exceedingly dear to them as the sons of their masters?
Why do I oppose them even while knowing this?
Why do I not, rather, serve them by becoming their slave, and further, by becoming their female servant?
For this reason as well, one should abandon doing harm to sentient beings and instead strive only to please them; thus it is said:

"In whose happiness the Lords of Sages find joy, and in whose suffering they enter into grief—it is by pleasing them that all the Lords of Sages are pleased; in harming them, one harms the Sages. (Bca 6.122)
For those beings who are like beloved sons, the Munīndras— the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones— experience joy and gladness in their physical and mental happiness,
and they enter into grief and find dissatisfaction in their suffering.
And this is stated by the Blessed One in this manner because it is not desired by them.
But the speech [of the Buddha] is not like a small piece of auspicious sandalwood;
for even among his disciples, there is no possibility of aversion or attachment.
The rest is easily understood.

But how could an injury to them constitute an injury to the Munis? To this he says: "Just as one whose body is ablaze on all sides finds no mental pleasure even through all desirable objects, likewise, when sentient beings suffer, there is no means for those whose nature is compassion to find joy. (Bca 6.123)
Just as for one whose body is set ablaze by fire, pervading all parts on every side, there is no mental well-being through the five strands of sensual pleasure,
nor is there even physical happiness, because that very state of being ablaze is overcome by suffering.
In the same way, when sentient beings are afflicted by pain or experience painful sensations, there is no means or cause for joy or mental gladness in the Blessed Ones whose nature is compassion.

Therefore, whatever unwholesome karma has been accumulated— whether through lack of full understanding, or by the power of being possessed by the seizing demon of the afflictions (*kleśa*), or by actions that harm sentient beings—
he now speaks while vomiting it up by way of this summary: "Therefore, whatever suffering I have caused to people who possess great compassion..."
Therefore, I now confess that evil; may those sages forgive me for having caused them distress.
Since harm done to sentient beings would thus be harm done to the Munis, I now, at this very moment, confess my evil;
filled with a sense of spiritual urgency, I reveal it before those very ones of great compassion.
Furthermore, being thus clearly aware, I shall not do so again;
therefore, I undertake restraint for the future.
If I have acted in a fitting manner, may they grant me forgiveness out of compassion.
Having asked for forgiveness, he now demonstrates his own single-minded devotion through the words beginning with "for the sake of propitiation":
"For the propitiation of the Tathāgatas today, I enter into servitude toward them with my whole being in this world.
Let the multitudes of people place their feet upon my head, or let them strike me down; may the Lord of the World be pleased. (Bca 6.125)

In order to fulfill the intentions of the Tathāgatas, I accept the state of a servant with my whole being—through body, speech, and mind—within the world and regarding all worldly objects. May they, showing me favor, place their feet upon my head;
with a joyful heart, I shall bear their feet upon my head.
By this, may the Blessed Lord, the Master of the worlds, cast aside my previous offense and become pleased in his mind.
(Bcp 114) Demonstrating that one who shows reverence for the Blessed Ones must not show disrespect toward sentient beings, he says:
"These entire worlds have been made their own by those whose very nature is compassion; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, these very protectors are seen here in the form of sentient beings—how can there be any disrespect toward them? (Bca 6.126)

Through the penetration of the all-pervading realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), or by means of establishing equality toward all sentient beings and the exchange of self for others, this entire world has been made one's own and accepted;
it is not merely a small portion.
This was done by those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whose mental continuums consist of the essence of compassion.
This is indeed well-determined;
otherwise, Buddhahood would be impossible.
Therefore, these sentient beings are seen as the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in the form of sentient beings.
Therefore, what lack of respect can there be here for those of deluded minds?
The sense is that it is by no means appropriate.
Since pleasing sentient beings serves many purposes, one should strive for that very end; thus it is said:
"This alone is the propitiation of the Tathāgatas; this alone is the accomplishment of one's own welfare;
this alone is the remover of the world's suffering. Therefore, let this alone be my vow. (Bca 6.127)
It is precisely for one's own benefit, characterized by the equipment for Buddhahood;
it removes the suffering of the world because it is the cause thereof.
"This very thing" refers to that.
"In all cases, one should apply the principle of pleasing sentient beings."
Furthermore, demonstrating through an illustration that one must practice turning away from harming others even by perceiving future dangers, he says:
"Just as a single king's officer may oppress a great multitude, yet that great multitude, being farsighted, is not at all able to retaliate. (Bca 6.128)
That royal official oppresses and crushes the great multitude of people residing in the king's realm— those dwelling in cities, market towns, villages, hamlets, and so forth.
Furthermore, because the great multitude perceives the fear of future royal punishment, they are incapable of undergoing even the slightest transformation at a mere word;
thus, even when struck by him, their conduct remains entirely contracted.
Why?
Because he is not truly alone, for the king’s army is his strength;
nor should that royal official be regarded as being without assistance.
But how is it that he is not without support? To this he says: "Of him" (tasya).
The king's power itself is his power, because of his taking that side.
Likewise, one should not humiliate anyone who has committed an offense, even if they are weak.
Therefore, one should not harm even a person of weak power who has committed an offense,
provided that he is not alone.
Since the guardians of hell and those who possess compassion have that power, one should therefore propitiate sentient beings, just as a servant serves a fierce king. (Bca 6.130)
Therefore, one should propitiate sentient beings.
Why? Because the guardians of hell act as if they were retaliating for the harm done to them, whereas the Compassionate Ones, the Victors and so forth, possess the power of those who take their side.
How indeed should one propitiate him?
Just as those who subsist by following the will of all must propitiate an invincible king, so too [should one act].
Furthermore, this has been stated here in accordance with worldly convention;
however, there is no actual equality between the fruit of the non-existence of sentient beings and the fruit of a king’s offense. Thus he says:
"What could an angry king do that would result in the agony of hell?"
For that which is experienced by means of the mental distress caused by sentient beings.
He asks with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*): "What kind of mass of suffering could the king possibly be capable of producing? The implication is: "Certainly not."
Of what nature is it? It is that collection of sufferings by which the sensation of a hell-being is experienced.
What could a pleased king give that would be equal to Buddhahood—that which is experienced through bringing joy to sentient beings? (Bca 6.132)
Let alone the future Buddhahood arising from pleasing sentient beings;
do you not see even in this very life the excellence of good fortune, fame, and well-being?
One who possesses patience, while wandering through cyclic existence, attains a pleasing appearance, health, joy, long life, and the abundant happiness of a universal monarch.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Forbearance," in the *Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā* composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 116) 7. The seventh chapter, titled "The Perfection of Vigor.
Having thus established the threefold patience by means of refuting its opposites, he speaks in order to establish vigor:
Thus, being patient, one should cultivate vigor, for awakening is established upon vigor;
indeed, without vigor there is no merit, just as there is no movement without wind.
In the manner thus described, one who is endowed with patience (*kṣamā*)— that is, one who is patient and has personally cultivated forbearance (*kṣānti*)—
should resort to vigor (*vīrya*), meaning he should initiate vigor. Otherwise, due to an inability to endure suffering, there would be no relaxation of vigor.
But why is vigor undertaken? To this he says:
"Vigor," and so forth—because Buddhahood is established in vigor, since Buddhahood depends upon it and has that as its cause.
Why is this so?
Because without vigor (vīrya), there is no merit (puṇya) nor the accumulation of merit (puṇyasaṃbhāra).
This is an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa).
Wisdom also is to be seen as such,
because energy is the cause of both;
thus, by means of this energy, the accumulations of merit and wisdom [are produced].
And by these two, it is stated that Buddhahood [is attained].
Because the true nature of vigor is not understood, he asks:
What is vigor? It is enthusiasm for the wholesome. What is said to be its opposite?
Laziness, attachment to what is base, despondency, and self-contempt. (Bca 7.2)
What is this so-called vigor (*vīrya*)? To this it is said: it is enthusiasm for the wholesome.
This refers to that exertion which is applied toward wholesome actions such as giving (*dāna*), as well as toward learning (*śruta*), and so forth.
That is what is called vigor (*vīrya*).
In the case of the unwholesome, however, it is merely laziness (*kausīdya*).

Since vigor that is impaired by its opposite is not at all a factor for the attainment of the desired goal, [the author] says "its opposite," and so forth, in order to demonstrate how to remove that opposite.
What is called the "opposing side" (*vipakṣa*)—the side contrary to that vigor (*vīrya*) for the sake of its destruction? The answer is given: "laziness," and so forth.
Laziness (*ālasya*) is indolence (*kausīdya*), the lack of serviceability in body and mind.
Attachment to what is contemptible and loathsome, such as laughter and dancing;
despondency is dejection;
and the turning back of the mind from difficult tasks.
The meaning is "lack of attachment.
By that [term], it refers to self-contempt or disregard;
this is its opposite.
To refute that laziness, he first explains its cause, saying:
"Laziness arises from a craving for the support of sleep and the tasting of the pleasure of inactivity, and from a lack of revulsion toward the suffering of saṃsāra. (Bca 7.3)
Due to a lack of agitation regarding the suffering of saṃsāra and a lack of spiritual urgency,
there arises this non-activity or state of being inactive;
therein, or by means of that, there is a relish for pleasure and a delight in pleasure.
That [is] sleep and the onset of *middha*;
by means of those two, through the onset of *middha*—which is a craving for support and a desire for leaning—laziness arises; thus the connection is to be understood.
Or alternatively,
due to a lack of revulsion toward the suffering of saṃsāra, there is inactivity,
meaning no engagement in any virtuous action whatsoever.
From that comes the relish for pleasure; from that, sleep;
and from that, a thirst for its support, by which [it is maintained].
Therefore, in order to turn back the lack of revulsion toward the suffering of saṃsāra, one should bring this cultivation of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) to the fore; thus he says:
"Smelled by the hunters that are the afflictions (*kleśa*), you have entered the snare of birth.
Even now, do you still not realize that you have come into the mouth of death? (Bca 7.4)
Those who catch fish and other creatures with nets are called *vāgurika*s, such as fishermen and the like; here,
the afflictions (*kleśa*) themselves are the *vāgurika*s,
and by them he has been "scented," meaning brought under their control.
If one asks how this is so:
he has entered the snare of birth; the very arising within a specific class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*) is the net of the trapper.
"Having entered that" means being contained within it;
this is the cause for making that one's own in this context.
Even now, having reached this state and having entered the jaws of death, why do you not understand?
The meaning is that once one is born, death is inevitable.

He states another cause for spiritual urgency: "Even as you see your own fellow beings being slaughtered one after another, you nevertheless fall asleep just like a buffalo belonging to a Caṇḍāla. (Bca 7.5)
A *yūtha* is a group; those belonging to it are *yūthyas*, with whom one has moved about— engaging in play, laughter, and so forth— during stages such as childhood.
"Those of your own class,
like a buffalo that must inevitably be killed by the Caṇḍālas—
do you not see that this same condition would be mine as well?"
"Death will inevitably come after lingering here for some time;

therefore, it is appropriate for me to experience pleasure for that duration. To this, he says: "Even if that were so, nevertheless, it is not proper to have confidence in death, since its occurrence is certain."
For one who is being watched by the King of Death and whose path is blocked on all sides, how can eating be pleasing to you?
How can sleep? How can pleasure?

Thus, for you who are being led to the place of execution, surrounded on all sides by executioners like a man condemned to death and seeing no way of escape, it is utterly inappropriate to rely on comfort.
Therefore, through this cultivation born of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), you must abandon laziness by turning away from its causes and practice the increase of enthusiasm for the side of virtue.
Furthermore, one might think: "Even if death is indeed inevitable, nevertheless, once I have realized its proximity, I shall cast off laziness.
Anticipating this, he says: "Death will arrive swiftly, with all its equipment fully assembled."
Even if you were to abandon that indolence now, what would you do when it is no longer time?
"Equipped" means that the equipment—the collection of conditions characterized by disease and old age—has been prepared for the purpose of slaughter.
"As soon as" is a common worldly expression;
it means "quickly" or "immediately," because there is no further deliberation.
Then, having entered the jaws of death, what will you do even if you abandon laziness at an improper time?
The sense is that nothing will be of any use then.
To support this very point regarding the inappropriateness of the time, he says in three verses:
"This has not yet been attained; this has been begun; this remains half-finished.
Thinking thus, "Death has arrived all of a sudden! Alas, I am ruined! (Bca 7.8)
Beholding his kinsmen, their faces red with tears swollen by the force of grief and devoid of hope, and beholding the faces of the messengers of Yama, (Bca 7.9).
Tormented by the memory of your own sins, hearing the cries of those in hell,
and with your limbs smeared by screams of terror, what will you do, overwhelmed as you are?
This is that which was intended to be done in the future but has not yet been attained;
this is the task already begun, which was desired to be performed from the very outset;
this remains half-finished.
"How much has been accomplished and how much remains unaccomplished?"—before I have even reached the end of my task, death has suddenly come upon me.
Alas! How exceedingly bitter this is!
Thinking "I am slain," one becomes distraught; the connection with the future phrase is "what will you do?
Grief (*śoka*) is the mental torment caused by separation from what is dear;
its "impetus" (*vega*) is its irresistible onset.
He beheld, that is, gazed upon, those kinsmen whose faces were such— faces upon which the eyes were swollen, elevated, tearful, weeping, and blood-red or copper-colored.
In this context, because the section concerns intransitive verbs, the verb *dṛś* takes the *parasmaipada* ending.
