Of what sort are they? They are "hopeless" (*nirāśān*). Wherein are they hopeless? They have abandoned hope regarding their resurrection.
Or, seeing those who lack such protection, and beholding the faces of the followers of Kṛtānta (Yama) standing at the moment of death—with their wrathful, harsh frowns—how will you remain unagitated?
Tormented by remorse at the time of death, thinking, "Why did I act in this way? as you remember the evil deeds committed by yourself.
It is not merely this; rather,
one hears the cries of the denizens of hell as they experience intense agonies— shouts arising from the hells that are themselves terrifying—
and upon hearing them, thinking "my own state will be exactly like this," there occurs a discharge of excrement, a flow of feces, due to that terror.
With your body thus smeared, agitated, and with the movements of your body, speech, and mind no longer under your control, what will you do? You have ceased all activity.
Thinking thus, in order to instruct that one must strive even while in a state of health, he says:
"It is only fitting for you to feel fear right here, thinking 'I am like a living fish';
how much more so for one who has committed sins, [fearing] the intense sufferings of hell! (Bca 7.11)
Living fish (*jīvamatsya*) are generally preserved for the purpose of eating by people residing in the eastern regions;

"living fish" refers to those very fish characterized by their being alive. This is their established convention, and it is a *madhyamapadalopa* (elision of the middle term) compound, following the rule for *śākapārthiva* and similar formations.
Just like that, thinking "I too will certainly die today or tomorrow," it is appropriate for you to feel fear right here; indeed,
it is appropriate for you to fear death while still in this very state of full awareness and not yet having met your end—
how much more so, then, is it fitting for you who have committed evil deeds to feel fear?
This too is to be understood as being brought about from the unbearable sufferings of hell.
With reference to one who delights in the savor of effortless bliss, it is said:
"O delicate one, you are tormented even by contact with warm water;
having committed the karma of hell-beings, why do you remain so at ease? (Bca 7.12)
"Even touched by warm water," this is an address meaning "O delicate one";
because of the extreme softness of your body, you are unable to endure it.
If this is so, then the passage beginning with "having performed" (kṛtvā ca) and so forth is easy to understand.
Furthermore, he says to him:
"O you who are devoid of effort yet crave results, O delicate one who suffers much, O immortal-like form seized by death—alas, you miserable one, you are being destroyed! (Bca 7.13)
You are devoid of effort to produce the causes of happiness,
and yet you long for its fruit, which is happiness;
you are unable to endure suffering.
Moreover, you are beset by much suffering because you are a mine of all miseries;
you have been brought under the power of death,
yet you consider yourself to be immortal by nature.
Observing his conduct thus perverted and feeling compassion for him, he said to him with weariness: "Alas, you who are suffering, you are being destroyed;
through an abundance of delusion, you have entered into a miserable state.
Or, he reflects upon this within himself.
In this way, it should be understood elsewhere as well, according to what is applicable;
and terms such as "without effort" (*nirudyama*) are used as vocatives.
Addressing one who is under the sway of sleep, he says:
"O fool, having obtained this human boat, cross the great river of suffering! This time for sleep is not [eternal]; this boat will be difficult to find again. (Bca 7.14)

Having obtained this human state, which is free from the eight inopportune conditions, like a boat for crossing to the further shore of prosperity and so forth, cross over the great river consisting of suffering. Cast all sufferings behind you;
that is to say, by relying upon diligence.
O you who are overcome by delusion, this is no time for sleep while this boat is still nearby.
If an effort is not made right now, then this boat will again become difficult to find for one who has fallen into the miserable realms. As it is said:
"Where else can such a reunion occur?"
Thus it is said.
[Bodhicaryāvatāra 1.4] Having thus dispelled laziness, in order to dispel attachment to what is contemptible, he says:
"Having abandoned the supreme delight in the Dharma, which is a continuous succession of uninterrupted joy..."
How can you find delight in restlessness, laughter, and the like, which are causes of suffering?
The supreme and most excellent delight of those who perform virtuous deeds—of what nature is it? It is a continuous succession of delights (*anantaratisaṃtati*).
Because it generates a succession of happy rebirths, it possesses an endless, inexhaustible flow of delight; such is its character.

For this very reason, it is said [in the verse] "in the highest"; having abandoned that [calmness], passion (*rati*) is what is delightful (*abhirāma*), while agitation (*auddhatya*) is loftiness (*unnatatā*).
It means having a disposition toward playing with body and mind; laughter is verbal restlessness, meaning a sudden alteration of speech.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), songs and so forth are included.
The intention is: how can there be delight for you in that? It is not appropriate.
Of what nature is it? It is the cause of suffering;
for by leading one to miserable rebirths such as the hells, it becomes the cause of suffering.
Having thus rejected even contemptible attachment, in order to reject despondency and self-deprecation— which are the opposites of vigor—
and further demonstrating the means to eliminate their opposites, he says: "The state of being subject to the self through the application of the array of the power of non-despondency."
The equality of self and others, and indeed the exchange of self and others.
Non-despair (*aviṣāda*) is the opposite of despair.
The array (*vyūha*) of powers is their collection, whose characteristics will be described later. Proficiency (*tātparya*) is skillfulness.
Submissiveness to oneself and being under one's own control;
all these form copulative compounds (*dvandva-samāsa*).
Alternatively:
(Bcp 120) Accompanied by these, there is self-mastery;
and self-equality with others and the exchange of self for others will be explained in the section on meditation (*dhyānapariccheda*) [in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*].
This entire collection is capable of abandoning laziness and accomplishing vigor; such is the summary.
Explaining the meaning that has been indicated in sequence, he says:
"One must not give way to despondency by thinking, 'How can there be awakening for me?
Regarding the phrase "How can there be awakening for me":
"How can I, a wretched person, be a vessel for perfect enlightenment?

For Buddhahood is achievable only by a certain exceptional person who possesses sharp faculties, has initiated heroic effort, and has accomplished extremely difficult deeds through immeasurable accumulations of merit and wisdom over many incalculable eons."
One should not engage in despondency or dejection through such a form of mental attention as "I am not like that; how could Buddhahood of such a kind be possible for those like me?",
because this is a cause for the loss of the great purpose.
As it has been said: "Despair, too, is a disadvantage" [Śikṣāsamuccaya 34]. Why?
Because the Tathāgata, who speaks the truth, has declared this to be true. (Bca 7.17)
Because the Tathāgata has spoken and declared this which is about to be stated as true and not false. How is this known? It says: "He is a speaker of truth.
This means he is one who speaks without error, due to the occurrence of both knowledge and action.
Therefore, this is a statement of the cause for speaking the truth.
What truth did he speak?
"They too were gadflies, mosquitoes, flies, and likewise worms, who by the power of their resolve attained the supreme enlightenment so difficult to reach. (Bca 7.18)

Thus he said: "Those Blessed Buddhas as well—Śākyamuni, Ratnaśikhin, Dīpaṃkara, and the others—while still within the whirlpools of the ocean of saṃsāra, wandering in the state of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), were exactly like this;

yet, by the power of their enthusiasm and through the capacity of their excellence in vigor, they accumulated the provisions and attained and realized the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment, which is difficult to reach and hard to obtain."
The sense is that for one who has initiated vigor, nothing is difficult to accomplish;
this is the truth.
Therefore, he says that for me, moreover, enlightenment is not at all difficult to attain:
"How much more so am I, a human by birth, capable of discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful;
why then should I not attain enlightenment by not abandoning the method of the Omniscient One? (Bca 7.19).
How much more so, then, being born as a human being, am I capable of knowing what is beneficial and what is harmful—
this is beneficial, this is harmful.
Having reflected, "It has been taught that there is both auspicious and inauspicious karma,

and I am capable of knowing and understanding it," [one considers] the *nīti*— the method or principle— of the Omniscient One, who knows the reality of all things, which is the exposition of what is to be adopted as truth.
Because of not relinquishing it, because of not abandoning it—
that is to say, because of grasping it, taking it up, and cultivating it—
I shall not attain Buddhahood.
"By reciting with a modulated tone (kākvā), one will surely attain [the goal]";
this was shown by the Blessed One in the *Ratnamegha*. As it is said:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva does not give rise to such a thought: 'Awakening is difficult to attain for one who has become a human being.'"
Moreover, this vigor of mine is limited and inferior;
I am indolent,
yet awakening must be fully accomplished through practice for many eons, many hundreds of eons, and many thousands of eons— by one who acts like someone whose head or clothing is on fire.
Therefore, I am not able to bear such a burden.
Rather, a bodhisattva should generate this thought: "Even those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who have already attained perfect enlightenment..."
And those who will also fully awaken,
they too shall do so by this very method and by this very path.
It was by such very vigor that they attained perfect awakening; yet even they did not attain perfect awakening while already being Tathāgatas.
I, too, shall strive in that same manner.

"In such and such a manner shall I exert myself with vigor shared with all sentient beings and with vigor directed toward all sentient beings, so that I too shall realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
This is indeed reasonable;
however, fearing that upon hearing of such extremely difficult deeds, one might become despondent and unable to proceed, he reflects and says:
"Nevertheless, I have fear that my hands, feet, and so forth must be given away."
If you think that because Buddhahood is not attained without the giving of hands, feet, head,
and so forth, one's enthusiasm necessarily turns away due to the fear of engaging in such extremely difficult deeds,
your own mind speaks thus:
Confusion regarding what is heavy and what is light would be mine through lack of reflection.
This very state of being confused about what is heavy and what is light—
thinking that what is small is greater and what is great is smaller— belongs to me due to the power of delusion, through lack of reflection and lack of discrimination;
it does not arise from reflection on the ultimate truth.
Demonstrating that, through an investigation into the ultimate truth, this is indeed a reversal of what is heavy and what is light, he says:
"I am to be cut, to be split, to be burned, and even to be torn asunder many times for incalculable millions of eons, yet awakening will not come to pass. (Bca 7.21)
Dwelling in the prison of *saṃsāra*, by the power of such karma, I am to be cut—my hands, feet, and other major and minor limbs—in the hells and other realms;
likewise, I am to be pierced with spears, pikes, and the like; and I am to be burned by the fires of hell and so forth.
Being split apart by flaming saws and other instruments many times,
that is, on numerous occasions,
while experiencing torment in the hells and other realms within the boundless path of saṃsāra.
For incalculable millions of eons, beyond the reach of calculation,
suffering of many kinds will befall one even against one's will, and that will not suffice for the equipment of Buddhahood.
Showing that this suffering of cyclic existence is more extensive and fruitless due to its lack of end, whereas that which accomplishes Buddhahood is much less and fruitful, he says:
"But this limited suffering of mine is the means for achieving perfect enlightenment."
It is like the pain of extracting a shaft that has already caused the pain of its removal.
That which accomplishes Buddhahood is this limited suffering of mine, because it arises at a specific time and is the cause for the pacification of suffering;
such being the case, that [suffering] is a thorn, and by it there is pain.
Its exclusion (*apoha*) is its cessation (*nivṛtti*). "For that purpose" means for the sake of removing it;
the meaning is: for the sake of abandoning the suffering caused by it as long as one lives.
The extraction of that lost splinter means its removal from the body;
that is to say, its drawing out.
By that [extraction], there arises a suffering that is restricted to a specific time and is relatively slight.
For the sake of pacifying long-term suffering,
this suffering as well ought to be endured in that same manner.
For this reason as well, he says that this is appropriate:
"All physicians bring about health through the pains of medical treatment;
therefore, to destroy many sufferings, a small amount [of suffering] must be endured. (Bca 7.23)
Not just some,

but all [physicians] provide health for those afflicted by disease through the sufferings of medical procedures— such as jumping, purgation, and so forth, as well as those produced by the restriction of food and lifestyle according to their needs;
otherwise, it would be impossible to do so.
Since this is so, therefore one must endure even the most minimal suffering with great effort.
For what purpose? To destroy many sufferings;
that is to say, for the sake of pacifying all long-term sufferings of oneself and of all sentient beings.
Thus, it is indeed proper for the wise person to accept this.
And showing that even this difficult task, though logical, was not permitted by the Blessed One for a beginner, he says:
"The excellent physician did not prescribe even this appropriate treatment"—
this treatment which has just been described, which produces suffering.
Although it was appropriate and worthy of being followed,
the Blessed One— the supreme physician who cures all diseases in every way—
did not grant it at first.
He did not present it as something to be practiced by a beginner.
How, then, does he remove the diseases of passion and so forth? He says:
"He treats those who are gravely ill with sweet remedies. (Bca 7.24)
The meaning is: by means of extremely gentle treatment and application, and by administering medical care according to what is appropriate;
he treats, that is, he makes [them] free from disease.
Those who are greatly afflicted, long-suffering from disease, and seized by the great maladies of passion and the like.
What, then, is this "sweet treatment"? He says:
"At first, the leader even enjoins one to the giving of vegetables and the like;
later, through that sequence, he causes one to do that which one would even give away one's own flesh. (Bca 7.25)

In order to remove the stain of stinginess and for the sake of increasing the accumulations with ease and happiness, the Blessed One, the Leader, first encourages [beings] by means of giving things that can be easily relinquished, such as vegetables, barley-meal, and balls of food; furthermore,
he employs them through such specific skillful means.
The word "tad" (that) refers to what is said in common worldly parlance:

just as a donor, through the gradual process of practicing mild giving, reaches the pinnacle of practicing extremely intense giving, and subsequently, at a later time, would offer even his own flesh, blood, and so forth with ease and with a serene mind.

Anticipating the doubt, "How, then, can this be so? he says: "When wisdom arises toward one's own flesh just as it does toward vegetables, then what indeed is difficult for one who abandons flesh and bone? (Bca 7.26)

At the time when, through the practice of giving reaching its highest excellence, a mind arises that is entirely free from stinginess and thus feels no attachment even toward one's own flesh as if it were mere vegetables, then—even regarding the gift of one's own flesh and so forth—there is no thought that it is impossible to perform. What, then, could be difficult at that time?
The meaning is: nothing at all.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "How can one who has been wandering for an exceedingly long time for the sake of others avoid that suffering? To this he says: "One is not miserable because of having abandoned sin; one is not dejected because of being wise. For it is through false conceptualization in the mind that pain arises in the body from sin. (Bca 7.27)
For suffering that arises as an affliction is indeed of two kinds: physical and mental.
Neither of these two occurs for the bodhisattva;
because he has desisted from all faults through body, speech, and mind, physical suffering does not arise for him.
And since both forms of selflessness are ascertained through reasoning and scripture, how could there be even mental [suffering]?

For suffering arises in the mind through false conceptualization—that is, through unreal discursive thought—which functions by grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, or through the insistence on the existence of phenomena and so forth;
and [suffering] arises in the body from evil deeds such as the taking of life.
Thus, it has first been demonstrated that suffering does not arise for him by means of avoiding the causes of suffering.
Now, demonstrating that he possesses nothing but happiness, it is said:
"By merit the body is happy; by wisdom the mind is happy.
Abiding in cyclic existence for the sake of others, how could the compassionate one be distressed? (Bca 7.28)
He is "happy" because this body has been born with ease;
he is "joyful" because happiness exists in his mind.
Thus, being endowed with both forms of happiness, why would a compassionate one, wandering through cyclic existence for the sake of others, be distressed by suffering?
Does one experience weariness? Or rather, by what is one wearied?
The meaning is that because there is no cause for weariness, one is not wearied by anything at all.
Why, then, is this aversion adopted out of groundless timidity?

It might be argued: "Perfect enlightenment is attained through a great accumulation of merit that has been practiced, cultivated, and multiplied over a long period of time; therefore, for those seeking liberation, it would be better to rely on the Śrāvaka vehicle because of its swiftness. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Exhausting former misdeeds and receiving oceans of merit,
one proceeds even more swiftly than the Śrāvakas solely through the power of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
By means of the power of the thought of awakening alone, one causes those sins committed in the past to be exhausted,
as it was said before:
"Like the fire at the end of an eon, it burns away great sins in an instant."
Thus, [Bodhicaryāvatāra 1.14]: likewise, by the power of the thought of awakening alone, receiving and taking up oceans of merit.
As it has been said:
"Uninterrupted streams of merit flow forth, equal to the sky."
A bodhisattva who has mounted the Mahāyāna by means of the speed of such power of skillful means travels faster and moves more swiftly even than the śrāvakas.
Thus, moving from happiness to happiness, what conscious person would despair after having obtained the chariot of the thought of awakening, which removes all weariness and fatigue? (Bca 7.30)
He demonstrates the very meaning already explained by summarizing it:

because of the abstention from all faults and the destruction of previously committed sins according to the sequence thus described, there is no going to an evil rebirth even in dreams; therefore, with intense resolve and manifold happiness, [one dwells] day and night pervading the realm of space.
And by increasing the ocean of merit, having obtained the bodhicitta— which is like a chariot for entering the excellent path of the succession of happy rebirths—
the meaning is "having mounted it.
"With all weariness" refers to exhaustion and fatigue caused by afflictions.
It is so called because it dispels darkness, or because it dispels all weariness and fatigue according to the method already established.

Who indeed that possesses discernment would fall into despondency while proceeding toward and attaining one bliss after another— each increasingly superior— the bliss characterized by the prosperity of gods and humans?
Thus, having established non-despondency by means of refuting the various causes of despondency, he speaks in order to establish the array of powers:
"The power of zeal, steadfastness, joy, and liberation is for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
One should cultivate zeal out of fear of suffering, while contemplating the benefits. (Bca 7.31)
This too is merely a statement of the headings.
Here, *chanda* is the aspiration for the wholesome;
*sthāma* is the firmness of what has been undertaken.
Delight is attachment to virtuous deeds; liberation is the relinquishment [of effort] for a time when one lacks the capacity [to act].
This is the fourfold army, because it consists of a collection of many constituent parts.
It is like the strength of an elephant and so forth;
the meaning is that because this vigor is the cause for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings, and because it is the means for achieving all that is desired.
In this regard, because the power of aspiration (*chanda*) is of great utility, he states its cause for arising with the words "aspiration" and so forth: "out of fear of suffering.
One should generate aspiration out of dread that suffering arises from unwholesome karma.
And one contemplates the benefits;
"benefits" refers to specific qualities by way of their results,
and these, by implication, belong only to wholesome action.
Cultivating those [ideas],
the meaning is that one repeatedly contemplates how various kinds of sweet fruits arise from virtuous actions.
Now, in order to demonstrate the function of the power (*bala*), he says:

"Having thus uprooted the opposing side, one should strive for the increase of enthusiasm by means of the powers of zeal (*chanda*), self-respect (*māna*), delight (*rati*), relinquishment (*tyāga*), application (*tātparya*), and mastery (*vaśitā*). (Bca 7.32)
"By the continuous sequence thus spoken," and so forth; "having uprooted the adversary, such as indolence," means having removed it by means of the method of cultivating the counteragent.
One should exert effort to increase one's vigor.
By what means? [It is as follows: Pride is the inflation of the mind.
This is either the nourishment of the power of steadfastness, or it is the power of steadfastness itself;
by means of their powers and capacities.
In this context, the word "power" (*bala*) is a synonym for "capacity" (*sāmarthya*).
In that regard, first, for the sake of generating the aspiration, he says:
"I must destroy the immeasurable faults of myself and others, wherein even a single fault would not be exhausted even in oceans of aeons. (Bca 7.33)
In that regard, not even a trace of my effort toward the destruction of faults is seen;
why does my chest not burst asunder while I am made to endure immeasurable agony?
Many virtues are to be acquired by me for both myself and others;
the cultivation of even a single one of these might not be accomplished in eons as numerous as the oceans.
Not even a trace of virtue has ever been cultivated by me.

Yet, for the sake of being a resource for all sentient beings, and for the abandonment of all my own afflictions and the production of every excellence without exception, I have generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
And having understood that this cannot be accomplished through lax effort, if—due to a lack of initiated vigor—I [fail to persevere]...

The collective meaning is that one should generate aspiration by bringing about a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), reflecting: "If I remain with such feeble exertion, there is no other destination for me except for falling into the miserable states of existence."
The meaning of the individual components is now stated: "Immeasurable" means impossible to measure.
"Faults" refers to those based upon body, speech, and mind.
"To be slain" means to be utterly destroyed.
"Of oneself and another" means of one's own self and of another's self;
"even of each one" implies that let alone many.
In those [cases] where, by one of weak vigor, exhaustion— that is, abandonment— is achieved through many oceans of eons, meaning hundreds of thousands of eons; therein, in those [cases],
regarding the undertaking of the destruction of faults, that is, the enthusiasm for abandoning faults.
Not even a *leśa*, not even the slightest bit, of me is seen or perceived.
Therefore, for me—who am a vessel for immeasurable suffering, a recipient of boundless pain—my chest bursts open and my heart rends asunder.
How? In what manner?
The passage beginning with "The qualities are mine" and so forth is easy to understand.
Having reflected thus, he demonstrates a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*):
"In vain has my birth been spent, though it was obtained by some extraordinary means. (Bca 7.36)
My birth has been spent in vain and fruitlessly; it was led away and wasted— meaning rendered useless—
even though it was somehow obtained after a very long time, like the neck of a turtle being inserted through the hole of a yoke floating upon the great ocean.
For this very reason, because it is a source of wonder, it is marvelous.
For this reason as well, he says it is fruitless:
"I have not attained the bliss of the great festival of worshiping the Blessed One; I have performed no service for the Teaching; and the hopes of the poor have not been fulfilled. (Bca 7.37)
I have not granted fearlessness to those who were afraid, nor have I brought happiness to the distressed;
I have gone only to cause my mother suffering, becoming a thorn in her womb. (Bca 7.38)

I have not attained or achieved the happiness and mental joy that comes from the extraordinary celebration and exultation of honoring the Tathāgatas; nor have I performed acts of service or worship by means of honoring images, stūpas, and the True Dharma within the Teaching, or through the giving of requisites such as monasteries, groves, and bedding.
Nor was the hope and desire of the poor and destitute fulfilled by providing them with all kinds of excellent requisites;
nor was fearlessness granted to those who were afraid, being overwhelmed by the dread of enemies and the like, with the words "Do not fear";
nor were those afflicted and tormented by the sufferings of body and mind made happy by removing those [sufferings].
Thus, because he is devoid of all the qualities of a true person (satpuruṣa), it is said:
"for the sake of suffering," and so forth; this is easy to understand.

He asks, "How did you come to reach this state regarding the Dharma? and says: "Due to my former lack of aspiration for the Dharma, such a misfortune has now befallen me; who would ever abandon aspiration for the Dharma? (Bca 7.39)

Due to the absence of a longing for the Dharma accumulated in previous births, such a calamity has now arisen for me in this life; it has emerged with the very nature of a total deficiency in all capability, as just described. Knowing this, who would abandon or relinquish their aspiration for the Dharma?
The sense is: what wise person indeed would not accept it?

Furthermore, anticipating the question of why there should be an effort to generate aspiration in those seeking the wholesome, he says the following—in order to clarify what was stated previously regarding how one should cultivate aspiration out of fear of suffering and so forth:
"The Sage declared that aspiration is the root of all wholesome qualities. (Bcp 126)
The root of that as well is the constant cultivation of the fruit of maturation.
The meaning of the word "and" (ca) is that one should strive to generate aspiration not only for the sake of avoiding misfortune, but also for the sake of accumulating pure qualities (*śukladharma*).
The phrase "of all" means not merely of some.
The Blessed One has stated that desire (*chanda*) is the root and the cause; the meaning is that this is not said merely by his own speculative reasoning.
Furthermore, the root of that very desire is the cultivation of the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) at all times and in every respect.
The ripened fruit of wholesome and unwholesome karma is characterized by the attainment of the desirable and undesirable in the next world;
its cultivation is the repeated bringing [of that fruit] to mind.
In that regard, demonstrating the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) of unwholesome karma, he says:
"Sufferings, mental distresses, and various fears, as well as the frustration of one's desires, arise for those who commit evil deeds. (Bca 7.41)
Whatever various and manifold kinds of physical and mental sufferings arise and exist within the realms of hell and so forth, all belong only to those who commit evil deeds;
as do the fears arising from execution, imprisonment, beating, and the like,
as well as the frustration of one's search for gain and the frustration of one's desires.
He speaks of the ripening fruit of well-performed actions:
"Wherever the desire of those who have done good goes, there they are honored by the value of its fruits through their merits. (Bca 7.42)

The mental construction that aspires for what is desired is *manoratha*, which is well known in the world as "the kingdom of the mind" (*manorājya*) for those who perform auspicious deeds and cultivate merit.
The phrase "in whatever [place]" uses repetition (*vīpsā*) to mean "nowhere else."
"Goes" means it extends.
"By the price of the fruit" (phalārgheṇa): the offering of the desired fruit itself is the "price" (argha), just as a price is an act of worship (pūjā).

Furthermore, he states the fruit of the unwholesome: "But wherever the evildoer goes who desires happiness, right there he is struck by the weapons of suffering produced by those very evils. (Bca 7.43)
The desire for happiness is the longing for pleasure.
In the phrase "by those sins," the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) denotes the agent; in "by the weapons of suffering," it denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*).
Sufferings themselves are like weapons, because they are the cause for the interruption of that desire.
He speaks of the uncommon fruit resulting from uncommon virtuous karma, which is not shared by ordinary worldlings:
"Seated within the calyxes of vast, fragrant, and cool lotuses,
their splendor is accumulated through feeding upon the sweet voice of the Jina."
Through their wholesome deeds, the sons of the Sugata emerge from the lotuses awakened by the hand of the Sage and appear before the Sugata.
For Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages beginning with *muditā* (joy) do not, against their will, take birth in a mother’s womb;
rather, they are born within the calyxes of the *viśvadala-kamala* (thousand-petaled lotus) in Sukhāvatī. By this [verse], he describes the manifestation of their bliss: "Vipulāni" (vast).
These are the lotuses, both those growing in ponds and those born from mud; they are expansive, fragrant, possessing a pleasing scent, cool, and pleasant to the touch when cool.
These are either attributes of the lotuses themselves, or rather, these are qualifiers of the "interiors" (garbha) of the lotuses.

The connection is as follows: those sons of the Sugata who have gone to and are established within them—possessing the bodhicitta which is infused with the *kalala* of merit and gnosis arising from wisdom (*prajñā*), skillful means (*upāya*), and great compassion—become such through their virtues. But how do they obtain nourishment within the hearts of the lotuses? To this he says: "With sweet," and so forth.

Those whose splendors—their bodies—are produced and accumulated by the food of the sound of the Dharma, which is sweet because it possesses all the qualities of musical tone and brings about supreme mental joy; they are thus described.

And as to how they emerge from that, he says "by the hands of the Sage," and so forth. Those lotuses, having been awakened and caused to blossom by the rays of the Tathāgatas once the time for their maturation had been discerned by the hands of the Sage—
those [beings] whose bodies have emerged or gone forth from them, being beautiful due to being adorned with the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana), are thus described.
Being thus, the sons of the Sugata become Bodhisattvas;
they are born in the presence of the Sugata, before the Blessed Amitābha in Sukhāvatī,
through wholesome deeds that are exclusively pure.
By this, it is demonstrated that for those being born within the mother’s womb, suffering is to be understood as the opposite of these aforementioned qualities.

For instance, having been produced there in that cramped, foul-smelling place heated by the fire of the stomach, born from the impurities of the mother and father, growing on what is like vomit consisting of the mother’s food and drink, submerged in the mire of fetal filth, at the time of full development—

In some way, like one whose life-breath has reached the throat or who is being crushed by a machine, there is an emergence from that state; thus, for the most part, the fruit of the ripening of mixed karma for one who has become human has been described.

Regarding the ripening fruit of that which is exclusively black, he says: "With all his luster stripped away by the messengers of Yama, crying out in agony, his body is as if poured with molten copper heated by fire."
With the flesh torn away by hundreds of blows from flaming swords and spears, he falls repeatedly upon the intensely heated iron ground due to his many evil deeds.
Led away and separated by the messengers of Yama, the messengers of Time, he whose entire skin, hide, or splendor has been shattered by blows from blazing hammers and other weapons is thus described;
being exceedingly afflicted, he falls upon the surfaces of intensely heated iron ground.
Furthermore, what is he like?

One whose body is drenched—that is, bathed—with copper that has been liquefied by the heat of a fierce fire; for this reason, every bit of its natural luster is stripped away. Blazing swords and *śaktis* (spears), which are types of weapons, [are used against him].
He falls, his flesh-slices— that is, his pieces of flesh— having been cut and severed by many hundreds of blows from those [weapons];
he falls upon well-heated iron grounds due to impure,
unwholesome actions (karma).
"Many times" means for many repetitions;
because its fruit is exhausted over a long period of time.

Having thus established the ripened fruit of virtuous and non-virtuous actions, he says, while concluding the section on the power of aspiration: "Therefore, one should cultivate a virtuous aspiration with such earnestness.
This is because the ripened fruits of virtuous and non-virtuous actions are, respectively, sweet and bitter.
Therefore, having reflected in this way, one should diligently cultivate the desire for virtue alone, abandoning unwholesome actions.
Now, in order to demonstrate the power of fortitude, he says: "One should cultivate pride, beginning with it, according to the method of the Vajradhvaja [Sūtra]. (Bca 7.46)
(Bcp 128) Furthermore, according to the procedure set forth in the *Vajradhvaja-sūtra*, one should perform the measurement and then meditate while undertaking the ritual action;
or alternatively,
"one should meditate while undertaking" means one should meditate with intense exertion.
One should make it firm in the mind;
the meaning is that one should not do so with a lax effort.
In order to teach the very commencement [of an action], he says:
"Having first examined the collection of conditions, one should either begin or not begin.
Having first—that is, at the very outset—examined the collection of conditions, which is the completeness of causes, for the sake of accomplishing the desired task;
Having deliberated upon its strength or weakness,
one should undertake it if there is strength,
or not undertake it if there is no strength.
If it is asked, "What is the purpose of such an investigation? he says: "It is better indeed not to begin at all than to turn back after having begun. (Bca 7.47)
It is indeed better not to begin at all from the very outset, rather than to turn back after having begun when one finds oneself lacking the capacity.
One might ask: "What is the fault here that this [practice] is not accepted?

To this he says: "Even in another life, that habituation persists; moreover, suffering increases due to evil. Furthermore, it is deficient at the time of action, and thus it has not been accomplished. (Bca 7.48)
When practiced in this manner, that very habituation continues even in another birth; this is what is called "cessation.
Furthermore, for one who fails to fulfill what has been promised, sin arises, and from that, suffering increases.
Moreover, there is the loss of that inferior thing which was abandoned when this [practice] was undertaken.
And "the time for the task" means inferior;
it refers to the time belonging to a task that has been commenced and then abandoned.
The meaning is: at that time, whatever other task ought to be performed, that [is what is meant].
Furthermore, that [gift] which was undertaken and then abandoned has neither been accomplished nor brought to completion;
thus, there are five types of defects here.
The intended meaning is that it is led by that.
Now, should this pride not be practiced in all circumstances? No, he says:
"Pride should be applied toward three things: actions, secondary afflictions, and capacities.
Toward which three? He says: toward actions, toward secondary afflictions, and toward capacity.

In that regard, the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) designated as the "Minor Matters" (*kṣudravastuka*) consist of seven, beginning with anger (*krodha*), enmity (*upanāha*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), and spite (*pradāśa*).
Alternatively, the fifty afflictions themselves, such as attachment (*rāga*) and so forth, are called secondary afflictions.
In this context, he speaks in order to explain the pride of action (*karmamāna*):
"I alone must do it"—this is the pride of action.
Whatever blameless deed has fallen to sentient beings,
all that must be performed by me alone; the meaning is that no opportunity should be given to anyone else.
Demonstrating this very point, he says:
"This world is independent of its afflictions and is incapable of accomplishing its own welfare;
therefore, I must act for their sake, so that I do not remain as powerless as other people. (Bca 7.50)
This entire mass of living beings, rendered dependent by the afflictions, is incapable of accomplishing its own welfare in any way;
therefore, I have generated the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*) for the sake of producing all happiness for them.
Since this is so, I am not as incapable of bearing such a burden as these people are.
Therefore, I myself must do everything for them.
(Bcp 129) He says that one should not give rise to aversion even toward a lowly task:
"How could another perform a lowly task while I am still present?
A lowly task is one highly despised in the world, such as carrying burdens and the like."
Even while I exist and remain as a servant to all sentient beings,
how can another perform what ought to be done by me? The sense is that it is fitting for me alone to do it.
Now, in order to prevent the inflation of the mind that thinks, "This improper act is my own doing," he says:
"If I do not perform this because of pride, it is better for my pride to perish. (Bca 7.51)
If, out of pride, I do not perform this work because I think, "Who is the son of such-and-such a person? And this task is exceedingly lowly; it is improper for me to do it," [then I am at fault].
In that case, let my pride perish; it would be better for me.
What use have I for this [pride] which causes the ruin of great goals, rather than engaging in base actions?
Having thus stated the measure regarding actions, he says the following to demonstrate the measure regarding the secondary afflictions (upakleśa):
"Even a crow acts like a Garuḍa upon encountering a dead Dundubha snake;
even a slight misfortune afflicts me if my mind is weak. (Bca 7.52)

If my mind were to have its activity weakened by having subdued the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), then calamity and transgression would afflict and overwhelm it, meaning that it would become possessed of an offense— even if that [offense] were slight and produced by a mild manifestation of a secondary affliction.
To explain how this is so, he says: just as even a crow, having found a dead dundubha snake whose life has departed, behaves like a garuḍa.
Why is this so? He says:
"Indeed, calamities are easily overcome by one who is rendered motionless by despair;
but one who has rallied and is striving is difficult to conquer even for the great. (Bca 7.53)

When one is devoid of mental upliftment, characterized by despondency, with the activity of body and mind sluggish, impaired by laziness, and possessed of lost mindfulness, calamities are easy to bring about and easily obtained; for even very slight calamities indeed arise because of such vulnerability.

However, one who has emerged from that state, with a highly uplifted mind, endowed once more with enthusiasm, exerting himself, and providing no opportunity for secondary afflictions through mindfulness and clear comprehension, is difficult even for the great to conquer and remains invincible.
It may be so.
Therefore, with a firm mind, I shall overcome misfortune with misfortune; for one who has succumbed to misfortune, the desire to conquer the three worlds becomes an object of ridicule.
Concluding the reliance on the power of steadfastness (*sthāmabala*), he demonstrates: "Since it is thus, therefore, with a firm mind, I shall don the mental armor (*mānasasannāha*).
I shall deal with calamities as if they were calamities—that is, as harmful—and by warding off their entry in every way, I shall uproot them from my continuum.
Otherwise, my undertaking of the conquest of the three worlds would be a mockery, an object of derision."
It will pass away for one who has been conquered by misfortune—a miserable thing that is dependent upon misfortune.
To explain what this is like, he says:
"For everything is to be conquered by me; I am not to be conquered by anyone. This pride must be borne by me, for I am the son of the Lion of the Victors. (Bca 7.55)
(BCP 130) Why? Because only the Victors, the Blessed Ones, are lions, since they cannot be approached by any of the beasts that are the Māras.

Having kept in mind that "I am their son; how could I incur the name of being defeated by others?", this pride must be borne by me. For just as a lion cub, having attained fearlessness, roams the forest entirely unvanquished by all other beasts, so too must I act.
The meaning is that I must likewise become firm.
This might be the case: if [pride] were indeed [a virtue], then why would even those who bear pride for the sake of conquering rivals and the like not be praised as "the proud"? To this, he says:
Those beings who have conquered pride are the best; they are not proud.
One who is proud falls under the power of the enemy, and those [who are not proud] are not under the power of the enemy-pride.
Those wretched ascetics who have been conquered by pride—that is, overcome by arrogance—will surely remain proud.
Why? Because one who possesses pride does not fall under the power of the enemy;
the meaning is that such a person does not comply with the will of those who harbor enmity.
Those whom you consider to be proud are actually under the sway of the enemy that is pride; their activities are dependent upon it.
To support this very point, he says in two verses:
"Led by pride to miserable rebirths, even when born as humans they are deprived of joy; subsisting on the alms of others, they are slaves, fools, ill-favored, and emaciated. (Bca 7.57)
Even those ascetics who are despised by all and stiff with pride—
if they too are among the proud, tell me, what kind of people are the truly wretched?
Led to miserable destinies and cast into the hells and other realms by one or another of the seven types of pride,
even if they should somehow obtain a human birth,
they remain there joyless and devoid of celebration due to the fruit of that disparagement.
The meaning is that their minds are base and dejected. "Eating the alms of others" means subsisting on food given by others due to a lack of provisions;
"servants" refers to those who live under the control of others, namely employees.
They are fools, devoid of all discernment;
they are unsightly, with misshapen bodies that produce no pleasure;
they are emaciated, with weak frames and lacking in capability.
From all sides and toward everyone, even those who have committed no offense become objects of physical and verbal contempt.
Who, then, are these?
They are ascetics stiff with pride—stiff with pride means unbending.
"Those wretched ascetics"— if even they, despite being such as these, are counted among the proud, then [the truly proud] are miserable, pitiable, and objects of compassion; this is the meaning.
"Furthermore, tell me, what are others who are miserable like? Speak!"—thus he addresses the questioner.
If those who are thus conceited are not so called, then what kind of people are they? He says:
"They are the conceited, and they alone are the victorious and the brave."
Those who carry pride for the sake of conquering the enemy that is pride,
and who, having struck down that very foe of pride even while it is surging, bestow upon people the fruit of victory as they desire; [to them I pay homage].

(Bcp 131) Only those Bodhisattvas are called "the proud" who, having struck down and shaken off that enemy of pride— even though it is surging and powerful— act according to their desire, as they wish; that is to say, they act with unrestrained freedom.
They manifest the fruit of victory in the world of beings, including the gods and others, at the stage of Buddhahood.
The intention is that such is the fruit of conquering the enemy of pride as it is seen in us;
they alone are the victors who have attained victory.
The two words "those very ones" (ta eva) and "heroes" (śūrāḥ) and "resplendent ones" (tejasvinaḥ) are to be applied according to their respective contexts.

Having explained pride regarding the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), he now speaks of pride regarding power: "One who stands in the midst of the faction of defilement may be arrogant a thousandfold.
The "faction of defilements" (*saṃkleśānāṃ pakṣaḥ*) refers to their class or group.
Standing in its midst, he would become a thousand times more arrogant and would rely upon an extraordinary strength of valor. Being of what nature? He says:
Duryodhana was [tormented] by multitudes of sufferings, like a lion by herds of deer.
He is called Duryodhana because he is "fought with difficulty";
the meaning is that he is not defeated by any means whatsoever.
How is this so? Just as the lion, the king of beasts, dwelling in the forest among the host of animals, endowed with great majesty and strength, overcomes all other beasts; so too is he.
And since he is not overcome by them, in this way a bodhisattva becomes difficult to conquer.
He says that this other sign should also be grasped:
"For even in great hardships, the eye does not perceive taste;
likewise, having encountered hardship, one should not fall under the power of the afflictions. (Bca 7.61)

Even when there are extremely intense hardships and sufferings, one does not see— that is, does not perceive or take as an object— the taste, such as sweetness and so forth, which is to be grasped by the sense organ of the tongue; this is because it is not within its range.
The meaning is that one does not engage with what is not one's proper object.
Thus, by the principle of the "eye for flavors" mentioned above, even when encountering hardship, one should not fall under the power of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Having established the power of steadfastness through the preceding discourse, he says the following to demonstrate the power of delight:
"Whatever task one undertakes, one should become devoted to that task;
one should be a connoisseur of that task and insatiable in spirit, like one who desires the pleasure that is the fruit of play. (Bca 7.62)
Whatever action characterized by meditation, study, and so forth, which is the basis for the accumulation [of merit], he undertakes;
having undertaken it through the application of sequential performance, he becomes devoted to that very action, his mind immersed in the flavor of its practice.
"Addicted to that karma" means greedy for its engagement;
"one whose soul is insatiable" means possessed of longing again and again.
Like what? Like one desiring to obtain the pleasure that is the fruit of games such as gambling—desirous of attaining that happiness which is the result of such play.
Showing that one should therefore develop a delight in action by reflecting even on this, he says:
"Action is performed for the sake of happiness, yet happiness may or may not result. But how can one who has no action be happy, when action itself is happiness? (Bca 7.63)
All perform actions out of a desire for the pleasure that is the fruit of those actions;
otherwise, there would be no engagement in them.
Nevertheless, even when one engages with such a mental attitude, the desired fruit of a particular action may still occur.
For some, however, it might not occur,
since even an undertaking that is fruitless is possible.
Nevertheless, people do not desist from undertaking actions because they still harbor the expectation of a result.
But for one for whom action itself is happiness, and who has no further desire for another happiness beyond that, how could such a person— being "niṣkarma," devoid of action— be happy?
The meaning is "not in any way whatsoever."
Thinking that one must apply oneself to action while cultivating this [meditation], he says:
"There is no satisfaction in cyclic existence through sensual desires, which are like honey on the edge of a razor;
how then could there be satisfaction through the nectar of merit, which is auspicious and sweet in its ripening? (Bca 7.64)
By means of objects such as form, one wanders again and again; this is what is called "saṃsāra. Non-contentment with unreal things is the lack of satiation.
Of what nature are they?

They are like honey on a razor’s edge. Just as when one tastes the sweet flavor of honey on a razor’s edge, suffering arises under the power of craving after the tongue has been cut off; those whose likeness is such as this are "like honey on a razor’s edge. Their comparison (upamā) is by means of that [suffering]. Those for whom the comparison is of such a kind are "those like honey on a razor’s edge."
The intention is that although they possess sweetness only at the moment of contact, they have a pungent nature due to the suffering of their ultimate transformation.
Meritorious deeds alone are like nectars;
how could there be satisfaction through them?

By what kind [of qualities]? By those that are sweet in their maturation (*vipāka*), because they possess a sweet flavor through transformation as the cause of the happiness that is the fruit of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*);
and by those that produce supreme bliss, being auspicious (*śiva*) and bringing about welfare (*kalyāṇa*) because they lead to the attainment of the ultimate good (*niḥśreyasa*).
The meaning is "by those which bring about the cessation of all suffering" because they are intent on bestowing the fruit of freedom from old age and death;
for this very reason, it serves as the explanatory reason for the phrase "by the nectars of merit."
Therefore, concluding with this summary, he speaks again to strengthen one's delight in action:
"Therefore, even at the conclusion of an action, one should immerse oneself in that very action, just as an elephant, scorched by the midday sun, plunges first into a lake. (Bca 7.65)
Even at the conclusion of that commenced action, he may sink;
he should release [the body] while still immersed in the flavor of his intense absorption.
How so? Just as one who, during the summer season when the sun is at its zenith, finds no water anywhere—

The overall meaning is as follows: a tormented elephant, possessed by extreme attachment, upon reaching a lake filled with exceptionally refreshing cool water, first plunges into it; "one who has reached the lake" means one by whom the lake has been attained.
The karmadhāraya compound follows later;
the word "at first" (ādau) is connected with the word "sinks" (nimajjati).

Now, having explained the power of delight (*ratibala*), he speaks in order to explain the power of liberation (*muktibala*): "But when there is a continuous attachment to the destruction of one's strength, one should abandon what was undertaken; and once it is well completed, one should let go of it through a desire for ever higher [attainments]. (Bca 7.66)

Having realized that one's own capacity for completing the task already begun has been exhausted, if one intends, "I shall do it again once capacity is regained," one may relinquish or abandon it for that duration;
by doing so, there would be no distraction for him.
Otherwise, even in such a case, if one does not relinquish it, there would only be the occurrence of misfortune.
Even when the action has been well-perfected and begun,
it must still be relinquished;
otherwise, even though it proceeds spontaneously, renewed effort toward it would result only in distraction.
Therefore, out of a desire for ever-increasing excellence, one should release— that is, abandon— it.
By this, the exception to that general rule previously stated in the verse beginning with "having first examined the totality of conditions" [7.47] has been declared.

Thus, having explained the array of forces in every way by demonstrating its internal distinctions, and now explaining the intended meaning—which was set forth in the first chapter but mentioned again in the section on the group beginning with "desire" (7.16)—[it says]:
"One should guard against the blows of the afflictions and strike firmly at the afflictions themselves, like one engaged in sword-fighting with a skilled enemy. (Bca 7.67)
One should guard against and ward off the blows and injuries of the afflictions (*kleśa*),
meaning that their blow should not prevail;
furthermore, one should strike back at the afflictions and destroy them.
"Solidly" means with a powerful blow, so that they may not find an opening again.

Regarding this, he provides an illustration: just as one who fights more skillfully with a sword against an enemy who is trained and endowed with expertise in the science of weapons overcomes that enemy.
And he is not overcome by that.

Thus, with the words "In that case," and so forth, he speaks again in order to teach the essential intent: "Just as one who is afraid would swiftly seize a sword that has fallen, so too should one seize the sword of mindfulness when it has slipped away, while recollecting the hells. (Bca 7.68)

In that sword-fight, the rule is that if the sword should somehow slip from one's hand, one must quickly retrieve and grasp it again, lest this enemy should strike me down by seizing an opportunity through deception; "tvaran" means acting with great haste.
It does not mean by the acquisition of time;
likewise, it is the same in the case of the loss of mindfulness.
Mindfulness itself is like a sword for the sake of conquering the enemy of the afflictions.
One should seize that which has slipped away and bring it back to the fore,
while recollecting the Raurava and other hells and reflecting upon the fact that one would partake in their suffering should one falter.

Now, one might ask: "Even if there is only the manifestation of subtle afflictions, what harm is done that equanimity should not be maintained toward them? To this he says: "Just as poison, having reached the blood, spreads through the body, even so does a fault, having found a fissure, spread within the mind. (Bca 7.69)
Not even the slightest opportunity for a fault should be granted;
otherwise, if even that much were to enter, it would be impossible to prevent its proliferation within the mind.
For it is just as when even a very small wound, having come into contact with blood, allows poison to spread through the body.
Therefore, one should apply oneself even to warding off the afflictions that are as small as an atom.
Furthermore, strengthening the intended meaning in another way, he says:

"Just as one carrying a vessel of oil, surrounded by men with swords in their hands, would be intent on his task out of fear of death should he stumble, so too should the practitioner of the vow. (Bca 7.70)

Suppose a certain man, by the command of a fierce king, were to take a vessel filled with oil and proceed along a slippery bridge, attended by royal guards with swords in their hands who declare, "If you spill even a single drop of oil, we shall deprive you of your life this very day. As he goes along, he thinks: "If I should somehow stumble here..."

Just as one becomes intent on [escaping] out of fear of death, thinking, "In that case, these people will surely kill me," so too a practitioner who has taken the vows (vratī) should become intent— that is, diligent— in order to prevent such lapses from occurring, out of dread of the sufferings of hell and other realms.
Summarizing what has been said, he says to show it:
"Therefore, just as one springs up quickly when a snake is in one's lap, so should one act with equal swiftness upon the arrival of sleep and laziness. (Bca 7.71)

Since this is so, therefore, just as one would rise with extreme haste when a venomous snake has entered one's lap, thinking "Lest this serpent bite me!", in the same way, when sleep and laziness arrive— that is, when torpor and lethargy manifest— one should apply a remedy; one should effect a counteraction through the cultivation of their opposites, such as the contemplation of impermanence.
Even for one who exerts effort in this way, some slight lapse might somehow occur according to the maxim of a hero's stumble.
In that case, having applied a remedy, one should again become diligent.
Demonstrating this, he says:
After having thoroughly repented for each single transgression, one should reflect:
"How shall I act so that this may not happen to me again? (Bca 7.72)

When there is a lapse of mindfulness, and when one by one, in each instance, a deception or a transgression occurs through some intrusion of the afflictions, one should feel remorse and, with a resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*), reflect deeply upon the mental anguish: "Alas! Having known [the truth], I have nonetheless stumbled. By what means shall I apply a remedy here, so that this deception may not occur again?"
Thus, one should dwell having undertaken such a firm exertion;
the sense is that one should not, however, become lax again.
For this very reason, permitting even that which is prohibited for those who desire solitude, he says: "By this means, one should desire or aspire to association or activity.

One should desire—that is, long for—association, which is meeting together, with the teacher (*ācārya*), the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), other fellow-students (*sabrahmacārin*), and so forth, who are deeply learned, knowers of the Tripitaka, and skilled in dispelling remorse.
The intended meaning is that one should remain dependent upon that very [instruction].
Or, "action" refers to that which has been attained, characterized by advice and instruction (*avavādānuśāsanī*),
as well as the removal of transgressions (*āpatti-samuddharaṇa*).
Or, one should desire to apply the administration of punishment by them when it arises;
this is for the purpose of protecting them from falling into [sin] through this very cause. He says this very thing:
"How indeed might there be the practice of mindfulness in these circumstances? (Bca 7.73).
By what method, indeed, might there be the practice of mindfulness during these states— the stages of the onset of afflictions—
such that there would be no loss of the object of focus even without effort?
It is with this intention [that he speaks].

This is the summarized meaning: due to the presence of a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), through his advice and instructions, and by observing his conduct, the afflictions (kleśa) find no entry for one who always dwells in mindfulness and clear comprehension (smṛti-saṃprajanya). Therefore, it is logical that one's enthusiasm increases precisely without conflict. Furthermore, one should never abandon a spiritual friend, even for the sake of one’s life.
Thus it is said: "Likewise, for those who act with reverence even out of fear of their preceptor’s instruction... [Bodhicaryāvatāra 5.102]...
For the fortunate, mindfulness arises easily through dwelling with the guru.
Thus [Bodhicaryāvatāra 5.30].

Having now demonstrated the intended meaning, he says the following to demonstrate that the self must be brought under control: "One should make oneself light by recollecting the discourse on heedfulness."
Just as before, one remains prepared for the arrival of karma in every situation.

(Bcp 135) One should make the self—characterized by body, speech, and mind—wholly serviceable; the meaning is that one should bring it under control through enthusiasm and practice. Just as before the arrival of a task or the commencement of an action, one is already prepared and brought under control, like a well-tamed horse, and engages in the work as if seated in expectation of its path.

Making clear the very point already stated by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as cotton is subject to the coming and going of the wind, so too should one come under the power of enthusiasm; in this way, prosperity truly flourishes. (Bca 7.75)

Just as cotton wool produced from *karpāsa* and other fibers is subject to and dependent upon the movement and coming-and-going of the wind, even so one should come under the sway of enthusiasm; one should become subject to the power of vigor (*vīrya*).
For one who is thus devoted to practice, supernatural power (*ṛddhi*)—characterized by traveling through the sky and other such feats—is accomplished and attained.

Furthermore, since both equanimity toward self and others (*parātmasamatā*) and the exchange of self and others (*parātmaparivartana*) are applicable in both cases, they should be explained precisely in the section on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Perfection of Vigor," in the *Pañjikā* on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
(Bcp 136) Chapter Eight: The Perfection of Meditation.
Thus, having explained diligence immediately after patience, it was said:
Then one should resort to the forest;
one should apply oneself to meditative concentration and cultivate the contemplation of the foul and so forth.
[Śikṣāsamuccaya Kārikā 20].
Having thus increased that [zeal], he begins to demonstrate it with the words "in this way" and so forth:
"Having thus increased enthusiasm, one should establish the mind in meditative concentration."

Having thus uprooted the adverse factors through the cultivation of their antidotes and having increased one's vigor, one should stabilize it by making it flow effortlessly; then, one should place the mind in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), in concentration (*samādhāna*), and in one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*).
One should cause it to enter therein; that is to say, one should establish it there.
To the question "For what purpose?", he says:
"But a person whose mind is distracted stands within the fangs of the afflictions. (Bca 8.1)
The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a reason.

Because, without meditative concentration (*samādhi*), even a man who possesses vigor—being one whose mind is distracted and whose conduct is not concentrated—stands as if caught between the fangs of the *rākṣasa*-like afflictions (*kleśa*); he remains as if already swallowed by them. Therefore...
In this regard, first establishing the introductory framework in order to eliminate the adversaries of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he says:
"Through physical and mental seclusion, distraction cannot arise.
Therefore, having abandoned the world, one should avoid discursive thoughts (*vitarka*). (Bca 8.2)
Physical seclusion is the avoidance of contact with people;
mental seclusion is the avoidance of discursive thoughts such as sensual desire and the like.
Thus it is said.

In the seclusion of body and mind, due to being free from attachment, there is no possibility— that is, no manifestation— of distraction, which consists in their elevation, or in other words, the non-abiding upon an objective referent.

Since this is so, therefore, having abandoned and left behind the world characterized by one's own kin, relatives, and so forth, one should first completely avoid—that is, renounce—the discursive thoughts that are the causes of mental distraction.
In that regard, first demonstrating the refutation of the reasons for not abandoning the world, he says:
"The world is not abandoned out of affection, nor out of craving for gain and the like;
therefore, in order to abandon it, the wise person should contemplate in this way. (Bca 8.3)
Attachment is the clinging set in motion by the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
because of it, the world is not abandoned,
nor is one free from craving for gain and the like.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), honor, fame, renown, and so forth are included.
Through craving for these, and through delusion—
by the word "and" (*ca*), it is further combined that one does not renounce them in this world.
Since this is the cause for not abandoning [the world], therefore, whether it be this affection or greed and the like,
the wise and discerning person should understand it as the reason for abandoning the world.
"In this way" means one should contemplate what is about to be described.
He says that very thing:

"Knowing that one who is well-yoked to insight through calm abiding effects the destruction of the afflictions, one should first seek calm abiding; and that [calm abiding] is attained through delight that is independent of the world. (Bca 8.4)
Śamatha is concentration (samādhi) characterized by one-pointedness of mind. The phrase "well-endowed with that" should be extracted [from the previous context] and applied here as well;
alternatively, the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause.
By means of *śamatha* as the cause, one is well-joined with *vipaśyanā*; or, in the sense of accompaniment,
one is well-joined with *vipaśyanā* together with *śamatha*.

Vipaśyanā is wisdom whose intrinsic nature is the thorough knowledge of reality as it truly is. One who is well-endowed with that [wisdom], through the yoga of the path that proceeds by way of the union of the two, effects the destruction—that is, the abandonment—of the afflictions. Having understood and known this, one who desires liberation from the afflictions should first, at the outset, seek out śamatha.
The meaning is "having produced [calm abiding]. Immediately after that comes insight (vipaśyanā).
The Sage said: "One who is concentrated understands reality as it truly is."
And the mind shall not waver from tranquility due to the cessation of external activity.
Thus it is said: [Śikṣāsamuccaya, Verse 9].
And that *śamatha* arises through a delight that is indifferent toward the world and its objects; it arises only for one who avoids attachment, and not otherwise.

To demonstrate that very same lack of regard for delight through the subsequent passage, he says: "For whom, being impermanent themselves, could there be affection for things that are impermanent, since one will not see a loved one again even after thousands of births? (Bca 8.5)
For what conscious being would it be appropriate or reasonable for affection to arise spontaneously toward impermanent things such as children and wife, which are themselves impermanent?
For what reason?
Because while wandering through countless thousands of births in the boundless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), one may never again see even a beloved person.
Because it pleases, it is called "dear" (priya).
And he says that even this is not present in him:
"Not seeing [the truth], he falls into discontent and does not abide in meditative concentration;
nor is he satisfied even upon seeing it, for as before, he is tormented by thirst. (Bca 8.6)
When he does not see him, then he experiences dissatisfaction and lack of fortitude;
because his mind is agitated by that very dejection, he does not abide in meditative concentration.
He does not remain at all; the meaning is that he is unable to maintain that [object] as a support.
Furthermore, even when a pleasant appearance arises for him,
Even then, he is not satisfied;
having seen it, his thirst is increased all the more,
and through the longing to see it, he suffers just as he did previously during the time when he could not see it.
Furthermore, demonstrating that association with loved ones is the source of all misfortune, he says:
"He does not see things as they truly are; he falls away from spiritual urgency.
He is consumed by that grief through his longing for union with the beloved. (Bca 8.7)
(Bcp 138) One who perceives things contrary to reality does not see or know faults and virtues;
through that very delusion, out of a longing for union with the beloved, one falls away from spiritual urgency and becomes ruined.
Likewise, by that same attachment, one is consumed by grief even at a momentary separation.
Thus, by that grief one is burned and tormented by that very mental anguish;
there is a longing for union with the beloved— union (*saṃyoga*) being the coming together (*saṃprayoga*) with the beloved— and the craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the desire for that.
By that which serves as the cause— namely,
by the ever-increasing and progressively more intense aspiration.
He says that even for this reason, association with them is indeed a cause of misfortune:
"By thinking of that, one's short life passes away in vain again and again.
This means by thinking of that beloved person or of that union with them, through the constant contemplation of their qualities.

The sense is: "How indeed might there not be a separation from this beloved union?"—thinking thus, with a mind absorbed in that [union], one's formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) perish fruitlessly at every moment;
they are of no use whatsoever for any wholesome action (*kuśala-karman*). This is the intended meaning.
And since that friend for whose sake one brings about the exhaustion of one's life is not stable, it is said: "By means of an impermanent phenomenon, the permanent Dharma is lost. (Bca 8.8)

Because of its inherent fragility and instability, through the cause of a friend who is not steadfast, one’s *dharma* falls away and declines. One might argue: "Since it is eternal and persists for a long time, and because it is included within the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*) and results in great fruit, this [friendship] must necessarily result in attaining some basis for welfare and happiness through that association;
why, then, is it rejected in every respect? To this, he says:
One who associates with fools will certainly go to an evil rebirth;
such association is not desired. What, then, can be gained from the company of fools?
Nor is anything else obtained here through association with them except for misfortune;
for one who shares the same conduct and possesses similar character as foolish ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) will certainly and inevitably go to an evil rebirth,
because of performing actions similar to theirs.
And because he stands outside the noble dharmas;

furthermore, if he were to act in a manner inconsistent with them by following the noble dharmas, then he would not be desired, would be disliked, and would be considered dissimilar— thus, he is one whose conduct is not the same [as theirs].
The connection is with the word "by fools" (*bālaiḥ*).
Here, the third case ending denotes the agent.
Thus, because of the subversion of both worlds, what has been obtained or attained from associating with fools—that which is the cause of benefit and happiness?
The meaning is "not anything at all."
And because they cannot be won over even by those whose conduct is agreeable, he says:
"In one moment they become friends, and in another moment they become enemies;
they fly into a rage at what would cause satisfaction—ordinary people are difficult to propitiate. (Bca 8.10)
In a mere moment, friends and allies are formed for some purpose of one's own;
yet in an instant, because of their contrary intentions, they become enemies and foes by taking up some pretext.
Moreover, even such a pretext for them is not fixed.
Because they sometimes become angry toward those who are objects of contentment or sources of joy due to the power of perversion—
thus ordinary people (*pṛthagjana*), being ignoble (*anārya*), are difficult to propitiate and can only be won over with great hardship.
(Bcp 139) Showing yet another characteristic of the foolish for the purpose of avoiding it, he says: "They become angry when told what is beneficial, and they restrain me from what is wholesome.
If their words are not heeded, they become enraged and go to an evil rebirth. (Bca 8.11)
When told or instructed that "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done," they become angry and harbor enmity.

Furthermore, they do not accept what was said as beneficial; on the contrary, they prevent me from that which is beneficial, saying, "What is the use of this performance of yours, which results only in mere exertion? and thus they dissuade me from engaging in it.
Now, "if their words are not heard"— the word "words" is to be supplied as the object—
[it means] if, having understood those words, one engages in what is beneficial.
Then, thinking "He does not desist from this because of our words," they become angry with that one who performs beneficial deeds; and, impelled by that karma, they go to a miserable rebirth.

Showing that one should cultivate another method for the sake of distancing oneself from this childish nature, he says: "Envy toward the superior, malice toward the equal, pride toward the inferior, intoxication from praise, and resentment at dispraise—when could any benefit ever come from a fool? (Bca 8.12)

Envy arises toward one who is superior or excellent due to their own learning, lineage, wealth, and so forth; it consists in the inability to endure the prosperity of others, directed specifically toward those very persons. From one who is equal to oneself—that is, similar—arises conflict, which is to say, dispute.

Pride (*māna*) is the conceit regarding oneself as inferior or low, arising from the thought "I am superior to this person. Intoxication (*mada*) is due to praise; it is a haughty arrogance (*avalepa*) resulting from the attribution of greatness through the recounting of one's own qualities, whether real or unreal, with the thought "I am great."

And there is hatred arising from hearing the proclamation of one's own faults due to disparagement; that is, toward the one who utters such disparagement. Thus, at what time and on what occasion could this ever be for the benefit of a fool?
The meaning is "never at any time."
To demonstrate that for this reason as well, one should dwell avoiding fools, he says:
Self-exaltation, disparagement of others, talk of delighting in cyclic existence—such things, and other impurities, inevitably arise from a fool toward a fool. (Bca 8.13)
From one fool toward another fool, and so forth, some kind of impure and unwholesome state necessarily and invariably arises.
What is that? It is self-exaltation and superiority through the praise of one's learning, knowledge, and so on;
and it is disparaging others, exposing their faults, and concealing one's own learning and such.
Whatever delight there is in cyclic existence— that is, the discourse and description of its pleasures— arising from the intense enjoyment of the qualities of sensual desire;
such is the nature of these things.
Thus, through association with him, there is an encounter with misfortune for that person as well.
Through association with another—that is, through contact with a second [such person]—some unwholesome state will necessarily arise.
For this reason, this association with fools is indeed an encounter with, and the attainment of, misfortune and what is not auspicious.
Therefore, for the sake of training in the noble dharmas:
"I shall dwell alone, happy, with an unafflicted mind. (Bca 8.14)
"Separated from the company of foolish people, I shall dwell alone;
from that solitude comes happiness.
This is an adverbial phrase.
How so? Because he is "one whose mind is undefiled," due to his avoidance of contact with them and the absence of affliction caused by them;
this is a statement of cause regarding the preceding [verse].
Alternatively:
"Physical pleasure" refers to bodily [pleasure];
"unafflicted mind" refers to mental [pleasure].
(Bcp 140) Therefore, in order to explain that one who wishes to avoid the suffering born from contact with foolish people should not associate with them, he says:

"One should flee far from the fool; if one encounters him, one should propitiate him with pleasant things. However, one should not engage in continuous intimacy, but rather remain like a neutral, virtuous person. (Bca 8.15)
From childhood, one should flee far away from all sides and withdraw,
so that there may not be even the slightest association with them;
yet, if by some chance it should happen through the power of fate, [one must remain vigilant].
Then, when he has arrived and met him, one should honor and please him with pleasing and delightful services;
yet even while honoring him, one should not do so out of a continuous attachment to intimacy or with the intention of cultivating a sense of familiarity.
Or rather, it is not out of attachment arising from intimacy;
what then? It is because of the avoidance of both aversion and attachment, like a virtuous neutral person who maintains right conduct with impartiality.
To teach another practice of virtuous people, he says:
"Taking only the essence of the Dharma, like a bee taking honey from flowers, I shall wander everywhere as if I were a stranger, unacquainted with anyone. (Bca 8.16)
