"For the sake of the Dharma" means for the purpose of the Dharma; that alone, nothing more. "Taking that" means having grasped it.
The meaning is "having extracted the essence.
Like a *bhṛṅga*, that is, like a *cañcarīka* (bee);
*madhu* means nectar (*makaranda*).
Alternatively, the analysis of the compound is as follows: "Dharma" itself is the "artha," meaning the purpose or objective of this [life] consisting of robes, alms-food, and so forth.
Averse to the company of fools, like the new moon that has never appeared before, I shall dwell everywhere, in every land or place.
"Unacquainted" means unfamiliar;
the meaning is that he is devoid of intimacy with the people living there.

Thus, having removed affection—the cause for association with loved ones—one must now abandon craving for gain and the like, which is the cause for not renouncing the world. Demonstrating this, he says:
"I am successful and honored, and many desire me"—from the attainment of such things, fear arises in a mortal regarding death. (Bca 8.17)
"I am one who possesses gain, for I am endowed with gains such as robes and alms-food;
I am honored and worshipped by people,
and many, indeed countless, desire and long for me."
The meaning is: "I am highly esteemed by the multitude.
For a mortal man who thinks in this way, fear arises from death—of what kind of death? From that which has arrived unexpectedly and without being anticipated.
Wherever the mind, deluded by pleasure, finds delight,
there that very thing becomes a thousandfold suffering and stands before one.
Therefore, the wise person should not desire that [suffering], for from desire fear is born; this [suffering] passes away of its own accord, so one should remain patient and wait.
Many became gainers and many became famous;
yet, along with their gains and fame, they were not known where they had gone.
(Bcp 141) Others despise me; why should I rejoice when praised? Others praise me; why should I despair when reviled? (Bca 8.21)
Sentient beings with diverse inclinations have not been satisfied even by the Victors;
how much less so by ignorant people like me? Therefore, what is the use of worrying about the world?
Thus, because death is necessarily inevitable at all times through such mental attention (*manasikāra*), what is the use of concern for the world of foolish people or for cultivating their conduct?
The sense is that there is no purpose whatsoever, as it is not to be adopted.
Thus, he says that association with foolish people is indeed a cause of suffering:
"They revile the being who gains nothing and they look down upon the one who gains;
how can delight arise from dwelling naturally with those whose company is so painful? (Bca 8.23)
They revile and disparage a being who has not obtained gain and is deprived of profit, saying,
"This poor fellow has performed no merit; it is because of this that he does not obtain even a mere portion of alms-food without great hardship."
Furthermore, they find fault with one who has obtained gains; yet they honor with offerings of robes and other requisites those who have been purified by faithful donors and patrons.
They also acquire gains such as robes by pleasing donors and patrons through hypocrisy and other such means.
Otherwise, why would others not possess such qualities?
Thinking, "By this means he alone obtains the boon and no other," they do not develop faith in him and utter such words.
Thus, in both ways, there is no peace in the mind derived from them.

Therefore, because they are by nature and by their very essence causes of suffering, those fools for whom dwelling together is suffering are "such. How can delight arise for one who dwells with such as these?
The meaning is "not at all."
Furthermore, a fool does not become a firm friend;
for this reason, the Tathāgatas have said that a fool is not the friend of anyone.
For no joy arises in a fool without some self-interest.
The joy that arises through the gateway of one's own interests is merely joy for the sake of the self;
for it is like the agitation felt at the loss of wealth, since that agitation is caused by the loss of happiness.
"A friend" means a well-wisher.
"Thus spoken by the Tathāgata" means it was stated in the scriptures (āgamas).
Why? Because for a fool, joy never arises except for his own self-interest.
Therefore, in its absence, the opposite occurs.
Furthermore, even when living among the ignorant, that [state] has not been described;
for even by one who practices loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it is impossible for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to feel joy in such a setting.

This being so, thinking, "In order to avoid the faults arising from living with them and to dwell in ease and cheerfulness, I must strive to resort to the forest out of a desire for solitude," they do not disregard its benefits; nor are trees difficult to propitiate with effort—when might I come to dwell together with those who provide such pleasant companionship? (Bca 8.26)
Trees are plants; they do not harbor ill will,
nor are they to be propitiated— that is, they are not to be diligently served with effort.

By practicing conduct favorable to that [state] while dwelling in forests and other such places, because one is free from harmful intentions—when will my dwelling together with those trees come to pass? He expresses this aspiration, wondering what they are like: "with those who are pleasant to dwell with."
It is called "happiness" because it is the cause of happiness, as explained previously.
Furthermore, he speaks of delighting in dwelling in solitude:
"When, staying in an empty temple, at the foot of a tree, or in caves, shall I go forth without concern, looking not back? (Bca 8.27)
Having stayed, dwelt, or remained for one or two nights in an empty temple free from the bustle of people,
or according to his desire at the foot of a tree— that is, beneath a tree—
or in secret places such as caves on mountains and the like.
When shall I go without regard for anything? Because there is nothing whatsoever that could be a basis for attachment.
For this very reason, not looking back, because there will be no further state of non-liberation.
Furthermore, he spoke otherwise:
"When shall I dwell, with my abode for moving about at will, in these regions which are vast by their very nature? (Bca 8.28)
In those [objects] which were previously not accepted by some adversary,
which are extensive, vast, and productive of mental joy,
and which are of such a nature that they [arise] spontaneously by themselves;
He does not hope, "When shall I dwell [in this way] by means of artifice?
Demonstrating the happiness that comes from dwelling in such a manner, he says: "Moving according to one's own will, one’s conduct is not dependent on others."
"Anilaya" means one for whom no abode, dwelling, or attachment exists due to being free from clinging; because he has no sense of ownership toward anything whatsoever,
such a person is unattached to anyone.
The remainder is easily understood.
Furthermore, demonstrating that one should aspire in this way through having few desires, he says:
"When, possessing no wealth other than a clay bowl and wearing robes that thieves cannot enjoy, shall I dwell without fear, no longer protecting my body? (Bca 8.29)
A clay vessel means an alms-bowl made of earthenware; he whose wealth and possessions consist solely of that, and nothing more—
likewise, his clothing consists of rags from a dust-heap, which are not to be enjoyed by thieves because they cannot be used [as plunder].
"Unused" means [not yet employed].
One who possesses such a robe or garment is described as "one who has such.
Both of these are also incapable of being taken away by others.

For this very reason he is fearless, due to his disregard for both body and life. He demonstrates this very point by saying, "not protecting the body," meaning not guarding it because of the absence of attachment to or grasping for anything external or internal.

Showing through three verses that this impermanence is the cause for abandoning attachment and must be cultivated at all times, he says: "When, having gone to my own place—the ground of corpses—will I compare my own body, which is subject to destruction, with other skeletons? (Bca 8.30)
For this very body of mine will become so putrid that even jackals would not approach its vicinity because of its stench.
Even for this single body, the fragments of bone born together will go their separate ways; how much more so for other dear people? (Bca 8.32)
"One makes one's own body a ground" means the ground of the charnel ground, because even after remaining for a long time, the body ultimately ends there.
"By other skeletons" refers to the skeletal frames— the bones— of those who died previously.
Decay is the state of putrefaction;
it has that [putrefaction] as its property and that as its intrinsic nature.
He explains that very comparison with the words "For this very... and so forth.
"Thus" refers to the similarity with the body falling from another skeleton.
It will become putrid and loathsome.
To the question "In what way?", he says: "Jackals," and so forth.
Because of its extreme foul odor, it is unbearable even for jackals, who are devoted to such food.
Thus, he says "even of this one," and so forth, to show that association with what is dear is impermanent:
"of this very body," which has been appropriated and conceived as a single entity.
The bone fragments born together with the body will become separate;
the meaning is that they will become dissociated.
How much more so, then, will other beloved people not become separate?
He who remains forever dissociated [from defilements].

It might be argued: "These sons, wife, and others are always my companions in pleasure and pain; therefore, it is only right to feel affection for them. To this he says: "Indeed, a living being is born alone, and dies alone as well."
No one else shares in that suffering; so what is the use of loved ones who only create obstacles?
No one whatsoever would be a sharer in the suffering of another, either at birth or at death;
rather, in the interval between, everyone experiences pleasure and pain solely as assigned by their own karma.
Therefore, this [notion of shared suffering] is merely a matter of conceit.
Because no other person, distinct from that self, shares in its suffering; rather,
it is the one who causes the pain who comes to have a share— that is, a portion— of that suffering.
She belongs to him,
because she is experienced by him alone;
therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever in those things dear to one that cause the destruction of the side of virtue.

Demonstrating that, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no association of anything with anything else, he says: "Just as one who has set out on a journey takes up temporary lodgings, so too does the traveler through existence take up the lodgings of birth. (Bca 8.34)
Just as one who has set out on a path and is intent on traveling toward a certain direction takes up residence in a single lodging, such as a pavilion or the like, together with other travelers;

so too, in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), for one wandering with a course dependent upon karma, the taking up of residence occurs within a single birth along with kinsmen, fellow clansmen, blood relations, and so forth.
Then, having abandoned that again, he goes somewhere else alone.
Furthermore, no companions follow him there;
therefore, a real association with anyone is impossible.
Consequently, one should not intentionally form an association with anyone, having fashioned it oneself—a thing that brings a thousand misfortunes.

Having thus stated the fault of association, he speaks—showing by means of three verses that these, moreover, are the virtues of solitude: "As long as he is not identified by four persons... [and so forth].
While one is still not being mourned by the world, at that very time one should go to the forest.
(Bcp 144) Through non-attachment and non-opposition, one who is alone in body and has already died to the world does not grieve when dying.
And no attendants nearby, though grieving, cause him any distress;
nor do any distract him from his recollection of the Buddha and the other [objects of mindfulness].
Even if one does not desire it, having now arrived at death while still in the state of being alive, one must be made to relinquish the household life by force;
therefore, it is fitting that one should renounce it oneself while still living.
"From there" means from the home.
While being grieved over with lamentations such as "Alas, my child! by the world—that is, by kinsmen and others—and while being mourned, he should depart for the forest even before that time.
To explain what specific advantage there is in this, he says: "Without intimacy," and so forth.
Due to the absence of attachment and aversion, he does not grieve when dying.
He does not become a partaker of the suffering produced by grief. Why? Because he has already died in the world even before he has departed from his home.
At that very time, regarding his kinsmen, relatives, and the world at large, he states that this is another quality of his: "And those who move near him," and so forth.
Those who move near him—kinsmen, members of the same lineage, and others staying close by—who, distressed by separation from him, grieve and produce sorrow, do not, indeed, cause him any pain.
The affliction of one's own body and mind,
or else,
seeing their grief, the mental anguish of one who is dying.
Not only is this a virtue,
but it also includes the recollection of the Buddha and so forth— the word "and so forth" (ādi) referring to the recollection of the Dharma and so on—
or the mental attention directed toward reality as its object.
Thus, for one who dwells in solitude away from the company of people at the time of death.
He concludes with the words beginning "Therefore":
"Therefore, solitude is delightful, effortless, and the source of auspiciousness;
it pacifies all distractions and should always be cultivated by me. (Bca 8.38)
Solitude is dwelling without attachment;
it is delightful because it is the cause of happiness,
and it is effortless because it is the antidote to suffering.
It is the "arising of Śiva" because it brings about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

It is the "pacifier of all distractions," meaning it pacifies and turns back all distractions—namely, misconduct of body, speech, and mind—because it is the cause of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Therefore, [it is said]: "I must practice this always."
The meaning is that one should form an attachment through clinging precisely to this.
Thus, having established physical seclusion by avoiding contact with people, he speaks in order to establish mental seclusion:
"Free from all other thoughts, with my mind one-pointed on my own consciousness, I shall strive for the concentration and the taming of the mind. (Bca 8.39)
He is liberated from all other thoughts, which are by nature false discursive reasoning, and is devoid of them.

"With a mind one-pointed in its own thought" (*svacittaikāgramānasaḥ*): that mental application (*mānasika*) in which one's own thought (*svacitta*) alone is "one-pointed" (*eka-agra*), meaning preeminent or primary, is so described; he whose mind is such is [called] "one with a mind one-pointed in its own thought.

Alternatively, the compound may be analyzed as: he whose mind has its own thought as its single focus (*ekāgra*), being intent on observing its own activity, or bound to a fixed object of observation.
Being thus disposed, I shall strive for the concentration and tranquility of the mind; I shall become intent upon that,
meaning I shall apply myself to one-pointedness.
"And for the sake of self-control" means for the purpose of repeatedly directing [the mind] toward that very same object,
or for the purpose of preventing outward distraction.
(Bcp 145) In that regard, because they are the adversaries of mental concentration, he says— in order to ward off thoughts of sensual desire:
"For sensual desires produce misfortune both in this world and in the next."
In this world through imprisonment, execution, and mutilation, and in the next world through rebirth in the hells and other such realms.
Because they are clung to as desirable by those who have not abandoned the fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*), forms and other objects are called "desires" (*kāma*).
The word *hi* (for) has the sense of "because";
thus, it connects with what will be said later: "therefore, having become weary of desires" [8.85].

And when these [sensual pleasures] are indulged in, they produce only misfortune... for whose sake one has many times joined the palms in reverence to male and female messengers, and for whose sake neither sin nor ill-repute was previously reckoned? (Bca 8.41)
I have cast myself into danger and squandered my wealth;
yet, by embracing those very things, I attained the highest bliss.
Why do you not attain peace by embracing at will those very same bones— neither other than them, nor belonging to anyone else, but under your own control and free from possessiveness?
That face which was formerly seen— whether covered by a veil, being raised with effort, or being lowered out of modesty— is now unseen.
Behold, that face has now been revealed by the vultures as if they could no longer endure your suffering; why do you flee now? (Bca 8.45)
That which was protected even from the falling glances of others has today been devoured; O envious one, why do you not protect it now?
Seeing this heap of flesh being devoured by vultures and other scavengers, one realizes that for others it is honored as food with garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments. (Bca 8.47)

"Having seen this heap of flesh, this mass of meat—which is being eaten by those vultures and others such as jackals—this loathsome form that was once honored by you with garlands and other offerings, why, O envious one, do you not protect it? This is how the connection should be made.
Or, there is a connection with the distant [word] "why do you now flee? (kim idānīm palāyase).
"Indeed, you too must be questioned regarding this," he says:
"You have fear even of a motionless skeleton when it is viewed in this way.
He asks with a rhetorical intonation (*kāku*): "Does fear arise for you even from something motionless, such as a piece of wood or a clod of earth?"
From a skeleton— that is, from a cage of bones—
even when seen as having such a loathsome form, if there is still such terror that you flee even further away than before; this is how it should be construed.
To the question, "How is there no fear when one is thus moving? he says: "Is there not fear of being moved by some kind of ghost (vetāla)? (Bca 8.48)
Is there not fear for one who is alive and moving while being shaken by a spirit-grasping demon?
Therefore, the meaning is that it is even more appropriate to feel extreme fear [of death].
(Bcp 146) Having thus established their loathsomeness, he speaks again in another way to establish it further:
"From a single morsel of food, both saliva and impurity arise from these [bodies]."
In that regard, since impurity is undesirable to you, how can the drinking of saliva be dear?

For one whose discrimination is shrouded by delusion and whose consciousness is swooned by the poison of passion— who, because of her extreme loveliness, desires to drink the saliva flowing from her mouth under the impression that it is the drinking of a woman's face—
the author poses this inquiry: "The cause for both [the saliva and wine] is indeed the same, since their nature consists of food and drink."
In that regard, between those two, the impure excrement is unpleasant to you;
how then can the drinking of saliva and phlegm be pleasant?
By what manner is there delight in that and not elsewhere?
The intended meaning is that it is logical for both as well.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even though the cause for both is the same,
there is aversion toward the one because of its extreme foul odor, whereas there is affection for the other because that [odor] is absent."
Demonstrating that even this is not a correct statement, he says:
"Those possessed by desire do not delight in pillows filled with soft cotton because they are foul-smelling or leaking; rather, they are deluded by impurity. (Bca 8.50)
Lovers do not find delight in pillows such as *masūraka* cushions filled with cotton and other soft materials, nor do they maintain contentment with them.
Why? Because they do not emit foul odors or the discharge of impurities; rather, they take pleasure only in the female body, which is filled with filth.
Why is this so?
Because those who possess desire—those who long for sensual pleasure—are deluded by impurity;
this is a statement of the reason.
Deluded by impurity regarding impure objects,
or through the perversion of perceiving the impure as pure, they experience an intense attachment to that very same [impurity].

It might be argued: "Granted that impurity is common to both the impure substance and the female body, nevertheless, in one case it is exposed while in the other it is concealed; therefore, one may feel attachment for this [latter] by avoiding the former. To this, he says:
If this passion exists even when concealed, why would that which is unconcealed be undesirable?
If there is no purpose in it, why is the concealed part being crushed?
In that which has an impure nature, whose form is concealed— meaning,
even when it is not seen—
there is such an attachment.
It is reasonable that when that [object] is uncovered and comes into view, it produces an exceeding degree of pleasure;
so why does such a thing become unpleasant to you?
Or, if you are entirely averse to such a thing, then the uncovered object serves no purpose for you whatsoever.
If this is so, then for what reason is the concealed specifically crushed, such that effort is made to bring about that alone while excluding everything else?
Furthermore, you should also be asked this: do you feel revulsion toward the impure or not?
Regarding the first alternative here, he says:
"If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another?
If you have no passion for the impure and no attachment whatsoever, then why do you embrace another woman?
What is it? He says:
"A cage of bones bound together by sinews and smeared with the mire of flesh. (Bca 8.52)
Flesh is like mud because of its common quality of being a coating; it is smeared or besmeared by that.
If one asks, "What is it like when it has become thus? [the answer follows].
A cage of bones bound together by sinews;
a skeletal frame held together, joined, and brought under control by sinews.
Otherwise, it would be shattered into fragments;
thus, he demonstrates that this [body] is an object of dispassion.
Now, if the second alternative—that passion is for what is pure—is accepted, he says in response: "one's own self," and so forth;
or alternatively:

It is introduced differently as follows: regarding what was stated by the opponent—that passion arises when [the object] is covered by skin and so forth, but not when it is uncovered—the author replies with the words "If," and so on.
If, for you, passion for the impure arises because of that cause, namely, because it is concealed by skin and so forth, [then...]
Then why do you embrace another's cage?
The rest is as before.
What then is appropriate in this case? He says:
"Since your own body is full of impurities, maintain your composure with that very thing; O consumer of excrement, forget about other bags of filth. (Bca 8.53)

Within yourself alone there is an abundance of impurities—saliva, mucus, brain-matter, urine, feces, and so forth; therefore, find contentment with that very impurity. Furthermore, [do not desire] another woman's body, which by its very nature is a bag of filth, a receptacle for excrement.
O you who greedily consume excrement, whose nature is to eat feces, forget it;
do not direct your mind toward that.
With the words "I am fond of meat," and so forth, he offers another rebuttal:
"You desire to see and touch this meat because you think, 'I am fond of it. But how can you desire meat, which by its very nature is insentient? (Bca 8.54)
He for whom meat is dear is "one who is fond of meat," such as I am;
[I am so] toward this cage of bones.
Or alternatively: "He is fond of meat; I am dear to him because I am fond of meat," as before;
up to: "I am fond of meat, and I am dear to him."
Even though [the compound] is dependent [on another word], the compound is valid because its meaning is intelligible.
Thus, out of greed for that [object], or with the thought of returning a favor, you desire to see and to touch;
you long for both seeing and touching.

To this, he says: [The self] is insentient (*acetana*), devoid of consciousness (*caitanya-śūnya*), and by its own nature (*svabhāvena*) or primordial substance (*prakṛtyā*), it is like a lump of clay;
it is not, however, as others describe—that which is insentient is called sentient because of its conjunction with consciousness.
Being a lustful person, how can you desire such meat, which is by nature insentient?
If it were perceived as such, that [desire] would apply even to a lump of clay;
and if that were the case, you yourself would not be sentient.
If it is argued that there exists therein a mind whose intrinsic nature is consciousness, and therefore one desires it, he says:
"That which you desire cannot be seen or touched."
And that which is possible, you do not know; why then do you embrace it in vain?
That mind which you consider to have the nature of consciousness cannot be seen because it is formless;
whereas that physical body, which has the nature of flesh and so forth, can both be seen and touched.
It does not perceive that,
it does not know it, because it is insentient.
Therefore, why do you embrace—that is, cling to—that which is insentient? It is in vain; it is fruitless.
The sense is that it is not at all appropriate to embrace [it];
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of embracing clods of earth and the like.

Furthermore, demonstrating that this too is utterly contemptible, he says: "It is no wonder that you do not perceive another's body as consisting of impurity; it is a marvel that you do not perceive your own body, which likewise consists of impurity. (Bca 8.56)
It is not at all surprising that you do not perceive the impure nature of another's body; indeed,
such ignorance is entirely appropriate.
Because another's continuum is separated from oneself by a barrier;
yet this is an even greater cause for wonder:
that you do not perceive, do not understand, that your own body consists of impurity.
Now the author of the treatise, seeking to incite a sense of spiritual urgency, says:
"Having abandoned the young lotus, which blooms at the rays of the cloudless sun, what pleasure can there be for a mind intoxicated by impurity within this cage of excrement? (Bca 8.57)

Having abandoned a fresh lotus— such as a young lotus that has blossomed wide under the rays of a cloudless sun— what pleasure can there be for one whose mind is intent upon impurity within this cage of excrement?
The meaning is that it is not logical.
Furthermore, he has said otherwise:
"If you do not wish to touch [the body] because it is smeared with impurities such as clay and the like, then how can you wish to touch that which has emerged from the body? (Bca 8.58)
By the word "etcetera," clothing and so forth are included;
because they are smeared with impurity,
if you do not wish to touch them.
Since that impurity has emerged and issued forth from this body, how can you wish to touch that very body?
Or, it might be argued: "This reproach is not appropriate for me."
Since I have no attachment to impurity, he says in response:
"If you have no passion for the impure, why do you embrace another?
That seed was produced from a field of impurity and was nurtured by it. (Bca 8.59)
The mother's womb is a field of impurity because it is a locus of manifold unclean things; the seed produced there, that which has arisen therein, is [the body].
That very seed, whose nature is the impurity of the mother’s and father’s semen and blood, is described as such.

"Nourished by that" means it was nourished and developed while situated in the womb by that impurity— the essence of what the mother had consumed, which is like vomit— and even after emerging from the womb,
it is nourished by the impure essence of the digestion of what one has personally eaten and drunk.
The connection is: "Why do you embrace another?"—meaning another woman's body. Thus, there is indeed a reproach directed at you.
Now, if you accept the position that "I am one who has passion for the impure," even so, the censure remains exactly as it was; thus he says:
"Because it arises from impurity and is small, you do not desire the impure worm."
You desire this body, which is composed of much impurity and born from impurity.
You do not desire a worm or any kind of living creature born from impurities such as excrement;
yet, by the same logic, you desire the body of a woman, which is even more fundamentally impure in nature and likewise born of impurity.
(Bcp 149) Furthermore, it might be argued: "What answer is there to be given here,
since I too am just as I am?"
Such is her body;
therefore, there is no fault in the contact of the impure with the impure.
He says that as is the yakṣa, so too is the offering (bali).
O consumer of excrement, you not only fail to feel disgust for your own impurity,
but you even desire other vessels of filth.
This is the power of great delusion,
that you do not first loathe the impure nature inherent within yourself,
yet instead desire other jars filled with impurity.
Thus, "fie" expresses a lack of discernment;
by the contemptuous word "devourer of excrement," he himself is being addressed.
Now, having realized this, he speaks in order to demonstrate the nature of impurity:
"Even the ground is considered impure when camphor and other such delightful things, or rice and condiments, have been spat out after being placed in the mouth. (Bca 8.62)
In this way, even objects that are pure and clean come to possess an impure nature through contact with the outflow from even a single part [of something impure].
Let alone those objects themselves,
even the ground, which is pure by nature, becomes impure through association with them.
If you do not believe even this impurity because it is evident to the senses,
then look at other terrifying bodies fallen in the charnel ground as well.
Thus, this conventional usage is established by direct perception;
nevertheless, if you still do not have conviction or do not accept it.
The meaning is that even having seen them, you do not believe it.
Then, look at bodies in a cemetery, an abode of putrefaction; of what nature are they? "Terrible," it says.
"Others" refers to those that are loathsome or terrifying by nature, such as being devoured, bluish-black, or festering, which are more [numerous] than these.
Furthermore, demonstrating that this body is by its very nature a transformation and not a fit object for delight, he says:
"Since great fear arises when the skin is flayed off, how can one feel delight again in that very same thing once it has been known [as such]? (Bca 8.64)
When it is torn out— that is, separated from the body— great terror arises [in one], thinking, "What is this?"
Thus, even having understood its true nature, how is it that at one time that very same place is apprehended as a source of fear, while at another time affection and attachment arise toward it?

It might be argued: "Even if the impure nature of the body is established by direct perception, nevertheless, when it is anointed with fragrant substances such as sandalwood, it becomes desirable. To this he says:
"Even when applied to the body, that fragrance comes from the sandalwood and so forth, not from anything else."
Why do you become attached elsewhere because of the scent belonging to another?

Even though this fragrance produced from sandalwood and the like is applied to the body, it is solely due to that [fragrance] itself that the perception of attractiveness arises toward the body. It does not arise from the body alone.
"Not from another" means not from the body.
Why, then, is delight taken here in the scent of another— such as that produced by sandalwood— when that scent does not belong to the one who possesses it elsewhere?
Moreover, demonstrating that even the refinement of sandalwood and the like serves only to harm oneself and does not lead to one's welfare, he says:
If passion does not arise here because of its inherent foul odor, then surely there is no well-being; why then does the world, delighting in what is harmful, smear it with perfume?
Because its inherent nature is foul-smelling, as it carries a natural stench;
"here" refers to this body— if passion does not arise [toward it].
In that case, surely it would be auspicious and beneficial.
Even though such qualities are possible, for what reason does the world, which is fond of what is harmful, smear that body with perfume?
The meaning is that this is not appropriate in any way.
And since there is no alteration of its intrinsic nature even if it consists of a thousand conditioned factors, he says:
"What has happened to the body here, if there is fragrant sandalwood?
What has happened to the body, which is by nature foul-smelling?
What has come into being? Nothing at all.
If it is sandalwood, it is "sugandhi" because it possesses a beautiful fragrance (*śobhana-gandha*), according to the rules for the suffixes used at the end of *bahuvrīhi* compounds.
Nevertheless, the point is that there is no loss of its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Now, regarding the claim that "by virtue of that [nature], taking its desirability as a basis, delight arises in it," he says:
"Why is one attached to one thing because of the fragrance belonging to another? (Bca 8.67)
And thus, the meaning is that there would be no discernment.

Showing by means of two verses that this body is indeed a cause of misfortune even through the refinement of the hair and so forth, he says: "If the body— with long hair and nails, with teeth stained yellowish-white by impurities, bearing filth and mud, naked, and terrifying by its very nature— " *Bca* 8.68.
Why is it being refined with such effort, like a weapon for self-destruction?
The earth is filled with madmen intent on deluding themselves.
"Long" means existing from birth; "unbroken" is the intended meaning.
"With teeth that are stained and pale" means with teeth and fangs that have not been refined by means of tooth-sticks, betel nut, and so forth.
"Bearer of the mire of impurity": impurity itself is the mire or mud;
he bears that, being thus [described], because of his lack of bathing, anointing, and so forth.
"Naked" means being devoid of clothing, remaining as if just born. Being in such a state,
if the body were by nature terrifying— frightening by its very essence like that of hungry ghosts (pretas)— then [this would be so].
Why is such a person as this adorned with effort?
By means of specific arrangements of hair and nails, by means of tooth-sticks, betel, and so forth— this is what is meant by "with effort."
By means of bathing, anointing, smearing with ointments, and so forth, or by means of garments and the like;
what is it like? It is like a weapon for the purpose of self-destruction.
Just as a sword or similar weapon is prepared for the purpose of killing oneself, so too is this the case.
Lamenting their behavior, which is brought under the sway of delusion, he says "ātma" and so forth:
by those who, like madmen with unbalanced minds, have exerted themselves to produce self-delusion through their own deliberate reflection.

And thus, because they perform actions that are contrary [to reality], the author of the treatise feels regret, thinking, "These wretched ones are not possessed of consciousness," and observes that "not a single person here is a knower of the Self; the earth is agitated and crowded with madmen."
Having concluded the incidental discussion, he says, continuing with the subject at hand:
"Indeed, you feel disgust upon seeing a few skeletons in a cemetery;
yet you delight in a village-cemetery crowded with moving skeletons. (Bca 8.70)

(Bcp 151) "A few specific skeletons of corpses"—this is what is meant. Having stated [the passage] beginning with "when the skin has been flayed" [8.64], that which was said regarding "how, even knowing this... and so forth, [is explained as follows].
To this, the opponent replies: This [body] is not similar to a corpse gone to the cremation ground, such that there would be no pleasure in it as well as in that [corpse];
rather, it is because the cremation ground is a place of loathing for that [corpse].
"Not here" means "not in this [place]," such as in a village cemetery and so forth.
"In a village cemetery" means in a cremation ground located within a village.
There is no distinction whatsoever here;
that very same body is a source of loathing in a cemetery, yet a source of delight in a village—this is what he says by way of irony.
The sense is that this is not consistent with the intellect of the wise.
By the phrase "crowded with moving skeletons," he shows this: however, there is this distinction;
yet by this distinction, the impure nature that is the cause of revulsion does not cease, such that this [worldly] activity might occur.
"Confused" (*saṃkula*) means crowded together (*samākīrṇa*).
Granted that such a thing, though its very nature is impure, may be a place of delight for those like swine;
nevertheless, demonstrating that even such a thing is not easily obtained by one devoid of wealth, he says:
"And thus, although this is impure, it is not obtained without a price."
For that purpose, there is the toil of acquisition and the suffering in the hells and other realms.
Without a price—that is, without wealth—it is not obtained, nor is it attained;
therefore, one who desires that [pleasure] must first acquire wealth.
Through the exertion involved in acquiring it—by resorting to agriculture, trade, service, and so forth—suffering arises right here in this very life.
And because it is acquired through unrighteousness, it leads to rebirth in the hells and other such realms;
thus, its acquisition is a cause of misfortune in both worlds,
and there is no attainment of happiness therein.
Demonstrating that there is only suffering resulting from its acquisition, he says:
"A child lacks the capacity for acquisition; by what means could he be happy in youth?
Youth passes away through acquisition; once old, what can one do with desires? (Bca 8.72)
One who remains in the state of childhood lacks the capacity to acquire wealth,
precisely because of being a child.
By what wealth or by what means could that child become happy in youth, in the stage of adolescence?
The meaning is that because of the lack of wealth, it does not exist anywhere.
Furthermore, even when someone is seen to be happy in their youth due to wealth acquired by their father or grandfather,
that too applies only to a specific individual and not to everyone.
Nor is he liberated from the two aforementioned types of suffering;

therefore, the acquisition of wealth should be undertaken first, as it is the means for achieving happiness. For one whose youth has already faded while engaged in its pursuit, there is no utility whatsoever in sense objects.
It might further be argued: "Even while acquiring that [wealth], sensual pleasure is indeed experienced. To this he says:
"Some of base desires, exhausted by their activities at the end of the day, return home in the evening and lie down as if they were dead. (Bca 8.73)

Whosoever have their minds seized by base desires, and whose bodies and minds are exhausted by day-long activities characterized by the labor of gathering wood, grass, leaves, and so forth for wages— being devoid of aspiration, they return to their own homes when the sun has set and lie down or sleep, as if dead, because they are overcome by deep sloth; then, rising again at dawn, they apply themselves once more to that same lowly work.
The word *sma* here serves as a rhetorical ornament (*vākyālaṃkāra*), because it does not refer to a past event.
In this way, some who are addicted to evil desires exhaust their life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) and yet do not obtain the taste of sensual pleasure.
(Bcp 152) Referring to those who serve others, he says:
Others are afflicted by the suffering of the hardships of travel due to military expeditions.
Even for many years, those who seek that [liberation] do not look after their children or wives.
"Others" refers to those other than the previously mentioned lovers of sensual pleasure; they are "evil-lovers," meaning servants.
They [are engaged] by means of military expeditions and the like;
"daṇḍa" (force) refers to an expedition (*yātrā*), that is, a military march for the purpose of conquering the armies of enemy kings.
Or, when there is a journey for the purpose of seizing the wealth of a foreign kingdom, and so forth— by means of such activities as sending [messengers] to other lands—
their exile consists in traveling to another country.
Because of that, there is affliction and exhaustion; because of that, they are suffering and oppressed,
remaining in such a state at all times.
Even after many years have passed—that is, even after the lapse of numerous years—they do not see, they do not behold, their sons and wives.
"Desiring those" means desiring those sons, wives, and so forth; the meaning is that for the sake of them alone, they accept service to others and other such labors.

Lamenting, "Alas! How fruitless is the practice of these people," he says: "That very purpose for which the self was sold by those deluded by desire has not been attained; instead, their life has been spent in vain through the labor of others. (Bca 8.75)
That for the sake of which the self was sold and made a slave to others by those deluded by desire—namely, that happiness—has not been attained;
it has not been acquired.
For only the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) have been brought to exhaustion in vain through the performance of another's work.
The meaning is that they have never been employed in any virtuous action whatsoever.
Demonstrating that for those who have set out in pursuit of pleasure, instead of happiness only suffering has befallen them, he says:
"For others whose very selves have been sold and who are constantly performing menial tasks, women give birth in forest thickets and similar places. (Bca 8.76)
Those who have sold their own self-nature—their very bodies—out of a desire for pleasure, making them dependent on others;
this refers to other servants. For this very reason, they are habitually engaged in performing errands at all times.
Furthermore, other women, while traveling for the sake of their masters,
give birth right on the road or in forest thickets and similar places.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it is meant] in difficult places such as mountains, ravines, rivers, and riverbanks.

Demonstrating that this is another of their misconceptions, he says: "Deceived by desire, these fools enter into life-threatening battles to live; for the sake of pride, they go into servitude. (Bca 8.77)

Having sold their very selves, they enter into battle, which is a collision of four tusks; of what nature is it? It is one where life is in doubt—that is, because there is a doubt regarding life as to whether one who has entered it will live or not.
"To live" means for the sake of livelihood;
the meaning here is that they think, "We shall maintain our lives with the gains we have obtained.
For the sake of honor, they enter into servitude.
Overpowered by someone powerful,
they accepted the cutting off of their fingers as a means of securing their release;
they were fools whose eyes of discrimination had been blinded by delusion.
Who are they? Those who are mocked by desire, or those who are mocked—that is, humiliated—by desire (kāma).
(Bcp 153) Describing the suffering seen in this very life for those whose minds are attached to sensual desires, he says:
"Some who are lustful are being cut; others are impaled upon stakes."
They are seen being burned and struck by spears.
Of such acts as the abduction of another's wife or the seizure of wealth.
The remainder is easily understood.
Furthermore, explaining that even this object, though pursued as a means to happiness, is indeed the cause for the production of a succession of misfortunes, he says:

"Know wealth to be an endless source of misfortune through the sorrows of acquiring, protecting, and losing it; for those whose minds are attached to riches and distracted by them, there is no opportunity for liberation from the suffering of existence. (Bca 8.79)
The acquisition of what has not yet been produced is suffering;
even once acquired, the protection of that which has been gathered from the five obstacles such as water, fire, and so forth, is more difficult.
Furthermore, even when protected, there is the calamity of dejection and mental distress caused by its occasional destruction through thieves and the like, which leads to torment.
Thus, because it is the primary cause of a succession of misfortunes, wealth itself is called "misfortune" through the metaphorical attribution of the effect to the cause.

Consequently, since those whose minds are attached to wealth are perpetually distracted by the pursuit of acquisition and so forth, they find no opportunity for even a moment’s composure; there is thus no occasion for them to be liberated from the sufferings of birth and the rest inherent in saṃsāra, as their lifespans are spent entirely with their mental attention fixed upon that [wealth].
Having summarized all this, he encourages [the practitioner] to abandon attachment to desires by means of a discourse on spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), beginning with the words "In this way":
"In this way, the danger for those possessed of desire is immense, while the gratification is meager—just like a draft animal pulling a cart that receives only a morsel of fodder. (Bca 8.80)
"Thus" (*evam*) refers to the manner previously described.
"Disadvantage" (*ādīnava*) means misfortune;
it is "great," meaning manifold in its varieties.
Moreover, there is not even a report of the arising of pleasure here;
and as for that which appears as pleasure in some way due to cognitive distortion,
that too is nothing at all.
It is like a beast whose body is exhausted by the burden of carrying an exceedingly heavy load, taking a mouthful of a mere scrap of fodder.
For the sake of that mere fragment of taste, which is not difficult even for a beast to obtain,
this extremely rare perfection of the moment has been destroyed by one cursed by fate.
For the sake of such a thing— a mere fragment of the taste of pleasure that is utterly trivial and common even to beasts—
this excellence of the moment, free from the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), has been struck down, destroyed;
the meaning is that it has been rendered futile.
Of what nature is she said to be so very difficult to attain?
By whom? By one struck by fate (*daiva*);
"fate" refers to past karma, and by that she is struck.
"Having a perverted intellect regarding the discernment of the beneficial and the harmful" means being utterly deluded;
in reality, however, this is a term of disparagement.
Thus, one who is deprived of their share is so called.

With these two verses beginning with "avaśyaṃ gantuḥ," he demonstrates that [this exertion] is indeed of the nature of a perversion: "This constant exertion which has been made for the sake of this body—which is destined to perish, is insignificant, and is liable to fall into the hells and other realms. (Bca 8.82)
"Of one who must inevitably go" means of one whose nature is unstable due to impermanence;
"of the small" means that which is extremely remote when compared to the supramundane body.
"Falling into hell and other realms" means being partakers of immeasurable suffering;
the meaning is that [the body] is incapable of producing even its own happiness.

This refers to the exertion and toil performed throughout all time, from the prior limit of saṃsāra, disregarding the sufferings of hell and so forth for the sake of the body—that is, one's own physical frame—in order to produce happiness.
Then, even by a hundredth part of a koṭi of that labor, there would be Buddhahood;
that is to say, from that labor, by a hundredth part of a koṭi of labor—a mere fraction—there would be Buddhahood;
compared to that, Buddhahood would be attained with a force of exertion that is exceedingly small.
Nevertheless, the meaning is that those of dull intellect do not venture for its sake.

Now, one might argue that even for one practicing the conduct of awakening (*bodhicaryā*), thousands of extraordinary sufferings surely arise due to the undertaking of hundreds of various difficult tasks; to this he says:
"The suffering of the [bodhisattva] conduct is a great suffering, yet that awakening does not belong to those who possess desire. (Bca 8.83)

In comparison to the suffering of [ascetic] practice, this alone is the great suffering: that of those who wander in saṃsāra for the sake of sensual desires, because they fall into the Avīci and other hells, and because they experience it for a long time under the power of others;
but not so for Bodhisattvas, who experience it for a specific duration by their own choice.

Thus, even for those who experience suffering for the sake of sensual desires, that awakening does not occur which belongs to the Bodhisattvas who experience suffering for the sake of others; such is the meaning.
Furthermore, explaining specifically the suffering caused by desire, he says:
Neither weapons, nor poison, nor fire, nor precipices, nor enemies can serve as a comparison for desires, when one recalls the agonies of hell and other such realms. (Bca 8.84)

These things such as weapons, which are well known for producing suffering, do not possess a resemblance to sensual desires. Why? Because of the recollection—through the bringing to mind by means of memory—of the suffering of miserable rebirths such as hell, as it has been understood from scripture.
For weapons and the like grant only the suffering of death at a restricted time, [whereas sensual desires lead to endless suffering].
But since sensual desires are the causes of long-lasting and intense suffering in the hells and other realms, what kind of comparison could there be with them?
Thus, having established mental seclusion immediately after physical seclusion, he says the following to apply it to the present context:
"Having become thus repelled by sensual desires, one should produce delight in seclusion."

Having become agitated and terrified by sensual desires, which are causes of fear, according to the sequence thus described, one should generate delight and intense attachment for the aforementioned solitude. As to where one should remain [therein], he says:
In the peaceful forest lands, devoid of the exhaustion of quarreling.
They are free from the fatigue of strife because of the absence of adversaries,
and they are delightful due to being devoid of wild beasts, predatory animals, reptiles, thieves, and the like.
Regarding this, he states the benefit:

"On fortunate stone slabs, vast as palace terraces, cooled by moonbeams like sandalwood and full of beauty, fanned by the silent and gentle forest breezes, one may walk to and fro and contemplate the welfare of others. (Bca 8.86)
(Bcp 155) By the fortunate ones who have performed meritorious deeds;
the rays (*karāḥ*) of the moon (*śaśāṅka*), being like sandalwood (*candana*) due to their common qualities of whiteness and coolness, are indeed the very beams of the moon.
The connection is that they walk upon those which are cool and smooth.
Of what kind are they? They are naturally pure and holy, and free from defects such as roughness.

In what kind of places do the virtuous practice walking meditation (*caṅkrama*)? In those as vast as palatial mansions, as expansive as white palaces; and of what nature are they? They are silent, being devoid of any disagreeable sounds.
"By gentle, non-intense [breezes]" means by those that are pleasant to the touch; "by forest winds" means by the breezes of the woods.
Being fanned by them, he "walks back and forth" (*caṅkramyate*), meaning that he turns around and wanders slowly again and again.
Not only does he walk, but he also reflects for the benefit of others and for the production of happiness for sentient beings.
All this is accomplished without effort for yogins,
whereas for those possessed by desire, it must be achieved through effort.
Thus, it is demonstrated that the happiness of discriminative discernment (viveka) is superior to the happiness of sovereign power.
Demonstrating that this is another uncommon happiness for one who dwells in solitude, he says:

"Having stayed wherever he pleases for as long as desired—in empty dwellings, at the foot of trees, or in caves—he wanders at will, free from the toil of protecting possessions and detached from expectations. (Bca 8.87)
This is easily understood.

He clarifies the very meaning already stated by means of the verse beginning with "roaming at will" (svacchandacārī): "Roaming at will, having no fixed abode, and dependent on nothing, the happiness of contentment that he enjoys is difficult even for Indra to obtain. (Bca 8.88)
"One's own *chanda* is one's desire; he whose nature it is to act according to that is *svecchācārī*— the meaning is "one who acts according to his own will."

Having thus described the qualities of discernment (*viveka*), and wishing to state the subject at hand, he says: "By cultivating the qualities of discernment through these and other such modes, one whose discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) have been stilled should cultivate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). (Bca 8.89)
"In this way" means by the aforementioned [means],
and by "and so forth," it includes other such modes as well;
that is, through the cultivation of the qualities of physical and mental seclusion (*viveka*).

Thus, because one repeatedly brings to mind that seclusion (*viveka*) is the cause for the attainment of all happiness, one's discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) are stilled and improper mental attention (*asat-manasikāra*) ceases;
being in such a state, one should cultivate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
By the word "but" (*tu*), he shows the distinction: when cultivated in a mind thus purified, the thought of awakening ascends to the stage of excellence.
In that regard, as long as one does not establish identity with others through oneself,
the mind does not properly incline toward the welfare and happiness of others, because the grasping at a self functions preeminently only with respect to the self.
Therefore, for the sake of its cessation,
one should first cultivate equanimity toward oneself and others with such earnestness;
"first" means at the very beginning.
The meaning is that there is subsequently an exchange of self and others.
"In this way" means according to the method that will be explained.
"With reverence" means with great earnestness.
He shows its very form: "All beings, being equal in suffering and happiness, must be protected by me as I am myself. (Bca 8.90)
(Bcp 156) There is no distinction whatsoever among these;
therefore, just as suffering is an affliction for me, so too is it for them.
"Just as my own happiness is beneficial, so too is theirs.
Thus, all living beings are equal in their experience of suffering and happiness;
therefore, they must be protected by me just like myself.
Just as oneself is rescued from suffering or the causes of suffering, so too should other sentient beings be rescued;
just as oneself is desired to be made happy in every way, [so should others].
In the same way, others as well should be protected like oneself.

Now, one might ask: "How can the oneness of sentient beings—who are divided by the distinctions of many types of rebirths—be established through the self, and how can they possess a non-different nature of pleasure and pain? To this, he says:
Just as a body, though manifold in its parts such as hands and so forth, is to be protected as one;
Likewise, this entire world, though distinct [in appearance], is of one nature in its suffering and happiness; it is exactly so.

The body, which is of many kinds due to its divisions such as hands, feet, and head, is determined to be one and thus becomes something to be protected, both for the sake of averting suffering and for the sake of providing happiness. Likewise, the world of sentient beings, determined to be non-different and one with oneself, becomes something to be protected;
it is characterized by a nature of non-distinct suffering and happiness.

The grammatical indication [in the original text] omits the letter *ca*. Just as with the various distinctions such as the hand and so forth, "all this" (*sarvam idam*) is likewise divided by many different modes of movement and distinctions.
This is the intended meaning: just as, through habituation, there is a conceptual determination of unity in this body even in the absence of actual unity.
Likewise, it is so even in the world in its many forms; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.
This might be the case: if the world were of one single nature with you, then how could your suffering not be an affliction for other mental continua?
One might suspect that this same logic should also apply to the reverse scenario; anticipating this, he says:
Although my own suffering does not afflict others in their bodies,
nevertheless, that very suffering of theirs is unbearable for me because of my attachment to myself.
Even if my suffering does not actually cause affliction in the bodies of others, nevertheless, that suffering is indeed mine.
Why? Because of attachment to the self (*ātman*), it is unbearable—that is, impossible to endure.
This is a statement of the reason;
the meaning is that even when it occurs partially, it does not relinquish its nature as suffering.
In this same way, the opposite case should also be explained.
Likewise, even if another's suffering is not perceived by me as my own, nevertheless,
that suffering of theirs becomes unbearable to me because of my attachment to self.
Therefore, setting aside the distinction between self and other, the very nature of suffering itself is the cause for its cessation. Thus he says:
"The suffering of others must be destroyed by me because it is suffering, just like my own suffering;
whatever is suffering, that must be destroyed by me."

Just as one's own suffering [is to be destroyed], so too is the suffering of other sentient beings; this is an application of the reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For the state of being subject to destruction follows merely from the fact of having the nature of suffering.
Nor is the reason unestablished,
because the fact that [all things] have suffering as their intrinsic nature has been proven without exception;
nor is it inconclusive.
"Even one's own suffering would not be something to be destroyed, because there is no distinction"—this is the subverting argument against the contrary position.
For this very reason, there would also be no contradiction [with the reason].
Furthermore, there is this other formal argument:
(Bcp 157) "Others, too, must be favored by me because they are sentient beings, just like my own self. (Bca 8.94)
"All those sentient beings are to be favored by me just as my own self is;
and other sentient beings are also living creatures"— this is indeed a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this case, the nature of being worthy of favor resides solely in the state of having a sentient being as its essence;
furthermore, this is not unestablished,
because the state of having a sentient being as its essence is well-known in the subject (pakṣa).
Because it would entail the consequence that the self lacks the quality of being capable of receiving benefit, [the reason] would not be inconclusive (anaikāntika);
as before, it is not contradictory (viruddha).
[Objection: Is there not a distinction from others, namely, an attachment to pleasure within one's own self?
Thus, this reason is inconclusive. To this, he replies:
"When happiness is equally dear to me and to others..."
What distinction is there for oneself such that effort toward happiness should be directed toward this [body] alone? (Bca 8.95)
Happiness that is equal and identical is likewise dear and desired. What, then, is the distinction between oneself and another?
None at all; the meaning is that for this very reason, one should apply oneself to the production of happiness for the other just as for oneself.
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness regarding the first reason, he says:
"When fear and suffering are not dear to me or to others, then what is the distinction of my own self such that I protect it and not another? (Bca 8.96)
"Fear" refers to the cause of suffering;
"not the other" means nothing else.
It might be argued: "Even if the nature of suffering is not differentiated, nevertheless, only he who is afflicted by suffering is worthy of protection, and no one else. To this, he says:
If it is not protected on the grounds that "I am not afflicted by their suffering," then why protect against the suffering of my future body, which does not afflict me now?
If one does not protect another on the grounds that "I have no affliction or pain from the suffering of that other person," then this other point would be contradicted: namely,

that no affliction whatsoever can possibly arise for this appropriated body from the suffering of a future body— that is, a body born in hell or elsewhere in the next world— which is of the nature of suffering.
Because it is different from that;
this is used in common parlance, or in the sense of "therefore."

Since this is so, with what intention is it protected? It is the body, because that is the subject under discussion; [it is protected] for the sake of turning away from evil and engaging in what is wholesome.
Now, it might be argued: "I am always one and the same;
therefore, there is no difference here between the two bodies.
To this, he says: "This is not a fault. [And he explains:]

"This is indeed I even then"—this conceptual construction is false. Since the self (ātman) is about to be refuted and has already been partially refuted, what could possibly be the object of this notion of "I"?
Therefore, because there is no single entity that serves as the object of the notion of "I," this conceptual construction and determination is false.
"I am that very same person even then" refers to even in another existence,
because this [recognition] has as its object merely the five aggregates of clinging which are like an illusion.

Thus, this too is spoken by the power of conceptual determination (adhyavasāya), but in reality, it has no objective referent whatsoever, because its nature is that of a mental construction (vikalpa).
But from where does this false conceptualization arise? He says:
"Because one who has died is indeed another, and it is yet another who is born. (Bca 8.98)
Since no single entity such as a self or the like exists that travels to the next world,
but there is only the mere collection of aggregates,
it is certainly not the case that the very same five aggregates which perish here [in this life]...

That very same [self] does not arise again in the next world; rather, upon the cessation of the previous [existence], something entirely new arises there—conditioned by this [present state] (idampratyayatā), fashioned by afflictions and karma, and produced through the continuity of the intermediate state (antarābhava).
Therefore, due to the force of the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization that have operated throughout beginningless saṃsāra, the notion of "I" arises as something utterly false.
Furthermore, he states that there is this additional refutation regarding that point:
"If it is held that the suffering belonging to one person must be protected by that very person, then why is the pain of the foot not protected by the hand? (Bca 8.99)
Let alone the argument that one need not strive for the sake of protecting against the suffering of a future body;
even in this present single body, there is distinct suffering due to the differentiation of its various members.
Therefore, when it is not logical for the suffering of one part to be protected by another, [how much less so for a future body].
In that case, how is it that when one sees a blow falling upon the foot or another limb, one reaches out with the hand to protect it?
The meaning is that this is not logical, since there is no difference in their being distinct from the self.

Now, even if this [world] proceeds from the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) despite being improper, that which is improper— whether it be one's own or another's— must be turned back according to one's strength. (Bca 8.100)

Because of the grasping at a self through the thought "I" regarding this body, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) proceeds and arises even though there is no self; thus, the mental attention that seeks to protect [the body] in the feet and other parts occurs.
This is not correct.
Whatever is improper and does not accord with reason must be set aside and removed— whether it be one's own or that of another— according to one's strength and capacity.
The underlying sense is that, due to a deficiency of power, it is appropriate to simply disregard such things.

It might be argued: "Even if there is no such thing as a self (ātman) and so forth, nevertheless, a continuum (saṃtāna) called 'one' is possible; likewise, a collection of many parts such as hands and feet constitutes one body."

These two, as applicable, will serve as the determinants for removing one's own suffering and so forth, both in this world and in the next. Therefore, suspecting that the reason "because there is no distinction" is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the previous reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says:
The continuum and the collection are false, like a row or an army;
since he who experiences suffering does not exist, to whom will that [suffering] belong?
That which is called a "continuum" (saṃtāna) does not exist as a single entity in the ultimate sense.
What then? It is merely the form of a flowing succession of moments proceeding through the relationship of cause and effect, because nothing distinct from that is perceived.
Therefore, for the sake of conventional usage, the Buddhas established the convention "continuum" (*saṃtāna*) as a single term to designate these very moments.
Thus, this is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*);
one should not form an attachment to it.

Otherwise, what wrong has the self committed that it is not accepted [as real]? Likewise, the collection (*samudāya*) also does not exist as a single, substantially real entity distinct from its constituents (*samudāyin*), because it is not perceived separately from them. (Bcp 159)
The conceptualization of identity and difference has already been resolved through the analysis of the "whole" (avayavin); therefore, it is not further elaborated upon here.
Consequently, this [self] is also merely conventionally existent, just like the previous cases.
He provides examples for these two respectively, saying: "like a row, an army, and so forth."
The continuum is like a mudbank;
the collection is like an army and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), garlands, forests, and the like are included.

Just as there is no single entity called a "line" apart from the individual nature of many ants and so forth situated in a prior-to-posterior sequence— just as [there is no line] distinct from the beads and the string—

and just as there is no other single entity called an "army" existing apart from the elephants, horses, foot soldiers, and so forth when they are assembled, so too is the case with a collection (*samudāya*).
And this has been investigated in detail elsewhere [at 9.73], so it is not investigated here.
Therefore, because there is no object that exists as a real entity, this cognition is false; or rather, the object is false, because it cannot withstand analysis.
Thus, since there is no owner such as a self or the like, there is no one to whom suffering belongs;
therefore, to whom will that suffering belong as its own? The meaning is that it belongs to no one at all.
Now, if the self and so forth do not exist, how can this analogy— “like the self” and “like a sentient being”— be valid?
This is true.
However, this argument is not stated out of a sense of hostility;
rather, it is for the purpose of removing another's persistent attachment to the grasping of a self.
Therefore, if that other person’s persistent attachment to the grasping of a self has indeed ceased, [then there is no need for further proof].
In that case, there would be no purpose whatsoever for the employment of inference.
If, on the other hand, [the opponent] has not ceased [from his position],
then it is precisely with reference to his intention that one establishes the distinction between self and other, and states the proof and the example for the sake of making that understood.
Thus, there is no failure of the example for the purpose of establishing conventional discourse.
Furthermore,
when this example is given with reference solely to these appropriated five aggregates, there is no defect whatsoever.
Because the word "self" (ātman) is applied precisely to this [consciousness].
Now, concluding the present topic, he says:
"All sufferings whatsoever are without an owner; because they are suffering, they must be warded off without distinction. What basis is there for restriction in this regard? (Bca 8.102)
The analysis of the compound is: "those for whom there are no owners according to the sequence stated.
The meaning is that they are *amamāni*, i.e., not bound to anyone.
Why? Are only some [of them] so? No.
All things indeed, without distinction;
nowhere does anyone possess ownership,
because there is an absence of distinction.

Precisely because they are suffering, one makes a distinction between self and others, and thus [objects] are to be avoided and prohibited. There is no other cause for this than [the notion of] "belonging to oneself" and so forth.
Therefore, by what is this restriction established?
By what distinction is it established that [these] are one's own waters and not those belonging to another?
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the reason "because of being suffering" (*duḥkhatvāt*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Now, one might raise this objection: "If indeed no such thing as a 'sufferer' exists within cyclic existence, then suffering would be unavoidable, since there would be no one to serve as a recipient of compassion. Anticipating this doubt, he says:

If it is asked why suffering must be averted, [the answer is] because there is no dispute among anyone that it should be so; and if it is to be averted, then all [suffering] must be averted in this way, for one's own self is no different from other sentient beings.
If you think that it cannot be prevented precisely because of its being devoid of self (nirātmakatva), then this is not tenable.
Why? Because there is no dispute and no disagreement among all [regarding this].
Even for the Cārvāka, activity in this world proceeds solely for the sake of avoiding his own suffering;
nor is it without fault because they do not admit a self.
Because its intrinsic nature is not perceived;
nor is its existence established by mere assertion, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could prove it,
and because many kinds of subverting arguments have been stated.
This being the case, if suffering is to be warded off, then everything must be warded off; if not everything is to be warded off, then the self as well [is not to be warded off].
The conclusion is that suffering, which has the nature of the five appropriated aggregates, cannot be avoided, because there is no distinction between it and the case of all sentient beings.

It might be argued: "Since one who suffers from the suffering of others due to being dependent on compassion strives to remove all their suffering, it would be better if that very [compassion], which is the source of much suffering, were not produced in the first place. Anticipating this opportunity for an opponent's objection, he says: "If, through compassion, much suffering arises, why does it arise so forcefully?"
"By force" means through effort.
To this, he gives the following reply:
"Having examined the suffering of the world, how can this suffering of compassion be considered great? (Bca 8.104)
Having observed the manifold suffering of the world caused by hells and other realms, how can this suffering produced by compassion be considered great?
The sense is that this suffering born of compassion is not great at all.
Furthermore, he states this other response to the objection:
"If the suffering of many were to cease through the suffering of one, then that suffering should certainly be produced by one who possesses compassion for both self and others. (Bca 8.105)
If, through the suffering of a single person, the suffering of many sentient beings is dispelled or ceases,
then such suffering must indeed be produced;
it should be brought forth by one who is compassionate and whose nature is pity, for the sake of both others and oneself.
To avoid the charge of contradicting the sūtras, he says:
"Therefore, even though Supuṣpacandra knew of the danger to the king, he did not eliminate his own suffering because it would have resulted in the destruction of many who were suffering. (Bca 8.106)
Precisely because that suffering of both oneself and others must be produced by one who possesses compassion, for this very reason, the Bodhisattva Supuṣpacandra—
though knowing and fully aware of it— [endured] the king's calamity or the misfortune of the sovereign.
One's own suffering has neither been destroyed nor averted;
that is to say, it has been neglected.
Likewise, the king also [neglects] the suffering of the next world.
Why is this? Because of the expenditure of many who suffer.
The word "of suffering" (*duḥkhasya*), which was previously mentioned, is connected here as a genitive case.
As it is said in the *Supuṣpacandra-itivṛttaka* [Samādhirāja Sūtra 35]: "For instance, in the past, there was a Tathāgata named Ratnapadmacandraviśuddhābhyudgatarāja."
That Blessed One, having performed the deeds of a Buddha and remained for a very long time, passed into parinirvāṇa.
When he had passed into parinirvāṇa and at the time of the disappearance of the teaching, there was a king named Śūradatta.
His royal capital was named Ratnāvatī.
At that time, sentient beings were corrupted by wrong views.
Out of compassion for them, many bodhisattvas arose and went forth into the religious life.
Having been banished from those kingdoms and districts, they settled in a forest grove named Samantabhadra and dwelt there together with the Dharma-preacher Supuṣpacandra.

Then, as the Bodhisattva Supuṣpacandra was feeling compassion for sentient beings while in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind: "What if I were to go to the provinces, kingdoms, and royal capitals, and establish those beings who have entered upon evil paths upon the auspicious path?"
He reported that matter to his fellow religious practitioners;
yet, even though they tried to dissuade him, he persisted in his own calamitous course and departed from that forest grove along with the king.

Gradually teaching the Dharma, he reached the capital city of that king and, having disciplined many beings—including princes, ministers, and priests—in various ways, established them on the true path.

While he was establishing [the boundary], he was seen by the king; upon seeing him, the king became enraged, and having observed that the entire body of people had become devoted to him, his heart was corrupted by envy,
and he commanded his own sons to kill him.
Perceiving that they were intent on sparing his life, he commanded Nandika, the executioner.
Following his orders, Nandika severed his hands, feet, and other limbs in succession, extracted his eyes with pincers, and deprived him of life.
Then, as the body of that monk, who had been executed while standing upon the royal highway, lay there, many wonders occurred.
Having observed those signs, the king became certain that "this monk is indeed a Bodhisattva," and overcome with distress, he lamented even more intensely.
Thus has the account of Supuṣpacandra been told in brief;
however, it is taught in detail in the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* [35], and should be understood from that very source.
And demonstrating that even great suffering does not cause affliction for those possessed of compassion who suffer with the suffering of others, he says:
"Those whose mental continuums have been cultivated in this way, for whom the suffering of others is as dear as their own, plunge into the Avīci hell as swans enter a lotus grove. (Bca 8.107)

Thus, those whose mental continuums have been cultivated through the equality of self and other possess mental continuums that function effortlessly. They are such that for them, what is dear is equal to and identical with the suffering of others;
the meaning is that even their own happiness is nothing but suffering due to the suffering of others.

They plunge into the Avīci hell for the sake of uprooting the calamities of others, regarding that very suffering as happiness. This is precisely what is meant by the verse: "Just as swans [enter] a lotus grove; for those who, for the sake of others, regard even the suffering of Avīci as happiness."
By what other cause of suffering will they become miserable?
Furthermore, demonstrating that even their happiness arises as something unique, not shared with the happiness of others, he says:
When sentient beings are being liberated, there arise those oceans of joy;
surely that alone is sufficient—what need is there for a liberation that is devoid of flavor?
While sentient beings are being separated from the bondage of suffering,
those [beings]—
because they are established only through personal experience (*anubhava*)— cannot be described by way of "this-ness" (*idantayā*).

For this very reason, oceans of joy and oceans of contentment arise within the mental continuums of the compassionate; by those very oceans of joy, they are fully satisfied and reach completion through their turning away from all other forms of happiness. Therefore, even after accomplishing the welfare of others, there is neither pride nor astonishment.
There is no longing for the fruit of karmic maturation, due to an exclusive thirst for the welfare of others.
Therefore, just as I protect myself even from the slightest disparagement,
I shall likewise cultivate a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward others.
Through habituation, the cognition "I" arises even with respect to drops of semen and blood belonging to another, even though the object is unreal.
Likewise, why is another's body not grasped as "self"? For one's own body to be regarded as "other" is already established and is by no means difficult. (Bca 8.112)
Having recognized oneself as being full of faults and others as oceans of virtues,
