one should cultivate the relinquishing of one's own self-identity and the taking up of the other.
Just as hands and other limbs are accepted as being parts of the body,
why are embodied beings not likewise accepted as parts of the world?

Just as the notion of a self arises through habituation toward this body of ours, which is devoid of a self, why should the sense of selfhood not likewise arise toward others through habituation? (Bca 8.115)
Thus, even after performing the welfare of others, there is neither pride nor astonishment;
and just as when one has fed oneself, no expectation for a reward arises.
Therefore, just as you wish to protect yourself from pain, grief, and the like,
so too should you practice a mind of protection and a mind of compassion toward the world.
Therefore, the Protector Avalokita bestowed his own name [upon him] in order to remove even the fear of timidity before an assembly for the sake of people.
One should not turn back from difficult tasks because of the power of habituation;
for that very thing which causes fear upon hearing it, by that same thing one finds delight.
He who wishes to quickly protect both himself and others should practice the supreme secret: the exchange of self and other.
Since one feels fear even at the slightest danger due to excessive attachment to this self, who would not hate that self? For the destruction of an enemy brings fear, whereas this [self] brings it.
He who kills birds, fish, and deer out of a desire to remedy his own weakness, hunger, thirst, and so forth, and he who stands as an ambush on the path; Bca 8.122.
One who, for the sake of gain and honor, would even kill his own parents or seize the property of the Three Jewels, thereby becomes fuel for the Avīci hell.
What wise person would desire, protect, or honor such a self?
One should not look upon him as an enemy, nor should anyone treat him with contempt.
"If I give, what shall I eat?"—this is the state of a *piśāca* for one's own sake; "If I eat, what shall I give?"—this is the state of a king of gods for the sake of others. (Bca 8.125)
Having oppressed another for one's own sake, one is cooked in the hells and other realms of suffering;
but by oppressing oneself for the sake of others, all forms of prosperity are attained.
By transferring that very desire for one's own exaltation— which leads to miserable rebirths, low status, and folly— onto another, one attains a happy rebirth, honor, and wisdom.
(Bcp 163) By commanding another for one's own sake, one experiences servitude and the like;
but by commanding that same person for the sake of another, one experiences lordship and the like.
Whoever in the world is suffering, all do so out of a desire for their own happiness;
whoever in the world is happy, all do so out of a desire for the happiness of others.
What is the use of saying more? Behold this difference between the fool who seeks his own interest and the sage who acts for the sake of others.

Indeed, Buddhahood is not something to be accomplished; how, then, could there be happiness even in cyclic existence for one who does not effect an exchange of their own happiness for the suffering of others? (Bca 8.131)
Let alone the next world; even a visible purpose in this life is not accomplished when a servant does not perform his work or when a master does not pay his wages.
Abandoning the production of mutual happiness and the festival of joy in both this world and the next,
deluded beings embrace terrible suffering born from mutual harm.
Whatever calamities arise in the world, and however many sufferings and fears there may be—all these result from the grasping for a self; so why do I grasp at this [body]? Bca 8.134.
Without abandoning the self, suffering cannot be abandoned;
just as without abandoning fire, burning cannot be abandoned. (Bca 8.135)
Therefore, for the sake of pacifying my own suffering and for the sake of pacifying the suffering of others,
I give myself to others and take others as myself.
"O mind, form the conviction: 'I am bound to others. Having renounced [all concern] for the sake of all sentient beings, nothing else should be thought of by you now. (Bca 8.137)
It is not right for one's own eyes and other faculties to perceive their respective objects;
it is likewise not right for the hands and other limbs belonging to another to exert themselves for one's own sake.
Therefore, being devoted to sentient beings, whatever you perceive within this body,
having cast that very thing away from it, act for the benefit of others.
Having conceived of yourself as inferior and others as superior,
you should cultivate envy and pride with a non-conceptual mind.
"This person is honored, but I am not; he gains profit, but I do not;
he is praised, while I am blamed; I am suffering, while he is happy. (Bca 8.141)
"I perform actions, while he remains well-established;
he is indeed great in the world, while I am truly base and devoid of merit. (Bca 8.142)

(Bcp 164) What can be done by one who lacks virtues? For everyone’s self is endowed with virtues. There are those among whom I am base; there are those among whom I am superior. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 8.143.

I am to be treated according to my capacity by the power of afflictions such as the failure of ethical discipline and right view, and not by my own will; even suffering has been accepted by me for that purpose.
Now, since I am incurable for him, why do you despise me?
What use have I for these virtues; he alone is the one possessed of virtue.
While still within the jaws of the beast of miserable rebirths, he feels compassion for people;
furthermore, out of pride in his virtues, he seeks to conquer the wise.
Since one observes oneself as equal [to others], for the sake of increasing one's own excellence,
one should secure gain and honor for oneself even through quarreling.
May my virtues become manifest throughout the entire world;
yet, may there be some of his virtues that no one at all shall ever hear.
"May my faults be concealed; may there be no worship for me, but rather for him.
Today I have gained great profit, for I am not the one being worshipped. (Bca 8.149)
Let us watch with joy for a long time this man who has been humiliated, laughed at by everyone, and reviled here and there. (Bca 8.150)
For even this wretched fellow indeed competes with me;
what learning does he have? What wisdom, beauty, lineage, or wealth? (Bca 8.151)
Having thus heard my own virtues being proclaimed here and there,
with my hair standing on end in joy, I shall enjoy a festival of happiness.
Even if he should obtain some gain, we must take it from him by force,
provided that, after giving him merely enough for his sustenance, he performs our work.
This person must always be made to fall from happiness and be joined with our own suffering;
by means of him, we have all been tormented by the pains of cyclic existence hundreds of times.
Immeasurable eons have passed while you have sought to know your own self-interest;
through this great exertion, you have acquired nothing but suffering.
At my request, act here likewise without hesitation;
you will see these benefits later, for the word of the Sage is indeed true.
If this karma had been performed by you in the past, then,
setting aside the bliss of the Buddha's perfection, this present state would not have come to pass.
Therefore, just as you have conceived an ego-sense toward drops of semen and blood belonging to others, cultivate that same attitude toward other things as well.
(Bcp 165) Acting as a spy for others, whatever you perceive within this body,
take that very thing away for their sake and act for the benefit of others. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 8.159.
"This one is well-off while that one is miserable; this one is lowly while that one is high;
that one does something while this one does not"—do not harbor such envy within yourself. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 8.160.

Deprive yourself of happiness and subject yourself to the suffering of others; examine his every move and his motives, asking: "What is he doing now? and "When will this [opportunity] arise? (Bca 8.161).
Cast even a fault committed by another upon his very head;
and reveal even the slightest fault of this great sage.
Defile his reputation with talk of the superior glory of others;
and make him carry out tasks for living beings like a lowly slave.
For this one is composed of faults; he is not to be praised on account of any adventitious qualities.
Act in such a way that no one may perceive his virtue.
In brief, whatever harm you have done to others for your own sake,
turn that very misfortune upon yourself for the sake of sentient beings.
One must not give him any encouragement that would make him talkative;
rather, he should be established in the conduct of a new bride—modest, fearful, and restrained.
"Do this; remain thus; you must not do this.
In this very way, he should be brought under control, and restrained when he transgresses.
Moreover, even if it is said thus, if you, O mind, will not do this,
I shall surely subdue you alone, for all faults are dependent upon you.
"Where will you go, now that you have been seen by me? I shall destroy all your pride! That was another time in the past when you were able to destroy me. (Bca 8.169)
Abandon now the hope that "I still have my own self-interest";
you have been sold by me to others, so do not think of your own great suffering.
If, out of negligence, I do not give you away among sentient beings,
you will undoubtedly deliver me to the guardians of hell.
Having thus given to me in many ways, you have long caused me suffering;
now, remembering those enmities, I shall destroy you, who act solely for your own self-interest.
If you have love for yourself, you should not take pleasure in [harming] yourself;
if this self is to be protected, it is not proper to protect it [by harming others].
Just as this body is provided with protection,
it becomes increasingly more delicate, and in that very same way, it inevitably falls [into ruin].
Even for one who has fallen into such a state, this entire earth is not sufficient to satisfy his desire; therefore, who will fulfill his longing? (Bca 8.175)
For one who desires the impossible, suffering and the frustration of hope arise;
but for one who is free from hope in all things, prosperity never decays.
Therefore, one must not grant the body any scope for the increase of its desires;
for that object which is not grasped because it is desired is indeed called "auspicious."
This body, which ends in a state of ashes, is motionless and moved by another;
it is a terrible vessel of impurity—why then do I have such attachment to it?
What is this machine of mine to me, whether living or dead? What difference is there between it and a clod of earth? Alas! Why do you not let go of this egoism?
Through partiality toward the body, suffering is acquired in vain;
what is the use of hatred or attachment toward this thing that is like a piece of wood? (Bca 8.180)
Whether it is thus protected by me or devoured by vultures and other scavengers, there is neither affection nor aversion toward it; why then do I feel attachment? (Bca 8.181)
If he whom I provoke to anger and he whom I honor with worship do not themselves know [the value of my actions], for whose sake then is my labor? (Bca 8.182)
Those who desire this body are indeed said to be my friends;
since everyone desires their own body, why are they not dear to me?
Therefore, disregarding my own interests, I have renounced my body for the welfare of the world;
hence, even though it is full of many defects, it is maintained like a vessel of karma.
Therefore, enough with worldly conduct; remembering the discourse on heedfulness and warding off sloth and torpor, I shall follow the wise.
Therefore, in order to destroy the obscurations, I shall practice meditative concentration,
drawing the mind away from the wrong path and making it continuous with its own object of focus.
The eighth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Meditation," in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
The ninth chapter, titled "The Perfection of Wisdom."
That which, by virtue of its stainlessness, is the unsurpassed state, free from all conceptual proliferation, and is designated by conventional terms such as "perfection of wisdom" (prajñāpāramitā)—
that which is untainted; having correctly realized that, those of pure intellect attain supreme nirvāṇa.
Having bowed to her according to the prescribed rite, I shall compose a commentary upon it in clear words. (1)
Where that teacher Śāntideva, a treasury of virtues who has reached the further shore of the great ocean of the scriptures, is able to speak with clarity;
how could I, of dull intellect, be capable of speaking for his sake? Nevertheless—
Through the practice of wisdom, I have set forth from that which is incomparable well-performed merit.
Indeed, there is not even a trace of the impression of virtue in me, nor have I acquired any quality of intellectual brilliance;
nevertheless, as the fruit of attending upon true friends, such speech as this flows forth from me. *3*

Now, suppose there is a certain noble being who, by virtue of his distinguished lineage and through having attended upon spiritual friends, shares in the suffering of all beings included within the three worlds;

who is intent on completely uprooting the suffering of all living creatures; who is indifferent to his own happiness; and who, regarding only Buddhahood as the means for its cessation, has generated the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) out of a desire to attain it, for the purpose of fulfilling the two accumulations that serve as the means for achieving the state of the Sugata.
One proceeds gradually in the practices of giving and so forth.

For one who thus proceeds—even if they have correctly practiced calm abiding (*śamatha*)—the perfections such as giving do not bring about Buddhahood, which is the cause for accomplishing the welfare of the world, because they are devoid of wisdom. With this intention, it must necessarily be understood that by one who seeks liberation from the suffering of *saṃsāra*...
One should strive for the production of wisdom, as it has been said:
"One who is well-engaged in insight through tranquility," and so forth. Among these, the presentation of tranquility has already been made.
Now, in order to establish *vipaśyanā*—which follows immediately after that and is also known by the name "wisdom"—he says: "The Sage taught this entire preparatory practice for the sake of wisdom;
therefore, one should generate wisdom out of a desire for the cessation of suffering. (Bca 9.1)
The word "this" (*imam*) refers by way of direct perception to the practice of giving and so forth, which has just been explained here in this treatise according to its characteristics;
"retinue" (*parikaram*) means the surrounding circle or the specific division;
and "provision" (*saṃbhāram*) means as much as is required.
All that has been stated in various ways, and furthermore:
the connection is that the Sage taught for the sake of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Wisdom is characterized by the discernment of the reality of things as they truly exist, namely, dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

That very thing is the "purpose" (*artha*), which is the objective; that retinue characterized by giving and so forth is "such," because it leads to the state of being a cause for perfect enlightenment.
This is because among the perfections of giving and the rest, wisdom—which has the nature of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*)—is predominant.
For indeed, giving is the primary cause for attaining the enlightenment of a perfectly awakened Buddha.

Because it is included within the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*), that [merit]— when adorned by ethical discipline (*śīla*)— brings about a succession of happy rebirths endowed with the requisites for the enjoyment of happiness, and serves as the cause for the attainment of unsurpassed knowledge (*anuttarajñāna*).

Patience (*kṣānti*) also, by acting as the antidote to hostility (*pratigha*), which is its opposite, protects the accumulation consisting of the well-performed acts of generosity and ethical discipline, and thus proceeds toward the realization of Buddhahood.

Furthermore, this merit known as the "accumulation of virtue" (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*), which arises from the triad of giving and the other [perfections], does not occur without vigor; thus, vigor also arises for the sake of abandoning all obscurations by being the cause for both accumulations.

Moreover, since the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) arises for one whose mind is concentrated, the perfection of meditation (*dhyānapāramitā*) is also established as a cause for unsurpassed gnosis (*anuttarajñāna*).

In this way, even if these [virtues] such as giving are properly cultivated, they do not become causes for attaining the state of a Sugata without wisdom, nor do they receive the designation of "perfection" (*pāramitā*).
Furthermore, those who possess purification produced by wisdom, by virtue of their unimpeded and noble activity, follow in accordance with that [wisdom] and attain its causal state,

thereby receiving the designation of "perfections" (*pāramitā*). Likewise, when purified by wisdom through the yoga of non-apprehension of the triad of giver, gift, and recipient, and practiced with diligence, continuity, and over a long period of time—

Reaching the ultimate limit, they bring forth the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata— which is free from the stains of the entire web of conceptual constructions set in motion by ignorance, liberated from the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, characterized by the realization of the two kinds of selflessness, the foundation for the attainment of all welfare for oneself and others, and consisting of the reality of the ultimate truth; thus,
the virtues such as generosity and the rest are said to have wisdom as their preeminent quality.

And this should not be said: "If wisdom is the primary [factor] among giving and the others, let that alone be the means for attaining perfect enlightenment; what is the use of the other factors such as giving?"

Since their utility has been described for others, generosity and the other perfections— being like those who are blind— are said to have wisdom as their guide, because they proceed toward the desired stage of the Sugata only when led by wisdom;
however, wisdom alone is not the means for achieving perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, it is established that the equipment consisting of generosity and the other perfections has wisdom as its purpose.

The Buddha, the Blessed One, is a *muni* because he is free from all conceptual construction (*sarvakalpanāviraha*), because he maintains silence regarding the two extremes of superimposition and denial (*samāropāpavādāntadvayamauna*), or because he is endowed with the threefold silence characterized by the actions of body, speech, and mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣakāyavāṅmanaḥkarmalakṣaṇamaunatrayayoga*).
He "sang"—that is, he spoke—with the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*) to protect the entire world suffering through the three types of suffering;
the meaning is that he has spoken.
In the noble *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, he has explained the prerequisites for wisdom, such as generosity and the rest, in their proper sequence.
As it is said in the noble *Śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā*:
"Subhūti, it is just as, for example, the orb of the sun and the orb of the moon perform their functions throughout the four continents."
Just as [the sun] follows and revolves around the four continents,
even so, Subhūti, the perfection of wisdom performs its function among the five perfections and follows after the five perfections.
They do not follow along; because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom, the five perfections do not receive the designation "perfection.
Subhūti, it is just as, for example, a wheel-turning monarch who is deprived of the seven treasures does not receive the designation "wheel-turning monarch."
In the same way, Subhūti, the five perfections do not receive the designation "perfection" because they are devoid of the perfection of wisdom.
Just as, Subhūti, whatever small rivers there may be, they all flow toward the great river Ganges; so it is with these.
Just as those [rivers] follow along with the great river Gaṅgā toward the great ocean,
even so, Subhūti, the five perfections, when embraced by the perfection of wisdom, proceed toward all-aspect omniscience;
such is the detailed explanation.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Kauśika, this perfection of wisdom surpasses the perfection of generosity of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas."
It surpasses the perfection of ethical discipline, it surpasses the perfection of patience,
[and it surpasses the perfection of vigor].
He surpasses the perfection of meditation.
Kauśika, it is just as if there were a hundred or a thousand people born blind who, being without a guide, would be incapable of entering upon the path,
let alone entering a city.

In the same way, Kauśika, the five perfections are without eyes and like those born blind without the perfection of wisdom; they are without a guide, and without the perfection of wisdom they are incapable of entering the path to awakening, let alone of entering the city of the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, Kauśika, when the five perfections are embraced by the perfection of wisdom,
then these five perfections become possessed of eyes;
and it is when embraced by the perfection of wisdom that these five perfections receive the designation "perfection."
Thus is the detailed explanation.
In the same way, this should be understood elsewhere as well according to the sūtra. And it is said:
"O blameless one, by means of all the stainless perfections, you are always followed, like the crescent moon by the stars."
Thus [Prajñāpāramitāstava 8].
Alternatively: "This" refers to the preceding composition consisting of *śamatha*;
"the equipment" (*parikara*) refers to the collection of causes that give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as the introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*).
"For the sake of wisdom" means that wisdom itself, as previously described, is the "object"—that is, the purpose or goal—as that which is to be accomplished.
This is because wisdom manifests within the mental continuum when it has been purified by calm abiding (*śamatha*), just as a harvest is produced in a well-cultivated field.
As it is said in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*:
What, then, is the greatness of this śamatha?
It is the power to generate knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūtajñāna). For it is said:
"The Sage has said that one who is concentrated knows things as they truly are.
This too was stated in the *Dharmasaṃgīti*:
For one whose mind is concentrated, there arises vision of things as they truly are;
for a bodhisattva who sees things as they truly are, great compassion toward sentient beings arises:
"I must bring this gateway of samādhi to fulfillment for all sentient beings."
Impelled by that great compassion, he fulfills the trainings in higher ethics, higher mind, and higher wisdom, and thereby awakens to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
such is the detailed account.

The word "hi" (for) means that since the Sage taught the equipment consisting of generosity and so forth, or the equipment consisting of tranquility (*śamatha*), for the sake of wisdom (*prajñā*), one should therefore generate wisdom— this is how it should be construed.
"One should generate" means one should accomplish, realize, cultivate, practice, or make much of [wisdom].
And that wisdom is of two kinds: that which is causal and that which is resultant.
The causal is also twofold: that of the bodhisattva who practices through resolute belief and that of the bodhisattva who has entered the stages.
The resultant, however, is endowed with the excellence of all aspects and has as its intrinsic nature the realization of the emptiness of all phenomena.

By means of the yoga of the signless (*animitta-yoga*), there first arises, through the sequence of practice, the wisdom consisting of hearing, reflection, and cultivation which serves as the cause; this brings about the wisdom of one who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*).

And that wisdom, increasing its excellence through the attainment of successive stages until the removal of both obscurations, accomplishes the wisdom whose nature is Buddhahood, free from the entire web of conceptual construction.
For this very reason, he said, "through the desire for the cessation of suffering.

This refers to suffering—comprising that which belongs to the mass of sentient beings included within the five destinies, that which pertains to oneself, and that which is characteristic of cyclic existence: namely, birth, sickness, old age, and death; separation from the beloved, union with the unloved, the failure to obtain what one seeks, and, in brief, that which consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Cessation is nirvāṇa, tranquility;
the meaning is its absolute eradication by virtue of being subject to the quality of non-arising again.
"By the longing for that" means by the desire for it.
"By desire," and so forth.

For instance, in one who possesses perverted perceptions, the host of afflictions such as attachment arises—produced by improper mental attention (ayoniśomanasikāra)—due to the occurrence of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self, which stems from the insistence on superimposing existence upon the non-existent;
from that [affliction], action (karman) arises.
From that comes birth,
and from that arise disease, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair;
thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.

Thus, for one who correctly contemplates dependent origination in its forward order with right wisdom, and who further perceives that very same process as being without self and without owner— seeing it, in ultimate reality, as being devoid of intrinsic nature due to its resemblance to illusions, mirages, cities of the Gandharvas, dreams, reflections, and so forth—
the limb of existence known as ignorance, which is by nature delusion, ceases through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are, owing to its being the antithesis of that [knowledge].
With the cessation of ignorance, the formative forces conditioned by it cease.
In this way, it should be understood that through the cessation of each preceding cause, each succeeding effect ceases;
thus, with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair also cease.
In this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
Therein, ignorance, craving, and grasping constitute the severance of the path of afflictions;
volitional formations and existence constitute the severance of the path of karma.
The remaining members constitute the severance of the path of suffering;
the cessation of the prior and subsequent limits constitutes the severance of the path of cessation.
In this very way, the threefold path is selfless, devoid of self and what belongs to a self, yet it arises through the principle of dependent origination.
And it ceases through the process of disintegration;
by its own nature, it is like a bundle of reeds.
This will be demonstrated in detail later through both reasoning and scripture.

Thus, for one who investigates the conditioned with wisdom as having the nature of a dream, an illusion, and so forth, there arises the realization of the ultimate truth through the understanding that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; consequently, the entire mass of defects along with their latent predispositions is completely eliminated.
Therefore, it is established that wisdom is the cause for the cessation of all suffering.

To demonstrate how the discernment of the non-erroneous reality of things arises for one who investigates through both reasoning and scripture, he states the establishment of the two truths, beginning with "Conventional reality," and so forth:
"This is held to be the two truths: conventional reality and ultimate reality."
Reality is beyond the scope of the intellect; the intellect is said to be conventional.

It is called *saṃvṭi* because by means of it, the knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*) is concealed (*saṃvriyate*) or covered (*āvriyate*), both due to the obscuration of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāvaraṇa*) and the manifestation of what is obscured.
Ignorance (*avidyā*), delusion (*moha*), and perversion (*viparyāsa*) are synonyms.
For ignorance, being that which superimposes the essential nature of non-existent entities and having the nature of obscuring the vision of intrinsic nature, is established as *saṃvṛti*.
As it is said in the *Āryaśālistamba-sūtra* (Bcp 171):
"Furthermore, non-engagement with reality and false engagement [constitute ignorance]."
Ignorance is nescience (*avidyā*).
And it has been said:
"It manifests an unreal object while concealing the real."
Ignorance, as soon as it arises, is like the manifestation of the affliction of jaundice.
Thus it is said.
And that nature of things which has been shown to be dependently originated is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti).
That very thing is designated as "worldly conventional truth" (lokasaṃvṛtisatya), because it is true for the world by way of convention. As it has been stated:

Delusion (moha) is the concealment of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and so forth; it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti). Whatever fabricated thing appears by means of that [delusion], the Sage declared that to be "conventional truth" (saṃvṛtisatya); he also designated a produced entity (kṛtaka) as the conventional.
Thus it is said [Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 6.28].
And that conventional reality (saṃvṛti) is of two kinds from the perspective of the world itself: correct conventional reality (tathyasaṃvṛti) and false conventional reality (mithyāsaṃvṛti).
For instance, certain objective forms such as blue and so forth, which arise dependently and are perceived by unimpaired sense faculties, are true from the perspective of the world itself.

On the other hand, that which arises dependently yet is perceived by impaired sense faculties—such as illusions, mirages, reflections, and the like—as well as that imagined through the tenets of various non-Buddhist schools, is false from the perspective of the world itself. As it has been said:
"That which is apprehended by the world through the six sense faculties, provided there is no impairment of those faculties..."
For that which is real is so according to the world alone; the remainder, being conceptualized, is false according to the world alone.
Thus, both of these are false for the noble ones who possess right vision,
because from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is unreal.
We shall demonstrate this immediately following [the present discussion] by means of logical proof.
Therefore, the intrinsic nature of things does not appear to those possessed of ignorance.
The ultimate object (*paramārtha*) is the supreme reality;
it is the unconditioned nature of things,
through the realization of which there occurs the abandonment of all obscurations, latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), and the underlying afflictions (*anuśaya-kleśa*).
The absence of intrinsic nature, emptiness, and suchness of all phenomena.
The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*),
the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), and so forth are synonyms.
For the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of every dependently originated entity is its ultimate form.
Because that which appears conventionally is not logically tenable;
for instance, an entity does not possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) in the form in which it is currently perceived,
because that [form] does not persist in subsequent moments.
And because intrinsic nature is never adventitious, it is by nature unchanging;
for how could that which is the intrinsic nature of something ever be revoked at any time?
Otherwise, because it would follow that its intrinsic nature is lost, it would be nothing but devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Furthermore, as it arises, it does not come from anywhere with the form of an existent intrinsic nature; nor, as it ceases, does it go to any accumulation.
Rather, it arises like an illusion depending on the assemblage of causes and conditions,
and it ceases due to their deficiency;
for that which is born depending on the assemblage of causes and conditions has its acquisition of self-nature dependent on others, like a reflected image.
Whence could there be an existent intrinsic nature (*satsvabhāvatā*)?
For it is not possible for any entity to arise from a collection of causes and conditions in an ultimate sense;

because that collection itself has its own nature produced by another collection, and thus, since its acquisition of selfhood is dependent on something else, it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
In this way, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of every other preceding [cause] must be understood as being produced by its own respective causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*).

Thus, for one who maintains that the effect conforms to its cause, how can the arising of something with intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāva*) from that which lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) be accepted?
As he will say:
That which is created by illusion and that which is produced by causes—from where does it come, and to where does it go? Let this be investigated.
That which is seen through the proximity of another is not seen due to its absence;
how can there be reality in that artificial thing, which is like a reflection?
Thus it has been said:
"That which is born from conditions is indeed unborn; for it has no arising by way of intrinsic nature."
That which is dependent on conditions is said to be empty; he who understands emptiness is heedful.
Thus, from the *Anavataptahrādāpasaṃkramaṇasūtra*:
"It is from empty phenomena alone that empty phenomena arise."

Furthermore, the arising of an entity— whether based on causes consisting of itself, another, or both, or even without a cause— is not at all tenable. For instance, if the intrinsic nature (*ātmasvarūpa*) of entities were the cause of their own arising,
it would have to be either already established or unestablished.

First of all, that which already exists as an accomplished entity cannot possess causal efficiency with respect to itself, because it has already been fully accomplished in its entirety; what further operation could there be for it?
Furthermore, since there is no other nature of this [entity] to be produced that remains unaccomplished, [it cannot act upon itself].
Furthermore, because this one [entity] is partless,

it is not logical for another entity arising subsequently to possess that same intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), since that which has not yet been produced lacks the state of possessing the intrinsic nature of the former once the latter has been completed.
Thus, there is no arising of anything from its own self as something already established.
Nor, under the view of arising from self, is it possible for anything to have a pre-established nature, because that would entail the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).
Furthermore, that which has an unestablished nature—resembling a lotus in the sky and devoid of all causal capacity—is not capable of becoming a cause for its own establishment.
Otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that even a donkey's horn would produce its own intrinsic nature.
Nor is the position that [things arise] from another tenable,
because it would entail the absurd consequence that darkness could arise even from the sun, or that everything could arise from anything at all.
Because there is no distinction in "remoteness" between those considered the progenitor and those not considered the progenitor with respect to the intended effect;
furthermore, the restriction to a single continuum based on the identity of the produced and the producer does not hold in reality, as it is merely conceptual so long as the effect has not arisen.
Nor is the conventional usage of "effect" and so forth real when based on dharmas existing in a future state.
This is because the existence of the intrinsic nature of objects will be examined [later].
Nor is there any non-conceptual otherness of the seed with respect to the sprout existing in the state of the seed, since the effect exists within the cause. (Bcp 173)
Because it is about to be refuted:
where even the form that is currently being perceived does not remain when subjected to analysis, what concern can there be regarding that which is merely imagined in the future and so forth?
Nor is the position that [the cause] consists of both [types] tenable, because it would entail the combined faults stated for each individual position,
and because, given the non-arising of the effect, a cause possessing both forms does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Or, if there were production, since there would be nothing at all to be produced, where could the operation of a cause possessing both forms take place?
Nor is the alternative of "without a cause" tenable, because this "without a cause" cannot logically be understood as a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

For if things were without cause, there would follow the consequence of no restriction regarding place and time, or else the consequence of their being either eternally existent or eternally non-existent; furthermore,
for those seeking a goal, there would be no performance of specific means.
Since causes such as Pradhāna, Īśvara, and so forth will be refuted,
entities do not acquire their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) from a lack of cause.
Therefore, entities possessing an existent intrinsic nature do not arise from causes that are of the nature of self, other, or both. As it has been said:
"Never, anywhere, are any entities found to have arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor even without a cause."
Thus, [Mūlamadhyamakakārikā 1.3]:
Even by investigating whether things possess a nature that is one or many, all entities lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they do not possess a real nature.

Consequently, let it be that this is merely "this-conditionality" (*idaṃpratyayatāmātra*), which is charming only so long as it is not subjected to analytical investigation, like a dream, an illusion, or a reflection.
What purpose, then, is there here in this clinging to the existence of things, which is the cause of all suffering?
Therefore, this is the true nature of objects: these things, as propounded by ourselves and others, are in reality devoid of intrinsic nature.
Because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, like a reflection.
Thus, the very absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) remains as the innate, ultimate form of all phenomena.
That alone, being the primary goal of the person, is designated as the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), meaning the supreme purpose.
In this regard, one should not form an attachment;
otherwise, there would be no distinction between attachment to existence and attachment to emptiness,
since both are conventional by virtue of being conceptual in nature.
Furthermore, non-existence has no intrinsic nature whatsoever by virtue of its being an imagined nature;
nor is non-existence of the nature of the cessation of existence, because cessation itself lacks intrinsic nature.
And if an entity itself were to possess some intrinsic nature (svabhāva), then non-existence, being of the nature of its negation, would also exist;
however, it has already been established that an entity possesses no intrinsic nature.
Therefore, there is no such thing as non-existence (abhāva) that consists in the cessation of existence (bhāva).

Furthermore, since it has been established through the aforementioned sequence that neither existence nor non-existence exists, it is impossible for there to be a nature that is a mixture of both, or a nature consisting in the negation of both;
for conceptualization regarding existence alone is the basis for all conceptual proliferation.
When that [position] is refuted, all these [other positions] are likewise discarded by a single stroke. Therefore:
Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither.
It should be understood as an object of some degree of attachment.
As it is said in the *Ārya-prajñāpāramitā*:

Subhūti said, "In this case, venerable Śāradvatīputra, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family belonging to the bodhisattva vehicle, being unskilled in means, perceives that 'form is empty,' that is an attachment."
To perceive feeling as empty is attachment; to perceive perception as empty is attachment;
to perceive mental formations as empty is attachment.
To perceive that consciousness is empty is attachment.
Likewise, [to perceive] the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind,
up to the emptiness of all phenomena as "empty," is attachment.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
And it is said:
"The teaching of the nectar of emptiness is for the sake of abandoning all conceptual constructions;
and for whomever..."
Even in that regard, this grasping of yours has been extinguished by you.

Thus: "Neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor even of the nature of neither—liberated from these four alternatives, such is the reality known by the Mādhyamikas. [Catuḥstavanirupama 21]
Thus,

we perceive the entire universe as being free from attachment and without a basis, like space, because it is devoid of conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) due to its nature of being liberated from the four extremes— being primordially quiescent, unarisen, unceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, and so forth.
"This is considered to be the two truths.
What are they? "The conventional and the ultimate"—this is to be connected with what follows. "This Brahmin woman is real," [so it is said].
Just as it is said, "This is a sowing, this is a handful," so too conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is one truth that is non-erroneous,
and ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is another truth.
The word "and" (ca) conjoins them as being of equal strength by virtue of their mere status as truths.
In this regard, the distinction is that conventional truth is the non-false form of the world, while ultimate truth is the truth, the non-deceptive reality, of the noble ones.
Thus, the particle "ca" (and) is also appropriate for the purpose of indicating a distinction.
This is what is meant: all these internal and external entities arise bearing two natures, namely, the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*).

Among these, one [nature] has its existence manifested as an object of false perception for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), whose eyes of intellect are veiled by the cataract of ignorance and who perceive unreal objects.

The other has its essential form presented as an object of correct perception for the Noble Ones (*ārya*), the knowers of reality, whose eye of right knowledge has had the film of ignorance removed by the surgical probe of analytical investigation.
All entities possess these two natures;
and that which is the object of these two natures for foolish people who perceive falsely is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
And that which is the object of those with right vision who have realized reality is established by the experts of the treatises as ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). As it has been said:
"All phenomena possess two natures, acquired through correct and false vision."
That which is the object of those with right vision is reality; that which is the object of those with false vision is said to be conventional truth.
Thus, it is logical that the combination of the two is called "the pair. (Ma. A. 6.23) (Bcp 175) Thus, the collection of the two is appropriately termed "the dyad."
"Is considered" means it is agreed upon and accepted.
Of whom? Of the Blessed Buddhas, whose intellects have abandoned all obscurations, and of the noble disciples, solitary realizers, and bodhisattvas who follow their path.
The particle "ca" (and) is also appropriate for the purpose of restriction, signifying that there are only these two truths and no other truth exists. As it has been said:
"The teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two truths:
the conventional truth of the world and the truth of the ultimate meaning."
Thus it is said.
And in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*, it is stated:
"These two truths have been taught by the Knower of the World himself, without having heard them from others."
If both the conventional and the ultimate truths do not exist, what third truth could there be?

Thus [it is asked]: "But surely the four noble truths—characterized as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—were taught by the Blessed One in the Abhidharma; so how can there be only two truths?"
True; however, these two truths are spoken of as four by virtue of the dispositions and latent tendencies of those to be trained, because they are included within these very two.
For indeed, the truths of suffering, origin, and the path are included within conventional truth, since their intrinsic nature is conventional.
But since the truth of cessation belongs to ultimate truth, there is no contradiction whatsoever.

It might be argued: "Since conventional reality (saṃvṛti) has as its nature the superimposition of the unreal because it is manifested by ignorance, how can it be true even when it falls apart under analysis hundreds of times?
This too is true;
however, it is called conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) from the perspective of worldly consensus.
For it is the world alone that has entered into conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) here;
following after that [world], even the Blessed Ones—who do not seek the ultimate reality—speak of conventional truth in that very same way.
For this very reason, the Master [Nāgārjuna] himself stated the distinction in the Treatise as "the conventional truth of the world" (lokasaṃvṛtisatya).
In reality, however, only the ultimate truth is the single truth; therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, there is only one supreme truth, namely, Nirvana, which is of a non-deceptive nature;
all conditioned phenomena, however, are false and of a deceptive nature."
Thus [it is said].
These two truths have been explained.
Among them, for those whose minds are overwhelmed by ignorance, it is recognized as conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) by virtue of its nature as such.
However, ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is not known: what is it like, what is its nature, and what are its characteristics?
Therefore, its essential nature must be stated; thus he says: "Reality is beyond the range of the intellect.
This means it is beyond the range—that is, not an object—of the intellect, which encompasses all forms of knowledge, because it transcends the domain of all cognition.
The meaning is that it cannot be made an object of any cognition whatsoever in any manner.
Thus, how can its true nature be demonstrated?
For such is the reality of ultimate truth, whose very essence is completely free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Therefore, because it is devoid of all adjuncts (*upādhi*), how could it be seen through any conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)?
Furthermore, its nature, which transcends conceptualization, is not an object of words;
for words, being born of conceptual thought, are not able to function with respect to that which is not an object of conceptual cognition.

Therefore, since it is devoid of all conceptual constructions and verbal expressions, being non-superimposed, non-conventional, and inexpressible, how indeed could the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) be demonstrated?
Nevertheless, for the sake of favoring those who are vessels and listeners, something is stated by means of conventional illustrations, having recourse to mental construction (*parikalpa*).
Just as a person with cataracts, due to the influence of the cataracts, sees the entire expanse of space as adorned with clusters of floating hairs even while moving his face here and there;

and just as one without cataracts, observing him acting thus, wonders "What is he doing? and approaches him, and although his eyes are directed toward the hairs perceived by the other, does not perceive the form of the hairs, nor does he conceptualize the specific qualities such as existence or non-existence regarding those hairs as their substratum.

Furthermore, when that person with cataracts reveals his own intention to one free of cataracts, saying, "I see hairs here," then, in order to remove that conceptual construction, the latter tells him the truth: "There are no hairs here.
He speaks this statement solely for the purpose of negation, in accordance with what was perceived by the one with cataracts.
And even by one who demonstrates in that manner, no negation or affirmation is made regarding anything;
for that reality of the hairs which one free from cataracts perceives, that is not perceived by one with cataracts.

Thus, that which fools— whose vision of reality is impaired by the cataracts of ignorance— perceive as the intrinsic nature of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, is their conventional form.

However, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, whose latent tendencies of all ignorance have been utterly eliminated, perceive those very same aggregates and so forth through an intrinsic nature according to the logic of one with clear vision perceiving hair where none exists for one suffering from ophthalmia.
Therefore, this is their ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
as the knower of the treatises has said:
"That which is conceptualized as the form of hair and so forth due to the influence of cataracts is indeed false."
Understand that here too, whatever is seen by one of pure vision through their own self is indeed reality (tattva).

Thus, although the reality of the ultimate (*paramārtha-tattva*) is ultimately inexpressible, it has been explained in some way by means of examples, relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*). However, its nature—which is devoid of all conventional linguistic usage—cannot be expressed in reality. As it has been said:
What is the hearing of the dharma that is beyond syllables, and what is its teaching?
The meaning that is heard and taught is beyond syllables only through superimposition.
Thus,
it is by abiding in conventional truth alone that ultimate truth is taught;
and from the understanding of the teaching on ultimate truth, the realization of ultimate truth occurs.
Because that [conventional reality] is the means to that [ultimate reality].
As it is said in the treatise:
"Without relying upon conventional usage, the ultimate truth is not taught."
Without attaining the ultimate truth, nirvana is not realized.
Thus, [as stated in the *Madhyamakālaṃkāra* 24.10]: (Bcp 177) in this way, conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) serves as the means for teaching ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

And the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that which is to be attained (*upeya*), because otherwise it would be impossible to teach it. Now, one might ask: "Why does such [realization] not, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), become an object of a corresponding cognition? To this he says: "Cognition is called the conventional (*saṃvṛti*)."
For every cognition, by virtue of having an object or being without an object, is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*);
and all conceptual construction is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), because it grasps what is not a real entity. As it has been said:
This conceptual construction itself has come to have the nature of ignorance;
thus, ignorance is the conventional.
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, no cognition whatsoever is logically tenable as a grasper of an ultimately real form.
Otherwise, by virtue of being apprehended by conventional cognition, its very nature as the ultimate would be lost,
because the ultimate is, in reality, not an object of conventional knowledge. Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One in the *Āryasatyadvayāvatāra*:
For if, O Devaputra, the ultimate truth from the perspective of ultimate reality were to fall within the domain of body, speech, and mind,
it would not be reckoned as ultimate truth;
it would merely be conventional truth.
Moreover, O Devaputra, ultimate truth transcends all conventional discourse;
it is without distinction, unarisen, and unceasing.
It is free from the expressed and the expression, the knowable and the knowledge;
it transcends the state of being an object for the omniscient wisdom endowed with the excellence of all aspects—this is the detailed description of ultimate truth.

For this very reason, that [reality] is not an object for any conceptual constructions; for real entities, there cannot exist such distinctions as existence and non-existence, self-nature and other-nature, truth and falsity, permanence and annihilation, eternity and non-eternity, pleasure and pain, purity and impurity, self and non-self, emptiness and non-emptiness, the characterized and the characteristic, unity and difference, arising and cessation, and so forth, because these belong to the nature of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
This was said by the Blessed One in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*:
"The knowable is just this much—namely, the conventional and the ultimate.
And that has been well-seen, well-understood, and well-realized by the Blessed One through emptiness."
Therefore, he is called "the Omniscient One. In that regard, conventional reality was perceived by the Tathāgata through its worldly operation; as for ultimate reality, however—
It is ineffable, unknowable, and incomprehensible.
unintelligible, untaught, and unrevealed.
...up to being without action, without doing, and so forth— neither gain nor loss, neither pleasure nor pain, neither fame nor infamy, neither form nor formlessness, and so on.

Thus, that which is called ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) by the Blessed One— whose inner self is illuminated by the light of knowledge pervading the expanse of infinite entities, and who has declared it to be free from all specific conventional things and devoid of every limiting adjunct (*upādhi*)— is to be personally realized by the Noble Ones (*ārya*) through its nature as their own direct experience.
Therefore, that alone is the authority (*pramāṇa*) in this matter.
Conventional truth, however, is elucidated by relying upon worldly convention.
Thus, through the thorough knowledge of the two truths according to their correct distinction, an unerring discernment of phenomena arises.

Having thus established the two kinds of truth through the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate, he says "In that regard, in the world," etc., demonstrating that the world concerned with them is likewise twofold:
"In that regard, the world is seen to be twofold: the yogi and likewise the ordinary person. Therein, the ordinary world is sublated by the world of the yogis. (Bca 9.3)
In that regard, "established" means being concerned with those two truths—conventional and ultimate;
that is to say, it refers to the realization of those truths.
"The world" refers to people.
"Twofold" means of two kinds: one who knows the conventional and ultimate truths.
"The world" is a collective term; by this, the meaning is that there are two groups.
It is accepted as "seen" on the basis of both reasoning and scripture.
Explaining how it is twofold, he says: "the yogi and likewise the ordinary person."
Yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi), characterized by the non-apprehension of all phenomena; one who possesses this is a "yogi," and thus "the world of yogis" constitutes one category or heap.
Likewise, primordial nature (prakṛti) refers to the causes of the progression of saṃsāra, namely ignorance (avidyā) and craving (tṛṣṇā).
The first is the "born from that" (tasyā jāta), which is the *prākṛta* (natural). The second is the *prākṛtaka*, meaning the world is merely natural (*prākṛta*).
In that regard, the yogi perceives the principle of *pradhāna* without error.
And the ordinary person perceives the reality of things in a distorted manner because of delusion.

It might be argued: since both [the yogi and the ordinary person] perceive reality according to their respective [standards], which of these two could possibly be mistaken such that one is sublated by the other? Furthermore, which of these two is sublated by which? To this he says: "In that case," and so forth.
The locative case in "tatra" (in that case) indicates a collective reference.
And the locative case is used here in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*).

Among those two worlds—the world of yogis and the world of ordinary people—the world of ordinary people is selected from the collection by way of the universal property of being "ordinary" (*prākṛtakatva-jāti*);
and having been so selected, it is sublated.
Thus, the sublation is enjoined.
To the question "By what? he says: "by the world of yogis" (*yogilokena*).
A yogi himself is the world; hence, "the world of yogis."
It is established that one whose mind is perverted is afflicted by that;
how so? It should be construed as "by a particular kind of cognition.
However, the yogi is not afflicted by what is ordinary.

This is what is intended here: just as the cognition of one whose eye is impaired by cataracts and who perceives non-existent hair-nets and the like—which has its existence projected by error—is not sublated by the cognition of one with unimpaired vision, which grasps the reality of things as they truly are;
so too, the cognition of an ordinary person, whose eye of the intellect is defiled by the cataract of the impurity of ignorance and which grasps the nature of objects erroneously, [is not sublated].

The knowledge of the world of yogis—who possess the eye of untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) cleansed of stains by the water of wisdom (prajñā), and who know reality born of meditative cultivation—is sublated by that [yogic] knowledge; however, the knowledge of the yogi is not sublated by other [ordinary] knowledge.
Thus it has been said:

Just as what is perceived by those with cataracts does not invalidate the cognition of those without cataracts, so too there is no sublation of pure cognition by a mind that is itself obscured by the lack of stainless knowledge; nor does it sublate that stainless cognition.
Thus, it is said:
"Therefore, only the knowledge of the ordinary person is erroneous and is sublated."
Now, are only ordinary people sublated by yogins, or are yogins also [sublated]?
To this he says: "They are sublated," and so forth— "Even yogins are sublated by subsequent [yogins] through their superior cognition."
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that even yogis are subverted by successive other yogis, not only ordinary people. By what kind [of yogis]?
"By those that are progressively higher":
"higher and higher" means *uttara* and *uttara*; by these [qualities], having attained excellence through the acquisition of specific qualities established according to their degrees of intensity.
The meaning is "by those increasingly superior.
In comparison with them, those with inferior qualities—the lower and lower ones—are sublated; they are overwhelmed by the greatness of knowledge and so forth.

How so? "By a distinction of intellect" (dhī-viśeṣeṇa). This refers to the excellence (prakarṣa) of the intellect—that is, of knowledge (jñāna) or wisdom (prajñā)—resulting from the removal of various obscurations; it is by means of this.
Furthermore, this is an illustrative indication (upalakṣaṇa).

It is also distinguished by the excellence of meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), concentrations (*samādhi*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and so forth. For instance, when compared with the qualities such as knowledge of a Bodhisattva who has attained the first stage called *Pramuditā*, the qualities such as the power of knowledge of a Bodhisattva who has attained the second stage named *Vimalā* that follows it are superior.
In this same way, it should be understood for others who attain successively higher stages;
likewise, one should apply the principle of being superseded by successive [attainments] to those who have attained the first dhyāna and so forth.
Up to: "by means of the uncontaminated [states] of those that are contaminated."

This may be the case: even though there is a distinction in the cognitions of yogis, how can it be understood that the knowledge of ordinary people is erroneous? To this he says: "By means of an example accepted by both, for the sake of a purpose, without further investigation" (Bca 9.4).
It is accepted and intended by both [parties], namely yogis and ordinary people;
by that example, that illustration—
this example which was taught by the Blessed One in the sūtras, such as an illusion, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, a reflection, and so forth.
And that [emptiness] is established for both [the proponent and the opponent] by virtue of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*),

because it is through its similarity to that [emptiness] that the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena is demonstrated. For instance, as for those things such as form (*rūpa*) whose essential natures are apprehended by all people:
These [entities] are established as being without intrinsic nature for yogins alone through their realization of ultimate truth;
however, those which are perceived in dreams, illusions, and so forth,
are [perceived] even by ordinary people.
Therefore, since there is no disagreement between the two parties regarding that point, the status of the example as a factual property (*dṛṣṭāntadharmatā*) is not undermined.

As for those such as the Mīmāṃsakas who hold the view that an object, consisting of a different nature in terms of place and time, appears exactly as it is, they have been refuted elsewhere; thus, their position is not refuted here.
As for those of our own school who believe that consciousness alone is substantially real and appears in such a way in dreams and so forth,
they too will be refuted later on when self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is rejected at the appropriate time.
Furthermore, even that which is established by reasoning is indeed established for both parties.
Therefore, by that example, it is established that the cognition of ordinary people is erroneous because it grasps the nature of things in a distorted manner;
the same should be stated for yogis as well, according to the circumstances.
Now, if it is the case that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)— this being the reality of things—
then how is it that even Bodhisattvas who know reality engage in practices such as generosity for the sake of fulfilling the accumulations, with the intention of uplifting all sentient beings?
For they too are devoid of intrinsic nature.
To this he says: "For the sake of the effect, without analysis.
"Effect" (kārya) means that which is to be accomplished, that which is to be adopted;
it is called the fruit (phala).
"For that purpose" means for that cause.
"By way of non-investigation" means because one engages with its cause precisely through non-investigation.

Even though things are such [as being empty], there is no contradiction in the relationship between cause and effect, because the necessity of "conditionality upon this" (*idaṃpratyayatā*) exists therein.
This is what is meant: although generosity and the other perfections are devoid of intrinsic nature because they have the nature of an illusion and so forth,
nevertheless, when practiced with the threefold purity and the application of reverence and so on, even while being of such a nature, they become the cause for the realization of ultimate reality,
because they are the means to that end.
And because dependent origination is inconceivable, such a fruit is attained from such a cause alone, since that [fruit] is to be reached by means of that [cause]. As it has been said:
"Conventional truth is the means (upāya), and ultimate truth is the goal (upeya).
Thus it is said [M. A. 6.80]; and this must necessarily be so.
Otherwise, how could the stainless state arise from the stainless state through the practice of the path, or the non-conceptual state arise from the conceptual state?
For, in the ultimate sense, that [stainless or non-conceptual state] would already have that as its intrinsic nature.
This is the same elsewhere as well;
because all phenomena are, from the perspective of ultimate reality, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), a result is everywhere held to correspond to its cause.
Therefore, even from a conventional cause that is devoid of intrinsic nature, the result is precisely the realization of the absence of intrinsic nature.
Otherwise, how could one attain the unconditioned nirvana even from the conditioned path?

Thus, although giving and the other perfections are in reality devoid of intrinsic nature, they are undertaken by bodhisattvas who feel compassion for all sentient beings in order to realize ultimate reality.
Otherwise, it would be impossible to realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Therefore, engagement in acts such as giving is not precluded.
Thus, for those who seek to attain desired results and avoid undesired ones, engagement in the wholesome and cessation from the unwholesome must be explained.
This, moreover, will be made clear later.

It might be argued: "If ordinary people also perceive that very nature of things which yogis perceive as having a nature identical to that of an illusion and so forth, then where is there any disagreement? To this, he says "by the world," and so on:
Worldly beings perceive and even conceptualize phenomena as being real;
however, there is no dispute between yogis and worldly people regarding the fact that these are like an illusion.
"By the world" means by ordinary people. "Entities" (bhāva) are so called because they come into being—that is, they acquire their own nature—by depending upon causes and conditions;
however, they do not possess an inherent, ultimate nature of their own.

Thus, by the word "entity" (bhāva), the expression of the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā) is understood. Things are not perceived as having an existent nature, nor are they even conceptualized as such in reality;
rather, they are determined from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha) precisely according to their nature as it is conventionally perceived.
They are "attached" insofar as they conceive that this nature of things, which is the object of our cognition,
is indeed real.
But it is not like an illusion; nor, moreover, is it as when illusions are seen by a yogi as being empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-śūnya) like an illusion,
such that they are perceived as such from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha).
Thus, "dispute" (*vivāda*) here refers to the disagreement (*vipratipatti*) between the yogi and the world—that is, between the world and the yogi.

This is because the world does not apprehend the true nature of reality as it has been apprehended by the yogi; or alternatively, it is the dispute of the yogi with the world, since the world denies the correspondence to reality (*yathārthatā*) of what has been apprehended by the yogi.
This is the intended meaning: all entities possess a twofold nature, namely the conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*).
Among these, that which is conventional is perceived by the world, whereas that which is ultimate is said to be perceived by the yogins.

Just as a person whose eyes are deluded by the power of mantras and the like perceives only the form of an elephant or other object created by a magician, while the magician himself knows its own true nature, such as its lack of intrinsic reality; in the same way, the understanding of both the yogi and the world-ling should be applied accordingly.

Furthermore, one might think: "How can this nature of things—which is common to all people, capable of causal efficiency, and cognized through the means of direct perception—be denied? Anticipating this objection from the opponent, he says: "Even direct perception," and so forth:
"Even direct perception, such as form and the rest, is not established by way of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
Furthermore, that which is designated as "direct perception," such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth—
whereby the word "and so forth" includes sound and the like, as well as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest—
that too exists only through conventional renown, established usage, and worldly parlance, and not by way of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The connection is that form and so forth are not perceived as real by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
because perception and the other [means of knowledge] are merely conventional valid cognitions (*sāṃvyavahārika-pramāṇa*),
form and so forth, as apprehended by them, are purely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).

Furthermore, a real nature is not something to be apprehended by worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for that would entail the absurd consequence that all people are knowers of reality. As it has been said:
"If that which is perceived by the sense faculties were to exist as reality," [it would follow that everyone perceives reality].
When fools have become knowers of reality, what then is the use of the knowledge of reality?
Thus, even perception has not been apprehended by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(Bcp 181) If the reality of form and so forth, though perceptible, has not been apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can there be its establishment?

If it is argued that [the self] is established by common consensus, how can it be false? To this he says: "Just as the notion of purity and so forth regarding what is impure and so forth, that [notion of self] is false. (Bca 9.6)

And just as, in the ultimate sense, a perception of purity arises toward impure things such as a woman’s corpse for those whose minds are perverted by attachment to them— the word "etc. includes the perception of permanence and so forth regarding what is impermanent and so on— and that [perception] is false because it apprehends something as being what it is not.
The meaning is that it grasps erroneously;
likewise, this applies to form and so forth as well, and thus there is no distinction.
If that [existence] is not established through the means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception, then it will be established through scripture;
for indeed, in the sūtras, the Blessed One has taught that entities have the nature of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.
And [it is so] by virtue of having momentariness and other such natures.
Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One:
"O Brahmin, 'everything, everything' refers only to the five aggregates."
The twelve sense bases and the eighteen elements; thus it is said. Furthermore—
All conditioned phenomena are momentary; how can there be action for things that are unstable?
That which is their very arising is itself the action, and it is also called the agent.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, it is not appropriate to establish the nature of things such as illusions as being momentary or non-momentary, because for those that are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), no intrinsic nature whatsoever exists.
To the question, "In that case, how is it that these are not ultimately real? he says: "For the purpose of introducing [beings] to the world," and so forth.
And entities were taught by the Protector for the sake of introducing the world [to the Dharma];
in reality they are not momentary, yet if one says this, it contradicts conventional truth.

The word "ca" (and) is used here in the sense of a reason (*hetu*): because, for the sake of leading those beings who are attached to the existence of things in the world, who are to be disciplined by the teaching of the aggregates and so forth, and who are not yet fit for the direct teaching of emptiness, one introduces them to emptiness through a gentle approach;
for [according to that approach], things characterized as the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth exist.
In reality, although all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature,

they were taught and revealed by the Buddha, the Blessed One— the Protector who rescues sentient beings from the sufferings of hell and other realms, who leads them to the happiness of higher rebirth and the ultimate good, and who knows the dispositions and intentions of sentient beings— and not [taught] from the perspective of ultimate truth.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtras. As it has been said: "Just as the Victors spoke of 'mine' and 'I' for the sake of a particular purpose, so too did they speak of the aggregates, bases, and elements for the sake of a particular purpose."

Thus [it is said in the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*]: "If they are not taught from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), how then are they momentary? To this he says: "In reality, these are not momentary."

In reality, from the perspective of the ultimate truth, these entities do not even exist as momentary, because they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*). The teaching on momentariness and so forth is for the sake of those to be trained, in order to reveal their true nature.
If they are not momentary in reality, how [is it so]? (Bcp 182)

Then, bearing in mind that they are indeed stated in the teaching, he says: "If [it is said] 'conventionally' (saṃvṛtyā)..."— anticipating the objection that if it is asserted that things are momentary conventionally,
he refutes this by stating that it would then be contradictory.
The claim that "they are momentary conventionally, but not ultimately" is contradictory and does not hold together;
because they are perceived as non-momentary, there is a contradiction with perception,
since worldly people perceive them as non-momentary— meaning, in short, that momentariness is not their conventional nature.

The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin) refutes this: "There is no fault from the perspective of the world by way of the conventional reality of yogis, for they are seers of reality; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the world in the case of the perception of a woman as impure. (Bca 9.8)
This is not a fault characterized by contradiction with common experience.
Why? Because for yogins who have attained the meditative concentration on the selflessness of persons, momentariness is perceived through their conventional discourse.
This is the intended meaning: even if momentariness is not perceived by those of limited vision, it nevertheless remains within the sphere of the activity of yogins;
and the activity of yogins, too, does not abandon its conventional nature.
Because of the statement, "Intellect (buddhi) is said to be the conventional (saṃvṛti)," that which is sublated by [ordinary] cognition is not necessarily sublated,
since such a cognition lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (apramāṇa).

But why is it that even such conventional [properties] as momentariness and so forth are perceived only by yogins and not by those of limited vision? To this he says: "From the world, they are seers of reality.
This means that compared to the world—those of limited vision—those yogins are seers of reality, seers of what transcends the senses;
this is a statement of the reason.
Since they are seers of reality,
they therefore realize such things as momentariness and selflessness, even though these are not recognized by the world;
for this very reason, their [realization] is not sublated by worldly consensus.
He states that this must necessarily be accepted, beginning with "Otherwise," etc.:
otherwise, if this were not admitted,
then there would be contradiction with common worldly experience even regarding what you yourself have accepted.
Where? In the contemplation of an impure woman.

At the time of meditating on impurity, when one contemplates—that is, analyzes—the woman who is an object of desire as being "impure," there would be contradiction with the world; that is, there would be opposition to what is commonly recognized by the world.
Because the world adheres to the female body as having a pure nature, the vision of the yogins does not contradict what is commonly recognized by the world. In this regard, it is said:
"Just as [forms] are perceived by those with cataracts..."
This should be applied as a reason for accumulation by means of such passages.
Thus, even according to scripture, there is no establishment of entities from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is certain that all phenomena have the nature of illusions, dreams, and so forth.
It might be argued: if the nature of being like an illusion pervades all things, then even a Buddha would be like an illusion and like a dream.
And this has been stated in the *Bhagavatī*:
When this had been said, Subhūti spoke thus to those sons of the gods: "Sons of the gods, these sentient beings are like an illusion;
sons of the gods, these sentient beings are like a dream. For indeed, illusion and sentient beings are non-dual; they are not divided into two."
O sons of the gods, all phenomena are like an illusion, like a dream;
even a stream-enterer is like an illusion, like a dream, and even the fruit of stream-entry is like an illusion, like a dream.
It is like an illusion, like a dream;
likewise, the once-returner and the fruit of once-returning,
as well as the non-returner and the fruit of non-returning.
Even an Arhat and even Arhatship are like an illusion, like a dream;
even a Pratyekabuddha is like an illusion, like a dream;
even Pratyekabuddhahood is like an illusion, like a dream.
Even the perfectly awakened one is like an illusion, like a dream;
even the state of perfect awakening is like an illusion, like a dream;
even nirvana is like an illusion, like a dream.
If there were even some dharma more distinguished than nirvāṇa, I would say that too is like an illusion and like a dream.
Anticipating the opponent's objection as to how merit and demerit can arise from honor or injury in that case, he says "like an illusion," and so forth:
"How can there be merit from a Victor who is like an illusion, even if he exists?
[The opponent asks: "If the Blessed One also has the nature of being like an illusion..."

Then, how—how indeed—do you conceive of the merit and well-performed deed arising from worship, honor, and prostrating at the feet of the Blessed Victor, who is like an illusion and devoid of intrinsic nature?
This is merely an illustration;
it should be understood that the same applies to the demerit resulting from harming him.
For it is not logical that merit or demerit should arise from the honoring or harming of a person created by a magician; such is the opponent's intention.
To this, the same answer previously stated applies. Furthermore, he questions the opponent here: "Even if [the person] exists, how could it be so?"
"Even though [the Blessed One] exists"—that is, even though he possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*)—how indeed could there be merit?
