The word "how" (*katham*) should be applied to both instances.
This is the intended meaning: just as for someone who is ultimately real, merit that is ultimately real arises from the Victor (*jina*).

Likewise, for another [proponent], it is "like an illusion" from that which is "like an illusion"; thus there is no distinction between us two, because the mere fact of being conditioned by this (idaṃpratyayatāmātra) is common to both.
Therefore, whatever answer you have, [that is our answer as well].
That very point applies to us as well;
it does not differ in the slightest.
Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that there is no such thing as a truly existent nature of things established by reasoning.
Granted that merit may indeed arise from a Victor who is like an illusion; but how is this [objection] resolved? To this he says:
"If a being is like an illusion, why is it born again after dying? (Bca 9.9).
Alternatively, it is introduced in another way: if even the Jina is like an illusion, what then can be said of the beings within saṃsāra?
We say that they, too, are likewise so.
"Those sons of gods, those sentient beings, are like an illusion," because of this statement.
This being so, a great fault would follow; thus he says, "If," and so forth.
If a sentient being, a living creature, is like an illusion—that is, possessing properties identical to the nature of an illusion—then...
In that case, what more is born when one has died?
The word "what" (kiṃ) is used either as an interrogative or to express incapacity;
[the question is]: "What more is born? or "What arises?"
"Dead" means having passed away from the homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāgatā*). An explanation must be given here as to why this [position] is not tenable.
For an illusory person, once destroyed, does not arise again;
therefore, it must be accepted that entities are ultimately real.
To show that this [illusion] is not to be understood as real, he says "as long as" and so forth:
"As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does illusion persist.
For as long as there is a collection—that is, an assembly—of conditions, namely causes such as mantras, medicinal herbs, and the like, [so long does illusion continue].
As long as the causes are complete,
even an illusion persists; it does not cease before that time.
Nor does it proceed beyond that.
Thus, as long as the causal complex consisting of ignorance, karma, and craving exists, so long does the illusion of the continuum of sentient beings continue.
Because its occurrence depends upon this-conditionality (*idaṃpratyayatā*).
If, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), no sentient being exists, how is it that the continuum of sentient beings proceeds as long as saṃsāra lasts?
"But does it not cease before long like an illusion?
To this it has been said: "As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does it proceed; but for that which does not have such [conditions], [it does not proceed]."
"He does not conform [to that view].
Furthermore,
he states "long continuity" and so forth, because long-term persistence is not the basis for establishing correctness.
How can a sentient being exist in reality merely by virtue of a long continuum?

"Long" refers to a continuum (*saṃtāna*) or flow that has persisted for a long time; "by that alone" means by that [continuum] exclusively. He asks "how?"—in what manner does a sentient being exist or subsist?
In truth and from the perspective of ultimate reality;
however, there is this distinction: for that which possesses specific causes and conditions for its persistence over a long period, it continues for a long time.
But for one who does not have it in that way, he does not conform;
yet, by that much alone, there is no state of being either correct or false.
Therefore, even though its nature is like an illusion, it is not the case that rebirth is impossible.
If that is the case, then just as there is no taking of life in the killing of an illusory person, so too there would be none in the killing of another person,
because their intrinsic nature is not different.
Regarding this, he says "māyāpuruṣa" and so forth:
"In the killing of an illusory person and the like, there is no sin because of the absence of mind.
This refers to the killing, such as the slaying, of an illusory person.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it refers to] one who takes what is not given and so forth.

Even though the mind and consciousness are equally devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), because they do not exist—that is, because they are non-existent—within the continuum of an illusory person (*māyāpuruṣa*), no evil or unwholesome [act], such as the taking of life, arises.
"Evil" (*pāpaka*) is simply "evil" (*pāpa*).
Because the suffix *kan* is prescribed in the sense of the base word itself;
even in that case, for one who delivers a blow with the intention of killing, there is indeed unwholesome karma (*aśubha*),
but it is not the taking of life (*prāṇātipāta*).
If it is asked, "How can there be the taking of life apart from an illusory person? he says: "But when the mind is accompanied by illusion, there arises the production of sin and merit. (Bca 9.11)
Mind itself is illusion; "mind-illusion" means being endowed with or joined to that [illusion].
The meaning is: bound by a mind whose intrinsic nature is illusion.
The word "tu" (but) serves to distinguish this from what preceded.
"Puṇyapāpe" means merit and demerit; the "samudbhavaḥ" of these two refers to their origin or production.
Regarding "benefit and harm": a specific effect arises from a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

Just as there is a difference in nature between two wicks produced respectively from cow dung and other materials—despite their similarity in form due to the difference in their causes—so too here, the aforementioned fault does not follow.
Regarding what was stated— that it is "mind-only"— another [opponent],
seeking to refute that, says "of mantras and so forth," etc.:
"Because mantras and so forth lack efficacy, there is no arising of a mind consisting of illusion."

Because mantras and so forth—where "and so forth" includes medicines and the like—are incapable of and do not function toward the arising of a mind, a mind that is an illusion does not arise; that is, a mind having the nature of an illusion does not come into being.
Just as, through the power of mantras and the like employed by a magician—which serve as the basis for deluding others—there is the manifestation of forms such as elephants.
"It is not so for the mind"—this is the opponent's position. Refuting this, he says: "That illusion, too, is of various kinds, arising from various conditions," and so forth.
The word "api" has the sense of restriction and its position in the sequence is shifted;
that illusion is indeed manifold, indeed of various kinds.

Therefore, it is described as "having its origination from various conditions," meaning that its arising or production (*saṃbhava*) occurs from various conditions, that is, from manifold types of causes.

This is the intended meaning: even if there is a similarity of words in the sense that both [illusion and the world] are called "illusion" (*māyā*), nevertheless, there is no identity even regarding their causes.
Even though an effect has the nature of illusion, it possesses diverse natures;
for it is not the case that because a certain cause is observed in one effect, it is appropriate to postulate that very same cause everywhere simply due to the commonality of the term "effect.
Rather, the capacity of a particular cause belongs only to a specific instance.
Even though the words are identical, there is a difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Not for one [cause] does there exist the capacity for everything in any circumstance" (Bca 9.12).

It is not possible for a single condition, cause, or reason whose capacity has been observed in one instance to possess or have the capacity for all capacities—that is, the capacity for every effect—simply because it was seen or accepted in some particular case; that is, at some time, place, or occasion. Furthermore, a certain illusion (*māyā*) possesses a nature acquired through the power of mantras and the like.
Furthermore, some [efficacy] proceeds from the power of ignorance and so forth, which has functioned with majesty throughout beginningless saṃsāra;
therefore, the potency of mantras and the like does not exist in all cases.
All this arises by depending upon a conventional reality that is constructed by conceptualization and follows worldly convention, but not from the perspective of ultimate truth.
Because in the state of ultimate reality there is an absence of conceptual constructions such as birth and death, arising and cessation, cause and effect, existence and non-existence, and so forth,
since all phenomena are by nature quiescent.
Unable to accept this, the opponent, attempting to prove the opposite, says: "If one who is *nirvṛta* were to transmigrate conventionally,
[it would follow that] he is *nirvṛta* because, being empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), he is devoid of arising and ceasing."

In the ultimate sense, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is primordially quiescent because it is by nature nirvana. If, however, one were to transmigrate through the conventional— by way of conventional truth and conceptual construction—
one would be subject to birth, aging, and death.
Thinking that this would result in a great contradiction, he says: "Even a Buddha would thus wander in saṃsāra," and so forth:
"Even a Buddha would thus wander in saṃsāra; what then is the use of the practice for enlightenment? (Bca 9.13)
If this were accepted, then even a Buddha—though extinguished through the abandonment of all obscurations—would still transmigrate and be subject to birth and so forth.
Since this is the case, for that reason, what is the use of the conduct of awakening (*bodhicaryā*)?

What is the point of that conduct for the sake of awakening—that is, for Buddhahood—which is characterized by hundreds of thousands of various hardships such as the giving away of hands, feet, and head?
There is no purpose [for it],
because it would be fruitless according to the sequence already stated;
for that [wisdom] is relied upon for the cessation of all worldly phenomena and for the attainment of Buddhahood, which rests upon the accumulation of all qualities.
Nevertheless, if there is no cessation of worldly phenomena (saṃsāradharma), the sense is: what has been accomplished by relying upon that [attainment]?
That has already been answered by the passage beginning with "as long as the collection of conditions," yet he speaks again, clarifying it further, starting with "of the conditions":
"If the conditions were not cut off, even illusion would certainly not be cut off."
But due to the severance of conditions, it cannot arise even conventionally.
Of conditions and causes; "in non-interruption" means in non-destruction;
"hi" (for) because.

The word "also" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction, indicating that it is not only saṃsāra [that does not cease]; [illusory appearance] (*māyā*) likewise is neither cut off nor does it cease.
However, [it ceases] when its conditions (*pratyaya*), that is, its causes, [are removed].
Due to the severance [of the causal chain],
there is no occurrence— that is, no transmigration— even by way of conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), that is, even through conceptual worldly discourse. Furthermore,

the total cessation of the conditions (*pratyaya*) is to be understood as occurring through the sequence of the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, based on the cultivation of reality (*tattva*).
As it is said in the Noble Śālistamba Sūtra:

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya spoke thus to the Venerable Śāriputra: "O monks, that which was spoken by the Blessed One, the Lord of Dharma, the Omniscient One—'He who sees dependent origination sees the Dharma.'"
Whoever sees the Dharma sees the Buddha.
In this regard, what is called "dependent origination"?
That is to say: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise;
with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;
with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises.
Conditioned by name-and-form are the six sense bases;
conditioned by the six sense bases is contact;
conditioned by contact is feeling.
With feeling as condition, craving arises; with craving as condition, clinging arises; with clinging as condition, existence arises.
With existence as condition, birth arises;
with birth as condition, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, dejection, and despair arise.
Thus occurs the origination of this entire great mass of suffering.
Therein, with the cessation of ignorance, the formative forces cease;
[and so on]... in this way, there is the cessation of this entire great mass of suffering.
This is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). [The passage continues:

He who, constantly and continuously, regards this dependent origination as being without a living soul (*nirjīva*), as it truly is, unerring, unborn, unbecome, unconditioned, non-obstructive, without objective support (*anālambana*), auspicious, fearless, indestructible, and having the nature of non-cessation—[he is one who sees correctly].
He perceives the Dharma;
and he who thus constantly and continuously perceives the Dharma as having a nature that is never-quiescent perceives the Buddha as the unsurpassed body of Dharma.
[The] abbreviated passage: In that regard, what is ignorance?
It is the notion of unity, the notion of a whole, the notion of permanence, the notion of stability, and the notion of eternity regarding these very six elements.

The perception of pleasure, the perception of a self, the perception of a sentient being, the perception of a living soul, the perception of a creature, the perception of a human, the perception of a person, and the perception of "I" and "mine"—
such various forms of ignorance as these.
This is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, when ignorance exists, attachment, aversion, and delusion arise with respect to sense objects.
Among these, those which are attachment, aversion, and delusion toward sense objects—
These are called the formative forces (saṃskāra) conditioned by ignorance.
Consciousness (vijñāna) is the discernment of objects.
And matter derived from the four great elements is the unified mass of matter.
The four formless appropriated aggregates that arise simultaneously with consciousness are "name"; that is name-and-form.
The sense faculties based upon name-and-form are the six sense bases.
The coming together of the three factors is contact;
the experience of contact is feeling;
the attachment to feeling is craving.
The expansion of craving is grasping (*upādāna*).
The karma born from grasping that produces renewed existence is becoming (*bhava*).
The manifestation of the aggregates caused by becoming is birth (*jāti*).
The maturation of the aggregates that have been produced by birth is aging;
the destruction of the aggregates is death.
The internal burning of one who is dying, being deluded, and possessed of attachment is sorrow.
Lamentation is wailing arising from sorrow.
Suffering is the experience of malice associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.
Mental distress is mental suffering associated with the mental application of pain.
And whatever other secondary afflictions (upakleśa) there are of this kind, these are called "distresses" (upāyāsa).
In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is so called in the sense of great darkness; volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) in the sense of formative activity;
and consciousness (*vijñāna*) in the sense of discernment.
Name-and-form is so called in the sense of mentalizing;
the six sense bases in the sense of being doors of arrival;
contact in the sense of touching.
Feeling (*vedanā*) is so called in the sense of experiencing;
craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the sense of thirsting;
and grasping (*upādāna*) in the sense of seizing.
"Becoming" (*bhava*) is so called in the sense of generating renewed existence;
"birth" (*jāti*) is so called in the sense of the manifestation of the aggregates;
"aging" (*jarā*) is so called in the sense of the maturation of the aggregates.
Death is so called in the sense of destruction;
sorrow in the sense of grieving;
lamentation in the sense of verbal wailing.
Suffering is in the sense of physical oppression;
mental distress is in the sense of mental oppression;
and despair is in the sense of secondary affliction.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
When the conditions thus demonstrated are not severed, saṃsāra proceeds in its entirety,
because the twelve-linked dependent origination itself is saṃsāra. As the venerable Master said:
Increasing gradually according to its projection, the continuum proceeds again to the next world through afflictions and karma; thus, the wheel of existence is beginningless.
"That dependent origination consists of twelve factors and three sections.
(Abhidharmakośa 3.19–20) Furthermore, if conditions were to be annihilated, there would be no transmigration whatsoever.
Because of the deficiency of causes;
and therefore, the consequence that "even a Buddha would thus wander in saṃsāra" does not follow.

Having thus set aside the objections of the Sautrāntikas and others, he speaks the verse beginning with "When even error does not exist," etc., in order to refute the misconceptions of the Yogācāras by presenting a refutation according to their own view:
"When even error does not exist, by whom is the illusion perceived? (Bca 9.15)

When the Madhyamikas have established that the entire world is empty of intrinsic nature because its essence is illusory, and when even your own cognition— which apprehends the conventional nature of illusion— does not exist externally,
then by what means is illusion perceived?
By what means is it cognized, in the absence of a cognition of a real entity that apprehends it?
The meaning is: by nothing at all.
However, for one for whom only one's own mind is ultimately real and appears in such a way due to the delusion of external form—
The sense is that this fault does not belong to him.

To refute this, he says: "When even illusion itself does not exist for you," and so forth. When even illusion itself does not exist for you, the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*), by way of its appearing as a perceived object in the form of an elephant and so on, then what is perceived?
For those who accept that the world is mind-only because of the absence of external objects,
what is it then that is perceived, and what is it that appears here?

The meaning is that, because external objects do not exist, an appearance characterized by spatial and temporal distinctions is not tenable. Anticipating the opponent's objection here, he says: "Even though that form belongs to the mind alone, in reality there is something else [external]. (Bca 9.16)
It has been stated here that it is the mind itself, appearing erroneously in an external form, that manifests in the shape of an elephant and so forth;
this indeed has been stated.
However, although that manifestation—the aspect appearing as an object of apprehension through a spatial and other such divisions—is nothing but the mind, the cognition itself, [it appears as such].
"Another" means something else; [it] exists, i.e., is found, in reality, i.e., as a substantial entity, distinct from the internal aspect of the apprehending mind.
Although this was stated as a concession with the words "even if," he says that even so, this does not cohere, beginning with: "When the mind itself is illusion, then what is seen by what?"
Mind alone, consciousness alone, is accepted as the experiencer;
for when illusion is not other [than that],
there is indeed no such thing as "illusion" apart from the experiencing mind.
Since it is admitted that it appears as such by virtue of having that as its nature, then at that time,
what is seen by what, and what is cognized by what?
For there is only seeing itself, and no object of sight;
without an object of sight, even seeing would not exist,
because it is dependent upon the object of sight.
Therefore, nothing would be seen by anyone; the implication is that total blindness would result for the entire world.
Now, this might indeed be the case if there were no self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of cognition.
"Since one perceives one's own nature through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), one would likewise perceive the appearance of illusion (*māyā*) and so forth as non-different from it;
and this being the case, there is no fault whatsoever.
Anticipating this intention of the Vijñānavādins, he says:
And it has been said by the Lord of the World: "The mind does not see the mind.

When it has been established through reasoning that the entire world is empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), then what, in reality, is the intrinsic nature of what? And by whom could there be a perception of what?
And it was said by the Blessed One: "All phenomena are empty; the mind has emptiness as its characteristic."
"All phenomena are secluded;
the mind has the characteristic of seclusion.
Furthermore, it was said and declared by the Lord of the World, the Buddha, the Blessed One—the protector and refuge of all beings in the world.
What has been said? "The mind does not see the mind," meaning the mind does not know itself;
for even though it possesses substantial reality, there is a contradiction in its own self acting upon itself. How is this so?
Just as the edge of a sword does not cut itself, so it is with the mind.

Just as even an extremely sharp sword-edge, the blade of a scimitar, does not cut or cleave itself— its own body— because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself, so it is with the mind.
It should be understood that even the mind, like the edge of a sword, does not perceive itself;
for it is not logical that a single cognition should possess a threefold nature consisting of the object of knowledge (*vedya*), the knower (*vedaka*), and the act of knowing (*vedana*).
This is because it is impossible for a single, partless entity to possess a triple nature.
Regarding this, it is said in the noble *Ratnacūḍa-sūtra*:
"Searching for the mind, he does not perceive the mind internally;
he does not perceive the mind externally."
One does not perceive the mind in the aggregates;
one does not perceive the mind in the elements;
one does not perceive the mind in the sense bases.
Not perceiving the mind, he investigates the stream of the mind, asking: "From where does the arising of the mind occur?
When there is an object, the mind arises.
Is that mind one thing and the object another?
Now, is that which is the object of cognition (ālambana) itself the mind (citta)? If, first of all, the object were one thing and the mind another, then there would be a duality of minds.
Now, if the object of perception is indeed the mind itself,
how can the mind see the mind?
For the mind does not perceive the mind.
For example, just as that very edge of a sword cannot be cut by that same edge of the sword,
and just as that very tip of a finger cannot be touched by that same tip of the finger, even so, that very mind cannot be seen by that same mind; such is the detailed explanation.

In this regard, the proponent of *cittamātra* (mind-only), wishing to resolve the contradiction of an action directed toward itself and to establish his own position, presents an example, saying "the nature of itself," and so forth:
"Just as a lamp illuminates its own nature.
That is to say, just as a lamp—a light—illuminates, i.e., makes manifest, its own nature, its own form.
For just as a lamp is indeed employed for the purpose of perceiving objects such as a jar enveloped in darkness, another lamp is not required for the illumination of that first lamp;
rather, while illuminating the jar and so forth, it illuminates itself as well.
The same should be understood regarding self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) in the present case as well;
and since no contradiction has been observed anywhere, this [principle] should be applied everywhere.
If you argue that, therefore, there is no contradiction at all— just as in the case of a lamp—
if you think this way, then you should not speak thus.
To the question "Why?", he says "not at all," and so forth:
"A lamp is not illuminated at all, because it is not enveloped by darkness. (Bca 9.18)
A lamp is not illuminated like a jar or similar object, nor is it made to shine forth, because it is not enveloped by darkness— that is, it is not shrouded in obscurity.
Illumination is the removal of an existing covering.
Therefore, the manifestation of jars and the like is logical, because they already exist prior [to their manifestation];
but it is not so for the lamp.
Because it did not exist previously,
and it is not logical for that which does not exist to be illuminated— since it is non-existent—
the lamp is not illuminated at all.
Thus, because of this dissimilarity, the probandum is not established by the example of the lamp.

It might be argued: by the passage beginning with "its own nature" (*ātmabhāvam*), it is not being asserted that the lamp illuminates the self as something enveloped in darkness like a jar; rather, what is being asserted is merely its independence with respect to its own nature.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "for not," and so forth.
For a blue crystal does not depend on anything else for its blueness;
likewise, some things are seen to be dependent on others, while others are independent.
The word *hi* means "because.

Just as a crystal stone, being itself not blue, requires another external condition (*upādhi*)— such as proximity to a blue leaf— as the cause for the arising of the quality of blueness when it appears blue.
Likewise, that very object which is blue does not depend on any other condition (upādhi) for its blueness;
similarly, in that same manner, some things such as a jar are seen to be manifest through dependence on another, such as a lamp.
Furthermore, some things, such as a lamp and the like, are seen and perceived to be self-luminous without depending on anything else;
this much alone is intended [to be said].

When the proponent of consciousness (vijñānavādin) has thus presented this distinction, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), refuting the example of "blue" itself as being independent of anything else with respect to its blueness, says:
"If it were not blue when it is not blue, then that would not be blue; for how is it observed to be the cause of blueness? Indeed, who could make the blue itself blue by means of itself? (Bca 9.20)
This too is not a suitable example, because even blue is not independent with respect to its blueness, like a crystal,
since it depends upon its own causes and conditions for that state.
When, then, would this be independent? If that [entity] were produced as non-blue from its own causes,
it would subsequently— being independent of anything else— make itself blue by its own power.
And this is not the case; for when there is "non-blue-ness," that is, the absence of the quality of blue,
the word "not" performs a negation.
The word "that" refers to the object intended as blue.
That which is blue—that is, possessing the quality of blueness—cannot, by itself, produce its own self-nature;
it is not capable of doing so.
As before, because of the contradiction in [the object] acting upon itself;
therefore, even blue does not possess independence with respect to its blueness, just like a crystal.
For instance, even a crystal stone, though its form is established in reality, does not experience the coloring of blue when in proximity to an adjunct (*upādhi*).

Rather, the established doctrine is this: due to the cessation of its own prior natural state through the operation of the specific limiting condition (*upādhi*) of "blue," an entirely different crystal stone, colored by the quality of blue, arises from the characteristic of taking up all its constituent parts.
Therefore, it is common to both that their respective qualities are dependent upon causes and conditions.
Thus, there is no difference whatsoever even when the probandum (sādhya) is the subject under discussion (prakṛta).

Is this not indeed something dear that has been performed by my beloved? For, since cognition arises from its own causes and conditions as an essence turned away from the nature of insentience, its very production—being independent of any other illuminator—is its self-illumination;
this is what is called "self-awareness" (svasaṃvedana).
And this very point has been established by you as well through the apprehension of the nature of the blue object.
It is for this much alone that even a lamp has been cited as an illustration;
we do not, however, maintain that cognition illuminates itself through a distinction between action, agent,
and activity, because it is impossible for a single existing entity to possess the threefold nature of object and so forth.

Therefore, even if there were a refutation based on distinctions such as action and so forth, nothing of ours would be refuted, because the self-luminosity produced by its own causes remains unimpaired.
Thus, the previously stated fault does not apply to self-cognition. As it has been said:
Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms;
this very quality of being non-insentient is its self-cognition.
However, there is no self-cognition of this [consciousness] through a distinction between action and agent,
because it is a single entity without parts, and thus a threefold nature is logically impossible for it.
Thus it is said: [Tattvasaṃgraha 2000–1].

To this it is replied: The refutation was stated after having understood the meaning of the word as established in conventional usage through the distinction between action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka), because the word "self-cognition" (svasaṃvedana) expresses that very meaning.
If, however, even a word-meaning well-known in the world is abandoned out of fear of logical faults, then you will incur contradiction from the world itself.
Even in this way, self-cognition is not established in an ultimate sense.
For it has been stated that, like a reflection produced by causes and conditions, [cognition] is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
And thus, self-cognition of knowledge is all the more impossible,
because in reality there is an absence of its own intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, in the absence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) is not tenable for a sky-lotus.
Nor, from the perspective of the Madhyamaka proponent, is a non-insentient nature established for anything ultimately,
such that there could be a non-insentient self-cognition excluded from the insentient.
Therefore, it is appropriate to say this only in response to those who maintain that things possess intrinsic reality (*vastuvādin*).
Consequently, due to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not established in any way whatsoever.
We shall, however, demonstrate this in detail later in the section on the presentation of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) [9.24].
Now, having granted for the sake of argument that a lamp is self-illuminating, [the author], demonstrating that the self-cognition of cognition is illogical, says "The lamp," and so forth:
"The lamp shines"—this is stated by means of a cognition after having known it.
But by what is it known and stated that "cognition shines"? (Bca 9.22)
Or, let it be granted that a lamp possesses the nature of illumination;
nevertheless, it is not a suitable example for establishing the cognition of consciousness—this is the collective meaning.
When it is said that "the lamp illuminates," it appears by itself, independent of any other illumination.
Having understood this through dependent cognition (*pratītyajñāna*), it is spoken of and established by means of the intellect (*buddhi*),
because a lamp is an object of cognition;
the intellect is cognition (*jñāna*).
Regarding the statement "it shines forth," he asks further by what cognition this is known and then expressed; thus,
he demonstrates the impossibility [of such a claim] by showing that there is no basis whatsoever for the apprehension of it by the intellect.
First of all, its apprehension cannot occur through the preceding cognition, because that [subsequent object] has not yet arisen at that time and is therefore non-existent.
Nor can it occur through a cognition arising at a later time, because by that point, due to momentariness, the object to be grasped has already passed away.
And because that [consciousness] is not assisted by what exists at the same time as it;
nor can there be the status of being an object for that which does not provide assistance, according to the statement: "That which is not a cause is not an object."
Nor does it [arise] by itself,
because there is disagreement regarding that very point;
thus, we do not know how its cognition occurs.

Thus, since cognition is in every way unperceived, its self-awareness is utterly untenable; so he says, beginning with "Whether luminous or non-luminous": "When [cognition] is not perceived by anyone, whether it be luminous or non-luminous, it is as futile as describing the playful dance of the daughter of a barren woman. (Bca 9.23)
Either it is luminous, having luminosity as its nature, like a lamp;
or it is non-luminous, having non-luminosity as its nature, like a jar and so forth.
The two uses of the word "vā" (or) indicate a mutual conjunction.
When the intellect (buddhi) is not perceived by anyone, nor apprehended by anyone— whether as an agent of apprehension or in its own form—
the word "yadā" (when) draws in the word "tadā" (then).
Then, like the playful grace, the charm, and the elegance of a daughter— the offspring— of a barren woman who by nature cannot bear children,
even though it is being told or described, it is in vain.
This is the understanding:
"Futile" means fruitless; the intention is that since the daughter of a barren woman is understood to be non-existent, her play is all the more unperceived.
Alternatively,
because its nature is unarisen and unceasing, cognition is like the daughter of a barren woman;
because that nature is not perceived, self-awareness is like her play.

Since that [object] is not perceived, its self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*)—even if it were asserted that "because that is not perceived, this too is not perceived"—is in vain as a mere word devoid of reasoning;
it is useless because it is not to be accepted.

It might be argued that this is merely a statement devoid of reasoning. To show that there is indeed reasoning here, he says: "If self-cognition does not exist, how is cognition remembered? and so forth. If self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) does not exist, how can cognition be recollected?
If self-awareness does not exist for consciousness,
then how is consciousness remembered?
Due to the absence of self-awareness in consciousness, there would be no recollection at a later time.
For it is not logical that there be a recollection of what has not been experienced, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Therefore, since recollection— the fruit of experience— is observed at a later time, it is inferred that there is a self-awareness (saṃvedana) of cognition.
This proof is not more convincing;
for if memory were ascertained to be the effect of self-awareness,
then memory would be the cause of self-awareness, just as smoke is the effect of fire.
Furthermore, as long as self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) has not been established through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
there can be no apprehension of memory as its effect;
for the apprehension of the causal relation is in every respect inseparable from the apprehension of both [the cause and the effect].
Nor can it be argued that, as in the case of the visual faculty (*cakṣus*) and so forth, memory— though not itself perceived— will be established as its effect;
for the effect of the eye is inferred by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), since in the absence of the eye, there is no cognition of blue and other such objects.
We shall demonstrate that memory occurs even without the experience of cognition; therefore,
since memory is not invariably concomitant with it [cognition] in the absence of a certainty regarding its being an effect of self-cognition, there is no proof of that [self-]cognition.
Therefore, it must be explained how even recollection is established, since it is a form of cognition;
for a mark that is not itself established cannot be an indicator of something else.
Nor is recollection a grasper of self-awareness by way of direct perception.
Because it is distinct from that [object],
cognition cannot have another cognition as its object;
for otherwise, defects such as the impossibility of establishing a relationship would follow, just as in the case of external objects.
Since there is no difference in their being distinct entities, there would be apprehension of that [object] even by a memory occurring in another continuum.

If it is argued that it is not remembered because it was not previously experienced by that [memory], then the same consequence follows: it was not previously experienced even by [the memory] belonging to the same continuum.
Furthermore, it is not tenable that the causal relationship itself acts as its regulator,
because the causal relationship does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality;
even if it did exist, it would be impossible to grasp it, since all cognitions are restricted to their own respective objects of apprehension.
If one accepts things according to conventional usage, they are conceptual;
and if they are conceptual, then because all conventional usages are constructed by conceptualization, they are merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). Thus, our thesis has been proven.
Therefore, the self-cognition of memory is not established.
To the question, "How then can there be memory in the absence of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) even for you [the opponent]? he says, beginning with "anyānubhūte":
"Memory arises from a connection with what was experienced by another, just as the poison of a rat [is transmitted]. (Bca 9.24)
When an object—that is, a thing to be grasped—other than cognition itself has been experienced, a memory, that is, a recollection, arises regarding that cognition.

[Objection: But if there were a recollection of one thing when another has been experienced, would this not lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga)? [Response: He says "due to a connection" (saṃbandhāt).
When an object has been experienced, the recollection of the cognition of that [object] occurs because of a connection.
For consciousness is connected to that [object] by way of being its grasper;
therefore, it is consciousness that is remembered, and nothing else.
If it is argued that even though there is a connection, if one thing were experienced and another were remembered, the memory would be erroneous—this is not so.
An object previously experienced, when being recollected at a later time, is recollected as qualified by that very experience; for it is grasped as characterized by that [experience].

Since the experience of the object is nothing other than cognition itself, the recollection of the cognition is said to occur through its connection with the recollection of the experience of the object.
However, there is no fault, because even cognition alone, devoid of its object, is not remembered.

One might ask: "How indeed could recollection occur at a later time without the seed of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of memory produced by the experience of cognition? To this he says: "Just like rat-poison.
Just as rat-poison—that is, the poison of a mouse—manifests after an interval of time due to its underlying connection, so too does recollection; such is the meaning.
For instance, poison from a rat that has entered the body in a single moment undergoes a transformation at another time upon hearing the thundering of clouds;

this occurs because its activity depends solely on the principle of "this-conditionality" (*idampratyayatāmātra*), even in the absence of the seed of latencies for memory established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
The sense is that, likewise, there is no fault in the present case either.

Furthermore, the Vijñānavādin, in order to establish the self-awareness of cognition, states another method: "pratyayāntara..."—because that which is conjoined with another condition (*pratyayāntara*) is seen, it manifests itself;
the "other condition" refers to another cause (*kāraṇāntara*) or another time (*kālāntara*).

The science of divination (*īkṣaṇikā*) and so forth, as well as the supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) of knowing the minds of others and the like— because for one endowed with these, the mind connected to that causal complex is seen,
that is, it appears, consciousness manifests its own nature; in other words, self-awareness exists.
For if that [object] were always of a nature beyond perception, how could it ever be perceived due to a particular collection of conditions?

Therefore, the point is this: just as another's mind is perceived through a particular collection of conditions, so too one's own mind is perceived through conditions such as the immediately preceding condition and the object-condition.
To show that this too is not due to the power of the cognition’s self-awareness, he says "siddhāñjana" and so forth:
"A jar seen through the application of a magical ointment does not itself become the ointment. (Bca 9.25)
And that collyrium is accomplished, or it is the collyrium of one who has attained accomplishment;
its procedure, method, or application [is as follows].
Therefore, a jar that is seen or perceived, or a treasure-trove and the like, does not become the act of coloring;
nor can a jar and such things be the act of coloring itself.
For that which is perceived from something else does not become that very thing.

In this way, even if the mind of another were perceived like a jar or other objects through knowledge assisted by sciences such as *īkṣaṇikā*, the fact of its being experienced would not thereby be established.
Therefore, this too is not a proof useful for establishing the thesis.
Now, if cognition were of an unknown nature, [how could it be known?]
There would also be no cognition of the object,
because cognition is characterized by the manifestation of what was previously unmanifest; for there is no manifestation of the object itself.
If that [cognition] is not perceived, how can there be perception of the object?
For it is so because self-awareness has been refuted,
and because it is impossible for one thing to be apprehended by another.

Furthermore, if one accepts the apprehension of that [cognition], then because one would have to pursue further cognitions for the sake of cognizing each subsequent, as yet uncognized [cognition], there would be the consequence of an infinite regress; thus, the object could not be cognized in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, what was stated [by you]—“In the case of what is experienced by another,” and so forth—is inconsistent.
Because there is no experience of the object.
He says "just as it is seen," and so forth, [arguing] that otherwise this entire worldly convention of seeing and so on would not exist.
As for what is said— that the convention of seeing and so on would not exist— would that [non-existence] be from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), or...
Or is it conventionally?
In that regard, if it is said that [it] would not exist ultimately,
then this is pleasing to us.
For that which is conventional has no place in the investigation of ultimate reality.
Now, if it is worldly renown [that is being considered], then:
"That which is seen, heard, and known is not here negated."
Thus: "seen" refers to what is apprehended through direct perception by means of visual and other sensory consciousnesses; "heard" refers to what is learned from another person or from scripture;
and "cognized" refers to what is ascertained through inference arising from a logical mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*).
Therefore, all this is neither prohibited nor prevented here with respect to conventional usage;
whatever is perceived in accordance with worldly convention, that is accepted.
That [nature] is accepted exactly as it is, with its true form unexamined, based on worldly consensus, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, defects such as the absence of the cognition of knowledge and the non-apprehension of objects do not apply here to the proponent of the ultimate position.
If that is accepted as being exactly so, then what precisely is being negated? To this he says "from the perspective of reality," and so forth:
"In this context, conceptual construction, which is the cause of suffering, is refuted from the perspective of reality. (Bca 9.26)
"From the perspective of reality" means from the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) means superimposition (*āropa*).
The word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "furthermore."
Furthermore, in this investigation or in the established doctrine (siddhānta), it is warded off—that is, it is prohibited.
Why? Because it is a cause of suffering.
This is a causal phrase; the meaning is: "because it is the cause, the reason for suffering, therefore."

And it is precisely because of the cause—the activity instigated by conceptual constructions such as existence and non-existence regarding the aggregates of clinging—that there is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, cyclic existence has suffering as its intrinsic nature.
These [aggregates] are suffering, the origin, the world, the locus of views, and becoming.
Because of this statement [Abhidharmakośa 1.8],
conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is, in truth, the cause of suffering.
Therefore, what is intended here is merely the negation of the insistence on the conceptual construction that superimposes what is non-existent; nothing real whatsoever is being negated.
Thus, self-cognition of knowledge is not in any way at all tenable. As it has been said:
The Tathāgatas have not perceived the mind as having the form of an awakener or that which is to be awakened;
where there is both an awakener and that which is to be awakened, there awakening does not exist.
Thus it is said.

As for the fact that the Blessed One has in some places spoken of the existence of mind-only (*cittamātra*), that will be explained as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), like [his teachings on] the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense-bases (*āyatana*).
Now, having concluded this incidental discussion, he says, beginning with "If it were other than the mind," etc., in order to apply it to the subject at hand:

"If illusion is not other than the mind, nor is it conceived as non-other; if it were a real entity, how could it be neither other nor non-other? If it is neither, it does not exist as a real entity. (Bca 9.27)
In that case, would illusion be other than the mind, or non-other than it,
or of the nature of both?
Or [it may be] of neither nature;
thus there are four alternatives.
Among these, first of all, it is not the first position.
Even if one were to accept [the existence of things] as other than mind, there would be a contradiction with the tenet of one who maintains that the world is mind-only (*cittamātra*).
As for the second position, however, the fault has already been established by the passage beginning, "When even illusion does not exist for you" (9.6).
Furthermore, the third alternative is not tenable.
Because two mutually contradictory things cannot exist in one place;
furthermore, the fourth alternative is also not tenable.
Based on that [illusion], it is said that "illusion is not other than the mind"; this is the negation of its being something else.
If one then asks, "Is it then non-other?", [the answer is] "nor is it non-other"; this is the negation of its being identical to reality (*tattva*).

If it is thus postulated and established that there is a falling back into both sides [of the dichotomy], that too is not tenable; for since two things are mutually exclusive, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other, and thus they cannot both exist in the same place. Therefore, a fourth alternative does not cohere either.
Moreover:
"If it were a real entity" means that if that illusion were substantially real, how could it not be something other— that is, not distinct from the mind?
Now, if they are not different—
if the mind itself were the illusion— then it would not exist in reality.
From the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing exists, because that [illusion] has that [emptiness] as its intrinsic nature; thus, it follows that there is only mind alone. As it has been said:
"When for you even illusion itself does not exist, then what is perceived?"
Thus it is said.
Now, having established the subject at hand, he concludes by saying "asatyapi" and so forth:
"Just as an illusion is seen even though it is non-existent, so too is the mind.
An illusion, although perceived, is non-existent in reality, having a nature that is unreal like that of an elephant or similar objects [within the illusion].
Even such [an object] is visible—that is, within the range of perception—just like an illusion; likewise, the mind is for the observer.
That very same unreal illusion is the visible example.
Likewise, the mind, although its nature is non-existent from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), will be capable of seeing.
Thus, having established what was stated by the opponent—that "when even error does not exist" (9.15)—and so forth, it has been demonstrated by way of conclusion.

Furthermore, intending to address the opponent's challenge in order to establish consciousness as ultimately real through another method, he says: "And that which has a basis in a real entity," and so on.
If saṃsāra were based on a real entity, it would be otherwise, like space.
For instance, both affliction (*saṃkleśa*) and purification (*vyavadāna*) must be understood correctly as this duality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.
In that regard, the mind covered by the stains of passion and so forth is said to be "afflicted.
And because they arise through the power of false superimposition, those [stains] function as adventitious factors residing in the mind.
The cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) arises as a continuous succession of births produced by abundant karma.

That very same mind, however, is in the ultimate sense luminous by nature (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*), non-adventitious, empty of the latencies of attachment to the superimposition of duality—such as the grasped and the grasper—which originate from unreal imagination (*abhūtaparikalpa*); it is non-dual by nature and, being free from adventitious defects, is called "purification" (*vyavadāna*) upon the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
Thus, they consider that the establishment of affliction and purification is not possible without a mind arisen from a real basis, because both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa have the nature of mind;
it is the mind alone that becomes afflicted.

Because of the statement that "the mind itself is purified," he explains that very position of the opponent: "vastvāśraya" means that which has a real entity (*vastu*)—namely, the mind existing as a real entity—as its basis (*āśraya*). If cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is established [in this way],...
In that case, saṃsāra would be something else; it would be other than the mind,
and if it were other than a real entity, it would be a non-entity.
And because the mind alone is the reality:
how so? Like space, like the sky.
That which is called saṃsāra is the very locus of the mind.
Is that a real entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*)?
If it is a real entity, is it the mind itself or something other than that?
In that regard, if it is a real entity, it must be the mind alone.
At that time, there is no saṃsāra other than the mind upon which it depends; rather, saṃsāra is the mind itself.
And because the mind is luminous by nature and has purification as its intrinsic essence, it is not something to be abandoned.
If, on the other hand, it were other than the mind,
then because something distinct from the mind would be admitted, there would be a contradiction of one's own tenet.
Or, if it were a non-entity, [the same fault would apply].
At that time, what is called "saṃsāra" does not exist at all,
like the horn of a donkey;
for this very reason, it is said to be "like space."
Just as space is a mere conceptual existence and non-existent, being incapable of any causal efficiency whatsoever,
so too would cyclic existence be for you.
Alternatively,
by the phrase "like space," because of its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), there is an entry into our own established doctrine.

It might be argued: "Even if it is indeed a non-entity (*avastu*), nevertheless, because it depends upon a mind that is a real entity (*vastu-sadbhūta*), it will possess the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*. To this, he says "by depending on an entity," and so forth: "How could a non-existence (*abhāva*) possess activity by depending on an entity?"
That which lacks an existent form cannot have any substratum,
because the relationship between a substratum and its dependent consists in the nature of cause and effect;
and non-existence is not the effect of anything.
Because its specific qualities are not subject to alteration;
even so, by depending upon a real entity— that is, by depending upon a mind that exists as a real entity— non-existence, which is of the nature of non-being, possesses activity.
How could there be causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*)?
The meaning is that it is not tenable at any time;
otherwise, it would possess the nature of a real entity (*bhāvasvabhāvatā*).

For power (*śakti*) is the defining characteristic of existence (*bhāva*), according to the statement that "the absence of all powers is the defining characteristic of non-existence (*abhāva*). To the question, "What then is present when this is being investigated? he says: "Assisted by the non-existent," and so forth.
For indeed, your mind falls into a state of being alone with unwholesome companions.
"Accompanied by the unreal" means that non-existence (*asat*) is its companion.
The particle *hi* is used for emphasis.
For you, who maintain that the mind alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the mind falls into a state that is singular and indeed without a second.
[Objection: But has it not already been stated that the mind is characterized by non-duality, being entirely free from the forms of the grasped, the grasper, and so forth?
Thus, in establishing the oneness of the mind, there is nothing undesirable for us.
[Reply: That is incorrect.
It has been stated that even affliction (*saṃkleśa*) possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*) because it is to be abandoned.
How then can the mind alone be the sole real entity?
Granting that this may be so, [the author] says "the object of apprehension is released," etc., to show that even so, there is no liberation from the obstructing factors.
When the mind is liberated from the apprehended object, then all are Tathāgatas.
"The apprehended" is an illustrative term;
it should be understood that [the mind] is likewise liberated from the apprehending subject and so forth as well.

Alternatively, since the state of being a grasper (grāhaka) is dependent upon the grasped (grāhya), the absence of the latter entails the absence of the former. Furthermore, because the expressible (abhilāpya) is fashioned by that grasper, the absence of the grasper results in the absence of expression; it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that "the grasped" was mentioned.
When the mind of the entire world is of a non-dual nature, free from the forms of the grasped and so forth—
At that time, because that mind is included within the mental continua of all sentient beings, all transmigrating beings would become Tathāgatas, Buddhas, and Blessed Ones;
there would be no ordinary person at all.
Consequently, it would follow that the cultivation of the noble path for the sake of abandoning afflictions (*saṃkleśa*) is rendered useless;
yet this is not the case.

Therefore, with the intention that—even though there is an absence of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject—the adherence to the reality of things (*bhāvābhiniveśa*) remains as it was, and thus the abandonment of all afflictions does not occur, he says "And thus," and so forth.
And what benefit is gained by conceiving even "mind-only" in this way? (Bca 9.30)
The compound particle *evaṃ ca* has the sense of "this being so" (*evaṃ sati*).
The particle *ca* has the sense of "even" (*api*).
[The question is: "Even if this is accepted, what benefit is obtained?"
Not at all;

for even though it is "mind-only" and even when "representation-only" is conceptually constructed and superposed by imagination, the outbursts of passion and other afflictions still persist within the mental continua of all sentient beings, despite their connection to the thorough knowledge of non-dual reality.

Now, raising the objection that this same [criticism] applies to you as well who propound the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), he states "even when it is known to be like an illusion," etc., in order to show that the fault is equal:
"Even when it is known to be like an illusion, how is affliction (*kleśa*) removed?
Even when it is known to be like an illusion—that is, even when the world is known to have the nature of an illusion—how is affliction removed?"
He asks: "How is the group of passions such as attachment abandoned?
He replies: "What is the reason for the impossibility of abandonment here that you ask about?"—namely, when it is said: "When passion arises even for the creator of an illusory woman... (Bca 9.31).

This is seen here as the seed for the impossibility of abandonment: when passion—that is, a state of mind characterized by attachment—arises toward a woman created by a magician through illusion, whose nature is that of a phantom, of whom does it arise?
It arises even of the creator himself.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that this [delusion] arises not only for those whom it was created to delude, but also for its creator— the one who fashioned that illusory woman.

For instance, when a certain magician, highly skilled in creating such forms, displays a woman who is the most beautiful in the land— produced through the power of mantras and medicinal herbs for the purpose of causing a delusion in the minds of others; she who is complete in all her major and minor limbs and physical characteristics, endowed with the perfection of fresh youth, possessing a clear and charming complexion, and radiant with an excellence of beauty.
At that time, it was not merely others who, upon beholding her, had their hearts pained by the strikes of the arrows of Love;
rather, even he who was the creator of her— her whose form was yearning for skill in the arts of love and whose perfection of lovely luster was such—
that expert in her nature [thought], "She was fashioned by me myself."
Even he, reaching the supreme state through the digit of desire (*kāmakalā*), was not at all able to steady his mind;
therefore, how could there be a severance of the continuity of saṃsāra even when its illusory nature (*māyopamatva*) has been ascertained?
Desiring to avoid this [objection], he says: "For that [desire] is not abandoned," and so forth.
For the latent predisposition toward the afflictions of the objects of knowledge has not been abandoned by its creator;
therefore, at the time of that [false] view, his predisposition for emptiness is weak. (Bca 9.32)
The word *hi* has the sense of "because.
This objection does not apply to us,
because [the afflictions] have not been abandoned and have not ceased.
Of its creator— that is, the creator of the illusory woman—
is it not abandoned?

The latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for the affliction of the knowable (*jñeya-saṃkleśa*) refers to the affliction of the knowable consisting of attachment and so forth, arising from the superimposition (*samāropa*) of intrinsic nature (*sasvabhāvatā*).
Or it is the superimposition of reality;
that is the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) in its entirety.

Its latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) is the depositing of karmic impressions (*saṃskāra*) within the continuum of consciousness, which has become the seed for those [obscurations] produced by false conceptualization practiced throughout the succession of births in beginningless saṃsāra.
Because that [ignorance] has not been abandoned.
Is this not an equally valid rebuttal for the Vijñānavādin as well?
Even though that non-dual reality exists, because the latencies of adventitious afflictions have not been abandoned, not all beings become Tathāgatas.
This is not the same [as the case of the stains], because stains, being of the nature of non-existence and lacking the capacity for causal efficacy, cannot constitute an obscuration.
This has already been stated.
For us, however, that which is produced and that which produces are indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva); thus, it is not the same [as your position].
Because that [defilement] has not been abandoned, [it persists].
Therefore, for this reason,
at the time of seeing that [object], there is the seeing— that is, the apprehension— of that knowable thing's own-nature.
"At that time" means at the time of seeing or perceiving that illusory woman;
"of him" refers to the observer who has not yet abandoned the latencies (vāsanā) of affliction.

"The impression of emptiness is weak" (*durbalā śūnyavāsanā*): the analysis of the compound is "of emptiness," meaning either of the reality of emptiness (*śūnyatattva*) or of emptiness itself (*śūnyatā*). The term *śūnya* is used [instead of *śūnyatā*] by omitting the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) in accordance with the requirements of the meter.
An impression (*vāsanā*) is the depositing of a latent disposition (*saṃskāra*).
That [consciousness] is weak and devoid of capacity, because it perceives what has been superimposed;
therefore, at that time, the latent impression of existence is powerful.
How, then, is that [habitual tendency] removed? He says "emptiness," and so forth:
"The habitual tendency toward existence is abandoned through the instillation of the habitual tendency toward emptiness.
The habitual tendency toward emptiness—that is, toward the lack of intrinsic nature whose nature is like an illusion—is its instillation, which is to say, its infusion.
This means strengthening through repeated practice. Therefore, one is deprived of— that is, turned away from— that contrary cognition, just as the sensation of cold ceases upon the presence of fire.

What is it? It is the latent impression of existence (*bhāvavāsanā*), which is the latent impression of the persistent clinging to things as real, practiced throughout beginningless and endless saṃsāra.
This is because that [clinging] has a real object and because it constitutes the intrinsic nature of things.
Because the other is false and adventitious.

Now, is there not indeed no distinction regarding attachment between attachment to existence or attachment to emptiness, since even that does not transcend the nature of conceptual construction? As it has been said:
Emptiness has been declared by the wise to be the relinquishing of all views;
however, those for whom emptiness itself is a view were said to be incurable.
Thus [it is said].
To refute this, he says "Nothing exists at all," and so forth:
"By the practice that 'nothing exists at all,' even that [notion] is later abandoned. (Bca 9.33)
"Something" refers to either an entity or emptiness;
"does not exist" means it is not found.
The word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction in reference to what precedes it.
Thus, through such practice, after the abandonment of the latent tendency toward existence (*bhāvavāsanā*), even that latent tendency toward emptiness (*śūnyavāsanā*) is abandoned and ceases.

This is the intended meaning: for the penetration of emptiness, being the antidote to the adherence to existence, serves as the means of abandonment; and once the goal has been attained, the abandonment of the means itself is subsequently practiced, because the means is like a raft. He says this very thing:
The teaching of the nectar of emptiness is for the sake of abandoning all conceptual constructions;
yet you have suppressed even that grasping which some may hold toward it.
Thus it is said: [Catuḥ-2.21].

This might be the case: even if the abandonment of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of emptiness occurs through the practice of mental attention (*manasikāra*) that "nothing exists," nevertheless, due to that very practice, the conceptualization of non-existence (*abhāva-kalpanā*) would arise again and could not be prevented.
And thus, when the pupil has entered the socket, the exit of the iris occurs; therefore, your wickedness remains in that same state.
To this, he says: "When [the object] is not perceived," and so forth.
When no entity is found that could be conceptualized as "non-existent," then how could non-existence,
being without a basis, appear before the mind?
This conceptualization of non-existence also does not hold up under analysis;
for there is that entity which is imagined as being non-existent, and that entity whose negation is performed.
If, when being investigated, that [imagined entity] is not found or obtained because it lacks intrinsic nature— just like the clusters of hair perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia—
then it is "without a basis," namely,
that entity which was imagined.
Since it lacks any correlate, how could this non-existence—which is without support and whose form is manifested by conceptual construction—stand before the mind?
How could it appear before the intellect when subjected to investigation?
It simply ceases of its own accord upon the realization that existence is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Alternatively, it is introduced in another way: "Granted that the cessation of the latent impression of existence may occur through the empowerment of emptiness, by what can the adherence to non-existence be prevented, since there is no negation of that [existence]? To this he says, "When [it] is not apprehended," and so forth.
Everything else is as before.
This is the collective meaning here: for the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) is adopted in order to abandon attachment to existence;
yet that very emptiness is subsequently abandoned once emptiness itself has been realized. Furthermore, whatever conceptualization of existence might arise in any way whatsoever—
That [investigation] too ceases immediately upon further investigation.

For this very reason, in order to turn back this entire web of conceptual construction, eighteen types of emptiness—beginning with internal emptiness—are taught in detail in the *Bhagavatī Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, emptiness is not distinct from existence.
Because that very nature belongs to existence itself;
otherwise, if emptiness were distinct from existence, phenomena would lack the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
It was established previously that the absence of intrinsic nature is its very nature.
This too has been stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:

"Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the *prajñāpāramitā* contemplates with mental attentions associated with the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) as follows: 'Form is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of form.'"
Form itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is form.
Feeling is not empty by virtue of the emptiness of feeling.
Feeling itself is empty;
emptiness itself is feeling.
It is not by means of the emptiness of perception that perception is empty.
Perception itself is empty, and emptiness itself is perception.
It is not by means of the emptiness of volitional formations that volitional formations are empty.
Formations themselves are empty; emptiness itself is formations.
It is not by means of the emptiness of consciousness that consciousness is empty.
Consciousness itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is consciousness.
Thus it is said in detail. And it has been stated:
"That which is dependent origination, that very thing you consider to be emptiness;
'there is no independent entity'—this is your peerless lion's roar."
Thus,
emptiness is not distinct from phenomena;
therefore, one should not form an attachment even to emptiness.

Demonstrating that the liberation from all obscurations arises through the subsiding of all conceptual constructions in this way, he says: "When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind," and so forth.
(Bcp 199) When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind, [then one is liberated].
Then, due to the absence of any other alternative, it becomes tranquil, being without a focal point.
When neither existence— meaning an entity with an ultimately real intrinsic nature— stands before the mind,
nor non-existence— that is, a non-existence characterized by the mere absence of existence— stands before the mind; [then...]
At that time, because there is no other alternative due to the absence of any other possibility through affirmation or negation—
and because both the positions of "both" and "neither" consist of these two [affirmation and negation],
and since those two are included within these [positions] as they are not distinct from them— those two [positions] are also subsumed; thus, [the tetralemma] is without a basis.
Because neither an existent nor a non-existent object can serve as a focal point, the intellect becomes stilled and subsides;
through the subsiding of all conceptual constructions, it attains extinction like a fire without fuel—this is the meaning.

How then does the Blessed One, having attained Buddhahood—which is free from all conceptual construction and has been desired for many incalculable eons as the means for achieving the welfare of others—accomplish the welfare of others? To this he says: "Just as the wish-fulfilling gem and the wish-granting tree fulfill desires, so too is the form of the Victor perceived through the power of those to be trained and his former vows. (Bca 9.36)
The *cintāmaṇi* is a particular kind of jewel that grants the fruits of one's thoughts;
the *kalpataru* is a particular kind of tree that grants the fruits of one's imaginings.
Just as these fulfill the desires and accomplish the aspirations of people according to their fortune, even without conceptual thought (*vikalpa*).
The connection is that "the image of the Victor (jinabimba) is likewise seen.
The Blessed One is the Victor (jina) because of his victory over the four Māras, or because of his victory over the dharmas that lead to evil.

The body of the Jina, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is an image resplendent with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man. In that manner, even in the absence of all conceptual construction, it is perceived as capable of accomplishing the welfare and happiness of others. But how can this come about by mere wish? To this he says: "By means of the disciples and their vows."

By the power of those to be trained— meaning, by virtue of the ripening of the wholesome karma that serves as the cause for obtaining the specific fruits dependent upon those who are to be trained by the Buddha, the Blessed One—
and also by the power of his former vows.

Because of the momentum of that manifold vow made by the Blessed One previously during his state as a bodhisattva to accomplish the welfare of sentient beings—which proceeds effortlessly according to the principle of the continued spinning of a potter’s wheel—the accomplishment of the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings is established. As it has been said:
"From the night the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment until the night he passed into parinirvāṇa..."
In the meantime, not even a single syllable was uttered by the Tathāgata.
For what reason? Because the Blessed One is eternally in meditative equipoise.
And those beings who are to be disciplined by means of syllables, sounds,
and voices hear the resonance issuing from the mouth of the Tathāgata, from the circle of hair between his brows (ūrṇākośa), and from the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa), and so forth. And it is said:
While he has entered that meditative absorption and remains like a wish-fulfilling gem, teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects.
Through them, human beings come to know all matters they wish to understand,
and they swiftly attain their benefits according to their individual capacity.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Catuḥstava*, it is stated: [Tattvasaṃgraha 3241–42] (Bcp 200).
Not even a single syllable has been uttered by you, O Lord;
yet the entire assembly of those to be trained has been satiated by the rain of Dharma.

Thus [Catuḥ-1.7]. Having thus explained the uncommon cause, he speaks again, demonstrating by means of two verses that, in another way, it is precisely from the state of the cause (*hetvavasthā*) itself that such a particular excellence of power arises, whereby a fruit capable of accomplishing the welfare of others is produced effortlessly (*anābhogena*). He says:
As in the case of the snake-charmer and so forth:
just as a snake-charmer, having accomplished a ritual pillar, passes away; even though he has long since perished, that pillar continues to pacify poisons and the like. (Bca 9.37)

Just as a snake-charmer who knows the nature of poisons and has attained the power of mantras, having prepared a pillar made of wood or something else and consecrated it with a mantra, thinks, "In my absence, this very thing will be skilled in removing all poisons," and then passes away,
his own activity ceasing of its own accord.

That pillar, consecrated by him, would pacify poisons and the like—even after that Garuda-practitioner has long since perished or ceased to exist for a great length of time; by the word "and the like" (ādi), it is meant that he would also remove afflictions caused by planetary spirits and other such disturbances.

In accordance with the rules of the Vedic grammatical tradition (*chāndasa-samaya*), although the rule [Pāṇini 7.3.55] requires a short vowel for the penultimate letter before the causative suffix (*ṇic*), the shortening was not applied here.
Or, it is because a grammatical operation preceded by a specific technical designation (saṃjñā) is not invariably obligatory.

Having thus established the analogy, he applies it to the subject of the illustration, saying: "In accordance with the practice of awakening, even a victory pillar, once consecrated, performs all its functions even when the Bodhisattva has passed into nirvana. (Bca 9.38)
The word "yathā" (as) draws in the word "tathā" (so).
Thus, "bodhicaryā" is the conduct for the sake of awakening, for the cause of awakening, and for the purpose of Buddhahood.
It applies even when the Bodhisattva has passed into nirvāṇa.
Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is Buddhahood;

it is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*) known as the *dharmakāya*, which is devoid of the nature of being one or many, unarisen and unceasing, neither annihilated nor eternal, liberated from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and equal to space.

It is precisely this that, by recourse to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), is designated by such terms as *prajñāpāramitā*, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
And it was with this very intention that it was said: "The Buddhas are to be seen through the Dharma, for the Guides are the Dharma-body;
yet the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is unknowable—it cannot be known."
Thus it is said in the *Vajracchedikā* (26):
"It is without characteristics, unarisen, unconditioned, and beyond the reach of speech."
Space and the mind of awakening are awakening, characterized by non-duality.
Thus:
in this context, a *bodhisattva* is one whose intention (*sattva*) is directed toward awakening (*bodhi*).
Even when that [awakening] has been realized, [the term applies].
The word "api" (even) is displaced [in the sentence]. It means:
even when one has attained supreme peace through non-abiding nirvāṇa—that is, upon the cessation of the causal state and the attainment of the resultant state.
Thus, in both ways, even though there is a total absence of conceptual construction, it is demonstrated that the accomplishment of the welfare of sentient beings remains unimpaired.

(Bcp 201) This might be the case: if the Blessed One has ceased all activity of mind and mental factors because all conceptual objects have subsided, then how can it be described that making offerings to the Tathāgata yields great fruit? Anticipating this doubt, he says "in one who is without mind," and so forth.
How can worship performed toward that which is without mind be fruitful?

When the Blessed One is devoid of conventional mind, how can worship—offered and presented to him—be fruitful; how could it bear fruit? How could there be a distinction in the act of making offerings?
How could it be productive of results?

In that case, if there is no experiencer, how can there be merit for the donors and patrons? To this, he gives the answer beginning with "It is indeed equal," etc.: "For it is taught to be exactly the same for one who remains [in the world] and for one who has attained nirvāṇa. (Bca 9.39)
It is exactly the same, precisely equal;
it is recited and established in the scripture (*āgama*).
Therefore, it should be construed as follows: "Consequently, it shall be fruitful for one who remains [in this world] and for one who has attained *nirvṛti* (extinction)."

There is no difference in the merit of making offerings whether [the Buddha] is staying and has not yet entered parinirvāṇa, or whether he has entered parinirvāṇa and attained the nirvāṇa without remainder (*nirupadhi-nirvāṇa*). This is the intended meaning: for merit is of two kinds—namely, that which follows from relinquishment (*tyāga-anvaya*) and...
That which arises solely from relinquishment;
and that which follows from enjoyment,
which arises from the enjoyment of the gift to be given.

In that regard, even if there is indeed no merit resulting from enjoyment due to the absence of a recipient once the Blessed One has passed into nirvāṇa, who can prevent the merit resulting from the act of relinquishment?
If no one accepts [the gift], how can there even be merit resulting from relinquishment?
Furthermore, what is the reason that merit must exist when there is a recipient, but not when there is none?
If you argue that it is because [the merit] would belong to no one at all,
this is simply not a valid reason.
For if merit were to arise solely from the benefit of others, it would not exist during the cultivation of the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) or of right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
