Therefore, it should be understood that merit originates from one's own mind even in the absence of benefiting others.
Likewise, even when the virtuous one has passed away, the merit arising from devotion toward him from one's own mind is not contradicted.
Moreover, since the existence of all merit and demerit is attested by scripture for everyone, he says "and from scripture" and so forth:
"And from scripture there is the fruit in that regard, whether conventionally or in reality;
what need is there here for another logical argument?"
From scripture—that is, from the word of the Blessed One—it is understood that the fruit resulting from making offerings to the Blessed One consists of great enjoyment and other such characteristics.
"Therein" refers to making offerings when the Blessed One has either passed into nirvāṇa or not yet passed into nirvāṇa.
However, this much is the distinction: for some, that fruit is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛta*).
However, for someone else, this is intended in an ultimate sense;
thus, disregarding the preceding analysis,
it is stated specifically that the fruit of the performance of merit and demerit— whether conventionally or in reality— is understood from the scripture of the Blessed One.
And in this regard, there is no dispute between us; for it was said by the Blessed One in the *Puṣpakūṭa-dhāraṇī*:
"O Siṃhavikrīḍita, whoever shall perform worship of the Tathāgata, whether he is present or has passed into parinirvāṇa, they shall all attain parinirvāṇa by means of one of the three vehicles."
Moreover, Siṃhavikrīḍita, whoever, having seen the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, should clarify their mind, and with a clarified mind should honor, revere, respect, worship,
and attend upon him, serving him with gains— namely, robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick— and with all articles of comfort; [that person would generate much merit].
And whoever should perform worship of the body of a Tathāgata who has attained final nirvāṇa toward a relic the size of a mustard seed, an equal ripening of fruit is to be expected;
likewise, for such worship, there is no distinction or difference whatsoever. Thus it is said.
And it is said:
"One should worship him who remains [in this world], as well as him who has attained final nirvāṇa."
Through the clarity of an even mind, there is no distinction in merit.
Thus it was said; furthermore, this was declared in the *Divya-avadāna*:
"Moreover, Siṃhavikrīḍita, suppose someone were to attend upon the Tathāgata for a hundred years or a thousand years, providing him with every article of comfort."

And whoever, for the sake of making an offering to the Tathāgata, should place even a single flower upon the stupa of a Tathāgata who has entered parinirvāṇa while embraced by the thought of awakening (bodhicitta), or should offer a handful of water,
or should sprinkle it with water;
Or he might offer a stalk of grass,
or remove withered flowers,
or perform the offering of anointing or the offering of a lamp.
With a joyful mind, having taken even a single step or having gone beyond it, you should utter these words: "Homage to that Buddha, the Blessed One.
O Siṃhavikrīḍita, let there be no doubt, uncertainty, or hesitation in you regarding this.
"That he should go to a state of miserable rebirth or downfall for an eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons—this is impossible.
Thus, one must necessarily accept this; therefore, he says "In the Buddha of Truth," and so forth.
How is it that an offering made to one who possesses true awakening becomes fruitful? Just as [in the following example].

"How is it that an offering made to the Blessed One— who possesses true wisdom and exists in the ultimate sense— is fruitful and productive of results? To explain how this is so, he provides an illustration.
The sense is that there is no other illustration for this than scripture (*āgama*).
Therefore, in every respect, the existence of a fruit in the worship of the Blessed One is understood from scripture.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "by instilling the impression of emptiness" (*śūnyatāvāsanādhānāt*), the Vaibhāṣikas and others—who cannot tolerate the abandonment of all obscurations through the emptiness of all phenomena and who desire the vision and cultivation of the four noble truths as the means for that—say: "Liberation comes from the vision of the truths; what is the use of the vision of emptiness?"
"By the vision" means by the perception or realization— meaning by the direct manifestation— of the four noble truths characterized as suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
"By the vision" is an elliptical expression [intended to include cultivation].
It should also be understood from the perspective of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). As it has been said:
"The abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) is declared to result from the vision and cultivation of the truths" (Abhidharmakośa 6.1).

In that regard, for one who is established in conduct, possesses learning and reflection, and has engaged in cultivation—practicing the cultivation of the foul, mindfulness of breathing, and the foundations of mindfulness—by way of the sequential accomplishment of these, he perceives the truths of suffering and so forth through these sixteen aspects: as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. By means of the four aids to penetration beginning with "heat" (*uṣmagata*), there arises the path of seeing, characterized by fifteen moments beginning with the receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).

Thereafter, through the realization of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the abandonment of the mass of afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) belonging to the three realms—which are to be abandoned by seeing and cultivation—there arises the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). This is, in brief, the sequence of clear realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding the Noble Truths.
In this way, liberation is said to result from the vision of the Noble Truths.
Therefore, let liberation arise from this very [view]; what is the use of the vision of emptiness, given that emptiness is the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena? (Bcp 203)
By means of vision, by means of realization—that is to say, by means of direct realization—what [is gained]? Nothing at all; there is no purpose whatsoever.
Because there exists no other means for liberation [than this]. To this, he says "not without," and so forth:
"For it is the scriptural tradition that there is no enlightenment without this path. (Bca 9.41)
There is no other means;
such is the meaning.
This is the reality of the Great Purpose.
For indeed, all entities possess a dual nature: that which is superimposed and that which is non-superimposed.

Among these, the superimposed form, which is carried along by the stream of ignorance, is common to all people; therefore, the abandonment of affliction does not logically follow from the perception of that [superimposed form].
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that all foolish people would be Tathāgatas.
Thus, reality itself, when not superimposed and being realized through the yoga of non-apprehension, is observed to possess the power for the exhaustion of the outflows of ignorance.

And when that [reality] is discerned by wisdom, it is determined to have the characteristic of the non-apprehension of all phenomena; therefore, it is understood that the emptiness of all phenomena alone is most effective for the abandonment of all obscurations and delusions.
This has already been established through reasoning and will be further examined later; here, however,
this matter is presented solely on the basis of scripture.
"Because there is no awakening without this path; such is the scripture," he said. As it is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
The Blessed One said: "In this regard, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing in the perfection of wisdom does not cultivate form as an entity;
he does not cultivate feeling as an entity;
he does not cultivate perception as an entity."

He does not cultivate the notion that the formative forces (saṃskāra) are an entity; likewise, he does not cultivate the notion that the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgākārajñatā) is an entity, up to and including the notion that the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) is an entity.
One does not cultivate the thought that "the abandonment of all afflictions along with their latencies and underlying tendencies is an entity.
For what reason?
One who perceives entities does not practice the perfection of wisdom.
As long as one possesses the perception of existence, there is no cultivation of the perfection of generosity;
there is no cultivation of the emptiness of non-existence for one who possesses the perception of existence;
and there is no cultivation of the six superknowledges for one who possesses the perception of existence.

As long as there is no cultivation of all meditative concentrations, all doors of dhāraṇīs, the powers of a Tathāgata, the grounds of self-confidence, the analytical knowledges, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the unique qualities of a Buddha— why is that?
Because that state is attached to the two extremes of "this" and "I am."
In generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom—
one who is attached to these two extremes thinks, "I am this. And whoever is attached to these two extremes, [is not liberated].
For him there is no liberation. Why is that?
Subhūti, for one who perceives entities, there is no giving.
As long as there is no wisdom, no path, and no knowledge, [so long is there no liberation].
There is no attainment,
there is no clear realization,
and there is no conformable patience.
There is no full comprehension of form, no full comprehension of feeling, and so on, up to no full comprehension of dependent origination.
There is no thorough comprehension of the notions of a self, a sentient being, a living soul, a creature, a nourisher, a person, a human, a man, an agent, an experiencer, a knower, or a seer;
indeed, there is no thorough comprehension of the abandonment of all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies and underlying connections.
How, then, can there be liberation for such a one?
For this very reason, it is stated again in that same place:
The Blessed One said, "So it is, Kauśika, so it is.
Even those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who existed in the past time..."
They too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
And those who will be Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the future time,
they too, having relied upon this very perfection of wisdom, will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

Furthermore, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas who currently reside, stay, and maintain themselves, teaching the Dharma, in the immeasurable and incalculable world-systems of the ten directions—
they too have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by relying on this very perfection of wisdom.
Those who were the disciples of the past Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones;

those who will be the disciples of the future Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones; and those who are now the disciples of the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones—
They too, by relying on this very perfection of wisdom, have attained, will attain, and are attaining pratyekabodhi.
For what reason?
In this Perfection of Wisdom, all three vehicles are taught in detail;

moreover, they are taught by way of the signless, by way of non-apprehension, by way of non-arising, by way of non-affliction, and by way of non-purification, up to: by way of worldly convention and by way of what is not the ultimate truth.
Thus is the detailed exposition.
And it has been said:
"You alone are the path to liberation, practiced by Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas; there is no other—this is the certainty."
Thus ends the *Prajñāpāramitā-stuti*.
Unable to endure these words of the Mahāyāna, he says: "Is it not the case that the Mahāyāna is unestablished," and so forth—namely, "Is it not the case that the Mahāyāna is unestablished?"
But, O proponent of emptiness,
the Mahāyāna is not established for me as a scriptural authority, nor is it accepted by me.
Therefore, its presentation as a means of proof is not sound.
Here, he states the opponent’s objection, which offers a similar rebuttal, beginning with "How...":
"How is your scripture established?"
If the Mahāyāna is not established [as the word of the Buddha], how and in what manner is your own scripture established as the word of the Blessed One?
In that regard, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that proves its status as scripture.
The opponent offers a rebuttal with the words "yasmāt" (because):
because this [scripture] is established for both— meaning, for that reason, this scripture of mine is established for both you and me, being ascertained as an authoritative tradition (*āgama*).
For even you, who follow the Mahāyāna, have no disagreement regarding my scripture being the word of the Buddha;
therefore, that [Mahāyāna] is established.
But I do not have full conviction in the Mahāyāna.
By this, the same [objection] would apply even to you.
The proponent of the established tenet (siddhāntavādin) says: "That is not established for you from the very beginning. (Bca 9.42)
Thus: although the fact that [your scripture] is established for both parties is the reason for establishing [the authority of] scripture, even so, this should not be stated,
because it is unestablished.
Because, for you yourself, this scripture of yours is not established—at what time? At the beginning, prior to its acceptance;
for prior to its formal admission, it is not established for you in any way whatsoever.
Thus, because it is unestablished for both [parties], it is not a valid means of proof due to its lack of establishment.
(Bcp 205) Even if being established for both parties is unproven,
let this then be the proof: that which has been handed down through the lineage of teacher and disciple as the word of the Buddha.
And that which enters into the Sūtras, appears in the Vinaya,
and does not contradict the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), namely dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
That is the word of the Buddha and nothing else.
To this, he says "that which is the condition," and so forth:
"Apply that same confidence toward the Mahāyāna which you have there."
That which is the condition and the basis for this adherence is so described;
that is to say, it has whatever [condition] as its condition and whatever [basis] as its basis.
"Reliance" means acceptability and respect. Therefore, maintain— that is, establish— here in this Mahāyāna as well that same reliance which you have toward your own scripture.
Because the grounds for confidence stated even in the Mahāyāna exist;
furthermore, this is the common and infallible characteristic shared by all the teachings, as it was said in the *Adhyāśayasaṃcodana-sūtra*:
"Moreover, Maitreya, by four reasons, eloquence should be known as spoken by all the Buddhas."
By which four?
Here, Maitreya, inspired eloquence is associated with the meaningful, not associated with the meaningless;
it is associated with the Dharma, not associated with what is non-Dharma.
It abandons the afflictions and does not increase them;
it demonstrates the qualities and benefits of nirvāṇa and does not demonstrate the qualities and benefits of saṃsāra.
By these four [criteria].

... [as before] ... Maitreya, whoever possesses these four kinds of inspired eloquence, or will possess them, faithful sons of good family or daughters of good family should conceive the notion of a Buddha toward them.
Having formed the perception of him as the Teacher, that Dharma should be heard.
For what reason?
Maitreya, whatever is well-spoken, all that is the word of the Buddha.
All of that was spoken by the Buddha.
In this regard, Maitreya, whoever should reject these inspired eloquences, saying, "These were not spoken by the Buddha," and should conceive a lack of respect for them—
Through his hatred for that person, he rejects all inspired eloquence spoken by the Buddha;
having rejected the Dharma, he becomes one who goes to the states of woe due to the karma conducive to the ruin of the Dharma.

Therefore, in this context, non-contradiction with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) alone is stated to be the correct characteristic. And it has been said: "Whatever speech is meaningful, endowed with the words of the Dharma, which eradicates the afflictions of the three realms, and which demonstrates the benefits of peace—that is the word of the Sage; otherwise, it is the opposite."
Thus,
since all this exists in the Mahāyāna, how could it not be accepted?
As for what was said, "That [reasoning] is not established for you from the outset," [it is refuted as follows:]
To this, the opponent states a distinction:

"I do not say that what is established for both of us is 'established for both' (ubhayasiddha); rather, my scripture is to be accepted because it is established for both of us and for others besides us."
It is not the Mahāyāna because it is the opposite of that; therefore, it should not be accepted. Thus he says, "The other, both, and desired," and so forth.
If both [the Buddhist and non-Buddhist views] were equally true, then the Vedas and other such scriptures would also be true.
If, because we two have entered into dispute, there are others besides us who are undecided regarding both [positions],
then that which is desired— that is, intended or agreed upon— by them.

If its truth— that is, its correspondence with reality— is accepted, then the truth of the Vedas and so forth would also follow; that is, the truth, or non-falsity, of the Vedic statement characterized by injunction (*codanā*),
as well as— by the force of the word "and so forth"— the truth of the words of Kaṇāda and others, would likewise obtain.
In that case as well, it is possible for there to be mutual agreement between both the proponent and the opponent;
therefore, even that [agreement] would have to be accepted by you.
Consequently, this too is not a distinguishing feature.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "There is no dispute regarding my teaching being the word of the Buddha, but there is such a dispute regarding the Mahāyāna;
therefore, that [my teaching] is to be accepted and not the other. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The Mahāyāna is subject to dispute," and so forth.
If you say that the Mahāyāna is subject to dispute, then abandon your own scripture as well,
for it is disputed by non-Buddhists, and other scriptures are disputed by both your own and others.
The Mahāyāna is subject to dispute and disagreement:
some accept it as the word of the Buddha because it serves as a factor for spiritual practice, while others do not accept it due to the superimposition of its opposite.
For this reason,
if it is not to be accepted, then abandon the scripture.
Abandon even your own scripture;
for that too would not be a basis for action.
Why? Because it is subject to dispute by non-Buddhist schools such as the Mīmāṃsakas, and because the possibility of contradiction exists, it deserves to be rejected.
He says "by their own" to show that it is not only by outsiders (tīrthika), but even by those of our own school;
for the teaching of the Blessed One is divided into four classes and eighteen sects.
In that regard, because many subdivisions can arise within even a single school (nikāya), mutual dispute is possible even among those belonging to one's own group (svayūthya).
"By one's own" means by those residing in other subdivisions within one's own school;
"by others" means by those residing in other schools.
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction with respect to what precedes it.
The connection is: "Because it is subject to dispute, abandon another scripture. "Another scripture" (*āgamāntaram*) refers to a scripture other than the one accepted by you.
That too, because it is subject to dispute, does not deserve acceptance;
for your scripture as well is equally subject to dispute in relation to others, so the logic for its rejection is exactly the same.
Or alternatively:

"By their own" means by those established within a single division—the Sautrāntikas, Abhidharmikas, and Vainayikas—who, because they dispute with one another, deserve the abandonment of the Sūtras, Abhidharma, and Vinaya;

for there is indeed mutual dispute among the Sautrāntikas and others who are situated within a single division. "By others" means by those belonging to different sub-divisions based on the same school (nikāya).
By this, that which was stated— that the word of the Buddha has come down through the lineage of gurus, disciples, and so forth—
should be understood as refuted by this very [argument].
Indeed, it is not reasonable for those who have not forgotten the oral tradition to engage in mutual dispute;
nor is there any mutual contradiction among the words of the Omniscient One;
and it is not possible for you to maintain that the Sūtras, Abhidharma, and Vinaya are mutually consistent in their meaning.
How then is it said that consistency with the Sūtras and other scriptures is the reason for its being the word of the Buddha?
Therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Having thus stated that the refutation applies equally to both sides, he speaks again, pointing out a specific defect in the opponent's position:
"The teaching has its root in the state of being a monk, yet the state of being a monk itself is ill-established.

He begins with the words "the teaching" (*śāsanam*), etc.: the "teaching" (*śāsana*) is characterized by the Blessed One’s instruction regarding the adoption of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful.
And that is rooted in the state of being a monk.
Alternatively,
having concluded the incidental discussion on the misconception regarding the scriptures, it was said:
Desiring to refute the claim, "Liberation comes from the vision of the truths; what is the use of the vision of emptiness? he says, "The teaching," and so forth.
"Teaching" refers to the issuing of commands: "This is to be done; this is not to be done."
That has the state of being a monk as its root.
"Monkhood" (*bhikṣutā*) means the condition of being a monk; that very thing is the root or bulbous base of which, and thus it is so described.
Because it is established upon that.

Just as a tree with firm roots, remaining for a long time, becomes capable of providing trunks, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, fruits, and shade, and of removing heat and other afflictions; so too the Bodhi-tree of the Blessed One’s teaching, having reached the root of the state of a monk (*bhikṣutā*), is endowed with the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, the meditations, the formless attainments, the concentrations, the factors conducive to enlightenment, and the fruits of asceticism along with the Noble Eightfold Path.

Through the miracles of supernatural power (*ṛddhiprātihārya*) and so forth, one becomes capable of removing the heat of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and other such torments; thus, this is the fundamental similarity to a monk (*bhikṣu*).
In this regard, there is the monk by designation,
the monk by profession,
and the monk by way of his habit of begging.

A monk who has received full ordination through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapticaturthakarman*), a monk whose afflictions are destroyed— thus there are five types of monks.
Among these, the fourth and fifth are the foremost.
Because the others are denotable merely by the same designation [as the former two],
both of these are likewise non-contradictory as causes for the endurance of the Teaching.
Even therein, the monk whose afflictions have been destroyed is preeminent.
It is precisely that which is intended here.
The state of being that is "monkhood" (*bhikṣutā*).
And since that [monkhood] is not logically consistent with the vision of the Noble Truths, he says: "And monkhood itself," and so forth.
"Bhikṣutā" (the state of being a monk) means the state of having destroyed the afflictions (*kleśa*);
that is to say, it refers to the abandonment of the afflictions.
The particle *ca* functions as a causal conjunction, gathering together the various points to be stated.
Since that state of being a monk itself is unstable— being inconsistent without the vision of emptiness and not tenable through the vision of the truths alone—
the intention is that one should not say that liberation comes from the vision of the truths.
For whom is it poorly situated?

It is for those whose minds possess an object of apprehension (*sāvalambana*). It is called "possessing an object" because it functions together with an object of apprehension, that is, with attachment to a thing (*vastu*).
Those yogins who possess such a mind are referred to as "those [so described]";
for it is your view that they apprehend the truths of suffering and so forth, as well as the dissociation from afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyoga*), as real entities (*vastu*).
Therefore, for those who hold the view of apprehension, [the path] is unstable.
Not for those whose minds are without an object of focus.
Furthermore, as for what was stated— that liberation results from the vision of the truths—
that must be examined;
for the vision of the truths is conceived in two ways.
Whether from the perspective of ultimate reality or from the perspective of conventional reality:
if it is the first alternative,
then there is no disagreement between us.
Because our position is the primary one,
for we accept that all phenomena are seen from the perspective of ultimate reality;
now, as for the second [position]:
We do not accept that, because it contradicts reason;
for liberation does not arise from the vision of conventional truth.
Because it would follow that all sentient beings are already liberated.
For, through the discernment of reality and unreality by means of both reasoning and scripture,
it is ultimate truth alone— not conventional truth— that is determined here for the sake of abandoning the afflictions.
And that has the characteristic of the non-apprehension of all phenomena;
for without it, the cessation of affliction is not tenable,
as long as there is adherence to the existence of things.
As long as conceptual construction does not cease,
and as long as there is conceptual construction, the afflictions— whose majesty remains unimpaired— dwell within the continuum of the mind.
And as long as there are afflictions, the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)— which is the production of a succession of births fashioned by karma— also proceeds with its course entirely unimpeded.
Therefore, it is determined that the emptiness of all phenomena alone— because it is the antidote to ignorance— is the cause for severing the continuity of saṃsāra,
and not the mere vision of the truths.
This very point was stated by the venerable Master:
Liberation arises from the vision of emptiness; for that purpose, one should practice all meditations without exception.
Thus, how the Noble Truths are included within the two truths has already been demonstrated previously. Enough of this digression. Moreover—
For those whose minds possess a focal point, even nirvana is unstable.
Thus, it is not only the state of being a monk,
but rather even nirvāṇa as well; such is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also).
Nirvana, through its dissociation from the afflictions, is without substrate-remainder; it is difficult to abide in and difficult to accomplish.
In that regard, he first states the inconsistency of being a monk:
"If liberation results from the abandonment of the afflictions, let it occur immediately thereafter.
And if the afflictions are abandoned through the vision of the Noble Truths,
and liberation arises from that,
then let that liberation occur immediately after that— right following the abandonment of the afflictions.
Let it be so;
for who indeed would say otherwise?
This is not the case.
Why is this so? He says:
"And their capacity is observed even in the case of karma that is free from afflictions. (Bca 9.46)

What is the reason? It is seen and understood through scripture (*āgama*). Because in those noble ones such as Ārya-Maudgalyāyana and Ārya-Aṅgulimāla, whose afflictions have been abandoned, there exists efficacy—the power with respect to the bestowing of the fruit.
Therefore, liberation does not occur immediately following that [death].
Of what is the efficacy observed?
It is the efficacy of karma, characterized as wholesome or unwholesome.
Is it [the case] previously, in the non-noble state, for karma accompanied by afflictions?
No, he says: even for karma that is without affliction—that is, devoid of the cooperation of afflictions.
But surely, through the vision of the truths, ignorance and the rest are abandoned;
through their abandonment, craving is also abandoned by way of the sequential abandonment of the formative forces and so forth;
and craving, as well as the perversions of mind, are the causes for the arising of renewed existence.
And therefore, due to the absence of those two [ignorance and craving], even though karma exists—just as a seed devoid of husks [does not sprout]—nothing at all is obstructed. As it has been said:
"By the power of false knowledge and the volition arising from the thirst born thereof, one undergoes birth and goes to inferior states; having abandoned these, one is not born again."
Thus it is said;
or alternatively, craving alone is the cause of renewed existence,
because it constitutes the aspect of origination (*samudaya*).
For it was said by the Blessed One: "In that regard, what is the noble truth of the origin?
It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there."
Nandinī, they are as follows: craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence.
Thus, for one who has no craving and for whom the origin [of suffering] has been abandoned, there is no possibility of rebirth due to the absence of its cause.
Raising this point as the opponent's intention, he says:
If it is thoroughly considered that craving does not exist as grasping— that is,
if it is determined and ascertained that, due to the abandonment of ignorance, craving is no longer the cause for grasping at renewed existence— then [it follows that there is no grasping].
Then this should not be said;
because for those who hold the view of apprehension (*upalambha-dṛṣṭi*), the abandonment of ignorance (*avidyā*) is impossible,
and due to its existence, the abandonment of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is likewise non-existent.
Or let it be so; nevertheless, it is said:
"Is it that even this non-afflicted craving does not exist for them, while delusion does? (Bca 9.47)

Even though it is non-afflicted (*akliṣṭa*) and even though it is not associated with the afflictions (*kleśāsaṃprayukta*), does this craving (*tṛṣṇā*) not exist, or is it impossible for these yogins?
How so? Like delusion (*saṃmoha*), that is, like non-afflicted ignorance (*akliṣṭājñāna*).
Thus, he says that even in this way, craving cannot be prevented:
"Craving has feeling as its condition, and these [beings] possess feelings;
feeling has contact as its condition."
And craving has feeling as its condition;
that feeling is the cause of craving for these [beings],
while craving is its effect.
How can it be asserted that [the effect] does not exist even when the cause is complete?
If it is argued that for one who is free from ignorance (*niravidya*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*) does not arise even in the presence of sensation (*vedanā*), we say no;
for it has already been stated that for those who are attached to the existence of things (*bhāvābhiniveśin*), freedom from ignorance itself is unestablished.
Therefore, even if craving is not admitted to exist like non-afflicted ignorance, it nevertheless follows by the force of logic that it must exist until there is the vision of emptiness.
This is the collective meaning here: when the capacity of karma to yield its fruit is observed even in the continuum of one who is liberated, (Bcp 209)
And since craving is possible only when sensation exists, the abandonment of the afflictions would likewise remain doubtful; how, then, could one reach a certainty regarding liberation?
Therefore, without emptiness, the state of a monk does not appear as firmly established. As it has been said:
"For those whose minds possess an object of focus, even nirvāṇa is unstable.
Demonstrating this, he says:
"A mind that possesses an object of focus must remain wherever it may be. (Bca 9.48)
One should abide with and become attached by means of a mind that has an object and possesses apprehension—
whether toward this or that, toward those various points of attachment such as the Noble Truths or the fruits of their cultivation.
If there is no cessation of rebirth when there is the possibility of attachment, how could even Nirvāṇa not be in doubt when there is the possibility of rebirth?

Therefore, it is said that emptiness itself is the cause of liberation; thus he says: "Without emptiness, the mind arises again bound; as in the case of the attainment of non-perception, one should therefore cultivate emptiness. (Bca 9.49)
Without emptiness—that is, apart from emptiness—the mind, which is consciousness, remains bound and constrained by the snare of attachment to its object.
Even though it may cease for some time through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it arises again; that is, it is subject to rebirth.

He asks, "Where has this been seen? and replies: "As in the case of the attainment of non-conception. The meaning is that just as for those entering the attainment of non-conception there is the re-arising of mind and mental factors after their cessation for a certain period of time, so it is in other cases as well.
And this is an illustration; it should also be understood as applying to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), for example.
Alternatively:

Just as when those entering the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti) are reborn among the non-percipient gods (asaṃjñideva), even though their minds and mental factors have ceased for many hundreds of eons, they arise once again upon the completion of the ripening fruit (vipākaphala) of that attainment; so it is here. For without emptiness (śūnyatā), neither the state of a monk nor nirvāṇa is possible.
Therefore, he says "one should cultivate" and so forth, [teaching] that emptiness alone should be cultivated by those who seek both [nirvāṇa and enlightenment].
For the reason that, without emptiness, the mind arises again bound,
for that reason one who seeks nirvāṇa and the like should cultivate emptiness itself.
For the cultivation of that [wisdom] brings about the abandonment of the afflictions and the attainment of nirvāṇa;
it is not the case that the cultivation of the truths and so forth alone does so,
because they possess an objective referent (sālambanatvāt).
As it is said in the noble *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*:
"What do you think, Subhūti, does it occur to a stream-enterer thus: 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied: "Certainly not, Blessed One."
For what reason?
Because, Blessed One, he has not entered into anything;
therefore he is called a "stream-enterer."
He has not entered into form, nor sounds, nor odors, nor tastes, nor tangibles, nor mental phenomena;
therefore he is called a "stream-enterer.
Blessed One, if it should occur to a stream-enterer, "I have attained the fruit of stream-entry," [he would no longer be a stream-enterer].
That itself would be for him a grasping at a self, a grasping at a sentient being, a grasping at a soul, and a grasping at a person. [The same applies to the rest.
What do you think, Subhūti? Does it ever occur to an Arhat, "I have attained Arhatship"?
Subhūti said: "Certainly not, Blessed One.
And why is that?
Because there is no dharma whatsoever that is called 'Arhat'."
If, Blessed One, it should occur to an Arhat, "I have attained Arhatship," that itself would be for him a grasping at a self.
[The same applies to the rest.]
The Blessed One said: "Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should thus generate a mind that is non-abiding;
he should generate a mind that does not abide anywhere;
he should not generate a mind that abides in form."
"One should not give rise to a mind that is established in sound, smell, taste, or tangible objects.
Therefore, it is established that emptiness alone is the path to enlightenment.
[Added:
If a statement is accepted as being spoken by the Buddha because it appears in a sūtra, why is the Mahāyāna not considered to be largely identical to your own sūtras? (Bca 9.50)
If everything were faulty because of one [text] that is not being studied,
then why is everything spoken by the Victor not [accepted as authoritative] simply because of one [text] that is equal to a sūtra?
"If even the words of those headed by Mahākāśyapa cannot be fathomed, who will accept that which you do not understand? [Who will make it their own? (Bca 9.52).
The three verses beginning with *yatsūtre 'vataret* appear to have been rejected by someone."
Because it was established by way of departure,
the introduction to this investigation is the contradiction regarding scripture;
for there is dispute concerning scripture in such cases as "the teaching" and "the state of being a monk."
It would have been more appropriate to state this earlier, as it belongs to a different stage of the argument;
for the author to introduce again a point of dispute that was interrupted by this [intermediate matter] would indicate a lack of skill in his exposition.
Furthermore, since the meaning of the two preceding verses has already been expressed by the words "yat-pratyaya" and so forth.
Because the statement beginning with "headed by Mahākāśyapa" is indecorous, it is certain that it was not employed by the author of the treatise;
therefore, this is indeed an interpolation.
It might be argued: "Just as liberation would not occur because attachment arises toward a mind that has an object (*sālambana*), so too fear arises even regarding emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Therefore, it is more appropriate to remain within cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) itself by avoiding both. To this, he says:
But through non-liberation from attachment and fear, one’s persistence in cyclic existence is established;
this is the fruit of emptiness for the sake of those who suffer due to delusion. (Bca 9.53)
Attachment is clinging;
terror is fear,
[arising] from hearing about emptiness.
This is because its meaning is not fully understood. "Attachment and fear" is a collective compound (*samāhāra*).
Therefore, by avoiding both extremes, one's establishment—that is, one's abiding—becomes realized within *saṃsāra*, which has the three realms as its intrinsic nature.
The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of refuting the objection;
that is to say, this would be a refutation [only] if emptiness were accepted,
whereas [our position] is a common refutation.
Why? Because of non-liberation (*anirmukti*).
The instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of cause;
the meaning is "due to the absence of liberation."
Of whom? Of those beings who are suffering, afflicted by the sufferings of birth and so forth within the saṃsāra of the five destinies.
How? Regarding the object—that is, with respect to the sphere of objects—through delusion, which is ignorance.
"By means of non-attachment to objects" is the meaning.
Therefore, this is the fruit of emptiness: that one returns once more and remains within saṃsāra.

This is the intended meaning: just as there can be no liberation for one who perceives through the view of apprehension (*upalambha-dṛṣṭi*) apart from emptiness (*śūnyatā*), so too the fool—whose mind is intent on the pleasure of attachment to sense objects, who is terrified and cowed by the fear of the emptiness of all phenomena, and who thinks it better to remain in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—turns away from the bliss of tranquility (*praśama-sukha*). Experiencing the sufferings of birth and so forth, he remains once again in that very same state.
Thus, what has been established by this?
Others, however, considering the reading to be *saktitrāsāntanirmuktayā*, explain it as follows: because it is the cause of attachment (*sakti*), "attachment" (*sakti*) is a locus of clinging;
because it is the cause of fear (*trāsa*), "fear" (*trāsa*) is a locus of dread. These two are the "extremes" (*anta*); thus, they are the extremes of attachment and fear (*saktitrāsāntau*).
This means the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism.
For it is thus: attachment arises from the view of eternalism, and fear arises from the view of nihilism.
By being freed from those two, that is, by their relinquishment;
the third [case] is as before:
that which is the avoidance of the extreme of eternalism through the investigation of ultimate reality.
And by the acceptance of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), the extreme of nihilism (ucchedānta) is abandoned;

thus, by avoiding the extremes of superimposition (samāropa) and denial (apavāda), this middle way (madhyamā pratipad) is demonstrated. To show what is thereby accomplished, he says: "In cyclic existence (saṃsāra), stability is established."
For one who is unstained by the defects of saṃsāra through wisdom, because of being dependent on compassion, a state—meaning a stable abiding—is accomplished and achieved within saṃsāra.

For what purpose? For the sake of those who suffer; that is, for the sake of those wandering in saṃsāra who suffer, due to the desire to completely uproot their suffering, arising from the quality of sharing in the suffering of others.
Now, one might object: "In ultimate reality, those called 'transmigrating beings' do not exist at all;

so how can they have such a state? To this he says: "Because of delusion (*moha*), because of error (*viparyāsa*), and because of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), a sentient being (*sattva*) is perceived.
This point will be made explicit later in the verse: "But for the sake of the cessation of suffering, the delusion regarding what is to be done is not prevented" (9.77).
Therefore, this is the fruit of emptiness:
that although one remains in cyclic existence through compassion, one is not defiled by the faults of cyclic existence due to the vision of emptiness.
This non-abiding nirvana is the fruit of emptiness.
Because this [abiding] does not exist apart from emptiness,
those who desire to remain for the sake of sentient beings throughout the cycle of existence must cultivate emptiness alone.
Demonstrating all of this by way of summary, he says:
"Thus, in this manner, a refutation against the position of emptiness is not tenable.

This means that the refutation stated above against the position of emptiness—that because of fear of emptiness, the characteristic of remaining in cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is neither tenable nor consistent—is [not valid], because of the resolution that will be stated hereafter.
Thus is the application [of the argument] to the first position. Since this is so:
"Therefore, emptiness must indeed be cultivated with freedom from doubt. (Bca 9.54)
Having emerged from doubt, being free from uncertainty and devoid of hesitation,
one who exists as such must indeed cultivate and repeatedly practice emptiness— the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena— by means of the yoga of non-apprehension.
By this, what was stated— "not without this path" [9.41]— is concluded. Furthermore, regarding what was asked— "what is the use of the vision of emptiness?"—
he states the specific distinction of emptiness therein:
For emptiness is the antidote to the darkness of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations;
how could one who desires omniscience quickly not cultivate it? (Bca 9.55)
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are attachment and the rest;
the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are fivefold.
The word "obscuration" (*āvṛti*), however, is connected with both.
The afflictions (*kleśa*) themselves are the obscuration;
furthermore, the knowable (*jñeya*) is the obscuration in the sense of being a veil—this should be applied by making such a distinction.
The knowable itself is the obscuration because its nature is superimposed.
That very [ignorance] is like darkness because it obscures the true nature of reality;
its opposite is the cause for its abandonment.
Indeed, because it is emptiness (*śūnyatā*),

therefore he is so described as one who possesses a desire or longing for omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), that is, for Buddhahood, quickly and with haste; or alternatively, "one who desires omniscience" (*sarvajñatākāma*) means one who wishes for omniscience.
"How does one not cultivate that? means: how does one not cultivate—that is, not practice—that emptiness? Rather, one should indeed cultivate it with great effort.
Regarding what was also said— that there would be no engagement with emptiness due to fear—
that too is not tenable; thus he says, "That which is suffering," and so forth.
Regarding the second position, however, it should be introduced in this way: "This benefit indeed exists in emptiness;
the only thing is that, because of fear toward it from the very outset, one would not engage with it. He says: "Let fear arise from that object which gives rise to suffering."
Emptiness is the pacifier of suffering; therefore, why should fear arise from it?
While fear and dread may indeed arise from an object that produces suffering and causes affliction,
emptiness, on the contrary, is the pacifier of suffering and the remover of all the miseries of saṃsāra.
Therefore, what kind of cause could there be for fear to arise in a timid person toward that emptiness, which is a state of fearlessness?
The intended meaning is that, because it is the source of all virtues, love alone is appropriate toward it.
For fear arises in those who do not know reality from the egoism produced by the grasping at a self.
And since that self has a form superimposed by conceptual construction, egoism too is without a basis due to its absence; demonstrating this, he says:
"If there were something called 'I' from which fear might arise, then let fear come from wherever it may."
If I myself am nothing at all, for whom will there be fear?
From whatever source—whether from a place of fear or a place of fearlessness—let there be fear.
When? If indeed "I" were something;
by "I," the object of the notion of self (ahaṃpratyaya) is indicated.
The word "I" (aham) refers to whatever entity whatsoever is known through the notion of "I";
it is neuter because its specific description is unmanifest.
In that case, fear is indeed appropriate.
Furthermore, when I myself am nothing at all— not a real entity when examined— and am nothing other than a mere verbal conceptualization, then for whom is there fear?
For the "I" does not exist.
"It will come to be" means "it will arise.
The sense is that through this very investigation, fear is turned away. As it has been said:
"I am not, I shall not be; there is nothing for me, there shall be nothing."
Thus, for the fool there is terror; for the wise man, there is the destruction of fear.
Thus.
And demonstrating how the object of the notion of "I" is non-existent because it is shown to be a mere conceptual construction, he says:
I am not the teeth, hair, or nails; nor am I the bone, nor am I the blood; nor am I the mucus, nor the phlegm, nor the pus, nor even the lymph.
The teeth, hair, and nails are not I; each of these individually is not an object of the notion of "I. Neither is the bone, nor am I the blood.
The bone is the market;
the blood is the gore.
These two as well are not "I," nor am I they.
Nasal mucus, phlegm, and pus:
nasal mucus is the moisture discharged from the nostrils;
phlegm is that which issues from the mouth cavity.
Pus is ripened blood in a wound;
these also do not constitute me, nor does the lymph.
The synovial fluid is the moisture of the wound; that too am not I.
I am not the fat, nor the sweat, nor the marrow, nor the blood;
I am not the entrails, the nirguṇḍī, nor the excrement and urine.
"I am not fat, nor am I sweat, nor am I marrow-fat.
Fat (*vasā*) is the bodily oil;
sweat (*sveda*) is perspiration.
Fat is the fourth element;
these too are not I, nor are the intestines I.
The intestines are well known;
I am not even they,
nor am I the *antranirguṇḍī*, the *antranirguṇḍī* that is subtle in nature.
That too is not me;
I am neither feces nor urine, nor is I excrement.
Even this duality does not exist, nor am I.
I am not flesh, nor sinew, nor heat, nor am I wind;
I am not the cavities, nor in any way the six consciousnesses.
I am not flesh, nor sinew, nor heat;
sinew is [flesh],
and heat is the element of bodily fire.
These are not me either;
nor am I the wind,
for the wind is characterized by inhalation, exhalation, and so forth.
That [body] is certainly not I,
nor are the apertures such as the eyes; they too are not I.
Nor are the six consciousnesses in every respect—
the six being eye-, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness;
these also do not constitute a self.
In every way and by every means—whether individually or collectively [the self is not perceived].
For, when analyzed, the body is perceived as consisting precisely of a collection of teeth and so forth; and that [collection], individually, is not something cognizable through the notion of "I."
Because the notion of "I" does not exist with respect to each of those [parts] individually;
for even according to others, hairs and so forth are not objects of the notion of "I" when taken one by one.
Even when combined, they remain merely those same [parts] as before.
Nor can any single entity exist within those things when they are combined,
because such a thing will be refuted later;
nor can multiple things, even when combined, be the object of a single cognition.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single cognition to be erroneous with respect to many [objects],
nor can reality be established on the basis of error.
Therefore, it is certain that this [notion] is merely a conceptual construction, appearing as the object "I" while being empty of any referent.
And this was stated in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* in the context of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*):
"In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth, dirt, filth, skin, flesh, bone, sinews, veins,
the heart, the spleen, the lungs, the intestines, the mesentery, the stomach, the large intestine, the abdominal fat, and the liver."
Feces, tears, sweat, saliva, nasal mucus, fat, lymph, marrow, adipose tissue, bile, phlegm, pus, blood, brain matter, and urine—
in these substances, the Bodhisattva is by nature one who investigates.
Furthermore, we shall explain this later at the conclusion of the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Thus, the specific notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) is indeed devoid of an objective referent.
It might be argued as follows: even if hair and so forth are not objects cognized by the "I-notion," nevertheless, it does not follow that this [notion] is without an object;
for the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that the "I-notion" has as its domain only a person (puruṣa) who functions internally.
This also is not tenable,
because this notion of "I" appears as consisting precisely of the reflective awareness in such forms as "I am fair," "I am thin," "I am tall," or "I am walking.
And yet, this nature is not accepted by others [the proponents of the self] as belonging to the self.
Furthermore, it is not logical for one thing to be apprehended by a cognition that has a different form [than that thing], because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For instance, [if that were the case,] one who possesses that [object]...
Others describe its characteristics as follows:

first, the Naiyāyikas maintain that the self (*ātman*) is eternal, omnipresent, distinct for each living being, insentient by nature, yet sentient through its conjunction with consciousness; it is the substratum of qualities such as pleasure and the like, the agent of auspicious and inauspicious actions, the enjoyer of their fruits, and one who transmigrates to the next world.

The Vaiśeṣikas are also like the Naiyāyikas. As it has been said: "Others, however, here maintain that the self is the substratum of desire and the rest; by its own nature it is insentient, eternal, and likewise all-pervading."
It is the agent of pure and impure actions and the experiencer of their fruit; it is conscious due to its association with consciousness, not by its own nature.

Thus [it is said]. The followers of Jaimini (Jaiminīyas), however, maintain that the self (*ātman*) consists of consciousness (*caitanya*) which, by its nature as cognition (*buddhi*), undergoes transformation (*pariṇāmin*) and possesses the character of both exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*). And that consciousness has the very nature of cognition (*buddhi*).
And for that [Self], there is neither engagement nor withdrawal, because it possesses a nature that persists in both states.
For example, when a snake’s coiled state ceases and its straight state arises, the essence of being a snake persists in both. As it has been said:
Others, however, maintain that the self consists of both exclusion and inclusion,
and that its nature is consciousness, where consciousness is defined as the characteristic of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Just as the coiled state of a snake departs and immediately thereafter the straightened state arises, yet its nature as a snake does not cease; so it is here.
In the very same way, for the Self, whose nature is eternal consciousness,
there is neither a complete disappearance of its form nor a universal pervasion.
Thus [it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verses 222–224].
This is the distinction;
everything else is as before.
The Jains, like the followers of Jaimini, maintain that the self is conscious and consists of both substance and modes, characterized by persistence and change as appropriate.
Thus it has been said:
"Like the followers of Jaimini, the Jains declare another definition of consciousness."
It consists of the nature of substance and modification, characterized by exclusion and inclusion.

The followers of Kapila, however, maintain that the self is eternal, all-pervading, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and consists of consciousness by its very nature, and not [consciousness] through connection with the intellect (buddhi);
for the intellect is by its own nature non-conscious (acit).
Because of the statement that consciousness is the essential nature of the *puruṣa*,
he is neither the agent of any effect nor the enjoyer of its fruit himself.
Because it is devoid of activity,
primordial nature alone is its agent and the bringer of its fruit.
Under the influence of error, he superimposes that [object] upon his own self. For instance, when a longing arises in a person characterized by the enjoyment of objects such as sound,
then Nature (prakṛti), having become aware of the person's longing, joins with the person.
Thereafter, it creates the evolution of sound and the other objects.
When sound and the rest have been grasped as objects by the functions of the ear and the other senses under the direction of the mind, the intellect performs determination (*adhyavasāya*).
Then, the Puruṣa becomes conscious of the object as determined by the intellect. Thus it is said.

Thus, because its nature is consciousness, it is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), and because it is all-pervasive, it is inactive; such is the specific characteristic of the Sāṃkhya Puruṣa. And it has been said:
"Others consider consciousness to be distinct from the nature of the intellect (buddhi)."
And they conceive of consciousness as the innate nature of the self.
(Bcp 215) He merely enjoys the fruit brought forth by Pradhāna;
he possesses no agency at all, for that is considered to belong to Prakṛti alone.

The ignorant person, whose consciousness is perverted because it is shrouded by darkness, falsely imagines that "I am the doer" regarding these qualities of nature as they evolve; he is not even the master of the bending of a blade of grass.
Thus [it is said in the Sāṃkhyakramadīpikā 43].
However, the proponents of the Upaniṣads maintain that there is but one single, all-pervading, and eternal consciousness inherent within the entire continuum of living beings;
it is as a manifestation (*vivarta*) of that [consciousness] that this entire world—consisting of earth, water, wind, fire, and so forth—appears.
And the self (*ātman*) has precisely that as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

There exists no external object of cognition whatsoever—neither a composite whole (*avayavin*) nor atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth—that is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And it is said:
"This world, consisting of earth, fire, water, and so forth, is an eternal transformation (*vivarta*) of consciousness."
Others, however, maintain that the self is of the nature of that [consciousness].
Nothing whatsoever endowed with the characteristic of an object of apprehension exists here;
therefore, all this is examined as a transformation of consciousness.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, the Pudgalavādins— who are among the heterodox sectarians (tīrthika) who wander within [the Buddhist fold]—
maintain that there is a self called "pudgala" which is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from the aggregates (skandha).
Otherwise, there would be the appearance of an adherence to the tenets of non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika). And it has been said:
"Some, though considering themselves followers of the Sugata, even proclaim a self.
(Tattvasaṃgraha 336)
How could the self be the object of the notion of "I"?
Because it does not appear there in its own essential nature. Therefore, how can it be said that the self appears as the notion of "I"?
Therefore, it is established that this is mere conceptual construction,
arising without an external object.

Now, the Sāṃkhyas and others who maintain that the self is of the nature of consciousness (citsvabhāva), being unable to tolerate the negation of the self in relation to the six types of cognition, say: "We designate the cognition of sound and so forth as being of the nature of consciousness, which is itself the self; how then can its status as the self be denied?
Having anticipated this objection from the opponent, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), employing a reductio ad absurdum, says:
If it were the cognition of sound, then sound would be perceived at all times.
Indeed, if the self consists of the cognition of sound, then because that [self] is eternal, the cognition of sound would also be eternal.
In that case, sound too would have to be perceived as always and eternally present during both the time of its existence and the time of its non-existence;
for its nature, which is the apprehension of sound, would persist at all times throughout those periods of its presence and absence.
Otherwise, its very permanence would be lost.
If it is argued, "Let it be so; let it be exactly thus," he says:
"But what does it know without an object of knowledge, by virtue of which it is designated as 'knowledge'? (Bca 9.61)
Knowledge alone is eternally present;
however, because the word [the name] is occasional, its manifestation of existence does not occur at all times.
Consequently, at the time when that [word] is absent, what would that knowledge know, or what would it cognize, without the object of knowledge—that is, without an external object?
The word "tu" (but/however) functions to specify the time of non-existence in the question.
By means of that object of knowledge (*jñeya*), even cognition (*jñāna*) is described—that is, it is designated as such;
for it is called "cognition" because it knows the object of knowledge.
The intention is: "In the absence of that [object], how can there be cognition?"
He says this very thing:
"If that which does not know were knowledge, it would follow that a piece of wood is knowledge;
for even that which does not know an object [would be knowledge]."
If even that were called "knowledge," then it would follow that wood, which has the nature of non-knowledge, is knowledge;
for it has committed no offense by which it should not be consciousness.
But this is not the case.
Therefore, because there is no thorough knowledge of the object, just as wood does not become cognition, so too would anything else not be [cognition]; thus he says:
Therefore, it is certain that there is no cognition of an object of knowledge that is not present.
Because there is no cognition that lacks an object,

for that reason it is certain— this is a definitive conclusion— that there exists no such cognition whose apprehended object (*grāhya*) is an absent thing, meaning an object situated in an inaccessible location. This is the absolute certainty.
Because it is dependent.
It might be argued: "Since the word (śabda) exists at all times, verbal cognition does not have a non-present object as its domain;
however, its non-apprehension occurs only occasionally because its manifestation is occasional, and thus the aforementioned fault does not follow.
This is not so.
Since that form of this cognition which is its object of determination is called "manifest," the cognizer is designated as "non-cognition" because its object is not always present;
however, in the case of the word, its constant existence or non-existence is not intended to be expressed.
Since the probandum is established merely by the fact that cognition is sometimes non-apprehending,
it follows that by the statement "the object of knowledge is not present," the non-apprehending nature of cognition itself is being proven.
For in whatever form an object is the apprehended content of cognition, [in that same form it must be present].
Since it is not the case that this [sound] is always present, how is it that the aforementioned fault does not follow?
Just as sound does not exist at all times,
it is not explained here for fear of prolixity.
Moreover, if the self were nothing other than the cognition of sound, then,
because it would consist solely in the apprehension of that [sound], there would be no apprehension of form;
but this is not the case.
If it is argued that "that very [cognition] is intended to be the grasper of form," to this he replies with the words beginning "tadeva":
"If that very [cognition] knows the form, why does it not also hear?
If it is the opinion that that very cognition of sound knows the form..."
If it does not hear even then,
then why does it not hear even at the time of perceiving form;
why does it not perceive sound as well?
Because it is a cognition of sound. Or rather, it certainly does apprehend it,
provided that it were present.
Anticipating the opponent’s reply that "there is no fault because of the mere absence [of the object]," he says "of the word," and so forth:
"If [it is argued] that it is due to the absence of the word, then from that [absence], the cognition of that [object] would also be non-existent. (Bca 9.63)
If it is argued that there would be no perception of sound because, having become an object, it is not present due to being in an unsuitable location, then in that case,
even that cognition would be non-existent.
Therefore, in that case, because the word is not present, that cognition—though called "cognition of the word"—is non-existent (asat), meaning it does not truly exist;
the sense is that it is not actually a cognition of the word at all.
Furthermore: if [the cognition] were a cognition of sound, then it would not be logical for it to have the nature of apprehending form; thus he says "the apprehension of sound," etc.:
"How could that which has the nature of apprehending sound be the apprehension of form?"

How can that cognition which has the nature of apprehending sound— that is to say, which has the intrinsic character of apprehending sound— be the apprehension of form, having the apprehension of form as its essence?
It could not be so in any way whatsoever, because it is impossible for a single partless entity to possess two forms. [Objection:
But is it not the case that one and the same person can be a father in relation to someone else?
And depending on someone, that very same person may be a son;
likewise, in the present case as well, there will be two forms for a single entity. Thus he says, "One is both father and son," and so forth:
"One is conceived of as both father and son, but not in reality. (Bca 9.64)
It is conceived that the father alone is the progenitor and the son alone is the born; yet he is established through conceptual construction in relation to that [other],
but not in reality.
But this is not so from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

There is only a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that possesses both aspects; it is merely designated through conceptual superimposition (*kalpanā-samāropita*). Furthermore, although it is one, it is not truly expressed as manifold through various designations due to the differentiation of forms (*rūpa-bheda*). The two real forms belonging to both must be unified within the one.
And that [position] does not cohere in any way whatsoever, because it would entail the consequence that the entity itself is twofold due to being differentiated by two forms.
Therefore, just as a real entity cannot possess two forms, such a state does not exist in the subject of the example.
And as for that which is merely conceptual, it is irrelevant to the present context; thus, this [objection] is trivial.
For this reason as well, he says that this designation is not ultimate:
"Sattva, rajas, or even tamas—since there is neither son nor father.
And this you must necessarily accept: for in the Sāṃkhya system, the world is a single entity consisting of the three guṇas.

Then, the word "api" (also/even) signifies a collective aggregate, meaning the collection of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Since these qualities (*guṇas*), whether existing individually or combined, abide in their own respective natures, therefore,
from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is neither father nor son.
At all times there exist only the qualities (guṇas) alone.

This is the meaning: those qualities characterized by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* which exist in the state of being a son, remain exactly the same in their essential nature (*svabhāva*) before and after [the birth], even when they have attained the status of being a father.
Therefore, in relation to that [prior state], one is called both "father" and "son," yet there is no actual distinction therein;
thus, this conventional usage is purely conceptual.
And if, even at the time of perceiving a form, that single cognition were essentially the perception of sound, then its nature as such would be perceived;
yet it is not so perceived.
Therefore, he says "the grasping of sound," etc., [to show] that it does not have the nature of grasping that [object]:
"But its own nature as being conjoined with the grasping of sound is not observed. (Bca 9.65)
"Endowed with the apprehension of sound" means connected or associated with it.
The word "but" (tu) is used to indicate a distinction.
Its intrinsic nature—that of the cognition which grasps form—is not observed; that is, it is not perceived.
Therefore, it is determined that at that time, he possesses no capacity for perceiving sound.
This might be the case: even if it is not perceived, nevertheless, it is still that very same thing.
To the question, "How then is there the apprehension of form? he says, "That very same," and so forth:

In that very same way, like an actor, it too is impermanent; that is, the cognition of sound [is impermanent]. The remainder of the sense is: by means of another form—that is, by means of its own nature consisting in the apprehension of color—it apprehends color.
In what way is there conformity for him? Like an actor.
Just as an actor who has entered the stage at the time of a performance appears in various forms, though he is but one; (Bcp 218) so too is it with him.
Thus, there is no fault even in the present case.
To this, he replies: "That too is non-eternal," meaning it is impermanent; by abandoning its previous nature, it enters into another form.
Nor is it of one and the same nature at the earlier and later times, because the actor is connected with various forms.
Otherwise, one would have to say that its two forms exist simultaneously;
thus, the example is deficient in respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Furthermore, it might be argued: "The entity is that very same thing."
Furthermore, its intrinsic nature arises and ceases in succession;
therefore, he says "that very same [nature] is other," etc., to show that this is not a fault:
"If that very same thing were of another nature, then this would be a novel kind of identity. (Bca 9.66)
That very self is like an actor; if it is said that it has one nature [at one time] and another nature [at another], then...
Then, this oneness is unprecedented; this such oneness has never been seen before. Even when another nature arises from that entity, its oneness is its undifferentiated self-nature.
For instance: "that very same thing" is declared to be its reality (*tattva*), whereas "having another nature" implies that very same thing's alterity.
And it is not logical for these two mutually contradictory properties to belong to a single entity.

For an entity (*bhāva*) is not something other than its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), such that those two—arising and cessation—would not belong to the entity even though they belong to the intrinsic nature.

Nor is it logical for the entity to remain in its original state while the intrinsic nature, which is non-different from it, undergoes arising and cessation; for that would entail the consequence of the absence of non-difference.
The meaning is that, in the case of difference, the relationship cannot be established.
It might be argued: "Let this undesirable consequence indeed follow if this self possessed two real forms;
however, having set aside its own innate form, it possesses another form that is unreal.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply."
Anticipating this objection, he says, "If the other form is unreal," and so forth:
"If the other form is unreal, let that which is its own form be stated.
That other form is conditioned by the object, like a crystal stone; it is unreal, meaning it is not intrinsic.
If this is so, then let its own form be stated; let its own, innate form—that is, the true nature (tattva) of that self—be declared.
For it certainly does possess another form.
What is that? If it is consciousness—then if it is consciousness, it follows that all persons would be one.
The very nature of that [cognition] as consisting of knowledge, which persists through prior and subsequent times, is its own intrinsic form.
What else need be said?
[If it is claimed that it is one because, despite being connected to prior and subsequent forms other than itself, it remains like a crystal.]
In this way, the identity of all persons would follow as a logical consequence,
because [consciousness] possesses a common nature by virtue of being knowledge.
For example, just as there is indeed oneness between two distinct cognitions of sound occurring at earlier and later times, despite their having different forms, so too [is it here].

Likewise, it follows— and indeed occurs— that all sentient beings belonging to the various states of existence must be of one self-nature, because there is no distinction [between them] despite their factual difference.
Furthermore, this leads to an over-extension; thus he says "cetanā" and so forth:
"The unity of the conscious and the unconscious [is asserted] because their existence is equal.

Alternatively, if unity is asserted by setting aside some specific distinction that serves as the basis for internal differentiation and relying instead upon a certain common form, then consciousness would be the property of the *puruṣa*, while unconsciousness would be the property of *prakṛti* and so forth.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate further defects.
Those two would also be a single, non-different entity.
How so? Because the existence (*astitā*) of those two—the conscious and the unconscious—is identical;
and that [existence] is the intrinsic nature (*nijam rūpam*) of all things.
"Equal" means the same for both.

Now, one might object: "In this case as well, unity is indeed accepted as being based on similarity even when there is a difference in the entities; therefore, since this establishes what is desired, there is no fault. To this, he says "And the distinction," and so forth.
And when the distinction itself is false, what then can be the basis for similarity?
The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate another fault.
When there is no fixed rule regarding the distinction or difference (*viśeṣa*) between all entities, such that they are false or unreal,
then their own inherent nature (*nijam rūpam*) alone is real.
In that case, what would be the basis for similarity?
Depending on what is similarity established?
For if there were actual distinctness, similarity could only exist through a degree of commonality consisting of some mere portion.
And in the absence of any distinction, that [cow] would be that very thing itself, not something similar;
for if one did not perceive the specific difference of the cow between a cow and a gavaya, the gavaya would not be "similar to a cow," but rather would be a cow itself.
Therefore, the particular (viśeṣa) alone is the substratum of similarity.
And when that [particular] is not ultimately real,
then what could be the substratum or the basis for the similarity— the common form— of persons or of anything else?
The meaning is that there is nothing at all;
therefore, in reality, identity itself results for you,
not something produced by similarity.
How then can it be said that there is no fault because the point is already established?
Thus, the existence of a self (ātman) whose nature is consciousness, as imagined by the followers of Kapila, the Jains, and Jaimini, is unestablished.
Furthermore, the refutation should be stated, as appropriate, regarding the self imagined by the proponents of the Upaniṣads as well.
Now, in order to refute the conventional usage of a non-conscious self as postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others, he says "And non-conscious," and so forth:
"And I am certainly not non-conscious, because of my lack of consciousness, like a cloth and the like.
First of all, it is not tenable for the self to be conscious according to the sequence already explained.
The meaning of the word "also" (*api*) is that it is not logical for even the insentient (*acetana*) to be the self (*ātman*).
Why? Because of its lack of sentience (*ācaitanyāt*), that is, due to the absence of consciousness (*caitanyābhāvāt*).
It is called "insentient" because consciousness does not exist in it.
The state of that [non-existence] is "insentience" (ācaitanya);
the vowel lengthening of both members of the compound occurs as in the case of *pāralaukika* and similar words.
Therefore:
The meaning is "because of being insentient.
How so? Like cloth and so forth.
Just as cloth, trees, mountains, and the like are not the self because they lack consciousness, [so too is the body].
Likewise, it is also accepted [as such],
because its status as both object and agent is admitted;
otherwise, there would be no purpose for it.
And that is not possible for that which is insentient,
such as a cloth and the like;
even if it were indeed itself insentient, [it could not act].

Nevertheless, anticipating the opponent's intention—that "the intellect (buddhi) conceives through its association with consciousness (cetanā), and therefore this fault does not apply"—he says, beginning with "Now, if it were a knower," etc.:
"Now, if [the self] were a knower by virtue of its association with consciousness, it would follow that when [consciousness] is absent, the [self] would be an ignorant, non-existent being. (Bca 9.69)
The word "atha" (now/then) is used here in the sense of an inquiry.
Now, this self (*ātman*), although itself insentient due to its connection with consciousness (*cetanā*) and its inherence in the intellect (*buddhi*), becomes a knower (*jña*).
The form "jñaḥ" is derived from the root *jñā* with the suffix *kap*. Thus, it means "one who knows."
If it were accepted in this way, it would follow that the ignorant [self] is destroyed.
For when, in a state of intoxication or fainting, consciousness has ceased and this self is ignorant and knows nothing at all,
then it follows that it is destroyed— ruined— due to the abandonment of its nature as previously connected with consciousness.

(Bcp 220) Anticipating the following objection— that this fault does not arise because the self possesses a single nature at both times, whether it is connected with consciousness or not— the author says "But if it is unmodified," and so forth:
"But if the self is indeed unmodified, what has been done to it by consciousness?"
Now, if the self remains unmodified during the arising and ceasing of consciousness, being by nature neither produced nor ceased— if this is so, then what has been done for it by consciousness?
What has been done for this self, which is insentient and eternally unmodified, by means of consciousness through its inherence in the intellect (*buddhi*)?
What extraordinary quality has been produced [in the self]? Nothing at all.
Even if there were a conjunction with cognition (*buddhi*), the self would remain exactly as it was before, without its original nature having fallen away; thus, the self remains purely insentient.
This being the case, he asks: "What, then, have you accomplished?"—meaning, what has been achieved by you?
Thus, the nature of space—which is ignorant and inactive—is considered to be the self.
For the ignorant one—incapable of discerning even the slightest benefit or harm—who is "inactive" (*niṣkriya*), meaning one from whom action has departed or who stands outside of it;
for such a person, who is devoid of all remedies and cannot be refined because no excellence can be imparted to him;
or alternatively, for one who is like space, being either lacking the capacity for any action or devoid of the activities of moving and so forth, due to his lack of utility for the subject at hand.
This being so, the state of selfhood—that is, the establishment of the intrinsic nature of a self—is established. And this is an illustration according to one's own position:
just as space, by virtue of its lack of intrinsic nature, is empty of all activity and is a mere conceptual existence.
The meaning is that the self is likewise; or else, even according to the view of the opponent,
just as space does not possess the nature of being an agent, an object of action, and so forth, because it is insentient and inactive.
