Likewise, there is the state of self-satisfaction.
Now, however, setting forth another objection against the negation of the self from the perspective of an opponent, he says "na karma" and so on:
"If the connection between action and its fruit were not tenable without a self,
then there would be no single entity that goes to the next world."
In that case, without that self which goes to the next world, a connection between action and its fruit would be untenable;
for "action" refers to what is wholesome or unwholesome,
and "fruit" refers to the desirable or undesirable result of that very same action.
The connection between those two;
or the connection of the performed action with its fruit—
that very person by whom the action was performed [is connected with it].
That the attainment of that very fruit belongs to him alone and not to another is neither logical nor tenable;
yet, the connection between karma and its fruit in the next world is accepted.
And regarding this point, there is no disagreement even among the followers of the Sugata;
as it is said in a Sūtra:
"By this very person was the karma performed."
Who else shall experience [the result]?
For, monks, actions that have been performed and accumulated do not ripen in the earth element, nor in the water element, nor in the fire element, nor in the wind element.
They ripen only in the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases... [and so forth].
And it has been said:
"Karmas do not perish even in hundreds of millions of eons;
having met with the necessary conditions and the [proper] time, they surely bear fruit for embodied beings."
Thus,
the connection between action and its fruit remains unrefuted even for you.
Therefore, the self must necessarily be accepted;
otherwise, all of this would be inconsistent.
To explain how the connection between action and its fruit is possible if the self does not exist, he says: "Having performed an action," and so forth.
For when the agent has perished after performing an action, to whom will the fruit belong?
For indeed, since the agent of the action has perished— that is, having performed and produced an action characterized as wholesome or unwholesome, once that agent has ceased—
of whom will the fruit be?
Because there is no self that goes to another world,
and because the mental moment by which the action was performed has ceased at the time of performing that action due to its momentariness;
To whom will the fruit of an action performed—consisting of pleasure or pain in a happy or miserable rebirth—belong, or how will it arise?
It would belong to no one at all;
for in the next world, some other person who was not the very one who performed the action would arise as the possessor of that fruit.
Thus, there would be the destruction of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done.
And this is merely an illustration;

if it were held that memory, recognition, doubt, ascertainment, the searching for a thing previously hidden by oneself, curiosity regarding a seen object, the cessation [of curiosity], the relation of cause and effect, the means of knowledge for apprehending those, bondage, liberation, and so forth, would also not exist.
He says "that is not tenable" and so forth: "In both of us," etc.—when the fruit of the action is established as having distinct substrata for both of us.
"In both of us" means for both of us.
For you, who maintain the doctrine of a self, and for me, who maintain the doctrine of selflessness,
this is established and certain.
What is established? He says: the action and its fruit have distinct substrata; the action occurs in this life, while its fruit occurs in the next world.
These two are established as having distinct substrata, that is, different loci.
For instance, one does not experience the fruit after death with the very same body by which one performed the action in that birth;
therefore, the agent of the action is indeed different [from the experiencer].
And that other [agent] is the enjoyer of the fruit;
therefore, the action and its fruit reside in different substrates. And on this point, there is no disagreement between us.

It might be argued: "Without the activity of a self, those very states of being an agent and an enjoyer would not exist. To this he says: "But surely, the claim that 'the self is inactive therein' is in vain. (Bca 9.72)
It is inactive, meaning devoid of activity.
In that regard, the self (ātman) is incapable of performing either of those two—namely, action or the enjoyment of its fruit—because it is devoid of action and lacks consciousness;
furthermore, due to its eternality, it is not capable of any action whatsoever.
As it has also been said:
"Its agency is said to consist in its connection with mere cognition and so forth;
whereas its state as an enjoyer consists in its inherence in the experience of pleasure, pain, and so on."
Thus, even that [position] is not tenable according to the aforementioned sequence for one whose nature remains unchanging across prior and subsequent times. Therefore,
regarding this self which is devoid of activity, both assertion and dispute are in vain and fruitless.
Because it is of no utility toward that purpose for which it was accepted;
the word "nanu" is used to address the opponent.
Now, one might object: "If the self does not exist, how then would faults such as the loss of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*) not occur?
Therefore, that doctrine [of the self] is not in vain. To this, he says "having a cause," and so forth:
"It is seen that one who possesses a cause is joined with a fruit; this is not possible" means that he who possesses a cause is conjoined with action.

That very one who possesses the fruit is connected with the fruit; thus, this possibility is neither seen nor perceived. Why? Because it is indeed one person who dies in the world and quite another who is born.
Consequently, the connection between a cause and its fruit is not perceived.
How, then, is this [scriptural passage] to be interpreted: "This very person performed the action; who else shall experience its result?"
Regarding this, it is said: "Relying on the unity of the continuum, it is taught that there is an agent and an enjoyer" (Bca 9.73).

Based on the unity of the continuum— which is characterized by a succession of many successive moments and functions through the relation of cause and effect— and taking as its basis the unity superimposed upon the many through the force of worldly convention, it is taught that there is an "agent" and an "experiencer," [expressed as]: "He who is the agent of the action is the very same one who experiences its fruit."
Although this has been taught, it was revealed by the Blessed One through the power of intentional meaning (*neyārtha*);
otherwise, people might imagine the annihilation of karma and its fruit. Yet, by that much alone, the existence of a being that migrates from one world to another was not declared.
And for this very reason, it is stated in that same [text]: "They ripen only within the appropriated aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.
Likewise, because of the statement: "Karma is volition (cetanā) and karma after having willed (cetayitvā). Thus it has been said:
The variety of the world is born of karma; that consists of volition and what is produced by it. Volition is mental karma; from it arise vocal and bodily karma.
Thus it is said.
It is also stated elsewhere:
"The mind alone constructs the world of sentient beings and the world of the environment, in all their great variety."
For it has been said that the entire world is born of karma; and karma does not exist apart from the mind.
Thus [it is said in the *Madhyamakāvatāra* 6.89]. Therefore, there is no karma other than that which is dissociated from the mind.

And that wholesome or unwholesome mind, upon arising and ceasing, deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*)—consisting of specific formative forces (*saṃskāra*) such as the wholesome and unwholesome—within the momentary mental state that it itself produces.

Furthermore, that [mind], imbued with the latent impressions (vāsanā) deposited by those [actions] and proceeding as a continuum through an uninterrupted succession of subsequent moments conditioned by them,

undergoes a specific transformation (pariṇativiśeṣa) and brings about in the next world a fruit consisting of the very nature of pleasure and so forth, which is mental in essence and corresponds to the particularity of the action.

For example, the earth, seeds, and so forth, having attained excellence through specific conditions of mutual proximity, produce a particular quality conducive to the arising of the effect within the second moment—which is their own appropriated collection—at the very first moment.

By means of generating this successive gradation, they reach the ultimate limit of excellence characterized by the final moment; and through a specific transformation of the continuum (*saṃtatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*), they produce a rice or *kodrava* sprout that corresponds to its seed.
And just as a seed of a citron or similar fruit, when saturated with lac-dye and sown, produces redness in its flowers and so forth due to the continuous succession of that refinement,
yet there is no single persisting entity therein that follows from the earlier time to the later time;
such is also the case for that which is common to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Because it is presented as a mental construction (*kalpanā*), its presentation [as a real entity] is not tenable. As it has been said:
"In whichever very continuum the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) is deposited..."
It bears fruit right there, just as redness appears in cotton.
Thus, just as in the case of seeds and the like, a specific effect and its production occur sequentially even in the absence of a self (ātman),

so too in the present case, even without a single entity that migrates to the next world, the result is strictly determined because the relationship between cause and effect itself acts as the regulator.
Because the continuum, conditioned by afflictions and karma, proceeds without interruption, the attainment of a fruit in a future life is explained;
thus, neither the "accrual of what was not done" nor the "loss of what was done" serves as a refutation.
Therefore, without a self, the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable.

And just as that [self] is not tenable even when a self exists, so too, were it to be explained in detail along with its elaborations, it would become excessively prolix; therefore, it is not expanded upon here. And it has been said:
"The self does not exist; there is only the aggregates, conditioned by afflictions and karma."
By means of the continuity of the intermediate state, it enters the womb like a lamp.
Thus,
because those who propound the person (pudgala) accept the position that it is neither identical to nor different from [the aggregates], they have themselves refuted its status as a real entity;
for a real entity cannot transcend the categories of being either identical to or different from [something else].
Because two things that are mutually exclusive are such that the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other;
the *Bhārahāra-sūtra* and others have also been established in this sense.
Therefore, this [notion] has been imagined by those who do not understand the Buddha’s intentional teaching.
It is not a real entity;
for if its status as a real entity were admitted, there would be no difference [between it and the self],
and thus it is refuted simply by the refutation of the self.
Thus, it has not been specifically refuted;
and this was said by the Blessed One:
"In this way, monks, there is karma."
There is a fruit,
but no agent is found who abandons these aggregates and takes up other aggregates.
Except for the conventional designation of phenomena (dharmasaṃketa).
Herein, this is the conventional designation of phenomena: when this exists, that comes to be.
"From the arising of this, that arises."

By this, the Blessed One has indeed demonstrated that the relationship between cause and effect is characterized solely by "conditionality upon this" (*idampratyayatāmātra*). Furthermore, by the phrase "of the continuum" (*saṃtānasya*)—or rather, by the phrase "the continuum is one"—it is indicated that its essential nature is not defined according to conventional usage; for by the term "continuum," one accepts only conditionality upon this.
Otherwise, there would be no continuum at all.
Therefore, the faults that arise from the existence of a real causal relationship are not avoided.
This very point was also stated by the venerable Master:
If it is argued that everything is powerless, [we reply: the power of seeds and so forth toward sprouts and so forth is observed;
if that power is held to exist, let it be so according to conventional reality (saṃvṛti).
Thus,
by the very fact of the specific determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), the absence of memory is also refuted;
since there is no single persisting self (*anugamātman*), no rememberer whatsoever exists here.
Rather, memory alone, by virtue of superimposition, has as its object the thing being remembered.
And there is no contradiction here even in the absence of a rememberer;

for when an object has been experienced, because the seed of memory is deposited within the continuum of consciousness, the effect called "memory" arises at a later time due to the ripening of that continuum.
In this same way, recognition and other such arguments are also to be understood.
For fear of excessive prolixity, they are not individually refuted here; therefore, their detailed justification should be sought elsewhere.
All this has been established by relying upon conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

However, in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), because all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and because all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have ceased, nothing whatsoever— whether possessing a self or being selfless— is produced or ceases.
Furthermore, when investigated, neither action nor its fruit exists,
nor does this world or the next;
for they are merely constructed by conceptualization.
Therefore, all this arises and ceases like a reflection, being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Cause and effect are described as having a self (*sātmaka*) or being without a self (*nirātmaka*), and as permanent or impermanent.
Like a dream, there is the state of being an agent and an object of action.
The enjoyment of its fruit, this world, and the next world.
And the going to happy or miserable destinies occurs because of the non-abandonment of conceptual constructions;
thus, everything is well-established.
As he will say:
Thus, in reality, there is neither cessation nor existence;
therefore, this entire world is unborn and unceasing.
"The realms of existence are like dreams; when investigated, they are like plantain trees," and so forth.
And it has been said:

You have stated that the agent is independent and that the action is also so, from the perspective of conventional usage; however, the establishment of both of these is intended by you to be mutually dependent.
There is no agent, nor is there an enjoyer; merit and demerit are born dependently.
O Lord of Speech, you have declared that whatever is dependently arisen is not truly born.
Thus: [Catuḥ 2.8–9] Just as all phenomena are selfless, yet there is no contradiction regarding the connection between action and its fruit,
and they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).

And just as there is no contradiction with all phenomena as they have been seen, so it was taught in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*. As it was said—the Blessed One declared: "In the very same way, Great King, an ignorant, unlearned ordinary person, having seen forms with the eye that are conducive to mental pleasure, becomes attached to them."
Being thus obsessed, he is led toward it; being led toward it, he becomes passionately attached;
being passionately attached, he performs threefold karma born of passion by means of the body.
It is fourfold by way of speech and threefold by way of mind.
And that karma, once it has been performed, is from the very beginning exhausted, ceased, vanished, and transformed; it does not remain depending upon the eastern direction.
not the south, not the west, nor the north;
Neither above, nor below, nor in the intermediate directions;
Not here, not across, nor in between the two.

Furthermore, at another time, when the moment of death has arrived, with the cessation of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) due to the exhaustion of the lifespan and the depletion of its corresponding karma, it becomes the objective support (*ālambana*) for the final consciousness as it is ceasing.
It is just like, for example, a "Beauty of the Land" (*janapadakalyāṇī*) to one who has just woken from sleep.

Thus, O Great King, with the final consciousness as the dominant condition and that karma as the object-condition, the first consciousness belonging to the stage of rebirth arises through these two conditions—
whether it be among the denizens of hell or in the animal realm.
whether in the world of Yama, or in the realm of the asuras, or among human beings;
Or [if it is] among the gods;
and immediately after that first consciousness belonging to the state of rebirth has ceased, a homogeneous mental continuum proceeds,
wherein there is maturation.
It is known through the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*):
therein, the cessation of the final consciousness is designated by the term "death" (*cyuti*).
The manifestation of the first consciousness is what is called "rebirth" there.
Thus, Great King, no dharma whatsoever goes from this world to the next world.
Death and rebirth are thus discerned.
And that final consciousness, O Great King, when arising, does not come from anywhere;
when ceasing, it does not go anywhere.
Karma, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go anywhere.
The first consciousness, too, when arising, does not come from anywhere.
When it ceases, it does not go anywhere.
Why is that? Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.
The final consciousness is empty of the final consciousness;
karma is empty of karma;
the initial consciousness is empty of the initial consciousness.
Death is empty of death; rebirth is empty of rebirth;
yet the non-futility of karmic actions is made known.
And there is the experience of the maturation;
therein there is no agent, nor any experiencer.
Except for the conventional designation of names.
Thus is the detailed explanation.
In the same way, the formation of karma through hatred and delusion should also be stated according to what is appropriate.
It is also said in the Śālistamba Sūtra:
"Furthermore, non-comprehension of reality, false comprehension, and ignorance are what constitute avidyā (ignorance).
When avidyā exists in this way, three kinds of saṃskāras (formative forces) are produced: those leading to merit,"
Those leading to demerit and those leading to the imperturbable—
these are called the formations conditioned by ignorance.
For formations leading to merit, there arises consciousness that leads only to merit.
For volitional formations leading to demerit, consciousness leads to demerit; for volitional formations leading to the imperturbable, consciousness leads to the imperturbable.
This is called "consciousness conditioned by volitional formations."
That very consciousness is the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Through the growth of name-and-form, functional activities proceed by way of the six sense bases;
therefore, that name-and-form is said to be the condition for the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
From the six sense bases, the six groups of contact arise;
this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.
Whatever the nature of the contact is, a feeling of that same nature arises.
This is called feeling conditioned by contact;
that which experiences it and specifically relishes it.
He rejoices in it, he resolves upon it, and he takes his stand upon it.
That is called craving conditioned by feeling; it is relishing, delighting,
and the state of attachment.
The thought, "May there be no separation from that which is dear and pleasant to the self," and the repeated prayer for non-abandonment—
this is called clinging (*upādāna*) conditioned by craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Praying in this way, one instigates karma that produces renewed existence through body, speech, and mind.
That which is conditioned by grasping is called "existence" (bhava).
The manifestation of the five aggregates produced by that karma is what is called "birth" (jāti) conditioned by existence.
That which is the destruction of the aggregates that have been produced by birth, resulting from their accumulation and maturation—
this is called "aging and death conditioned by birth.
[The rest is as before.]
In this context, consciousness is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a seed;
karma is the cause by virtue of having the nature of a field;
and ignorance and craving are causes by virtue of having the nature of afflictions.
Karma and the afflictions produce the seed of consciousness.
In this process, karma performs the function of the field for the seed of consciousness,
while craving moistens the seed of consciousness.
Ignorance sows the seed of consciousness.
In the absence of these conditions, the production of the seed of consciousness does not occur.
In this regard, it does not occur to the karmas: "I am performing the function of a field for the seed of consciousness."
(Bcp 226) Even in craving, it does not occur thus: "I moisten the seed of consciousness.
In ignorance as well, it does not occur thus: "I sow the seed of consciousness.
In the seed of consciousness too, it does not occur thus: "I am produced by these conditions."
Rather, the seed of consciousness, established in the field of karma, moistened by the moisture of craving, and covered with the soil of ignorance, sprouts;
thus the production of the sprout of name-and-form occurs.

And that sprout of name-and-form is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, not created by a Lord, not transformed by time, not dependent on a single cause, nor is it arisen without a cause.

And yet, through the union of mother and father, the coincidence of the season, and the convergence of other conditions, the seed of consciousness— bound by craving— brings forth the sprout of name-and-form in the mother’s womb at the point of rebirth in various places of birth;
all this occurs amidst phenomena that are without owner, without "mine," without possession, without adversary, equal to space, and having the nature of the characteristic of an illusion.
Because there is no deficiency in causes and conditions—
and so forth— no dharma whatsoever transmigrates from this world to the next world.
There is indeed the fruit of karma, and there is indeed informative action,
because of the non-deficiency of causes and conditions.
...and so on;
just as fire does not burn due to a deficiency of fuel,
but burns when there is no deficiency of fuel.

In the very same way, the seed of consciousness, produced by karma and afflictions, brings forth the sprout of name-and-form in the mother’s womb at the moment of rebirth in various places of birth, due to the non-deficiency of causes and conditions— despite phenomena being without an owner, without "mine-ness," without possession, without adversaries, equal to space, and having the nature of the characteristic of illusion.
In this way, the conditional dependence of internal dependent origination is to be understood.
In this regard, internal dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
Which five? Not as eternal, nor...
Not through annihilation,
not through transmigration,
but through the production of a vast fruit from a small cause.
And because of the continuity of what is similar to that.
How is it not eternal?
Because the final aggregates at the time of death are different [from those of the previous life].
Other aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear; however,
those very aggregates that belong to the end of life do not themselves appear as the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth.
Therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not subject to annihilation?
It is because the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth do not manifest when the aggregates at the end of life have already ceased.
Nor do they arise when [the former aggregates] have not ceased; rather, at the very moment the aggregates of the time of death cease, the aggregates belonging to the state of rebirth appear.
It is like the rising and falling of the arms of a balance scale;
therefore, it is not through annihilation.
How is it not through transmigration?
From a dissimilar class of beings, aggregates of a different nature are produced in another birth;
therefore, it is not by way of transmigration.
How is it that a vast fruit is produced from a small cause?
A small deed is performed,
yet a vast ripening of fruit is experienced;
therefore, from a small cause there arises a vast result.
How is it "by way of a continuous succession similar to that"?
Just as karma is performed to be experienced in a certain way, so too is its ripening experienced in a corresponding way.
Therefore, because of the continuity of similar [factors],
internal dependent origination should be viewed in this way through five [causes— modes].
Thus is the detailed explanation.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that even in the absence of a self (*ātman*) and so forth, the connection between action and its fruit remains entirely intact, as shown by the Blessed One himself in the Sūtras;
therefore, nothing at all is contradicted by the fact that there is no single entity persisting through both [the action and its result].
If the self does not exist in any way whatsoever, how then is it said:
"The self is indeed its own protector; what other protector could there possibly be?"?
For by means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven.
Is this stated in the verse [of the Dhammapada] as follows? (Bcp 227)
It is mind alone that is expressed by the word "self" in this context, because it is the basis for the conceit of "I. As stated in another sutra:
"The taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."
This is because of the statement regarding the taming of the mind in the *Dhammapada*.

Furthermore, for those who are attached to the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), the mind was taught as being the "self" according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*) and as having a provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), in order to eliminate the conceptual construction of grasping at a self elsewhere; it was not so taught from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
By this, that which was stated in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*—
“The person, the continuum, the aggregates, conditions, as well as atoms, primordial matter, and the Lord as creator— I declare these to be mind-only”— is explained.
Thus, that [verse from the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra] is also explained;
for that statement elsewhere as well was spoken for the purpose of refuting attachment to a person (pudgala) and so forth.
However, by that much alone, the ultimate reality of the mind has not been asserted.
Likewise, in other cases as well, the teaching of a self with respect to the aggregates and so forth is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Therefore, even the mind is not, in reality, the object of the notion of "I."
Or, let it be granted that the mind exists as an ultimate reality;
nevertheless, demonstrating that it is not in fact the object of the notion of "I," he says "past," and so forth:
"The past and future mind is not 'I,' for that does not exist."
For the mind arises in three ways based on conceptual construction: as past, future, and present.
Among these, the past and future minds—being destroyed and unborn respectively—are neither "I" nor objects of the vision of "I."
Why? Because,
since that past and future mind does not exist and does not exist at present, [it is non-existent].
Because of its being destroyed and unborn:
that which is past is exhausted, ceased, departed, and transformed;
that which is future—
"That too has not been attained. Well then, one might think, "I shall be the future mind"; to this he says:
"Or if the mind has arisen, once this has perished, I no longer exist" (Bca 9.74).
That the presently arisen mind should be "I" is also not tenable;
for when this [mind] has perished, the "I" no longer exists.

When this present mind has perished and become past in the second moment, the "I" no longer exists; subsequently, the object of the notion of "I" would not be established. Furthermore, the persistence of the present [mind] is not perceived.
Therefore, from what could the mind be apprehended such that it would have an object?
Consequently, since even the mind is not an object, this notion of "I" arises as being entirely without an object.
Thus, because the self does not exist, there is no self;

and because the mind existing in the three times has that [self] as its object, it is established that the mind is also not the object of the ego-conception (*ahaṃkāra*). Concluding this, he says "just as," and so forth: *Yathaiva...* etc.
Just as the trunk of a plantain tree is nothing when dissected part by part,
so too am I non-existent when sought through analytical investigation.
Just as a plantain trunk, when broken down part by part and limb by limb, is shaken apart and nothing whatsoever is found that exists as a real entity; so it is with all things.
Likewise, I too am non-existent, like the trunk of a plantain tree;
I, though the object of the notion of "I," am also non-existent and devoid of substantial reality,
like the son of a barren woman.
The meaning is that there is no object whatsoever for this [consciousness].
How so? When sought through investigation—that is, through analytical determination.
Furthermore, raising another objection against the negation of the self, he says "yadi" and so forth:
"If a sentient being does not exist, for whom would there be compassion?
If, when analyzed in every respect, a sentient being, a self, or a person (*pudgala*) is not found to exist, [then for whom would compassion be directed?].
If that were not so, upon whom would the compassion and pity of the bodhisattvas be directed; and in the absence of sentient beings, with what as its object would it function?

And compassion is the means for accomplishing perfect enlightenment, because it is precisely preceded by compassion that one engages in the practices of giving and so forth, which are the causes for the accumulations.
Therefore, all the qualities of a Buddha proceed with compassion as their precursor.
And so it is said in the *Ārya-dharmasaṃgīti*:

"Then indeed, the noble Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara said this to the Blessed One: 'O Blessed One, a bodhisattva need not train in too many dharmas. A bodhisattva should make just one single dharma well-mastered and thoroughly understood.'"
All the qualities of a Buddha come to be within the palm of his hand;
just as, for example, wherever the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch proceeds, there the entire army follows.

In the same way, Blessed One, wherever the great compassion of a bodhisattva goes, there all the qualities of a Buddha go. Just as, Blessed One, when the life-faculty exists, the other faculties function; so it is with the great compassion of a bodhisattva.
In the same way, Blessed One, it is when great compassion exists that the factors which bring about awakening come into operation.
And it is said in the *Ārya-gayāśīrṣa*:
"Mañjuśrī, what is the undertaking of the conduct of bodhisattvas, and what is its basis?"
Mañjuśrī said: "O Devaputra, the conduct of bodhisattvas begins with great compassion and has sentient beings as its basis."
Thus is the detailed exposition.
Therefore, one must necessarily first accept compassion that has sentient beings as its object, because it arises based upon suffering sentient beings.
If you think that it would not exist in the absence of sentient beings:
To show that this [objection] should not be stated at that time, he says "for the sake of the task," and so forth:
"That which was imagined through delusion by one who has accepted [the self] for the sake of accomplishing a task... (Bca 9.76).
The task to be accomplished, which is the desired goal, is called the "human aim" (puruṣārtha).

The meaning is: with respect to that "being" (sattva) which is imagined and superimposed by means of delusion (moha)—that is, by means of conventional reality (saṃvṛti)—which has been accepted and embraced for the sake of that [aim].
For instance, Buddhahood—which is free from the entire web of conceptual construction and liberated from all obscurations—is the goal to be accomplished here as the supreme human aim.
And that [Buddhahood] is not attained without the non-apprehension of all phenomena;
and that [non-apprehension] is brought about by reaching the excellence of wisdom (*prajñā*).
And that [compassion] arises from practice that is respectful, uninterrupted, and long-lasting;
its undertaking occurs through the power of compassion.

Since that compassion, when first directed toward suffering beings, becomes the cause for the commencement of the accumulations, conventional truth—in the form of delusion—is accepted for the sake of the goal to be accomplished.
Therefore, first there is compassion having sentient beings as its object; after that, compassion having phenomena as its object; and finally, compassion without an object.
This is the intended meaning: it is not that a sentient being (*sattva*) is non-existent in every respect.
For the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are designated by the word "self" (*ātman*) according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).
As it was said by the Blessed One:
(Bcp 229) "Monks, whatever recluses or brahmins regard anything as 'self,' they all regard these very five aggregates of clinging as such."

Therefore, even if indeed there is a non-apprehension of sentient beings from the perspective of ultimate reality when one investigates with wisdom, nevertheless, they are not negated conventionally. As it has been said:
"Since wisdom resorts to the ultimate truth, while compassion resorts to the conventional."
When you reflected on the truth that the world was devoid of intrinsic essence,
and when you were permeated by the compassion of the Mother of the Ten Powers,
then, O Son, love for the world arose in you like a father’s love for his suffering child.
Thus [ends the *Guṇaparyanta-stotra* composed by Ratnadāsa, verse 33].
Also, in the *Catuḥstava*:
"O Protector, the notion of a 'sentient being' does not occur to you in any way whatsoever."
And toward sentient beings afflicted by suffering, you are exceedingly compassionate in nature.
Thus, [Catuḥ-1.9]:
therefore, it is these very things—form and so forth—that are conventionally designated by the word "sentient being.
Consequently, compassion is not without an object.
Now, one might object: "If there is no sentient being in the ultimate sense, for whom does that effect belong?
How, then, can anyone engage in activity for its accomplishment? Having this in mind, he says "the effect," and so forth:
"If there is no sentient being, whose is the effect? True; however, this striving is due to delusion."
"If there is no sentient being" means:
if a sentient being does not exist, then,
because there is no single persisting entity and because form and the other aggregates are subject to arising and perishing, for whom would there be an effect?
The meaning is that it would not belong to anyone.
Regarding the phrase "in the admission [of the opponent] that this is true":
it is exactly so; this very view is our own—that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no effect whatsoever belonging to anyone.
Because all phenomena are without an owner.
If this is so, one might ask: how then does activity first arise for the sake of accomplishing them?
[The answer is: "Such striving, however, arises from delusion."
Furthermore, *īhā* (striving) is an activity (*ceṣṭā*) arising from the desire for its result due to delusion (*moha*).

It occurs through the determination of oneness, thinking "this result shall belong to me alone," even though there is no real sentient being, because all things are by convention of the nature of illusion (*māyā-svabhāva*).
In reality, however, all phenomena are devoid of striving, except for dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As it has been said:
O Protector, you have revealed that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature— imperturbable, powerless, empty, and arising from conditions like an illusion.
Thus it is said [Catuḥ-2.22].
Therefore, the activity regarding the purpose of an effect belongs to conventional reality alone.
Now, one might object: delusion, being by its very nature ignorance, is in every respect entirely unacceptable.
How then can there be acceptance of that very same [delusion]? To this he says "duḥkha" and so forth:
"But for the sake of the cessation of suffering, the delusion regarding what is to be done is not prevented. (Bca 9.77)
For delusion is of two kinds: that which is the cause of the progression of saṃsāra, and that which is the cause of its pacification.
Of these, that which is the basis of saṃsāra must indeed be abandoned.

But that other delusion which, for the sake of the gradual cessation of suffering and as a cause for the welfare of all beings regarding birth and so forth, is a delusion concerning what is to be done— that is, the delusion for the sake of attaining the ultimate truth characterized by what is to be done— is not, however, to be prevented.
It is not prohibited;
indeed, it is adopted,
because it is useful for the ultimate truth.
This is what is under discussion here: even that task is not undertaken by the great out of a desire for their own happiness,
but rather for the sake of the ultimate cessation of all suffering of all sentient beings.
And in that regard, the ultimate goal (*upeya*) is precisely the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*);
its means (*upāya*) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*),
because without conventional truth, the ultimate truth cannot be realized.

Thus, the fact that the delusion regarding the task has the purpose of pacifying suffering was already established previously in the context of the verse: "This is for the sake of the task, through non-investigation" (9.4). It is stated again here in order to elaborate upon it.

It might be argued as follows: just as the delusion regarding the effect (kāryamoha) is accepted as being of the nature of ignorance (avidyā) because it is a cause for the cessation of suffering, so too let there be delusion regarding the self (ātmamoha), since it is likewise a cause for that [cessation].
Why, then, is the self (ātman) so laboriously denied?
Even if that [self] exists, since egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) is eliminated through the cultivation of selflessness (*anātman*), there will be the cessation of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
To the question, "What then is the use of the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya*? he says: "Egoism is the cause of suffering, yet it increases from delusion regarding the self," and so forth.
Just as delusion regarding the objective world (*kāryamoha*) is a cause for the pacification of suffering,
so it is not with the second type, delusion regarding the self (*ātmamoha*); for as long as that exists, there can be no destruction of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

However, due to self-delusion (*ātmamoha*), because of the perception of the inversion of self (*ātmaviparyāsa*) regarding that which is not-self, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) increases; having increased, it arises.
Of what nature is it? It is the cause of suffering—the cause and reason for the suffering of cyclic existence characterized by the three types of suffering.
Furthermore, the cessation of suffering is held to result from the destruction of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
But as long as the view of a self (ātmadarśana) exists, how could that [ego-sense] be averted?
For it is impossible for an effect to cease while its cause remains with unimpaired capacity.
Consequently, suffering does not cease.
For instance, in one who perceives a self within the conditioned aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandhadhātvāyatana*), an exceedingly firm attachment arises in the form of "I.

From that, through the desire to counteract that suffering, there arises a longing for pleasure; this conceals faults, and through the superimposition of virtues due to that yearning, one engages in the means for its attainment.
The thought "they are our benefactors" arises toward those who help us;
and from the perception of "I" and "mine," aversion arises toward those who act as obstacles.
Consequently, all the afflictions and secondary afflictions, which are the source of all suffering, proceed having gained their opportunity.
Thus, egoism (*ahaṃkāra*), which is the cause of suffering, is set in motion by delusion regarding the self (*ātmamoha*).
As it was said by the venerable Teacher:
"For one who perceives a self, there arises here a permanent attachment of 'I'."
Through attachment, one thirsts for pleasures; craving conceals the faults.
Seeing qualities and thirsting for them, one grasps at the means to achieve them with the thought "this is mine"; as long as there is this adherence to a self, so long is there cyclic existence.
When there is a self, there is the notion of "other"; from the division of self and other arise attachment and aversion. Bound up with these two, all faults are produced.
Thus it is said.
Thus, the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) cannot be turned back from its attachment to the self;
if it cannot be turned back even from that [attachment], [what can be done]?
If the ego-sense cannot be turned back— that is, if it is impossible to turn one away even from that very view of a self— then the cultivation of selflessness is better.
The cultivation (*bhāvanā*), that is, the repeated practice, of selflessness (*nairātmya*)— the absence of a person (*pudgala*) and so forth—
is superior (*varam*), meaning supreme, because it is the cause for the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) that functions through the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*).
Let it remain for that duration;
later, even this will be abandoned,
because it is a view of apprehension— this is the intended meaning.

For instance, by reaching the culmination of the cultivation of that [insight] and through the direct perception of selflessness (*nairātmya*), the opposing view of a real self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is eliminated.
Upon its elimination, because there is no perception of a single persisting entity, there occurs the perception of a mere moment (*kṣaṇa*) devoid of prior and subsequent forms.
Consequently, due to the absence of the superimposition (*samāropa*) of a prior and subsequent [identity], one does not perceive anything as a means for the self’s future happiness.
Consequently, no passion arises in him toward any object,
nor does aversion arise toward its opposite,
precisely because of the absence of attachment.
Nor does he perceive an object of harm toward one who has not acted [as an offender],
because both he by whom the harm was done and the one against whom it was done cease to exist in the second moment.

Furthermore, it is not fitting for a discerning person to seek vengeance elsewhere when an injury has been committed by someone else, nor is it fitting for the one who committed the act to seek vengeance against another.
Likewise, when passion and the like have ceased, other afflictions and secondary afflictions arising from them do not arise.
Nor is anyone in reality a wrongdoer to another,
because of the vision of dependent origination— that "this arising, that arises.

For when there is the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the view of a self-existent body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) has ceased, the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not manifest, as their root has been severed.

As it is said in the *Āryatathāgataguhya-sūtra*: "Śāntamati, just as when the root of a tree is cut, all its branches, leaves, and foliage wither, even so, Śāntamati, through the pacification of the view of a self-existent body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), all afflictions (*kleśa*) are pacified."
Therefore, the cultivation of selflessness is superior.
This incidental discussion is concluded.
Now, however, he begins to examine the object of the "I-notion" (ahaṃkāra).
It might be argued that if the self, upon investigation, is like the horn of a donkey and thus not the object of the "I-notion," [then what is its object?]
Nevertheless, one might argue that the body as a whole will be the object [of perception]; to this he says, "The body is not":
The body is not the feet, nor the shanks, nor the thighs; the body is not the hips, nor the belly, nor the back, nor the chest, nor the arms. (Bca 9.79)
There are no hands, nor these sides, nor the armpits, nor the characteristics of the shoulders;
there is no neck, nor the head. Of all these, which one then is the body?
He demonstrates that even the body, when analyzed, does not exist as a single entity at all: for in this way, only parts such as hands and feet are seen;
however, what is called a "single body" does not appear.
Nor is it logical that any one of those [parts] is the body.
For the body is not the feet,
nor the ankles, nor the shanks;
and the shanks do not constitute the body.
The thighs and the specific parts of the shanks are not the body;
the hips are not it, nor is the pelvis the body;
the abdomen is not it, and the belly also does not constitute the body.
Nor is this the back;
this body is not even the back. Nor is it the chest; the chest, the breast, is also not the body.
Nor is he the arms;
that body is not the two arms either.
It is not the hands, nor are the two hands the body.
Nor are these the sides; this body does not consist even of the sides.
Nor are they the armpits; the body is not even the roots of the arms.
The body does not have the characteristic of flesh, nor is the body of the nature of the aggregates;
the body is neither the neck nor the throat.
The head is not the body,
nor does the head constitute the body;
for, as will be examined below regarding the feet and other members, [the body] does not exist even as far as its constituent atoms.
Because the cutting off of any one of the hands, feet, or other limbs would entail death through the destruction of the body,
and because there is no acceptance by others [that they are the self], the body does not have the nature of the self in each of these individually.
Thus, when these are not each of the nature of the body, [how could their collection be so?]
And this body is merely a collection; among these parts before us— the feet and so forth— which serve as the basis for the conceptual construction of a "body," which one, then, is the body?
In short, when examined, not even a single thing that constitutes the nature of the body is apprehended.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is not stated that the hands and so forth are individually the body; rather, because the whole (avayavin) pervades all its parts, it exists in all the parts. To this, he says "yadi" and so forth:
"If this body exists in all [the parts] by way of a single part..."
Does this [body], which exists in all its parts, exist in them by way of a single part, or simultaneously by way of its entire self?
In that regard, if the body, as the whole, were present in all the parts such as the hands and feet, [it would follow that it is manifold].
It exists by way of one part; it pervades some portion or some member,
but not everything by means of its entire self— this is the meaning.
Then this should not be said;
for, as to those parts by which it exists in the constituent members, does it exist in those parts also by means of other parts, or by a single part?
The alternative—that it exists by its entire self—does not avoid the [same] dilemma. Furthermore, if one again imagines that it exists in only one part, there would be no end to the infinite regress.
Moreover:
Because there is no space for it, it does not reside in its parts; thus he says, "The parts," and so forth:
"The parts reside in the parts, but where does it itself abide? (Bca 9.81)

Parts (*aṃśāḥ*), which are portions, exist—that is, they remain established—within their respective parts; for all entities are established within their own respective parts. And where is that [whole] itself situated?
Furthermore, we do not know where this body itself, as a whole possessing parts, is actually situated.
Now, as for the second alternative,
he says "in its entirety" (sarvātmanā):
"If the body were present in its entirety in all parts, such as the hands and so forth..."
There would indeed be as many bodies as there are those hands and other limbs.

Even if one assumes the possibility of its occurrence through its entire self, since there is no room for it within the parts, the consequence—namely, "where then does it itself abide?"—is not yet resolved.
Nevertheless, another point is further stated: "by its entire self" means by its whole being, not by a single part.

If the body as a whole were to exist as an inherent whole (samaveta) in all its parts, such as the hands and so forth—the word "and so forth" including the feet and other limbs—then this further fault would arise; thus he says: "The bodies... [as follows].
The whole of the body would then be as many [as its parts];
it would necessarily result in being limited by that same number.
How many? As many as those hands and so forth are.
Those parts, such as the hands and feet, possess limits; whatever number they are delimited by, the wholes inhering in them must likewise be that many,
because the whole, being partless, is entirely contained within them in its totality.

Because it has multiple relations, it must be manifold; otherwise, it could not subsist in many [loci]. This same reductio ad absurdum should also be applied to the position that [a universal] subsists in many [loci] by means of only a part.
In the same way, cases such as being covered by red or non-red [colors], being obstructed or unobstructed, trembling, and so forth, should also be stated according to their respective applications.
(Bcp 233) Thus, it has been demonstrated that a body cognizable through means of valid cognition such as direct perception does not exist;
furthermore, showing that there exists an immediate sublation (*bādhaka*) of this [position], he says: "Neither within," and so forth.
The body exists neither internally nor externally; how, then, could the body be in the hands and other limbs?
Since the internal agent (puruṣa) was previously refuted and since flesh, blood, and so forth have been analyzed, the body does not exist within the interior.
Furthermore, because the whole (avayavin) is now refuted, the body is not external—that is, it is not an object of perception and the like.
Thus, how can the body be established as being [identical to] the hands and so forth?
Now, to address the possibility that it might exist as something distinct from the hands and so forth, he says "from the hands and so forth," etc.:
It does not exist separately from the hands and so forth; how, then, indeed, could it exist? (Bca 9.83)
A body that is distinct and separate from its parts, such as the hands and so forth, does not exist; it is not perceived, for it has not met the conditions for perception.
Indeed, only the hands and other parts themselves appear.
Thus, that which is neither of the nature of the hands and so forth, nor is it supported by them, nor inherent in them, nor contained within them,
nor even distinct from them;
How indeed does that body exist?
By the phrase "how indeed" (*kathaṃ nu khalu*), he asks—failing to perceive the body in any way whatsoever and finding its existence inconceivable—in what manner, by what means?
The particle *nu* expresses deliberation.
Is it established that it exists?
And when, through such analysis, the body cannot be established, then one should conclude that it is indeed non-existent; thus he says, "Therefore, it does not exist," and so forth.
That body does not exist; however, due to delusion, there is the cognition of a "body" with respect to the hands and so forth.
That body does not exist because, through the aforementioned analysis, it is not apprehended.

Therefore, since it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, the body does not exist. If it does not exist, how then can there be the cognition of a "body" with respect to the hands and so forth? To this he says: "But from delusion," and so on.
But furthermore, due to delusion—that is, by the power of ignorance—the cognition of a "body" arises with respect to the hands and so forth, which are devoid of being a single, unitary substance.
But not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).
Or, the word "but" (*tu*) serves to emphasize;

for indeed, due to the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) of false habitual practice accumulated through the succession of births in the beginningless and endless cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there arises the conceptual construction of a superimposition contrary to reality, even when one has realized the true nature of things as they actually exist.
It arises;
bound to that [conceptualization], this worldly convention regarding the body and so forth proceeds,
but it is not ultimate.
To the question of how that [perception] does not occur in other cases, he says: "By means of a particular configuration, as in the case of the cognition of a person in a tree stump" (Bca 9.84).
The configuration of the hands, feet, and so forth is "saṃsthāna" (structure);
that itself is the "viśeṣa" (particularity), the distinction from others;
by means of that cause of delusion, [the cognition occurs] only with respect to the hands and other parts.
It does not occur everywhere, for errors are held to have restricted objects. How so? Like the cognition of a person in a post.

The meaning is as follows: just as someone who perceives a particular configuration—such as verticality—which is common to both a post and a person, might through delusion conceive of a post that lacks the nature of a person as being a person because they have not distinguished its specific differences from afar, so it is in the present case as well.
It might be asked: "How, then, is it determined that the cognition of a body arises from delusion and not from the reality of the object itself? To this, he says "as long as," and so forth:
"As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does the body appear like a person."

(Bcp 234) To whatever extent the collection of conditions and causes— consisting of the six elements such as earth, the six bases of contact, and the eighteen mental explorations, whose functioning is dependent upon karma— remains delimited by a certain temporal limit, for that same duration the body exists, like a person.
Just as, although devoid of the intrinsic nature of a person from the perspective of ultimate reality, it appears and is conventionally designated as a "person" by way of its imagined form;
and this is merely an illustration—
it should also be understood to apply to a "woman."

It does not exist previously in states such as the *kalala* (embryonic stage), nor does it exist afterwards because it has been disintegrated, as in states such as ashes; this is because its own intrinsic nature (*nijasvabhāva*) is absent.
Demonstrating that this is also common to the present case, he says "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, as long as [the parts] such as the hands exist, to that extent the body is seen here. (*Bca* 9.85)
Just as the body appears like a person when the totality of conditions is present,
and appears as being real,
so too [does it appear] in the hands and other parts, as long as that totality of conditions exists.
To that extent, the body is seen here in the hands and so forth;
it appears through the power of conceptual construction,
but not in ultimate reality.
Therefore, the cognition of a body occurs when the totality of conditions is present, and it does not occur in their absence;
hence, it is certain that the cognition of a body with respect to the hands and other limbs arises solely from delusion.

This is the collective meaning here: when the respective collection of conditions (*pratyaya-sāmagrī*) is present, this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) arises through the power of delusion, manifesting an unreal reality even in the absence of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those respective things.
By virtue of that [construction], the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "woman," "man," "body," and so forth proceeds with respect to particular configurations (*saṃniveśa-viśeṣa*).
For this very reason, it ceases in states such as [the body becoming] ashes, due to the deficiency of the collection of conditions.
Therefore, he will state that this conventional usage of "body" and so forth is not ultimately real. As it has been said:
"The intrinsic nature of the body must be described as that which remains even when devoid of its states;
yet if the body were merely the form of a statue, it would not exist in the embryo or in ashes."
If it remains there in a subtle state, having abandoned its grossness,
how can that which is inherently indescribable be called a "body"?
Thus it has been said:
"That which has its origination from a cause does not have its persistence without conditions."
Since its disappearance results from the absence of conditions, how can it be understood to exist?
Thus it is said; in some recensions of the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*, the reading is:
"As long as the collection of conditions exists, so long does the person persist, like a piece of wood."
Thus it is said;

here this is to be explained: as long as the causal complex of error persists, the perception of a person occurs in what is actually a post, and for that long the wood, though its nature is that of a post, is perceived as a person.
It does not exist in their absence.
In this very way, as long as that collection of conditions exists in the hand and so forth, the body is perceived here in the hand and so forth, but not afterwards.
Therefore, it is certain that the cognition of the body arises solely from delusion.

Now, one might object: "Granted that the body does not exist, yet its parts, such as the hands and feet, cannot be denied because they are perceived through direct perception. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] says the following to demonstrate that even the hands and so forth possess only an imagined intrinsic nature:
In this way, because it is a collection of fingers, what indeed would the foot be?
Just as the body does not exist when analyzed,
so too the hands, feet, and so forth do not exist.
For a "cluster" (*puñja*) is a collection (*samudāya*) of fingers;
the mention of "fingers" is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*),
and it should be understood to include the heels and so forth as well.
Its state is its reality (*tattva*);
therefore, the meaning is "from that intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, which one would it be—the foot or the leg?
The meaning is that, when analyzed apart from that collection, nothing whatsoever exists.

He says "that too," and so forth, to show that even a heap of fingers does not have a single intrinsic nature: "That too, because it is a collection of joints; and a joint as well, due to the division of its own parts. (Bca 9.86)
Even that collection of fingers, when analyzed, is not substantially real. Why? Because it is a collection of joints;
because it is a collection—that is, an aggregate—of the joints which are the parts of the fingers. This is to be connected with the preceding statement: "What could it possibly be?"
Since each of the parts (*parvan*) is also not a real entity, he says: "The part, too, is not a real entity.
Why? Because of the division of its own constituent parts—that is, because of the differentiation of the parts (*aṃśa*), which are the limbs (*avayava*) of itself, its own self.
He states that even parts do not exist in reality:

"Even parts, by means of the division into atoms. Even parts—that is, constituent portions—are merely conceptual constructs because they are subject to division into atoms through the analysis of ultimate particles.
He states that even atoms are not ultimately real individually:
"That atom, too, [is not real] because of its division according to directions.
This is because of its manifoldness due to division through connection with the directions—namely, those whose natures are east, west, south, north, below, and above.

Due to the division of those [directions], the atom being divided would possess six parts. Alternatively, there would be divisions in the directions, consisting of various parts of different forms situated in various directions;
therefore, by virtue of that differentiation, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) cannot remain established.

According to the principle that "that which possesses a distinction of spatial directions cannot logically be a unity," it is as follows: Is that form belonging to the central atom which faces the atoms situated in the eastern, western, and other directions actually one and the same?
Or are they distinct from one another?
If the position is that they are indeed one and the same,
then it follows that all atoms situated surrounding [one another] would occupy the same location.

For, without occupying the same location as the atom situated in the eastern direction and other directions, the atom situated in the western direction and so forth could not face the same form that faces the atom situated in the eastern direction;

otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a difference in their forms. And this occupation of the same location cannot occur without the latter being included within the essential nature of the former.

Furthermore, because that atom situated in the eastern direction would be included within the nature of the other atom through a connection with its entire essence, the substance would become a mere atom.
This being the case, mountains and the like, which consist of accumulated forms, would not exist.
Therefore, one who desires the accumulation of entities such as mountains must accept the second position alone.

And at that time, because it would simultaneously connect with six [atoms] in successive forms, the central atom would consist of six parts; for its atomic form would be differentiated by its connection with various other atoms situated in their respective locations.
Thus, it is not logical for even an atom to possess a single nature.
As it was stated by the venerable Ācārya:
"Through simultaneous conjunction with six [other atoms], the atom would have six parts."
Because the six [atoms] occupy the same location, the aggregate would be the size of a single atom.
Thus [it is said in verse 12 of the *Viṃśatikā*]:

"Furthermore, those even more minute parts, when analyzed in the same way, are established as being selfless and having the nature of space. Therefore, he says: "The division of directions also... and so forth:
"The division of directions, because it is partless, is space; therefore, there is no atom. (Bca 9.87)
Even regarding spatial division, when an atom is divided according to the different directions, being split into six parts as before, what [atom] would remain?
It would not be any real entity at all.
This [analysis] should be applied everywhere to the preceding cases.
Why? Because it lacks parts.
Therefore, when it is analyzed, being devoid of intrinsic nature, it is simply empty like space.
For that reason, the atom does not exist.
An atom does not exist;
likewise, when analyzed, the hands and other parts should be seen as lacking intrinsic nature.
Therefore, even the body does not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Because it has been established that they are devoid of a nature that is either one or many,
in this way, neither hair and so forth exist, nor does the self.
Neither the mind nor the body is, in reality, the object of the notion of "I.

Therefore, this cognition of "I," which arises even in the absence of a real self or such entities due to the presence of a selfhood projected by ignorance, occurs entirely without an objective referent.
Therefore, what was stated—
“If I myself do not exist as anything at all, for whom will there be fear?”—
is established.
By all of this, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is demonstrated.
As it is said in the *Dharmasaṃgītisūtra*:

"Furthermore, noble son, a bodhisattva establishes mindfulness of the body in this way: 'This body is merely a collection consisting of the feet, toes, calves, thighs, groin, belly, navel, backbone, heart, ribs, costal cartilages, hands, forearms, upper arms, shoulders, neck, jaw, forehead, and skull.'"
It is accumulated by the agent of karmic existence and is the abode of hundreds of thousands of various primary and secondary afflictions, conceptualizations, and discursive thoughts.

Furthermore, many substances are gathered therein, namely: head hair, body hair, nails, teeth, bones, skin, flesh, fat, sinews, marrow, grease, lymph, liver, urine, feces, the stomach, the large intestine, blood, saliva, bile, pus, nasal mucus, brain, and the cerebral membrane—such is the collection of many substances.
What, then, is this body? As he examines it, it occurs to him: "This body is equal to space.
He establishes mindfulness upon the body as being like space.
He perceives that all this is space;
because of his thorough understanding of the body, his mindfulness no longer extends or disperses anywhere.
"He does not resort [to them]."
It has been stated again:

this body does not come from the past, nor does it transition to the future; it does not abide in the past or the future, but arises otherwise from unreal inversions. It is devoid of an agent or an experiencer, and its root is not established in the beginning, the end, or the middle.
It is ownerless, without "mine-ness," and without possession.
Through adventitious conventional designations, this body is referred to as the "body," the "physical frame," "enjoyment," the "basis," the "corpse," or the "sense-sphere.
This body is devoid of essence; it is produced from the semen and blood of the mother and father, having a nature that is impure, putrid, and foul-smelling.

It is crowded with the thieves of passion, hatred, delusion, and despondency; it is by nature constantly subject to falling apart, collapsing, breaking, scattering, and destruction; and it is a nest for hundreds of thousands of various diseases.

Thus, when the body is investigated and found to be in reality like space due to its empty nature, then fools—superimposing a false reality upon it and generating passion and the like—nurture cyclic existence. To this effect, he says "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, what discerning person would feel attachment for a form that is like a dream?"

In this way, according to the sequence described, who would become attached, who would become obsessed, with regard to a form that is like a dream, perceived as if in a dream, and which is a basis for displeasure?
And by extension of this [example], who would feel aversion?
It should also be understood: "Who would be deluded?
For example, having seen with the eye forms that are conducive to mental pleasure, lust arises.
Having seen with the eye forms that are conducive to mental distress, hatred arises;
having seen with the eye forms that are conducive to equanimity, delusion arises. Thus, when one moves with attachment toward those forms that are disagreeable to the mind, [it is called attachment].
Because of that, attachment arises in him;
he acts with hostility toward disagreeable forms, and because of that, aversion arises in him.
He does not wander deluded among either agreeable or disagreeable things;
therefore, delusion arises in him.
In this way, he experiences the threefold object in sounds and so forth, as previously described.

In this regard, one who is of a wise nature understands that the sense-base of the eye is absolutely empty of the intrinsic nature of the sense-base of the eye; it is not apprehended even from the perspective of the past limit,
nor is it apprehended from the perspective of the future limit.
It is not apprehended in the middle because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The same should be stated for the other [bases], such as the ear and so forth.
Thus, in an ultimate sense, the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) is not the sphere of form by way of the intrinsic nature of the sphere of form, and so on, as previously described.
The same should be stated regarding sound and the other sense objects.
For thus one perceives the sense faculties as being like an illusion and the objects as being like a dream;
how, then, could passion and the like arise in such a person?
It is for this very reason that he is called "the investigator."
The discerning and wise person,

seeing this thus as it truly is with right wisdom— who would feel passion, hatred, or delusion? In this regard, the examples spoken of by the Blessed One, such as the beautiful woman of the country perceived in a dream, should be illustrated.
Furthermore, since the body does not exist, attachment—even by way of conceptualizing it as "woman" and so forth—is not tenable; thus he says, "And the body," etc.:
"And when the body itself does not exist in this way, then what is a woman, and who is a man? (Bca 9.88)
In the *Hetusamuccaya*,
the word "ca" (and) is used because passion does not arise through the conceptualization of women and so forth;
since the body does not exist in this manner according to the explained principle, [passion is absent].
If it is devoid of intrinsic nature,
then, due to the absence of a body, who is the woman who is a "lover," by whose loveliness passion would arise in a man?
And who is the man who is a "lustful one," by whose attractiveness passion would arise in a woman?
For a woman, having conceived the notion "woman" with respect to herself, generates passion for a man externally as "man.
Likewise, a man also, having conceived the notion "man" with respect to himself, generates passion for a woman externally as "woman.
However, in the absence of a body, the notion "woman" does not exist with respect to a woman.
A person is not found within a person;
and that which is not found by way of intrinsic nature is neither woman nor man.
Therefore, in the absence of a body, even passion produced by the conceptualization of women and so forth is not tenable.
Why is that?
Because all phenomena are indeed devoid of conceit.
This explanation is given according to what is primary;
in this very same way, it should be understood that even garlands, sandalwood, and so forth are devoid of intrinsic nature,
as are the objects of hatred and delusion.
And this was said by the Blessed One in the *Pitāputrasamāgama*:
"O Great King, this person consists of six elements."
Having six bases of contact and eighteen mental explorations—
O Great King, it is indeed appropriate to say that this person consists of six elements.
And depending on what does this exist?
Great King, there are these six elements.
Which six? Namely: the earth element, [the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element].
the water element,
the fire element,
and the wind element.
The space element and the consciousness element—
these, O Great King, are the six elements.
Furthermore, Great King, there are these six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatanāni*).
Which six?
The base of eye-contact for the seeing of forms, up to the base of mind-contact for the cognizing of mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
These, O Great King, are the six bases of contact...
[as before] ...these, O Great King, are the eighteen mental applications.
Which are the eighteen?
Here, a person, having seen forms with the eye, dwells upon those forms that are bases for joy, grief, or equanimity.
The same should be stated for the ear and the other [senses].
Thus, through each of the six sense-faculties, there are eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*) due to the threefold division of joy and so forth. [The same applies to the others.
And what, O Great King, is the internal earth element?
Whatever internal hardness or solidity there is in this body that is appropriated—what, then, is that? It is as follows: hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, and so forth.
And what, Great King, is the external earth element? Whatever is external, characterized by hardness, having the nature of solidity, and non-appropriated—
this is called the external earth element.
In this regard, Great King, the internal earth element, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation.
There comes a time, Great King, when a woman internally conceives the notion, "I am a woman."

Having internally conceptualized "I am a woman," she conceptualizes an external person as "a man. Having externally conceptualized a person as "a man," being filled with passion, she desires union with that external person.
It should be understood that the man also, as before, internally conceptualizes "I am a man."
When there is a desire for the union of those two, union occurs;
from the condition of that union, the *kalala* is born.
In this regard, Your Majesty, that which is conceptualized—
And that which is the conceptualizer—
both of these do not exist;
in a woman, "woman" does not exist.
"In a person, no person is found. Thus, indeed, a non-existent and unreal conceptualization arises;
yet that conceptualization, too, does not exist by way of true being.
Just as intention does not exist,
so too does conjunction;
even the *kalala* does not exist by way of its own intrinsic nature.
And that which does not exist by way of intrinsic nature—how could it produce solidity?
Thus, O Great King, having understood this conceptual construction, solidity should be known as follows: when solidity arises, it does not come from anywhere.
Great King, there comes a time when this body reaches its end in the cemetery;
as its hardness dissolves and ceases, it does not go to the eastern direction.
not to the south, not to the west, nor to the north;
It does not go upward, nor downward, nor into the intermediate directions.
In this way, Great King, the internal earth element is to be viewed. [And so on.
In that regard, Great King, even the arising of the earth element is empty;
Destruction is also empty;
even when the earth element has arisen, it is empty of intrinsic nature.
Thus, O Great King, the earth element is not apprehended as "earth element-ness."
Except for conventional usage;
and even that conventional usage is neither woman nor man.
Thus, O Great King, it should be seen as it truly is with right wisdom.
What is that conceit? Conceit is the domain of Māra.
For what reason?
For all phenomena are indeed free from conceit. Thus it is said.

Having thus established the application of mindfulness to the body, he speaks while analyzing sensation (*vedanā*) in order to demonstrate the application of mindfulness to sensation, beginning with "If it exists," and so forth:
"If suffering exists in reality, why does it not afflict those who are intensely joyful?"
If things such as delicious food were pleasant for one afflicted by grief and the like, why would they not be pleasing?
For feelings are of three kinds: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
In that regard, even feeling does not exist from the perspective of ultimate truth, just as form does not.
If one asks how this is so: if suffering were to exist [ultimately],...
Unpleasant feeling—
truly and from the perspective of ultimate reality—
why does it not afflict those who are then intensely joyful?
What does not cause suffering for those endowed with contentment?
If even happiness exists in reality, then it [causes suffering] to one afflicted by grief and the like.
From the word "etcetera" (ādi), [it includes] those afflicted by desire, fear, and madness.
If "delicious things and so forth" (mṛṣṭādi) mean pleasure, then it refers to delicious food, drink, and the like that possess excellent flavor.
From the word "etcetera," garlands, sandalwood, and so forth are included as pleasure because they are causes of pleasure.
If it is indeed pleasure,
why is it not pleasing?
For a real entity possessing an intrinsic nature can never be made to cease;
therefore, it is only pleasure and pain presented by conceptual construction that are to be experienced.
Regarding what was asked— “Why does [pleasure] not afflict those who are intensely joyful?”— the opponent provides the following resolution, beginning with the words “by the more powerful,” etc.:
“If that [pain] is not experienced because it is overwhelmed by something more powerful...”
For it is not the case that suffering is entirely non-existent during a state of intense joy;
rather, although it exists, it is not experienced because it is obscured by the arising and persisting pleasure—
that is, because it is overwhelmed and impaired by a pleasure that is powerful and exceedingly strong.
If it is argued that even though that suffering exists, it is not experienced or felt, then this is not tenable; thus he says "the nature of sensation," and so forth:
"How can there be the nature of sensation for that which lacks the essence of experience? (Bca 9.90)

How, and in what manner, can there be the state of being feeling (*vedanātva*), that is, the intrinsic nature of feeling (*vedanā-svabhāvatva*), for that unmanifest pleasure which lacks the nature of experience (*anubhava-ātmatā*) and lacks the nature of being experienced?
For it is said that "feeling" (*vedanā*) is so called because it is felt; as it is stated: "feeling is experience."
And if feeling were to exist even while not being experienced, then there would be nothing that is not feeling; thus, there would be the logical fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is not that it is not experienced in every respect;
rather, although it is experienced in a subtle manner, it is as if not experienced at all. To this, he says "asti" and so forth:
"Suffering does exist in a subtle form; its grossness has indeed been removed."
If there should be another [state] consisting of mere contentment, then that too is its subtlety.
If suffering exists and persists because it is subtle and thus unperceived, then what has been done to it by powerful pleasure? Has not its very grossness merely been removed?
In the state of intense joy, the powerful pleasure that has arisen has destroyed—that is, overcome—the grossness and intensity of this suffering.
"Nanu," "nanu"—these are used for addressing another.
"Is this your view, O sir? [is the meaning].
For no such thing as subtlety of suffering is perceived at the time of experiencing pleasure;

so how can it be said that pleasure has subtlety? If, however, it is merely a state of satisfaction arising from that very pleasure when its manifestation has subsided, [then it is not a distinct entity].
