But another [state] would be merely contentment, the second would be merely pleasure— a very small fragment of pleasure—
and there would be a subtlety of suffering, if that were intended.
Is it not so that even this subtlety of his is merely another form of contentment?
Furthermore, this subtlety belongs to pleasure itself, and not to suffering.
Because satisfaction is a species of pleasure,
it is certain that the subtlety of suffering— which is of an imperceptible nature— does not exist at all during the time of the experience of pleasure.

It might be argued: "Suffering is not merely occasional by virtue of being conceptual; rather, it is simply not perceived at certain times due to the deficiency of its causes. To this, he says "contradictory," and so forth (Bcp 240):
If there is no arising of suffering when a contrary cognition arises—
provided that there is the arising, or the presence, of that contact which is the cause or condition for pleasure, which is itself contrary to suffering.
Alternatively:
when there is the arising—i.e., birth—of a contrary condition that is a cause of pleasure; or, it is that which has a contrary condition as its [cause].
Even when there is an expectation [of the word] "by means of suffering" (*duḥkhena*), a compound is formed because it conveys the meaning.

If it is said that when that [pleasure] arises—in a state of intense joy—there is a non-arising of suffering due to the deficiency of its causes, then is it not the case that one has arrived at the conclusion: "Feeling is indeed an adherence to conceptual construction"? (Bca 9.92)
Is it not the case that exactly what we have stated has now arrived?
What is that? It is attachment through conceptual construction;
that is, the attachment produced by conceptual construction.
The word "hi" is used for emphasis:
that very sensation itself is pleasure, pain, or something other than those;
there exists nothing else that is real, whether it be pleasure and so forth, or the cause of non-pleasure and so forth.
For instance, even that which is devoid of its own intrinsic nature, when imagined as a means to pleasure,
gives rise to the experience of pleasure through attachment to it; from other [conditions], other [experiences arise].

Otherwise, how could that which is a means of suffering for one person be a means of happiness for another? For instance, how could that very same thing which caused suffering even from the mere hearing of its sound for one person...
Furthermore, pleasure arises from seeing that [object] again after a lapse of time;
therefore, pleasure and its means are merely conceptual, not real. And it has been said:
Poison becomes a source of pleasure for the peacock, and an elixir for one accustomed to poison;
likewise, thorns that prick the mouth become causes of particular delight for the young camel.
Thus, because sensation has the very nature of attachment, it can be turned back through investigation; hence he says "for this very reason," and so forth:
"For this very reason, this investigation is cultivated as its antidote."
"Precisely for this reason": because feeling has the nature of attachment (*abhiniveśa*), for that very reason this investigation, this inquiry, is the antidote and the opposite;
it is cultivated—that is, it is reflected upon—because it serves as the cause for the refutation of this attachment consisting of pleasure and so forth.
Because, in the absence of its means of accomplishment, there is an absence of attachment to it.
Furthermore,
he says "conceptualization," etc., stating that attachment is likewise feeling.
For yogins have meditative concentration as their sustenance, which arises from the field of conceptual construction.
The phrase "for this very reason" carries over from the previous context.
Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) itself is the field, because it is the ground of birth. Meditation that has arisen or been born therein is "secluded from sensual desires."
"Secluded from evil, unwholesome states, accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, born of concentration, with rapture and bliss," and so forth.
The cultivation of the dhyānas and so on consists of the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi-samāpatti*), because it arises from conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
that very state is "nutriment" because it is the cause for sustaining the body.
Those for whom this is so are thus described.
Who are they? They are the yogins.
For (hi) because the bodies of the yogins are sustained by the food of the joy and bliss produced through mental construction.
Therefore, it has been established that feeling is the attachment to conceptual construction.
Now, because a cause cannot be established, it is argued that sensation is not logically real as a substantial entity; thus he says "with an interval," and so forth:
"If the sense-faculty and the object have an interval between them, how can there be contact between these two?
This is the collective meaning here: feeling has contact as its condition;
and contact is the coming together of the three—object, sense faculty, and consciousness—because of the statement:
"The six types of contact are born from the coming together" (Abhidharmakośa 3.30).
Contact arising from the conjunction of the triad is not possible at all; how then could there be feeling conditioned by it?
For instance, would [contact] occur between the sense faculty and the object when they are separated by an interval, or when they are contiguous?
In that regard, if the sense faculty and the object were at a distance from one another— that is, separated by an interval—
then how, for what reason, could there be a conjunction, a coming together, or a meeting of these two, the sense faculty and the object? It is simply not tenable.
For contact (*sparśa*) is said to be conjunction (*saṃparka*); the point is: how could that exist when there is an interval?
Now, as for the second alternative:
That too is not tenable; thus he says, "Even if there is no interval," and so forth:
"Even if there is no interval, how could there be oneness? With what could there be a conjunction? (Bca 9.94)
Even when there is contiguity—that is, even when there is an absence of any intervening space—there is oneness, meaning identity, between the sense organ and the object.
For such complete contiguity of those two would only occur if there were no intervention by even the slightest part and if they possessed identical properties.
In that case, their inclusion within one another would constitute their very identity.
And in this way, what could have conjunction with what?
Since there is no difference when there is oneness, what could be conjoined with what?
Indeed, the conjunction of a self with itself is not logical.
It might be argued: the conjunction of partless atoms is indeed real;
nor is the conventional distinction between parts and the whole appropriate there, since that possibility exists only for gross forms.
Regarding that refutation of conjunction, he says "not [of] an atom," and so forth:
"There is no entry of one atom into another, for it is devoid of space and is equal;
even the contact of atoms is not at all logical."
Because there is no entry of even a single atom into another atom, nor is there any inclusion within it.
Why? Because (the word) "ca" means "since."
That atom is spaceless and without interstices;
it is equal and uniform, due to the absence of depressions and elevations.
Thus, how can there be a conjunction of that which is partless?
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there be no entry of one atom into another; let there be merely conjunction alone."
He says "non-entry" to show that our point to be proven is established by that much alone:
"In the absence of entry there is no mixing; in the absence of mixing there is no conjunction. (Bca 9.95)
For the conjunction of two atoms must be by way of their entire selves;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of them having parts.
And thus, their conjunction with that [other atom] occurs only for one who pervades it by means of its own self.
Thus, in the absence of such mutual intermingling of their essential natures, there would be no connection;
and that intermingling would not occur without entry into one another.
In this way, when there is no entry—that is, in the absence of entry—there is neither intermingling nor a state of non-distinct form.
In the state of non-mixture and in the absence of mixture, there is neither conjunction nor non-conjunction.
He states that "the conjunction of that which is partless is not possible in any way whatsoever" with the words beginning "And of the partless," etc.:
"And how indeed can the conjunction of a partless thing— that is,
an entity devoid of parts— be logically established?"
In the context of a collection of refutations,
how indeed can "conjunction" (saṃsarga)— meaning a coming together— be possible?
The word "nāma" (indeed) is used here to express a concession.
How can association be conceived?
Even the smallest possible thing must necessarily possess at least one part;
for that which has no part whatsoever [cannot exist].
The implication is that if this formless entity lacks parts, it necessarily follows that it is non-existent.
Furthermore, you yourself do not perceive such a thing anywhere through any means of valid cognition; thus he says "In the case of conjunction," and so forth:
"And if partlessness is observed in the case of conjunction, then demonstrate it. (Bca 9.96)
(Bcp 242) ...he said, beginning with "But of consciousness," etc.:
"But for consciousness, which is formless, conjunction is simply not tenable."
In the case of expressing an excellence,
it is not at all logical for there to be a reunion of consciousness— that is, of the cognition of an object— with [the past].
It is not tenable.
Why? Because of the phrase "of that which is formless";
that is, of consciousness, which is devoid of material form.
The meaning is "because of formlessness.
For conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is indeed mutual contact,
and that exists only for things that possess form.
But for that which has no form at all, how could there be a conjunction?
Thus, having refuted the conjunction of all three [possibilities], he now says "of the collection also," etc., demonstrating that even the collection itself does not exist as a real entity.
Since even a collection is not a real entity, as was previously analyzed.
Furthermore, even in the case of a collection (*samuccaya*),
since a multitude (*samūha*) or an aggregate (*saṃghāta*) is not a real entity—
that is, it lacks substantiality— a conjunction (*saṃsarga*) is not at all tenable, just as in the case of a horse and a horn; this is how it connects with the subject at hand.
Because the collection itself does not exist. How, then, is it devoid of a real entity (*avastuka*)?
As was previously analyzed:
As was previously established,
[it is so] by such arguments as "because it is a collection of fingers" and so forth.
Concluding the very impossibility of the cause, he says "tadevam" and so forth:
"Thus, in the absence of contact, how can there be the occurrence of sensation?
Therefore, by the sequence thus established, in the absence of contact—that is, in the absence of the conjunction of the triad—how can there be the occurrence of sensation?"
From what source could there be the occurrence, that is, the arising, of feeling in the form of pleasure and so forth?
It is not at all tenable,
because an effect cannot possibly arise in the absence of a cause.
Thus, since from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) there is an absence of feeling (*vedanā*), and consequently no possibility of objects that are beneficial or harmful,
for what purpose is this exertion?
For what purpose is this exertion performed which consists in the acquisition of the means for happiness and the avoidance of the means for suffering?
The sense is that it is not at all appropriate, as if for the purpose of chewing the sky.
Let it not be for the sake of attaining happiness;
but suppose it were for the sake of avoiding suffering, since suffering is impossible to endure? To this, he says:
Whose affliction could there be, and from what source?

Because sensation (*vedanā*) is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) when analyzed, there is no sublation (*bādhā*) when not analyzed; and since the self (*ātman*) and so forth have been previously refuted, there is an absence of a feeler (*vedaka*).
Furthermore, because even the cause of injury is constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpaka*), it has no existence from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Thus, in this way, since there is an absence of the sensation of pain and injury, for whom could there be sublation, given the absence of a feeler?
How could there be [feeling] from the absence of a cause for its impairment?
From the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing could arise from anything at all.
Therefore, feeling is also not tenable due to the non-existence of a feeler.

Now, in order to demonstrate that because sensation (*vedanā*) is absent, its condition—craving (*tṛṣṇā*)—also cannot arise in the ultimate sense due to the lack of its cause, he says "When no one... and so forth:
"When there is no feeler whatsoever and sensation does not exist, then, seeing this state, O craving, why do you not shatter? (Bca 9.99)
(Bcp 243) That which experiences feeling is the feeler;
when there is no self or anything else whatsoever, [who is it that feels?]
Because of the absence of that [contact] and because of the immediate investigation [of its non-existence], feeling does not exist.
Then, having seen and perceived this very state, which is thus deprived of its own birth, O Thirst, why do you not burst asunder;
though pained by that suffering, why do you not fall apart?
That even now, distressed by separation from him, you do not release yourself.

This might be the case: if there were no experiencer and no feeling, then by what means would this conventional usage regarding entities—such as "seen" and so forth, based on their being instruments of pleasure and the like—be set in motion? To this, he says "it is seen," and so on: dṛśyate ityādi— It is seen, and so forth.
It is seen and even touched by means of a mind that is like a dream or an illusion;
because it arises simultaneously with that mind, feeling is not perceived as something separate.
It is seen by the mind born of the visual faculty; it is touched by the mind born of the tactile faculty; and it is known by the mind through cognition.
If it is then argued that, in this case, the mind alone exists as a real entity that experiences, [the author] replies: "By way of being like a dream or an illusion."
By means of a mind that is dependently originated, having the nature of being like a dream and the nature of being like an illusion,
but not as something ultimately real.
How is that which is distinct from the mind seen by the mind?
Because it is co-nascent;
because it has arisen together with the mind, there is the seeing of that which has its birth together with the mind.
Because dependent origination is bound to a single causal complex and because it is inconceivable,
there is no seeing in the ultimate sense by which such conventional designations as "seen" and so forth could exist;
therefore, feeling is not perceived.
Since even the conventional usage of "means for attaining seen pleasure" and so forth arises from something else,
for that reason feeling is not perceived;
it is not seen in reality.
Now, it might be argued: "The simultaneous [perception] is not observed; rather, cognition, arising from that object by assuming its form, is said to be the apprehender of it at a later time.
To refute this, he says "previously," and so forth:
That which is born before and after is remembered, not directly experienced;
necessarily, there must be a cognition of that which is co-nascent.
Otherwise, what occurred previously—that which existed earlier—would be remembered, not experienced, by the knowledge produced at a later time, being made an object in the form of memory.
It does not exist directly,
because at the time of that cognition, it has already passed away; and it is not appropriate for that which has passed away to be known in its own essential nature.
Because it does not exist [as an external object],
and because experience is the cognition of its own nature,
therefore this is merely a memory.
In that case, it is not logical for there to be self-awareness.
He states "its own self," etc., meaning that the very definition which establishes the intrinsic nature of cognition is itself untenable;
[cognition] does not experience its own self.
It does not experience its own self, its own nature, nor does it perceive it,
because self-awareness has already been refuted.
"Is that feeling then experienced by another cognition? He replied:
"And it is not experienced by another. (Bca 9.101)
Nor is it the case that it is not experienced at all; rather, it is experienced— that is, cognized— by another cognition occurring at the same time as it,
because one cognition is not cognized by another cognition.
There is no experiencer whatsoever distinct from the feeling; thus, it does not exist in reality.
Yet, it is not the case that there is no experiencer at all who experiences the feeling.
Whether it be the mind or something else,

for this reason, sensation is "experience"; yet, because it is empty of the defining characteristic of sensation, sensation does not exist in reality or in the ultimate sense, other than as a result of conceptual attachment, since there is nothing whatsoever that establishes its own intrinsic nature.
This is stated in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*:
"Moreover, indeed, attachment is feeling."
Appropriation is feeling, grasping is feeling,
and apprehension is feeling.
Perverted perception is feeling; conceptualization is feeling, and so forth.
It is also said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra*:
"Feeling is declared to be experience; by what is it experienced? A feeler, a feeling, and the object of feeling do not exist as separate entities."
Thus should mindfulness be established by the wise regarding feeling;
for as is awakening, so too is this [feeling]: peaceful, pure, and luminous.

Thus, for this reason, this body appears as something that is empty of the nature of a knower and a feeling, merely dependently originated, devoid of activity, ownerless, and having entered the sphere of perception like a magical illusion (*māyā-prapañca*); therefore, neither pleasure nor pain belongs to anyone as their own. Thus he says "without self" (*nirātmaka*), and so forth.
In this collection which is devoid of self, who indeed is thus oppressed by it?

In that which is selfless (*nirātman*), because there is no experiencer such as a self, and in this collection of factors which has no owner due to the absence of any single persisting entity, and which is merely dependently originated and has entered the sphere of perception like the nature of an illusion—seeing it thus, like a magical display (*indrajāla*), he speaks with wonder: "Who indeed is afflicted by this?
For, according to the sequence thus described, there is an absence of any experiencer and an absence of [an intrinsic] sensation (*vedanā*).
Who, in ultimate reality, is afflicted or oppressed by this sensation?
Upon investigation, no one at all.
Therefore, this determination regarding the means of pleasure and so forth is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Thus, this application of mindfulness to sensation has been demonstrated.
Now, in order to demonstrate the application of mindfulness to the mind (*cittasmṛtyupasthāna*), he says "not in the faculties," and so forth:
The mind does not abide in the sense-faculties, nor in forms and the like, nor in between them;
the mind is found neither within, nor without, nor anywhere else. (Bca 9.103)
In this regard, he first examines the sixth, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*): "Where, then, does this mental consciousness itself arise?
In that case, the mind (*manas*) does not abide, nor has it attained a state of stability, within the sense faculties such as the eye and so forth;
nor does the mind abide in objects such as visible forms."
The mind does not abide in the interval, nor does it abide in the middle between the sense faculty and its object,
because its own nature is not determined even in a single location;
nor is the mind within, nor is it without.

Nor is the mind found within, that is, in the middle of the body; nor is it found outside, that is, in the external parts of the body. It is not found elsewhere either—not in any other location apart from those mentioned, nor anywhere else whatsoever.
It is not found when subjected to analysis.
In this way, since it exists in some place and in some manner, how can it be negated? To address this, he says "That which is not in the body," and so forth:
"That which is neither in the body nor elsewhere, neither mixed nor separate anywhere..."
Therefore, there is nothing [ultimately real] therein; thus, sentient beings are by nature in a state of parinirvāṇa.
That mind is not in the body— the internal or external body—
nor is it elsewhere;
it is certainly not in any external object other than the body.
It is not mixed;
this is an adverbial modifier.
Even as a mixture of the two—the internal and the external—it does not exist.
That mind which is not separate from the body,
nor does it abide anywhere independently as something distinct— that mind,
in the ultimate sense, does not exist.
Nothing at all exists as a real entity;
it is merely displayed by conceptual construction.
As long as saṃsāra lasts, the mind appears like an illusion because it is devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, for this reason, sentient beings—living creatures—are by nature (*prakṛtyā*) and by their own essence (*svabhāvena*) already in *parinirvāṇa*, having a nature that is completely liberated;
because the *prakṛti-nirvāṇa*, characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), is always present within the mental continua (*saṃtāna*) of all sentient beings.

Yet, through the power of unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), they themselves superimpose reality upon what is unreal; with their mental continua afflicted by the latencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), their independent functioning is obstructed by confinement in the prison of *saṃsāra*, and thus they remain unliberated.
Thus they are called, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Having thus investigated the mind, while investigating the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, he says "from the object of knowledge" and so on:
If cognition were prior to the object of knowledge, by depending upon what could it arise?
If cognition were simultaneous with the object of knowledge, by depending upon what could it arise? (Bca 9.105)
For indeed, cognition does not exist at any time as something eternally established in its own nature;
rather, it is said to be the grasper of objects of knowledge such as form when it arises in dependence upon the causal complex of the eye and so forth.
Anticipating this intention of the opponent, he analyzes it: "Furthermore, that [cognition] must exist either prior to the object of knowledge,"
Either simultaneous with the object of knowledge, or subsequent to the object of knowledge.
In that regard, if it is the former alternative, [then...]
Regarding this, he says: If it is asserted that cognition has already arisen even before the object of knowledge— that is, prior to, and while the object of apprehension is still unarisen—
then depending upon what could its occurrence possibly take place?
First, in the absence of an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as an objective support (*ālambana*), depending on what and relying on what could its occurrence—that is, its arising—take place?

Relying on the second position, he asks: if cognition exists at the same time as the object of knowledge, which is the apprehended object (*grāhya-viṣaya*), depending on what could its occurrence take place?
Because an object of cognition that is simultaneous [with the cognition] cannot be its cause, it lacks the status of an objective support (*ālambana*);
for it is stated that "that which is not a cause is not an object (*viṣaya*)."
Now, if the third alternative is accepted, then [the text says] "atha" and so forth:
"If [the object] were to exist after the knowable, then from where would knowledge arise?
Here, "atha" is used in the sense of an inquiry.
Regarding the phrase "from the object of knowledge" (jñeyāt): first there is the object of knowledge;
subsequently, immediately after that, once the object of knowledge has ceased, knowledge would come into being—that is, it would arise.
In that case, from where would knowledge arise?
Since the object of knowledge has ceased at the time of knowledge,
from what objective support could knowledge arise?
Depending on what could it arise?
Therefore, even from the totality of objects and so forth, cognition is not established in the ultimate sense.
This application of mindfulness to the mind (cittasmṛtyupasthāna) has been explained in the *Āryaratnakūṭa* and other such scriptures.
He thus searches for the mind: "Which is that mind that becomes attached, or becomes hostile, or becomes deluded? Is it past, future, or present?
In this regard, that which is past has ceased.
That which is future has not yet been reached;
for that which is present, there is no duration.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is formless, invisible, non-obstructive, non-communicative, baseless, and homeless.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, has not been seen by any of the Buddhas.
They do not see,
nor will they see,
that which has not been seen by all the Buddhas.
They have not seen it, nor will they see it; of what nature, then, should its movement be regarded as being?
Apart from this, phenomena proceed by means of perceptions fallen into falsehood.
For, Kāśyapa, the mind is like an illusion; through unreal conceptualization, it grasps at various types of rebirth. [The rest as before.]
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like the current of a river—unstable, arising, breaking up, and dissolving.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like the flame of a lamp; it proceeds by way of causes and conditions.
For the mind, Kāśyapa, is like a flash of lightning.
O Kāśyapa, the mind is momentary and unstable; indeed, like space,
it is defiled by adventitious afflictions and secondary afflictions.
... [as before] ... up to: For, Kāśyapa, when the mind is thoroughly sought after, it is not found; and that which is not found—
That is not apprehended;
it is neither past, nor future, nor present.
It transcends the three times.
That which has transcended the three times neither exists nor does not exist, and so forth.

Having thus established the application of mindfulness to the mind, he says "And thus," and so forth, applying the very same sequence in order to establish the application of mindfulness to phenomena: "And thus, the arising of all phenomena is not perceived. (Bca 9.106)
The particle *ca* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.
In this very way, according to the logic already stated, the arising—that is, the production—of all phenomena and all entities is not determined and is not perceived.
Furthermore, regarding their arising prior to their own causes, simultaneously with them, or subsequently, this same refutation should be stated as applicable in each case.
Since there is no arising, cessation is also not tenable,
because that which has not arisen cannot undergo cessation.
For this very reason, because all phenomena have the nature of being neither arisen nor ceased and are thus free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), they are oriented toward liberation.
They are said to have issued from the *dharmadhātu*, to culminate in the *ākāśadhātu*, and to be non-designatable, beyond conventional expression, ineffable, and inexpressible.
Thus, through the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), there arises a non-attached knowledge regarding all phenomena.
Furthermore, the cultivation of the application of mindfulness to phenomena is shown in the *Āryākṣayamati-sūtra*, where it is said:
Dwelling in the contemplation of phenomena within phenomena, the bodhisattva does not perceive any phenomenon whatsoever;
for there are no Buddha-qualities,
and there is no awakening.
Knowing that there is no path and no escape, and that all phenomena are themselves the escape, he enters the samādhi of unobstructed great compassion.
He acquires the perception that all phenomena and all afflictions are artificial: "These phenomena are without affliction; these are not possessed of affliction.
Why is that?
Because they converge upon the meaning in the sense of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
There is no accumulation or heaping up of afflictions;
there is no state of passion, nor any state of hatred.
There is no state of delusion;
awakening (bodhi) arises from the very thorough understanding of these [afflictions].
And whatever is the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the afflictions, [that is awakening].
Enlightenment has that as its intrinsic nature; thus one establishes mindfulness. So it is said.
And it has been said:
"For that which has no arising at all, what cessation could there be? Since it is like the manifestation of an illusory elephant, it is primordially quiescent without effort."
That which is dependent origination is itself considered by you to be emptiness;
such is the True Dharma, and the Tathāgata is equal thereto.
That reality is also the ultimate truth, suchness, and is held to be the substance;
it is the real and non-deceptive, and one is called a Buddha because of the awakening to that.
Thus,
by demonstrating the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) in this way, it is revealed that all phenomena are neither produced nor ceased.

If that were so, it would be said that conventional truth is untenable; consequently, the establishment of the two truths would not be possible. To resolve this, he raises an objection, saying "If it is thus," and so forth:
If that were so, then conventional reality would not exist; consequently, from where would the two truths arise?
If, from the perspective of ultimate truth, all phenomena have a nature that is neither produced nor ceased, then in that case, conventional reality does not exist.
Conventional practice would not exist,

and there would be only the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). Consequently, because conventional reality (saṃvṛti) would be absent, that which was stated— namely, that there are two truths, conventional truth and ultimate truth— would be undermined.
"Conventional reality and ultimate reality—these two truths are thus considered.
From what, then, would these two truths arise? They would not exist at all.
And because of their absence, there would be no going to another world, no connection between action and its fruit, and no acquisition of intrinsic nature, and so forth.
Because all conventional transactions would be absent.

Nevertheless, it might be argued: even if [the object] does not exist, it is nonetheless established by the intellect through conceptualization—which has the nature of the conventional—just as there is the conceptualization of water in mirages and the like.
Then, anticipating the objection that two truths would consequently follow, he says "atha sāpi" (and that too): "atha" is used here as an interrogative particle.
"And that [conventional reality] too [is established] by another conventional reality.
Thus, the word "atha" functions as a question.
"‘That too’ refers to conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*); the meaning of ‘too’ (*api*) is that it is not only ultimate reality (*paramārthasatya*).
It is established by another convention, which consists of the nature of conceptualizing cognition."
Alternatively,
the particle *api* is used for emphasis and its position is displaced;
it should be construed as "by means of a completely different conventional reality" (*anyayaiva saṃvṛtyā*).
Showing that while one thing is being joined together, another falls away, he says:
"How could a sentient being be liberated? (Bca 9.107).
If, from the perspective of ultimate reality, even that which is empty of intrinsic nature is called "conventional" because it is made an object of conceptualizing thought,

then how could even that being who, having realized the ultimate truth characterized by the lack of intrinsic nature in all phenomena, has attained final nirvāṇa through the yoga of non-apprehension and is thus free from all conceptual proliferation,
be one who has truly passed into nirvāṇa or been liberated? He certainly would not be.
Because that [nirvāṇa] too is made an object by cognition,
and because every cognition is a conventional reality (saṃvṛti) due to its nature as conceptual construction (kalpanā)—
according to the statement "cognition is called conventional reality"— then even nirvāṇa would be a conventional reality.
Regarding this, he states the refutation beginning with "paracitta" and so forth:

"This is a conceptual construction regarding another's mind"—that is, the mind of another being, distinct from a being who has attained nirvāṇa; this is the conceptual construction concerning that [mind].
This refers to the fact that even one who has attained nirvāṇa is made an object by another's cognition.
For it is not logical that the conventional reality of one person should be [determined] by the conceptual construction of another's mind;
therefore, even when made an object by another's cognition, he remains indeed in nirvāṇa.
Why? Because:
"But by its own conventional reality, it does not exist.
The word "but" (tu) expresses a distinction from what preceded.
By his own convention—that is, by his own worldly consensus or by his own conceptual construction—he does not exist as one who has attained final nirvāṇa; he is not found [as such].
He is indeed one who has attained final nirvāṇa because all conceptual constructions have ceased for him of their own accord.
To the question, "In that case, how could there be another's convention elsewhere? he says, beginning with "He afterwards," and so forth:
If that [conventional reality] does not exist as something subsequently determined, then conventional reality does not exist at all.
"When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this, that arises"—this mere conditionality (*idampratyayatāmātra*) is conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*).
Thus, a phenomenon arising from other phenomena would be posterior [to them].
Therefore, that Dharma which is subsequently established—
if it exists, then conventional reality (saṃvṛti) certainly exists.
If that [dependent origination] does not exist, then conventional reality itself does not exist;
for in cases such as a sky-lotus, the principle of "this-conditionality" (idaṃpratyayatā) is absent.
This is what is meant: even if one who has attained final nirvāṇa is indeed made an object of the mind, his non-nirvāṇa does not occur merely by virtue of another's mental conceptualization;
for he himself has brought to rest all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
One whose mind is not stained by passion, having himself abandoned all afflictive obscurations, would—though free from desire—be as one who has not transcended desire [for others].

Therefore, because he is devoid of all conceptual construction, even though he relies upon other conventionalities, he is himself truly extinguished (*parinirvṛta*) from the perspective of ultimate reality.

For this very reason, all phenomena are said to be naturally extinguished and primordially quiescent, because they are empty of all conceptual construction and possess a nature that is neither arisen nor ceased.
Nevertheless, from such [causes] alone, other such phenomena arise and cease,
like the nature of an illusion.
And because they are apprehended as objects once again through the power of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) in that form, they are conventional (*sāṃvrta*).
And because they lack any real nature, they are said to be unarisen and unceasing, like the horn of a donkey. As it has been said:
"From empty phenomena alone do empty phenomena arise."
It is also said in the *Ārya-lalitavistara*:
"Formations are like the flame of a lamp, having the nature of rapid arising and ceasing;
they are unstable like the wind, and as insubstantial and weak as a mass of foam."
Formations are inactive and empty; when observed, they are like the trunk of a plantain tree.
Like an illusion, they delude the mind; they are like an empty fist that deceives children.
* * * * [The same applies] in detail:
Just as a rope made of balvaja grass is twisted by the power of exertion,
and the water-wheel with its mechanism revolves, yet among those [parts] there is no revolving in each one individually.
In the same way, that which exists within all factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is dependent upon mutual accumulation;
yet, when examined one by one among them, no progression from the prior limit to the subsequent limit can be found.
Just as a seal is seen in its impression, the transfer of the seal is not itself perceived.

It is not there, nor indeed is it elsewhere; thus the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) are neither annihilated nor eternal. Just as fire arises from the conjunction of the lower fire-drill, the upper fire-drill, and the exertion of the hands—born of such conditions—it quickly ceases once its purpose has been achieved.
Then, if some wise person searches for where this has come from or where it goes—
searching through all the intermediate and cardinal directions— it is found that there is neither its coming nor its going.

The aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, as well as craving and ignorance, have karma as their condition; however, the designation "sentient being" is merely a collection [of these factors], and that [being] is not found in the ultimate sense.
Thus it is said.
Also, in the *Catuḥstava*, it is stated: [Lalita-vistara 13.97, 98, 100, 101, 104, 108–110] (Bcp 249).
Whether from a seed that has ceased or one that has not ceased, the arising of a sprout occurs;
indeed, you state that all arising is like the production of a magical illusion.
Therefore, you have thoroughly understood that this world arises from conceptual construction; it is unreal, unarisen, and does not perish.
There is no cyclic existence for that which is eternal, nor is there cyclic existence for that which is impermanent;
O best among those who know reality, you have declared that cyclic existence is like a dream.
Thus, although from the perspective of ultimate truth there is an absence of arising and cessation, there is no contradiction with conventional truth; therefore, everything is consistent.
Now, if all phenomena are ultimately unarisen and unceasing, then neither knowledge nor the object of knowledge exists in reality;
in that case, what is investigated here by whom? Thus, even investigation itself would not exist.
Therefore, one might think that one should simply remain silent; to this, he says "conceptual construction," and so forth:
"Conceptual construction and the conceptually constructed—these two are mutually dependent. All investigation is said to proceed by relying on what is conventionally established. (Bca 9.109)
Conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a superimposing cognition;
"the constructed" (*kalpitam*) refers to that which is superimposed by it. The particle *ca* indicates a conjunction of what has been stated.
Thus, these two are mutually dependent and rely upon one another:
in relation to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), there is the imagined (*kalpita*); and in relation to the imagined, there is conceptual construction.
Relying upon and taking as a basis what is determined according to worldly convention as it is commonly established, all investigation— that is, all critical examination— is said, or expressed.
The word "all" implies that not even a single investigation is extended by relying on conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) alone,
but rather [it proceeds] by means of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The meaning is that it transcends all conventional linguistic usage.

If it is argued that analysis (*vicāra*) itself must be analyzed, because its nature is conceptual just like external analysis, [the author] says "by the analyzed," etc., intending that analysis cannot be analyzed:
"But when that which has been analyzed is analyzed by means of analysis..."
Then there would be an infinite regress, because that very analysis would itself require further analysis.

But when that which has already been investigated and examined is further investigated and scrutinized by another investigation, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and a lack of foundation (*apratiṣṭhāna*).
Why? Because that investigation, too, must be investigated.
Because that very investigation which is undertaken for the purpose of investigating [the previous] investigation must itself be investigated.

If one asks, "In that case, when the object of investigation is being investigated, how can this infinite regress not occur? he says "When the object of investigation has been investigated," and so forth: "But when the object of investigation has been investigated, there is no further basis for investigation. Because it is without a basis, it does not arise; and that is called Nirvāṇa. (Bca 9.111)
But when an object to be investigated has been examined and determined, there is no further basis for investigation or determination to be performed at a later time,
by depending upon which an infinite regress would occur through the pursuit of further inquiry;
for once the object of investigation has been scrutinized, its purpose having been fulfilled, there is no further desire [for more].
Precisely because it is without a basis, it does not arise;
and due to the absence of a basis, further investigation does not proceed.

Having established the negation of all superimpositions, one has fulfilled all that was to be done through the thorough knowledge of the reality of things, and thus there is neither engagement nor withdrawal. (Bcp 250)
It is attached nowhere, nor does it become detached;
and that is called nirvāṇa.
Because all conventional transactions have ceased and it is utterly tranquil due to being devoid of activity in every respect, that very state is designated as "nirvāṇa."

He states that "in every case, investigation regarding an imagined object is necessarily true, but not from the perspective of ultimate reality" with the words beginning "But for whom this..."— but for whom these two, namely investigation and the object of investigation, are both true as ultimately real, he alone is extremely poorly situated. However, for one who asserts the existence of ultimate reality, both of these— investigation and the object of investigation— are true as ultimate reality.
That proponent of the intrinsic nature of entities (*bhāvasvabhāvavādin*) is extremely ill-situated—meaning he stands in extreme and excessive misery—because his position is difficult to maintain.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "if," and so forth:
"If the object exists by the power of cognition, then what is the status of the existence of cognition itself? (Bca 9.112)
If the object of cognition— the *prameya*— is established by virtue of knowledge— that is, by the power or capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—
then let the establishment of the *prameya* from the *pramāṇa* indeed occur;
who can prevent it?

Only this remains to be examined here: what is the status regarding the existence of cognition? Furthermore, it must be stated from what source the existence of cognition—which is itself a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—is ascertained?

Since self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is absent, if one were to search for another means of valid cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*). Therefore, what course should be adopted?
This might be the case— there would indeed be an infinite regress if a means of valid cognition were sought for the existence of cognition;
however, the establishment of the means of valid cognition proceeds from the object of cognition itself.
Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how could there be an infinite regress? he says "atha" and so forth:
"Now, if cognition [exists] by virtue of the object of cognition, what is the recourse when the object exists?
The word 'atha' (now/then) serves to indicate the intention of the opponent."
Now, if knowledge is established by virtue of the object of cognition— that is, the object of valid apprehension— then what is the status of the existence of that object of cognition?
If knowledge is established by virtue of the object of cognition, [what follows?]
In that case, the object of knowledge itself would have to be the basis for establishing the existence of the cognition;
and one asks from what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that [object] is established: "But what is the recourse regarding the existence of the object of knowledge?
If one pursues another cognition in order to establish the object of cognition, it must be explained from where that other cognition is established.
If it is argued that [the object] is established from that very object of knowledge, then from what is the object of knowledge itself established?
If another cognition must be pursued for its establishment, there would again be an infinite regress without end.

It might be argued: "This [objection] would hold true if there were a requirement for another cognition in order to establish either the cognition or the object of cognition; however, rather than that, their establishment is mutual.
Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not follow. Revealing this intention of the opponent, he says: "Now, if they are mutually... and so forth.
Moreover, by virtue of their mutual dependence, both existence and non-existence would belong to both.

Now, however, it might be argued as follows: by virtue of, that is, through the power of, each other—namely, knowledge and the object of knowledge—the existence or being of both knowledge and the object of knowledge is determined; that is to say, the object of knowledge exists by virtue of knowledge, and knowledge exists by virtue of the object of knowledge. If this were the case, there would be a non-existence of both.
There would be the non-existence of both the cognition and the cognizable; the existence of even one of them could not be established.
Because they are mutually dependent, if one is unestablished, the second is also unestablished.
In this regard, he states an appropriate example for the subject at hand, beginning with "If the father," and so forth:
"If there is no father without a son, how can there be the birth of a son?
In the absence of a son, there is no father."
(Bcp 251) If the father, the progenitor, were not to exist without a son— that is, in the absence of a son—
this designation [of "father"] would not occur, because it is dependent upon the birth of a son.
In that case, from where could the son arise? From what—that is, due to the absence of the father—could there be the arising, the birth, of the son who is to be produced?
Why is this so? Because in the absence of a son, there is no father.
This is a statement regarding the cause:
because in the absence of a son—that is, when he does not exist—the father does not exist, nor does he come to be;
for it is by means of a father that a son is to be produced.
And as long as he does not beget a son, he is not yet a father;
and as long as he is not a father, [he is not a father].
Therefore, the birth of the son from that [cause] does not exist.

Consequently, due to mutual dependence, the absence of one would entail the absence of the other; thus, the collective meaning is that both of these are non-existent. Applying this point to the case under discussion (the *dārṣṭāntika*), he says "tathā" (so too):
Likewise, there is the non-existence of those two.
Just as in this illustration of the father and son, so too is there non-existence— that is, the absence— of both of those, namely the cognition and the object of cognition.
For it is said that cognition is so called because it arises from the object of cognition.
Furthermore, as long as knowledge is not established by way of being that which delimits, so long is the object of knowledge not established;
and as long as thorough comprehension is not established, so long is the object of knowledge not established by way of being that which is delimited.
The point is that because of mutual dependence, there would be the non-existence of both.
It might be argued: "We do not say that the establishment of these two occurs through mutual dependence; rather, cognition is the effect of the object of cognition.
Therefore, from that cognition, the object of cognition will be established, just as a seed is [inferred] from a sprout.
Anticipating this objection, he says "the sprout," and so forth.
A sprout is born from a seed, and by that very [sprout] the seed is indicated;
why then is the existence of that [seed] not understood through the knowledge produced from the object of knowledge?
A sprout is born and arises from a seed located within a grain pit;
by that very sprout born from the seed, the seed is indicated—that is, it is made known.

Just so, why is the existence—the actual being—of that object of knowledge (*jñeya*) not likewise made known here by the cognition (*jñāna*) that has arisen or been produced from that object of knowledge?
Why is it not accepted?
Because here too, as in the case of the seed and the sprout, the relationship of cause and effect exists.
"This is not a comparable illustration," he says, beginning with "from the sprout, etc.": "From the sprout and other [effects], it is understood that the seed exists;
but from what is the existence of the cognition known, such that the object of cognition is understood by it? (Bca 9.116)

When it is understood from the effect, namely the sprout, that "the seed exists," this is not the power of the seed alone; rather, it is understood that "it exists" through another cognition distinct from the sprout itself.
For instance, an effect does not indicate its cause by mere capacity; otherwise, even a seed that has not yet produced a sprout would possess the status of an indicator.

Nor does it do so by the mere cognition of its own nature, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of such an indication occurring even for one who has not apprehended the relationship of cause and effect.

Rather, it is ascertained through the state of being inseparable (avinābhāvitva). Therefore, for one who has previously established the relationship of cause and effect and subsequently perceives a sprout that is invariably concomitant with a seed, there arises an inference consisting of a determinative cognition (adhyavasāyātmaka) from the sprout;
from this, it is determined that "the seed exists."
Therefore, it is only when the sprout has been made an object of cognition that it becomes the cause for the apprehension of the seed.
From what is the existence of cognition known? From what is its presence understood?
Because self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) does not exist, and because one does not pursue a further cognition out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
That which is to be known is understood by it; that is to say, because the object of knowledge is understood—that is, determined—by that cognition which is the effect of the object of knowledge.
For a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is itself not ascertained [cannot lead to certainty].
It is logical that [the reason] makes known the probandum;
for, because it is a "reason as a cognizer" (*jñāpaka-hetu*), it possesses the capacity to make known the object to be known (*jñeya*).
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*vāstava-pakṣa*), since neither cognition nor the object of cognition is established, investigation cannot be carried out.
However, it is certain that in the case of the conceptualist position, [the matter] can be established by relying upon conventional usage as it is commonly recognized.
Never, anywhere, do any entities whatsoever exist that have arisen from themselves, nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause.

In order to support this point [from *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* 1.3], and for the sake of establishing the fourth alternative— that things do not arise without a cause— he first speaks the verse beginning with "The world," etc., in order to refute the position of those who maintain that things arise from their own nature (*svabhāvavāda*):
"The world, for its part, perceives through direct perception that everything depends upon a cause."
For they describe it thus: the diversity of the multitude of entities arises entirely independent of all causes, whether intrinsic or extrinsic.

For instance, insentient things such as water and mud are not capable of producing the diverse variety of lotuses and the like, with their stalks, petals, leaves, filaments, and so forth, distinguished by many different types of differences. Nor is any other sentient being observed who, through action, is skilled in such a creation.
Nor does it take account [of such causes], because that action has no end and because it is impossible for it to operate simultaneously upon infinite particulars.
Therefore, their view is that this entire variety of the world arises without any cause at all; as it has been said:
The birth of entities is described by the proponents of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādins) as being independent of all causes; yet they do not even call that [intrinsic nature] a cause.
Who indeed creates the variegated beauty of the lotus filaments and so forth?
By whom was the multicolored eye of the peacock's tail and such things fashioned?
Just as the sharpness and other qualities of thorns and the like are without cause, so too,
because they occur only occasionally, those various sufferings and the like are without cause.

Thus, he demonstrates that for one who speaks in this way, there would be a sublation [of their position] by the very power of causes as they are commonly recognized in the world: "the world" refers to all people;
"from perception" means from knowledge based on the sense faculties.
The phrase "by means of direct perception" (*pratyakṣataḥ*) is an elliptical expression, implying that its cognition also occurs through inference (*anumānataḥ*);
that is to say, by both direct perception and inference.
"All" refers to every kind of cause, the cause of the world's diversity.
One observes that the effect arises in conformity with the presence and absence of that [cause];
for it is understood that whatever effect occurs when something exists, and does not occur when that thing is absent, [belongs to that cause].
It is determined that this is its cause;
thus, by the very operation of causality as it is commonly recognized in the world, his thesis of causelessness is contradicted.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "From the lotus-stalk, etc. and so forth.
For indeed, the differentiation of the lotus stalk and so forth arises from a difference in their causes.
Those things, such as the petals and filaments of a lotus (*padma*), which have the stalk of the *rājīva* lotus as their beginning, are so designated;
their "division" (*bheda*) is their manifoldness (*nānātva*). "For" (*hi*) means because.
It arises—that is, it is produced—by way of a distinction in the cause, meaning by way of a specific causal factor, and not otherwise;
for if there were no such restriction, the consequence would follow that [the effect] exists everywhere.
Therefore, whatever is perceived as following the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of something [else], [that is its cause].
Therefore, it must be accepted that this effect belongs to that [specific cause] alone and not to any other;
for since the production of a specific distinction arises from a specifically determined cause, and because its difference follows from the difference of that [cause], it is not without a cause.
(Bcp 253) But surely this distinction would hold if this very distinction were established by the reason itself; however, it must be explained from what that [distinction] arises for that [reason].
Nor can there be the production of a particularity from that which is devoid of particularity, for that would lead to the consequence of causelessness;
thus, in order to dispel this doubt, he says "By what is it made? and so forth.
If it is asked what causes the distinction between causes, [the answer is] "from the differentiation of prior causes.
If it is asked what causes it, by whom was it made, from where did it come—
if this distinction of causes is asserted as a specific difference in the cause— then [it is said to arise] from the differentiation of prior causes.
"By way of the differentiation of the prior cause" means by way of the differentiation—that is, the distinction—of the prior, that is, the preceding cause that produces it.
If it is asked, "From what does even that prior cause derive its distinction?
one must reply, "Again, in that case as well, it is from the distinction of a prior cause."
Thus, when there is a desire for a further distinction regarding each subsequent [term], the answer must be stated as "because of the distinction of each preceding one.
Nor does such an infinite regress entail any undesirable consequence, because it is accepted that "the prior limit of this beginningless and endless saṃsāra is not known.
For this very reason, he says "And from what? and so forth, to show that even the non-perversion of the fruit does not occur by itself.
And why? Because the cause yields its fruit through the power of the preceding cause.
For what reason is it that the cause is capable of yielding a fruit—that is, capable of bestowing a distinguished fruit?

Because of the power of the prior cause; by the efficacy of the preceding cause that produced it, it was born with such a nature through its own cause, such that, undergoing a transformation consisting of a succession of specific qualities conducive to the production of the effect when assisted by specific auxiliary factors, it attains [that state].
When there is no obstruction or deficiency [in the causal conditions], it produces exactly such a result.
Therefore, even the non-erroneous yielding of a result is produced solely by the capacity of its own cause.
Consequently, from a cause that is the means for achieving prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), the results of prosperity and the supreme good arise respectively.
Since the opposite of that [is] the opposite of this, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Moreover, the proponent of intrinsic nature (svabhāvavādin) must necessarily accept that things possess causes, even if unwillingly;
otherwise, how could the causelessness of entities—which he has asserted—be established in the absence of a cause?
For no one accepts it on the basis of a mere assertion alone.

For one who seeks to establish that [thesis] through the operation of a reason, since he himself must again accept its being caused by a reason, there would be a contradiction of his own thesis by his own words—just like one who says, "My mother is barren. Thus, this poor fellow has fallen into a dilemma; as it is said: "Like a rope with two nooses at both ends, he has reached a strait."
By asserting that "there is no cause," does he not thereby himself undermine his own thesis which possesses a reason?
Or, if he were to be indolent in adducing a reason, what would become of him with a mere thesis alone?
Thus,
this is merely the manifestation of a false view, because it is contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Having thus refuted the proponent of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and in order to establish the fourth alternative, he introduces the doctrine of God as the cause of the world in order to reject it, saying "God," and so forth. For those who maintain that God is the cause of the world—the proponents of the doctrine of God as the cause—having heard the refutation of the position of the proponent of intrinsic nature, think, "Half the burden has been completed; we shall state the distinction," and say: "In this way, assistance has indeed been rendered."

By you [it must be admitted that this is so]; for the diversity of the world cannot possibly arise without a cause, as that would entail the consequence of there being no restriction regarding place and other factors.

However, it is logical that he stated these things— water, mud, and so forth— are merely insentient and lack the capacity for such diversity. In this regard, there indeed exists that Blessed One, who is skilled in the creation of the world's manifold variety, the sole architect of the universe, the primordial source of the entire world, whose power and majesty are never impaired due to his eternal nature, and who knows the true reality of all things, such as the relationship between cause and effect.
"God possesses a majesty that is beyond the scope of all modern philosophical systems;
for that reason, what conscious person would venture to assert otherwise than that this entire world, including all things moving and unmoving, is caused by Him?
Having thus stated the doctrine of the Naiyāyikas and others, he refutes it: "God is not the cause of the world."
"Īśvara" is a name for Śaṅkara;
he alone is the cause of the entire universe, the cause of its creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
From him alone this entire universe arises without exception.
Otherwise, however, since they would lack a conscious cause, how could these mountains, rivers, earth, oceans, and so forth come into being?
It is only through the superintendence of a conscious being that these are able to arise, for they proceed solely by means of its activity. As it has been said:
Others declare the Lord to be the cause of all things that have an origin;
for it is said that a non-conscious entity cannot, of its own accord, initiate its own effects.
This would not be Mount Meru, nor this earth, nor this ocean; these two,
the sun and moon, beautiful in their abode, would not be the eyes of the world,
were it not for Īśāna, who acts as the potter in the creation of the universe.
It is said that some indeed assert that this world has been created by a creator who is the Lord, characterized by existence and other qualities.
Thus [it is said in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, verses 46–47].
Therefore, he asserts for himself that the world, which is thus insentient by nature, has Īśvara as its cause.
To this it is replied: What is the use of this proliferation of verbal elaboration, this construction of objects of cognition fabricated within one's own house?

Even when stated thus, this [position] does not produce satisfaction for the wise, as it is devoid of valid proof and fails to please those of dull intellect who are dogmatically attached to their own systems.
For instance: if he is compassionate, for what purpose does he again create these living beings who are tormented by the sufferings of hell and other realms?
And this being the case, his compassion would be something to be understood through faith alone.

If it is argued that he cannot be called "lacking in compassion" because he exerts himself to remove that [suffering] by making [the being] experience the fruits of the unwholesome karma he himself committed, we say no.
Why does the Compassionate One cause that action to be performed by which an undesirable fruit is experienced?
Because He is active even in that regard, as He is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all things that arise.
Furthermore, when that [agent] is not performing [the action], is the fruit of that karma experienced or not?
If the first position is held, then how is this so— ?
This ignorant creature is not its own master over its pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed into the pit.
Thus [Mahābhārata 3.30.28]:
because by this very [argument], there would follow the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding the admission of its operation in all causal activities.
Now, as for the second [alternative]:
In that case, why does this compassionate one not maintain equanimity toward it, but instead exerts effort to provide assistance?
If it is argued that he acts for the sake of its experience because the performed action is never lost and its fruit must necessarily be experienced by him, [then we reply:]

But how is it that, even while this [destruction] is not functioning, [the action] must necessarily be experienced by it due to the deficiency of the causal complex? Furthermore, what is the fault even in this case of "perishing"?
Therefore, it is appropriate for the Compassionate One to turn back from that very effort.
For if he were to remain there, his activity being dependent on their will, his own sovereignty would be demonstrated through their lack of spiritual maturity.
In this regard, although he is compassionate, he is unable to remain because he is impelled by the karma of sentient beings.
Indeed, his own sovereignty would be greatly illuminated otherwise;
for even if he were drawn along by the action of another, he would not attain mastery over himself,
and thus it would be the great power of karma alone that is revealed as being superior to God.
Therefore, it is better to attend solely to action, by the power of which even Maheśvara is unable to remain [unmoved] when drawn forth;
hence this remains unrefuted:
"Homage to those good deeds, before which even Brahmā has no power."
Thus [it is said in Bhartṛhari’s Vairāgyaśataka 92].
Now, if he is not compassionate, is he one who is free from passion or one who possesses passion?
If the first alternative is taken,
then it must be explained: even if [the creator] does not bestow happiness because he is devoid of compassion, why does he produce suffering for living beings?
For suffering is indeed brought upon someone by the power of passion and the like;
yet these do not exist in him. How then can he cause suffering to people without any cause?
If it is argued that he causes suffering for the sake of sport,
or that the activity of one free from passion is for the sake of sport, then it is certain that he is not free from passion.
Even for those possessed of passion and so forth who have conquered their senses, activity for the sake of play is not observed;
how much less, then, could it be so for those free from passion?
For no one other than a *rakṣas*, a *piśāca*, or similar beings can be imagined to take pleasure in the suffering of others.
Now, if the position is that he is not free from passion,

then how can he be the Lord (Īśvara) when he is common with other ordinary people? For one whose activity is subject to the bonds of afflictions such as passion is incapable of possessing sovereignty over the world.

Otherwise, it would follow that anything else of a similar nature would also possess that [power]. Nor is it logical for one whose autonomy is confined within the prison of saṃsāra to possess the skill in crafting the manifold variety of the universe, as if he were someone else.
Thus, it is existence itself that deceives you, in that such sovereignty is attributed even to one who is in such a state.
Or, let it be granted that such a being possesses agency;
nevertheless, is this person one whose self is healthy or one whose self is unwell?
If his self is healthy, then...
In that case, why does he cause suffering to people so suddenly and without cause?
For one who is composed in mind is never seen to afflict a person who is innocent.
If it is argued that he afflicts only those who go astray and have committed an offense, then [the following applies]:
He causes even one who has gone down a wrong path to act in that very way;

and having caused him to become such, he torments him again. Thus, he surpasses even the worldly lords in his baseness of conduct, for they punish only the offender for the transgression he himself has committed.
Furthermore, the fact that he acts by himself constitutes his great distinction.
Now, if he were of unsound mind,
then the engagement of discerning people seeking heaven and liberation in propitiating him would be improper.
For no one other than a madman would venture to propitiate a madman;
for discerning people engage in his propitiation out of a desire for heaven and the like,
and that [desire] is not possible from him because his nature is entirely uncertain.
Or rather, the opposite result of propitiating him is also possible.
However, those engaged in propitiating him, under the influence of extremely intense faith, would call themselves insane while calling him mad;
otherwise, how could they proceed with his propitiation?
What offense have these other madmen committed that they are not attended upon? If you say it is because they lack a superior power (*prabhāvātiśaya*),
we certainly do not perceive any such superior power in the case of the subject under discussion either.

Who other than a madman would dare to say that a madman possesses power that transcends the entire world? Thus, when this matter is thoroughly investigated, it finds no firm footing anywhere; therefore, enough with paying heed to the outpourings of such a misguided mind.
Consequently, what was said is well-stated:
(Bcp 256) There is no giver of pleasure or pain; the notion that another gives them is a false conception.
For the world is strung together by the thread of its own karma; the pride of thinking "I am the doer" is in vain.

Thus, this entire world is indeed without a creator; there is no other independent agent, whether conscious or otherwise, who acts as its creator apart from the causes that are directly perceived. To demonstrate this point in detail, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādī) says:
"Tell me, who indeed is the Lord?
He asks the proponent of the doctrine that God is the cause: "Tell me, declare—what is this 'Lord' intended by you?

By the word "indeed" (*tāvat*), he intends this: for those things such as the earth and so forth, whose effects are observed to follow upon [the presence and absence of] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
In that regard, what do you designate as Īśvara?
Furthermore, it is not logical to postulate causality for one whose operation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is unperceived,
because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, one who desires that [the self] be the cause must accept that it possesses the very operation of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) as observed [in other cases]. Furthermore, no effect is ever seen to follow the positive and negative concomitance of anything else distinct from the earth, seed, and so forth.
How, then, can its utility for the production of the effect be established? As it has been said:
When those [conditions] exist, that [effect] necessarily arises; yet, if something other than them is postulated as its cause, there would be an infinite regress of causes in every case.
Thus it is said.
Now, anticipating the opponent's view that "let the elements such as earth and so forth themselves be the Lord," he says: "If it is the elements... and so on:
"If it is the elements, let it be so; what effort is required even for a mere name? (Bca 9.119)
If the elements, such as earth and so forth, are called "Lord," then that is indeed accepted.
Let it be so.
"Let it be so;
we do not disagree on this point,
because we observe that an effect conforms to the positive and negative concomitance of earth and the other [elements]."
What effort is there even in a mere name?
"Mere name" (*nāmamātra*) means simply a name devoid of any distinct referent. The particle *api* is used here for emphasis.
What is the use of this great undertaking here; why is such effort and exertion made to establish that?
When I speak of earth and the other elements, and you likewise call those very same things "God," is there not any difference in meaning whatsoever?
And in this case, no fruit whatsoever is perceived from a dispute that is devoid of meaning.
Now, if there is indeed a distinction in their objects, then it is not logical for them to possess lordship; thus he says "But rather," and so forth:
"But rather, they are many, impermanent, inactive, and not deities."
Since earth and the other elements are subject to leaping over and are impure, he is not the Lord.
By the word "but" (apitu), he states an additional point:
it is not appropriate to conceive of these [elements], such as earth and so forth, as your Lord (īśvara), because they lack the characteristics [of a Lord].
How so? Because they are manifold with diverse intrinsic natures,
and they are impermanent, having a nature that perishes.
They are motionless;
being insentient, they are devoid of activity,
and they are not deities.
Nor are they of a form to be propitiated;
they are to be leaped over and bypassed because they cannot be approached,
and they are indeed impure and unholy.
Because earth and the other elements are present even in impure substances and the like.
"Earth and the others" refers to those beginning with earth—namely, earth, water, fire, and air.
He is not the Lord.
That Lord does not possess such a nature,
because he is the opposite of those six types.
If earth and the other elements are not the Lord, then perhaps space will be; to this he says "not space," and so forth:
"Space is not the Lord, because it is devoid of activity."
Even space is not a lord or an Ishvara. Why? Because it is devoid of activity; due to its lack of intrinsic nature, it is devoid of functional operation.
Even according to the opponent's view, [the self] lacks activity;
therefore, let it be the self— [but] no, for the self has already been refuted previously.
Since the self has already been refuted in detail, it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), like the horn of a hare.

Nevertheless, one might argue that because its majesty is inconceivable, its true nature cannot be discerned as "this is such-and-such" by those of limited vision. To this he says, beginning with "of the inconceivable," etc.:
"And if agency belongs to the inconceivable, why is it called 'inconceivable'? (Bca 9.121)

If he possesses a majesty that transcends thought, then why is it said— that is, what is being asserted— regarding the agency and simultaneous causality of Īśvara, which are themselves inconceivable and beyond the path of reasoning?
The meaning is that its agency, too, should not be spoken of, because it is inconceivable.
It might be argued: "Since its essential nature is extremely difficult to discern, it cannot be conceptualized;
however, its effect, being common to the perception of all people, must certainly be conceptualized.
To one who speaks thus, he replies with the words beginning "By that, what [is gained]? and so forth.
Granted that one might consider what he intends to create as his purpose, nevertheless, what is it that he intends to create?
Anticipating the opponent's reply— asking what it is that this Lord of inconceivable majesty desires or intends to create or fashion— he says:
"If [it is] the Self..."
In this case, the sandhi has not been applied with the vowel *ā* of the preceding word for the sake of metrical conformity.
If it is held that the Self is intended to be created by Him,
he refutes this as follows:
Is he not indeed constant? Indeed, sir, this self is intended by you to be constant and eternal;
how then can it be produced?
Otherwise, it would not be eternal at all;
for this would entail the absence of the defining characteristic of eternity, namely that "that which exists without a cause is eternal.
Furthermore, its activity of creation is not observed elsewhere either; thus he says "the earth and so forth," etc.
The Lord has the earth and other elements as his nature, and knowledge is beginningless, arising from the object of knowledge.
From karma arise pleasure and pain;
by the word "etcetera," water, fire, air, space, time, direction, and mind are included.
Their intrinsic nature is constant.
That [effect] is also not produced by that [cause],
because it is admitted that the atoms of earth and the other elements are eternal,
and because the operation of those [atoms] upon gross form will be refuted later.
Because space and the other [elements] are also eternal;
and as for "the Lord" (īśa),
since the Lord too is permanent, he does not create himself.
"Knowledge is beginningless from the object of knowledge":
knowledge, too, being produced from the object of knowledge, is beginningless,
because it proceeds by taking the object of knowledge as its support throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Even that [result] is not produced by it;
rather, pleasure and pain arise from that action—
namely, from wholesome and unwholesome karma— and pleasure and pain occur according to possibility, born from desirable and undesirable maturation.
Even in that case, he has no activity.
This being so—tell me, what was created by him?
Speak: what has been created or fashioned now by that Lord (Īśvara)?
Thus, no capacity whatsoever is observed in him;
so how can he be said to be the creator of the world?
Now, he states a refutation that applies universally: "Because of the cause," and so forth.
If there is no beginning to the cause, how could there be a beginning to the effect?
For instance, would this cause of the world be eternal or non-eternal?
It has been conceptualized by its proponents as being precisely eternal.
In that case, if the cause—the causal agent—is eternal, it has no beginning.
If that were so, from where would the beginning of the fruit arise?
The meaning is that it could not exist at all.
If the cause, possessing a capable nature, were eternally present, the effect produced by it would likewise arise incessantly;
thus, the effect, being constrained by its capacity, would always be obtained. Why, then, does it not produce [the effect] at all times?
For what reason does it not act at all times—that is, at every moment—and why does it not produce every effect? How is it that there is ever a cessation of the activity of any particular effect?
Alternatively, it is introduced in another way: "If God were not the creator of the world, how could this [world] undergo creation from the very beginning after a period of dissolution?
To this, he says "Because of the cause," and so forth: "For the cycle of births is indeed without beginning or end."

And for that reason, if there is no beginning— that is, no prior limit— of the cause characterized by afflictions, karma, and so forth, how could there be a beginning, that is, a first commencement, of the result characterized by the evolution of the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world?
The meaning is that such a thing does not exist at all.
For in beginningless saṃsāra, the processes of subsistence, dissolution, and evolution proceed by the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings;
and this has already been stated by the verse: "From karma come pleasure and pain" (9.123).
Alternatively, even here, it is said "of the cause" (hetoh) with reference specifically to Īśvara.
