If there is no beginning to the cause, namely Īśvara— since his majesty is admitted to remain unimpaired even at the time of dissolution— how could there be a beginning to the effect produced by him, characterized as creation and so forth?
Because its cause would be eternally capable by virtue of its permanence, even the creation and so forth would necessarily be eternal.
Therefore, while that [cause] is eternally capable, there could be no beginning at all for the creation and so forth.
Consequently, how could its operation occur even at the beginning of the creation? Moreover:
If he were the creator,
then, because of his eternity,
why does he not act at all times?
The word "creation and so forth" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
For instance, if he were to create at some time, then, by virtue of having that [creative] nature as his cause, he would always perform that very act.
The same should be said regarding maintenance and destruction as well;
or else, its activities of creation and so forth would have to occur simultaneously,
precisely because there would be no cessation for that very reason.
There is also no cessation of the fruit;
the rest is as before.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if that [cause] were always of a capable nature, it still does not act at times due to the absence of auxiliary conditions. To this he says:
"For it does not depend on anything else."
(Bcp 259) Thus: the Lord (Īśvara) is the cause because his nature is efficacious; "hi" means "since."
It does not depend upon another auxiliary cause,
because it is impossible for that which is eternal and possesses a capable nature to depend on anything;
for that which, by virtue of its eternity, cannot have any excellence added to it, has no dependence whatsoever.
Alternatively, if a particularity (viśeṣa) were produced, it would follow that the entity itself—whose nature is non-different from that particularity—must also be produced.

Or, if there were a difference [between the entity and the particularity], the production of the effect would arise from the particularity alone, and the [entity] would be a non-agent. As it has been said:
If something were to depend upon another in order to perform some action,
then why would that which is incapable of performing any action at all depend upon anything?
Thus [it is said].
Or let there be auxiliaries for it;
nevertheless, would they be eternal or non-eternal?

As for those things that are eternal, such as atoms and the like, it is impossible for them to lack existence, nor is it possible for there to be a deficiency in the presence of those things whose proximity depends upon them.

Furthermore, since even impermanent things have their arising and presence dependent upon that [cause], how could there be any deficiency in them such that it could be said, "It does not produce [the effect] due to a deficiency of auxiliary causes"?
Therefore, this is not a valid rebuttal here.
Therefore, he says "by that, it is not made," and so forth:
"Since there is nothing else whatsoever not made by that, what could it possibly depend upon? (Bca 9.124)
That which was not created by that Lord, namely that which has an origin, does not exist at all.
There exists no other [cause] in the world besides him;
for that reason, since his auxiliary causes—upon which his activity depends—are always present, why would this eternal creator depend on anything?
Depending on what could he ever fail to produce an effect?
Thus, since he has no dependence whatsoever, one should always perform one's duty.

Furthermore, it might be argued that an effect arises from a triad of causes: the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), and the instrumental cause (nimittakāraṇa).

Anticipating the opponent’s intention— that because it is an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), there is no occurrence of the aforementioned fault since it produces the effect in dependence upon a collection of conditions (*sāmagrī*)— the author says "if it depends," and so forth:
"If it indeed depends upon a collection of conditions, even though it is always capable of producing all effects..."
Nevertheless, it still requires a causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For indeed, even if an agent is capable, the effect does not arise in the absence of a causal complex.
Just as, for example, even when there is a certain cause capable of producing a cloth, no cloth arises without the shuttle, the threads, the loom, and so forth.
If it is the same in the present case as well, he says: "The cause is not, moreover, God;
if [He] acts when the totality of conditions (sāmagrī) is present,"
And if it is admitted that he does not act in their absence,
then God would no longer be the cause,
since the production of the effect arises from the causal complex alone.
Furthermore, because [the effect] does not arise [independently],
we observe the presence or absence of the effect based on the presence or absence of that [cause],
but not based on the presence or absence of God.
Even at the time when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, that [agent] does not act by means of another nature;
and since its own nature remains exactly as it was previously capable, how could there ever be a cessation of activity?
As for what was also said—that it acts only occasionally, like a weaver and so forth—[that is untenable].
That too is not tenable;
for weavers and the like are indeed incapable at first,
yet later, through the acquisition of the causal complex consisting of the shuttle and so forth, they attain a previously non-existent capacity and thus produce effects such as cloth.
Otherwise, even if their capacity existed previously, the consequence that those actions would still occur does not cease; thus, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Furthermore, that very [capacity] is the cause even for the production of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
And since its nature is always present, how could there ever be a deficiency in its causal conditions (*sāmagrī*)?
Therefore, demonstrating this very point, he says:
"It is not capable of not acting when the causal conditions are present."
Thus, he is not capable of non-doing; that is, he is not able to refrain from action.
This refers to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), that is, within the sphere of the causal conditions.
Because it is capable of performing all its functions, it cannot remain indifferent even toward the production of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
If it is argued, "Then let it produce the causal complex," he says:
"[It cannot do so], because that [complex] is absent. (Bca 9.125)
He is not even capable of acting within the causal complex.
Why? Because of its absence—that is, because that causal complex is absent and non-existent.
And nothing can be done with that which lacks an intrinsic nature, like the son of a barren woman, because it is devoid of form.
As he will say:
"There is no modification of a non-entity; [it is] conceptual... [hetu?]
"Even by hundreds of millions. Thus,
let it be granted that there is indeed an agent only when the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) is present.
Nevertheless, there are two alternatives: does he act, though unwilling, being drawn by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or does he act with desire?
Anticipating the first alternative, he says "he acts," and so forth.
If the Lord acts even without desiring it, he follows as a consequence that he is dependent on another.
"Acts" means he brings about the effect; "without desiring" means without wishing;
"Lord" means the Sovereign (Īśvara).
If this is your view, it follows that [the agent] would be dependent on another;
"dependent on another" means being subject to another.
For it would follow that one is under the control of that [collection], acting even against one's will by the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for one who experiences dependence to possess sovereignty,
as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
With reference to the second alternative, he says:
Even if one desires, one would be dependent on desire;
furthermore, if the position is accepted that "one acts because one desires," even then one would be dependent on desire.
Because there is activity toward an effect when desire exists, and no such activity when it is absent;
this is due to the presence of dependence upon that [desire].
For one who acts [independently], how can there be lordship?
For one who acts in this way and brings about an effect, from where could there be lordship, and from where could there be sovereignty?
By this, that which was said by someone— namely, "this fault does not apply to God because He possesses intelligence"— is refuted.
For one devoid of intelligence would indeed produce an effect that arises solely from its own existence and without any sequence;
but an intelligent being, though capable of acting, does not act if he does not so desire— so what cause for reproach can there be for him?
That too has been refuted;
for in that case, the same reproach applies: why does he not also produce those very desires, since they too are dependent solely upon his own existence?
Furthermore:

If they are not its auxiliaries, why does it not act even when they are absent? Or, if it does not produce the effect even in the absence of non-auxiliaries, is it always dependent upon them? If they are indeed auxiliaries, [then...]

Likewise, even when that [permanent cause] exists, why does it not produce every effect? If you argue that it is capable only when there is a totality of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), and that what is incapable in isolation cannot be a producer; then:
In that case, does this [agent] act by means of another's nature? If so, it is not an agent at all;
for it does not [act] by means of its own nature. (Bcp 261)
If it is argued that the non-agent is indeed called the agent because its own nature, which is denoted by the term "intrinsic power" (nija-śakti), is serviceable for the effect,
then there is no further need for dependence on adventitious powers (āgantuka-śakti).

If it is argued that although this [entity] is by nature capable, it does not act because of the non-proximity of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), then the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Fools) would also have to say that a woman who is actually a mother is by nature barren; let us leave that matter aside for now.
Furthermore, a non-eternal [cause] is not accepted by those who propound that [theory].
And this being the case, how can that which possesses a nature common to others be the Lord? Thus it is established that the diversity of the world is not the work of a Lord.

If the world is not created by an intelligent agent, then let it consist of a collection of eternal atoms, arising in the sequence of dyads and so forth, such as the earth, trees, mountains, and so on; to this he says "ye 'pi" and so forth:
"Those who assert that atoms are eternal have also already been refuted."
Even those proponents such as the Mīmāṃsakas who assert that eternal atoms exist and declare them to be the cause of the world’s diversity—

those proponents too have already been refuted and rejected during the investigation of atoms in the passage beginning with, “Even parts [are excluded] by the analysis of atoms” (9.87). Therefore, this world is not composed of eternal atoms either.

Having thus refuted, by means of half a verse, the doctrine of God as the cause and the nature of the world as consisting of eternal atoms in the interim, [the author] now sets forth the Sāṃkhya view in order to refute the idea that the world is a transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), for the sake of establishing that very fourth alternative; he says "The Sāṃkhyas," and so on:
"The Sāṃkhyas maintain that *pradhāna* is the eternal cause of the world. (Bca 9.127)
The Sāṃkhyas, followers of Kapila, maintain that *pradhāna*—which has the alternative name *prakṛti*—is the eternal cause of the world;
they consider it to be permanent and of an indestructible nature, and they hold it to be the cause of the entire world, including all moving and non-moving beings, by way of transformation.

If one asks, "What is this so-called *pradhāna*? he says: "Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities (*guṇa*), when existing in equilibrium, are called *pradhāna*; when they are unbalanced, the world is said to arise. (Bca 9.128)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these three qualities, when existing in an undisturbed state, having reached a state of equilibrium, are called *pradhāna*;
they are termed *pradhāna*.
This, then, is their state as primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
The world is said to be "uneven" because it has reached an uneven state through these very same qualities; thus, the transformation of the world's manifold diversity is described.
For their system is as follows: when a longing arises in the *puruṣa* for the experience of objects, then *prakṛti*, having become aware of the *puruṣa*'s longing, unites with the *puruṣa*.
Thereupon, she brings about a transformation in the form of the creation of sound and the other sense-objects.
Then the sequence is as follows:
from primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five among those sixteen, the five gross elements arise.
This is its meaning: from *prakṛti* comes the Great One (*mahān*); from *pradhāna* comes the Great One.
"The Great One" is a designation for the intellect (*buddhi*).
From that [mahat] arises the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the cognition "I am.
From that ego-sense arises the group of sixteen.
The "sixteenfold" consists of the eleven sense-faculties and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*).
Among these, the five faculties of action (*karmendriya*) are characterized as speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals;
and the five faculties of cognition (*buddhīndriya*)—(Bcp 262).
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose;
the mind (*manas*), which is of both natures, makes eleven.
Furthermore, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.
From the five [tanmātras], the five elements arise;
from the five, beginning with sound, the five elements come into being, and these five elements are known as space, air, fire, water, and earth.
However, the primordial nature (prakṛti) is solely a cause and not an effect.
The Great Principle (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), and the five [subtle elements] beginning with sound constitute both effect and cause.
The eleven organs and the five [gross elements] beginning with space are only effects, not causes.
The Person (puruṣa), moreover, is devoid of the nature of both. As it has been said:
Root nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved;
the group of sixteen is only evolved; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolved.
Thus [it is said in Sāṃkhyakārikā 3]:
"And that Pradhāna, consisting of the potencies for all effects and composed of the three guṇas, brings about the production of the effect.
Otherwise, how could the manifold variety of effects, which does not exist therein [prior to creation], arise?"
And so it has been said:
"From Pradhāna alone, which is accumulated with all powers, various effects proceed; in reality, they are of that very same nature."
If, however, the effect were non-existent within the nature of the cause by virtue of its potentiality,
it could not be produced at all, because of its lack of form, like a lotus in the sky.

Thus, the followers of Kapila (the Sāṃkhyas) indeed maintain that the world evolves from the Primal Nature (pradhāna) in the form of its effects. Considering all of this to appear like a painting drawn in the sky, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntavādin), wishing to refute it, says "of the one": *Tattvasaṃgraha* 7–8. Considering all of this to appear like a painting drawn in the sky, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddh
It is illogical for a single entity to possess the nature of the three self-natures; therefore, that does not exist.
It is illogical—that is, inconsistent—for a single existent *pradhāna* to have a tripartite nature consisting of the distinctions of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
For that reason, it does not exist.
That *pradhāna*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, does not exist;
the claim that it is both one and possesses a manifold nature is mutually contradictory. Therefore, once that [pradhāna] is discarded, all its effects are likewise refuted.

Granted that it may not have a single nature consisting of the three qualities (*guṇa*), at least the qualities themselves must exist by way of their own nature; thus he says "in this way," and so forth:
"In this way, the qualities do not exist, for each of them is likewise threefold. (Bca 9.129)
In this very way, the qualities (guṇas) consisting of sattva, rajas, and tamas do not exist as being primary (pradhāna);
for they too are threefold,
because— hi— of this reason.
Those qualities (*guṇa*) as well are each threefold, consisting of three types.
For, according to those who assert that everything consists of the three qualities, it follows that even the individual qualities themselves must consist of the three qualities by their very nature.
Thus, because they consist of the three qualities, even those qualities do not possess a single inherent nature (*svabhāva*).

And when, upon such investigation, qualities do not exist, then even sound and the other [objects], which are of the nature of their manifestations, are not tenable; thus he says, "In the absence of qualities," and so forth:
"In the absence of qualities, the existence of sound and the rest is exceedingly remote."
"In the absence" (abhāve) means in the non-existence (asattve) of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest.
The word "and" (*ca*) serves to aggregate other refutations.
By the inclusion of "etcetera" (*ādi*) in "sound etcetera," the inclusion of touch and so forth is intended.
Existence, that is, being, is utterly remote;
it is not possible in any way whatsoever,
because in the absence of a cause, the existence of an effect is untenable.
As for what was also said:
"For this manifest [world] is clearly observed to be endowed with pleasure and so forth."
Because states such as serenity, distress, and dejection are perceived as a single [unitary] experience.
Thus [it is said]. That too is not tenable.

Furthermore, as for the reason stated—that the transformation of manifest form and so forth, which consists of the nature of pleasure and so on, is the cause for establishing that existence and the other [qualities] have the nature of pleasure and so forth—[that is also flawed].
He says that even that does not exist, beginning with "insentient," etc.:
"And in insentient things such as clothing and the like, there is no possibility of pleasure and so forth either. (Bca 9.130)

And in that which is insentient and of an inert nature— the word "and" (ca) functions as before— in cloth and so forth, which are of the nature of non-consciousness such as woven fabric, there is the impossibility, that is, the absence, of pleasure and the like, even though they are of the nature of consciousness, due to [their] identity [with the substrate].
Since it is precisely sattva, rajas, and tamas that are called pleasure, pain, and delusion,
and those qualities (guṇas) do not exist [in the Self],
how could pleasure and the others exist therein?

Furthermore, it might be argued: "We do not say that pleasure and the other [feelings] have the nature of pleasure and so forth because they are identical in essence to pleasure and so forth, but rather because pleasure and so forth arise from them.
Anticipating this objection, he says "taddhetu... and so on:
"If entities have the form of the causes of those [feelings], then surely entities have already been analyzed."
If it is your view that external entities such as cloth and so forth are the causes— that is, they possess the nature of being the causal basis— of that pleasure and the rest,
then surely those entities have already been analyzed.
These [objects] such as cloth do not exist in the form of a composite whole (*avayavin*).
Furthermore, entities have been thus examined and established through reasoning as being neither of the nature of atoms nor composed of the three qualities (triguṇa),
because those things appearing [to perception] are devoid of intrinsic nature, like an illusion.
What, then, could these entities be that serve as the cause of pleasure and so forth?

Furthermore, if manifest things were of the nature of pleasure and so on, then cloth and other such objects would themselves be produced from pleasure and the like; thus he says, "pleasure and so forth alone," etc.:
"And pleasure and so forth alone are their cause."
Furthermore, for you, the Sāṃkhya, even the cloth would have pleasure and so forth as its cause.
Because the manifest is of the nature of pleasure and so forth;
nevertheless—therefore, cloth and the like do not [arise] from that.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), sandalwood garlands and so forth are included.
On the contrary, the opposite is observed here; thus he says "but of cloth, etc. and so forth:
"But from cloth, etc., pleasure and so forth would arise; in the absence of that [cloth], pleasure and so forth do not exist.
"From cloth, etc."—by the word "etc.," garlands and the like are included.
Furthermore, pleasure and so forth would arise;
by the word "and so forth," suffering and so forth would also occur.
Because of the absence of that [pleasure], [suffering and so forth would likewise be absent].

Because those [causes], such as cloth and so forth, are absent, pleasure and the like do not exist; since pleasure and the like are effects of cloth and so forth, they would likewise not exist. Thus, because pleasure and the like conform to the presence and absence of those [causes], they are their effects.

Furthermore, as for the claim that pleasure and the like are eternal because they consist of the qualities such as *sattva*, that too is not correct; thus he says, "And of pleasure and the like," and so forth:
"And the eternity of pleasure and the like is never perceived. (Bca 9.132)
And [it is so] regarding pleasure, pain, and delusion;
the word "and" (ca) is used here to indicate the intention to express further faults.
Permanence—that is, the state of having an eternal intrinsic nature—is never perceived, nor is it ever seen.
Because qualities themselves do not exist, it is impossible for them to possess such properties as permanence.
And if pleasure and the other [feelings] were eternal, then they would be perceived eternally; thus he says, "When [the cause] exists," and so forth:
(Bcp 264) If pleasure and the like were eternal, then they would be perceived at all times; therefore, he says "satyām" and so on.
If pleasure were indeed manifest, why is it not perceived?
If pleasure and the other [feelings] truly exist as stable entities, then they would be experienced at all times.
The collective meaning is: "because of not abandoning its own nature.
That is, while a manifestation of pleasure actually exists—that is, when a manifestation of pleasure has once arisen—if pleasure were eternal.
Why is consciousness not apprehended?
Why would there not always be the experience of pleasure? Yet, such constant experience does not exist.
Therefore, since it is certain that something which is not perceived at some time does not exist then, how can there be permanence?
It might be argued: "This fault would apply if it were always in a manifest form;
however, when that very same thing has entered into dissolution in the form of a latent power (*śakti*),"
To the objection that "in that case there would be no fault," he says "tadeva" and so forth:
"That very same thing becomes subtle; how can that which is gross be subtle? (Bca 9.133)
Having established itself in manifestation through its reliance on existing entities,
it subsequently attains subtlety at the time of non-perception; like stars by day, it resorts to a state of unperceivable nature.
This is inconsistent.
Why? Because that which is gross has a manifest nature; how then can it be subtle?
How can that pleasure and so forth have an unmanifest nature?
The point is that it is not logical for a single entity to possess a manifold nature by virtue of being eternal.

Furthermore, it might be argued that while two mutually contradictory things cannot coexist at one time, there is no fault in the case where, upon the cessation of a prior property, another property arises. To this he says "sthaulyam" and so forth:
"Having abandoned grossness, the subtle would exist; in the impermanent, there are grossness and subtlety.
Having abandoned—that is, having relinquished—the state of manifestation, grossness would become subtle, meaning it would take a concealed form.
If this is accepted, then since grossness and subtlety are impermanent—being permeated by arising and destruction—they would be unstable.
To the objection, "Let them be impermanent for you; what is the harm? he says: "Of everything," and so forth.
Why is impermanence not likewise accepted for every entity? // Bca_9.134 //

Why is impermanence not accepted for every entity characterized by the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), just as there is both grossness and subtlety? Why is total destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*) not admitted?

This is the intended meaning: even in the case of grossness and subtlety, manifestation and disappearance are not tenable without the destruction of the preceding state without residue and the arising of the subsequent state as something previously non-existent.
Otherwise, because it would persist in some form or other, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being perceived again, just as before;
and the same applies to pleasure and the rest.
Therefore, one must necessarily accept that for those two, there is destruction without residue and the arising of what was non-existent;
and just as these two occur for them, they would likewise occur for others as well, since there is no distinction between them.
Furthermore, if the destruction of grossness and the arising of subtlety are admitted,
then it would follow that pleasure and the other [feelings] are impermanent.
For instance, would that grossness be different from the pleasure or non-different?
In that case, if [the two] were distinct,
then even when that [feeling] had ceased, there would still be the experience of pleasure as before;
for it is not logical that a jar should remain unperceived simply because a cloth has ceased to exist.
For if one were to postulate a relationship between them expressed as "this belongs to that," it would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress.
Furthermore, even if a relationship existed, the cessation of one thing would not logically entail the cessation of another if the latter were not its cause—
just as the cessation of a cow does not necessarily entail the cessation of its owner.
Nor is that the cause of pleasure, since pleasure arises from the cloth and so forth themselves;
nor is even that [the cloth] the cause.
Because it is simultaneous with pleasure and the other [feelings].
(Bcp 265) Now, if the position is that [pleasure] is non-different [from the self], it is said in response: "If grossness is not other than pleasure..."
If grossness were not distinct from pleasure— that is, if it were not different from it—
then that would be nothing but pleasure; in that case,
the impermanence of pleasure would be evident.
Since pleasure ceases when grossness is removed due to that very nature [of pleasure], the impermanence—that is, the perishability—of pleasure is clearly ascertained.
It might be argued: if there were destruction in every respect, then pleasure could not arise again;
for that which is absolutely non-existent, like a sky-lotus, cannot undergo production.
Thus, demonstrating the opinion of others, he says "nāsat" and so forth:
"If it is thought that nothing non-existent arises because of its lack of existence—
[then] that which does not exist at all within the nature of the cause does not arise."
Just like a lotus in the sky,
if anything else were likewise to exist, it would not arise.
Therefore, nothing arises from non-existence, nor does anything arise that has an absolutely non-existent nature.
Why? Because of its non-existence.
If it is thought that [the object] does not exist because of its non-existence,
and if this is indeed accepted, then one should not say this; thus he says "of the manifested," and so forth.
The arising of a manifest thing from what is non-existent is established for you, even against your will.

The production (utpāda) of that which is manifest and previously non-existent—that is, of a manifest thing not existing in its state of potentiality—is its subsequent arising. Even for you, who maintain that what exists is produced, this [consequence] stands; otherwise, if it existed even prior [to production], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its being perceived even before, just as it is after.
Just as there is the arising of a manifest thing that was previously non-existent,
if it were the same for another [thing],
then nothing would be contradictory.

Moreover, since for the proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*), the effect is already present in the state of the cause, another objection is raised; thus he says, beginning with "eater of food" (*annāda*): "An eater of food would be an eater of impurity.

An "eater of food" (*annāda*) is one who eats food (*anna-ad*); [if the effect were pre-existent], he would be an eater of impurity (*amedhya-bhakṣa*), meaning he would be a consumer of the unclean. How so?
If the effect were already present in the cause— that is,
if the effect existed as a real entity within the cause— then it would follow that the effect, such as excrement, is identical in nature to its cause, the food.
And since this [consequence] exists for the proponent of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavādin*) precisely at the stage of the seed,
you suspect that by eating the seed, one eats that [cloth].
Furthermore, introducing another undesirable consequence for the proponent of the theory of the pre-existent effect, he says "by the price of the cloth," and so forth.
Having purchased cotton seeds with the very price intended for the cloth, let it be worn.
The connection is: "if the fruit exists within the cause.
Since the effect, which is the cloth, exists potentially within its cause, the cotton seed, one might buy and take the cotton seed at the price and value of the cloth, and then wear it.

Furthermore, one might think: "Even if the effect exists in the cause from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, this worldly person engaged in conventional practice, whose eyes are impaired by the cataracts of ignorance regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), does not perceive it. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says "from delusion" and so forth (Bcp 266): mohād dhetuphalātmānaṃ kalpayitvā hy abhidhīyate / kāraṇe 'sti phalaṃ ceti tasmān mohaḥ prakalpyate // 17 // For, having imagined the nature of cause and effect through delusion (*moha*), it is indeed asserted that "the effect exists in the cause"; therefore, delusion is postulated.
If the world does not perceive [it] due to delusion—
if, out of delusion, that is, ignorance, the world does not perceive or see the reality of things even though it exists—
then the aforementioned logical fault does not follow.
If [it is argued that it does not exist],
then surely that same state exists even for one who knows reality.
Even if the world does not engage in such conventional usage while failing to see [the truth],
it would be appropriate for one who knows reality;
however, this is not the case.
For this reason, even for the Sāṃkhya who knows the ultimate truth—that the effect exists within the cause—the same position holds;
that very same established order is common to all people engaged in worldly affairs.
Even they are seen engaging in activities such as eating food, while those seeking cloth avoid the cotton seed.
Nor is this rebuttal appropriate here, as he says "of the world" and so forth:
"And that knowledge belongs even to the world; why does it not see?
That knowledge belongs even to the world—that is, to ordinary people engaged in worldly transactions.
That by which one understands that the effect exists in the cause does not belong to the knower of reality alone.
For instance, the certainty that "the effect exists in the cause" upon seeing the effect is common to both the knower of reality and the worldly person.
Therefore, for what reason does the world not see it?
In that regard, the cause for the world's non-perception must be stated.
If it is argued that the world’s perception is invalid, he says "the world," and so forth:

If the world were not a valid authority— that is, if the people of the world, those engaged in conventional practice, were not authoritative— then even the perception of the manifest would be non-existent, given that their cognition lacks validity. (Bca 9.138)
The manifestation of the manifest, that is, the appearance of its manifested nature—
that too would be non-existent and lack valid authority.
Therefore, the determination of the reality of things cannot be established on that basis.
And this is indeed accepted by us,
because all conventional means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), not valid cognitions.
Thus, you too have relegated [the validity of our position] to our own side.

Having thus reached a conclusion, the follower of Kapila (the Sāṃkhya), even while leveling a common objection against the proponent of the established doctrine, says "If it is a means of valid cognition," and so forth:
"If that which is a means of valid cognition is invalid, then surely what is cognized by it is false.
If your position is that even a means of valid cognition is not, in the ultimate sense, a means of valid cognition, [then...]
Is it not the case that what is cognized by that [means] is false?
If the means of cognition lacks validity, then that which is cognized by it—that is, determined by that means of cognition—would result in being false or unreal.
What follows from this?
Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality, emptiness is not established for entities.
If that which is cognized by a means of valid cognition is false because that means of valid cognition lacks validity,

then this emptiness of phenomena and entities— which is established through that means of valid cognition as being their reality and ultimate truth, namely the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena— that too would not be tenable.
It is not tenable;

for since everything demonstrated by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has a false nature, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena is likewise demonstrated solely by the means of valid cognition that investigate it—the logic being identical.
Regarding this, he states the refutation beginning with "the imagined," etc.:
"Without contacting the imagined entity, its non-existence cannot be apprehended.
Without touching—that is, without grasping by means of the conceptualizing intellect—a thing that is imagined and superimposed by conceptualization, its non-existence is not grasped nor apprehended.
For instance, having conceptually constructed a jar by way of a superimposed form, people in the world understand the non-existence of the jar as being related to it.
When, through investigation, not even the slightest intrinsic nature of the jar remains according to worldly consensus, [then its non-existence is understood].
At that time, its non-existence—which would be of the nature of the opposite of that [existence]—is all the more not anything at all.
Demonstrating this very point, he says "Therefore," and so forth:
"Therefore, since existence itself is false, its non-existence is clearly false. (Bca 9.140)
Since non-existence is apprehended through the exclusion of an imagined entity,
therefore that existence which has a non-existent nature is false;
its non-existence is clearly false as well.
The non-existence— that is, the absence or lack— of that entity which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is clearly and certainly false and unreal,
because that [non-existence] too has a purely imagined form (*parikalpitarūpa*).
And thus, when both existence and non-existence have an imagined form, the very absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena (*sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā*) remains established.
Furthermore, clarifying this very point under the guise of a summary, he says "Therefore, in a dream," and so forth: "Therefore,
when a son is lost in a dream, the conceptualization that 'he does not exist' [is false],
because existence and non-existence are unreal objects since they are established by conceptual construction."

Therefore, when a son has been born and then perished during the state of sleep while the mind is overcome by *middha* (torpor), the conceptualization that "that son does not exist" is the conceptualization of his non-existence. What does it do?
It obstructs the arising of the conceptualization of his existence.

"His existence" (*tadbhāva*) means his being present; "conceptualization of that" (*tasya kalpanā*) is the superimposition of reality (*sattvasamāropa*); "the arising of that" (*tasyotpādaḥ*) is its emergence—that [conceptualization] it obstructs.
He refutes this: "If you say that it is indeed so, then it is false. (Bca 9.141)
That conceptual construction obstructs the conceptualization of its existence, even though it is false;
for in a dream, a fictitious son is neither produced nor ceased. Alternatively, this entire [argument] should be applied even to a son who is regarded as real, once he has perished in a dream.
In this way, the arising and ceasing of all phenomena are to be seen as demonstrated by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

This is what is meant: just as for an object perceived in a dream—which, though neither arisen nor ceased, has existence and non-existence demonstrated by conceptual construction that are not ultimately real—nevertheless, they appear as having entered the sphere of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) through conceptual construction.
Nor is that conceptual construction invalid because it has an unreal object for its domain,
since that object is, from the perspective of ultimate reality, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*);

for in the same way, even existence and non-existence, which are perceived during the waking state and enter the path of conventional usage, are established as being presented by conceptual construction.
Thus, even if that [scripture] lacks authority, the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena is not undermined.
As Nāgārjuna said in the *Catuḥstava*:
"In reality, you have stated that the world is arisen, abiding, and destroyed."
Because all phenomena are revealed as being mere conceptual construction.
Even conceptual construction is said to be non-existent, by which emptiness is conceptually constructed.
Thus, everything is consistent.

Having thus refuted the view that the world has as its creator a non-causal inherent nature (*svabhāva*), a Lord (*īśvara*), or primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and having established the meaning of the statement "nor from no cause," he concludes by saying: "Therefore, in this way," and so forth—
(Bcp 268) "Therefore, through such investigation, nothing exists without a cause."
Since no effect whatsoever is logically possible as arising from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth,
therefore, through such an investigation and the immediate analysis just described, nothing exists without a cause; that is,
there is no effect found to have arisen from a non-cause, such as intrinsic nature or other such uncaused origins.
And this is merely an illustration;
it is also not produced by a person, time, or other such factors, because those too lack causal efficacy.
Therefore, it is established that things do not arise without a cause either.

Now, one might object: even if nothing whatsoever arises without a cause—such as from intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), God (*īśvara*), or primordial matter (*pradhāna*)—nevertheless, things will ultimately arise from causes that are empirically observed.

Anticipating the objection, "In that case, how will the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena be established?", he says the following, supporting the three alternatives—that it does not arise from itself, nor from another, nor from both: "And it is not established in conditions, whether taken individually or collectively. (Bca 9.142)
And it is not that they do not exist at all; "in the separate and the combined" means in both the separate and the combined.
Therein, they do not exist in the separate, that is, individually, neither from themselves nor from another.
Nor is there anything established— that is, existing as something produced— within all conditions or causes taken together, whether by both self and other.
In that regard, things do not first arise from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since that intrinsic nature does not exist prior to arising, from what could they arise?
And once it has arisen, even if its own-form (*svarūpa*) exists, since that too is already established, what would there be to arise? Furthermore:
If birth were from itself, there would be a rebirth of that which has already been born;
and that is not logical,
because it would entail the performance of what has already been performed.

Furthermore, if there were the rebirth of what has already been born, then because seeds and the like would continue to function throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), sprouts and so forth would never find an opportunity to arise.
Nor does this [position] reach the path of proof even for one who accepts it, as it encounters contradiction by common worldly experience,
since we observe that sprouts and the like do indeed arise from seeds and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no identity between the seed and the sprout,
because both possess distinct forms, tastes, potencies, and maturations; moreover,
if things were produced solely from their own intrinsic nature, the arising of anything at all would be impossible.
Because they would involve mutual dependence;
for as long as the intrinsic nature does not exist, so long would there be no arising.
And as long as there is no arising,
so long there can be no intrinsic nature;
therefore, nothing whatsoever arises from itself.
Nor [does it arise] from another.
For if arising from another were accepted, it would follow that even from a rice seed (*śālibīja*) a sprout of *kodrava* grain could be produced;
moreover, with respect to a *kodrava* sprout, the status of being "other" is no different for both rice and *kodrava*.
Or else, the birth of everything would occur from everything,
because there is no distinction in the mutual otherness of all things.
Now, even if this otherness is indeed undifferentiated, [the objection remains].

If it is argued that, nevertheless, because the relationship between cause and effect is governed by the principle of mutual production and production (janyajanakabhāva), not everything arises, we say: no.
For as long as the effect has not yet arisen, it must be stated in what [effect] this [cause] possesses its power.
Moreover, since cause and effect do not exist simultaneously, there can be no fixed determination of the relationship of producer and produced.
For this very reason, even the restriction to a single continuum is not tenable, because a continuum does not exist apart from cause and effect;
and since that [continuum] does not persist for even a single moment, what indeed is this so-called "continuum"?
Furthermore, because the flow of preceding and succeeding moments is a conceptual superimposition, there is no real continuity (*saṃtati*).
By this, similarity as a regulating factor here is also refuted.
Thus, nothing whatsoever exists that falls within a single continuum, whether it be similar or determined by the relationship of producer and produced.
Since it is precisely the relationship of producer and produced that must be examined here, how can there be a resolution by means of that very same relationship?
Therefore, even from another [cause], the arising of anything is impossible.
Nor [is it produced] by both, because that would entail all the faults already stated for each individual position.
Furthermore, because two things that are individually incapable remain incapable even when combined,
it is not possible for many blind people to see a path that has not been seen by a single blind person;
nor do grains of sand, which are individually incapable of yielding oil, become capable of doing so when combined.
Therefore, because the faults adduced by both positions would follow, the production of anything from either of the two [causes] together is impossible.
Thus, in reality, nothing exists that is produced by itself, by another, by both, or without a cause.

Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the entire universe appears as dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), having an essence that is neither arisen nor ceased, equal to an illusion, a mirage, a reflection, or an echo, and empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvaśūnya*).
However, it is not the mere fact of being conditioned by this or that (*idampratyayatāmātra*) on the conventional level (*sāṃvṛta*) that is here denied.
As it was said here by the Blessed One in the *Śālistamba Sūtra*:
"In that regard, how does one perceive dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)?

Here, the Blessed One has said: 'One who perceives this dependent origination as constant and continuous—devoid of a life-principle (*nirjīva*), exactly as it is, unerring, without a living soul (*ajīva*), unborn, unbecome, unmade, unconditioned, non-obstructive, and without objective support (*anālambana*)..."
He who perceives that which is auspicious, fearless, unassailable, immutable, and of a nature that is not subject to cessation—
that person perceives the Dharma. Furthermore,

he who thus constantly and continuously perceives it as being without a living soul (*nirjīva*), and so forth as previously described, up to its nature of not being subject to cessation— he perceives the Buddha, whose body is the unsurpassed Dharma.
[Through the application of right knowledge in the realization of the noble dharmas?
Why is it called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*)? It is said to be with cause and with condition, not without cause and not without condition.
[And so on] as before.
Furthermore, this dependent origination arises from two causes.
From which two causes does it arise?
It is by way of causal connection and by way of conditional connection.
That, too, should be seen as twofold: external and internal.
Among these, what is the causal connection of external dependent origination?
That is to say: from the seed comes the sprout;
from the sprout, the leaf; from the leaf, the stalk.
From the stalk comes the stem; from the stem, the node; from the node, the interior.
From the embryo comes the awn; from the awn, the flower;
from the flower, the fruit.
When the seed does not exist, the sprout does not arise; likewise, up to the point that when the flower does not exist, the fruit does not arise.
But when the seed exists, the production of the sprout occurs.

In this way, up until the production of the fruit when there is a flower, it does not occur to the seed: "I am producing the sprout," nor does it occur to the sprout: "I have been produced by the seed."
In this way, up to the flower, it does not occur to it: "I am producing the fruit";
nor does it occur to the fruit: "I have been produced by the flower.
Nevertheless, when the seed exists, the production and manifestation of the sprout occurs.
In this way, as long as there is a flower, the production and manifestation of the fruit occurs;
thus should the causal connection of external dependent origination be viewed.
How is the conditional dependence of external dependent origination to be viewed? It is through the coming together of six elements. Through the coming together of which six elements?
That is to say, the conditional dependence of external dependent origination should be seen as resulting from the combination of earth, water, fire, air, space, and the season.
In this regard, the earth element performs the function of supporting the seed;
the water element moistens the seed.
The fire element ripens the seed;
the wind element brings forth the seed;
the space element performs the function of non-obstruction for the seed.
The season also performs the function of transforming the seed.
In the absence of these conditions, the production of the sprout from the seed does not occur.
When the external earth element is complete, and...
In this way, when the elements of water, fire, wind, space,
and season are complete, then through the conjunction of all these, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.
In that regard, it does not occur to the earth element: "I perform the function of supporting the seed.
Likewise, it does not occur to the season: "I perform the function of transforming the seed.
Nor does it occur to the sprout: "I am produced by these conditions."
Furthermore, when these conditions exist, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.

And this sprout is not self-made, not made by another, not made by both, not created by a Lord (īśvara), not transformed by time, not arisen from primordial nature (prakṛti), nor dependent on a single cause, nor produced without a cause;
rather, through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, air, space, and the season, as the seed ceases, the production of the sprout occurs.
In this way, the conditional dependence of external dependent origination is to be understood.
In this regard, external dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
Which five?
Not as eternal, not as annihilated, not as transmigrating, from a small cause there is the production of a vast fruit, and there is a continuous succession of similar [states].
How is it not eternal?
Because the sprout is one thing and the seed is another; it is not the case that the seed itself is the sprout.
Alternatively, again: the seed ceases and the sprout arises;
therefore, it is not eternal.
How is it not from annihilation? A sprout is not produced from a seed that has already ceased,
nor is it produced from a seed that has not ceased.
Moreover, at the very moment the seed ceases, the sprout arises.
It is like the rising and falling of the beam of a scale;
therefore, it is not through annihilation.
How is it not through transmigration?
The sprout is dissimilar to the seed;
therefore, it is not by way of transmigration.
How is it that a vast fruit is produced from a small cause?
A small seed is sown,
yet it brings forth abundant fruits;
therefore, there is the production of abundant fruit from a small cause.
How is it "by way of a continuous succession similar to that"?
It is because whatever kind of seed is sown, such a kind of fruit is produced;
therefore, it is said to be "by way of a continuous succession similar to that."
Thus, external dependent origination is to be viewed through five reasons.
As for internal dependent origination, it has already been explained in detail previously;
it should also be applied here.
Thus, when analyzing from the perspective of ultimate truth, the conventional is simply not refuted.
Is it not the case that entities do not arise from absolute non-existence?
Rather, through the power of causes and conditions, they come from the future time-path to the present time-path,
and from the present, again through the power of impermanence, they go to the past time-path.
Thus, the designations of arising, abiding, and ceasing [are explained].

Anticipating the objection that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) likewise coheres exactly in this way according to the doctrine of those who maintain the three times, he says "not from another," and so forth:
It does not come from elsewhere, nor does it abide, nor does it go.
Nothing has come from any other place or time,
nor does anything, having arrived, go anywhere from the present path of time.
Nor does it abide anywhere with that single nature;
for instance, if it were to come from the future path to the present,
or from the present to the past, [it would follow that it had moved].
In that case, even the conditioned would be eternal, because it exists at all times;
there is no such thing as the non-eternal.
And how will it be established that "this dharma is neither eternal"?
Perhaps you argue that there is a distinction of the dharma across the time-periods (adhvan) due to its being devoid of activity (kāritra) in the prior and posterior times;
for instance, when it has not yet attained activity, it does not perform its function.
Then it is called "future";
when it performs its function, it is "present";
but when it has ceased from performing its function, it is "past"—this is the distinction.
This too is nothing [of consequence].
Since that very self exists at that very time, it must be explained how its activity (*kāritra*) could not also exist.
Furthermore, dependence on other conditions is impossible for that which exists with a permanently fixed nature.
Moreover, if a thing were to exist while being devoid of causal activity (*kāritra*), it would follow that even things like a horse's horn would possess reality.
Or else, how could such an activity be said to be past, future, or present?
Is that [past state] due to the existence of another activity, or does it exist by itself?
In the former case, there is an infinite regress;
in the latter case, nothing is lost even if the dharma itself is established as being past and so forth.
And if, just as the present exists substantially, so too do the past and the future exist, [then...]
In that case, it is not so.
How can a phenomenon (*dharma*) that exists by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*) have the nature of being unarisen and destroyed?
What did it previously lack, such that, due to the absence of that, it is said to be "unborn"?
Furthermore, what is it that does not exist subsequently, such that by its absence one could say "it has perished"?
If it were to persist in that very same self-nature during both prior and subsequent times, there would follow the consequence of its being perceived and so forth, just as it is in the present.
Therefore, because it has not come into being and because its nature is non-arising, the connection with the three time-periods is in no way tenable.
The existence of the past and so forth does not follow from the acceptance of [the reality of] the principles (*tattva*).
Regarding this, there is the following summary verse:
"Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) never exists, and it is not admitted that an entity (*bhāva*) is eternal."
And an entity is not other than its intrinsic nature; this is clearly the work of the Lord.
Thus [it is said].
As for what is also said— that because of the scriptural statement, "Past karma exists; future fruit exists," there exists the state of being past and so forth—
Furthermore, regarding that denial of cause and effect, the Blessed One spoke for the purpose of refuting such a misconception: "The past exists;
the future exists.
For the past is that which, having previously not existed, arose and then perished.
The future is that which will come to be when a cause exists;
for in this way it is said that "the cause and so forth exist," since the word *asti* is a particle (*nipāta*) and thus functions across all three times.
And thus, this is exactly what was stated by the Blessed One in the *Paramārthaśūnyatā-sūtra*:
"O monks, when the eye arises, it does not come from anywhere; when it ceases, it does not go to any accumulation."
Thus, monks, the eye comes into being after not having been, and having come into being, it passes away.
And if the future eye were already existent,
it would not have been said that "having not existed, it comes to be.
Therefore, there is no transmigration of the time-periods (adhvan).
And if this is so,
no coming from anywhere nor going to anywhere is perceived.
Furthermore, when that which appears in the present is analyzed, not even the slightest form remains; therefore:
"What difference is there between this and an illusion, such that it has been regarded as real by the deluded? (Bca 9.143)

Since even the forms of elephants and so forth produced by a magician through illusion are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), there is no difference whatsoever between them and this visible form of a thing produced by causes and conditions;
how could there not be a difference?
Again, clarifying this very point, he says "by illusion," and so forth:
That which is created by illusion and that which is produced by causes—from where does it come, and to where does it go? Let this be investigated. (Bca 9.144)

Here, by the word "māyā," a specific state of consciousness and so forth that serves as the cause for the creation of illusions is expressed; this is a metaphorical designation of the effect by the name of the cause, intended to demonstrate that even the cause possesses the nature of an illusion. That which is created by it—
And that form of an entity which is fashioned by the cause of illusion— that is, by the nature of illusion—
and that other form of an entity which is produced by causes well-known in the world;
the two particles *ca* serve the purpose of indicating their mutual conjunction.
It comes; it arrives.
From where, or for what reason, does that form of a thing—which is either produced by illusion or produced by causes—arise?
Where does it go,
and once destroyed, where does this [form] go again?
Let this be examined and investigated with subtle scrutiny.
If it were perceived as coming from somewhere or going to somewhere, it would exist.
But surely, if the nature of a thing is produced by the power of causes and conditions, how could it be false?
For this very reason, he says "that which is other," and so forth, explaining that it is indeed false.
That which is seen through the proximity of another is not seen due to its own absence;
since it is artificial and like a reflection, how can there be reality in it?
Whatever form of an entity is seen or perceived due to the proximity of another cause and condition,
that is not seen due to the absence of that other; it is not seen because of the non-existence of that other.
Because its mode of existence is dependent on another;
it is "equal to a reflection" (pratibimbasama), meaning it is similar to a reflection appearing in the surface of a mirror through its resemblance to the face and so forth.
Just as a reflection appears through the proximity of the original object, such as a face, to the surface of a mirror and so forth.
Likewise, the nature of a thing [arises] from the proximity of causes and conditions.
Since such a nature of a thing is artificial and lacks intrinsic nature (*asvābhāvika*) because its activity is dependent on others, how could there be truth or non-falsity?
It is simply not tenable.
For it is not logical that things whose nature consists of another's designation should possess an uncontrived reality. As it has been said:
"For those things which arise from causes, and which do not exist in the absence of those [causes], how indeed could they not be clearly considered equal to reflections?"
Thus, from the *Yuktiṣaṣṭikā*:
"Therefore, nothing whatsoever produced by causes and conditions exists as ultimately real;
nor does the efficacy of causes and conditions ever exist in any way from the perspective of ultimate reality."
For instance: would an entity that exists, or one that does not exist, or one that possesses both natures, be produced by causes consisting of self, other, or both?
Regarding this, he states that what already exists is not produced, beginning with the words "of that which exists":
"What purpose is there for a cause regarding an existing entity?
That is to say, what purpose is there for a cause—that is, for a causal factor—regarding an entity whose nature is already existent prior to the operation of its causes?

Because the effect, being of a nature already accomplished, lacks an inherent state to be produced, the operation of a cause would be useless. With reference to the second alternative, he says "athāpi" and so forth:
"But even if it does not exist, what is the purpose of a cause? (Bca 9.146)
The phrase "even so" (*athāpi*) indicates another alternative.
That which does not exist lacks an existent intrinsic nature (*satsvabhāva*).
If that is the case, what is the purpose of a logical reason (*hetu*)?
Even then, there is no purpose whatsoever served by a cause, because even in that case, due to the absence of an existent intrinsic nature, there is an absence of causal operation.

It might be argued: "Granted that for an existing thing there is no need for a cause because it has already been produced and thus nothing remains to be done, why should this not be the case for a non-existent thing? To this he says:
"There is no modification of a non-entity, even by hundreds of millions of causes," and so forth.

There is no modification of a non-entity— that is, of that which lacks an existing intrinsic nature— nor is there any alteration into the state of having an intrinsic nature, because, being devoid of form, it likewise lacks anything to be produced.
Even by hundreds of millions of causes—
let alone by hundreds of causes or thousands of causes—
even by hundreds of millions of causes.

Because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is impossible for it to be altered by anything whatsoever. [The opponent might argue: "Let there be no alteration; let this [entity] simply possess the nature of an existent (*bhāvasvabhāvatā*). To this, he replies: "In that state" (*tadavastha*).
In that state, how could it be an entity?
Being in that state, not having abandoned its nature as non-existence, it would simply not be an entity;
for non-existence itself does not become an entity.
"Only upon the cessation of the nature of non-existence does the nature of existence come to be. To this, he says:
"Or who else has attained the state of existence? (Bca 9.147)
If prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) does not have the nature of an entity (*bhāvasvabhāva*),
then what other thing besides non-existence could possibly become an entity by abandoning its nature as non-existence and attaining the form of an entity?
Nothing else whatsoever is perceived,
because the identity of the cause with the effect has already been refuted.

It might be argued: "No other entity whatsoever comes into being; rather, because of the existence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), which is opposed to the entity, the entity does not exist at that time.
Later, however, when that [non-existence] has departed, it certainly does come into being. To this, he says:
If there is no entity at the time of non-existence, when will the entity ever come to be?
If it is not an entity at the time of non-existence— that is, at the time when non-existence exists—
and if the entity does not exist [then], [when will it arise?]
When will existence come to be?
If existence does not arise at the time of non-existence, then existence would never emerge.
Because it is always embraced by its contradictory, namely non-existence.
If it is argued that the destruction of non-existence will occur by means of that very entity as it arises, he says:
"For that non-existence will not depart by means of an entity that has not yet arisen. (Bca 9.148)
As long as that entity has not arisen, there is simply no destruction of non-existence;
for (hi) this reason.
Therefore, that non-existence in the form of prior non-existence will not be removed—that is, it will not be turned back—by means of an entity that is unborn and unarisen.

Now, it might be argued: "Let it be that non-existence (abhāva) does not depart; even while it has not departed, existence (bhāva) arises. And once existence has arisen, because existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive, non-existence will subsequently depart of its own accord. To this, he says "na ca" and so forth: Furthermore, it is not the case that while non-existence remains undeparted, existence arises; nor, when existence has arisen, does non-existence subsequently depart of its own accord through mutual exclusion. Why? Because [existence and non-existence] are not established as distinct entities. For if they were distinct, then one could say that while the one remains, the other arises or departs. But since they are not established as distinct, how could there be such a sequence? Moreover, if existence were to arise while non-existence remained undeparted, then existence would be produced from that very non-existence, which is untenable. Furthermore, if non-existence were to depart after existence has arisen, then existence would be subject to destruction, for it would vanish along with the departure of non-existence. Therefore, this position is also illogical. Thus, it is established that neither existence nor non-existence exists. Consequently, since the two do not exist, their conjunction also does not exist. Therefore, the statement that "the cessation of suffering occurs through the complete abandonment of the two extremes" is merely a conventional expression used to guide those who are to be trained. It is not, however, an ultimate reality. This is what was intended. Thus, it is said: "Existence and non-existence are both empty; The two extremes are likewise empty. Therefore, the wise do not rely on them, For they are devoid of intrinsic nature. Thus, the meaning of the middle way is established. This concludes the refutation of the views of existence and non-existence. Now, the refutation of the views of permanence and annihilation follows. As it is said: "The view of permanence is the grasping of existence; The view of annihilation is the grasping of non-existence. Since these two views are abandoned, The wise do not fall into either extreme. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If existence were real, Then non-existence would follow. Since existence itself is not established, How could non-existence arise? Thus, the refutation of permanence and annihilation is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of the two extremes. Now, the refutation of the views of cause and effect follows. As it is said: "Effect does not exist within the cause, Nor does it exist outside the cause. It is not produced from something else, Nor does it arise without a cause. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If the effect existed previously, There would be no production of it. If it did not exist previously, What is produced from what? Thus, the refutation of cause and effect is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of cause and effect. Now, the refutation of the views of self and non-self follows. As it is said: "Self does not exist, Nor does non-self exist. These two are mere designations, Used to express the aggregates. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If the self were real, Then bondage and liberation would be real. Since the self is not established, Bondage and liberation are also not real. Thus, the refutation of self and non-self is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of self and non-self. Now, the refutation of the views of eternity and cessation follows. As it is said: "Eternity is the grasping of existence; Cessation is the grasping of non-existence. Since existence and non-existence are refuted, Eternity and cessation are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If things were eternal, Then there would be no change. If things were subject to cessation, Then all actions would be fruitless. Thus, the refutation of eternity and cessation is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of eternity and cessation. Now, the refutation of the views of unity and diversity follows. As it is said: "Unity is the grasping of identity; Diversity is the grasping of difference. Since identity and difference are refuted, Unity and diversity are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If things were identical, Then there would be no distinction between cause and effect. If things were different, Then they would be unrelated, like a fire and a pot. Thus, the refutation of unity and diversity is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of unity and diversity. Now, the refutation of the views of arising and ceasing follows. As it is said: "Arising is the grasping of existence; Ceasing is the grasping of non-existence. Since existence and non-existence are refuted, Arising and ceasing are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If arising were real, Then there would be no end to birth. If ceasing were real, Then all beings would be eternally extinguished. Thus, the refutation of arising and ceasing is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of arising and ceasing. Now, the refutation of the views of coming and going follows. As it is said: "Coming is the grasping of arrival; Going is the grasping of departure. Since arrival and departure are refuted, Coming and going are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If there were a coming, Then there would be no place of rest. If there were a going, Then there would be no place of origin. Thus, the refutation of coming and going is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of coming and going. Now, the refutation of the views of oneness and manyness follows. As it is said: "Oneness is the grasping of identity; Manyness is the grasping of difference. Since identity and difference are refuted, Oneness and manyness are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If things were one, Then there would be no variety of phenomena. If things were many, Then they would be fragmented and unstable. Thus, the refutation of oneness and manyness is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of oneness and manyness. Now, the refutation of the views of existence and non-existence follows. As it is said: "Existence is the grasping of being; Non-existence is the grasping of nothingness. Since being and nothingness are refuted, Existence and non-existence are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If existence were real, Then there would be no liberation. If non-existence were real, Then there would be no path to traverse. Thus, the refutation of existence and non-existence is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of existence and non-existence. Now, the refutation of the views of permanence and annihilation follows. As it is said: "Permanence is the grasping of eternity; Annihilation is the grasping of cessation. Since eternity and cessation are refuted, Permanence and annihilation are also refuted. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If things were permanent, Then there would be no change or transformation. If things were annihilated, Then there would be no continuity of karma. Thus, the refutation of permanence and annihilation is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of permanence and annihilation. Now, the refutation of the views of cause and effect follows. As it is said: "Effect does not exist within the cause, Nor does it exist outside the cause. It is not produced from something else, Nor does it arise without a cause. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If the effect existed previously, There would be no production of it. If it did not exist previously, What is produced from what? Thus, the refutation of cause and effect is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of cause and effect. Now, the refutation of the views of self and non-self follows. As it is said: "Self does not exist, Nor does non-self exist. These two are mere designations, Used to express the aggregates. This is the meaning. Furthermore, it is said: "If the self were real, Then bondage and liberation would be real. Since the self is not established, Bondage and liberation are also not real. Thus, the refutation of self and non-self is also established. This concludes the section on the refutation of self and non-self. Now, the refutation of the views of eternity and cessation follows. As it is said: "Eternity is the grasping of existence; Cessation is the grasping of non-existence. Since existence and non-existence are
And as long as non-existence has not departed, there is no possibility for existence to arise;
yet succession does indeed occur,
provided that existence itself were to exist first.
And this is not the case;
for since it is so,
there is no occasion or opportunity for an entity (bhāva) to exist as long as non-existence (abhāva) has not departed or ceased.
Its occurrence is due to the very existence of non-existence, which is the opposite of the arising of an entity. If it is argued that its absence will be removed by the cause itself, we say no.
Since the operation of a cause consists solely in the production of its effect,
if it is argued that "in producing the effect, it simultaneously brings about its own non-existence," [we reply:
it indeed produces the effect.
If [the cause] is capable of producing [the effect] because of the absence of its opposite,
yet it is not capable of producing that effect while that [opposite] possesses unimpeded power,
then there is no contradiction between the cause and the absence of that [opposite].
Because even at the time of the cause, its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) exists— that is, it persists as a state of being— therefore,
the causal operation upon an effect that is either existent by nature or non-existent by nature is not tenable.

Furthermore, regarding the positions of both [existence and non-existence] or neither, it should be understood that the refutation of the causal operation is accomplished precisely through the refutation of each individual position.
Nor is the occurrence of those two possible, because it is impossible for affirmation and negation, which are contradictory, to exist together in one place at one time. As it has been said:
An entity that exists does not arise, nor does one that does not exist, nor one that both exists and does not exist;
it is not born from itself, nor from another, nor from both—how then could it be born?
Thus, in this way, the arising of an entity does not in any way whatsoever accord with ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Nor is the cessation of an arisen entity that possesses an existent intrinsic nature (*satsvabhāva*) in any way tenable; thus he says "an entity," and so forth.
Furthermore, an existent entity does not become non-existence, for that would entail the consequence of it possessing two natures.
The particle *ca* (and) refers back to what precedes it:
just as non-existence does not attain the state of existence, so too existence does not attain the state of non-existence; [on the contrary,] it goes [to it].
Why? Because it would entail the consequence of two intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
When an existing entity possesses the nature of non-existence, then there would be the consequence of two intrinsic natures for that very same single thing.
Because a single entity possesses the nature of both existence and non-existence,
it is not appropriate to say that it abandons its state of existence and attains the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, since at that time the very existence [of the entity] has ceased, we do not know what it is that attains the nature of non-existence.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which possesses an existent intrinsic nature to cease if it is ultimately real,
because that would entail the consequence of its ultimate reality being non-existent.
Having thus established that the arising and destruction of an entity do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality, he concludes by saying "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, there is neither cessation nor is there any entity at any time;
for, according to the sequence just described, arising and destruction are untenable."
What is the reason? Because there is no cessation,
there is no destruction.
And there is no existence;
there is no substantial reality.
The word "and" (ca) is used for conjunction.

"At all times, at every moment— whether Tathāgatas arise or whether Tathāgatas do not arise— this true nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the sameness of phenomena (dharma-samatā), the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthititā), the fixed order of phenomena (dharma-niyāmatā), the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu), suchness (tathatā),
and non-falsity (avitathatā) remain ever established."
Because of such statements as these: "Since it is thus—unborn and unceasing—therefore this entire world [is so]. (Bca 9.150)
It is unarisen and unproduced,
and it is unceased and undestroyed from the perspective of ultimate truth;
therefore, because of the aforementioned absence of arising and destruction.

"Everything without exception" refers to this entire world, which shares the common locus of being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), designated as the world of sentient beings and the world of the vessel, including all that is moving and stationary. Furthermore,
arising and ceasing exist by way of conventional usage, like the arising and ceasing of an illusion.
By this, the non-repudiation of conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya) has been stated.
And this was said in the *Dharmasaṃgīti*:
"O son of good family, 'suchness, suchness' is a designation for emptiness (śūnyatā)."
And that emptiness neither arises nor ceases. It is said: "If all phenomena have been declared by the Blessed One to be empty in this way, then all phenomena will neither arise nor cease."
The Bodhisattva is without undertaking.
He said: "It is so, noble son, just as you have realized."
All phenomena do not arise, nor do they cease.
[A questioner] asks: "Regarding that which was spoken by the Blessed One—that conditioned phenomena arise and cease—what is the intended meaning of this teaching of the Tathāgata?"
He said: "Noble son, the world's abode is characterized by adherence to arising and cessation.
In that regard, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion, spoke of 'arising' and 'ceasing' by way of conventional usage, for the sake of removing the world's ground for fear.
Yet, herein there is neither the arising nor the cessation of any dharma whatsoever."
Therefore, because all phenomena have the nature of being neither arisen nor ceased, they are primordially quiescent and naturally in a state of parinirvāṇa.
