Thus, demonstrating that since the world is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the realms of existence such as the hells contained within it are likewise devoid of intrinsic nature, he says "like a dream," and so forth: (Bcp 275) Therefore, because all phenomena have the nature of being neither arisen nor ceased, they are primordially quiescent and naturally in a state of parinirvāṇa; thus, since the world is devoid of intrinsic nature, the realms of existence such as the hells contained within it are also devoid of intrinsic nature—demonstrating this, he says "like a dream," and so forth:
The realms of existence are like dreams; upon investigation, they are like plantain trees.
Those for which there is a comparison equal to a dream are described as such.
The particle "tu" (but/then) serves as a restriction.
The specific distinctions among the common lot (*sabhāgatā*) of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods have a nature that is like what is perceived in a dream.
Just as in a dream there is the coming and going between different places and the experiencing of pleasure, pain, and so forth,
so too should it be understood regarding the experiences in the hells and other realms for one who has not realized the reality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-tattva*).
But not in reality.
How so? "In analysis, they are like plantains"—this is a statement of reason.

The meaning is: because, when one investigates and examines all phenomena through their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), the realms of existence (*gati*) are like plantain trees—devoid of core, just as a plantain tree is.
By this, that which was stated previously [at 4.47] is explained.

"Since this is mere illusion, therefore, O heart, abandon your fear," and so forth; that too has been demonstrated after being established. And because all phenomena are unarisen and unceasing, [they are like an illusion].
Therefore, he says "nirvṛta" and so forth: "In reality, there is no distinction between those who have attained nirvāṇa and those who have not. (Bca 9.151)

Those who are "extinguished" (*nirvṛta*) are those who, through the abandonment of all obscurations, are liberated from all bonds. Those who are "not extinguished" (*anirvṛta*) are those whose mental continuums are subject to the snares of afflictions such as passion and who remain within the prison of saṃsāra.
Between these two groups, there is no distinction or difference whatsoever.
It is not possible.
Why? Because, in reality and from the perspective of ultimate truth, all phenomena are by nature in a state of parinirvāṇa due to their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
However, from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*), there certainly is a distinction.

Thus it has been demonstrated in many ways. For this very reason, he said: "Because, in reality, there is no difference between the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings, and because of the equality of oneself and others, they are considered as such."
Thus, [Catuḥ-3.40].

Demonstrating that ignorant people, due to their lack of understanding of the reality of ultimate truth and their false attachment, construct a superimposed web of the world and thereby only confound themselves, he says "In this way," and so forth:
"In this way, when all phenomena are empty, what could be gained and what could be lost?"
Who will be honored, or by whom will anyone be insulted?
Whence comes pleasure or pain, what is dear or what is not dear?
What is craving, and where is that craving when sought by way of its own nature?
Upon reflection, who is this world of living beings? Who indeed here will die? Who will come to be, who has been, who is a kinsman, and who is whose friend? (Bca 9.154)
Thus, by the logic already established, since all phenomena are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, what has been gained?
What has been obtained from anywhere such that one rejoices in gains? What has been taken away? What could have been stolen from anyone, and by whom?
By the loss of what do they become angry?
Who is honored or worshipped, or who is insulted or harmed; by whom will anyone exist?
The meaning is that, in the absence of the intrinsic nature of entities, nothing exists by means of anything.
Whence could there be pleasure, since the cause of pleasure is absent; or whence could there be suffering, since the cause of suffering is absent?
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in both instances to signify a mutual conjunction.
For what purpose is effort exerted for the sake of attaining or avoiding something? Is it because of something pleasant or something beloved?
For the nature of being "pleasant" is merely a mental construction.
What is unpleasant, and what is undesirable? Since nothing whatsoever exists that is truly unpleasant in the ultimate sense,
for what purpose is effort exerted for the sake of union with or separation from the pleasant and the unpleasant?
What is this craving by which people thirst for the sake of gain and the like?
Where is that craving;
and where, moreover, is the object of attachment in which craving resides?
When sought by way of intrinsic nature and investigated by way of its own form,
it too is non-existent due to the absence of its object, because of being devoid of an object.
By virtue of which those various karmas are accumulated.
When there is investigation into the nature of ultimate reality, who is this world of living beings, this world of sentient beings?
None at all. Since that does not exist, who indeed here will die?
Upon investigation of the world of living beings, because they are by nature non-existent, who indeed in this world of living beings will die—
that is, whose life-faculty will cease?
Who will come to be?
Who will arise?
Who has previously arisen?
Thus, the conventional usage of "past" and so forth is purely conceptual.
Who is a kinsman, who is one's own kin?
To whom does anyone belong as a friend,
and who is whose ally?
The word "here" (atra) is to be applied everywhere in this context.
Why is it that even unwholesome [actions] are not counted when one is possessed by such attachment?
Thus, because they are empty of intrinsic nature, he says "all," and so forth, explaining that reality is merely superimposed by conceptual construction.
Let those like me regard everything as being like space;
they become angry or delighted due to the causes of quarrels and festivals.
All this has been stated, and furthermore:
"resembling space" means it is like space because its true nature is empty of superimpositions.
"But those like me, having superimposed an essential nature that does not even exist, grasp it"—with these words, the author uses himself as the very illustration.
Foolish people like me, who have not realized the reality of the ultimate truth and whose minds are agitated by improper reflections, become enraged;
through false attachment, they fall into anger. Through the pursuit of unreal gain, they become overjoyed and elated.
By what means? By causes of strife and causes of festivals—that is, by causes of quarrel and disputes, and by causes of celebration and joy, as appropriate.
Therefore, those who have not realized the reality of the ultimate truth, being attached to the conventional form of things as being real, conceive of all this [in such a way].
But this is not the case for those who know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). As it has been said:
"The knowable is precisely this much: namely, the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*paramārtha*).
And these have been well-seen, well-understood, and well-realized by the Blessed One through emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
Therefore, he is called "the Omniscient One. In that regard, the Tathāgata perceives conventional reality through its worldly operation; as for ultimate reality, however—

It is ineffable, unknowable, inconceivable, untaught, and unrevealed; it is, moreover, without action and without agency, and so forth, until: neither gain nor loss, neither suffering nor happiness, neither fame nor infamy, neither form nor formlessness, and so on.
Therein, for the sake of people and for the benefit of the world, the Victor taught the conventional truth,
by which the world may here generate serene confidence in the presence of the Sugata for the sake of happiness.
The Lion among Men established conventional designations, declaring the six destinies for the multitudes of sentient beings:
the destiny of hell-beings, as well as that of hungry ghosts, the hosts of asuras, humans, and gods.
Those from low-born families as well as those from high-born families, those from wealthy families and those from poor families.
And so forth.
He says that this too is the fruit of not realizing reality, beginning with the words "by sorrows and labors":
"Desiring happiness for themselves, they pass their time with great difficulty through sorrows, labors, despondencies, and mutual cutting and piercing, due to their sinful deeds. (Bca 9.156)
The connection is as follows: sorrows are those caused by separation from sons, wives, and so forth;
fatigues are the exertions undertaken for the sake of attaining happiness and avoiding suffering; by means of these sorrows and fatigues, people like me pass their time with great difficulty.
And by despondencies— that is, by the mental distresses of despondency regarding gain, honor, and so forth—
and by mutual cutting and piercing;
"mutual" meaning one another's cutting of hands, feet, head, nose, ears, and so on.

"Cuttings" refers to those of the arms, calves, thighs, chest, sides, belly, and so forth; the word "and" (ca) is understood [from the previous context]. By means of these cuttings and piercings, they cause them to endure.
In the course of time, they exhaust their life-formations;
with great difficulty and immense hardship, they somehow obtain food, drink, and clothing. Being in what state?
"Those who desire their own happiness through evil deeds" means those whose nature is to long for the happiness of themselves, their own selves, by means of evil, unwholesome actions.
And by such specific modes of conduct,
those who have died fall into states of woe characterized by long-lasting and intense suffering;
"died" means being separated from the life-faculty.
They fall and go to the miserable states— among hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—
in which [states] there are long-lasting and intense sufferings.

In those states of woe which are described as such because they possess suffering that is long-lasting— meaning it persists for a great length of time— and intense— meaning its ripening is experienced as being exceedingly difficult to endure. And in those [states].
The word *ca* is used either as a conjunction (*uktasamuccaye*) or with a shifted word order (*bhinnakrame*).
To the question "In what manner?", he says:
"Having come again and again to a happy rebirth, having become accustomed to happiness," and so forth (Bca 9.157).
Having been repeatedly nurtured in happiness—
how so? By coming again and again, having attained and attained the good rebirths, namely the excellent destinies of gods and humans.
Furthermore, demonstrating how those who have become such are submerged and emerge from the ocean of the succession of sufferings, he says "In existence," and so forth:
"In existence there are many precipices, and therein such a lack of reality; therein there is mutual contradiction, and therein no such reality exists. (Bca 9.158)
In existence—that is, in *saṃsāra*, which has the nature of the realms of desire, form, and formlessness—there are many precipices and even greater injuries.

Within that existence, or within those precipices, there is such a lack of reality; therein lies such unreality, a manifestation of delusion, common to all people, of the kind already explained, currently being observed, or as it appears.
In that regard, there is mutual contradiction;
for when such a non-reality exists,
there is mutual contradiction, which is to say, reciprocal disagreement.
For what reason would such a thing not be reality?
Therefore, this nature of things is such because of the superimposition of manifold forms.
And therein lie incomparable, intense, and infinite oceans of suffering;
and it is even so:
they are "incomparable" because there exists no other suffering like them, making them impossible to compare.
"Intense" means extremely fierce pains.

"Infinite" means either because their maturation lasts for an unlimited time, or because they are boundless due to the extreme vastness of the sufferings; they are like "oceans" because it is impossible to cross them without attaining the Mahāyāna.

Nevertheless, since they can somehow be exhausted by accumulating the side of virtue through great vigor and reaching a happy rebirth after a long period of time, he says, "In that case, thus," and so forth.
In that regard, there is such weakness of strength; even therein, there is the brevity of life.
Even there, one is occupied with the activities of sustaining life and health, with hunger, fatigue,
and exhaustion, with sleep, with afflictions, and likewise with fruitless associations with the foolish.
Life passes away quickly and in vain; therein, discernment is difficult to find.
In such a state of immersion as that, there is this observed condition of feebleness, which is to say, a lack of vigor.
There too, there is the shortness of life;
even in such a state as that,
"shortness" means meagreness.
Regarding life, there are the formative forces of life (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*).
In that regard as well, there are activities for sustaining life and health, such as bathing, anointing the body, and so forth.
For the sake of health, or for the pacification of illness, there are specific activities, such as drinking pungent, bitter, and astringent medicinal decoctions and the like.
The connection is with what will be said later: "Without the acquisition of merit, life passes away quickly and in vain.
Likewise, [it is wasted] by hunger, exhaustion, and fatigue;
*kṣut* means hunger.
By fatigue, which is exhaustion;
by weariness, such as the fatigue of travel and so forth;
and by sleep, which are disturbances.
By sleep and dreams;

by calamities caused by laughter, mockery, and harassment, or by those caused by reptiles, beasts of prey, wild animals, stinging insects, mosquitoes, and the like, characterized by killing, binding, and beating;
and likewise by fruitless associations with the foolish.
Likewise, through association and contact with foolish ordinary persons—
of what kind?
Fruitless, and abounding in self-exaltation and other forms of frivolous chatter.
"So be it"— not only according to the sequence previously stated,
but also in this way, life passes away quickly and in vain;
indeed, it passes and goes swiftly, being entirely fruitless because it is devoid of the accumulation of the side of wholesome qualities (kuśalapakṣa).

Because of the consequence of engaging in what is non-existent, [the mind] would perish very quickly; even so, for those who remain [in this state], discernment (*viveka*) is extremely difficult to attain—
discernment being either the knowledge of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, or the relinquishing of attachment.
It is extremely difficult to obtain;
it cannot be found even with the greatest effort.
Let it be so.
Nevertheless, if by some means a resolution were to arise, that would be auspicious;
yet even that does not exist, as he says in the passage beginning with "tatrāpi" (even there):
In that case as well, how can there be the practice of warding off distractions? (Bca 9.161)
Even there, Māra exerts himself to cast them into the great hells.

Even when they have reached such a state, how could there be any access for him—the one whose distraction has become habitual and whose restlessness has been thoroughly practiced—to prevent, to turn back, or to enter upon that [state]? It is simply not possible.

Even in that situation, while they remain in this succession of misfortunes, Māra exerts himself to cast them into the great hells whenever he perceives even a slight inclination toward the side of virtue.
The Māra of the afflictions or the Māra who is a son of the gods exerts himself and strives for the purpose of casting [beings] down into the great precipices of the miserable states— that is to say,
for the sake of throwing them into the Avīci hell and other such hells.

Even so, one might occasionally achieve some degree of spiritual excellence through the power of conviction regarding the Jewels of Truth and the like; thus he says: "In that case, due to the abundance of wrong paths, doubt is difficult to overcome" (Bca 9.162).

Furthermore, the opportunity for a favorable moment is difficult to find, the appearance of a Buddha is exceedingly rare, and the flood of afflictions is hard to restrain—alas, what a succession of sufferings! (Bca 9.163)

In that regard, one reaches this state: because the false path—the antithesis of right view—expounded by the Cārvākas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others, is so prevalent and abundant, there arises doubt and a lack of conviction regarding the true path;
and such doubt cannot be abandoned by any means.
Even if one somehow attains a fortunate rebirth, the rarity of the opportune moment (kṣaṇa) remains.

The rarity of this moment, which is free from the eight inopportune states (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), is of the utmost difficulty— comparable to a turtle inserting its neck through the hole of a yoke floating upon a vast ocean. Even if some other favorable moment should somehow occur, the appearance of a Buddha is exceedingly rare.

The arising and manifestation of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones—who bring light to the entire world and extract the thorns of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that serve as the source of all suffering—is exceedingly rare. It occurs only somehow and at some time, being as difficult to encounter as the flower of the *udumbara* tree; it serves as the means for crossing the ocean of *saṃsāra*.
Even when the arising of a Buddha occurs somehow, the flood of afflictions—the continuous flow of birth, old age, death, and so forth—remains unbroken.
It is difficult to ward off;
it cannot be prevented even with great effort. Oh, what a succession of sufferings!
Thus it is;
"aho" expresses distress; [it refers to] a succession of suffering and hardship.
Because even upon emerging from one suffering, one falls back into another suffering.

Having just now observed these beings who are so deeply afflicted, the author of the treatise—his heart overflowing with compassion and himself pained by the suffering of others—expresses his grief for the suffering of sentient beings, saying: "Alas! The phrase "alas" (*aho bata*) is a collection of particles used to express lamentation.
"Alas! How exceedingly pitiable are these [beings] who are caught in the flood of suffering! Thus he speaks.
"Exceedingly pitiable" means being most worthy of compassion.

This refers to those beings who are devoid of the discernment between the beneficial and the harmful, whose minds are agitated by the continuous succession of waves in the ocean of suffering, sinking and surfacing within it.
To the question, "Who, then, are these beings worthy of compassion? he says "those who," and so forth.
Those who do not perceive their own miserable state remain thus exceedingly miserable.
Those beings whose eyes of wisdom are blinded by ignorance do not look, they do not see their own wretched state—their own condition of suffering.
Even so, being "exceedingly ill-situated" means that, in the manner described, they are exceedingly ill-situated, remaining in a state of extreme suffering;
that is to say, they are encompassed by suffering.

Clarifying this with a corresponding illustration, he says "Having bathed," and so forth: "Just as someone, having bathed again and again, might repeatedly enter the fire, yet consider themselves to be in a state of well-being—even so do those who are in extreme misery. (Bca 9.165)
Having bathed again and again, having repeatedly immersed himself in water, just as someone of impaired intellect, afflicted by cold and desiring comfort,
might enter— indeed, enter into— the fire.
"Again and again" means at every moment or repeatedly;
likewise, these sentient beings [seek] their own well-being.
They imagine and perceive the attainment of their own happiness;
yet even so, they remain in an extremely wretched state—extremely wretched indeed by this aforementioned sequence, swallowed by the blazing flames of the fire of suffering.

"Alas! How great is the onset of the darkness of ignorance upon these people, that they do not perceive even the heedlessness inherent within themselves! Thus he says, beginning with "ajarāmaralīlānām":
"While those who sport as if they were ageless and immortal are thus diverting themselves, terrible calamities will come upon them, having placed death right before them. (Bca 9.166)
Those for whom aging—that is, decrepitude—does not exist are "ageless" (*ajara*). Those who do not die are "immortal" (*amara*).
Those whose playful movements (*līlā-viceṣṭita*) are like those of the ageless and immortal are so described.
As they thus sport in this manner, wandering about with such certainty,
calamities will come upon them and press down upon them incessantly—
all those causes of suffering, namely old age, disease, and misfortune.
Terrible and exceedingly fearsome—
how will they come?
Having placed death before them.
Having placed before oneself death— mortality that cannot be remedied or avoided—
it is said in the *Rājāvavādaka-sūtra*:
"For example, O Great King, suppose four mountains were to come from the four directions..."
Firm, substantial, and unbroken.
They were without flaws or hollows, well-compacted, solid, touching the sky and scraping the earth.
They crush all grass, wood, branches, leaves, foliage, and all living beings, creatures, and sentient things;
it is not easy for them to escape by speed,
nor to turn them back by means of strength, substances, mantras, or medicinal herbs.
In the same way, Great King, these four great terrors approach, for which it is not easy to flee by means of speed, nor to turn them back by means of strength, wealth, mantras, or medicines.
Which four?
Old age, sickness, death, and misfortune. Great King, old age comes, crushing youth.
"O Great King, disease approaches, crushing health;
O Great King, death approaches, crushing life;
O Great King, misfortune approaches, crushing all prosperity."
For what reason?

It is like this, Great King: just as the lion, the king of beasts, endowed with beauty, endowed with speed, and formidable with well-formed claws and fangs, enters among the herds of deer, seizes a deer, and does with it as he pleases;
yet that very king of beasts, having encountered an exceedingly powerful beast of prey, becomes helpless.

In the same way, O Great King, when one has been pierced by the arrow of death—devoid of intoxication, without protection, without refuge, and without resort; while the vital organs are being severed, the flesh and blood are drying up; with a face overwhelmed by distress and parched with thirst; occupied with the tossing of hands and feet; rendered incapable and powerless; and smeared with saliva, snot, pus, urine, and excrement.

For one whose life remains but a little, who is grasping for rebirth from the existence of karma, terrified by the fear of the messengers of Yama, fallen under the power of the Night of Death, while his final inhalations and exhalations are being obstructed— alone, without a second, without a companion, abandoning this world and entering the next, treading the great path, and plunging into the vast wilderness.
For one plunging into a great thicket, entering a vast wilderness, being carried away by the great ocean,
being led by the winds of karma, and traveling toward a direction determined by signs, there is no other protection, no other refuge, and no other final resort than the Dharma.
For at that time, O Great King, the Dharma becomes a protection, a shelter, and a refuge— just as the heat of fire is for one afflicted by cold,
or the extinguishing of fire for one who has entered into it.
Or coolness for one afflicted by heat,
or a grove with very cool shade for one who has set out upon a journey.
Cool water for one who is thirsty, or exquisite food for one who is hungry, or physicians, medicines, and attendants for one who is ill;
For one who is terrified by fear, the powerful and the virtuous become companions and a refuge.
Thus is the detailed exposition.
Therefore, in order to avoid this fear, one should apply effort toward the factors of the wholesome side alone, which have been purified by wisdom.
Now, expressing his own intention to remove the suffering of those tormented by the miseries of birth and so forth, he says "In this way," and so on:
"In this way, when shall I bring peace to those scorched by the fire of suffering, with my own provisions for happiness produced from clouds of merit? (Bca 9.167)

In this manner, according to the principle just stated, when shall I bring peace— that is, the cessation of the burning heat of the fires of suffering such as birth— to those beings tormented by the fires of suffering? When shall I effect the quelling of the scorching heat of the fire of suffering?
At what time should I act—that is, perform it?
How? With the requisites of happiness;
the requisites of happiness are the means for achieving happiness, such as clothing, ornaments, ointments, beds, seats, and so forth.
Is it by those [merits] acquired by others?
No, he says: "by one's own," meaning by those belonging to oneself;
that is to say, by those acquired by me myself.
What is the use of displaying emanations and the like?
He says "no," [explaining that they are] "arisen from clouds of merit.
Merits themselves are indeed clouds, because they serve as the cause for providing a cool rain that pacifies the suffering and distress of all miseries and provides the requisites for happiness.
Arising from or produced by them; by means of them.

Having thus established the minds of others in the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), he speaks the verse beginning with "When? to demonstrate the attainment of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*):

"When, through the non-apprehension of conventional reality, shall I respectfully teach emptiness to those whose views are based on apprehension, so that they may gather the equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*)? (Bca 9.168)

When, at what time, shall I teach and reveal emptiness—the absence of intrinsic nature in all phenomena—to those who hold the view of apprehension and are attached to the grasping of entities? How? By means of conventional usage.
Otherwise, because it is not an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), emptiness—which is empty of ultimate reality—could not be taught.

Thus, the cause for the accumulation of knowledge (*jñāna-sambhāra*) which leads to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has been shown. Now, demonstrating its cause, the basis for the accumulation of merit (*puṇya-sambhāra*), he says "merit," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "When shall I teach the equipment of merit, knowledge, and so forth, to those who hold the view of apprehension?
"With respect" means with great reverence;
"having honored [them]," not casually.
In what manner?
By way of non-apprehension,
through the yoga of the non-apprehension of the triad consisting of the gift, the giver, and the recipient.
This refers to the purification through the three spheres (*trikoṭipariśuddhi*).
Thus, the accumulated equipment of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*) arises for the attainment of Buddhahood.

Therefore, by all of this, because it serves as the means for abandoning all obscurations through its nature as the antidote to all superimpositions and conceptual constructions that are the causes of all afflictions (*saṃkleśa*), [it leads to the goal].
And because it is the cause for the realization of all Tathāgatas, it is demonstrated that the wisdom which is the means for the pacification of all suffering arises.
Those wise ones who have cast away delusion through sharp wisdom that plunges into the profound method,
and who are elevated by stainless knowledge regarding the sides of affliction and purification—
they, being virtuous, [discern] the essence even within the mixture of virtues and faults.
Everything that is blameless should be accepted; however, if it is ill-spoken, it should be rejected like poison.
Whatever improper thing I have said here, that alone is my greatest transgression;
will not the virtuous, however, now perceive my true intention through this very act of mine?
Moreover:
That which somehow enters the range of the mind by way of conventional reality— how [could it be otherwise]?
Whose intellect would not falter regarding such a subject as this, even for one like me? Yet,
having seen here a mere fragment of virtue in those who possess the Middle Way and who investigate the meaning of well-spoken words, may there arise the thought that it is worth adopting.

Having composed this exposition of wisdom with clear words of detailed commentary— conducive to the pacification of the dense delusion of views that oppose right knowledge— may all people, by the merit I have thereby acquired which bears the fruit of benefit, quickly [attain it].
May he become a mine of wisdom, like Mañjuśrī, the sole abode of excellent qualities.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the Perfection of Wisdom, in the *Pañjikā* commentary on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, composed by Prajñākaramati.
This work is the composition of the scholar-monk Prajñākaramati.
[The eulogy composed by the scribe: This commentary is supreme, with well-constructed words, pure, and gladdening to the mind.
For those people who are crossing to the further shore of the ocean of saṃsāra, this [work] is like a ship;
it brings about the swift attainment of the state of a Jina. Whatever merit has been acquired by me through having now written this, may all beings thereby attain the state of a Buddha.
In the year one hundred and ninety-eight,
on the fifth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, on a Tuesday.
During the victorious reign of the illustrious Lord Śaṅkara,
this auspicious commentary on the *Bodhicaryāvatāra* was written.
In the beautiful city of Śrī-Lalitapura, at the place known as Śrīmānīśvala,
in the Sugata temple called the Vihāra of the one named Śrī-Rāghava.
Blessed is this book of the Elder Bhikṣu Buddacandra;
through its merit, one attains the state of a Bodhisattva, the supreme station.
May the clouds pour forth water as they desire;
may the earth be endowed with abundant crops;
and may the king protect his subjects without fear.
May there be a great increase in the happiness of the Lord of Jewels.
Thus [it is said].
It was written by the scribe Bhuvanākāravarman.
(Bcp 283) 10. The Tenth Chapter: Dedication.
Whatever merit I have gained from reflecting upon this *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, [may it lead all beings to the state of omniscience].
By this, may all people be adorned with the conduct of awakening.
May all those in every direction who are afflicted by physical and mental suffering obtain oceans of happiness and joy through my merits.
May there never be any loss of happiness for them as long as saṃsāra lasts;
may the world attain the unceasing bliss of a bodhisattva.
In as many hells as exist throughout all the world-systems,
may the embodied beings therein rejoice with the bliss and joy of Sukhāvatī.
May those afflicted by cold obtain warmth, and may those afflicted by heat become cool,
through oceans of water produced from the great clouds of the Bodhisattva.
May the Forest of Sword-Leaves for them have the splendor of the Nandana grove,
and may the thorny Śālmalī trees become wish-fulfilling kalpa-trees.

May the regions of hell become delightful, with lakes possessing the charming splendor of the clamor of kadamba ducks, kāraṇḍava ducks, ruddy geese, swans, and the like, and the fragrance of abundant lotuses.
May that heap of coals become a heap of jewels, and may the scorched earth become a floor of crystal;
may the mountains of the world-system become celestial palaces for worship, filled with Sugatas.

From this day forward, let there be a rain of charcoal, heated stones, and weapons; let that mutual battle with weapons henceforth be a flower-rain for the sake of sport, and let it be a battle of words today.
With all their flesh fallen away, their skeletal bodies the color of jasmine, they were submerged in the Vaitaraṇī river whose waters are like fire; now,
through the power of my merit, they have attained divine forms.
May they dwell upon the Mandākinī together with the celestial maidens.
Terrified, the messengers of Yama and the fierce crows and vultures suddenly behold here the darkness destroyed on all sides; whose gentle sovereign is this, who produces happiness and joy?
Thus, looking upward and seeing Vajrapāṇi blazing in the expanse of the sky, may they, their misdeeds dispelled by the force of their joy, go together with him.

A rain of lotuses mixed with fragrant water falls, seen extinguishing the fires of hell with a *chhamiti* sound; suddenly, those who had been crying out in distress ask, "What is this? and are comforted by it.
Let there be a vision of Kamalapāṇi for the denizens of hell.
"Come, come quickly! O brothers, dispel our fear! We have been restored to life;
this certain young Cīrin has arrived for us, blazing and bestowing fearlessness. By his power alone, all calamity has vanished and a surge of joy has arisen."
The thought of awakening that has arisen, and compassion, which is the mother who protects all beings.
Behold him, whose lotus-feet are worshipped by the crowns of hundreds of gods,
whose gaze is moist with compassion, and upon whose head falls a rain of many heaps of flowers;
he is surrounded by delightful gabled pavilions and the songs of thousands of celestial women whose voices are raised in praise.
Upon seeing Mañjughoṣa before them, let there now be a tumultuous clamor from the denizens of hell!
Thus, may those in the hells rejoice upon beholding the clouds of bodhisattvas headed by Samantabhadra, brought forth by my own virtues, raining down pleasant, cool, and fragrant breezes.
May the intense sufferings and the fears of the hell-beings be stilled;
may all those dwelling in the miserable realms be liberated from those states of woe.
May the fear of devouring one another depart from the animals;
may the hungry ghosts become happy, like the humans in Uttarakuru.
May the hungry ghosts be fully satiated, may they be bathed,
and may they always remain cool by means of the streams of milk flowing from the hands of the noble Avalokiteśvara.
May the blind see forms, and may the deaf always hear;
may pregnant women give birth without pain, like Queen Māyā.
May they obtain clothing, food, drink, garlands, sandalwood, and ornaments—
everything their hearts desire— that is conducive to their welfare.
May those who are terrified be fearless; may those afflicted by grief obtain joy;
and may those who are agitated become free from agitation and possessed of steadfastness.
May those who are ill attain health; may all be released from their bonds;
may the weak become strong, and may they have affectionate hearts toward one another.
(Bcp 285) May all directions be auspicious for all those traveling on their paths;
may whatever purpose they pursue be accomplished by the appropriate means. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 10.23.
May those embarked on sea voyages have their desires fulfilled;
having reached the shore in safety, may they rejoice together with their kinsmen.
May those who have strayed onto the wrong paths in the wilderness find the company of a caravan,
and may they travel without fatigue, free from fear of robbers, tigers, and other dangers.
May the deities provide protection for those who are asleep, intoxicated, or deranged; for those in the perils of disease, forests, and the like; and for the helpless, the young, and the elderly.
May they be forever free from all unfavorable conditions, endowed with faith, wisdom, and compassion,
perfected in appearance and conduct, and always remember their past lives.
May they possess inexhaustible treasuries, as vast as the treasury of space;
may they be free from conflict and hardship, living with self-reliant independence.
May those beings who have little splendor possess great splendor;
may those ascetics who are deformed become endowed with perfect beauty.
Whatever women there are in the world, let them attain manhood;
let the lowly attain high status, and let those with pride be humbled.
By this merit of mine, may all sentient beings without exception,
having desisted from all misdeeds, always perform what is wholesome.
They are never parted from the thought of awakening, are devoted to the conduct of awakening,
are embraced by the Buddhas, and are free from the deeds of Māra.
May all those sentient beings have immeasurable lifespans;
may they always live in happiness, and may even the word "death" perish.
May all directions become beautiful with gardens of wish-fulfilling trees, filled with Buddhas and their sons, enchanting with the sounds of the Dharma.
May the ground everywhere be free from pebbles and the like, level like the palm of a hand, soft, and made of lapis lazuli.
May the great assemblies of Bodhisattvas sit all around and adorn the surface of the earth with their own splendors.
Let the sound of the Dharma be heard without ceasing by all embodied beings—from the birds, from all the trees, from the rays of light, and even from the sky. (Bca 10.37)
May they always attain union with the Buddhas and the sons of the Buddhas,
and may they worship the Teacher of the World with infinite clouds of offerings.
May the god send rain in due season, and may there be an abundance of crops; may the world be prosperous, and may the king be righteous. (Bca 10.39)
May medicinal herbs be efficacious; may mantras be effective for those who recite them;
and may ḍākinīs, rākṣasas, and others be filled with compassion.
May no sentient being be suffering, may none be sinful, and may none be diseased;
may none be inferior or despised, and may no one be dejected in mind.
May the monasteries be well-established, filled with the recitation and study of the scriptures;
may there always be harmony within the Saṅgha, and may the work of the Saṅgha be accomplished.
May the monks, having attained discernment and desiring training,
meditate with pliant minds, free from all distractions.
May the bhikṣuṇīs be successful and free from strife and fatigue;
likewise, may all those who have gone forth possess unbroken morality.
May those of immoral conduct be filled with spiritual urgency and always delight in the destruction of evil;
may they attain a good rebirth and there maintain their vows without violation.
May the wise be refined and receive alms-food;
may they possess pure mental continuums and have their fame renowned in all directions.
Without experiencing the suffering of the miserable realms and without the practice of austerities,
may one attain the state of Buddhahood for the sake of the world with a single divine body.
May all the perfectly awakened Buddhas be worshipped by all sentient beings in manifold ways;
may they be exceedingly happy with the inconceivable bliss of a Buddha.
May the aspirations of the Bodhisattvas for the sake of the world be fulfilled;
may whatever those Protectors intend for sentient beings come to fruition.
May the Pratyekabuddhas and likewise the Śrāvakas be happy,
being constantly honored with reverence by gods, asuras, and humans.
Through the protection of Mañjughoṣa, may I always attain the recollection of past lives and the state of renunciation, until I reach the Stage of Joy.
May I sustain myself with whatever seat [of practice] so that I may be endowed with strength;
and may I obtain the necessary conditions for dwelling in solitude throughout all my births.
And whenever I should desire to see him or wish to ask anything,
may I behold that very protector, Mañjunātha, without hindrance.
In accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings as far as the limits of space in the ten directions,
may my conduct be exactly the same as that of Mañjuśrī.
(Bcp 287) As long as space endures, and as long as the world endures, may I remain, destroying the sufferings of the world. *Bodhicaryāvatāra* 10.55.
Whatever suffering there is in the world, may it all ripen upon me;
and by all the virtues of the Bodhisattvas, may the world be made happy.
May the Teaching— the sole medicine for the suffering of the world, the source of all prosperity and happiness— endure for a long time, accompanied by gain and honor.
I pay homage to Mañjughoṣa, by whose grace my mind is directed toward what is auspicious;
I revere my spiritual friend, by whose grace it flourishes. (Bca 10.58)
The Tenth Chapter: Dedication, from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*.
This *Bodhicaryāvatāra* is completed.
It is the work of the master Śāntideva.
